MBSE-DEVSECOPS Primer
A Case Study
A case study: Jim, Bob and Tom take Tidewater from SysML v1 to SysML v2 in GitLab in twelve weeks • October 2026

MBSE-DEVSECOPS Primer

A case study: Jim, Bob and Tom take Tidewater from SysML v1 to SysML v2 in GitLab in twelve weeks
The agile kit
First edition, October 2026

Tidewater, its people, its prime contractor and every number in this book are fictional and notional. Any resemblance to a real program, organization or person is coincidental. Nothing here describes a real system.

The commands, scripts, templates and pipeline in this book are real: they ship with the agile kit (core Perl, Git for Windows, Vim) and every artifact quoted was produced by running them. Rebuild the evidence with perl sim/tidewater-sim.pl and this book with perl sim/primer.pl.

Typeset with XeLaTeX in TeX Gyre Pagella, TeX Gyre Heros and DejaVu Sans Mono.

For every engineer who was told to go digital
and was not told why.

Bottom line up front

54% of the work the team finished in the first twelve weeks is actual systems engineering, and the share rises sprint by sprint. The rest is a one-time investment in tools and learning: 73% of sprint 1, down to 18% of sprint 6. The figure for the whole eighteen months follows in the next edition, when the later sprints have run.

If you read nothing else in this book, read this page. It is written for the people who have to approve the change, and for the engineers who have to live with it.

Where the team's work goes

Every story on the team's board carries one of three labels. Engineering is work on the system itself: requirements, structure, behavior, interfaces, verification. Platform is the DevSecOps machinery that checks and publishes that work: the GitLab project, the pipeline, the runner. Learning is time the team spends learning the new tools, budgeted on purpose so it does not happen on nights and weekends.

Table 0.1. Task points closed in each sprint, by kind of work. One point is one ideal person-day.
SprintTask points doneSystems engineeringDevSecOps platformLearning
116.527%48%24%
21932%53%16%
31553%30%17%
41774%18%9%
516.564%30%6%
61482%14%4%
Sprints 1-69854%33%13%

These are task points: every finished task counts, including the finished tasks of a story that carried over, so a sprint's figure can be higher than its story points done (Section 13.8, Two ways to count "done").

Where all the time goes, meetings included

Points cover the work on the board. The agile meetings come on top: a fifteen-minute stand-up each day, a kickoff, a refinement session, and a review with a retrospective at the end of each sprint. Together they take about 7 hours per person per sprint, or 9% of an eighty-hour sprint.

Table 0.2. All paid hours of the three-person team in the first twelve weeks.
Activity, sprints 1-6Share of all paid hours
Systems engineering29%
DevSecOps platform18%
Learning7%
Agile meetings9%
Not on the board: holidays and leave, the lead's management duties, interruptions37%

What this means

  • The overhead is real, visible and temporary. Platform and learning work dominate the first two sprints, because the team is building the shop and learning to use it. By sprint 6 most of the board is engineering again. A plan that hides this cost is a plan that fails in week three.
  • The meetings cost less than a tenth of the team's time, and they replace status meetings, review meetings and the slide-building that used to come before every milestone.
  • The engineering that remains is faster and checked. Every change is checked automatically and reviewed before it is accepted. Problems the team used to find at the next milestone review are found the same day. The measured results -- requirements traced, model items ported, review turnaround, problems caught early -- are in Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard, and the briefing the team gave management at the end of the twelve weeks is in Chapter 35, The briefing.
  • What management must provide is the learning time in this table, a runner machine, the tool approvals and a GitLab tier decision, asked for in writing in sprint 2 (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim).
Note: Where these numbers come from

The tables are computed from the team's plan (sim/tidewater-plan.pl) by perl sim/tidewater-split.pl, and the book cites the resulting file, docs/tidewater/work-split.json, rather than typing the numbers. When the simulation's results replace the plan in that file, these tables follow. The method is described in Chapter 46, Systems engineering work, not pipeline work; you can apply it to your own project's backlog in Chapter 50, Your project in twelve weeks: a playbook.

Preface

From what you know

You know

how a program document opens: purpose, scope, applicable documents, then the content.

Here it is called

the preface: who the book is for, the cast, the calendar, and how to read and type along.

What is new

every command in this book has been run, and you are expected to type it too.

This book is a parachute drop.

Picture three systems engineers standing at the door of an aircraft. They have spent their careers writing specifications, reconciling spreadsheets and briefing chiefs. A few years ago someone handed them a modeling tool and told them to put everything they knew into it. They did, by hand, one box and one line at a time. Now the jump light is on again. Below them is a place called "MBSE DevSecOps," and they have been told to land there, set up camp, and show progress within twelve weeks. They have no map of that place. They have no software background. They have never written a pipeline, opened a merge request or resolved a merge conflict. They have the clothes on their backs, and one tool they trust: the Vim editor, which all three of them have used for years to write notes, edit requirement lists and clean up exported text files.

This book is written for people in that position. It follows Jim, Bob and Tom, the three government engineers responsible for the Tidewater system model, through their first twelve weeks. It shows what they did each day, what they typed, what broke, what they argued about and what they measured. It also explains, as plainly as we can, why each step is worth taking. By the end of the twelve weeks the team has a SysML v2 model under configuration control in GitLab, an automated pipeline that checks every change, a trace report that used to take two days and now takes seconds, and a management briefing built from measurements instead of opinions. They also, somewhat to their own surprise, like working this way. The book tries to show how that change of mind happened, without pretending it was easy.

Note: What you have, what you need

What you have: a Windows laptop, the Vim editor, years of systems engineering experience, and a model in a tool you were never comfortable with.

What you need from this preface: a picture of the people, the system and the calendar, so the rest of the book has somewhere to hang. Nothing to install yet; that starts in Chapter 9, The survival kit.

Who this book is for

You will get the most from this book if you are a systems engineer who:

  • knows what a requirement, an interface, a verification method and a baseline are;
  • has worked with documents (a SEMP, an SRS, ICDs), spreadsheets (requirement matrices, trace tables, action item lists) and briefings (design reviews, CCB packages);
  • has seen or used a SysML v1 tool such as Cameo Systems Modeler, even if you did not enjoy it;
  • has been told that the program is "moving to DevSecOps" and is not yet sure what that means for you.

You do not need to know how to program. You will type commands into a terminal, edit text files and read the output of automated checks, and the book explains every one of those things the first time it appears. If you already know git, GitLab or SysML v2, you can skim the chapters that teach them and spend your time on the case study chapters in Part III and the chapters about making the case to management in Part IV.

The book is also for the people around such a team: the program manager who issued the directive and wants to know what to expect, the information system security manager (ISSM) who has to approve the new tools, and the contractor who delivers the models. Each of them appears in the story, and each chapter notes what they need to do and when.

How to read this book

The book has five parts.

  • Part I, Where they start, tells the team's history: decades of documents, then the Cameo years, then the directive that started this story. It shows that the systems-engineering Vee stays (Chapter 4, The Vee, kept: the systems-engineering V in MBSE DevSecOps), explains DevSecOps in systems engineering words, introduces SysML v2 to people who know SysML v1, and ends with a workbook you type. Read it first even if you are impatient. The objections raised in Part I are the objections you will hear (or raise) yourself, and the rest of the book answers them one at a time.
  • Part II, Week zero, sets everything up, starting with what you already use: the survival kit on the laptop, Vim for models, diagrams generated from the model, then git from zero, the operating model and stories, GitLab, the DevSecOps tools worth turning on, CI/CD and the pipeline, and the daily rhythm. Part II is the part you type along with.
  • Part III, Twelve weeks, is the case study proper: six two-week sprints, one chapter each, with the real issues, merge requests, pipeline logs, stand-up notes and metrics from the run.
  • Part IV, Making the case, assembles the twelve-week scorecard, walks through the management briefing slide by slide, and revisits each objection from Part I against the evidence.
  • Part V, Living with it, covers what comes after the first twelve weeks: administration, maintenance through the life cycle (every prime contractor delivery, every baseline, the remaining months of the project), scaling up to several segments and hardware blocks (Chapter 49, Scaling up: segments, blocks and a ladder of fidelity), and the mistakes to avoid.

The appendices hold a command reference, every template, checklists, a glossary that translates between systems engineering, DevSecOps and SysML v2, and answers to the exercises.

From what you know to what you do not

The order is deliberate. Each chapter starts from something you already do, says what it is called here, and only then shows what is new; a box headed "From what you know" opens every chapter to make that step explicit. The chapters climb the same ladder the team climbed: first the things you know, then the things that are quick to learn because they are your own work in a new form, and only then the things that are genuinely new.

If a chapter feels too far up the ladder, go down one rung: the study plan (Appendix L, A twelve-week study plan per role) lists the chapters in ladder order for each role.

Type along

This book is meant to be read with a terminal open. Every command shown in a code block is real and has been run against the material that ships with the agile kit this book comes from. When you see

type it, press Enter, and compare what you see with what the book shows. (The commands in this book are not only shown; they are run: a test in the kit runs every command a reader is told to type, chapter by chapter, against the same material, before the book is printed.) If they differ, that is useful information: either your setup differs (and Chapter 9, The survival kit will help you find out how), or the material has changed since this book was generated. Either way you will learn more from the difference than from reading.

Commands are written for the Git Bash terminal that comes with Git for Windows, because that is what Jim, Bob and Tom have on their government laptops. They also work in a Linux terminal. Paths use forward slashes. When a command is long it is broken across lines with a trailing backslash, which the shell joins back together.

Vim commands are written the way Vim's own help writes them: :w means type a colon, then w, then press Enter; \mf means press the backslash key, then m, then f in normal mode. The kit's Vim help is always one command away: :help agile.

Tip: The exercises

Most chapters end with exercises. Some ask you to type and observe; some ask you to decide something and defend the decision. Answers are in Appendix N, Answers to the exercises. The decision exercises have more than one defensible answer; the answers appendix gives the one the team chose and why.

Conventions used in this book

  • Fixed-width text is something you type or something a program prints: a command, a file name, a line of SysML.
  • A code block that starts with a command is meant to be typed. In a block whose lines start with $ , type what follows each $ (not the $ itself); the other lines are what the command prints.
  • $KIT stands for the folder the agile kit is in (~/projects/agile on Tidewater's laptops); Chapter 9, The survival kit shows how to set it once, the way the pipeline sets it. File paths without $KIT are relative to the folder you are in unless they start with / or ~. ~/w2s is the practice folder the book uses; use any folder you like.
  • Bold marks a term the first time it is defined. The glossary in Appendix K, Glossary has all of them.
  • Boxes are labeled by kind. Note and tip boxes add detail; warning boxes mark a mistake the team made or nearly made; sidebar boxes step back from the story; objection boxes record a skeptic's argument in the speaker's words, followed by the answer and where the evidence is; exercise boxes are for you.
  • Quotations from Jim, Bob and Tom come from the team's notes, retrospectives and stand-up answers, lightly edited.
  • Numbers from the document era are reconstructions and are labeled notional. Numbers from the twelve weeks come from the records the tools kept, and each table says where it came from.

The system: Tidewater

Tidewater is a fictional coastal weather-observation network, invented for this book. Nothing in it describes a real system, a real program or a real organization, and every number in it is notional.

Tidewater has three segments:

  • Stations. Moored buoys offshore and shore stations on masts. Each station measures wind, air pressure and air temperature; buoys also measure waves. A buoy runs on its own solar panel and battery and sends its observations over a radio link; when the link is down it keeps them and sends them later.
  • The data center. It ingests every observation, checks its quality, archives it with a quality flag, and publishes a marine bulletin on a fixed schedule for forecasters and mariners.
  • Operations. A maintenance depot, a service vessel with a deck crane, and a pool of spare parts that keep the stations running.

The system is small on purpose. A real program's model has thousands of elements; Tidewater's v1 model has a few hundred. Small enough to read in an afternoon, large enough to have every problem a real model has: requirements that nothing satisfies, requirements that nothing verifies, text in the requirements database that no longer matches the text in the model, diagrams nobody updates, and packages so tangled that a change in one place surprises someone in another.

The cast

Jim is the MBSE lead and the person responsible for the Tidewater system model on the government side. Jim owns the big picture: what the model must contain, which work comes first, what "done" means, and what gets reported upward. In this story Jim is also the one who received the directive to adopt DevSecOps, which makes Jim the person who has to explain it to the other two without fully understanding it yet. Jim has twenty-six years in systems engineering, most of them writing and reviewing specifications.

Bob is the MBSE engineer. Bob built most of the Cameo model during the document port and knows where every block came from, including the ones that should not be there. Bob is the most skeptical member of the team about the new direction, and the one whose skepticism is most useful, because Bob asks precise questions: "Who approves a change?", "Where is the baseline?", "What happens when the contractor's model changes?"

Tom is the configuration management engineer, and in this story becomes the team's DevSecOps engineer. Tom volunteered to build the pipeline, mostly because somebody had to and Tom has run the program's CM database for a decade. Tom has never written a pipeline, never administered a GitLab project, and never written a line of code beyond spreadsheet formulas and Vim macros. Tom likes procedures, checklists and things that can be audited.

Around the team:

  • The program manager issued the directive and will judge the results at the end of the twelve weeks. The program manager is not hostile, but needs to show the program's leadership that the money spent on tools and training produces something measurable.
  • The deputy program manager chairs the configuration control board (CCB) and cares about one question above all: can a change be traced from request to approval to implementation?
  • The ISSM (information system security manager) must approve any new tool or data flow on the program's network. The ISSM is careful, busy and, for three days in week six, unreachable.
  • The prime contractor, Northwind Marine Systems (fictional), builds Tidewater and maintains the authoritative SysML v1 model in Cameo under a contract data requirement (CDRL A003, "System Model"). The prime delivers the model to the government as "drops": an XMI export of the model, a ReqIF export of the DOORS requirements, a CSV copy of the requirements and a manifest with checksums.
  • The prime's modeler is the contractor engineer the team talks to about the content of each drop.
  • The enterprise GitLab administrators run the organization's GitLab server. They create groups and projects on request, register runners and enforce the organization's settings. They are helpful and slow.
Note: A note on pronouns

The book refers to every person by name or by role, and uses "they" when a pronoun is needed.

The calendar

The project in this book lasts eighteen months: thirty-nine two-week sprints from Monday 5 October 2026 to Friday 31 March 2028. The first twelve weeks, sprints 1 to 6, are the subject of Part III. The rest of the project is summarized in Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle.

Table 0.1. The eighteen months at a glance (the twelve weeks are sprints 1 to 6)
SprintDatesWhat happens
15 to 16 Oct 2026GitLab project created; the first pipeline; drop 1 received and assessed
219 to 30 Oct 2026drop 1 imported through the vendor branch; every change gated
32 to 13 Nov 2026Network and Types cleaned up; DOORS requirements imported; the hardest week for morale
416 to 27 Nov 2026Stations cleaned up; gaps reported to the prime; the model site shown to management
530 Nov to 11 Dec 2026Data center and operations cleaned up; release procedure rehearsed
614 to 25 Dec 2026behavior work starts; interim baseline; the management briefing
7 to 20Dec 2026 to Jul 2027the port completed; drops 2 and 3 absorbed; baseline 1 accepted
17 to 39May 2027 to Mar 2028maintenance against drops 4 to 7; baselines 2 and 3

The prime delivers seven drops over the eighteen months:

Table 0.2. The prime contractor's drops
DropVersionDeliveredWhat changed upstream
1v1.0Fri 2 Oct 2026the model at contract start
2v1.1Fri 8 Jan 2027a humidity sensor and its requirement; one requirement text corrected

Federal holidays fall inside the twelve weeks on 12 October, 11 November, 26 November and 25 December, and each team member takes some leave. The plans in Part III account for both, because a plan that ignores the calendar is the first thing a skeptic will pick apart.

What "done" looks like after twelve weeks

So that you know where the story is going, here is the state of things at the end of sprint 6, in the terms the program manager asked for:

  • every change to the model goes through a merge request, is checked automatically by a pipeline, and is approved by a code owner other than its author; nothing reaches the integration branch any other way;
  • the model's conversion debt, the number of places where the converter could not carry a SysML v1 construct into SysML v2, is measured on every change and has fallen sprint by sprint;
  • the trace between the DOORS requirements and the model is computed on every change, including the text drift between them that nobody had ever checked systematically;
  • every problem in the contractor's model is tracked as a discrepancy report with an owner, a due drop and a closing condition;
  • an interim baseline is tagged, reproducible and published with release notes;
  • the team can show all of the above in a browser, live, in a management review, instead of in screenshots pasted into slides.

None of these things require the team to become software developers. They require the team to do what systems engineers already know how to do (control configuration, trace requirements, review changes, verify) with tools that make those things cheap instead of expensive. That is the argument of this book, and the twelve weeks are the evidence.

Part I: Where they start

1 Thirty years of documents

From what you know

You know

the SEMP, the SRS, the SSDD, the ICDs, the VCRM spreadsheet and the milestone briefing. Thirty years of them.

Here it is called

the document era, described honestly, strengths included.

What is new

nothing yet. This chapter names the costs you already pay, so later chapters can show what replaces them.

Note: What you have, what you need

What you have: a career's worth of habits for controlling documents, reviewing changes and briefing decisions.

What you need from this chapter: a clear list of which of those habits are worth keeping (most of them) and which costs they hid. Nothing to type yet.

1.1 A Tuesday in 2019

The request arrived at 4:10 on a Tuesday afternoon, the way such requests always arrived: as a one-line email from the deputy program manager, copied to the program manager, with the subject line "Quick question."

Jim -- before Thursday's program review, can you tell me which Tidewater requirements don't have a verification method yet? Just a list is fine. Thanks.

It was not a quick question, and everybody on the distribution knew it. The answer lived in four places. The System Requirements Specification (SRS), revision C, held the requirement text and a section 4 "Qualification provisions" table. The Verification Cross-Reference Matrix (VCRM) was an Excel workbook with one row per requirement and a column for the method (test, analysis, inspection, demonstration). The prime contractor kept the authoritative requirement text in DOORS and sent a CSV export every month. And the action item tracker, a different spreadsheet, held the open items from the last design review, several of which said things like "Contractor to propose verification approach for SRS 3.2.7."

Jim forwarded the email to Bob with a single line ("Can you pull this together?") and Bob spent Wednesday doing what Bob had done many times before. Bob opened the latest DOORS CSV in Excel, sorted it by object identifier, and pasted it next to the VCRM. A lookup formula matched the identifiers. Forty rows did not match, because the VCRM still used the paragraph numbers from revision B and DOORS used the new object identifiers. Bob fixed those by hand from the cross-reference table in the SRS appendix, found three requirements in DOORS that were not in the VCRM at all, found two in the VCRM that DOORS had deleted, checked the action item tracker for the ones with open actions, and by 3 p.m. on Wednesday had a list of eleven requirements with no verification method. Jim reformatted it as a slide, the deputy program manager presented it on Thursday, and the program review moved on to the next topic.

Two weeks later the prime delivered revision D of the VCRM. Four of the eleven had been fixed. Nobody updated the slide, and nobody ran the comparison again until the next "quick question."

Case study: Why this scene matters

Nothing in the scene is a failure. Every person did their job well. Bob's answer was correct on Wednesday afternoon. The trouble is that it was correct only on Wednesday afternoon, it cost a skilled engineer a day and a half, and the work that produced it left no trace that anyone could re-run. Keep that last point in mind; it is the whole argument of Chapter 5, DevSecOps in systems-engineering words in one sentence.

1.2 The document set

For most of Jim's career, systems engineering on a government program meant producing, reviewing and controlling a set of documents. The names vary by organization; Tidewater's set was typical:

Table 1.1. The document-era artifact set (typical; Tidewater's names)
DocumentWhat it heldWho changed it
SEMP (Systems Engineering Management Plan)how the program does systems engineeringthe government, rarely
ConOps (Concept of Operations)who uses the system and how, in prosethe government, once
SRS (System Requirements Specification)the "shall" statements, numbered paragraphsthe prime, through the CCB
SSDD (System/Subsystem Design Description)the architecture: segments, subsystems, block diagrams as picturesthe prime
ICDs (Interface Control Documents)each interface: messages, fields, timing, connectorsthe prime, both sides sign
VCRM (Verification Cross-Reference Matrix)each requirement's verification method and eventthe prime, a spreadsheet
RTM (Requirements Traceability Matrix)parent-child links between requirement levelsthe prime, a spreadsheet or DOORS
Risk register, action item trackeropen risks and actionsthe government, spreadsheets
Design review packagesslides summarizing all of the aboveeverybody, for each review

Each document had an owner, a revision letter, a change history page and a signature block. Changes moved through a formal process: somebody wrote an engineering change proposal (ECP) or a document change request, the request went into the queue for the monthly configuration control board (CCB), the board approved, rejected or deferred it, and the owner incorporated approved changes into the next revision. Between revisions, changes were tracked as "redlines": a marked-up copy of the document, usually a PDF with comments, sometimes a Word file with tracked changes, occasionally a printout with handwriting.

The spreadsheets lived alongside the documents and did the work the documents could not. The VCRM was a spreadsheet because a matrix is a spreadsheet. The RTM was a spreadsheet because parent-child links between a few hundred requirements are rows. The action item tracker was a spreadsheet because everything that did not fit anywhere else was a spreadsheet.

The briefings sat on top. Every review, every status meeting and every decision produced slides. The slides summarized the documents and spreadsheets, and for the people in the room the slides were the system: few decision makers read the SRS, but everybody saw the chart.

1.3 What worked

It is fashionable to sneer at document-based systems engineering. This book will not. The document era got a great deal right, and almost everything it got right survives into the way of working this book describes.

Everybody could read the documents. A Word document or a PDF needs no special software, no license and no training. An operator, a test engineer, a contracting officer and a general can all open the SRS. This is a real virtue, and the team's fear of losing it is one of the objections in Chapter 3, The directive.

The documents were the contract. The CDRL told the prime to deliver an SRS, and the government accepted or rejected it. Signatures meant something. When a dispute arose, the signed revision settled it.

Changes were reviewed. Nothing went into a controlled document without a second pair of eyes and a board decision. The review culture of the CCB, the habit of asking "who approved this, and when?", is exactly what DevSecOps calls change control, and it is the habit Tom will build the pipeline around.

Baselines existed. "SRS revision C" named a fixed, known set of requirements. Everyone could point at it.

Traceability was taken seriously. The RTM and VCRM were tedious to maintain, but the program knew that every requirement needed a parent and a verification, and it checked, at least at each review.

Tip: Keep this list

Hold on to these five virtues: readable by anyone, contractually meaningful, reviewed, baselined, traced. When someone tells you DevSecOps throws away good systems engineering practice, ask which of the five it throws away. In the chapters that follow, each one is kept, and each one gets cheaper.

1.4 What it cost

The costs of the document era were real but hidden, because they were paid in engineers' time rather than in a budget line. Nobody ever wrote "1.5 days to answer the deputy's question" on a timecard; it was just Wednesday.

To make those costs visible, Jim later reconstructed four of them from the program's last document-era review cycle. They are reconstructions, not measurements, and this book labels them as notional wherever they appear. They are the "before" column of the scorecard in Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard.

Table 1.2. The document-era baseline (notional, reconstructed from the last review cycle)
Activity in the document eraTypical effort or elapsed time (notional)
A requirement change, from change request to incorporated revision23 working days
"Which requirements are unverified?", answered from the VCRM, DOORS export and SRS2 working days
A model or design review: screenshots in a 60-slide briefing, prepared, reviewed and presented3 weeks
Finding text that differs between DOORS and the documents (or the model)never done systematically

Where did the 23 working days of a requirement change go? Almost none of it was engineering. Jim's reconstruction of one change, a clarification to a data-latency requirement, looked like this:

Table 1.3. Where the time went in one requirement change (notional)
StepWorking days (notional)
Engineer drafts the change request in the CR template1
Change request waits for the next monthly CCB agenda11
CCB meeting; approved with a comment1
Comment resolved by email; revised wording approved by the chair3
Prime incorporates the change into the next SRS revision draft4
Government reviews the draft revision, signs3

Most of the elapsed time is waiting: for a meeting, for a revision, for a signature. The meeting itself took a day, and the engineering, deciding what the requirement should say, took less than that. The process was designed for a world where making a copy of a document was expensive and distributing it was slow, so changes were batched into monthly meetings and quarterly revisions. Batching is efficient when each batch costs a lot. It is wasteful when each change could be reviewed, approved and incorporated on the day it is proposed.

The other hidden costs were less visible still.

Every answer was a one-off. Bob's Wednesday produced a correct list and a slide. It did not produce anything that could be run again. The next time someone asked, Bob started from scratch, because the spreadsheet formulas were in a copy of the VCRM that was now two revisions out of date.

Consistency was nobody's job. The SRS, the VCRM, the RTM, the DOORS database and the ICDs each held part of the truth, and each was maintained by a different person on a different schedule. When they disagreed, which they always did a little, the disagreement was found by accident, usually by someone preparing for a review. Requirement text in DOORS that differed from the text in the SRS was a known problem with no known size.

The briefing became the truth. Because decision makers saw slides, the slides were where decisions were made, and the slides were copies of copies. A block diagram drawn for a 2017 review would reappear, slightly edited, in 2019, long after the architecture had changed. Nobody could say which picture was current.

Configuration management meant file names. The program's shared drive held files named SRS_RevC_final.docx, SRS_RevC_final_v2.docx, SRS_RevC_final_v2_JIM_comments.docx and, memorably, SRS_RevC_FINAL_use_this_one.docx. Tom, who ran the CM database, could tell you which file was the signed revision. Nobody else could, and the CM database did not know about the working copies at all.

Knowledge lived in people. Bob knew why the VCRM's row 214 had a strange formula. Jim knew which ICD paragraph had been "temporarily" waived in 2016. When people moved on, the knowledge went with them.

Objection: "The documents worked. We delivered systems with them for thirty years."

That is true, and nothing in this book disputes it.

Answer

The question is not whether documents can work but what they cost and what they make impossible. The document process worked by spending skilled engineers' time on copying, reconciling and waiting. It made it impossible to ask the same question twice and get a fresh answer cheaply. The chapters in Part III measure what the same questions cost in the new way; Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard puts the two side by side.

1.5 The habits worth keeping

Before the team moves on, it is worth naming the document-era habits that will survive the transition, because the team's discouragement in Chapter 3, The directive comes partly from believing that everything they know is being thrown out. It is not. Here is the translation the book will use, one habit at a time. Chapter 5, DevSecOps in systems-engineering words gives the full table.

  • Change requests become merge requests: a proposed change, with a description, reviewed and approved before it is incorporated. The difference is that a merge request contains the actual change, not a description of it, and can be approved the day it is written.
  • The CCB's approval becomes a code owner's approval: a named person, responsible for an area, approves changes to that area. The board still exists for decisions that need a board; it no longer has to touch every editorial fix.
  • Baselines become tags: a name fixed to an exact, retrievable state of the model. Revision C becomes baseline-1.
  • The VCRM and RTM become reports computed from the model: instead of maintaining a matrix by hand, the team writes the trace into the model and lets a program compute the matrix whenever anyone asks.
  • The design review package becomes a published site: the current model, its diagrams and its reports, always generated from the baseline, never pasted.
  • Redlines become diffs: a precise, line-by-line record of what changed, produced automatically.
  • The CM database becomes the repository's history: every change, who made it, when, why, and who approved it, kept automatically.

None of these translations is perfect, and the book points out where they break. But the shape of the work is recognizably the same. Systems engineering still means knowing what the system must do, how it is put together, how each requirement will be shown to be met, and how changes are controlled. What changes is how much of that work is done by hand.

1.6 What the spreadsheets were really doing

Every program has a spreadsheet that nobody is allowed to touch. On Tidewater it was the VCRM, and Tom, who had seen every revision of it, once described it as "the most important database on the program, stored in the least reliable format we have."

Spreadsheets did three jobs on the program, and it is worth separating them, because each job has a better home in the new way of working.

The spreadsheet as a database. The VCRM, the RTM, the interface list and the action item tracker were all tables of records with identifiers, attributes and relationships between them. That is a database. Spreadsheets are a poor database: nothing stops two rows from having the same identifier, a formula from referring to the wrong column after someone inserts one, or a copy of the file from drifting away from the original. In the new way, the records live in the model (requirements, satisfy and verify relationships) or in GitLab (issues), both of which enforce identity and keep history.

The spreadsheet as a calculator. Bob's lookup formulas, the trace coverage percentages and the "requirements without a verification method" count were calculations over the records. Each calculation was written by hand, in one copy of one file, and lost when the file was replaced. In the new way, calculations are small programs that run in the pipeline against the current model, every time. The trace report in Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job is Bob's Wednesday, written once and run thousands of times.

The spreadsheet as a report. The colored cells, the filtered views and the pivot tables pasted into slides were how the records reached decision makers. In the new way, reports are generated from the model and published (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep); nobody formats a cell.

Case study: The VCRM's row 214

Row 214 of the VCRM held a formula that combined three columns and a lookup into a hidden sheet. It computed whether a requirement's verification event had been scheduled. Bob wrote it in 2017. In 2021 someone sorted the sheet without including the hidden columns, and for four months row 214's formula pointed at the wrong requirement. Nobody noticed until a test readiness review. The formula was right; the format was the problem. A calculation that lives in a cell is only as safe as every edit anyone ever makes to that file.

1.7 A year in the document era

To see the pattern of the old way, it helps to look at a whole year rather than a single Tuesday. Here is Tidewater's systems engineering calendar for a typical year before the Cameo port, reconstructed from the team's old meeting invitations. The effort figures are notional.

Table 1.4. A document-era year, reconstructed (effort notional)
WhenEventWhat the team didEffort (notional)
monthlyCCBassemble change requests, write the agenda, record decisions, update the change log2 days per month
monthlyDOORS export from the primereconcile the export against the VCRM and SRS1 to 2 days
quarterlySRS / ICD revisionreview the prime's revision against approved changes, comment, sign1 to 2 weeks
quarterlyprogram management reviewbuild the SE section of the briefing (status, risks, TBD/TBR counts)3 to 5 days
twice a yeartechnical review (SRR, PDR, CDR, TRR ...)review packages, comment matrices, action items3 to 6 weeks
ad hoc"quick questions"one-off answers from the spreadsheetsabout a day each, several a month

Add it up and roughly a third of the team's year went into reconciling, reformatting and re-answering: work that produced no new engineering knowledge, only fresh copies of old knowledge in a new format. Nobody on the team thought of it that way at the time, because each piece of it was necessary given how the information was stored. The waste was in the storage, not in the people.

That third of a year is the budget the new way of working draws on. When Chapter 3, The directive asks what the team can stop doing, and when Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard compares effort before and after, this table is where the comparison starts.

1.8 Why the document era lasted

If the costs were this large, why did the document era last thirty years? It is worth answering honestly, because the same forces will push back against the new way.

  • The costs were invisible. Time spent reconciling spreadsheets was never charged to "reconciling spreadsheets." It was charged to systems engineering. Nobody could see it, so nobody could argue to reduce it.
  • The contract required documents. CDRLs named document deliverables with data item descriptions that assumed a document. Changing what the prime delivered meant changing the contract.
  • Everyone knew how. A new engineer could be productive with Word and Excel on the first day. Any new way had to compete with zero training cost.
  • Failures were rare and quiet. Most of the time, the reconciliations caught the inconsistencies before they mattered. When they did not, the failure appeared months later as a test problem or a rework, far from its cause.
  • Nothing better was available to this team. Until SysML v2's textual notation, the alternatives were diagram tools that, as Chapter 2, The Cameo years shows, kept most of the costs and added new ones.

The last point matters most. The team's resistance to the directive is not stubbornness; it is the reasonable conclusion of people who were offered an alternative once before and found it worse. The new way has to be better on the measures they care about, and it has to show that early.

1.9 Exercises

Exercise 1.1: Count the copies

Pick one requirement on a program you know. List every place its text appears (documents, spreadsheets, databases, slides, emails). For each, write who maintains it and when it was last updated. How many of those places agree, word for word, today? How would you find out without reading them all?

Exercise 1.2: Reconstruct a change

Take one recent change to a controlled document on your program. Reconstruct its timeline as in the table "Where the time went in one requirement change". Separate the time spent deciding from the time spent waiting. What fraction was waiting?

Exercise 1.3: The five virtues

For each of the five virtues of the document era (readable by anyone, contractually meaningful, reviewed, baselined, traced), write one sentence on how your current process achieves it and one on what it costs. Keep the page; you will revisit it after Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard.

2 The Cameo years

From what you know

You know

Cameo: its diagrams, its containment tree, the XMI export and the DOORS link.

Here it is called

SysML v1, and the spider web it became.

What is new

measuring the spider web (diagrams, duplicates, cycles, relationships per block) instead of only feeling it.

Note: What you have, what you need

What you have: a SysML v1 model in Cameo that you built by hand, that the prime contractor now maintains, and that nobody on the team enjoys opening.

What you need from this chapter: an honest, measured picture of that model, and an understanding of why SysML v1 in a diagram tool did not scale for this team. You will run two commands to measure it yourself.

2.1 "Go MBSE"

The first directive came in the spring of 2022, and it was shorter than the one in Chapter 3, The directive. The program's leadership had attended a conference, seen a demonstration of model-based systems engineering, and decided that Tidewater would "transition to MBSE." Licenses for Cameo Systems Modeler arrived in June. Jim, Bob and Tom attended a three-day vendor training course in July. The course taught them which buttons to press to create a block, a port, a requirement and a diagram. It did not teach them what to put in the model, how to organize it, how to review it, or how it would stay consistent with the documents and DOORS. Those questions were left, as the course instructor put it, "to your organization's modeling guidelines." The organization did not have modeling guidelines.

So the team did the only thing that made sense to them: they ported the documents. Every block diagram in the SSDD became a block definition diagram. Every interface table in the ICDs became an internal block diagram with ports and connectors. Every "shall" in the SRS became a requirement element. Every row in the VCRM became a verify relationship. The work took most of two years, done between other duties, by clicking.

I drew the PowerSystem IBD four times. Once from the SSDD figure, once when the ICD changed, once when Cameo crashed and I lost the layout, and once for the CDR briefing because the real one didn't fit on a slide.

— Bob, recalling 2023

In 2025 the program changed the contract. The prime contractor, Northwind Marine Systems, took over maintenance of the Cameo model under a new contract data requirement, CDRL A003 "System Model." From then on the prime made the changes and delivered the model to the government every few months; the government reviewed it. The team's role shifted from building the model to checking it, which in practice meant opening Cameo, clicking through diagrams, taking screenshots and pasting them into review comments.

2.2 What the team built

The prime's first delivery under this book's timeline, drop 1 (version 1.0, delivered Friday 2 October 2026), is the model as the team built it and the prime inherited it. It is an XMI file: Cameo's export format, an XML file in which every model element is a tagged record with a long, unique identifier. You can generate the drop yourself:

($KIT is the folder the kit is in; Chapter 9, The survival kit sets it up, and ~/w2s is the practice folder the book uses.) The command writes four files into ~/w2s/drop1, exactly as the prime delivers them:

Table 2.1. What a prime drop contains
FileWhat it is
tidewater.xmithe Cameo model, exported as Eclipse UML2 XMI (what Cameo calls "Export To > Eclipse UML2 (v5.x) XMI File")
tidewater.reqifthe DOORS requirement modules, exported in the standard ReqIF exchange format
tidewater.csvthe same requirements as a DOORS CSV export, for people who want a spreadsheet
MANIFEST.txtthe delivery record: version, date, CDRL, the prime's build (Jenkins job and commit) and tools, and a SHA-256 checksum for each file

Here is one block, the solar panel on a buoy, as it appears in the XMI. You do not need to read XML fluently; just notice the shape.

Three things are worth noticing, because each one comes back later.

First, the solar panel is not one record but several, scattered across the file. The block itself is a UML class near the middle. The fact that it is a SysML block is a separate record near the end (sysml:Block), pointing back at the class by its identifier. The team's own "assembly level" tag and the supplier data are two more records from the team's custom profile. To know everything about the solar panel you have to collect all four.

Second, the type of the ratedPower property is not written as a name. It is an identifier, _22_1_7f3a0c1_dd4fe0cc913f, that you have to look up elsewhere in the file to discover it means Power. The same is true of the port's type. The file is written for machines, not for people.

Third, the diagrams are not here at all. The XMI holds the model's elements and relationships; the diagrams that people actually looked at, with their boxes, lines and layout, live in Cameo's own project file and appear in the export only as a list of names. When the team "reviewed the model," they reviewed the diagrams, and the diagrams are precisely the part that cannot be exported, compared or checked.

2.3 Measuring the spider web

"The model looks like a giant spider web" is Bob's phrase, and it was meant as a complaint, not a measurement. Jim's first act as the person responsible for the model was to turn the complaint into numbers, because numbers can be tracked and complaints cannot. The measures are simple counts from the drop-1 XMI:

Table 2.2. The spider web, measured from drop 1
MeasureDrop 1What it tells you
Model elements (records with an identifier)819the size of the export, including comments and stereotype applications
Packages20how the model is organized
Blocks / requirements40 / 30the parts of the system and the "shall" statements
Diagrams47the pictures people review; 11 of them are stale copies or briefing snapshots
Relationships124satisfy, verify, trace, derive, allocate, connectors, generalizations, associations
Relationship ends per block, maximum17 (ObservingStation)how tangled the most-connected block is
Relationship ends per block, mean1.4how tangled a typical block is
Package dependency cycles2pairs of packages that each depend on the other
Unused blocks4 (three clutter blocks, plus the context block, unused by design)blocks nothing refers to
Duplicate or stale blocks2copies left behind by the document port

Two ways of counting elements. The 819 above counts every record in the XMI file that carries an identifier, including comments and stereotype applications, because that is what makes the file big. The converter counts differently: it counts the model elements it walks, and its own report on drop 1 ends with this line (columns: in, mapped, folded, TODO):

Both numbers are right; they answer different questions. Elsewhere in this book, "elements" means the converter's count unless a table says otherwise. The relationship and per-block counts in the table are Jim's own counts of relationship ends in the XMI; the converter's report and the generator's spider-web summary count only the relationship kinds they handle, so their numbers are a little lower.

A few of these deserve explanation.

Diagrams. The model has 47 diagrams for 40 blocks. Some of that is legitimate: a block definition diagram per segment, an internal block diagram per assembly that has connections, an activity diagram, a state machine, a sequence diagram, use cases, a requirements diagram and two matrices. The rest is what happens when diagrams are the main way to look at a model and nobody is allowed to delete one in case someone needs it. Their names tell the story:

Package dependency cycles. A package depends on another when something in it refers to something in the other: a part typed by a block over there, a trace relationship pointing over there. A cycle means two packages each depend on the other, so neither can be understood, reviewed or changed alone. In drop 1 the cycles are: Stations with DataCenter, and Network with Operations. Each one began as a reasonable shortcut during the document port (a trace link drawn from a station block straight to a data center requirement, because that was where the ICD paragraph pointed) and nobody untangled it afterwards. (The SysML v2 tools count the same tangle in their own ways; Section 11.4, The five views, read explains why the numbers differ.)

The most-connected block. ObservingStation carries 17 relationship ends. Most of them are trace relationships the team drew from the block to every requirement that mentioned it in any document. Some of those are real satisfy relationships under another name; some duplicate a satisfy that already exists; some are simply wrong. In a diagram, those links are the strands of the web.

The Legacy Import package. When the team first ported the documents, they imported a spreadsheet of requirements and blocks with Cameo's Excel import. The import created elements the team later rebuilt by hand, and the originals were never deleted. They sit in a package called "Legacy Import": a Battery_old, a Copy of SensorSuite, a TBD Component that nothing uses, and a requirement-like class called "Requirement from slide 14" with no identifier. Every review since 2023 has had a comment saying "clean up Legacy Import." It is still there.

You can measure the spider web yourself. The converter's report lists every element type and what happens to it:

These lines from the report summarize the conversion:

Read the total line as four counts: 560 elements came in; 444 were mapped to SysML v2; 65 were folded into something else (a connector end becomes part of its connector, a multiplicity becomes part of its property); and 51 fall under a TODO. The 51 are fewer things than they sound: the three lifelines, three messages and six message events of one sequence diagram, for instance, all sit under a single TODO for that diagram. The unmapped line says they produce 12 TODO lines. Add one TODO line for each of the 39 custom stereotypes listed above it, and one note about the constraint expression, and the converted files contain 52 TODO lines.

Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers explains the rest of the report. For now, the TODO lines are what matter. They are the places where the model contains something the converter could not carry into SysML v2. They are the conversion debt, and counting them will become the team's main measure of progress. Notice also the ported vs remaining line: every block, port, property, connector and activity in the model, 206 of 206, came across. The debt is real but bounded.

The converter writes one file per top-level package of the Cameo model, so the converted drop doubles as a map of the model's organization. Counting what is in each file gives a first look at where the size, the debt and the tangles are. These are real counts from the converted drop 1.
