requirements/Requirements.sysml18830 requirements, 29 satisfy, the derivations and traces0DataCenter, Network, Stations, RequirementDerivation
verification/Verification.sysml606 verification defs (the v1 test cases)0Requirements
behavior/Behavior.sysml558 action defs: the observation cycle4Interfaces
datacenter/DataCenter.sysml515 part defs: ingest, quality control, archive, publisher5Interfaces, Stations
network/Network.sysml475 part defs, actors, 4 use cases, the context3DataCenter, Operations, Stations
interfaces/Interfaces.sysml404 port defs, 3 item defs0Types
operations/Operations.sysml305 part defs: depot, vessel, crane, spares5Network
legacy-import/Legacy_Import.sysml274 part defs left from the document port0Interfaces, Stations, Types
types/Types.sysml22value types, units, an enumeration3none
allocations/Allocations.sysml147 allocations of activities to blocks0Behavior, DataCenter, Stations
analysis/Analysis.sysml13the energy balance constraint2Types
tidewater/Tidewater.sysml4the custom profile's placeholder1none

Three things jump out of that table, and the team noticed all of them in the first week.

The size is small. The whole model is about 740 lines of text. Bob had spent two years building it, and it fits in a long afternoon's reading. The point is not that two years were wasted; the content took that long to decide. The point is that once decided, the content is compact, and the work of keeping it current should be proportionate.

The debt is concentrated. Twenty-nine of the 52 TODO lines are in one file, Stations.sysml, and almost all of them are level stereotypes. That told Jim where the first weeks' effort would go, and that it would go quickly.

The tangles are written down. Look at the last column. Stations imports DataCenter, and DataCenter imports Stations. Network imports Operations, and Operations imports Network. Those are the two package dependency cycles from the spider-web table, and in the text they are not hidden in a model browser: they are two pairs of import lines, at the top of four files, that anyone can read. Stations also imports Requirements, because a dozen trace links were drawn from station blocks straight to requirements. In Cameo, finding these took a dependency matrix and an afternoon. In text, they are on the first screen of each file.

Bob's reaction to that last point is worth recording:

I always knew the stations and the data center were tangled. I could never show anyone. Now it's four lines.

— Bob, sprint 1

2.5 Why it did not scale

The team's experience with Cameo is common, and it is worth being precise about why, because "we hate the tool" is not an argument that management will accept, and it is not quite true either. Cameo is a capable tool. The problems the team ran into come from the combination of SysML v1, a diagram-first way of working and a team that was never given the practices that make a shared model work.

2.5.1 The diagram is not the model, but everyone treats it as if it were

In SysML v1 tools, the model and the diagrams are separate things: a block exists once in the model and can appear on many diagrams. That separation is correct and powerful. In practice it confused everyone. Reviewers looked at diagrams, so a relationship that existed in the model but not on any diagram was invisible, and a stale diagram that nobody had opened since 2023 still looked like part of the design to anyone who found it. When Bob redrew the PowerSystem IBD for a briefing, the briefing version had a different layout and fewer ports, and for the people in the room it was the PowerSystem.

2.5.2 Nothing could be compared

The question a reviewer most needs answered is: what changed since last time? In the document era the answer was the redline. In Cameo there was no good answer. Cameo has a model-comparison feature, but it compares two projects element by element in a tree that runs to thousands of rows, and the team could not turn its output into anything a reviewer could read. The XMI export changes in ways unrelated to the model (element order, generated identifiers on some exports, tool-version headers), so comparing two XMI files with a text comparison tool shows thousands of meaningless differences. When drop 2 arrived, the team's review consisted of opening both versions side by side and clicking through the diagrams looking for differences by eye.

2.5.3 Nothing could be merged

A shared model needs a way for two people to work at once and combine their work. Cameo's answer is a server (Teamwork Cloud) that locks elements while someone edits them. The program never bought the server, so the team passed the project file around by email, and only one person could edit at a time. Bob owned the model in practice because Bob had the file. When the prime took over, the file moved to the prime, and the government lost the ability to change it at all.

2.5.4 Nothing was checked automatically

Cameo has a validation feature with rules, and the team ran it once, during the training course. It produced eight hundred warnings, most of them about diagram formatting, and nobody ran it again. The questions the team cared about (is every requirement satisfied, is every requirement verified, does the requirement text in the model match DOORS, does every assembly carry its level tag) were never encoded anywhere. They were answered, when they were answered, by Bob clicking through matrices before a review.

2.5.5 Seats, licenses and one machine

Cameo is licensed per seat. The program bought three. A fourth engineer who wanted to look at the model had to ask for screenshots. The model lived on the machines where Cameo was installed. The data center's engineers, the test engineers and the program office never saw the model, only pictures of it.

2.5.6 The team never had a workflow, only a tool

This is the deepest reason, and it is not Cameo's fault. The team was given a tool and told to use it. Nobody gave them a way of working with it: how changes are proposed, reviewed, approved and recorded; how the model is baselined; how it is checked; how it is kept consistent with DOORS. Without those practices, the model behaved exactly like the documents had, except that it was harder to read and nobody outside the team could open it. It inherited the document era's costs and added new ones.

Case study: The scaling problem, stated plainly

SysML v1 in a diagram tool scales with the number of people who can click. Changes are made one at a time, by one person, in one tool, and reviewed by looking at pictures. A team of three can keep up with a small model that way. It cannot keep up with a model that changes every few months from a contractor, has to stay consistent with a requirements database, and has to be reviewed by people who do not own a license.

2.6 What the team believed, and what was true

By 2026 the team had drawn a conclusion from the Cameo years: modeling does not work for us. It is worth separating that conclusion into its parts, because some parts are true and some are not.

Table 2.4. The Cameo years: belief and fact
What the team believedWhat was actually true
"Modeling is slower than documents."Point-and-click modeling of content that already existed in documents is slower than the documents. Modeling as the primary record, with automated checks, is a different activity.
"The model is a spider web."Measurably true: duplicates, stale diagrams, package cycles and tangled trace links. The web was built by the port, and can be untangled.
"Nobody uses the model."True: nobody outside the team could open it. That is a distribution problem, not a modeling problem.
"We can't tell what changed in a drop."True with XMI and screenshots. Not true with a text model in version control (see Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers and Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers).
"The contractor owns the model now; we just review it."True contractually. The government can still keep its own derived copy, check it, and report discrepancies; that is the plan in Chapter 13, The operating model.
"We are engineers, not programmers."True, and this book does not ask anyone to become a programmer. Text files, reviews and checklists are engineering tools.
Objection: "We already tried modeling. It took two years and gave us a spider web."

Bob, at the first team meeting about the directive in Chapter 3, The directive.

Answer

The two years went into porting documents by hand into a tool with no workflow. The spider web is measured above, and the measures are the starting point of the twelve weeks. Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated through Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself show the web being untangled package by package, with each tangle reported to the prime as a discrepancy, and Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard shows the same measures at the end.

Objection: "If we couldn't make Cameo work, why would SysML v2 be different?"

Tom, same meeting.

Answer

Because the problems in this chapter are about comparison, merging, automated checking and distribution, and those are exactly what a text model in version control does well. The language matters less than the fact that SysML v2 has a standard text notation. Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers shows the same Tidewater elements in both forms; Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers shows what comparison and merging look like for text.

2.7 Reviewing a drop by screenshot

The clearest picture of why the Cameo years were painful is the government's review of a prime delivery in 2025, the first year the prime maintained the model. It is worth walking through, because Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated repeats the same job the new way and the contrast is the core of the case.

The prime delivered the Cameo project file and a delivery letter listing "significant changes" in prose: "Updated PowerSystem to reflect ECP-0117. Added maintenance states. Updated requirement allocations per CDR action items." The government had thirty days to accept or reject the delivery.

Bob opened the new project in Cameo next to the previous one, on two monitors. For two weeks, Bob clicked through every diagram in both versions, looking for differences by eye. Each difference went into a comment matrix, a spreadsheet with columns for the diagram, the element, the change observed, whether it matched the delivery letter, and the government's comment. To make the comments understandable to the prime, Bob took screenshots of both versions and pasted them into a slide deck, one slide per finding.

Table 2.5. The government's review of one Cameo delivery (notional)
Review activity, 2025 deliveryEffort (notional)
comparing diagrams by eye, two versions side by side7 working days
screenshots and the comment slides (61 slides)3 working days
comment matrix (48 comments)2 working days
review meeting with the prime1 day
following up the prime's responses2 working days over the next month

Three things about this review deserve attention.

It could not be complete. Bob compared diagrams, not the model. A change to an element that appeared on no diagram, or a relationship added in the model browser, was invisible. Bob knew this and said so in the review memo: "Review limited to changes visible on diagrams."

It could not be repeated. The comparison lived in Bob's head and in screenshots. When the prime delivered again three months later, the review started from zero.

It produced no record the model could use. The 48 comments lived in a spreadsheet. Whether each was resolved in the next delivery was checked, again, by eye.

In Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated, the same job, reviewing what changed in a drop, is a report generated in seconds from the two XMI files, element by element, including changes that no diagram shows. Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle repeats it for six more drops.

2.8 Who owns what, after the contract change

The 2025 contract change matters to everything in this book, so it is worth stating precisely.

Table 2.6. Ownership after the 2025 contract change
ItemOwnerWhat the government can do
the SysML v1 model in Cameothe prime (CDRL A003)receive each drop, review it, accept or reject it, report discrepancies
the DOORS requirements databasethe prime, with government approval of changes through the CCBreceive exports, review, approve changes through the CCB
the government's derived SysML v2 modelthe government team (this book)everything: edit, check, baseline, publish
discrepancy reports against the prime's modelthe government raises; the prime resolvestrack each to the drop that fixes it

The directive in Chapter 3, The directive keeps this split: the prime's v1 model "remains the contractual baseline," and the government maintains a derived v2 model. That word, derived, shapes every technical decision in Part II. The government cannot fix a problem in the prime's model; it can only report it and wait for a later drop. But it can fix the problem in its own v2 model immediately, record that it did, and check, when the next drop arrives, whether the prime fixed it too. Chapter 13, The operating model shows how a vendor branch makes that possible without the government's fixes being overwritten by each new drop.

2.9 What a model is, and what a diagram is

One last idea from the Cameo years, because the team confused it for three years and it matters for everything after. A model is a set of elements and relationships: a block named PowerSystem that has a part solar typed by the block SolarPanel, a satisfy relationship from PowerSystem to requirement TW-SYS-011, and so on. A diagram is a picture of some of those elements and relationships, chosen and laid out by a person for a purpose.

Diagrams are views. They are excellent for explaining, for seeing shape, for spotting a missing connection at a glance. They are poor as a record, because a picture shows only what someone chose to draw, and because the layout (where the boxes are, how the lines bend) carries no engineering meaning but takes most of the effort.

In the Cameo years, the team treated diagrams as the record. In the new way of working, the text is the record, and diagrams are generated from it whenever someone needs a picture. The kit draws part trees, trace diagrams, interface diagrams and package diagrams from the text (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep), and a viewer redraws them live beside Vim as the text changes (Chapter 10, Vim for models). The diagrams still exist. They have just stopped being the thing that has to be kept consistent by hand.

2.10 Exercises

Exercise 2.1: Measure it yourself

Generate drop 1 with perl sim/tidewater-v1.pl --drop 1 /tmp/drop1. Open /tmp/drop1/tidewater.xmi in Vim. Use /name="Battery and n to find every element whose name starts with "Battery". How many are there? Which one is the real battery? How did you decide?

Exercise 2.2: Read the manifest

Open /tmp/drop1/MANIFEST.txt. Then, in the terminal, run sha256sum /tmp/drop1/tidewater.xmi. Does the checksum match the manifest? What would it mean if it did not, and who should you call?

Exercise 2.3: Belief and fact

Write your own version of the table "The Cameo years: belief and fact" for a model on your program. Which of the beliefs are about the language, which about the tool, and which about the way the team was asked to work?

3 The directive

From what you know

You know

a directive that arrives with a date and no resources, and the meeting where the team works out what it really means.

Here it is called

the DevSecOps directive and the twelve-week scorecard.

What is new

agreeing in week zero on what will be measured, so success is a number, not an opinion.

Note: What you have, what you need

What you have: a memo telling you to adopt something you have never done, a skeptical team and twelve weeks.

What you need from this chapter: a precise reading of what the memo asks, the team's objections written down so none of them get lost, and a definition of "measurable progress" that everyone, including management, agrees to before the work starts.

3.1 The memo

The memo arrived on a Thursday in late September 2026, attached to an email from the program manager with the subject line "FYSA -- DevSecOps for SE artifacts -- action required." It was two pages long. The first page is reproduced here because the team read it so many times that Bob could later quote it from memory.

The second page listed training resources (a link to the enterprise platform's documentation and a recorded webinar), a point of contact in the enterprise DevSecOps office, and a sentence that Tom underlined twice: "Teams are encouraged to start small and iterate."

3.2 Reading it carefully

Jim read the memo three times before showing it to anyone. On the third reading Jim did what twenty-six years of requirements work had trained Jim to do: treat it as a specification, and separate what it requires from what it assumes and what it leaves open.

Table 3.1. The directive, read as a specification
The memo saysWhat it actually requiresWhat it leaves open
model "developed and maintained using DevSecOps practices"changes made, reviewed, checked and recorded through the platformwhich practices; how much is enough
"transitioned ... to SysML v2 textual notation"a SysML v2 text model exists and is the government's working copyhow faithful the port must be; what to do with what the converter cannot carry
prime's v1 "remains the contractual baseline"the government cannot change the authoritative modelhow the derived v2 model stays current with each drop
"automated quality checks on every model change"a pipeline that runs on every change and blocks bad oneswhich checks
"traceability ... computed rather than hand-maintained"a trace report produced by a program from the model and DOORSwhich measures
"peer review and approval of every change, with a complete audit record"merge requests, approvals, protected brancheswho approves what
"reproducible baselines"tags that can be rebuilt identicallyhow often
"measurable progress reported at regular intervals"numbers, every sprintwhich numbers
"brief initial results at the December PMR"a briefing in about twelve weekswhat "initial results" must show
"ISSM approval before use with program data"the toolchain must be approvedhow long that takes

The right-hand column is long. That is not a complaint about the memo. A directive from leadership is supposed to say what and leave how to the people doing the work. But it meant that most of the important decisions were now Jim's, and that the team would have to make them without experience. Jim wrote on the printout: "We decide the 'how'. Write every decision down, with the reason. If we're wrong, we'll at least know why."

That note became a habit, and it is why this book can explain the thought process behind each decision: the team recorded them, first in the wiki and later in merge request descriptions.

3.3 The meeting with the program manager

Jim asked for thirty minutes with the program manager the next morning and brought two questions.

The first was: what does success look like in December? The program manager's answer was frank. "Leadership has spent money on the platform and on licenses. They want to see that programs are using it and that it does something. I need a story I can tell with numbers. I don't need perfection. I need progress I can measure, and I need your team not to hate it."

The second question was: what are we allowed to stop doing? This mattered more than it sounded. A team of three could not port a model, learn a new way of working and keep doing every document-era activity at the same time. After some discussion, the program manager agreed to three things:

  • the monthly screenshot-based model review package would be replaced by whatever the team could publish from the new system, starting when it was ready;
  • the government's VCRM spreadsheet would be frozen at its current revision and replaced by the computed trace report once the trace report existed;
  • the team would spend no time on Cameo beyond reading each drop, for the duration of the twelve weeks.
Tip: Ask what you can stop doing

Every change program adds work. Few of them say what to remove. Ask, early, in writing. The three things Jim negotiated freed roughly a fifth of the team's time, and that time is what paid for the learning curve.

3.4 The team meeting

Jim scheduled the team meeting for Monday afternoon, 28 September, in the small conference room with the broken projector. Jim printed the memo three times, handed out copies, and let Bob and Tom read it in silence.

Bob finished first and put the memo face down on the table.

So we're doing it again. Three years ago it was "go MBSE." We spent two years clicking every box in the SSDD into Cameo. Now it's "go DevSecOps," and we get to do it all again in a different tool. What happens in three years?

— Bob

Tom read the memo twice, underlined "start small and iterate," and asked a question that sounded practical and was actually the deepest objection in the room.

I run CM. I know what a baseline is, I know what a CCB is, I know what an audit is. What I don't know is what any of these words mean. Pipeline. Merge request. I've never written code. Why can't we just do systems engineering the way we know how to do it, and put the documents in GitLab if they want them in GitLab?

— Tom

Jim did not have good answers yet, and said so. What Jim did instead turned out to be the most useful thing anyone did in the first week: Jim went to the whiteboard and wrote down every objection, in the speaker's words, without arguing with any of them. "If we can't answer these with evidence by December," Jim said, "then we'll put that in the briefing too."

The whiteboard photo went into the team's notes that afternoon. The objections are reproduced here, each with a pointer to the part of the book where it is answered. They are worth reading slowly; if you are in the team's position, most of them are yours.

Objection: "We already did this once. Modeling took two years and gave us a spider web."

Bob.

Answer

The spider web is measured in Chapter 2, The Cameo years and untangled a strand at a time: one package loop broken in Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed, the Legacy Import clutter removed and the trace spaghetti pruned in Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself. The last loop, between Stations and DataCenter, is still open after twelve weeks and stays on the scorecard (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web). The two years went into porting documents by hand into a tool without a workflow; this time the content already exists, a converter carries most of it, and the workflow is the point. Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard compares the two efforts.

Objection: "Why can't we just do systems engineering the old way?"

Tom.

Answer

You can keep doing systems engineering; nothing in this book changes what a requirement, a baseline or a review is. What changes is how much of it is done by hand. Chapter 5, DevSecOps in systems-engineering words translates every DevSecOps practice into the systems engineering practice it implements, and Chapter 38, How the team changed its mind revisits this objection against twelve weeks of evidence.

Objection: "We're systems engineers, not programmers. We don't know how to code."

Tom and Bob.

Answer

Nothing in the twelve weeks requires programming. The team edits text files in Vim (which they already use), types a small number of commands (listed in full in Chapter 9, The survival kit and Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers) and reads reports. The pipeline is a configuration file of about a hundred lines that calls tools other people wrote; Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job explains every line.

Objection: "The contractor owns the model. Anything we do is a copy that will go stale."

Bob.

Answer

It would, if keeping it current were done by hand. Chapter 13, The operating model sets up a vendor branch that holds exactly what the prime delivered, converted, so each new drop is merged into the government's model like any other change, with the conflicts shown precisely. Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle shows six more drops absorbed this way over the following fifteen months.

Objection: "Nobody outside our team will be able to read SysML v2 text."

Jim, playing devil's advocate.

Answer

Fewer people could read the Cameo model, because only three people had licenses. The v2 model publishes itself as a website with generated diagrams and reports on every baseline (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep, Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed), readable in a browser by anyone with access. The text is for the people who maintain the model; the site is for everybody else.

Objection: "The ISSM will never approve this in time."

Tom.

Answer

The toolchain is small (Git for Windows, Perl and Vim, already approved on the laptops, plus the enterprise GitLab, already approved for the enterprise) and Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated starts the ISSM conversation in week three with a written system description. It does cause a three-day block in Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named, and the plan absorbs it.

Objection: "We'll spend twelve weeks learning tools and have nothing to show."

Bob.

Answer

The plan in Chapter 13, The operating model delivers something measurable every sprint, starting in Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in with a working project and a first pipeline, run locally on drop 1 until the runner arrives in Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated. The scorecard below is defined before the work starts, so progress is measured against targets the team set, not against hope.

Objection: "Management will just move the goalposts."

Tom, quietly, at the end of the meeting.

Answer

Possibly. The defense is the scorecard: agreed in writing in week one, measured automatically, reported every sprint. Chapter 35, The briefing shows the December briefing built from it.

Objection: "In three years there'll be another directive."

Bob.

Answer

Very likely. What survives a change of tools is the habit of keeping the system's description as reviewed, versioned, checked text with a computed trace. That habit is tool-independent; Chapter 51, Pitfalls and anti-patterns discusses how not to lock it into GitLab either.

3.5 The prime's view

Jim called the prime's modeler on Friday 2 October, the afternoon drop 1 arrived, to explain what the government was about to do with it. Jim expected resistance. The prime's modeler was cautiously relieved.

We've been getting comment matrices with screenshots for a year. Half the time we can't tell which diagram the screenshot came from. If you can tell us exactly which element is wrong, by its ID, we can fix it in the next drop.

— the prime's modeler, 2 October

The call settled three working agreements that the rest of the book relies on:

  • The prime keeps delivering what the CDRL requires, unchanged: XMI, ReqIF, CSV and a manifest with checksums. The government will not ask the prime to change tools or formats.
  • The government reports problems as discrepancy reports, one per problem, each naming the element by its v1 identifier (the xmi:id that the converter keeps on every TODO line and that the drop-to-drop comparison reports), with the evidence and the drop by which the government would like it fixed.
  • The prime keeps element identifiers stable between drops, which Cameo does by default as long as elements are edited rather than deleted and recreated. This one agreement is what makes the government's drop-to-drop comparison and merge possible (Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).
Tip: Talk to the contractor early

The government's derived model depends on the contractor's deliveries in ways the contract does not spell out: stable identifiers, consistent export settings, a manifest with checksums. A friendly call before the first drop is processed costs an hour and avoids months of friction. Write down what was agreed and send it to the contracting officer's representative.

3.6 Defining measurable progress

The most important thing the team produced in the week before sprint 1 was not a tool or a file. It was a single page that defined what "measurable progress" would mean, agreed by Jim, the program manager and the deputy program manager. The page has three columns that matter: the measure, how it is computed (automatically, from the system, never by hand), and the target for week twelve. A fourth column holds the document-era baseline where one exists, so the comparison in December is fair.

The rule Jim set for choosing measures was simple: every measure must be computed by a program from the repository or GitLab, and every measure must be something a skeptic in the room would accept as meaningful. No "percentage complete" judged by eye, no counts of meetings held.

Table 3.2. The twelve-week scorecard, as agreed before sprint 1
#MeasureHow it is computedWeek-12 targetDocument-era baseline (notional)
1Conversion debt: TODO lines left by the convertercounted by the pipeline's todo job on every changeall structure TODOs closed; behavior startednot applicable
2Change lead timemedian hours from merge request opened to merged, from GitLabunder 3 working days23 working days
3Gated changesshare of changes to the integration branch that passed the pipeline and were approved by a code owner other than the author100%not measured
4Trace answer timewall-clock time of the pipeline's trace jobunder one minute2 working days
5Trace measuresrequirements linked (C), orphans (F), unverified (G), completeness (I), text driftcomputed on every change; every gap has an ownercomputed at reviews only
6Discrepancies reported to the primediscrepancy report issues opened, each with a due dropevery gap found is reportedad hoc emails
7Spider web in the v2 modelpackage dependency cycles, duplicate/stale blocks, max relationship ends per blockno cycles, no duplicatessee Chapter 2, The Cameo years
8Pipeline healthshare of pipelines passing on the integration branch; longest time from a failure to the next passabove 90%; restore within one working daynot applicable
9Reproducible baselinesbaseline tags whose rebuild matches the recorded checksuminterim baseline tagged and reproduciblerevision letters, not reproducible
10Review turnaroundmedian hours from merge request opened to first approvalunder 1 working day3 weeks per review package
11Delivery against planstory points done / committed per sprint, from the journal80% or betternot measured
12Team moralefive-question pulse survey (1 to 5) at each retrospective3.5 or better, risingnot measured

A few choices on this page deserve explanation, because they reveal the team's thinking.

Conversion debt is the primary progress measure. The converter carries most of the v1 model into SysML v2 automatically, but leaves a // TODO comment wherever it meets something it cannot carry (see Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers). Those lines are a precise, countable, shrinking list of work. Unlike "percent complete," a TODO count cannot be argued with: either the line is there or it is not. Jim chose it because it is the measure Bob, the strongest skeptic, would accept.

Lead time and review turnaround have document-era baselines. These are the measures where the new way should be dramatically better, and where management will look first. The team was careful to use the same definition on both sides (from request to incorporation) and to label the old numbers as notional reconstructions.

Gated changes must be 100%. This is the one measure with no tolerance. The memo asks for review and approval of every change. If even one change reaches the integration branch without a passing pipeline and an approval, the audit record has a hole. GitLab's protected branches make this a setting rather than a promise, as Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab shows.

Morale is measured. Including it was the program manager's idea, and it surprised the team. "If your team hates this in December," the program manager said, "the numbers won't matter, because it won't last." The pulse survey is five questions, answered anonymously at each retrospective on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree):

  1. I understand why we are working this way.
  2. I can do my work in the new tools without help.
  3. The checks catch problems I would have missed.
  4. I can see our progress.
  5. I would choose to keep working this way.

Nothing is measured by hand. Every measure on the page comes from the repository, GitLab's records or the team's journal, and the pipeline or a script computes it. This was a deliberate break from the document era, where every status number was a one-off, like Bob's Wednesday list in Chapter 1, Thirty years of documents.

Warning: Agree on the measures before you start

If you define your measures after the work, you will be accused (correctly) of choosing the ones that look good. Define them first, get them signed, and report all of them every sprint, including the ones that look bad. Several of the team's measures looked bad in sprint 3. Reporting them anyway is what made the December briefing credible.

3.7 Jim's plan in one page

With the scorecard agreed, Jim sketched the twelve weeks as six two-week sprints, each with a goal that produced something measurable. The detailed plan, and the reasoning behind the sprint length and the size rules for work, is in Chapter 13, The operating model; this is the outline that went to the program manager on Friday 2 October, the same day the prime delivered drop 1:

Table 3.3. The twelve-week plan, as sent to the program manager
SprintGoalEvidence at the end
1A GitLab project the team can work in; drop 1 received and assessedproject, protected branches, a first pipeline drafted and run locally on drop 1 (gating every change starts in sprint 2, when the runner is online), TODO inventory
2Drop 1 on the integration branch through the vendor branch; every change gatedvendor branch, gated merges, TODO burn-down starts
3Network and Types cleaned up; DOORS importedtrace report on every change; first drift found
4Stations cleaned up; gaps reported to the primediscrepancy reports; the model site
5Data center and operations cleaned up; release rehearsedstructure TODOs closed; release procedure
6Behavior work started; interim baseline; the briefingbaseline-0, release notes, the December briefing

At the bottom of the page Jim wrote one more line, which the program manager initialed: "We will report every measure every sprint, including the bad ones."

3.8 The email Jim sent that night

After the team meeting, Jim went home and wrote an email to Bob and Tom. Jim almost did not send it, and later said it was the most important thing written in the twelve weeks. It is reproduced here because it set the tone for everything that followed.

Bob replied the next morning with one line: "Twelve weeks. Then we talk." Tom did not reply, but on Wednesday Tom had already requested a GitLab group from the enterprise administrators, three days before Jim had planned to.

Tip: What the email does

The email does four things a change leader has to do: it admits what is not known, commits to specific behaviors, asks for specific behaviors in return, and sets an exit condition. It does not argue with the objections, and it does not promise that the new way will be better. It promises that the team will find out honestly.

3.9 Week zero

The week between the memo and sprint 1 (29 September to 2 October 2026) was not part of any sprint, and Jim used it to prepare the ground. Nothing in it required DevSecOps knowledge; all of it was ordinary program work. The full checklist is in Appendix J, Checklists; the main items were:

  • Request access early. Tom asked the enterprise GitLab administrators for a group (tidewater), a project (tidewater/model), three accounts with the right roles, and a runner, the machine that will execute the pipeline. The administrators' standard turnaround was five working days, so the request had to go in before sprint 1, not during it.
  • Book the ISSM. Jim asked for an hour with the ISSM in the second week of sprint 2 to present the toolchain, knowing that approvals take time and that sprint 3 would need them.
  • Confirm the laptops. Git for Windows (which includes Git Bash and Perl), Vim and the kit were already on the program's approved software list. Tom checked each laptop's versions so nobody would discover a missing tool on day one.
  • Agree the scorecard. The scorecard above was agreed by Thursday 1 October, signed by the program manager and the deputy program manager.
  • Receive drop 1. The prime delivered drop 1 on Friday 2 October. Jim logged the delivery against CDRL A003 that afternoon and did nothing else with it until Monday. The receipt is the first story of Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in.
  • Set the calendar. Fifteen-minute stand-ups at 09:00 every working day; sprint planning on the first Monday of each sprint; review and retrospective on the last Friday. Holidays and leave were entered before planning, so sprint capacities would be honest.
Warning: Access requests are on the critical path

The longest lead time in the first two weeks was not learning git or writing a pipeline. It was waiting for accounts, a project and a runner from the enterprise administrators. Submit those requests before you do anything else, even before you are sure exactly what you need. You can adjust a project's settings later; you cannot get back the week you spent waiting.

3.10 What management needed to hear, and when

The program manager's request ("a story I can tell with numbers") shaped the reporting rhythm for the twelve weeks. Jim agreed to three kinds of report, each built from the scorecard:

Table 3.4. The twelve-week reporting rhythm
ReportWhenContentBuilt from
sprint reviewevery second Fridaywhat was finished, demonstrated live; scorecard for the sprintGitLab, the journal, the pipeline
weekly noteevery Friday in betweenone paragraph: progress, risks, help neededthe journal's weekly quad
December PMR briefingend of sprint 6the twelve-week scorecard, before and after, the live demoeverything above; see Chapter 35, The briefing

No report would contain a number that had been typed by hand. That rule was hard to keep in sprint 1, when there was almost nothing to measure, and Jim kept it anyway: the first sprint review reported a scorecard with most cells marked "not yet measurable" and an explanation of when each would become measurable. The program manager later said that page was what convinced them the team was serious.

3.11 Exercises

Exercise 3.1: Read your own directive

Take a directive, policy or tasking memo you have received. Build the three-column table from "The directive, read as a specification": what it says, what it requires, what it leaves open. Who decides the open items?

Exercise 3.2: Write down the objections

Hold a thirty-minute meeting with your team about a change you have been asked to make. Write every objection on a whiteboard in the speaker's words, without arguing. Afterwards, for each, write where and how you will answer it, and with what evidence.

Exercise 3.3: Pick your measures

Choose five measures for your own first twelve weeks. For each, write how it will be computed without human judgment, what the target is, and what the old-way baseline was. Which of your measures would your most skeptical colleague reject, and why?

4 The Vee, kept: the systems-engineering V in MBSE DevSecOps

From what you know

You know

the Vee. Decompose on the left arm, from stakeholder needs to design; integrate, verify and validate on the right arm; tie each level on the left to its check on the right; hold a technical review at each gate.

Here it is called

still the Vee. The left arm is the model's layers, changed by merge requests. The right arm is the pipeline's checks plus the test events. The horizontal lines are verify relationships. The reviews are baselines: protected tags with a review package the pipeline generates.

What is new

the cadence. The program still walks one big Vee across its reviews, but every merge request now walks a small one in minutes, and every baseline walks a medium one. Nothing on the right arm waits for a milestone.

This chapter is CORE: it is the frame for everything that follows. Read it before Chapter 5, DevSecOps in systems-engineering words, which translates the vocabulary; this chapter explains the shape.

4.1 Jim's whiteboard

The second time the team met about the directive (Chapter 3, The directive), Bob walked to the whiteboard, drew a large V and put the marker down.

Every program I've been on runs on this. Requirements down the left, test up the right, a review at every corner. The memo says "continuous delivery". Where does the V go? Do we throw it away?

— Bob, the week before sprint 1

It was the right question, and the honest answer took Jim most of the afternoon to work out: the V stays. What changes is how often you walk it, and who does the walking on the right-hand side. In the document era the team walked the right arm by hand, a few times a year, in the weeks before a review. In the new way a machine walks the lowest rungs of the right arm on every change, and people spend their time on the rungs only people can climb.

This chapter is that afternoon, written down.

4.2 The Vee in one paragraph

The systems-engineering Vee draws the life of a system as a letter V. Down the left arm the team decomposes: stakeholder needs become system requirements, requirements become an architecture, the architecture becomes a detailed design. At the bottom something gets built. Up the right arm the team integrates the pieces and checks them, level by level, against what the left arm said: the design against its specification, the integrated system against its requirements, the delivered system against the stakeholders' needs. The horizontal lines across the V are the promise that every statement on the left has a check on the right. The gates on the arms are the technical reviews -- SRR, SDR or PDR, CDR, TRR, PRR, and the configuration audits -- where a board looks at the evidence and decides whether the program moves on.

Nothing in that paragraph mentions documents, tools or a calendar. That is why the Vee survives the move.

4.3 What DevSecOps changes: three Vees, not one

In the document era there was one Vee per program, walked once, with reviews months apart. In MBSE DevSecOps the same shape repeats at three time scales:

  • The program's Vee, across the technical reviews. It is the one you already know, and it still takes years. The reviews still happen and a board still decides; what arrives at each review is different (Section 4.7, The gates: technical reviews as baselines).
  • A baseline's Vee, release by release. Between reviews the team cuts baselines (Tidewater's are baseline-0, baseline-1 ...). Each one goes down the left arm (what changed), through the build (the release branch), and up the right arm (the baseline audit, the verification matrix, the people who approve it).
  • A merge request's Vee, in minutes. One change goes down the left arm (Bob edits a requirement and its satisfy relationship), is built (the merge request), and comes up the right arm (grammar, lint, the trace check, the verification matrix, a code owner's review) before it lands. The lowest rungs of the right arm are walked hundreds of times between two reviews instead of once.

The middle of the figure is where the shift happens: a change to the model sits at the bottom of the V, and the model checks are its first rung up. Bob's worry was that continuous delivery would flatten the V into a line. It does the opposite: it makes the V small enough to walk every day.

4.4 The left arm: the model's layers

On the left arm the document era had a specification tree: the SRS, the SSDD, the ICDs, the design documents, each with its own revision letter. In the new way the same content lives in one model, arranged in layers that mirror the left arm (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where):

Table 4.1. The left arm of the Vee as folders in the model.
Left arm levelWhere it lives in the modelHow it changes
Stakeholder needsmodel/requirements/stakeholder/ (from the DOORS needs module)DOORS export, imported by the vendor branch
System requirementsmodel/requirements/system/, each with its doorsIdmerge request; the recipe check grades the wording (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe)
Architecturemodel/logical/ and the parts, ports and interfaces of model/physical/merge request; the layers and complexity checks guard the structure
Designdetail inside model/physical/merge request, by the package's code owner

The arm is still walked top to bottom: a stakeholder need is still decomposed into requirements before anyone designs. What changed is the unit of work. A decomposition step is a story, its pieces are tasks of under a week, and each lands as a merge request that a second engineer reviews (Chapter 13, The operating model, Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).

4.5 The right arm: checks at every level

The right arm is where DevSecOps changes the most. In the document era every rung was a manual event: a desk check, an integration test, a review of a verification matrix someone had assembled by hand. Now each rung has an owner, and the lowest rungs are machines.

  • Model checks, the first rung (MIL, model in the loop). On every merge request the pipeline checks the grammar, resolves every name, checks the outline, the layers and the complexity, compares the trace with DOORS, regenerates the verification matrix and grades the requirement wording. Minutes, not weeks.
  • Integration. Interfaces are checked when they change: the interface tables and the connection view are generated from the model (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text), and an interface change needs the systems lead's approval through CODEOWNERS. Where a program has a simulation, a nightly software-in-the-loop job runs it (SIL).
  • System verification. The trace ratchet keeps every requirement's verification case in place, the verification matrix (VCRM) shows each requirement's latest verdict, and a lab bench runs hardware-in-the-loop tests (HIL) when a person starts them (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop).
  • Validation and acceptance. Test events and the customer's review: people and real conditions. The pipeline's job here is evidence, not judgement: the signed verdicts and the matrix go into the baseline's release.

You can see the rungs the pipeline walks for each kind of event. Start the practice project from lesson 11 (a copy of the team's model repository on an offline GitLab), then ask the pipeline what it would run for a merge request:

Ten jobs: the first rung of the right arm, on every change. Now the same question for a baseline tag:

The same ten checks run again, and three more join them: baseline (the configuration audit), publish-package and publish-release (the review package). That is the baseline's Vee coming up the right arm. Finally, the nightly schedule with a simulation and a lab bench switched on:

sil-regression runs by itself every night; hil-test waits, manual, for a person who has checked the bench. Tidewater has neither switched on, because the government team owns no simulation and no lab; the template carries them for the day a program does (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop).

4.6 The horizontal lines: verify, in the same merge request

The horizontal lines are the Vee's most important promise and its most neglected one. In the document era the promise was a verification cross-reference matrix, assembled in a spreadsheet before each review, out of date the day after. Here a horizontal line is a verify relationship in the model: a verification case that names the requirement it verifies. Two rules keep the line from breaking:

  1. A requirement and its verification case change in the same merge request. The reviewer sees both.
  2. The trace check compares the model with DOORS on every merge request and fails when a change adds a gap: a requirement that loses its satisfy (an orphan) or its verify (unverified). Gaps that were already there are reported, not blocked: they are someone else's to fix, often the prime's (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

Break a horizontal line on purpose and watch the check catch it. On a scratch branch, delete one verify and run the trace job as a merge request into develop would:

The nine unverified requirements that were already there did not block anyone. The tenth, the one this change created, does, and the message names it. In the document era that line would have broken silently, and the review in three months' time would have found it, if anyone looked.

4.7 The gates: technical reviews as baselines

The technical reviews keep their names, their boards and their decisions. Three things about them change.

  • What a review looks at. A review used to look at a document set assembled for it. Now it looks at a baseline: a protected tag, baseline-N, on a commit of the model. Everything the board reads -- the generated documents, the verification matrix, the trace report, the toolchain list -- is produced from that tag by the pipeline, so it describes exactly what was tagged.
  • How the baseline is audited. The configuration audit used to be a person comparing a document list with a library. Now the baseline job rebuilds the generated documents from the tagged model and compares a checksum with the one recorded in the tag. If the tag's documents were edited by hand, or the model changed without its documents, the audit fails.
  • Who decides. Nobody new. The board still decides; in GitLab its decision is an approval on the release merge request, by the people CODEOWNERS names, with the change-board concurrence written as a comment (Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0).

Cut a baseline by hand and audit it. The tag records the checksum of the generated documents; the baseline job rebuilds them and checks:

Now tag a commit whose model changed without its generated documents, the way a hurried hand edit would:

The audit refuses the baseline. A board looking at that tag would have been reading documents that no longer described the model; the machine noticed before the board met.

4.8 Change control between the reviews

Between two reviews the document era ran change control through engineering change proposals, a change board meeting every few weeks, and a revision letter on each document. In the new way:

  • A change proposal is a merge request. Its description says what and why, cites the requirement or the prime's change request, and links its issue (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).
  • Board approval is a code owner's approval, enforced by GitLab: an interface change cannot merge without the systems lead, a requirement change without its owner (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).
  • The revision letter is the commit, and the release of record is the baseline tag.
  • Changes the government does not own -- the prime's -- arrive as drops, are assessed by element id and dispositioned by the board before anyone edits the model (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).

The board meets less often for routine changes and more productively for the ones that matter, because the routine ones have been checked and approved in the merge request.

4.9 The Vee, then and now

Table 4.2. Each Vee element in the document era and in MBSE DevSecOps.
Vee elementDocument eraMBSE DevSecOps
Stakeholder needsa needs document, a DOORS modulethe DOORS module, imported into model/requirements/stakeholder/
System requirementsthe SRS, revised before each reviewrequirement definitions in the model, changed by merge request, wording graded on each change
Architecture and designblock diagrams in Cameo, SSDD, ICDsparts, ports and interfaces as text; the diagrams and interface tables generated from them
Buildthe design is drawn and documenteda change is made to the model on a branch
Unit and model checksdesk checks before a reviewgrammar, lint, outline, layers on every merge request
Integrationinterface review meetingsgenerated interface tables; the systems lead approves interface changes; SIL where it exists
System verificationa VCRM assembled by hand before TRRthe trace ratchet and a VCRM regenerated on every change; HIL results ingested
Validation, acceptancetest events, customer acceptancethe same, with the evidence attached to the baseline's release
Horizontal linesa spreadsheet cross-referenceverify relationships, changed in the same merge request as the requirement
Technical reviewa document set assembled for the reviewa baseline tag and the review package the pipeline generates from it
Configuration audita person compares liststhe baseline job rebuilds and checks the checksum
Change controlECP, CCB meeting, revision lettersmerge request, code-owner approval, commit and tag

4.10 What stays the same, and what changes

What stays the same:

  • The shape: decompose, build, integrate and check, and the promise that every statement has a check.
  • The reviews, their names, their entry and exit criteria, and the board that decides.
  • The roles: who owns the requirements, who owns each part of the design, who approves.
  • Validation by people, in real conditions. No pipeline validates a system.

What changes:

  • Cadence. The right arm's lowest rungs run on every change, not once before a review.
  • Evidence. What a review reads is generated from a tag, so it cannot drift from the model.
  • Who walks which rung. Machines walk the repetitive checks; people spend their time on design, judgement and the tests only people can run.
  • When a problem is found. A broken horizontal line is found the day it breaks, by the person who broke it.

4.11 Where Tidewater sits on the Vee

Tidewater is not a new program. Its buoys and shore stations are fielded, and the program is in production and sustainment, long past CDR: on the program's Vee it sits near the top of the right arm, with the prime maintaining the design. That shapes the team's whole twelve weeks:

  • The port is a small Vee of its own, on the model. On the left, the team planned the port: what the v2 model must hold, in what layers, with what conventions (Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in, Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated). At the bottom, the conversion and the hand work that closed the TODO lines. On the right, the checks that prove the port is complete and correct (Chapter 34, Proving the port is complete and correct), the interim baseline, and the management briefing, which is the port's validation: did it give the program what it needed (Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0)?
  • Each prime drop is a change Vee. The prime's change requests come down the left arm (what changed, by element id), the impact report finds where the change lands in the government's model, the vendor merge builds it, and the checks and the board's disposition take it up the right arm (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition, Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).
  • The government's role is mostly the right arm. The prime designs; the government verifies, accepts and keeps the authoritative view of verification. That is why the trace ratchet and the verification matrix matter more to Jim's team than any design tool.

A team at the start of a program sits at the top of the left arm instead. Everything in this chapter still applies; the stories are about decomposition rather than conversion.

4.12 Variants you may meet

  • Incremental Vee. The system is delivered in increments, each walking its own Vee, often sharing the upper left arm. In GitLab each increment is a release line: a release branch per delivered configuration, fixes landing on develop first (Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).
  • Iterative or spiral. The upper left arm is walked several times as the requirements mature. Each pass is a set of sprints ending in a baseline; the baselines are the spiral's turns.
  • Dual Vee. An architecture Vee for the system and an entity Vee for each element, walked by different teams. In GitLab the entity Vees are separate projects (one per subsystem) feeding the system project through tagged, published interface packages; this is the federation described in Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where.

4.13 Digital thread and digital twin

Two more terms travel with MBSE, and management will use both. This section is CORE for understanding and LATER for the twelve weeks: the team builds the thread from the first sprint, and nobody builds a twin in the first year.

Definitions
digital thread
the unbroken chain of identifiers that connects a need to the requirements derived from it, to the design elements that satisfy them, to the verification cases and their verdicts, to the configuration that was fielded, so that anyone can follow any element forward or backward through the life cycle.
digital twin
a live digital counterpart of a fielded system, built from the model and kept in step with the real thing by its operational data, used to predict, diagnose and decide.

In plain words: the thread is a promise about the records -- every element has one id that every later record uses, and every baseline keeps the ids. The twin is a working copy of the system that runs beside the real one.

The figure puts them together. The model in GitLab is the spine; both arms of the Vee read and write it. The thread runs through it from requirement to design to verification to the fielded configuration, kept in every baseline. The twin sits beyond the top of the right arm, built from the fielded configuration and fed by real data. Its findings come back along the top to the left arm as new needs, discrepancy reports and change requests, which start the next small Vee.

What Tidewater's twin would be. A model of the live observation network: each buoy and shore station from the v2 model's part tree, with its power system and sensors, fed by the real observation and health streams the stations already send. It could predict when a buoy's battery will not last the winter, show which stations a storm will take offline, or test a new transmission schedule before the prime changes it.

What the kit builds: the thread.

  • One stable id per element, carried from the prime's Cameo model through every drop (the prime agreed to stable ids in week zero) and into the v2 text, with a map from each v1 id to its v2 element (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).
  • doorsId on every requirement, so DOORS and the model meet on one key.
  • satisfy and verify relationships, checked on every merge request by the trace ratchet.
  • A verification matrix that ties each requirement to its cases and their latest verdicts.
  • Baselines that freeze all of it under one tag, audited by checksum.

What the kit does not build: the twin. A twin needs live data feeds from the fielded system, a simulation that runs the model's behavior, and a synchronization layer that keeps the copy in step with the real configuration. None of that is in this kit, and none of it is a twelve-week job.

What a team needs before a twin is worth building.

  1. A thread that holds: stable ids, baselines that rebuild, a trace with no unexplained gaps. A twin built on a broken thread mirrors the wrong system.
  2. Behavior and parameters in the model, not only structure: states, flows, the energy balance with real values (Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook).
  3. Access to operational data, approved for the purpose, with its own data rights and markings.
  4. A question worth the cost: one decision the twin would change, with a number attached.

Tidewater's team has the first by sprint 6 and part of the second; the third and fourth are a program decision. When management asks "are we building a digital twin?", the honest answer is: "We are building the thread a twin would need, and here is what it would take after that."

4.14 Pitfalls

  • Calling sprints "phases". A sprint is a timebox, not a stage of the Vee. A sprint can hold work from both arms: one story decomposes a requirement while another closes a verification gap. Teams that map sprints to Vee phases rebuild the waterfall at a two-week scale.
  • Skipping the right arm because the pipeline is green. The pipeline walks the lowest rungs. A green pipeline says the model is well formed and its trace is intact; it does not say the system works. Integration, test events and validation still need people, plans and dates (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop).
  • Reviews with nothing to review. If the review package is not generated from the tag, the board reads something the model has already moved past. Generate it, tag it, audit it.
  • Treating the twin as the goal. A twin is the last step of a long chain. Start with the thread.
Exercise 4.1: Map your program's Vee

Draw your program's Vee and mark where it is today. For each rung of the right arm, write who walks it now (a machine, a person, nobody) and how often. Circle the rung where a machine would save the most time.

Exercise 4.2: Find the three Vees

In the practice project, name one example of each Vee: a merge request's (which change, which checks), a baseline's (which tag, which jobs), the program's (which review would read that baseline). Use gitlab.pl ci --list with the right --event to show the checks.

Exercise 4.3: Break and mend a horizontal line

On a scratch branch, remove one satisfy relationship instead of a verify, run the trace job as a merge request, and read the message. Then explain to a program manager, in two sentences, why the check blocked this change but not the nine unverified requirements already in the model.

Exercise 4.4: The thread before the twin

Using the four prerequisites in Section 4.13, Digital thread and digital twin, write five lines for your own program: which you have, which you lack, and one decision a twin would change.

4.15 You can now

  • Show where each element of the systems-engineering Vee lives in an MBSE DevSecOps project, and say what changed and what did not.
  • Explain the three Vees -- the merge request's, the baseline's and the program's -- and show each with the pipeline.
  • Demonstrate that a broken horizontal line is caught on the day it breaks, and that a baseline's documents are audited before a board reads them.
  • Tell a digital thread from a digital twin, and say what has to exist before a twin is worth building.

4.16 Applying this to your project

Copy the mapping in Section 4.9, The Vee, then and now and fill in your own program's names for each element: your review names, your requirement modules, your test events. Keep the shape and the reviews; change the cadence of the right arm first, starting with the rung where checks are most repetitive. Decide locally which reviews read baselines from the first day and which keep their current package until a pilot proves the generated one. Build the thread before anyone mentions a twin: stable ids from your prime, doorsId on every requirement, the trace check on every merge request.

5 DevSecOps in systems-engineering words

From what you know

You know

configuration management, peer review, the CCB, configuration audits, baselines and CDRL deliveries.

Here it is called

version control, merge requests, code-owner approval, the pipeline, protected tags and the vendor branch.

What is new

all of it happens on every change, automatically, in minutes, instead of at milestones.

Note: What you have, what you need

What you have: a working knowledge of configuration management, change control, reviews, audits and verification, built over a career.

What you need from this chapter: the realization that DevSecOps is mostly those same disciplines, made cheap by keeping everything as text and letting machines do the repetitive checking. You will finish with a translation table you can keep beside you for the rest of the book.

5.1 Tom's Saturday

Tom spent the Saturday after the team meeting reading. The enterprise DevSecOps office's recorded webinar was ninety minutes long, and Tom watched all of it with a notepad, writing down every word that sounded like jargon. The list filled two pages: pipeline, CI/CD, merge request, branch, commit, shift left, artifact, runner, YAML, SAST, secret detection, protected branch, code owner, tag, release, infrastructure as code, GitOps, trunk, feature flag, observability.

On Sunday Tom tried something that turned out to be the key to the whole twelve weeks. Next to each word, Tom wrote the configuration management or systems engineering term that seemed closest. Some were easy: a tag was obviously a baseline label. Some took a while: a pipeline turned out to be something like a configuration audit, run automatically every time anything changed. Some had no equivalent at all, and those went on a separate list of things to ask about. By Sunday evening the second list had six words on it and the first had thirty.

On Monday Tom showed the list to Jim and Bob. Bob read it twice and said, "So it's CM. It's just CM that runs itself." That was not quite right, but it was close enough to start, and it was the first time anyone on the team had said something about DevSecOps that was not a complaint.

This chapter is Tom's list, cleaned up and explained.

5.2 What the word means

DevSecOps is a compound of three words from the software world:

  • Dev, development: making changes to the thing being built. For this team, the thing being built is the system model, so "development" means changing the model.
  • Sec, security: protecting the thing and the process that builds it. For a model, this means controlling who can change what, keeping secrets (passwords, tokens) out of files, checking that what the contractor delivered is what arrived, and recording who did what.
  • Ops, operations: running the thing and keeping it running. For a model, this means publishing it so people can use it, keeping it current with each contractor delivery, and keeping the tools that check it working.

The word was coined because software organizations used to separate those three jobs into different teams with different goals, and the hand-offs between them were slow and error-prone. Developers threw code "over the wall" to operations; security reviewed it at the end, if at all. DevSecOps means doing all three continuously, as one activity, with the checks built into the process instead of bolted on at the end.

Systems engineers will recognize the problem immediately, because the document era had the same walls. Engineers wrote documents; CM controlled them; reviews happened at milestones; security looked at the system at the end. The fix is the same too: build the checks into every change, so nothing has to wait for a milestone to be found.

Definitions: The one-sentence version
DevSecOps for a system model
every change to the model is made as text, recorded, reviewed by a person, checked by

a machine and published, every time, with security controls applied throughout instead of at the end.

5.3 Eight ideas, in systems engineering terms

The DevSecOps literature is large and full of slogans. For a team maintaining a system model, eight ideas carry almost all the value. Each one is explained below in systems engineering terms, with what it costs and what it saves.

5.3.1 1. Everything is text, and the text is under version control

In the document era, the authoritative record was a set of Word files, spreadsheets and a Cameo project. None of them could be compared reliably, because they were binary files whose contents only their own tools could read. In DevSecOps, the authoritative record is plain text: the SysML v2 model, the pipeline configuration, the issue templates, even the project settings. Plain text can be read by any editor (Vim, in this team's case), compared line by line by a program, and stored in a version control system that records every change.

The version control system this book uses is git. Think of git as a configuration management database that records, for every change: exactly which lines changed, who changed them, when, and the reason they gave. Unlike the CM database Tom ran for a decade, git records the change itself, not a description of it, and it does so automatically every time someone saves their work into it. Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers teaches git from zero.

What it costs: the model has to be text. That is why the memo says SysML v2 textual notation, and why Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers matters.

What it saves: every comparison question ("what changed since the last baseline?", "who changed this requirement and why?", "what did the model look like on 1 November?") becomes a command that answers in seconds.

5.3.2 2. Small batches

The document era batched changes: a month of change requests went to one CCB, a quarter of approved changes went into one revision. Batching was rational when each revision cost weeks of editing and distribution. With text under version control, a change costs almost nothing to record and distribute, so batching only adds waiting.

DevSecOps works in small batches: a change is proposed, reviewed and incorporated on its own, often the same day. The team's size rules in Chapter 13, The operating model (a task is less than a week of work) exist to keep batches small.

What it costs: discipline about splitting work into small pieces, and the habit of reviewing small things often instead of large things rarely.

What it saves: waiting, which Chapter 1, Thirty years of documents showed was most of the 23 days of a requirement change. Small changes are also easier to review well, because a reviewer can actually read all of a ten-line change.

5.3.3 3. Every change is reviewed and approved, by a named person

This is the CCB, made continuous. In GitLab, a proposed change is a merge request: a request to merge (combine) a set of changes into the shared model. The merge request shows the exact lines changed, carries a description of why, and cannot be merged until the people responsible for that part of the model approve it. Those people are named in a file called CODEOWNERS, so the approval rule is itself under configuration control.

What it costs: every change needs a second person's attention. On a three-person team this matters, and Chapter 13, The operating model sets the rules so nobody approves their own work and nobody waits long.

What it saves: the monthly CCB queue for routine changes. The board still decides what needs a board (interface changes with the prime, requirement changes in DOORS); it no longer has to see a corrected typo.

5.3.4 4. Machines check what machines can check, on every change

Before a merge request can be merged, a pipeline runs: a fixed list of automated checks, defined in a text file in the repository, executed by a server every time the model changes. If any required check fails, the merge is blocked.

This is the idea that converted Tom. A pipeline is a configuration audit that runs on every change instead of once a year. It asks questions like: does every file follow the SysML v2 grammar? Does every assembly carry its level tag? Is every requirement satisfied by something and verified by something? Does the requirement text in the model match the text in DOORS? Are the generated documents up to date with the model? Has anyone pasted a password into a file? Each question is a short program, written once and run forever. Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job walks through every check.

The software world calls this "shifting left": moving checks earlier in the process (to the left on a timeline), where problems are cheap to fix. A grammar error found by the pipeline ten minutes after Bob typed it costs Bob ten minutes. The same error found at a design review costs a review comment, an action item and a re-review.

What it costs: someone has to set up the pipeline (Tom, in this story) and keep it working.

What it saves: almost all of the manual checking that was done before reviews, and all of the problems that manual checking missed.

5.3.5 5. Security is built in, not added at the end

For a model, "security" mostly means controlling access and protecting the integrity of the record:

  • who can change what: members, roles and protected branches, which make it impossible (not just against the rules) to change the integrated model without a merge request;
  • integrity of what arrives: every contractor drop carries a checksum, and the intake process checks it before anything else happens;
  • no secrets in files: an automated scan rejects passwords and access tokens pasted into the repository;
  • a complete audit record: every change, approval and pipeline result is kept, and cannot be quietly edited;
  • least privilege for tools: the server that runs the pipeline has only the access it needs.

In the document era, security for engineering data meant marking the documents correctly and storing them in the right place. Those obligations remain (and Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab covers marking), but DevSecOps adds controls on the process itself, enforced by the platform rather than by procedure.

5.3.6 6. The model is published continuously

Every time the integrated model changes, the pipeline regenerates the human-readable products (documents, diagrams, trace reports) and publishes them as a website. Nobody pastes screenshots; nobody wonders which picture is current. This is what software people call continuous delivery, and for a model it means the review package is always ready.

This idea answers the strongest document-era virtue: everybody could read the documents. With a published site, everybody can still read them, in a browser, without a license, and what they read is generated from the current model.

5.3.7 7. Measure, and use the measures

Because every change, review and check is recorded by machines, the process measures itself. Lead time, review turnaround, pipeline pass rate and the number of problems found are byproducts, not extra work. The team's scorecard in Chapter 3, The directive is built entirely from such byproducts.

5.3.8 8. Improve in small steps, without blame

Each sprint ends with a retrospective: what worked, what did not, what to change next sprint. When something breaks (a pipeline fails, a merge goes wrong), the question is "what in the process let this happen?", not "who did this?". Systems engineers know this as lessons learned; the difference is that it happens every two weeks instead of at the end of a program, when nobody can use the lessons.

5.4 The translation table

Here is Tom's list, cleaned up. Keep it nearby. The glossary in Appendix K, Glossary has the complete version, including SysML v2 terms.

Table 5.1. Systems engineering to DevSecOps, the translation table
Systems engineering / CM termDevSecOps / GitLab termWhat is the sameWhat is different

baseline (revision C)tag (baseline-1)a fixed, named stateexact and reproducible; created in seconds

IMS milestonemilestonea date by which work is dueholds the issues due then

CDRL deliveryprime drop on the vendor branchthe contractor's deliverableconverted and merged like any change
deficiency report to the contractordiscrepancy report issue (owner::prime)a problem the contractor must fixtracked to the drop that fixes it
