And the six words that had no equivalent on Tom's Sunday list, with what the team decided they meant:

  • branch: a separate line of work, where changes can be made without affecting the integrated model until they are reviewed and merged. Closest equivalent: a working copy of a document with tracked changes, except that any number of people can have one at once and git combines them afterwards. Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers.
  • commit: one recorded change, with a message saying why. Closest equivalent: one entry in the change history page of a document, except that it holds the change itself.
  • runner: the computer that executes the pipeline's checks. Closest equivalent: the person who used to run the checks before a review, except that it is a machine and never gets tired. Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep.
  • YAML: the text format the pipeline is written in. It is a way of writing lists and key-value pairs in plain text. Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job shows the whole file.
  • artifact: a file produced by a pipeline job and kept with its results (a report, a generated document). Closest equivalent: an attachment to a test report.
  • merge conflict: what happens when two changes touch the same lines and git cannot combine them automatically. Closest equivalent: two people redlining the same paragraph differently. A person has to decide. Chapter 10, Vim for models shows how.
Case study: What DevSecOps is not

DevSecOps is not "agile" by another name, although it is usually practiced together with short iterations. It is not about writing software; this team writes none. It is not a product you buy: GitLab is a platform that makes the practices easy, but the practices work with other platforms. And it is not about moving fast and breaking things. For a system model, the point is to move safely, with every change checked and approved, at a pace set by the work instead of by the meeting calendar.

5.5 One change, end to end

To make the ideas concrete, here is one small change of the kind the team made in Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named, followed from start to finish. It is shown in outline here, with an illustrative issue number; Part III shows the real issues, commands and output.

The converter left a TODO line in the Network package where the v1 model had a custom "level" stereotype on the top block:

The government's convention (set up in Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated) is to write the level as a metadata annotation, @L1Network;.

  1. The work is an issue. A task issue in GitLab says "Close the level-tag TODOs in Network", is linked to its story, assigned to Bob, and estimated at one day. (Action item, with an owner and an estimate.)
  2. Bob starts a branch. One command creates a separate line of work named after the issue. (A working copy.)
  3. Bob edits the file in Vim, replacing the TODO line with @L1Network; and adding the import of the conventions package at the top. (The edit.)
  4. Bob checks locally, running the same grammar and lint checks the pipeline will run, from inside Vim. (Self-check before submitting.)
  5. Bob commits with a message: "Close the L1Network level TODO in Network (#14)". (Change history entry.)
  6. Bob pushes the branch to GitLab and opens a merge request whose description says what changed, why, and "Closes #14". (Change request.)
  7. The pipeline runs on the merge request: grammar, lint, outline, TODO count, trace, docs, secrets. All pass. The TODO count shows one fewer than the integrated model. (Configuration audit.)
  8. Jim reviews: reads the two-line diff and the pipeline results, and approves. Jim is the code owner for the model/physical/network/ folder. (CCB approval, by the responsible person.)
  9. Bob merges. The change joins the integrated model on the develop branch; the issue closes automatically. (Incorporation.)
  10. The pipeline runs again on develop, regenerates the docs and diagrams, and publishes the model site. (Distribution of the new revision.)

Elapsed time for a change like this is typically an hour or two, most of it waiting for the reviewer to finish a meeting; engineering time is about fifteen minutes. Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named has the real timestamps. Every step left a record: the issue, the branch, the commit, the merge request, the pipeline log, the approval, the merge. If the deputy program manager asks in six months who changed the Network package's level tag, and why, and who approved it, the answer takes one click.

Compare that with the 23 working days in Chapter 1, Thirty years of documents. The engineering content is the same. What vanished is the waiting and the copying.

Objection: "Fifteen minutes for a one-line change is still slower than just typing it into Cameo."

Bob, on reading an early draft of this example.

Answer

True for the typing. But the Cameo edit had no review, no check, no record anyone could find, and no published result. The comparison that matters is with the controlled change: the change request, the CCB, the revision. Against that, fifteen minutes and two hours elapsed is a different world. And for a truly trivial change, Chapter 51, Pitfalls and anti-patterns discusses batching several into one merge request.

5.6 Security for a model team, in practice

"Sec" was the part of DevSecOps that worried Tom most, because Tom had spent years on the receiving end of security audits and knew how much paperwork they produced. It helped to make the threats concrete. For a team maintaining a system model, the realistic threats are not exotic. Here are the ones the team listed in Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated, with the control for each.

Table 5.2. Threats to a model repository and the controls the team used
What could go wrongExampleControl in the new way
an unauthorized change to the modelsomeone edits the integrated model directly, without reviewprotected branches: nobody can push to main or develop; changes arrive only through approved merge requests
a change approved by the wrong personthe author approves their own changeapproval rules and CODEOWNERS; GitLab blocks self-approval
a tampered or corrupted deliverya drop altered in transit or storageSHA-256 checksums in the prime's manifest, checked before import; drops stored in the package registry
a secret leaked into the repositorya password or access token pasted into a file or commit messagesecret detection in the pipeline; tokens kept in masked CI/CD variables, never in files
the history rewritten to hide a changesomeone force-pushes over the recordforce push disabled on protected branches; protected tags cannot be moved or deleted
access outlives needa departed engineer keeps accessquarterly access review of project members (Chapter 42, Administration)
the pipeline's machine is compromisedthe runner is used to reach other systemsa dedicated runner with only the access it needs, patched on a schedule (Chapter 42, Administration)
marked information in the wrong placecontent above the repository's approved levelmarking rules, banners, and the project kept on approved infrastructure (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab)

Most of these controls are settings rather than procedures. That is the important difference from the document era. A procedure says "do not change the baseline without approval," and depends on everyone following it. A protected branch makes the unapproved change impossible. Tom, who had spent years writing CM procedures that people ignored, found this the most persuasive thing in DevSecOps: "I can stop writing rules and start setting them."

Note: Security reviews still happen

Settings do not replace the ISSM. The ISSM still has to approve the toolchain, the data flows and the controls, and the team still owes the ISSM documentation. What changes is that the documentation describes settings that can be inspected, rather than procedures that have to be trusted. Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named and Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself show the ISSM review.

5.7 Reading a pipeline log, before you ever see one

The first time a pipeline fails on your change, you will be looking at a log: the text output of the job that failed. Logs look intimidating, but they have a simple structure, and knowing it in advance removes most of the fear. Here is the shape of a failed grammar job, of the kind Bob saw in Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named. The error line is the grammar checker's real output for a level tag written without its closing semicolon; the runner lines around it are abbreviated:

Read it from the bottom up:

  1. The last line says the job failed and that the command returned a non-zero exit status. Every command reports success (zero) or failure (anything else); the pipeline stops a job at the first failing command.
  2. The lines above it are the output of the commands the job ran. The last of them (ci-reports.pl) only turns the result into the report GitLab shows on the merge request; the check itself is the sysml.pl line, and its output is where the problem is. Here: one error, in model/physical/network/Network.sysml, line 5, column 9. The checker met the word doc where it expected the semicolon that should have ended the line above (@L1Network written without its ;). Errors are reported where the checker noticed them, which is often just after the real mistake.
  3. The lines starting with $ are the commands the job ran. The first, perl ci/job.pl grammar, is the whole job: the one line in the pipeline file. Run exactly that in your clone and you get the same check on your own laptop, which is how you fix the problem without guessing (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job, Chapter 10, Vim for models).
  4. The lines at the top say which machine ran the job and which version of the model it checked. You will rarely need them, except when a job works on your laptop and fails on the runner.

That is all. A pipeline log is a record of a check that someone wrote down so the machine could run it. The skill of reading one is the skill of reading a test report, which every systems engineer already has.

5.8 What changes for each person

The translation table maps practices; it is also worth mapping people. On a three-person team, each person's job changes in a different way.

Jim, the MBSE lead, stops assembling status by hand and starts reading it from the system. Jim's main new activities are reviewing and approving merge requests in the areas Jim owns, keeping the backlog of stories in order, deciding what goes to the prime as a discrepancy, and presenting the scorecard. Jim's main lost activity is the quarterly briefing build.

Bob, the MBSE engineer, stops drawing and starts writing. Bob's main new activities are editing the model as text, closing TODOs, writing what the converter could not, and resolving merge conflicts when a new drop touches something the government changed. Bob's lost activity is the side-by-side diagram comparison.

Tom, the CM engineer turned DevSecOps engineer, stops maintaining the CM database by hand and starts maintaining the system that maintains it. Tom's main new activities are the GitLab project settings, the pipeline, the runner, the drop intake and the baselines. Tom's lost activity is the change log, which git now keeps.

All three still do systems engineering. None of them writes software.

5.9 Exercises

Exercise 5.1: Make your own list

Do what Tom did. Write down every DevSecOps term you have heard on your program. Next to each, write the closest systems engineering or CM term. Mark the ones with no equivalent. Compare your list with the translation table.

Exercise 5.2: Which idea first?

Of the eight ideas in this chapter, which one would save your team the most time in the next month? Which one would meet the most resistance? Are they the same idea?

Exercise 5.3: Follow a change

Take a real change your team made recently. Write it out as the ten steps of "One change, end to end." Which steps existed in your current process? Which were missing? Where did the time go?

6 SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers

From what you know

You know

SysML v1 in Cameo: blocks, ports, activities and requirement diagrams.

Here it is called

SysML v2 textual notation: part defs, port defs, action defs and requirement defs.

What is new

the model is plain text you can read, compare and review line by line, and the converter shows exactly what it carried and what it left as a TODO.

Note: What you have, what you need

What you have: you know SysML v1: blocks, parts, ports, connectors, requirements, satisfy and verify, activities and state machines. You learned them as boxes and lines on diagrams.

What you need from this chapter: to recognize the same things written as text in SysML v2, to read the converter's output with confidence, and to understand exactly what the converter leaves for a person to do. You will type a few commands and check a few files with the grammar checker.

6.1 Bob reads the converter output

On Monday 5 October, the first day of sprint 1, Bob ran the converter on drop 1 for the first time. Bob had been dreading it. The Cameo model had taken two years to build, and Bob expected the conversion to be either useless or incomprehensible.

To follow along you need drop 1. Section 9.5, The commands you need shows how to set up a practice folder; in short:

Then Bob's command, from ~/w2s:

The command ran in under a second and wrote a folder of text files, one per top-level package of the Cameo model. Bob opened the stations file in Vim:

and scrolled to the power system. Bob looked at it for a long time, then called Jim over.

That's the IBD. That's the whole IBD, the one I drew four times. It's twelve lines. I can read it. I can read it faster than I could read the diagram.

— Bob, sprint 1, day 1

It is worth being careful about what Bob was and was not saying. Bob was not saying text is always better than diagrams. Diagrams are better for seeing shape, and the kit can draw them from the text (see Chapter 10, Vim for models and Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep). Bob was saying that as a record, something to review, compare, check and keep, twelve lines of text are better than a diagram whose meaning is spread across a layout, a property panel and a model tree. That observation, on day one, was the first crack in Bob's skepticism.

This chapter teaches you to read what Bob read.

6.2 Why text, and why now

SysML v1 was defined as an extension of UML, and like UML it had no standard text notation. The model was whatever the tool stored; the exchange format, XMI, was XML written for machines (you saw it in Chapter 2, The Cameo years). Every tool vendor stored models differently, and moving a model between tools was unreliable.

SysML v2 is a new language, standardized by the Object Management Group, with two notations defined together: a graphical notation (diagrams) and a textual notation (the text you are about to read). Both describe the same model, and the textual notation is complete: anything you can model, you can write as text. The language also comes with a standard API for tools to exchange models.

For this team, the textual notation is what makes DevSecOps possible. Text can be:

  • compared: line by line, by git, showing exactly what changed between two versions (Cameo could not do this usefully, see Chapter 2, The Cameo years);
  • merged: two people's changes to different lines combined automatically, and conflicts shown precisely when they touch the same line;
  • checked: by small programs that read the text (the grammar checker, the linter, the trace report);
  • edited in any editor: including Vim, which the whole team already uses;
  • reviewed: in a merge request, as a diff, by anyone with a browser.
Note: The grammar checker

The kit includes a SysML v2 syntax checker built from the official SysML v2 grammar files. Every v2 snippet in this book has been checked with it:

A file that follows the grammar prints sysml: 1 file(s), 0 error(s). A file that does not prints each error with its line number, in a format Vim can jump to (Chapter 10, Vim for models).

6.3 Five ideas that cover most of SysML v2

SysML v2 has a large specification, but a model like Tidewater uses a small part of it. Five ideas cover almost everything in this book.

6.3.1 Idea 1: definitions and usages

The single most important idea in SysML v2 is the separation between a definition (a kind of thing) and a usage (a use of that kind of thing in a particular place). You already know this idea from SysML v1, under different names:

Table 6.1. Definitions and usages, from SysML v1 to SysML v2
SysML v1SysML v2 definitionSysML v2 usage
blockpart def SolarPanelpart solar : SolarPanel; (a part property typed by the block)
value typeattribute def Powerattribute ratedPower : Power;
interface block (port type)port def PowerIFport supplyOut : PowerIF;
signalitem def ObservationRecorditem record : ObservationRecord;
activityaction def SampleSensorsaction sample : SampleSensors; (a call behavior action)
state machinestate def BuoyModesexhibit state modes : BuoyModes;
constraint blockconstraint def EnergyBalanceconstraint balance : EnergyBalance; (or part, as the converter writes)
requirementrequirement defrequirement TW_SYS_011 { ... }
test caseverification def TestDataFlowverification testDataFlow : TestDataFlow;

The keyword def marks a definition. A line without def, with a colon, is a usage: "a part named solar, of kind SolarPanel." That is exactly a SysML v1 part property whose type is the SolarPanel block. The difference is that SysML v2 applies the same pattern to everything, consistently.

6.3.2 Idea 2: everything lives in a package, and packages import each other

A SysML v2 file contains packages, and packages contain definitions and usages:

The import lines say which other packages this one uses names from. Interfaces::* means "every name in the Interfaces package." private means the imported names are visible inside this package but not passed on to packages that import this one. Imports are how SysML v2 makes dependencies between packages explicit, and they are exactly what you need to see the package dependency cycles from Chapter 2, The Cameo years: if Stations imports DataCenter and DataCenter imports Stations, the cycle is written right there in the text.

6.3.3 Idea 3: the body of a definition is its structure

Inside the braces of a part def go its features: parts, attributes, ports and connections. Compare the converter's output for PowerSystem (above) with what you would have drawn in v1:

  • the part lines are the part properties, the boxes inside the IBD frame;
  • the attribute line is a value property;
  • the port line is a port on the frame;
  • each connection ... connect A to B line is a connector between two ports, written with dotted paths (solar.'out' means "the port named out on the part named solar");
  • each bind A = B line is a binding connector, the kind used in parametric diagrams to tie a constraint parameter to a value property.

Notice 'out' and 'in' in quotes. out and in are SysML v2 keywords (they mark directions), so a name that happens to be a keyword must be quoted. The converter does this automatically. You will see the same with 'send' in the behavior package.

6.3.4 Idea 4: documentation is part of the model

A doc comment is attached to the element it sits in and is part of the model, not a note on a diagram. The converter turns every v1 comment into a doc. Plain comments, which the model ignores, start with //; the converter uses them for its TODO lines, which is why the TODO lines can be counted and removed without changing the model's meaning.

6.3.5 Idea 5: metadata replaces stereotypes

In SysML v1, the team extended the language with a profile: custom stereotypes like L5Assembly (the level of a block in the part tree) and Procured (a part bought from a supplier, with tagged values for the supplier and part number). In SysML v2 the equivalent is metadata: a metadata def declares the annotation, and @Name applies it:

The converter does not know the team's custom profile, so it cannot translate the stereotypes; it leaves a TODO line on every element that carried one. Closing those TODOs is the team's first big piece of work in Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated and Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named, and it is mechanical: write the metadata def once, then replace each TODO line with the matching @Level; line.

6.4 Side by side: the solar panel

Here is the solar panel from Chapter 2, The Cameo years again, in both forms. On the left of the comparison (first block) the v1 XMI, on the right (second block) what the converter writes.

Everything the XMI says about the solar panel is in those seven lines. The type identifiers have become names (Power, PowerIF). The sysml:Block record has become the word part def. The default value is = 40. The two custom stereotypes are TODO lines that name exactly what was not carried and give the v1 identifier, so a person can find the original. After the team's conventions are in place, the finished version reads:

That version was checked with the grammar checker (inside a small package that declares Power, PowerIF and the two metadata definitions), as was every snippet in this chapter.

6.5 Side by side: a requirement and its satisfy

In v1, a requirement is a UML class with a stereotype application that holds its identifier and text, and a satisfy relationship is a UML abstraction with another stereotype application:

Reading that takes work: the abstraction's client is the PowerSystem block (by identifier), its supplier is the requirement (by identifier), and only the stereotype application at the bottom says it is a satisfy. The converter writes:

The requirement's name is its DOORS identifier with the hyphens changed to underscores (TW_SYS_011), because a SysML v2 name cannot contain a hyphen without quotes. The identifier itself is kept, exactly, as an attribute named doorsId, and that attribute is how the trace report matches the model against DOORS (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). The v1 name ("Own power") becomes the title. The satisfy relationship is one line that says what it means.

Derivation (the v1 deriveReqt relationship) becomes a connection using the standard library's derivation definitions:

Verification lives inside a verification def (the v1 test case), in its objective:

6.6 Where the converter stops

The converter (bin/xmi2sysml.pl, in the kit) maps every SysML v1 construct it understands into SysML v2, and for everything else it writes a // TODO line at the place the construct belonged, naming the v1 type and identifier. It never drops anything silently. This design choice is what makes the port measurable: the TODO lines are the remaining work.

Here is what the converter carries and what it leaves, in general:

Table 6.2. What the converter carries (from the converter's own mapping table)

ConstraintBlockconstraint def with its parameters; the expression becomes a TODO
Signalitem def
ValueType, DataTypeattribute def (primitive types map to ScalarValues); units become a comment and a TODO
Enumerationenum def
Activityaction def with parameters, call actions and control flows as first ... then ...
UseCaseuse case def (skeleton)
Requirement (and Cameo's requirement kinds)requirement with doc, doorsId, title, verificationMethod
TestCaseverification def
part, reference, value and flow propertiespart, ref part, attribute, in/out features
ports (flow, proxy, full)port
Connector, BindingConnectorconnection ... connect ... to ..., bind ... = ...
Generalization:> (specialization)
Satisfy, Verify, DeriveReqtsatisfy, verify in an objective, #derivation connection
Trace, Refine, other dependenciesdependency from ... to ...
Allocateallocate ... to ...
Commentdoc
State machine, interaction, include/extend, fork/join/decision nodes, pins, object flows, constraint expressions, custom stereotypes, instance specifications// TODO line
Diagrams and tool extensionscounted and skipped

Table 6.3. Drop 1's conversion debt, by kind
TODO kindLinesWhat a person must do

That table is the shape of the port. The 39 stereotype lines are mechanical and fast, so the TODO count will fall quickly in the first sprints. The last nine are judgment calls that need the v1 diagrams open beside the text, and they take longer. Chapter 13, The operating model turns the table into stories and tasks.

6.7 Writing what the converter could not

Three of the hand-written replacements are worth seeing now, because they show SysML v2 constructs the converter never writes.

6.7.1 The buoy's state machine

The v1 model has a state machine with four states and seven transitions on the moored buoy. The converter leaves:

Bob wrote the replacement in Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0 from the v1 diagram. A version that passes the grammar check:

Each transition reads as a sentence: first in this state, accept this event, then go to that state. The v1 diagram also had a transition from degraded to maintenance; a complete version adds it the same way. Note what this means for the future: when the prime adds a "Storm" state to the v1 state machine in drop 3, the converter's output will not change at all, because the converter writes only the TODO line. The change is invisible in the converted text. Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle shows how the team catches it anyway, by comparing the v1 drops directly.

6.7.2 The energy balance

The v1 constraint block's expression was written in English-like text, which v1 tools store but do not check:

Look closely: the expression uses sunHours, but the constraint block has no parameter named sunHours. The v1 tool never noticed, because an "opaque expression" is just a string. In SysML v2 the expression is part of the language, so the hand-written version has to declare everything it uses:

Writing it by hand surfaced a modeling error that had been in the v1 model for three years. This happened again and again during the port, and it became one of the team's favorite arguments in Chapter 38, How the team changed its mind: the act of writing the model as text found mistakes the diagrams had hidden. Each such finding became a discrepancy report to the prime.

6.7.3 The observation cycle's fork

The v1 activity ObserveCoast has a fork after the quality check, so that archiving and health logging can proceed in parallel. The converter carried the call actions and the simple control flows, and left TODOs for the fork, the pin and the object flow. A hand-written version:

(The real activity also has send and ingest steps; they are left out here to keep the example short.)

6.8 Bob's Wednesday, again

On the third day of sprint 1, Bob ran the requirements converter's trace against the converted drop 1. The command reads the DOORS export from the drop and the converted model, and compares them requirement by requirement:

The last lines of its report:

It ran in about a seventh of a second. Bob read it twice, then went back to the 2019 email in Chapter 1, Thirty years of documents and checked: the question "which requirements don't have a verification method?" was answered by the unverified line, and the answer included things Bob's spreadsheet method would never have found.

Line by line:

  • C, linked: 29 of 30. One DOORS requirement, TW-SYS-016 (a common time reference), does not appear in the model at all. Nobody had noticed in three years.
  • F, orphans: 2. Nothing in the model satisfies TW-SYS-012 (stations serviceable from the vessel) or TW-SYS-016. TW-SYS-012 has a trace from the mast block, which looks like coverage on a diagram but is not a satisfy.
  • G, unverified: 9. Six of the nine are stakeholder needs, which are verified through the system requirements derived from them; that is a modeling convention to agree, not a defect. The other three (TW-SYS-011, TW-SYS-016, TW-SEG-002) are real gaps.
  • I, completeness: 66.7%. The share of requirements that are both satisfied and verified.
  • In the model but not in DOORS: 1. TW-SEG-009 (a lowerable mast) exists in Cameo but not in DOORS. Either the prime added it to the model and forgot DOORS, or DOORS deleted it and the model kept it.
  • Text drift: 1. TW-SYS-006 says "twice a day" in DOORS and not in the model. Which one is right is a question for the CCB; that they differ is now a fact that anyone can see, on every run.

Each of those findings becomes a discrepancy report to the prime in Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed, and the run itself becomes the pipeline's trace job in Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named. Bob summed it up at the stand-up the next morning:

Y: ran the trace against drop 1 -- found the drift in two minutes, it used to take a week, and we never found this one. T: TODO inventory by package. B: none.

— Bob, stand-up, 8 October

6.9 Three rules for reading SysML v2 text

When you open a converted file for the first time, these three rules will carry you most of the way.

  1. Find the defs first. Each part def, port def, action def, requirement and verification def is a thing in the system's vocabulary. Read the names and the doc lines before reading any bodies. That gives you the map.
  2. Read every line inside a body as a sentence. part solar : SolarPanel; reads "has a part, solar, which is a SolarPanel." connection charge connect solar.'out' to regulator.'in'; reads "a connection named charge joins the solar panel's out port to the regulator's in port." satisfy TW_SYS_011 by PowerSystem; reads "PowerSystem satisfies TW-SYS-011."
  3. Treat every // TODO as an open action item. It names what the converter could not carry and where the original is. Until it is closed, the model is incomplete at exactly that spot, and nowhere else.
Objection: "Engineers outside the team won't read this."

Jim, again in the devil's advocate role.

Answer

Many will not, and they do not have to. The text is the record that the maintainers edit, review and check. Everyone else reads what is generated from it: the published site with diagrams, trees and trace reports (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep). In the Cameo era, the record was readable only by three license holders, and everyone else saw screenshots. Now the record is readable by anyone with an editor, and the generated views by anyone with a browser.

Objection: "The converter will get things wrong, and we won't notice."

Bob.

Answer

The converter reports what it mapped, folded and left as TODO, element type by element type, and the pipeline runs the grammar checker and a structure check on every change (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). The trace report compares every requirement against DOORS. What remains is semantic review by a person, which is what the merge request is for. Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in shows the team's assessment of the converter's output, package by package, before anything was merged.

6.10 Names, identifiers and the way back to v1

A port has to keep a thread back to the original, so that every element in the v2 model can be traced to the v1 element it came from, and every requirement to DOORS. The converter keeps three such threads.

  • DOORS identifiers. Every requirement keeps its DOORS identifier as attribute doorsId = "TW-SYS-011";. Its SysML v2 name (TW_SYS_011) is derived from the identifier, but the attribute is what the trace report reads, so renaming a requirement never breaks the trace.
  • v1 identifiers on every TODO. Each TODO line carries the xmi:id of the v1 element it stands for. When Bob writes the state machine by hand, the TODO line being replaced names the exact v1 element it stood for; that identifier goes into the merge request description, so the record shows which v1 element each hand-written part replaced.
  • Stable names. The converter names v2 elements after their v1 names (with spaces and keywords quoted: 'serial number', 'out'). Because the prime's tool keeps an element's identifier stable from drop to drop, and the converter is deterministic, converting the same element in two drops produces the same text. That property is what lets git compare and merge successive drops, as Chapter 13, The operating model explains.

6.11 The standard library

SysML v2 comes with a standard library of definitions that every model can use. The converter uses a few of them:

  • ScalarValues::Real, ScalarValues::Integer, ScalarValues::String, ScalarValues::Boolean for the v1 primitive types;
  • RequirementDerivation for the derivation connections;
  • the ISQ (International System of Quantities) packages for physical quantities, which the team uses when closing the unit TODOs (a Power attribute should eventually specialize the ISQ power quantity rather than a bare Real).

You do not need to read the library. You do need to know it exists, because the grammar checker and the structure check accept names from it without a declaration in your files, and because when you see ScalarValues:: or ISQ:: in the model, the definition is in the standard, not in Tidewater.

6.12 A first session with the text, in Vim

Chapter 10, Vim for models covers the kit's Vim support in full. Here is enough to read the converter's output comfortably on day one, using only plain Vim commands the team already knew:

Table 6.4. Reading converted SysML v2 in plain Vim
To do thisType
open every converted file at oncevim /tmp/drop1-v2/*/*.sysml
go to the next file / previous file:next / :prev
find the next definition/def then n for the next
jump from an opening brace to its closing brace%
fold everything between braces, to see only the definitions:set foldmethod=syntax then zM (open with zo)
list every TODO in every file, as a jump list:vimgrep /TODO/ /tmp/drop1-v2/**/*.sysml then :copen
jump to the next / previous TODO in that list:cnext / :cprev
find every use of a name under the cursor*

The :vimgrep line is the one Bob used most in the first week. It turns the 52 TODO lines into a list Vim can step through, one at a time, with the file opened at the right line each time. Bob called it "the action item list I always wanted."

With the kit's Vim files loaded (see Chapter 9, The survival kit), .sysml files also get syntax highlighting, and :make runs the grammar checker and lint and puts every error into the same jump list.

6.13 Habits from SysML v1 to unlearn

Some habits that served the team well in Cameo work against them in text. The team found these the hard way; listing them here may save you some of the trouble.

  • Drawing to think. In Cameo, the way to design was to draw. In text, sketch on paper or a whiteboard if that helps, then write. Do not try to keep a hand-drawn diagram "in sync" with the text; generate diagrams from the text when you need them.
  • One giant change before anyone sees it. In Cameo, Bob would work for a week and then show the result. In the new way, a change that takes more than a day or two to review is too big; split it (Chapter 13, The operating model). Small changes are reviewed better and merged sooner.
  • Fixing the layout. A surprising share of Cameo time went into moving boxes so lines did not cross. In text there is no layout. Whitespace and order in the file are for readability, and the team agreed a simple convention (definitions in the order of the part tree, one blank line between definitions) and stopped thinking about it.
  • Copying an element to make a variant. Cameo makes copying easy, which is how Battery_old and Copy of SensorSuite came to exist. In SysML v2, a variant is a specialization (part def B :> A) or a redefinition, and the original stays the single source.
  • Trace links to everything that mentions a block. The ObservingStation block carries 17 relationship ends because the team drew a trace to every requirement that mentioned it in any document. A trace link should mean something specific (satisfy, verify, derive, refine). If it does not, leave it out; the trace report (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job) computes the useful relationships.
  • The model as a private workspace. In Cameo, the model lived on Bob's machine. In the new way, the model is a shared record; every change is visible to the team the moment its merge request opens. That feels exposed at first. It is also what makes help possible.

6.14 Reading the converter report, column by column

The first table in the converter's report has a row for every element type in the XMI and four columns. Learning to read it takes five minutes and saves hours.

Table 6.5. The converter report's four columns
ColumnMeaningWhat to look for
inhow many elements of this type the XMI holdssurprises: types you did not know the model used
mappedhow many became a SysML v2 element of their ownshould equal in for blocks, ports, properties, requirements
foldedhow many were absorbed into another element (a connector end into its connector, a multiplicity into its property, a generalization into :>)nothing to do; folded is fine
todohow many fall under a TODO linethe types to plan work for

Below that table, the report lists the stereotype applications (including the custom ones it could not convert), the ported vs remaining count (the elements that the status metrics in the kit call "in scope": classes, ports, properties, connectors and activities), what the output contains by SysML v2 keyword, and every TODO with its v1 identifier. When the prime delivers a new drop, comparing two of these reports is the quickest first look at what changed in size and debt, before the detailed comparison in Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle.

6.15 Exercises

Exercise 6.1: Convert and count

Run perl sim/tidewater-v1.pl --drop 1 /tmp/drop1 and then perl bin/xmi2sysml.pl --report --out /tmp/drop1-v2 /tmp/drop1/tidewater.xmi. In the terminal, count the TODO lines with grep -r "// TODO" /tmp/drop1-v2 | wc -l. Does your count match the table "Drop 1's conversion debt, by kind"?

Exercise 6.2: Read a package

Open /tmp/drop1-v2/datacenter/DataCenter.sysml in Vim. Without looking at any diagram, draw the data center's internal block diagram on paper from the text: the parts, the ports and the connections. Then compare with the v1 diagram list in Chapter 2, The Cameo years. Which was faster to understand?

Exercise 6.3: Find a hidden error

The energy balance expression used a parameter that was never declared. Search the drop-1 XMI for other opaque expressions (/OpaqueExpression in Vim). Are there others? What would you write in a discrepancy report to the prime about the one you found?

Exercise 6.4: Write a state machine

Add the missing transition from degraded to maintenance (event CrewOnSite) to the BuoyModes example, save it as /tmp/modes.sysml, and check it with perl tools/sysml/sysml.pl check /tmp/modes.sysml.

7 Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe

From what you know

You know

how to write a "shall" statement, and the review comments that come back on weak ones.

Here it is called

the requirement recipe and the recipe checker.

What is new

a script grades every requirement on every change, so the comments arrive before the review.

Note: What you have, what you need

What you have: decades of writing and reviewing requirements. You know a bad one when you see it: "the system shall provide adequate performance" makes every reviewer reach for a red pen. You also know that red pens run out of ink. In a 400-requirement specification, the twentieth weak verb gets through because the reviewer is tired.

What you need from this chapter: one explicit pattern for a good requirement statement, so that "good" stops being a matter of taste; the vocabulary to talk about each part of a statement; and a tool that reads every requirement against the pattern on every change, so the red pen never runs out. You will run the tool on Tidewater and on the recipe's own worked example.

This is a core chapter: read it in the first four weeks, and type the commands. It sits here, between the SysML v2 introduction and the setup chapters, because the requirement statement is where systems engineering and the pipeline first meet. A pipeline cannot judge an architecture. It can judge a sentence.

7.1 Jim's red pen

Jim kept a one-page sheet pinned above the desk for most of the document era. It was a requirements recipe: one sentence pattern, eighteen numbered parts, six of them required, and a list of verbs nobody could verify. Jim had used it for years to review specifications by hand. A review meant printing the SRS, reading every paragraph with the sheet beside it, and marking up the margins. A careful review of a 300-requirement specification took Jim about three days.

In the Cameo years the sheet did not help much. The requirements were in DOORS, synchronized into the model, and the review happened on screen, one requirement at a time in a property panel. Jim stopped using the sheet; there was no margin to write in.

In sprint 5 Jim pinned it back up, for a different reason. The team had a pipeline that read every model file on every change, and the trace job had already shown that the pipeline could find what tired reviewers missed. Jim asked a simple question at refinement: could the pipeline read the requirement text against the recipe?

I've been doing this with a pen for twenty years. If a script can do the first pass, I can spend my three days on the requirements that are actually wrong, instead of the ones that just say "provide".

— Jim, sprint 5 refinement

The answer was yes, with a qualification this chapter is careful about. A script can check the form of a requirement: is there exactly one operative verb, is the target verb concrete, is there a measurable threshold, is the referenced document identified down to the section. It cannot check whether the requirement is the right requirement. The recipe makes the form checkable, so that the human review time goes to the substance.

7.2 The recipe in one sentence

The recipe is the user's own requirement-writing standard, developed from industry practice for requirement specifications. Its premise is simple: if every requirement follows one sentence pattern, then every requirement meets the static criteria of a good requirement by construction: it is verifiable, atomic and clear.

The recipe applies to every requirement in a project's requirement specifications. One paragraph holds one requirement and the statements that belong to it. A requirement is a single sentence that applies functional or performance criteria to the specification target. These single-sentence structures stand alone as paragraphs, or as elements of larger documents and databases.

Here is the pattern. The numbers in brackets are the part numbers used throughout this chapter.

Table 7.1. The eighteen parts of the requirement recipe
PartNameRequired
1ClassificationYes
2State
3Trigger
4Pre-condition(s)
5Specification targetYes
6Allocated function
7Operative verbYes
8Target verbYes
9Precise object(s)Yes
10Modifier
11Modification(s)
12Specification
13Document number
14Section number
15Exception(s)
16Informational statement(s)
17Requirement IDYes
18Requirement tags

Six parts are required: the classification, the specification target, the operative verb, the target verb, the precise objects and the requirement ID. Everything else appears when the requirement needs it. A short requirement is not a bad requirement: "(U) The data logger shall store 72 hours of observation records. (TW-SEG-011)" has all six required parts and nothing else, and it is a perfectly good requirement.

The pattern reads like a form with blanks. That is deliberate. The recipe is not prose style advice; it is a structure, and structures can be checked.

7.3 The parts, one at a time

7.3.1 Classification (part 1)

A classification portion mark is required in most defense-related requirement specifications. The portion mark for the requirement statement comes at the beginning of the paragraph. Portion marks include (U), (U//FOUO), (S), (S//NF), (S//FRD) and so on. The project's security classification guide (SCG) and its portion-marking instructions govern the details. Typical guidance is that every paragraph of a document is portion marked, and since a single requirement sits in its own paragraph, every requirement carries its own mark.

Note: FOUO is gone

The recipe's examples use "(U//FOUO)", For Official Use Only, which is how many existing specifications are marked. In current US government practice FOUO has been replaced by Controlled Unclassified Information: CUI, with its own categories and banner rules. When you rewrite or port an older specification, follow your program's CUI guide for the replacement marking rather than copying FOUO forward. Tidewater is fictional and unmarked; its rewrites below use "(U)" only to show where the mark goes.

The tool you will use in this chapter treats the classification as optional by default, because a notional project like Tidewater carries none, and --require classification makes it required. A real program turns that option on in its pipeline on day one.

7.3.2 State, trigger and pre-conditions (parts 2, 3 and 4)

Some requirements, functional or performance, apply only in a specific context. There are two ways to define the context: a state and a trigger.

  • A state is a specific operating mode or status of the element. Common state words are "while" and "when".
  • A trigger is an event that causes the action, or that applies the threshold the requirement specifies. Common trigger words are "upon" and "every".

The words after "while" or "upon" are the pre-conditions. It is not necessary to put pre-conditions at the beginning of the statement, but placing them first gives the reader the context before the requirement itself, and the recipe recommends putting all of them at the head of the statement.

In Tidewater terms: "While in observing mode" is a state; "upon each scheduled transmission time" is a trigger.

7.3.3 Specification target and allocated function (parts 5 and 6)

As a rule, the specification target is always the subject of the specification itself, at least for performance and functional requirements. A requirement found in the "data processor" specification always has "data processor" as its specification target. If a requirement in the telemetry unit specification has "the data center" as its subject, it is in the wrong specification.

The allocated function is optional. It applies the requirement to a structural or functional component of the specification target. If the data processor consists of the "data collector", "data extractor" and "message passer" top-level functions, stating that the required function is allocated to one of them gives greater resolution to the design space.

The only time the specification target may be something other than the subject of the specification is for tertiary requirements on a related entity: the developer who builds the specification target, or the tester who evaluates it. "The developer shall deliver the source code..." in a software specification is the classic case.

In SysML v2 the specification target becomes the requirement's subject, and the allocated function becomes an allocate relationship or the subject's feature. We come back to that in Section 7.9, The recipe in SysML v2.

7.3.4 Operative and target verbs (parts 7 and 8)

The core of a requirement statement is a pair of verbs: an operative verb and a target verb. There are four main operative verbs in requirements language.

Table 7.2. The four operative verbs
Operative verbMeaning
shallThe strongest verb. It applies a requisite function or performance threshold to the system. In most contracts every "shall" in a project specification has legal force.
willA weaker verb. Usage varies, but it typically states something about an external actor, mirroring a "shall" for that actor.
shouldA design or implementation guideline: how the system should behave or how a function should be implemented. It is not a requirement.
mayGives resolution to the available design space. Often an informational statement below a "shall" or "should".

There may be others. The specification, or a parent document it references, defines the available operative verbs and their precise meanings.

The target verb is the action or performance the system must meet. Target verbs must be specific and verifiable. Some target verbs are common and yet rarely or never verifiable: provide, have, be, be capable of, establish. Use specific, concrete verbs that belong to the engineering domain instead: send, store, measure, report, detect, compute, display, isolate.

The kit's checker adds a few verbs of its own to the recipe's list, because they fail the same test in practice: support, allow, enable, handle, ensure, facilitate, accommodate and permit. It also treats "be able to" as a weak verb: "shall be able to read" is a promise about capability, and the requirement should state the action itself, "shall read", with its threshold.

7.3.5 Precise objects (part 9)

The precise objects say what the operative and target verbs act on. They give definition to what the specification target is or does. As in ordinary language, the domain of the object is a function of the verb. If the verb is "store", the precise object is what is stored, and it must be something the specification target can store. If the verb is "maintain", the precise object is a measurable state: altitude, temperature, quantity, state of charge.

7.3.6 Modifiers and modifications (parts 10 and 11)

Modifiers apply specificity and constraint to the verb and its objects. A statement can have any number of them, as prepositional phrases following the noun-verb-object triple. Almost every preposition in the statement is, by definition, a modification. Strictly speaking the state, trigger and exception are modifiers too; this part refers to the modifiers that are not states, triggers or exceptions.

The available modifiers follow from the noun-verb-object structure. If a component "shall hand over bus control", a prepositional phrase should follow, most likely starting with "to", naming the component that receives bus control. And just as the first component must be capable of handing over bus control, the object of the preposition must be capable of receiving it and operating accordingly. A modifier is a claim about two things, not one.

Thresholds live here. "Within", "less than", "above", "at least", "every" all introduce a performance threshold, and a performance verb without one is a requirement nobody can fail.

7.3.7 Specification reference (parts 12, 13 and 14)

Often a requirement is levied on a specification target in one document, but its technical details are found in another. A software item required to use floating-point arithmetic would not define every case, exception and behavior of floating-point operations; its specification would reference IEEE 754, the standard for binary floating-point arithmetic, over and over.

Whenever an external specification is referenced within a requirement, best practice is to include the document number (unless it is part of the title) and the specific section or sections that apply. If the requirement is about multiplying floating-point numbers, the reference names the sections that define multiplication. It is also acceptable to put the document number in the references list rather than in every requirement that cites it.

Used sparingly, the reference can also levy some or all of an external specification's requirements on the current target. If an interface specification exists, the specifications of the components at either end may each carry a single statement applying the interface specification's requirements to the component.

7.3.8 Exceptions (part 15)

Exceptions modify where the requirement applies, for example when the system is in an error state or off-nominal condition. Requirements must be true all the time, so a requirement must carry the statements that define precisely when it applies. Exceptions are the cut-outs from the state or trigger: they establish the sub-state in which the requirement applies.

The position of an exception is more variable than any other part. Depending on how the sentence flows, it can come at the end of the statement (as in the pattern), as a modifier (exceptions are prepositional too), or as part of the state or trigger.

7.3.9 Informational statements (part 16)

Informational statements sit beside the requirement statement to give additional detail or constraint outside the statement itself. Sometimes they keep the requirement sentence grammatically clean: requirement statements have a specific language, but they must also function as proper English. An informational statement is not part of the requirement and carries no obligation. It can carry design constraints or hints for the verification method.

7.3.10 Requirement identifier (part 17)

Every requirement has a project-unique identifier that labels it independently of all other requirements. Most identifiers combine a number with an acronym that shows where in the system hierarchy the requirement sits: TW-SYS-002 is Tidewater's second system requirement, NC_112358 a navigation computer requirement.

The identifier is what makes a requirement findable in a database, traceable in a model and citable in a merge request. In the SysML v2 port it becomes the doorsId attribute, and it is how the trace job matches the model to DOORS (Section 6.10, Names, identifiers and the way back to v1).

7.3.11 Requirement tags (part 18)

A tag is an optional short indicator that draws special attention to a requirement.

Table 7.3. Requirement tags
TagMeaningDetails
SCSafety-criticalThe requirement specifies a safety-critical subsystem, element or function. Treatment of SC requirements follows specific processes in the Quality, Safety and Mission Assurance Plan (QSMAP).
SRSafety-relatedThe requirement can affect a safety-critical subsystem, element or function without causing a safety-critical issue directly.
MCMission-criticalThe requirement is mission-critical, subject to the additional rigor established in the QSMAP or a similar document.
RMFRisk Mitigation FrameworkThe requirement has specific cybersecurity equity under the RMF.1

Tagging safety-critical and mission-critical requirements is common practice, so they are easy to find and can be held to the additional rigor those requirements must meet. In SysML v2 a tag becomes metadata (@MC;), which a pipeline can count and a view can filter on.

7.4 The worked example, decomposed

The recipe comes with a worked example. In a hypothetical project, the following requirement is found in the Navigation Computer CIDS (D12340005):

Here it is taken apart, element by element.

Table 7.4. The worked example, part by part
ElementSource textEvaluation
Classification"(U//FOUO)"Unclassified, but labeled For Official Use Only. Care must be taken when extracting this requirement from its specification and storing or sending it through other media, because it is controlled unclassified information.
State indicator"While"The system, subsystem or component is in a specific state as the predicate for performing the required function.
Trigger indicatornoneThere is no trigger keyword, but an element of the modification defines a trigger.
Pre-conditions1. "in normal flight mode"; 2. "the 10 Hz clock signal"1. The requirement applies only while the system is in normal flight mode. The mode need not be defined in this requirement, but it must be defined or referenced in the specification, the Navigation Computer CIDS. 2. A specific trigger, the 10 Hz clock signal, a standard clock signal defined elsewhere in the specification. It appears alongside the modification for grammar and readability.
Specification target"navigation computer"The specification is the Navigation Computer CIDS, so the target of its functional and performance requirements is always the navigation computer. The specification may also levy workmanship, security and other requirements on the developer, tester and so on.
Allocated functionnoneNo allocated function is defined. The allocation of the "send" function will be derived in a lower-level specification descending from the CIDS, or left as design space for the developer to define in the design documentation.
Operative verb"shall"The strongest operative verb: complete requisite functionality or performance. In most contracts every "shall" in a project specification has legal force.
Target verb"send"Specific and verifiable, given the right objects. The target verb must be something the target can do, and a navigation computer can send a message. "Send" leads us to expect the what and the where: what is sent, and to whom?
Precise object"guidance solution message"The navigation computer sends the guidance solution message. The message is identified elsewhere in this specification or a related one (we find later that it is referenced in the Navigation Computer IRS).
Modifier1. "to"; 2. "within"1. "To" introduces the destination. Modifiers are not universally required, but this requirement would be incomplete without the destination. 2. "Within" signals a performance threshold. Words such as within, less than and above all indicate thresholds.
Modifications1. "the main computer"; 2. "30 msec"1. The destination of the message, the main computer. 2. The maximum allowable latency for sending the message, coupled with "within".
Specification"Navigation Computer IRS"Additional information about this message passing between the navigation computer and the main computer is in the Navigation Computer IRS.
Document number"D12340000"The IRS's document number. If the project uses an integrated data environment or library system, the number makes the document quick to locate.
Section number"Section 5.1.4"The specific subsection of the IRS where the information is found. This makes it far easier for an analyst to line up the family of specifications.
Exceptions"during the navigational upset condition"Placed at the front, like a pre-condition, purely for readability. The requirement applies while the computer is in normal flight mode but the upset condition has not been asserted: a very precise state.
Informational statements"The 10 Hz clock signal driver is either directly or indirectly sampled from the main CCA clock source."Not part of the requirement. Related information, design-space constraints or verification elements. Here it says the clock signal is measured against the clock source on the circuit card, which will shape the verification method.
Requirement identifier"NC_112358"Project-unique. An acronym for the specification target (NC) and a number (112358) separated by an underscore; searchable in a requirements database, with all its links.
Requirement tags"MC"Mission-critical. Quality and mission assurance use the tag to segregate and evaluate requirements under QSMA procedures.

Now let a program read it. The kit's checker, tools/sysml/req-recipe.pl, takes a plain text file with one requirement per paragraph and decomposes each one the same way. Type this into an empty folder; the first command writes the example into a file:

The output lists every part it found, then the summary line every run ends with:

Compare it with the table. The program found the same parts a careful human found. It did not find the trigger hidden inside the modification ("of the 10 Hz clock signal"), and it does not need to: the requirement has a threshold and a context, and the score is 100. The decomposition is a reading aid. The findings are the point, and this requirement has none.

Tip: Read the summary line first

Every run of the checker ends with requirements=N findings=F missing=M. The pipeline reads that line; so should you. N is how many requirements were read, F how many problems were found, M how many required parts were missing. A score per requirement (100 minus a penalty per problem) helps you sort, but the counts are what you report.

7.5 What the checker looks for

Here is a deliberately weak requirement, the kind every specification has a dozen of:

--strict makes the checker exit with status 1 when it finds anything, which is how a pipeline job fails. The finding is the recipe's first rule:

The findings the checker reports, and their weight:

Table 7.5. What the checker reports
FindingSeverityExample
A required part is missingmajorno requirement ID; no target verb
A weak target verbmajorprovide, have, be, establish, be capable of, be able to, support, enable, ensure
More than one operative verb, or more than one sentencemajor"... shall measure wind ... and each buoy shall also measure waves."
Passive voiceminor"Past observations shall be kept ..."
A performance verb with no measurable thresholdminor"shall report its operating mode" (how often? to whom?)
A reference without a document number or sectionminor"in accordance with the interface control document"
Vague wordsminoras appropriate, etc., and/or, user-friendly, fast, timely, adequate, robust, minimize
"must" instead of "shall", or will/should/may as the operative verbinfo"The logger must store ..."
A tag the project does not defineminor[XYZ]

The checker parses by heuristics: it finds the first operative verb, reads the clauses before it as state, trigger, exception, allocated function and target, and reads the words after it as target verb, objects and modifiers. A human reads a sentence better. That is fine: the checker does not replace the reviewer, it makes sure the reviewer never has to spend attention on the mechanical problems.

7.6 Tidewater's requirements, read by the recipe

Now the real thing. Make drop 1, the prime's first delivery, and grade its DOORS export:

Thirty requirements, fifteen findings, no missing parts. Every requirement has a target, a "shall", a verb, an object and an ID; the problems are all in how the requirements are worded. To see which requirements, list the ones that scored below 100:

Thirteen requirements, fifteen findings: two requirements have two findings each. Jim read them the way Jim used to read a marked-up SRS, looking for the pattern rather than the instances.

The stakeholder needs are written as wishes. TW-STK-001 says the network "shall provide" observations; TW-STK-003 and TW-STK-004 say mariners and field crews "shall be able to" read and service. That is normal for stakeholder needs, which state what users want in their own words. The recipe still applies, because a need that cannot be verified cannot be traced to anything that can. The fix is not to make the needs technical; it is to make each one name something observable: what is measured, how often, where.

One system requirement is two requirements. TW-SYS-001 reads "Each station shall measure wind, air pressure and air temperature, and each buoy shall also measure waves." Two "shall"s, two subjects, two requirements. The checker reports it as a major finding and scores it lowest, 77. Two requirements in one sentence break traceability: a verification case can pass the first half and fail the second, and the trace cannot say which.

The interface requirements have no thresholds. TW-SYS-002, -008, -009 and -014 and the segment requirements TW-SEG-003 and -004 say "transmit", "send", "report" and "retry" with no number: no latency, no rate, no limit. These are the findings that matter most for verification, because a test needs a pass criterion, and a requirement with no threshold leaves the test engineer to invent one.

One requirement is a quality, not an action. TW-SYS-012 says "Every station shall be serviceable from the service vessel." "Be" is the weakest verb on the list. "Serviceable" is a judgement; the requirement does not say what the crew must be able to reach, from where, or under what conditions.

Case study: The drift shows up again

Grade the converted model instead of the DOORS export and you get thirty requirements and seventeen findings, two more than DOORS. One of the two is TW-SYS-006, the planted drift from Section 6.8, Bob's Wednesday, again: the DOORS text says the bulletin is published "twice a day", the model's copy says only "on a fixed schedule", so the model's version has lost its threshold and earns a finding the DOORS version does not. The other is TW-SEG-009, which exists only in the model. The recipe check and the trace check are independent, and they found the same problem from two directions.

7.7 Rewriting to the recipe

Jim rewrote five of the requirements to show what the recipe asks for. The values are notional, like everything in Tidewater. Each rewrite sits in examples/tidewater-v1/recipe-rewrites.txt with the as-delivered text and its finding as comments:

Look at TW-SYS-002 before and after:

The rewrite added a state (observing mode), a trigger (each scheduled transmission time), a threshold (within 60 s), a reference down to the section (TW-ICD-001 Section 3.2) and an exception (maintenance mode). It also changed the specification target from "each station" to "the telemetry unit", because the telemetry unit is the thing that sends. And it is now testable: a test engineer can write a pass criterion for it without inventing anything.

All five pass the strict check, with classification required:

Warning: Longer is not the goal

The rewrites are longer than the originals, and that is not the point. The point is that every word is now doing a job: naming a state, a threshold, a reference. A long requirement full of vague words ("in a timely and appropriate manner as required") scores worse than a short one. If a rewrite gets long because it is trying to say two things, split it, as TW-SYS-001 must be split.

7.8 Who may change the words

Here the recipe meets the contract. Tidewater's requirements live in DOORS, and DOORS belongs to the prime. The government team cannot fix TW-STK-001 by editing its copy in the model, for the same reason it never edits the prime's Cameo model: the words are the prime's deliverable, and changing them unilaterally would make the government's copy disagree with the contract baseline (Section 6.6, Where the converter stops).

So in Tidewater, recipe findings on DOORS text become a discrepancy report to the prime. In sprint 5 Jim's story "Grade our requirements with the recipe" ended with DR-6, "weak verbs and missing parts in the DOORS text", which listed the thirteen requirements, the finding for each, and the five rewrites as suggested wording. The prime dispositions it like any other DR: accept the wording, propose its own, or explain why the original stands. When a later drop delivers new text, the checker grades it again, and the DR closes when the findings do.

Two consequences are worth stating plainly, because they are where teams go wrong:

  • Fix the source, not the copy. If the model's copy of a requirement is edited to satisfy the recipe and DOORS is not, the drift check reports a new drift, and the team has created the problem it was trying to remove.
  • Requirements the government owns can be fixed directly. If your program's stakeholder needs live in the government's own repository, the recipe findings on them become ordinary stories, fixed by merge request, and the recipe job can be made a gate for those files.

7.9 The recipe in SysML v2

A requirement in SysML v2 text is more than its sentence. The sentence stays, as the requirement's documentation, because the sentence is the contractual text. Around it, SysML v2 gives the recipe's parts a home the model can use:

Table 7.6. Where the recipe's parts live in SysML v2
Recipe partSysML v2
Classificationan attribute, or a marking metadata (@Marking) on the requirement or its package
State, trigger, pre-conditionsan assume constraint: the conditions under which the requirement applies
Specification targetthe requirement's subject
Allocated functionan allocate relationship, or a feature of the subject
Operative verb, target verb, objectsthe documentation text (the sentence itself)
Modifications with a thresholdan attribute with a unit, and a require constraint that compares against it
Specification referencethe documentation text; optionally a dependency to the referenced document's element
Requirement IDthe doorsId attribute
Requirement tagsmetadata (@MC;)

Here is TW-SYS-002 written that way. The requirement definition captures the kind of requirement (an observation latency limit on a telemetry unit), and the requirement usage gives the specific limit and carries the recipe sentence:

The grammar checker accepts it. Now the recipe checker, which reads .sysml files directly, finding the requirement's documentation, its doorsId, the classification attribute and the tag metadata:

Why bother with the constraint when the sentence already says "within 60 s"? Because the sentence is for people and the constraint is for the model. The constraint makes the threshold a value the model holds, with a unit, that an analysis can read, that a verification case can cite, and that a pipeline can compare against a design value. When the prime changes the threshold to 45 s, the change shows up in the model as one changed attribute, which the delta report can find, instead of as a changed word inside a paragraph.

Note: Tidewater does not do this yet, on purpose

Tidewater's converted requirements carry only the sentence and the doorsId, because that is what the DOORS export gives the converter, and because the DOORS text is the prime's. Adding subjects and constraints to the prime's requirements would be a government edit to the prime's deliverable. The pattern above is what the team does for requirements it owns, and what it proposed to the prime, in the model exchange agreement, as the target form for future drops. Treat it as the direction of travel, not week-one work.

7.10 The recipe in the pipeline

The model repository's pipeline runs the checker on every change, in the recipe job. It reads the model's requirement files (but not the DOORS conversion, which the trace job compares separately), writes a text report, and turns the findings into a Code Quality report so they appear on the merge request:

The job reports and never fails, because in Tidewater the findings are the prime's to fix. A program whose requirements are its own can make it a gate in two steps: first a ratchet (fail only when a merge request adds a finding, compared with develop), then, once the count reaches zero, --strict.

You can produce the same reports by hand. The Code Quality format is what GitLab shows in the merge request widget; JUnit is what it shows in the Tests tab:

Thirty tests, thirteen failures: each requirement is one test, and a requirement with any finding fails. That is the view management sees in the Tests tab: "13 of 30 requirements have wording problems", which is a sentence anyone can act on.

7.11 Habits

Checklist: Before you file or approve a requirement
  • ☐ One sentence, one "shall"
  • ☐ The subject is the thing the specification is about
  • ☐ A concrete target verb: not provide, have, be, establish, be able to, support
  • ☐ The object is something the subject can act on
  • ☐ A threshold with a unit, when the verb is about performance
  • ☐ References carry the document number and the section
  • ☐ Exceptions stated, not implied
  • ☐ Informational notes marked "Note:" and kept out of the obligation
  • ☐ An ID, and the tags the project uses
  • ☐ The checker's summary line, before and after your change

7.12 Exercises

Exercise 7.1: Decompose by hand, then check

Take TW-SEG-003 as delivered ("The power system shall report the battery state of charge.") and fill in the eighteen-part table by hand. Which required parts are present? Which optional parts would a test engineer need? Then run the checker with --only TW-SEG-003 on the drop-1 DOORS export and compare.

Exercise 7.2: Split TW-SYS-001

Rewrite TW-SYS-001 as two requirements that each pass --strict. Put them in a text file, one per paragraph, with IDs TW-SYS-001a and TW-SYS-001b, and run the checker on it. What did you have to decide that the original left open?

Exercise 7.3: A need that can be traced

TW-STK-003 says mariners "shall be able to read the latest bulletin and observations from a public service." Rewrite it so it is verifiable without turning it into a system requirement. Hint: what would the program office accept as evidence that the need is met?

Exercise 7.4: Add a constraint

Extend Recipe.sysml with a second requirement, TW-SEG-003, as a requirement def with the power system as subject and a reporting period attribute with a unit, and a usage carrying the rewritten sentence from recipe-rewrites.txt. Grammar-check it and grade it.

Exercise 7.5: Write the DR

Draft the description of DR-6 for the prime: the thirteen requirements, the finding for each in one line, and the suggested wording for the five that have it. Keep it to one screen. Which findings would you ask the prime to fix first, and why?

7.13 Applying this to your project

  • Agree the recipe before you grade anything. Put the pattern, the weak-verb list and the tag list in your conventions (docs/conventions/ in a repository made by kickoff.pl scaffold). If your program already has a requirements style guide, map its rules onto the eighteen parts; the checker's --tag option adds your tags.
  • Grade the baseline first, as a report. Run the checker on the requirements as they are today and publish the summary line. That number is your starting point, not a failure.
  • Fix at the source. Requirements someone else owns go back to them as a discrepancy report; requirements you own get stories.
  • Ratchet, then gate. Fail a merge request only when it adds a finding. Make the job strict when the count reaches zero.
  • Turn classification on. On a real program, run with --require classification from the first day, so an unmarked requirement can never be merged.
  1. In NIST usage, RMF stands for the Risk Management Framework (NIST SP 800-37). Use your program's expansion; the tag means the same thing either way: this requirement has cybersecurity equity. ↩

8 SysML v2 by example: a workbook

From what you know

You know

drawing blocks, ports and activities on Cameo diagrams.

Here it is called

writing part, port, action and requirement definitions as text.

What is new

you type the model, and the grammar check tells you within a second whether it is valid.

Note: What you have, what you need

What you have: you can read SysML v2 text now (Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers). You know what a part def, a port and a satisfy relationship are, because you drew them for years in SysML v1.

What you need from this chapter: to write them. Every construct the Tidewater team writes, one at a time: what it is, what it was in SysML v1, a short Tidewater example you type in and check, what to notice, and an exercise. By the end you will build a small model that passes the same checks the pipeline runs.

This is a core chapter, and it is a workbook, not a reference. Do it with a terminal open. Budget two sessions: the first half (packages to verification cases) in week 2, the second half (states to views) in week 3. The plan in Chapter 13, The operating model gives you that time as learning stories; take it.

8.1 How to use this workbook

Every section has the same shape:

  1. A sentence on what the construct is for, and what it was called in SysML v1.
  2. A snippet to type. Each one is complete: a package you can check on its own. Type it rather than pasting it; typing is how the keywords get into your fingers.
  3. The check. Every snippet goes through the same grammar checker the pipeline's grammar job runs.
  4. What to notice: the two or three things that trip v1 modelers.
  5. An exercise that changes the snippet.

Work in an empty folder. The snippets are written with cat > file <<'EOF', which writes everything up to the EOF line into the file; you can equally open the file in Vim and type the lines between. $KIT is where the kit lives on your laptop (the survival kit, Chapter 9, The survival kit, set it up).

8.1.1 The check loop

Before the first construct, learn what a mistake looks like, because you will make many. Here is a v1 habit written as v2 text, a "block":

Read it the way you would read a review comment. The file and position come first: line 2, column 11, which is the word Hull. The checker read block as a name it did not know and expected a punctuation mark after it; it found another name instead. The fix is the v2 keyword: part def Hull. The last line is the summary, and the exit status is 1, which is how a pipeline job knows it failed.

The same check runs from Vim. In a .sysml buffer :make runs the checker (or the project's lint, inside a model repository) and fills the quickfix list, so :cnext takes you from error to error (Chapter 10, Vim for models). Here it is headless, the way the book's tests run it, writing the quickfix list to a file so you can see it:

Two rules for reading errors, which save hours:

  • Fix the first error first. One missing brace can produce ten errors below it. Fix the first, check again.
  • Look one line up. A missing ; is reported where the next statement starts, which is usually the line after the real mistake.

8.1.2 Your own model, for comparison

Every section below ends by finding the same construct in Tidewater's real converted model, so you can see the textbook form next to what the converter wrote from the prime's Cameo model. Make the drop and convert it once now:

The converter writes one folder per top-level package of the Cameo model: tw/stations/Stations.sysml, tw/interfaces/Interfaces.sysml and so on. Keep this folder; the sections below read it.

Exercise 8.1: Break it three ways

In typo.sysml, fix block to part def and check that it passes. Then make three mistakes one at a time and read each error: delete the ; after Ballast, delete the closing } of the package, and misspell part as prat. Which error message points at the line that is actually wrong?

8.2 Packages, imports and visibility

A package is a namespace: a folder for names. In SysML v1 it was the Package in the containment tree. In v2 text it is the outermost thing in almost every file, and Tidewater has one top-level package per file.

What to notice:

  • import Types::*; brings every name in Types into scope, so you can write StationMode instead of Types::StationMode. Interfaces::ObservationPort imports one name. Prefer the narrow import in files you write: it makes dependencies visible in a merge request diff (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web).
  • private and public say whether a name is visible to whoever imports this package. private import keeps Types out of what Stations offers to others; public import passes ObservationPort on. Default to private. A chain of public imports is how a model quietly becomes a spider web.
  • private part def Ballast is a part def nobody outside Stations can see. Use it for details that are nobody else's business.
  • doc /* ... */ is documentation that belongs to the element, not a comment. It shows in generated documents. // comments do not.

8.2.1 In the Tidewater drop
