Every converted package starts with a list of private import ...::* lines: wildcards, one per package it uses, including quoted names such as Requirements::'System Requirements'::Functions::* for packages whose v1 names had spaces. The converter imports widely because it cannot know which names each file really needs. The government team leaves these as delivered (hand-editing them would conflict with every future drop) and writes narrow imports only in the files it owns (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web).

8.2.2 A common mistake

The missing semicolon after an import is the most common first error. Notice where it is reported:

The mistake is on line 2; the error is on line 3, where the checker found part while still waiting for the ;. Look one line up.

Exercise 8.2: Narrow the imports

Add a part def Mooring to Stations that uses StationMode as an attribute type. Change the wildcard import of Types to a narrow one. Check. What happens if you make the import public and import Stations::* from a fourth package: which names can that package see?

8.3 Names, documentation and comments

Three kinds of text can sit in a model file, and they are not the same. In SysML v1 the difference was hidden in the tool: the documentation field of a block, a comment shape on a diagram, a note nobody exported. In text it is visible, and it matters, because generated documents and reviews treat the three differently.

What to notice:

  • doc /* ... */ is the element's documentation. It is model content: generated documents print it, the recipe checker reads requirement text from it, and a merge request that changes it is a model change.
  • // ... is a note to whoever edits the file next. It is not model content. The converter's TODO lines are // comments on purpose: they are instructions for a person, and they disappear when the person does the work.
  • comment about X /* ... */ is a model comment attached to an element: v1's comment shape with an anchor line. Use it for review notes that should travel with the model; prefer doc for what the element is.
  • Quoted names ('Data Center', 'in', 'records per hour') let a name contain spaces or be a keyword. The converter uses them to keep v1 names unchanged. In files you write, prefer plain names: DataCenter, recordsPerHour. The conventions most SysML v2 projects use, and Tidewater's docs/conventions/naming.md, are UpperCamelCase for definitions and lowerCamelCase for usages.
Exercise 8.3: Document a decision

Add a comment about QualityControl recording why quality control flags observations instead of deleting them, and a doc that says what quality control is. Check. Then ask: which of the two would you want in the generated document a forecaster reads, and which only in the review?

8.4 Parts: definitions, usages, multiplicity

A part def is a kind of thing; a part is a use of it inside something else. In SysML v1 these were the Block and the part property typed by it. The v2 vocabulary says what v1 left implicit: definitions are reusable, usages are where they are used (Section 6.3, Five ideas that cover most of SysML v2).

What to notice:

  • : means "is typed by". part sensors : SensorSuite; reads "sensors, a SensorSuite".
  • :> means "specializes". MooredBuoy :> ObservingStation is v1's generalization arrow: a moored buoy is an observing station and has everything one has, plus its own parts.
  • Multiplicity in brackets. [4] exactly four, [0..2] up to two, [1..*] one or more.
  • A usage can have a body. part battery : Battery { part cells : Cell[4]; } says this station's battery has four cells, without changing the Battery definition. In v1 that needed a new block or a redefinition in a property panel.
  • A usage at package level (part network : StationSegment;) is a specific thing, not a kind. Tidewater uses these for the system context.

8.4.1 In the Tidewater drop

The converter turned v1's generalization into :> and every part property into a part usage. The second line is a converter TODO: the v1 level stereotype on the block, which the team replaces with @L3Station; (Section 8.17, Metadata, and practice lesson 10).

8.4.2 A common mistake

Leaving out the colon, which reads naturally in English ("part sensors SensorSuite"):

Exercise 8.4: A shore station

Add part def ShoreStation :> ObservingStation with a part mast of a new part def Mast, and give StationSegment a part shoreStations with multiplicity one or more. Check. Then draw the part tree in your head: how many levels deep is a cell in a buoy in the segment?

8.5 Redefinition and subsetting

When one definition specializes another (:>), it can narrow what it inherited. Subsetting (:> on a usage) says a feature is one of the inherited feature's values; redefinition (:>>) replaces an inherited feature, for example with a new default. In SysML v1 this was the redefinition and subsetting fields in a property's specification dialog, which few modelers ever opened. In v2 it is two characters, and you will see :>> in every Tidewater requirement that gives a limit a value.

What to notice:

  • part anemometer : Anemometer :> sensors; says the buoy's anemometer is one of its sensors. The suite still has its general sensors collection; the anemometer is a named member of it.
  • attribute :>> samplePeriod = 1 [min]; replaces the inherited ten-minute default with one minute for buoys. Without :>> you would have declared a second, unrelated attribute with the same name, which lint reports as a duplicate.
  • Read the three symbols aloud until they are automatic: : "is a", :> "is a kind of / is one of", :>> "replaces".
Exercise 8.5: A shore-station suite

Write ShoreSensorSuite :> SensorSuite with a barometer : Barometer :> sensors and a sample period of five minutes. Check. Then try leaving out the :>> and run the file through lint in a copy of the lintdemo project from Section 8.8, Attributes, values and units. What does lint say?

8.6 Ports and interfaces

A port def says what can cross a boundary; an interface def says how two ports connect. In SysML v1 these were proxy ports typed by interface blocks with flow properties, and connectors on an IBD. v2 keeps the idea and drops the ceremony.

What to notice:

  • Direction lives in the port def. out item observation says observations leave through this port.
  • ~ conjugates. ~ObservationPort is the same port seen from the other side: the out becomes in. One port def serves both ends; in v1 you either made two interface blocks or ticked "conjugated" in a dialog.
  • The interface usage names its ends. connect transmitter ::> telemetry.obsOut to receiver ::> ingest.obsIn binds each end of the interface def to a real port. ::> reads "is bound to" (strictly, references).
  • The dot is a path. telemetry.obsOut is the obsOut port of the telemetry part.

8.6.1 In the Tidewater drop

The v1 interface block ObservationIF, with its flow property, became a port def with an out item. The v1 name kept its "IF" suffix: the converter preserves names so the prime's v1 ids and names still line up with the v2 text.

8.6.2 A common mistake

Drawing the connector the v1 way, with an arrow:

A connection needs the word connect and the word to: connection connect a.p to b.p;. The checker stops at the first dot because, without connect, it reads a as the connection's name.

Exercise 8.6: A health interface

Add a HealthReport item, a HealthPort port def with out item health : HealthReport, a healthOut port on the telemetry unit, a conjugated healthIn on the ingest service, and a second interface usage connecting them. Check.

8.7 Connections and flows

A connection joins two parts or ports; a flow says something moves along it. In v1 these were connectors and item flows on an IBD. In Tidewater the converter wrote connections for every v1 connector.

What to notice:

  • An item def is a thing that moves (a record, a message, a fuel load). It replaces v1's signals and the types of flow properties.
  • connection NAME connect A to B; joins two features. The name is optional but worth giving; a named connection can be traced, allocated and found in a diff.
  • flow of T from A to B; is the item flow, with its type and both ends. Flows also connect actions (see Section 8.14, Actions, successions, forks and flows); the same keyword covers what v1 split between item flows and object flows.

8.7.1 In the Tidewater drop

Every v1 connector became a connection ... connect ... to ..., named when the v1 connector had a name (toQc, toArchive). Some names are quoted, ingest.'out', because out and in are SysML v2 keywords: a quoted name is how v2 uses a keyword as a name.

Exercise 8.7: Two flows

Add a HealthReport item that also flows from the logger to the telemetry unit. Do you need a second connection, or can two flows share the parts? Check your answer with the grammar checker, then argue it with a teammate: which is clearer to a reviewer?

8.8 Attributes, values and units

An attribute is a value a part has: a mass, a power rating, a mode. In v1 these were value properties typed by value types with units. In v2 the units come from the standard library's International System of Quantities (ISQ) and SI packages, so a power is a PowerValue and "40 W" is 40 [W].

What to notice:

  • attribute def Power :> PowerValue; makes a project value type that is an ISQ power. This is what replaced Tidewater's converter TODO for the v1 unit instance specifications (Section 6.6, Where the converter stops).
  • = 40 [W] gives a default value with a unit. The brackets hold the unit; W, kg, s and h come from SI.
  • enum def is v1's enumeration, and StationMode::observing names one literal.

8.8.1 What the grammar check does not see

The grammar checker reads the shape of the text. It does not know whether PowerValue exists. Misspell it, and the grammar check still passes:

Inside a model repository, the project's lint resolves names, and it catches what the grammar missed. Make a one-file project and lint it:

This is why the pipeline runs both jobs: grammar for shape, lint for names. It is also why an AI assistant's output must go through both (Chapter 18, A local AI assistant on the laptop): an invented library name is perfectly good grammar.

8.8.2 In the Tidewater drop

The converter could not know which ISQ quantity a v1 value type meant, so it made Power a plain Real and left a comment telling a person to finish the job. That person writes attribute def Power :> ISQ::PowerValue;, exactly the form you typed above, and the unit TODO lines below it go away.

8.8.3 A common mistake

Writing the unit without brackets:

The unit is an expression in square brackets: 40 [W].

Exercise 8.8: A power budget's inputs

Give Battery a stateOfCharge attribute as a percentage (hint: the library has a Real you can constrain, or look for a ratio type, see Section 8.21, Reading the official library), and give Station an averageLoad : Power. Check with both the grammar checker and, in a copy of lintdemo, the lint.

8.9 Expressions: the small language inside constraints

Constraints, calculations, default values and requirement limits are all expressions: arithmetic, comparisons, Boolean logic and navigation through the model. In SysML v1 they were opaque strings in OCL or plain English that no tool read, which is why Tidewater's converter could only quote them in a TODO line. In v2 they are part of the language, and the grammar checks them.

What to notice:

  • Units compose. [W*h] is watt-hours; the multiplication is inside the brackets.
  • Arithmetic and comparison read as you would write them: capacity * stateOfCharge, stateOfCharge < 0.2. Boolean operators are words: and, or, not, implies.
  • if c ? a else b is the conditional expression.
  • Navigation with dots reaches through multiplicity. batteries.usable is the usable energy of each battery, and sum(...) adds them up. ->forAll { in s; s > 0.1 } applies a condition to every value.
  • The grammar checks the shape, not the arithmetic. It will not tell you that a power was compared with an energy; an execution engine, or a reviewer, will.
Exercise 8.9: A reserve

Add an attribute reserve to Station: the total usable energy minus one day of a 15 W load (15 [W] * 24 [h]), and a constraint that the reserve is positive. Check. Then write the same rule as one English sentence a reviewer could check by hand, and compare the two.

8.10 Requirements: definitions, usages, subjects and constraints

A requirement def is a kind of requirement; a requirement usage is a specific one. In SysML v1 a requirement was a stereotyped class with an id and a text. In v2 it can also say what it constrains (its subject) and how (its constraints), so the model can check it. The recipe chapter shows how the recipe's parts map onto this (Section 7.9, The recipe in SysML v2).

What to notice:

  • subject is what the requirement is about: the recipe's specification target.
  • require constraint { ... } is the measurable part, a Boolean expression over the subject's values. assume constraint is the condition under which it applies (the recipe's state and pre-conditions); true here means always.
  • attribute :>> maxLatency = 60 [s]; redefines (:>>) the def's attribute with a value. One def, many usages, each with its own limit.
  • Tidewater's converted requirements look like tw_stk_002: a doorsId and the text, no subject or constraint, because that is what DOORS carries. Both forms are legal; the first is the direction of travel.

8.10.1 In the Tidewater drop

The converted requirement is one line: the name made from the DOORS id (dashes become underscores), the text as doc, and the DOORS attributes. No subject and no constraint, because the v1 model had none. This is the form your trace and recipe checks read today.

8.10.2 A common mistake

Writing the requirement sentence directly in the body, as you would in a document:

Text goes inside doc /* ... */. Everything else in a body is model, and the checker reads it as model.

Exercise 8.10: The battery requirement

Write a requirement def StateOfChargeReporting with the power system as subject and a reportingPeriod : DurationValue, and a usage tw_seg_003 with doorsId TW-SEG-003 and a period of 10 minutes (10 [min]). Check.

8.11 Satisfy, verify and derive

These are the trace relationships: which design element satisfies a requirement, which verification case verifies it, and which requirement is derived from which. In v1 they were stereotyped dependencies drawn on requirement diagrams and maintained in matrices. In v2 they are statements in the text.

What to notice:

  • satisfy R by X; names the requirement and the element that satisfies it. Satisfy at the level that actually carries the responsibility, not lower; a hundred fine-grained satisfies nobody reviews is how the spider web grows back (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web).
  • Derivation is a connection from the standard library's RequirementDerivation package, with metadata (#derivation, #original, #derive) marking which end is which. This is exactly what the converter writes for v1's deriveReqt, so you will read it in every Tidewater drop.
  • verify lives inside a verification case's objective; the next section shows it.
  • Write each relationship once, in the element that owns the responsibility. The matrices, the trace report and the VCRM are generated from these statements; never maintain the reverse direction by hand.

8.11.1 In the Tidewater drop

The prime drew satisfies and derives in Cameo; the converter wrote each one as a statement, all in the Requirements package. Count them: that list is the v1 trace matrix, now reviewable line by line.

8.11.2 A common mistake

Forgetting the by:

Exercise 8.11: Trace a new requirement

Add tw_sys_013 ("store and forward") derived from tw_stk_002 and satisfied by a new DataLogger part of Station. Check. Then predict what the pipeline's trace job would report for tw_sys_013 (hint: is anything verifying it?).

8.12 Verification cases

A verification def describes how requirements are verified: the subject under test, the objective naming the requirements, and the verdict. In v1 a test case was an activity stereotyped TestCase with verify dependencies to requirements.

What to notice:

  • objective { verify R; } is where the verify relationship lives. One case can verify several requirements; list them all in its objective.
  • return verdict : VerdictKind; uses the library's verdict (pass, fail, inconclusive, error). The VCRM job reads verdicts from the results file, not from the model (Section 8.21, Reading the official library shows where VerdictKind lives).
  • The verification method (test, analysis, inspection, demonstration) is metadata or an attribute in Tidewater (verificationMethod from DOORS). The recipe's parts and the method together are what a test engineer needs.

8.12.1 In the Tidewater drop

One converted verification case verifies four requirements; the v1 test case had four verify dependencies, and the converter gathered them into the objective. There is no subject yet: v1 test cases did not say what they tested, so that is part of the team's verification work (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop).

8.12.2 A common mistake

Putting verify straight into the body:

verify belongs inside objective { ... }.

Exercise 8.12: Inspect the vessel access

TW-SYS-012 is verified by inspection. Write InspectVesselAccess with the service vessel as subject and an objective verifying tw_sys_012. Where would you record that it is an inspection, so the VCRM can show the method?

8.13 States

A state def describes modes and the transitions between them. In v1 this was a state machine owned by a block. It is the construct Tidewater's converter could not carry (Section 6.7, Writing what the converter could not), so the team writes it by hand.

What to notice:

  • entry; then observing; is the initial state: where the machine starts.
  • transition first A accept E then B; reads "from A, on receiving E, go to B". A transition without accept happens when the source state's behavior completes.
  • The triggers are types. LowBattery is an attribute def here; in a fuller model it would be an item or signal the power system sends.
  • exhibit state is how a part has a state machine. v1 owned the state machine inside the block; v2 says the part exhibits it.

8.13.1 In the Tidewater drop

This is the converter's limit: a whole v1 state machine becomes one TODO line inside MooredBuoy. The snippet you typed is the start of its replacement; the full version, with the Storm mode drop 3 adds, is Bob's sprint 6 story (Section 6.7, Writing what the converter could not).

8.13.2 A common mistake

The v1 arrow again:

A transition reads as a sentence: transition first observing then degraded;, with accept SIGNAL between the two when an event triggers it.

Exercise 8.13: The Storm mode

Drop 3 adds a Storm mode: from observing on a storm warning, and back to observing when the warning ends. Add it, with two attribute defs for the triggers. Check. Then look at drop 3's delta report in Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition and compare your model with what the prime drew.

8.14 Actions, successions, forks and flows

An action def is a function: inputs, outputs and the steps inside it. In v1 this was an activity with actions, pins, control flows and object flows. v2 keeps the semantics in a much smaller notation.

What to notice:

  • Parameters are directed features. in record, out checked: v1's pins and parameter nodes.
  • first A then B; is a succession, v1's control flow. start is the built-in beginning of the action.
  • fork afterCheck; is a fork node: after it, store and publish both run. A join node collects them back.
  • flow A.x to B.y; is v1's object flow, between the output of one step and the input of another.
  • This is the shape of Tidewater's ObserveCoast, and the IDEF0 plates are drawn from it (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text).

8.14.1 In the Tidewater drop

The converter carried the control flows as first ... then ... successions and the call actions as action usages, and left TODO lines for the fork, the pin and the object flow: exactly the three things your snippet wrote by hand.

8.14.2 A common mistake

Successions use then, never an arrow.

Exercise 8.14: Join and finish

Add a join after store and publish, and a final step logBulletin that runs after the join. Route the bulletin out of ObserveCoast with a flow from publish.bulletin. Check.

8.15 Calculations, constraints and analysis cases

A calc def computes a value; a constraint def is a condition that must hold; an analysis def is a question asked of a subject, answered by calculation. In v1 these were constraint blocks, parametric diagrams and binding connectors, usually the least-maintained part of a Cameo model because the diagrams were so laborious. In v2 they are short.

What to notice:

  • return names a calc's result; the expression after = computes it.
  • A constraint def's body is a Boolean expression, here Tidewater's energy balance, the expression the converter could only carry as a TODO line.
  • constraint balance : EnergyBalance { in generation = ...; } is v1's binding connectors, written as assignments of the constraint's parameters to the part's attributes.
  • An analysis def frames the question; the kit does not evaluate it. Evaluating calcs and constraints needs an execution engine (the OMG pilot implementation, or a commercial tool), which Tidewater leaves for later (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).

8.15.1 In the Tidewater drop

The v1 constraint block's parameters came across; its expression did not, because v1 stored it as opaque English text. The TODO line quotes it, so the person writing the v2 constraint has it in front of them. Drop 5 changes that expression, and the TODO line changes with it: the drop-5 conflict in Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition.

Exercise 8.15: Use the calc

Write a calc usage inside PowerSystem that computes the daily load energy with DailyEnergy, and rewrite the constraint to compare against it. Check. Which form would a reviewer find easier to verify by hand?

8.16 Allocations

An allocation says a function is performed by a part. In v1 it was the allocate dependency, often drawn in swimlanes. In Tidewater the converter carried every v1 allocation, at the definition level.

What to notice:

  • Definition-level (allocate SampleSensors to SensorSuite;) says every sensor suite performs sampling. Usage-level (allocate sample to sensors; inside Station) says this station's sensors perform this station's sample step. Pick one level per project and say which in your conventions; mixing them is a classic source of the web.
  • The IDEF0 plates read allocations as mechanisms: the part that performs a function (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text).

8.16.1 In the Tidewater drop

All six v1 allocations, at the definition level, in their own package. This is what the IDEF0 plates read as mechanisms.

8.16.2 A common mistake

allocate S to P;

Exercise 8.16: Allocate the cycle

Allocate CheckQuality to a QualityControl part def and ArchiveObservations to an Archive part def, at the definition level. Check. Then decide: should PublishBulletin be allocated to the data center or to the publisher inside it? Write down why.

8.17 Metadata

Metadata labels elements with project-specific information: level tags, markings, procurement data, the recipe's tags. In v1 these were stereotypes from a profile, the source of most of Tidewater's converter TODOs (Section 6.3, Five ideas that cover most of SysML v2). In v2 a project defines a small set of metadata defs in one package and the pipeline checks their use.

What to notice:

  • @Name; inside a body applies metadata; @Name { attr = value; } applies it with values.
  • #Name in front of a declaration is the short prefix form of the same thing.
  • Level tags are checked. In a model repository, model.pl check verifies every part def carries the right @L tag for its depth in the part tree (Chapter 10, Vim for models, and practice lesson 10).
  • Keep the set small. A metadata def per real need, defined once in Conventions, is the v2 answer to v1's stereotype sprawl.

8.17.1 In the Tidewater drop

Every v1 stereotype application became a TODO line, most of them level stereotypes in Stations. Replacing them with @L metadata is the bulk of the structure port in sprints 2 to 5, and the reason the pipeline's TODO count falls the way it does.

8.17.2 A common mistake

The v1 guillemets:

#L3Station part def ShoreStation; or @L3Station; inside the body.

Exercise 8.17: A marking

Add a metadata def Marking with a level : String attribute and mark the Stations package @Marking { level = "U"; } (metadata can apply to a package too). Check. In a real program, who decides the value?

8.18 Use cases

A use case def describes what an actor achieves with the system. In v1, use case diagrams with actors and include/extend relationships. Tidewater's converter carried the use cases as skeletons and left the include as a TODO.

What to notice:

  • subject is the system the use case is about; actor declares who takes part.
  • include use case is v1's include relationship, written inside the including use case. This is exactly the hand fix for Tidewater's include TODO.

8.18.1 In the Tidewater drop

The use cases came across as skeletons, with the include as a TODO line inside ReviewObservations. One line of the snippet above closes it.

Exercise 8.18: Read a bulletin

Add ReadBulletin with a mariner actor and the network as subject. Should it include QueryArchive? Decide, then check.

8.19 Variants

A variation declares alternatives; a variant is one of them. In v1, variants were usually separate copies of blocks or whole branches of the model, a major source of v1 complexity. Tidewater's telemetry unit can use a cellular or a satellite modem.

What to notice:

  • variation part modem : Modem { variant ... } says the modem is one of the listed variants.
  • A configuration chooses by redefining the variation: the shore telemetry unit uses the cellular modem.
  • The grammar check accepts the choice; whether modem::cellular names a real variant is a semantic question for a full validator. This is advanced: Tidewater uses it in the later telemetry trade study (Chapter 46, Systems engineering work, not pipeline work), not in the first twelve weeks.
Exercise 8.19: A hybrid

Add a HybridModem variant and a buoyTelemetry usage that picks the satellite modem. Check. What would the trade study need from each variant to compare them?

8.20 Views and viewpoints

A viewpoint states a stakeholder's concern; a view exposes the part of the model that answers it. In v1 the diagrams were the views, drawn by hand and maintained by hand. In v2 a view is defined in the text, and drawings are generated from it (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text).

What to notice:

  • A viewpoint is a requirement on a view: the view def satisfys it.
  • The expose statement, expose network::**;, puts the network and everything inside it into the view.
  • Tidewater's drawings (part tree, trace, interconnection, packages, IDEF0) are generated by the kit's drawers, not yet from view usages. Defining views in the text is how a program records which views each stakeholder gets, which keeps view sprawl in check (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web).
Exercise 8.20: A test view

Write a TestViewpoint for the test organization ("which requirements each verification case covers") and a view def and usage that satisfy it. What would you expose?

8.21 Reading the official library

Every snippet above imported something from the standard library: ISQ, SI, VerificationCases, RequirementDerivation, ScalarValues. The library is plain SysML v2 text, and the kit carries the official release under tools/sysml/vendor. When you want to know whether a type exists, or what it is called, read the library rather than guessing:

Find where a value type is defined:

And the verdict a verification case returns:

What to notice:

  • Three folders. Kernel Libraries (the foundations: scalar values, base types), Systems Library (parts, ports, requirements, verification cases, states, views), Domain Libraries (quantities and units, analysis, metadata, requirement derivation).
  • ISQ re-exports the quantity packages. ISQ.sysml publicly imports ISQBase, ISQMechanics, ISQThermodynamics and the rest, which is why private import ISQ::*; was enough for PowerValue (mechanics) and EnergyValue (thermodynamics).
  • The library is the spec's own example. Reading how VerificationCases is written teaches more about verification cases than any summary. From Vim, :SysTags builds a tags file that includes the library, so Ctrl-] on a library name jumps to its definition (Chapter 10, Vim for models).
Exercise 8.21: Find three types

Find, in the library, the value types for a temperature, a length and an electric current, and the unit symbols for degrees Celsius and metres. Use them in a Thermometer part def with an attribute range and a default value. Check with the grammar checker and with lint.

8.22 Reading a converted file, top to bottom

You have written each construct once. Now read a whole file the converter wrote, the way Bob did on day one and the way every reviewer of a drop merge request has to. The stations file is the biggest in drop 1. Start with its head:

Read it in five passes, each looking for one thing. This is the habit that makes a 190-line file reviewable in ten minutes.

  1. The header line. "generated by xmi2sysml.pl ... TODO lines need a person". A file with this line came from the converter; on the vendor branch it is never edited by hand, and on develop the government's edits to it are the TODO closures and nothing else (Section 6.6, Where the converter stops).
  2. The imports. Stations imports DataCenter, and (you will find) DataCenter imports Stations. That pair is one of the two package dependency cycles in the v1 spider web (Chapter 2, The Cameo years); the cycle-break story in sprint 4 removes it.
  3. The definitions and their bodies. Each part def reads as a parts list, its ports, then its connections: the block's BDD and IBD in one place (Section 8.4, Parts: definitions, usages, multiplicity, Section 8.6, Ports and interfaces).
  4. The TODO lines. One per v1 construct the converter could not carry, each naming the v1 type and its xmi:id, so a person can find it in Cameo. In this file almost all of them are level stereotypes.
  5. The documentation. Every doc should say what the element is. Some say more than they should.

Look at the power system to see the last point:

Two documentation blocks. The first describes the element. The second is document prose pasted into Cameo during the port from documents: a reference to a section of a design document, a TBD from a trade study two years ago, and a process instruction. It is exactly the kind of clutter that made the v1 model a spider web, and it is now visible in a text diff instead of hidden in a property panel. It is also the prime's text: the government does not delete it from the converted file; it raises a discrepancy report, and the prime removes it in a later drop. If it were your own model, the decision would be yours: move the reference to a dependency, the TBD to an issue, and the process rule to docs/conventions/, and keep doc for what the element is.

Exercise 8.22: Review a file in five passes

Pick tw/datacenter/DataCenter.sysml and do the five passes. Write down: the packages it imports and which of them import it back, the number of TODO lines and their kinds, and any doc that says something other than what the element is. Which of your findings would go to the prime as a discrepancy report, and which are the government's to fix?

8.23 Putting it together: a model the pipeline accepts

The snippets above are each a package on its own. A real model is several packages in several files, under a model/ folder, with a sysml.conf that tells the kit's model tool where the trees start. Here is a small Tidewater in seven files that passes every check the pipeline's check stage runs.

Make the project and its conventions:

The structure, with level tags and one connection:

The behavior, the requirements with their satisfies, and the verification cases:

Now run the four checks the pipeline runs on every merge request: grammar, lint, the outline and level-tag check, and the trace. The first command moves into the project folder; stay there for the rest of the section:

And see the part tree you wrote, drawn as text and as a picture:

Tip: The outline rule bit Bob too

The first time Bob built this model, model.pl check reported one violation: the Verification package had a single member. The kit's outline rule wants two to nine children under every parent, the same rule of thumb a document outline follows (a section with one subsection is a sign the outline is wrong). Bob added the second verification case, which the model needed anyway. When the rule fires, ask what the outline is telling you before you reach for a waiver.

Exercise 8.23: Grow the mini model

Add the moored buoy's state machine from Section 8.13, States to Network.sysml (with exhibit state on MooredBuoy), add a third requirement satisfied by Archive and a verification case for it, and rerun all four checks. Then break the trace on purpose: remove the new verification case and run model.pl trace again. What does it report, and what would the pipeline's trace job do on a merge request?

The workbook's constructs are not an abstract syllabus. Every converter TODO line in Tidewater's drop 1 is one of them, waiting to be written. Go back up to the folder where you converted the drop, and count the TODO lines by kind:

And total them:

That number is the port's starting burn-down: the pipeline's todo job counts the same lines on every change (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). Here is where each kind is taught:

Read the table the way Jim read it at the sprint 1 estimate: two thirds of the port is one mechanical construct (level tags), which goes fast once one person has done it twice; the rest is a handful of real modeling problems, each a story of its own. Exercise 8.24: Your first TODO

Open tw/network/Network.sysml in Vim, find the level-tag TODO on ObservationNetwork with /\/\/ TODO, and write down the one line that replaces it and the import the package needs. (Practice lesson 10 has you do exactly this and checks it.)

8.25 What the workbook leaves out

The checks you ran are real, and they are what the pipeline runs, but be clear about what they prove:

  • The grammar checker proves the text is well formed SysML v2, against the official grammar.
  • model.pl lint resolves names and imports, finds duplicates and checks a set of structural rules.
  • model.pl check applies the outline rule and the level tags.
  • None of them evaluates constraints, checks that a redefinition is type-compatible in every case, or proves the model means what you intended. Full semantic validation needs the OMG pilot implementation (model.pl validate, with Java) or a commercial tool; meaning needs a reviewer (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).

The workbook also left out constructs Tidewater does not use yet: individuals and snapshots, occurrences and messages in detail, trade studies with full analysis cases, and the textual notation for diagrams. The library and the specification's examples, under tools/sysml/vendor/sysml-v2-release/examples, show all of them.

8.26 Applying this to your project

  • Give everyone the workbook time. Two sessions per person, as learning stories with points, in the first three weeks. A team that never typed a part def will not review one well.
  • Keep the snippets. The folder you worked in is a personal phrasebook. Copy from it; it is faster than the specification.
  • Check everything twice. Grammar for shape, lint for names, in Vim with :make before you commit and in the pipeline after.
  • Start from your converted model. The best exercises are your own converter TODO lines: each one is a construct from this workbook waiting to be written (Section 6.6, Where the converter stops).
  • Write your conventions down. Which level of allocation, which metadata, which import style: one page in docs/conventions/, agreed once, checked by the pipeline where it can be.

Part II: Week zero

Part I ended on Friday 2 October 2026 with a signed scorecard, a one-page plan, an email that promised honesty, and a zip file from the prime contractor that nobody had opened yet. Part II is everything that has to be true before the first sprint can start on Monday, and everything a reader needs to know to follow the twelve weeks in Part III with a terminal open.

It is the part you type along with. Jim, Bob and Tom did not learn these things in a classroom. They learned them in the gaps of real work: Tom reading about protected branches at the kitchen table on a Saturday, Bob trying git commands in a throwaway folder on a Tuesday afternoon until the words "merge conflict" stopped being frightening, Jim rewriting the Definition of Done three times because the first two versions were documents nobody would read. The chapters here put those lessons in the order a newcomer needs them, which is not the order the team learned them.

Survival kit

What you have

a Windows laptop with Git for Windows and Vim; the agile kit checked out; a SysML v1 model you exported from Cameo (or, for this book, the Tidewater drops); years of systems engineering judgment.

What you need by the end of Part II: a working terminal and a set of commands you trust; enough git to make a branch, commit, push and resolve a conflict; Vim set up to edit and check SysML v2 text; the operating model (who does what, how big each piece of work may be, when the team meets); a GitLab project configured from a file; the DevSecOps tools worth turning on; a pipeline you can read job by job; and the daily rhythm of stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo and retrospective.

The chapters build on each other:

  • Chapter 13, The operating model describes how the work is organized: the project, tomes, epics, stories and tasks, with the size rule for each; the two-week cadence; who decides what. It comes first because every later chapter refers to it, and because it is the part a systems engineer will find most familiar. It is a work breakdown structure and a schedule, with a few new words.
  • Chapter 9, The survival kit sets up the laptop. It is written for someone who has never opened a terminal on purpose.
  • Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers teaches version control from zero in a practice repository, with every command shown and its real output, and each idea tied to the configuration management practice it replaces.
  • Chapter 10, Vim for models turns the editor you already know into a model workbench: syntax, checks, jump lists, tags, merge conflicts and Markdown for GitLab.
  • Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab, Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep, Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero, Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job, Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board and Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro set up the shared platform, explain continuous integration, walk through the pipeline file, and establish the daily rhythm.
Tip: If you are short of time

Read Chapter 13, The operating model and Chapter 9, The survival kit in full. Work through Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers with your hands on the keyboard; it is the chapter people most regret skipping. Skim Chapter 10, Vim for models and come back to each section when Part III first needs it.

A word about pace. None of this is hard, but much of it is new at once, and new things in bulk feel hard. The team found that an hour a day of deliberate practice in week zero was worth more than a full day of reading. Bob's rule, written on a sticky note on the monitor, was: type it, break it, fix it, then read about it. The exercises at the end of each chapter are built on that rule.

9 The survival kit

From what you know

You know

your laptop, Windows, the shared drive, and Vim.

Here it is called

the survival kit: Git Bash, Perl, the kit and the doctor check.

What is new

a terminal you type commands into, and a check that tells you exactly what is missing.

Survival kit

What you have

a government Windows 11 laptop with Git for Windows and Vim on it (both on the approved software list); a network account; a login to the enterprise GitLab server that the administrators created last week; and the agile kit, which Tom copied from the enterprise GitLab.

What you need

to open a terminal and not be afraid of it; about fifteen commands you can type without looking them up; git configured with your name; a key or token so GitLab knows who you are; Vim set up with the kit; and a list of what to do when something goes wrong. Budget half a day. The team spent most of Monday morning of sprint 1 on this, together, and it was the best half day of the sprint.

9.1 Monday, 08:00

Tom arrived early on the first day of sprint 1 with a printed page. It was a checklist, of course; Tom had run the program's configuration management database for ten years and trusted checklists the way other people trust coffee. At the top it said Survival kit: every box ticked before stand-up. There were nineteen boxes.

Bob read it over Tom's shoulder. "What's a terminal?"

"The black window," Tom said. "Git Bash. It came with Git for Windows. You've had it on your laptop for two years."

"I've never opened it."

"Neither had I, until Saturday."

That exchange is the starting point of this chapter. If you have opened a terminal and typed commands into it, you can skim the next three sections. If you have not, read them slowly and type everything. The terminal is the one new tool in this book you cannot avoid. Everything else (git, GitLab, the converters, the checks) is driven from it, and once it stops being strange, everything else gets much easier.

9.2 What is on the laptop

Every tool the team used in the twelve weeks was either already on the government laptop or arrived as plain files inside the kit. Nothing needed an administrator to install. That mattered: an installation request would have taken two weeks and an ISSM review, and the team had neither.

On Tom's laptop in October 2026 the versions were:

Your versions will differ. Anything from the last few years works; the kit is written to run on old and new versions alike.

Note: Why Perl?

The kit's tools are Perl scripts because Perl ships inside Git for Windows, which is already approved almost everywhere. That one fact removed an entire category of approval from the team's critical path. You will not write Perl in this book. You will run Perl scripts, the way you run any program: perl followed by the script's name and its arguments.

9.3 The terminal

A terminal is a window where you type instructions to the computer, one line at a time, and it types back. The program that reads your line and carries it out is called the shell; in Git Bash the shell is called bash. The words "terminal," "shell," "command line" and "Git Bash" are used almost interchangeably, including in this book.

A systems engineering analogy: a terminal is a procedure executed step by step, where each step is one line, you can see exactly what happened after every step, and the whole record stays on the screen. A graphical tool hides the steps behind clicks. The terminal shows them. That is why everything in DevSecOps is driven from it: a sequence of typed commands can be written down, reviewed, repeated exactly and, eventually, run by a machine.

To open Git Bash: Start menu, type "Git Bash", press Enter. You see something like this:

That is the prompt. It tells you who you are (bob), which computer you are on (TWLAPTOP03), and which folder you are in (~, which means your home folder). The $ means "ready for a command." In this book, the $ at the start of a line means "type what follows"; do not type the $ itself.

Type pwd and press Enter:

pwd means print working directory: which folder you are in. Every command runs "in" a folder, and many commands act on files relative to it.

A command line has three kinds of parts:

  • ls is the command: the program to run.
  • -l is an option: it changes how the command behaves. Options start with - (one letter) or -- (a word): -l and --report are both options.
  • drop1 is an argument: what the command acts on, here a folder.

Five keys make the terminal pleasant:

Table 9.2. Five keys that make the terminal pleasant
KeyWhat it does
Up arrowbrings back the previous command, to run it again or edit it
Tabcompletes a file or folder name: type dr then Tab and it becomes drop1/
Ctrl-Cstops the running command (it does not copy, in a terminal)
Shift-Insert, or right-click then Pastepastes
qleaves a screen that is showing a long file or help page (the "pager")
Warning: Ctrl-C does not copy

In Windows, Ctrl-C copies. In a terminal, Ctrl-C interrupts whatever is running. To copy text from Git Bash, select it with the mouse (it is copied as soon as you release the button); to paste, use Shift-Insert or right-click. This catches everyone once. When it caught Jim, it stopped a long-running conversion halfway, which was harmless; the command was simply run again.

9.4 Files, folders and paths

A path is the address of a file or folder. Git Bash writes paths with forward slashes, the way Unix computers do, and shows the Windows drive C: as /c:

Table 9.3. The same folder in Windows and in Git Bash
Windows writesGit Bash writes
C:\Users\bob\projects\agile/c/Users/bob/projects/agile
C:\Users\bob (your home folder)~ or /c/Users/bob

A path that starts with / or ~ is absolute: it means the same place wherever you are. A path that does not is relative: it is relative to the folder you are in. drop1/MANIFEST.txt means "the file MANIFEST.txt in the folder drop1 inside the folder I am in now." Two special names help: . is the current folder and .. is the folder above it.

Three habits save trouble:

  • Avoid spaces in names you create. drop1 and prime-drop-v1.0 are easy to type; Prime Drop v1.0 must be quoted every time ("Prime Drop v1.0"), and forgetting the quotes produces confusing errors. The kit and GitLab handle spaces correctly; your fingers will not.
  • Names starting with a dot are hidden. .git, .vimrc and .gitlab-ci.yml are ordinary files and folders that ls does not show unless you ask with ls -a. Many of the most important files in this book start with a dot.
  • Line endings differ. Windows ends each line of a text file with two invisible characters (carriage return and line feed, written CRLF); Unix and the kit use one (LF). Most tools cope with both, but not all. The prime's manifest files arrive with Windows line endings; the command file tells you which you have:

Section 9.7, Setting up git shows the one git setting that stops line endings from changing silently.

9.5 The commands you need

Here are the commands the team used every week, each with a real example on the first prime drop. To follow along, create the drop the way the book does throughout, by asking the kit's generator for it (the real prime would deliver a zip file; the result is the same four files):

The kit lives in the folder ~/projects/agile (Section 9.6, Getting the kit shows how to get it). Commands in this book call that folder $KIT, the same name the pipeline uses for it, so tell the shell once where it is, and make a folder to practise in:

(export sets a variable, a name the shell replaces with its value wherever you write $KIT. It lasts until the window closes; Section 9.10, Shell shortcuts puts it in ~/.bashrc so every new window knows it.) Then ask for the drop and convert it:

The first line writes the four files the prime would deliver; the second runs the converter, which turns the v1 model into SysML v2 text in a folder of its own. Part I showed what it produces (Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers). Now the commands.

9.5.1 Where am I, and what is here: pwd, ls, cd

ls -l shows the long form: permissions, owner, size in bytes, date and name. The XMI file is 122,711 bytes, about 120 KB. cd FOLDER moves into a folder; cd .. moves up one; cd alone goes home; cd - goes back to where you were.

9.5.2 Make, copy, move and remove: mkdir, cp, mv, rm

mkdir -p makes a folder, including any missing folders above it. cp copies; cp -r copies a folder and everything in it. mv moves or renames. rm removes a file; rm -r removes a folder and everything in it.

Warning: rm has no recycle bin

A file removed with rm is gone. There is no undo and no recycle bin. Before you type rm -r, type ls with the same path and read what it would remove. Inside a git repository you are much safer, because anything that was committed can be brought back (Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers); that is one of the first comforts of version control.

9.5.3 Read a file: cat, less, head, tail

The manifest says who built the drop (the prime's Jenkins server, build 137), from which commit of the prime's own repository, with which tools, and how it was delivered: the provenance a receiver checks before trusting the files (Section 45.9, The prime's Jenkins: a delivery interface explains the prime's side). cat prints a whole file; use it for short files. less FILE shows a long file one screen at a time: Space for the next page, b for back, /word to search, q to quit. head -N and tail -N show the first or last N lines.

9.5.4 Search: grep

grep finds lines that contain a piece of text. It is the command the team used more than any other, because a model in text can be searched like any other text:

-n prints line numbers, -c counts matching lines instead of printing them, -r searches every file in a folder and the folders below it, and -i ignores upper and lower case. The quotes around "TODO uml:StateMachine" keep the two words together as one piece of text; without them, grep would look for TODO in a file called uml:StateMachine, fail, and print a confusing error. When in doubt, quote.

Compare the first line with what Bob used to do in the document era to find one requirement's text in the delivered CSV: open Excel, wait, use Find, wait. It is not that grep is faster (although it is); it is that the grep line can be written down, sent to someone else, and run again next quarter on the next drop, unchanged.

9.5.5 Find files and count lines: find, wc

find FOLDER -name 'PATTERN' lists files whose names match; * in a pattern means "anything," and the quotes stop the shell from expanding it early. wc -l counts lines.

The second line is worth stopping on. It counts every line in the converted model that contains // TODO, which is the converter's mark for "I could not carry this; a person must." That number, 52, is the team's conversion debt for drop 1, the primary progress measure on the scorecard (Section 3.6, Defining measurable progress). It was computed with one line of shell, and from sprint 2 on the pipeline computes it the same way on every change.

9.5.6 Pipes and redirection: | and >

Two symbols let commands work together. The pipe, |, sends one command's output into the next command as its input: find ... | wc -l means "list the files, then count the lines of that list." Redirection, >, sends a command's output into a file instead of the screen:

> replaces the file if it exists; >> adds to the end of it. A line of commands joined by pipes is called a pipeline in the shell. It is the same idea, on a small scale, as the GitLab pipeline in Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job: small steps, each doing one thing, connected so that the output of one is the input of the next.

9.5.7 Check a delivery: sha256sum

A checksum is a short fingerprint computed from a file's exact contents. Change one byte of the file and the fingerprint changes completely. The prime's manifest lists a SHA-256 checksum (the kind used throughout the government) for each delivered file, so the receiver can prove that what arrived is exactly what was sent:

The first command computes the fingerprint of one file; compare it by eye with the manifest's first line. The second does the comparison for you: grep picks the three checksum lines out of the manifest, and sha256sum -c checks each file against its listed checksum. In the document era, receipt inspection of a CDRL delivery was a signature on a transmittal form. This is receipt inspection that actually inspects. It is the first task of the first story Jim did in sprint 1 (Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in).

Note: On Linux, strip the carriage returns

Git for Windows' sha256sum reads the manifest's Windows line endings without complaint. On a Linux machine (or in WSL) the same command fails with No such file or directory for each file, because the invisible carriage return becomes part of the file name. Remove the carriage returns and the leading spaces first:

Use this form in anything that may run on Linux, such as a pipeline job (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job); it works everywhere.

9.6 Getting the kit

The agile kit is the folder of tools this book uses. On Tidewater, Tom cloned it from the enterprise GitLab, where the program keeps an approved copy:

(git clone copies a repository from GitLab to your laptop; Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers explains it.) Most teams get the kit the other way, as the slim MBSE zip that START-MBSE.md describes: the tools, templates, Vim files and practice lessons this book uses, without the kit's own development files. Unzip it into C:\Users\you\projects and it makes the same folder, ~/projects/agile. The book works with either form, and always calls that folder $KIT.

Check that it works on your machine. The kit's doctor checks Perl, git and Vim, and runs a small self-test: two of the kit's own test suites, and the converter and grammar checker on the Tidewater sample drop:

"All 223 passed" is a better answer to "does the tool work here?" than any installation guide: the checks ran on this laptop, with this Perl. The last line converted a sample drop and checked every file it wrote against the SysML v2 grammar. If a self-test line fails, stop and find out why before going further; Section 9.12, When something goes wrong lists the usual causes. The team found one laptop with an old Git for Windows this way, on day one rather than in the middle of a sprint.

Tip: Full kit only: run the whole test set once

If you cloned the full kit rather than the slim zip, run every test suite once on the first day: perl "$KIT/tests/run.pl". It takes a few minutes and prints one line per suite. The slim zip carries only the suites doctor runs.

Run doctor again without the grep once the rest of this chapter is done: it checks the whole laptop. It changes nothing; every line is PASS, WARN or FAIL, and every problem comes with the exact command that fixes it:

It checks Perl and the modules the kit uses, git and the settings below, Vim and the kit's Vim setup, curl, a short self-test of the converters, your SSH key, and whether GitLab answers. Run it on every laptop in week zero, and again whenever something odd happens.

9.7 Setting up git

Git records who made every change. Before your first change, tell it who you are, and set four other options the team agreed on. These settings are global: they apply to every repository on your laptop, and you set them once.

Table 9.5. The five git settings, and why
SettingWhy
user.name, user.emailEvery commit records them. Use your real name and your work email, the same one as your GitLab account, so GitLab links your commits to you.
init.defaultBranch mainNew repositories start with a branch called main, matching GitLab's default. Older git versions call it master, which causes confusion when the two meet.
core.editor vimWhen git needs you to write a message (a commit message, a merge message), it opens Vim.
core.autocrlf falseGit does not change line endings when files go in or out. The kit's files use LF; letting git rewrite them changes checksums and can make a baseline impossible to reproduce.
Warning: core.autocrlf is not optional on Tidewater

Git for Windows' installer offers to convert line endings automatically, and many laptops have it turned on. With it on, a file's bytes on the laptop differ from its bytes in the repository. Most of the time nobody notices. Then a baseline's checksum does not match on rebuild, and it takes a day to find out why. Tom found this on one of the three laptops in week zero. Set it to false, and leave line endings to the repository's own .gitattributes file, which the kit's templates provide.

9.8 Proving who you are to GitLab: SSH keys and tokens

When your laptop sends changes to GitLab (a push) or fetches them (a pull or clone), GitLab has to know who you are. There are two ways, and your enterprise administrators decide which you may use.

9.8.1 An SSH key

An SSH key is a pair of files: a private key, which stays on your laptop and is never shown to anyone, and a public key, which you give to GitLab. Anything signed by the private key can be checked with the public one. The analogy is a signature card on file at a bank: the bank holds a sample of your signature, and you hold the pen.

Make a key pair with one command (the -C text is just a label so you can recognize the key later):

Press Enter to accept the file name. When asked for a passphrase, type one: it protects the private key if the laptop is lost. Then print the public key and copy it:

It is one line starting ssh-ed25519 AAAA.... In GitLab's web page, open your avatar (top left), then Preferences, then SSH Keys, paste the line into the Key box, set an expiry date, and choose Add key. Test it:

GitLab answers Welcome to GitLab, @bob! and the connection closes. That is all it should do. (This is the one step in the chapter that needs your real GitLab server: the practice lessons and every other example here work offline.)

9.8.2 A personal access token

Some organizations block SSH and allow only HTTPS (the protocol web pages use). Then you prove your identity with a personal access token, a long random password created in GitLab for one purpose, with an expiry date. In GitLab: avatar, Preferences, Access tokens, Add new token. Give it a name ("Bob's laptop"), an expiry date (the enterprise maximum, often 90 days), and only the scopes (permissions) it needs: read_repository and write_repository for git. The kit's GitLab client (gitlab.pl, Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab) also needs api.

The first time git asks for a password over HTTPS, give your GitLab user name and paste the token as the password. Git for Windows includes a credential manager that stores it in Windows' own protected store, so you are not asked again until it expires.

Warning: Never put a token or a private key in a file you might commit

A token is a password. A private key is a password. Never paste either into a text file, a script, a Vim buffer you might save, a chat or an email. If one leaks, revoke it in GitLab at once (the same page that created it) and make a new one. The pipeline's secret detection job (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep) looks for exactly this mistake in every change, and the kit's token handling reads tokens from an environment variable, never from a file. The team's rule, from the ISSM's first review: a secret that has been typed into anything other than its one proper place is a secret that has leaked.

9.9 Setting up Vim

You already use Vim. The kit adds file types, syntax colors, commands and help for the files this book uses: SysML v2 models, stand-up notes, the journal, chat pastes. Turn it on by adding one line to your Vim settings file.

Open your Vim settings file (in Git Bash it is ~/.vimrc; create it if it does not exist):

and add these lines (adjust the path if you put the kit somewhere else):

Save and quit (:wq), then start Vim again. Check that it worked, in Vim:

The kit's help opens: the same text as perl agile.pl help, in Vim's own help format, with links you follow with Ctrl-] and come back from with Ctrl-T. Close it with :q. Now open a converted model file and check its type:

Vim answers filetype=sysml. The kit's SysML settings are active: four-space indentation, // comments, folding by braces, and the :Sys commands and \m keys that Chapter 10, Vim for models teaches. Type :Sys and press Tab to see the commands cycle through: :SysLint, :SysCheck, :SysSyntax, :SysTrace and the others.

9.10 Shell shortcuts

Typing perl ~/projects/agile/bin/daily.pl every morning gets old. An alias is a short name for a longer command. Add these lines to ~/.bashrc (Git Bash reads it every time it starts):

Close Git Bash and open it again: echo $KIT prints the kit's folder, and daily status now means the long form. The book always shows the long form, so you can see what is being run; use the short form in your own work.

9.11 GitLab in the browser

Most of the team's day happens in the terminal and in Vim, but GitLab's web pages are where the shared work is seen: issues, merge requests, pipelines, the board, the wiki. Log in to your organization's GitLab (for Tidewater, https://gitlab.example.com) with your network account.

On a project's page, the left sidebar holds everything this book uses. GitLab moves its menus around between versions, so look for the words rather than a position:

9.14 Applying this to your project

Copy: the checklist, the five git settings, the rule about secrets, and the habit of proving a tool works by running its own tests on your machine.

Adapt: the tool list to what your organization has approved. The essential capabilities are a terminal, git, a scripting runtime for the converters and checks, an editor you are fluent in, and a browser. If your laptops have Python approved and not Perl, the ideas in this book carry over; the commands do not.

Decide locally, before sprint 1: SSH or HTTPS tokens (ask your GitLab administrators and your ISSM together, once); where the approved copy of your tools lives and who updates it; and who on the team is the person others ask when the terminal does something strange. On Tidewater it was Tom, by default; name yours on purpose.

9.15 Exercises

Exercise 9.1: Find a requirement

Using only grep on drop 1's tidewater.csv, find every requirement whose verification method is Inspection. How many are there? Then find which converted .sysml file mentions TW-SYS-012.

Exercise 9.2: Count the debt by package

Using grep -c (which counts per file when given several files), print the number of // TODO lines in each converted file of drop 1. Which package holds most of the conversion debt? Why might that be? (Hint: look at what kind of TODO most of them are.)

Exercise 9.3: Break a checksum

Copy drop 1 to a new folder, change one character in the copy of tidewater.csv with Vim, and run the manifest check again. What does sha256sum -c print? What would you do if this happened to a real delivery?

Exercise 9.4: Make each mistake on purpose

Make three of the mistakes in Section 9.12, When something goes wrong deliberately (a misspelled command, a wrong path, a git command outside a repository) and read each error message aloud. The goal is to make the messages familiar while nothing is at stake.

10 Vim for models

From what you know

You know

Vim: opening files, searching, substituting and saving.

Here it is called

Vim for models: the kit's SysML keys, :make and the quickfix list.

What is new

the editor runs the model checks and jumps you to each error.

Survival kit

What you have

years of Vim. You can move, search, change, yank and put without thinking; you have a .vimrc with a few lines you copied from someone in 2009; and the kit is now sourced from it (Section 9.9, Setting up Vim).

What you need

to read a converted model comfortably; to turn the converter's TODO lines into a jump list and close them one by one; to run the model checks from inside Vim and land on each error; to jump to any definition or DOORS id by name; to resolve a merge conflict without leaving the editor; and to write commit messages, issue descriptions and merge request descriptions in Vim instead of a web text box.

10.1 The one thing they brought

When the directive arrived, the team's inventory of relevant skills was short. None of the three had written code. None had used git. But all three had used Vim for years, for the most unglamorous reasons: Jim to clean up DOORS exports before pasting them into Excel, Bob to fix the XML of a Cameo export that would not import, Tom to edit the CM database's load files with macros nobody else understood. In the Cameo years, Vim was the tool they used when the real tools failed.

The parachute drop turned that around. In the new way the model is text, and the best tool any of them had for text was already in their hands. Bob put it this way at the end of sprint 2: "For three years the model was the one thing I couldn't edit in Vim. Now it's the only thing I edit in Vim."

This chapter is not a Vim tutorial. It assumes you can already edit text in Vim and shows what the kit adds, and which ordinary Vim features matter most for model work. Every command shown was run against the converted Tidewater drop.

10.2 What the kit adds

Sourcing the kit's vim/scrum.vim from your .vimrc (Section 9.9, Setting up Vim) does four things:

  • File types. Files ending .sysml become type sysml; stand-up notes, the journal, pasted chat, drill sheets and IDEF0 models get their own types too. Each type has syntax colors and settings.
  • Commands and keys. :Sys... commands and \m keys in SysML buffers; :S... commands and \s keys for the stand-up and the journal (Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board); :Idef... for IDEF0 models.
  • A compiler. :make in a SysML buffer runs the kit's model checks and loads every error into Vim's quickfix list.
  • Help. :help agile and every topic under it, including :help agile-vim-sysml for this chapter's commands.

In a SysML buffer the kit sets these options (you can see each with :set OPTION?):

Table 10.1. What the kit sets in a SysML buffer
OptionValueEffect
filetypesysmlsyntax colors for keywords, names, strings, comments
shiftwidth, expandtab4, onindentation is four spaces, never tabs (the converter's style)
commentstring, comments// %sgq and comment formatting know SysML comments

foldmethodsyntaxevery { ... } block can be folded
tags./tags;,tagsCtrl-] finds the project's tags file from any subfolder
makeprgthe kit's model.pl for this project:make lint, :make check run the model checks

The leader key is backslash unless you have changed it, so \ml means backslash, then m, then l, typed in normal mode. (Strictly, the SysML keys use the local leader, which is also backslash by default.)

10.3 Reading a model

A converted model is a folder of files, one per package. Open them all at once from the model's top folder:

(If you no longer have the converted drop from Section 9.5, The commands you need, make it again in ~/w2s first:)

Then move around with commands you mostly know:

Table 10.2. Reading a converted model
ToType

Folding is the one the team found most useful. Stations.sysml is 180 lines; zM folds it to the list of its definitions, one line each, which reads like a block definition diagram's list of blocks. Open the one you care about with zo. Bob's habit, from the first week: open a file, zM, read the outline, then zo into the part that matters.

10.4 The TODO list as a jump list

Vim's quickfix list is a list of positions in files (file, line, column, message) that Vim can step through, opening each file at the right line. Compilers fill it with errors; :vimgrep fills it with search results. For model work it is the most valuable feature Vim has, because it turns any list of places into an action-item list where every item opens itself.

The converter marks everything it could not carry with a // TODO comment. Make them a jump list:

:vimgrep /PATTERN/ FILES searches every file and fills the quickfix list; ** means "this folder and every folder below it." The pattern is // TODO with each slash escaped as \/, because / ends a Vim pattern. :copen opens the list in a window at the bottom. On drop 1 it holds 52 entries, the conversion debt.

Warning: Search for "// TODO", not "TODO"

:vimgrep /TODO/ finds 65 lines, not 52. Every converted file starts with a header comment ("review before committing; TODO lines need a person") that contains the word TODO but is not a TODO line. The pipeline's count uses the same // TODO pattern as this chapter. If your count and the pipeline's disagree, check the pattern first.

Now work through the list:

Table 10.3. Moving through the quickfix list
ToType
open the entry under the cursor in the listEnter
go to the next / previous entry:cnext / :cprev (:cn / :cp)
go to the first / last:cfirst / :clast
close / reopen the list window:cclose / :copen
see older lists (after running another search or check):colder / :cnewer

Map :cnext to a key you like. Bob used ]q and [q (from a plugin Bob already had), Tom mapped F8. The kit leaves the choice to you.

10.5 Closing a TODO line: a worked edit

Thirty-six of drop 1's 52 TODO lines are the same kind: a stereotype from the v1 project profile (Tidewater_Profile:L3Station and its siblings) that the converter could not carry, because SysML v2 has no stereotypes. In SysML v2 the equivalent is metadata (Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers): a metadata def declared once, applied to an element with @. The government's plan was to declare the six level tags once, in a package of its own in the lowest layer of the model, model/library/conventions/, and to replace each TODO line with the matching tag.

To follow along, make a model repository the way week zero does (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab): the kit's scaffold, with Tidewater's level names, then drop 1 converted into it with the layout map that puts each package in its layer (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where):

First, the declarations. They live in model/library/conventions/Conventions.sysml, which the scaffold writes from the level names it was given; on Tidewater Bob wrote the first version by hand in Vim, and it reads:

Then each TODO line. One at a time, in the Network package, the line

becomes

That is cc and typing, for one line. For thirty-six lines, use a substitution. In the file you are editing:

Read it in pieces: %s substitutes on every line of the file; the pattern matches the TODO comment, capturing the level name (L followed by a digit and more word characters) inside \( and \); .*$ swallows the rest of the line; the replacement is @, the captured name (\1) and a semicolon. The indentation in front of the comment is not part of the match, so it stays. Add c at the end (.../@\1;/c) to confirm each change one by one; the team always did, the first time in each file.

In the repository just made, the whole edit for the Network package, including the import line described next, is four Vim commands (practice lesson 10, perl $KIT/agile.pl practice 10, walks through the same edit with a checker that tells you when it is right):

Finally the package must be able to see the new definitions. Add one import line at the top of the package, next to the converter's imports:

Check the result with the grammar checker, from Vim (next section) or the terminal:

One TODO line closed is one fewer in the pipeline's count. Two weeks of such edits, in small merge requests, is how the structural TODOs of drop 1 were closed in sprints 2 to 5.

Warning: A misspelled tag is not caught by lint

While testing this chapter's edit, a deliberately misspelled tag (@L1Netwrk;) passed both the grammar check and the kit's lint. The grammar check checks form, not names, and lint resolves the types of parts and attributes but not metadata names. The outline check (\mk, Section 10.6, Checking from Vim) does compare level tags with the part tree, but only tags it recognizes, so it reported nothing either. Use the substitution (which copies the name from the converter's own TODO line, so it cannot be misspelled), or Ctrl-N completion, rather than typing tag names. A wrongly placed tag is caught: putting @L2Segment; on ObservationNetwork makes the outline check report ObservationNetwork: tagged L2, first reached at L1.

10.6 Checking from Vim

The kit runs the same checks the pipeline runs (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job), from inside Vim, with every finding loaded into the quickfix list. Run them before you commit; then the pipeline never tells you anything you did not already know.

Table 10.4. Model checks from Vim
KeyCommandChecksScope
\mx:SysSyntaxthe official SysML v2 grammar (sysml.pl check)this file
\ml:SysLintgrammar, unresolved types, imports, duplicates (model.pl lint)the whole model
\mk:SysCheckthe outline rule (2 to 9 children per parent) and level tags (model.pl check)the whole model
\mg:SysGatethe security gate: markings, trust zones, threats (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep)the whole model
\mv:SysValidatea full compile with the SysML v2 Pilot implementation, if Java is installedthe whole model

Each saves the file first, runs the check, and opens the quickfix window if there are findings. :make lint and :make check do the same as \ml and \mk.

Here is a real finding. Change the type of the shore station's mast from Mast to Mastt (a typo) and press \ml. Lint prints:

and the quickfix list holds one entry: model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml:47:21, error, unresolved type 'Mastt'. Enter on it puts the cursor on the M of Mastt, line 47, column 21. Fix it, press \ml again, and the list is empty. The last line, elements=148 errors=0 warnings=0, is the line the pipeline's lint job reads; anything other than zero errors and zero warnings fails the job.

A syntax error (here a missing semicolon after part mast : Mast) looks like this from \mx:

Notice that the error is reported on line 48, the line after the mistake: the parser only discovers the semicolon is missing when it meets the closing brace. Grammar errors often point just past the real problem. Look one line up.

The outline check, \mk, reports something different: not errors in what is written, but shape. On the raw drop 1 conversion it reports eighteen violations, such as 25 package Stations: members (a package with 25 direct members, more than the nine the outline rule allows) and 1 part def Battery: parts (a definition with only one part). Each violation goes into the quickfix list at the line of the part def or package it is about (a folder's at the first line of its first file), so :cnext walks the shape findings the same way it walks errors. These are not mistakes. They are the spider web of Chapter 2, The Cameo years measured in another way, and closing them is part of the port's later stories (Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself).

10.7 Tags: jumping by name and by DOORS id

A tags file is an index of where every name is defined. With one, Ctrl-] on any name jumps to its definition in whichever file holds it, and Ctrl-T jumps back. You may have used tags for code; the kit builds them for models.

Press \mt (:SysTags) in any SysML buffer:

Now put the cursor on ObservingStation anywhere and press Ctrl-]; Vim opens model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml at the definition. Press Ctrl-T to come back. The tags file also indexes requirements by their DOORS identifier, so Ctrl-] on TW-SYS-006, in a requirement, a satisfy line, an issue description you are editing in Vim or a pasted chat, opens the requirement. You can also type the jump directly:

(Because the kit adds - to iskeyword, the whole id is one word for Ctrl-] and *.)

Rebuild the tags with \mt after a merge brings in new definitions. The file is called tags at the top of the project; list it in the model repository's .gitignore, since everyone builds their own.

10.8 Seeing the model

Text is the source, but people also need to see the structure. The kit can show it without leaving Vim:

Table 10.5. Seeing the model from Vim

\mb:SysVerbsthe function (action) tree, in a split
\mr:SysTraceregenerates the trace matrix and opens docs/Traceability.md
\md:SysDocsregenerates everything in docs/
