The part tree of the converted drop 1, from \mn (the first lines):

This needs a sysml.conf file at the project's top that names the roots of the trees (noun_root = ObservationNetwork, verb_root = ObserveCoast); the model repository has one from the first commit (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab).

\mW starts the live viewer, a separate window (built with the Tcl/Tk toolkit that ships in Git for Windows) that draws the part tree, trace, internal block diagram or package diagram and redraws whenever you save. Put it on the second monitor. \mf on a name highlights that element in the drawing; clicking an element in the drawing and pressing \mo in Vim opens the file at its line. It is the closest thing to Cameo's diagrams the new way has, with the difference that the drawing is always generated from the text and never edited.

Note: The trace from Vim and the trace in the pipeline

\mr runs the kit's model-side trace, which reads only the model. On drop 1 it reports six requirements "not satisfied," and only one of them, TW-SYS-012, really is: it treats a requirement satisfied by a port or an attribute (TW-SYS-008, satisfied by ObservingStation.obsOut, and likewise TW-SYS-009, TW-SYS-010, TW-SYS-014 and TW-SEG-003) as unsatisfied. The pipeline's trace job uses the DOORS export as well and counts it correctly. Use \mr for a quick look while editing, and the pipeline's report as the number of record.

10.9 Merge conflicts in Vim

This section belongs with git, which the next chapters teach: Section 12.11, Merge conflicts explains what a merge conflict is and where one comes from. If you are reading in order, skim it now and come back after Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers; if you already know git, here is how to resolve a conflict quickly in Vim.

First, one setting. Tell git to show the common ancestor in conflicts as well as the two sides:

With it, the vendor-branch conflict that Section 12.19, The vendor branch walks through looks like this:

The middle section, between ||||||| and =======, is the line as it was before either side changed it. Now the conflict explains itself: the team replaced the L3 TODO with a tag; the prime changed the level from L3 to L2. The right resolution is the team's form with the prime's level, @L2Segment;. Without the middle section you would have to work that out from the history. For vendor merges, where every conflict is "our edit versus their change," the team found the ancestor indispensable.

Resolving in plain Vim. Open the file and find the markers:

That pattern matches any line starting with seven of <, |, = or >, so n steps through every marker in the file. At each conflict, edit the lines into the right result and delete the marker lines with dd. When no markers are left (the search finds nothing), save, then in the terminal git add FILE and git commit.

Resolving with vimdiff. For a file with several conflicts, git can open Vim with each version side by side:

Vim opens four windows: LOCAL (yours), BASE (the ancestor) and REMOTE (theirs) across the top, and MERGED (the file you are fixing) below. In the MERGED window, ]c and [c jump to the next and previous difference, and

copy that side's version of the current difference into MERGED. Edit by hand when neither side is right. :wqa saves and closes everything, and git marks the file resolved. (git mergetool leaves .orig backup files; add *.orig to the model repository's .gitignore, or run git config --global mergetool.keepBackup false.)

Tip: Check before you commit a resolution

A resolved conflict is a hand edit, so check it like one: \mx on the file and \ml on the model before git commit. A stray ======= line left behind by a hurried resolution is a grammar error, and \mx catches it before anyone else sees it.

10.10 Commit messages, issues and merge requests in Vim

Everything you write for GitLab is plain text, and you can write all of it in Vim. Commits arrive in Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers and merge requests in Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab; this section shows how Vim handles the text they need, so you have it ready when they come.

Commit messages. With core.editor set to vim (Section 9.7, Setting up git), git commit opens Vim with Vim's built-in gitcommit file type: the subject line turns a warning color past 50 characters, and the second line is flagged if it is not blank. Write the message (Section 12.7, Commit messages a CCB would accept), :wq.

Issue and merge request descriptions. GitLab's descriptions and comments are GitLab-flavored Markdown, plain text with light markup: # headings, - lists, - [ ] checkboxes, | tables, three backticks around code. The model project keeps templates for each kind of issue and merge request in .gitlab/issue_templates/ and .gitlab/merge_request_templates/. Here is the story template the team filled in for every story:

Copy the template, fill it in with Vim, and create the issue from the file with the kit's GitLab client (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab):

gitlab.pl mr new ... --template FILE does the same for a merge request description. Bob preferred this to GitLab's web text box from the first week: Vim's editing, spell checking (:setlocal spell), and no lost text when the browser session times out.

For Markdown files, set the type and teach Vim's Markdown syntax to color code blocks:

(Put the let line in your .vimrc.) Then a SysML snippet inside three backticks with sysml after them is colored as SysML inside the Markdown.

Pulling command output into what you are writing. :r !COMMAND runs a command and inserts its output below the cursor. In a merge request description:

inserts the list of commits on your branch, or the files changed, exactly. The reviewer sees facts, not a summary.

10.14 Applying this to your project

Copy: the quickfix habit (every list of places becomes a jump list); running the pipeline's checks from the editor before committing; tags for names and requirement ids; merge.conflictstyle diff3; writing GitLab text in the editor.

Adapt: if your team does not use Vim, the same ideas exist in other editors (a problems list, go-to-definition, a merge editor). What matters is that the editor runs the same checks as the pipeline, from the same commands, so the pipeline's verdict is never a surprise.

Decide locally: key mappings for the quickfix list; whether generated files (tags, drawings) are committed or ignored; and a shared .vimrc fragment for the team's conventions, kept in the model repository so new members get it with their first clone.

10.15 Exercises

Exercise 10.1: The debt as a jump list

Convert drop 1 and load its TODO lines into the quickfix list. Step through the first ten. Group the 52 lines by kind (level stereotype, procured part, unit, activity construct, other): how many of each? Which kind would you close first, and why?

Exercise 10.2: Close the level tags in one package

In a converted copy of drop 1, close every level-tag TODO line in Stations.sysml with one substitution (confirm each), add the Conventions package and the import, and check with \mx and \ml. How many TODO lines are left in the file, and what kinds are they?

Exercise 10.3: Break it three ways

In the same copy, make three mistakes: a misspelled type, a missing semicolon, and a level tag on the wrong level. Which check finds each one, and on which line does it report it?

Exercise 10.4: Resolve with the ancestor

Recreate the vendor-branch conflict from Section 12.19, The vendor branch with merge.conflictstyle diff3 set, and resolve it once by hand with the marker search and once with git mergetool. Which did you prefer for a single conflict? For ten?

Exercise 10.5: Write a merge request description in Vim

Copy the Default merge request template from the model project's templates, fill it in for the change you made in the substitution exercise, and use :r !git diff --stat to insert the files changed. Could a reviewer approve your change from the description and the diff alone?

11 Seeing the model: diagrams from text

From what you know

You know

Cameo diagrams you drew and laid out by hand.

Here it is called

views generated from the text: part tree, trace, interconnection, packages and IDEF0 plates.

What is new

nobody draws them. They are regenerated from the model on every change and never go stale.

Survival kit

What you have

three years of Cameo diagrams. You think in block definition diagrams and internal block diagrams; you know what a model looks like because you have drawn it, box by box, line by line, and moved the boxes so the lines would not cross.

What you need

the same pictures, without drawing them. A part tree, a requirement trace, the connections inside each block, the package dependencies, and IDEF0 plates of what the system does -- each produced from the text in seconds, on your laptop, in Vim, and on the model site for management, always current.

Note: Core path

This chapter is CORE. You draw the views from week two; the model site that shows them to management arrives in sprint 4 (Section 17.6, Sprint 4: the model as a website).

11.1 "Where are my diagrams?"

On the Tuesday of sprint 2, Bob opened the converted Stations package in Vim, scrolled through ninety lines of text, and said the thing all three of them had been thinking since the directive: "Where are my diagrams?"

It is the right question, and the most important objection a Cameo modeler has. For three years the diagrams were the model. Reviews were diagrams in a briefing. A change was a box moved on a diagram. When the team talked about the power system they pointed at the IBD on the wall.

The answer this chapter gives is that the diagrams are still there, and better: they are drawn for you, from the text, every time the text changes. Nobody spends an afternoon moving boxes so lines do not cross, and nobody ever looks at a diagram that is three months out of date. What you lose is the ability to put a box somewhere the model does not say it is. That turns out to be the point.

Objection: "A generated diagram will never look as good as one I drew."

Answer

True, and it does not need to. The drawn diagram was beautiful on the day it was finished and wrong a month later; the team counted eleven stale diagrams in drop 1 (Section 2.3, Measuring the spider web). A generated view is never wrong about what the model says. When the layout matters for a briefing, the plates command puts views in a titled frame (Section 11.9, Plates for briefings), and you can still draw a slide by hand from a current view -- but you start from the truth.

11.2 Views are outputs, not inputs

In SysML v1 under Cameo, a diagram is a stored object with its own position data, separate from the elements it shows. Two people can disagree about where a box goes and both be "right." In SysML v2 text, the model is the text alone. A diagram is a view: a function from the text to a picture. Same text, same picture, every time.

The kit's view tools follow three rules:

  • Every view comes from the text, through one command, with no hand positioning.
  • Every view is deterministic: the same model gives the same bytes, so a view can be committed, compared and reviewed like any other file.
  • Every view also reports what it found: the trace view counts requirements with gaps, the package view counts dependency cycles, the connection view counts boundary crossings. A view is also a check.

The five views you will use:

Table 11.1. The five views
ViewCommandShowsCameo's nearest
Part treemodel.pl draw treethe composition hierarchy from the root part, each part at its levelblock definition diagram (composition)
Tracemodel.pl draw tracerequirements, what satisfies each, what verifies each, the gapsrequirement diagram, satisfy/verify matrix
Interconnectionmodel.pl draw ibdthe parts inside each block and the connections between their portsinternal block diagram
Packagesmodel.pl draw pkgpackages and their dependencies, with cycles markedpackage diagram
IDEF0model.pl idef0the function tree as IDEF0 plates: inputs, controls, outputs, mechanismsactivity diagram (sort of)

11.3 Drawing them from the shell

Practice lesson 10's sandbox holds Tidewater's drop 1 converted into a model folder with its sysml.conf. Draw the part tree first:

The command prints one summary line -- how many files it read, how many part definitions it found, how many trees and nodes it drew -- and writes tree.svg. Open it in a web browser (Edge on the laptop opens SVG files directly: start tree.svg from Git Bash). The root is the noun_root named in sysml.conf, ObservationNetwork.

Now the other three structural views. Each prints its own summary, and the summaries are worth reading:

The trace view reports how many leaf requirements it drew and how many have gaps -- the same planted gaps the trace job reports (Section 6.8, Bob's Wednesday, again). The interconnection view reports diagrams and connections. The package view prints a line for each package dependency cycle, then a summary ending in the count of cycles. That count is the spider web of chapter 3, measured. (Your sandbox prints a smaller count than the drop-1 figure below: the sandbox already has the layered folders, the government's conventions package and the DOORS modules, which change which packages depend on which. The figure is drop 1 exactly as converted.)

Note: The package view and markings

The package view was built to check security markings too: every package marked, nothing more sensitive flowing into something less. A converted model has no markings yet, so draw pkg says so on its first line and draws packages, dependencies and cycles only. The security gate (model.pl gate) still insists on markings; that comes later, in the security epic (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system).

11.4 The five views, read

Here is each view of Tidewater's drop 1 as converted, before the government had changed a line. These are the committed renderings in docs/tidewater/views/, made by sim/tidewater-views.pl with exactly the commands above.

11.4.1 The part tree

Read it from the left. Each box is a part definition; each line is "is made of." The level tags (@L2Segment, @L3Station ...) are what the team adds in the structure epic; in drop 1 they are still TODO lines, so the tree has no level shading yet. What to look for: a part that appears in two places (the duplicates of the Legacy Import package), a branch that is much deeper than its neighbors, a part with nine or more children.

11.4.2 The trace

Each row is a requirement, by DOORS id. To its left, what satisfies it; to its right, what verifies it. A requirement with nothing on one side is a gap and is marked. Drop 1's gaps are the ones the team reported to the prime as DR-2 to DR-4 (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed). This view is the one Jim showed the program office in sprint 4, because it answers their first question -- what is not covered? -- without anyone reading text.

11.4.3 Interconnection

One diagram per block that has internal connections. Ports sit on the edge of their part; connections join them. When the security epic adds trust zones, this view also marks every connection that crosses from one zone to another -- the attack surface.

11.4.4 Packages

Each box is a package; each arrow is "depends on" (an import, a type it uses, a relationship that reaches into it). Arrows that close a cycle are drawn dashed. Network depends on Stations, which depends on DataCenter, which depends back on Network; the drawing marks each arrow that closes such a loop.

Three ways to count the same tangle. The drawer counts dashed arrows, and which arrow it dashes depends on the order it visits the packages, so the same model gives a different number in a different folder layout: six on drop 1 in the converter's flat layout (this figure), four in Tidewater's layered layout (your sandbox, and the model site). The pipeline's complexity job counts something steadier: groups of packages that are tangled together, however many arrows tie them. On drop 1 that is one group of five packages. Jim's count in Chapter 2, The Cameo years was a third measure: pairs of packages in the v1 model that each depend on the other, two. All three are the spider web; the team tracks the complexity job's number, because it does not move when someone renames a folder.

The cleanup stories are judged by this picture: "Break the Network to Operations cycle" in sprint 4 removed one loop; the Stations and DataCenter loop was still there at the end of sprint 6 (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web).

11.4.5 IDEF0

The verbs of the model, not the nouns. The kit reads the function tree under the verb_root named in sysml.conf (ObserveCoast, one cycle of the network) and draws it as IDEF0 plates: a context plate (O-0) with the whole function as one box, and a decomposition plate (O0) with its steps -- Sample, Transmit, Ingest, Check, Archive, Publish -- each with its inputs on the left, controls on top, output on the right and mechanism underneath. The mechanisms come from the model's allocate statements: Sample is performed by the Sensor Suite, Transmit by the Telemetry Unit.

Systems engineers who came up through structured analysis read an IDEF0 plate faster than any SysML diagram, and program offices often still ask for them. Here they cost nothing.

11.5 IDEF0 plates from the shell

The IDEF0 plates need two more lines in sysml.conf: the name of the IDEF0 model and its letter. Without them the kit uses the defaults of its first example (a model named KillChain, letter K), which is not what you want on Tidewater's plates:

idef0_models = auto tells the kit how to cut the function tree into IDEF0 models. When the top-level steps are themselves decomposed, each becomes its own IDEF0 model; when they are all leaves, as in Tidewater, the whole tree is one model and the steps are the boxes of its A0 plate. The command writes docs/idef0/plates.html (all plates on one page), the plates as SVG under docs/idef0/svg/, and an INTERFACES file listing the hand-offs between steps.

Warning: Converted behavior is thin

A v1 activity converted to v2 carries its steps and their parameters, not its object flows. The IDEF0 bridge fills the gap by feeding each step's inputs from the nearest earlier step whose output has the right type, and says so in the generated notes. That is good enough to see the shape of the function; it is not a substitute for writing the flows by hand, which is the behavior epic's job (Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0).

11.6 Drawing them from Vim

In a SysML buffer the kit's Vim support has one key per view. Each saves the buffer, runs the same model.pl draw command for the project the file belongs to, shows the summary, and writes the SVG in Vim's current directory:

11.7 The live viewer beside Vim

For editing sessions, the kit has a live viewer: bin/sysml-view.tcl, a small window drawn with the Tk toolkit that ships with Git for Windows. It shows one view of the project at a time and redraws whenever you save a .sysml file. Start it from Vim with \mW, or from Git Bash:

It talks to Vim in both directions:

  • \mf in Vim (focus) tells the viewer to center on the definition under the cursor.
  • Clicking a box in the viewer records where that element is defined; \mo in Vim (open) jumps there.

Bob kept it open on a second monitor from sprint 3 on. "It's the part of Cameo I missed," Bob said at the retro, "without the part I hated." The viewer draws, it never edits.

11.8 Comparing two versions

A view of one version answers "what is it?" The question in a review is "what changed?" model.pl diff draws the views of two versions with the differences colored, and writes a plain change list beside them. Make a small change in the sandbox -- tag the station segment with its level, the first thing practice lesson 10 asks for -- commit it, and compare the commit with the one before: (a commit is a recorded version of the files; Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers, the next chapter, explains it -- here you only need the two commands below)

(The first line of that block is a scripted edit so the test can run; you would make the change in Vim.) The command writes diff-tree.svg, diff-trace.svg, diff-packages.svg and diff-ibd.svg with added, removed and changed elements colored, and diff-changes.txt with one line per change. Its summary also says whether the change opened any new trace gap -- the question a reviewer cares most about (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).

11.9 Plates for briefings

A briefing wants a picture with a title block: what it is, which baseline, which date, which sheet. model.pl plates puts the model's views into ISO-style drawing plates with a title block filled from the model and sysml.conf:

The plates are what Jim printed for the sprint 6 briefing (Chapter 35, The briefing): the part tree and the package view, each on one sheet, titled and dated, with the baseline tag in the corner.

11.10 The model site: views for management

From sprint 4, the pipeline's pages job (Section 20.10, Stage publish: the model site) draws all four views and copies the IDEF0 plates into the model site on every merge to develop, and the nightly schedule redraws them. The site's front page shows each view with the date and commit it was drawn from. Management never asks for a diagram again; they open the site.

Two choices the team made about the site, worth copying:

  • The site shows the views, not the text. Management does not need to read SysML v2. Every page leads with a picture or a count, and links to the text for whoever wants it.
  • A view that cannot be drawn says so. If a draw fails, the job leaves a note on the site instead of silently dropping the picture. A missing picture that nobody notices is worse than a red pipeline.

11.11 The trees as text

Not every question needs a picture. "What is under the Moored Buoy?" is answered fastest by the part tree as text, which prints in the terminal (or, from Vim, in a split with \mn):

--plain turns names like MooredBuoy into words ("Moored Buoy"), which is how Jim pasted the tree into the first status note. The function tree prints the same way with verbs:

The text trees are also the easiest thing to put in an issue or a merge request description: paste them inside a code block and GitLab keeps the tree drawing characters aligned.

11.12 Views as measures

Every view prints a summary line, and those lines are measures the team tracked from sprint to sprint. They are cheap -- each takes a second to compute -- and each one answers a question the program office asks:

Table 11.3. The view summaries as measures
ViewSummary measureThe question it answersWhich way is good
Part treepart definitions, trees, nodeshow big is the structure, and is it one tree?one tree; growth only when the prime adds parts
Traceleaf requirements, how many with gapswhat is not covered?gaps going down
Interconnectiondiagrams, connections, boundary crossingswhere do the parts talk to each other?crossings that each trace to a security requirement
Packagespackages, dependencies, cyclesis the spider web getting better?cycles going to zero
IDEF0models, activities, linkswhat does the system do, step by step?every step with a mechanism

The spider-web number on every sprint review slide from sprint 4 is the complexity job's count of tangled package groups, the scorecard's spider-web line: 2 after the DOORS import in sprint 3, 1 once sprint 4 broke the Network and Operations loop, and still 1 at the end of sprint 6, because Stations and DataCenter still depend on each other. The package view is the picture behind that number, and the cleanup stories change it in front of management's eyes.

11.13 What a view cannot show

A view is honest about what the model says, which means it shows nothing the model does not say. Four limits the team ran into:

  • Layout is automatic. Boxes go where the layout puts them. A view of a large block can be wide; the answer is a narrower view (one block, one package), not hand placement.
  • Converted behavior is thin. Until the behavior epic writes flows by hand, activities show steps without object flows, and state machines are TODO lines that no view draws.
  • The model tool's own trace has a known gap. model.pl trace (and \mr in Vim) counts a requirement satisfied by a port or an attribute as unsatisfied. On Tidewater that misreports five requirements. The pipeline's trace job, which compares the model with DOORS, does not have this gap; use its numbers as the record.
  • A view shows one version. "What changed?" is the diff (Section 11.8, Comparing two versions), not two views side by side by eye.

11.14 When a view will not draw

Table 11.4. When a view will not draw
Message or symptomCauseFix
no model/ directory here or aboveyou are not inside the projectcd to the project's top folder, or pass --root DIR
the tree is empty or starts at the wrong partnoun_root in sysml.conf names the wrong part definitionset noun_root to the top part definition's name
IDEF0 plates named K and KillChainidef0_name and model_letter are not setadd both to sysml.conf (Section 11.5, IDEF0 plates from the shell)
draw pkg reports errors about markingssome packages are marked and some are notmark them all, or none until the security epic
wish: command not foundthe live viewer's Tk is not on the pathrun it from Git Bash, where wish is installed with Git for Windows
a draw in the pipeline is missing from the sitethe job could not draw it; the site has a note in its placeread the pages job's log for that view

11.15 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: draw the views from the first week, put them on the model site, and treat the view summaries (gaps, cycles, crossings) as measures.
  • Adapt: set noun_root, verb_root, idef0_name and model_letter in your sysml.conf; choose idef0_models to match how deep your function tree is.
  • Decide locally: which views go in which briefing, and whether plates replace your program's drawing templates. Expect the first briefing with generated views to look plainer than the old slides; by the second, the program office will notice they are never out of date.
Exercise 11.1: Find a cycle

Draw the package view of the practice-10 sandbox. Pick one dependency cycle from the printed warnings, open the two files it names in Vim, and find the import or reference that closes the loop. Which package should own the shared element so the cycle disappears?

Exercise 11.2: Read a plate

Open docs/idef0/plates.html after running model.pl idef0. For the Check step, name its input, its output and its mechanism, and say which allocate statement in the model supplied the mechanism.

You can now draw the part tree, trace, interconnection and package views from the shell and from Vim, generate IDEF0 plates, run the live viewer beside Vim, compare two versions as colored views, and find the spider web in a picture.

12 Git from zero, for systems engineers

From what you know

You know

configuration management: versions, baselines, change records, who changed what and when.

Here it is called

git: commits, branches, merges, tags and the log.

What is new

every change is recorded as you make it, a branch lets you work without disturbing anyone, and merging is routine, not a crisis.

Survival kit

What you have

a terminal you can use (Chapter 9, The survival kit), git configured with your name, and decades of configuration management experience: baselines, change requests, redlines, revision letters, the CM library.

What you need

the git commands the team used every day, each one tied to the CM idea it replaces, practiced in a throwaway repository until they are boring. Then the commands for working with GitLab (clone, push, pull), and an understanding of branching strategies good enough to defend Tidewater's choice, or to make a different one for your own project.

12.1 Tuesday afternoon, a throwaway folder

On the Tuesday of sprint 1, after stand-up, Bob blocked out the afternoon in the team calendar with the title "Breaking git on purpose." Tom had given Bob a one-page list of commands on Monday. Bob had read it and understood none of it in any way that would survive contact with a real model.

So Bob made a folder called practice, put a copy of one small SysML file in it, and spent three hours doing everything on Tom's list, then doing it wrong on purpose to see what happened. Bob made two branches change the same line and watched git refuse to merge them. Bob deleted a file, panicked, and got it back. Bob made a commit with a typo in the message and fixed it. At 16:30 Bob wrote in the team chat:

It's a CM library where every change record contains the actual change, and you can't lose anything unless you really try. Why didn't anyone tell us that?

— Bob, team chat, 6 October 2026

This chapter is Bob's afternoon, written down. Every command was run on a Git for Windows laptop; the output is what git printed, with only the commit identifiers (which will differ on your machine) left as they came out. Make your own practice folder and type along. Nothing you do in it can affect anything else.

12.2 Version control in configuration management words

Git is a version control system: a program that keeps every version of every file in a folder, with a record of who changed what, when and why. The folder, together with that history, is a repository (often "repo").

You already know version control. The program's CM library was version control, done by hand: controlled items, revision letters, change records, a librarian who checked documents in and out. Git does the same job with three differences that change everything:

  1. Every change record contains the change itself, line by line, not a description of it. You never have to compare revision B and revision C by eye; git shows exactly which lines differ.
  2. Every person has the whole library, history included, on their own laptop. You can work without a network, and you can look at any past version instantly.
  3. Combining parallel work is automatic wherever the changes do not touch the same lines. Two people can change the same file at the same time, and git merges their changes. Only when both changed the same lines does a person have to decide.
Table 12.1. Configuration management to git
Configuration managementGitNotes
CM libraryrepositorythe folder plus its complete history
controlled itema file in the repositoryevery file is controlled; there is no "uncontrolled draft" inside
change record (who, when, why, what)commita snapshot of the changed files with author, date and message
revision identifiercommit hash (3bcc7d4)a fingerprint of the content, unique to that commit
the change package being assembledthe staging areathe changes you have chosen to include in the next commit
a working copy checked out for editingthe working folderthe files you edit
an alternative line of developmentbrancha named line of commits; cheap to make, cheap to delete
incorporating a changemergecombining one branch's commits into another
baselinetaga permanent name on one commit (baseline-0)
the central library serverremote (GitLab)the shared copy everyone pushes to and pulls from
check out a copy to your deskclonecopy the whole repository, history included
check in to the librarypushsend your commits to the remote
get the latest from the librarypullfetch others' commits and merge them into yours
redlinediffthe exact lines removed and added

12.3 Three places a change lives

The single idea that makes git make sense is that a change passes through three places:

You edit files in the working folder with Vim, as you always have. When a set of edits belongs together, you stage them with git add, which puts them into the package for the next commit. When the package is right, you commit it with a message saying why, and it becomes a permanent part of the history.

Why the middle step? Because a person's edits in an afternoon often belong to more than one change. Bob might fix a TODO line in Stations.sysml and, while there, notice a typo in Network.sysml. Those are two changes with two reasons; the staging area lets Bob commit them separately, each with its own message, so the history says exactly what was done and why. Tom's analogy, which stuck: the staging area is the change package on the CM librarian's desk before it is signed.

12.4 A practice repository

Start from your home folder and make a new repository:

git init made a folder practice with a hidden folder .git inside it. The .git folder is the repository: the whole history lives there. Never edit anything inside it by hand. Everything else in practice is your working folder.

git status is the command you will type more than any other. It tells you which branch you are on and what state your files are in. Type it whenever you are unsure, before and after every other command, until you no longer need to.

12.5 The first commit

Make a folder and a small SysML file. Use Vim (vim model/stations/Battery.sysml after mkdir -p model/stations) and type:

If you would rather paste than type, this makes the same folder and file:

Now ask git what it sees:

Untracked means git sees a file it has never been told to control. Stage it, and look again:

The file is staged: it is in the package for the next commit. Commit it, with a message:

That is a change record. It says who (from your git settings), when, why (the message), and, though git log does not show it here, exactly what. The long string after commit is the commit hash, a fingerprint computed from the commit's content, author, date and parent. Any change to any of them would produce a different hash, which is what makes git's history tamper-evident. People usually quote only the first seven characters (07f494b); git understands the short form.

12.6 Changing a file: the diff

Edit the file: change "Stores power" to "Stores solar power." Type it in Vim, or give the change on Vim's command line, which is how this book's own test of the chapter makes it:

Then:

git status --short is the compact form: M means modified (the column it is in says whether the change is staged; here it is not yet). git diff shows the diff, the redline: lines starting with - were removed, lines starting with + were added, and the lines around them are context. The @@ -1,6 +1,6 @@ line says which lines of the old and new file are shown.

This is the moment the document-era habit of "compare revision B and C by eye" dies. Every change, in every review, from now on, is shown this way: exactly the lines that changed, nothing else. When Bob showed the deputy program manager a diff in sprint 2, the deputy's first words were "That's a redline." It is.

Commit it:

git add -A stages every change in the working folder at once; use it when you know everything you changed belongs in this commit. git log --oneline shows one line per commit, newest first.

12.7 Commit messages a CCB would accept

The commit message is the "reason for change" field of the change record. In six months someone will run git log on a file to find out why a line is the way it is, and the message is all they will have. The team's convention:

  • A subject line of at most 72 characters, saying what the commit does, starting with the area: Stations: close the level-tag TODOs. No full stop at the end.
  • A blank line, then a body when the reason is not obvious from the subject: why the change was made, what was considered and rejected, what the reviewer should look at.
  • A reference to the task: Part of #23 or Closes #23, where 23 is the GitLab issue number. GitLab turns these into links, and Closes closes the issue when the change is merged (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab).
Table 12.2. Commit messages
PoorBetter
fixStations: type Battery.capacity as an energy value
changes per BobNetwork: replace the include TODO with an include use case (Closes #31)
WIP(do not commit work in progress to a shared branch; see Section 12.12, Putting work aside: stash)
updated modelRequirements: import DOORS module System Requirements (Part of #18)

Because core.editor is set to Vim (Section 9.7, Setting up git), typing git commit without -m opens Vim with an empty message. Write the subject on the first line, leave the second blank, write the body below, then :wq. Git commits when Vim exits. If you quit without saving (:q!), git cancels the commit. For anything with a body, this is easier than -m.

12.8 Undoing things

Fear of breaking something is the biggest obstacle for newcomers, so learn the undo commands early. Which one to use depends on how far the change has travelled.

A change you have not staged, that you want to throw away. Make a throwaway edit, then throw it away:

git restore FILE puts the file back the way it was at the last commit. This one cannot be undone: the edits are gone. (They were never committed, so git never had them.)

A change you have staged, that you want to take back out of the package. Add an owner line under the first line, stage it, then take it back out of the package:

git restore --staged FILE un-stages it: the edit stays in the working folder, it is just no longer in the package. (Notice the M move from the first column to the second.) Older guides show git rm --cached or git reset HEAD FILE for this; git restore --staged is the modern form.

The last commit, before you have pushed it, has a typo in the message or is missing a file:

--amend replaces the last commit with a corrected one (note the new hash). Use it only before you push: once others have the commit, replacing it rewrites shared history, which the protected branches in GitLab refuse anyway.

A commit that has been pushed, that turned out to be wrong:

git revert COMMIT makes a new commit that undoes an old one. History is not rewritten; it grows. That is exactly how a CM system should behave: the wrong change and its correction are both on the record. HEAD means "the commit I am on now," and HEAD~1 the one before it.

Tip: Committed means safe

Once something is committed, it is very hard to lose. Even a branch you delete keeps its commits for weeks in git's internal log (git reflog lists them). The things you can lose are the things you never committed. That is the practical argument for committing small and often.

12.9 Branches

A branch is a named line of commits. Every repository starts with one (main). Making another is instant, and it lets you make changes without touching anyone else's work until you choose to combine them. On Tidewater, every task that changes the model is done on its own branch, named for its GitLab issue: feature/23-network-levels.

git switch -c NAME creates a branch and moves onto it (git checkout -b NAME is the older form, and does the same). Edit the file so the capacity has a type (attribute capacity : ISQ::EnergyValue;) and commit:

(commit -a stages every modified, already-tracked file and commits in one step. It does not pick up new files.)

git log --oneline --all --graph draws every branch's history as a graph. Make it a habit; it is the map of the repository. Now switch back to main and look at the file:

The typed capacity is not there. It exists only on the branch. This is the point of branches: main is untouched until the change is reviewed and merged.

12.10 Merging

To incorporate the branch's work, merge it into the branch you are on:

The graph shows the branch going off and coming back. The merge commit (84f88cb) records the incorporation itself: when the change was incorporated, by whom, and (in GitLab) through which merge request and with whose approval. Deleting the branch afterwards removes only the name; its commits stay in the history.

--no-ff ("no fast-forward") forces git to make a merge commit even when it could simply move main forward to the branch's last commit. Without it, the graph would be a straight line and the fact that these commits arrived together, as one reviewed change, would be lost. Tidewater always merges this way; GitLab does it for you when the project's merge method is set to "merge commit" (decision D-3 in Section 13.11, The decisions the team wrote down).

On Tidewater you will almost never type git merge into a shared branch yourself. Merges into develop and main happen in GitLab, through a merge request, after the pipeline passes and a code owner approves (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab). You practice it here so that you know what GitLab is doing for you.

12.11 Merge conflicts

A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines differently, and git cannot know which to keep. It is two people redlining the same sentence: a person has to decide. Make one on purpose. On a branch, change the battery's documentation one way:

Edit the line to Stores solar power for the night. (from Vim's command line, as below, or by hand) and commit:

Then go back to main and change the same line another way (Stores solar power for night, cloud and storms.), commit, and merge the branch in:

When git merge stops like this it reports an error: the merge is half done, and git waits for you. Ask for the state:

Git stopped half way and wrote both versions into the file, between conflict markers:

Between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is the version on the branch you are on (main); between ======= and >>>>>>> feature/8-doc-bob is the incoming version. The middle section, from ||||||| (with the common ancestor's commit id) to =======, is the original line both sides started from; it appears because of the merge.conflictstyle diff3 setting from Section 10.9, Merge conflicts in Vim, and without that setting it is simply absent. Everything outside the markers merged cleanly (notice that the typed capacity from the earlier merge is there). Resolve it by editing the file into what it should be, with the markers removed. Here the right answer combines both:

In Vim, delete the lines from <<<<<<< to >>>>>>> and type the combined line in their place; or let Vim's command line do it, which is also how this book's test of the chapter does it:

Then tell git the conflict is resolved and finish the merge:

If you start a merge and want to back out of it, git merge --abort returns everything to how it was before.

Note: Conflicts are information

Bob's first conflict produced a moment of panic, then a realization. In the Cameo years, two people changing the same element produced no warning at all: the second save silently won, and the first person's work vanished until someone noticed, sometimes months later. A conflict is git refusing to lose anyone's work. It is the system working. The Vim chapter (Section 10.9, Merge conflicts in Vim) showed how to resolve conflicts quickly in Vim; now that you know what a conflict is, go back to that section; Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle shows how the team handled the conflicts that each prime drop produced.

12.12 Putting work aside: stash

Sometimes you are in the middle of an edit and need a clean working folder for a few minutes: to look at another branch, or to pull a colleague's change. You do not want to commit half-finished work. Make an edit (here, adding gales to the documentation), then stash it:

git stash shelves your uncommitted changes and leaves a clean working folder. git stash list shows the shelf. git stash pop puts the most recent shelved changes back and removes them from the shelf; git stash apply puts them back and keeps them on the shelf. git stash clear empties the shelf (carefully: that is a real delete). Stash is for minutes, not days. If work will take longer, commit it on its own branch.

12.13 Remotes: clone, push and pull

So far everything has been on one laptop. A remote is another copy of the repository that you exchange commits with. On Tidewater the remote is the GitLab project; here, a second folder plays GitLab's part, so you can practice without a server. (A bare repository is one with no working folder, only history: what a server keeps.)

git remote add origin URL names the remote origin (the conventional name). git push -u origin main sends the main branch there; -u remembers the pairing, so later a plain git push or git pull knows where to go.

Now be Tom. Clone the "server" into a second folder, as Tom would on another laptop, and make a change:

The clone has the whole history. In the clone, set Tom's name and email without --global, so these commits are Tom's; then add a README and push it:

Back in Bob's folder, bring in Tom's work:

git pull is two steps: git fetch (download the remote's new commits) and then a merge of them into your branch. Here Bob had no new commits of their own, so git simply moved Bob's main forward: a fast-forward.

12.13.1 When the push is rejected

What if both have committed? Tom adds a line to the README and pushes it:

Bob, who has not pulled since, commits the gales edit still in the working folder from Section 12.12, Putting work aside: stash, and pushes:

Pull, which merges Tom's commit into Bob's, then push again:

The server refused Bob's push because accepting it would have discarded Tom's commit. That refusal is a safety feature, not an error to be worked around. The fix is always: pull, resolve any conflicts, push again.

On Tidewater this situation almost never arises, because nobody pushes to a shared branch. Each person pushes only their own feature branches, and shared branches change only through merge requests. Your local copy of develop only ever moves forward, by pulling. One more setting makes that safe:

With it, git pull refuses to make a merge commit on your behalf; it only fast-forwards. If it ever refuses, you committed on a branch you should not have, and you want to know.

12.14 Tags: baselines

A tag is a permanent name on one commit. On Tidewater, tags are baselines: baseline-0, baseline-1. An annotated tag also records who made it, when, and a message:

Tags are not pushed with git push alone; push them by name. Anyone can then check out exactly that baseline (git switch --detach baseline-0), years later, and get the identical files. Compare the document era's "Revision C," which named a document but not the exact state of everything that document depended on.

In GitLab, baseline tags are protected (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab): only maintainers can create them, and nobody can move or delete them. That turns a convention into a control.

12.15 Reading history: log, show and blame

Three commands answer the questions a CM auditor asks.

What changed, and when? git log, with options. git log --oneline --all --graph for the map; git log --oneline -- FILE for one file's history:

What exactly was in that change? git show COMMIT prints the change record and its diff; with --stat, only a summary:

Who last changed each line, and in which change? git blame FILE:

Each line shows the commit that last touched it. Line 3 came from the last change, the gales; line 4 from the typed capacity. Bob's reaction, the first time: "In Cameo, nobody could tell me who changed a block or why. This tells me for every line."

12.16 Files git should ignore

Some files belong in the working folder but not in the repository: editor swap files, generated drawings you can rebuild, scratch output. List them in a file called .gitignore at the top of the repository, one pattern per line:

The docs/tree.svg made first stands for a generated drawing; git no longer reports it, because it matches the pattern. (?? means untracked.) Commit the .gitignore itself. The team's model repository ignores Vim's swap files, the tags file, merge backups and the local pipeline runner's logs, and deliberately does not ignore the generated docs/ folder, because the team decided to commit generated documentation so that reviewers see it change (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

12.17 The rules the team adopted

By the end of sprint 1 the team had settled on eight rules. They are on the wiki's Gitflow page and on a card taped to each monitor.

  1. Never commit on main or develop. Every change starts on a feature branch. GitLab enforces this for pushes; the rule exists so you do not make the local mess that a rejected push leaves behind.
  2. One task, one branch, one merge request. The branch is named for the task's issue: feature/23-network-levels.
  3. Start from the latest develop. git switch develop, git pull, then git switch -c feature/....
  4. Commit small and often, each commit with a message that says why (Section 12.7, Commit messages a CCB would accept).
  5. Push at least at the end of every day. Your branch on GitLab is your backup, and others can see your work.
  6. Never rewrite history that has been pushed. No force push; GitLab's protections refuse it on shared branches, and the team agreed not to do it on feature branches either.
  7. Never commit secrets or files you did not mean to. Look at git status before every commit.
  8. When unsure, stop and type git status, then git log --oneline --all --graph. Most confusion ends there.

The day-to-day sequence for one task, start to merge request, looks like this. Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab adds the GitLab side, and shows the kit's gitlab.pl flow commands, which do these steps for you and fill in the merge request:

When you push a new branch, GitLab's reply includes a link: To create a merge request for feature/23-network-levels, visit: https://gitlab.example.com/tidewater/model/-/merge_requests/new?.... Open it, and you are in Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab.

12.18 Branching strategies

A branching strategy is a team's rule for which long-lived branches exist and how changes move between them. It is the part of git that most resembles a CM plan, and the one where your project may reasonably choose differently from Tidewater. There are three common strategies.

GitHub flow is the simplest. There is one long-lived branch, main. Every change is a short-lived branch from main, reviewed in a merge request (GitHub calls it a pull request), checked by automated tests, and merged back into main. main is always the current state, and anything on it may be published at any time. It suits small teams that publish continuously and never need to maintain an older released version.

Git flow (or gitflow) is the most structured. There are two long-lived branches: develop, where integrated work accumulates, and main, which holds only released versions, each tagged. Features branch from develop and merge back into it. When a release is due, a release/ branch is cut from develop, stabilized (only fixes, release notes, version numbers), then merged into main and tagged, and merged back into develop. Urgent fixes to a released version are hotfix/ branches from main, merged into both main and develop.

GitLab flow sits between the two and comes in two variants. In the environment variant, main is the integration branch and further branches represent places the work is deployed (pre-production, production); changes are promoted from one to the next by merge requests, and the testing at each step widens. In the release variant, main is the integration branch and a release/ branch is cut for each released version as late as possible, receiving only serious fixes. Both variants follow an upstream-first rule: a fix always lands on main first and is then carried to the release or environment branch, never the other way round, so no fix is ever lost.

Table 12.3. Three branching strategies compared
GitHub flowGitLab flowGit flow
Long-lived branchesmainmain plus environment or release branchesmain (releases) and develop (integration)
Where daily work mergesmainmaindevelop
How a release is madeany commit on main; tag itpromote by MR to the next environment, or cut a release branch laterelease branch from develop, stabilize, merge to main, tag, merge back
Fixes to a released versionnone (you release again)upstream first: fix on main, carry to the release branchhotfix branch from main, merged to main and develop
Complexitylowmediumhigh
Suitscontinuous publishing; one current versionstaged deployment, or a few supported releasesformal, numbered releases that others depend on

12.18.1 Why Tidewater chose git flow

Jim, Bob and Tom argued about this for most of an afternoon in week zero, and the decision (D-2 in Section 13.11, The decisions the team wrote down) rests on three facts about Tidewater:

  1. Tidewater has formal baselines. Analyses, contracts and the program's other teams cite a specific baseline of the system model, and the CCB approves each one. Git flow's main is exactly the list of approved baselines: every commit on main is a baseline merge, and every baseline is a protected tag on main. The deputy program manager understood that in one sentence.
  2. Daily work must never wait for a baseline. Preparing baseline-1 took a week of review and release notes. With git flow, that happened on a release branch while Bob and Tom kept merging into develop. In GitHub flow, the team would have had to freeze main for a week, or publish a baseline that included half-reviewed work.
  3. A released baseline may need a correction. In sprint 24 the program office found a wrong satisfy relationship in baseline-1, which another program was using. A hotfix branch from main corrected it and the fix reached develop too (Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).

The team made two adjustments to textbook git flow. develop is GitLab's default branch, the one merge requests target unless told otherwise and the one where "Closes #N" closes issues, so that day-to-day work flows to the right place without anyone thinking about it. And a seventh kind of branch, vendor/prime, holds the prime's deliveries, which is the next section.

12.18.2 When your project should choose differently

Choose GitLab flow (release variant) if your model is published continuously (a model site everyone reads) and formal baselines are rare, or if you want one integration branch and find develop plus main confusing. Most of Tidewater's practices carry over unchanged: release branches become baselines, and the vendor branch works the same.

Choose GitHub flow if your model has no formal releases at all: an internal model used only by its own team, or a short study. It is the easiest to teach and the hardest to get wrong.

Choose git flow if, like Tidewater, people outside the team depend on specific approved versions, and those versions sometimes need corrections while new work continues.

Whatever you choose, write it down with its reason (Section 13.11, The decisions the team wrote down), protect the long-lived branches in GitLab, and keep the rule that nothing reaches a long-lived branch except through a reviewed merge request.

12.19 The vendor branch

The prime contractor delivers a new v1 model every quarter. The team converts each delivery to SysML v2 and then edits the converted text: closing TODO lines, removing clutter, writing what the converter could not. The question that kept Bob awake in week zero was: when drop 2 arrives, what happens to all our edits?

Converting drop 2 produces fresh text with every TODO back in place. Copying it over the team's edited files would erase three months of work. Hand-merging thirteen files every quarter would be the Cameo years again. The answer is a vendor branch: a branch that holds the deliveries exactly as converted, never edited by hand, and is merged into develop like any other branch. Git then does a three-way merge: it compares the prime's old and new version and applies the prime's changes to the team's edited version, leaving the team's edits alone wherever the prime did not touch the same lines.

You can see it work in a practice repository of its own. Make a skeleton:

Then a vendor branch holding the first delivery's converted file (pasted here; on Tidewater the converter writes it):

The delivered file has a TODO line where the converter could not carry a level stereotype. On develop, the team closes it (replacing the TODO line with @L3Station;) and commits:

Now drop 2 arrives. The prime added a mooring. Its converted text still has the TODO line, because the converter cannot carry the stereotype now any more than before. It goes onto the vendor branch exactly as converted:

The merged file has both: the team's @L3Station; and the prime's new mooring. Git knew the TODO line had not changed between v1.0 and v1.1 on the prime's side, so the team's replacement of it stands. Bob stared at this for a long time.

When the prime does change a line the team also changed, git stops and asks. In drop 1.2 of the practice repository the prime changed the stereotype on the very element the team had tagged:

This conflict is exactly right. The prime reclassified the buoy, and the team's tag is now out of date. A person must look and decide (here: @L2Segment;). The conflict is not a failure of the method; it is the method telling the team precisely where the prime's change and the team's work collide. On Tidewater, each drop's merge produced a handful of these, and resolving them was a task in the drop's story (Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).

Three things make the vendor branch work, and each became a rule:

  • The converter's output must be stable. The same v1 element must produce the same lines, in the same file, every time. The prime agreed to keep element identifiers stable between drops (Part I, Section 3.5, The prime's view), and the converter is deterministic.
  • Nobody edits the vendor branch by hand. It holds only what the converter produced from what the prime delivered. Only Tom can push to it, enforced in GitLab.
  • The team's own additions go in files the converter never writes (for Tidewater, model/library/conventions/ and other government-owned files), or in place of TODO lines, so that conflicts appear only where they mean something.

12.20 Applying this to your project

Copy: the practice repository exercise, for everyone, in the first week. The eight rules. Merge commits, never squash, if your metrics or audits rely on history. Annotated, protected tags for baselines. The vendor branch, if a contractor keeps delivering a model you must keep editing.

Adapt: the branching strategy. Use the comparison table and the three facts that decided Tidewater's choice; your facts may point elsewhere. Branch naming: any scheme works if it contains the issue number.

Decide locally: SSH or HTTPS; whether feature branches may ever be force-pushed (Tidewater said no, to keep the rule simple); who may push to the vendor branch; and which files are generated and committed versus ignored.

12.21 Exercises

Exercise 12.1: The practice afternoon

Make a practice repository and do every command in this chapter, in order, with your own small SysML file. Then do each of these on purpose and recover: restore a file you broke; un-stage a file you staged; amend a commit message; revert a commit; abort a merge.

Exercise 12.2: A conflict with three sides

In your practice repository, make two branches from main that each change the same line differently, and a third change on main itself. Merge both branches into main one after the other. How many conflicts do you get? Resolve them so that the final line makes sense, and look at the result with git log --oneline --all --graph.

Exercise 12.3: The auditor's questions

In your practice repository, answer with one command each: who last changed line 3 of your SysML file, and in which commit? What did that commit change? What was the message of the commit three before the latest?

Exercise 12.4: A vendor branch of your own

Reproduce the vendor-branch session in Section 12.19, The vendor branch. Then make a fourth "drop" in which the prime deletes the Hull part definition, after the team has added a doc comment to Hull on develop. What does git do with a change on one side and a deletion on the other? What should the team do?

Exercise 12.5: Choose a strategy

For a project you know, list the facts that matter for a branching strategy: are there formal baselines? Do others depend on specific versions? Do released versions get corrected? How often is the model published? Which strategy do the facts point to, and what would you write as its decision record?

13 The operating model

From what you know

You know

the integrated master schedule, phases, milestones and the weekly status meeting.

Here it is called

the operating model: project, tomes, epics, stories and tasks, in two-week sprints.

What is new

work is cut into pieces small enough to finish in days, and progress is counted, not reported.

Survival kit

What you have

a directive, a signed scorecard, a twelve-week outline, three people and a contractor who delivers a model every quarter.

What you need

a way to cut the work into pieces of a known size, a calendar the team keeps, a clear answer to "who decides?", and a written list of the decisions that shape everything else. That is the operating model.

13.1 Sunday evening, the whiteboard

On the Sunday before sprint 1, Jim stood in front of the whiteboard in the team room with a marker and a question the program manager had asked on Thursday: "When you say twelve weeks, twelve weeks of what?"

The honest answer, at that moment, was "twelve weeks of figuring it out." Jim knew that would not survive the first review. In the document era the answer would have been a work breakdown structure, an integrated master schedule and a systems engineering management plan: three documents, a month to write, approved by people who would never read them again. Jim did not have a month, and did not want three more documents. What Jim wanted was something the team could carry in their heads, check every morning, and change on a Wednesday without a CCB.

By the time Bob and Tom arrived on Monday morning, the board held five boxes stacked like a parts tree, each with a size limit written next to it, a two-week calendar with the meetings marked, and three names with arrows to the things each would own. Bob looked at it for a while and said, "So it's a WBS and a schedule."

"It's a WBS and a schedule," Jim agreed. "With size limits that we actually enforce, and a schedule that repeats every two weeks instead of running for three years."

That whiteboard is this chapter.

13.2 Why an operating model, and why so small

An operating model is the answer to four questions: how is the work divided, when does the team meet and plan, who decides what, and which decisions have already been made. Every systems engineering organization has one, whether it writes it down or not. In the document era the written version was the SEMP, and the real version was the set of habits the team had built over twenty years: who you called before you changed an ICD, which spreadsheet held the truth this month, which review package was actually read.

DevSecOps does not abolish any of that. It changes three things about it.

First, the pieces of work are small and of a known size. In the document era a work package was sized to the contract: "System Specification, revision C" might be six months of effort with one milestone at the end. Nobody knew whether it was on track until the review. In the new way, no piece of work the team commits to is larger than two weeks, and most are a few days. Progress becomes visible because things finish.

Second, the calendar is a heartbeat, not a timeline. Instead of an integrated master schedule that runs for years with a few dozen milestones, the team runs the same two-week cycle again and again: plan, work, show, reflect. The long-range plan still exists (Tidewater's runs for thirty-nine sprints), but it is built out of these repeating cycles, and it is re-planned at every one.

Third, the process is enforced by the platform, not by memory. "Every change is reviewed" stops being a sentence in a SEMP and becomes a setting on a protected branch in GitLab (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab). "Nobody changes a baseline" becomes a protected tag. The operating model says what the rule is; the tools make it true.

Case study: The SEMP the team did not write

Tom asked, in the first week, whether the team should update the SEMP to describe the new way of working. Jim's answer was to write a two-page "operating model" page in the GitLab wiki instead, and to put a one-paragraph pointer to it in the next SEMP revision. The wiki page is under version control like everything else, and it changed eleven times in the first twelve weeks. A SEMP revision takes a CCB. The team would have spent the twelve weeks either violating its own SEMP or waiting for approval to change it.

13.3 The five levels

Tidewater's work is divided into five levels. Each has a size limit, and the limit is the point: a level is defined by how long its pieces are allowed to take, not by what kind of work they hold.

Table 13.1. The five levels of work, with their size limits
LevelSize limitTidewater exampleWhere it livesWho owns it
Projectyears"Tidewater SysML v2 port", 18 months (39 sprints)the journal (one per project)Jim, with the program manager
Tomeunder 1 year (2 semesters, 26 sprints)T2 "Port Tidewater v1 to SysML v2", sprints 1 to 20the journal (t: tag); GitLab label tome::portJim
Epicunder 1 semester (13 sprints)E6 "Structure: close the structure TODOs", sprints 2 to 8the journal (e: tag); GitLab label epic::structureJim
Storyunder 1 sprint (2 weeks)"Close the Network TODOs", sprint 3the journal (an item); a GitLab issue labeled type::storythe person assigned
Taskunder 1 week (5 points or fewer)"Replace the level stereotype TODOs in Network.sysml with @L tags", 1 pointGitLab only: an issue labeled type::task, closed by a merge requestthe person assigned

A project is the whole effort, with a start, an end and a purpose a manager can state in a sentence. Tidewater's is "port the Tidewater system model from SysML v1 to SysML v2 in GitLab, then keep it current with the prime's deliveries." A project lasts years. It is the level the program manager funds and the level the program's leadership hears about.

A tome is a major body of work inside the project, the size of a large contract line item or a major phase. The word is unusual on purpose (it is the agile kit's word, and it means "a big book"): it does not collide with any term the team already uses, so nobody confuses a tome with a contractual "phase" or "increment." A tome must finish within a year. Tidewater has three.

An epic is a body of work inside a tome that delivers one recognizable capability or outcome, the size of a work package in an old WBS. An epic must finish within a semester, thirteen sprints. Tidewater has fourteen.

A story is a slice of work that produces something the team can show at the end of a sprint: a package with its TODO lines closed, a pipeline job that blocks a bad change, a set of discrepancy reports sent to the prime. A story must finish within one sprint. Stories are what the team plans with, commits to, and demonstrates.

A task is one step of a story that one person can finish in a week or less, usually a day or two: convert this file, write that job, review the other merge request. Tasks are what the team does each day. They are tracked in GitLab, where the work happens, and each model-changing task ends in exactly one merge request.

13.3.1 What a point is

Size is measured in points. On Tidewater one point is one ideal person-day: a day of focused work on the task by the person who will do it, with no meetings, no interruptions and no waiting. Nobody has ideal days, and that is fine. Points are not hours on a timecard. They are a unit for comparing pieces of work with each other and with what the team has finished before.

Why ideal days rather than hours? Three reasons the team found persuasive:

  • An estimate in hours invites false precision. Nobody knows whether converting a package will take 6 or 9 hours. Most people can tell whether it is a one-day job or a three-day job.
  • Hours get compared with timecards, and then the conversation becomes about the timecard, not the work.
  • Ideal days are easy to sanity-check against the calendar. A person has about eight points of capacity in a ten-day sprint once meetings, email and interruptions are taken out (see Section 13.7, Capacity).

The size limits translate directly: a task is at most 5 points (a person's working week), and a story is at most what fits in one sprint for the people working on it, which on Tidewater rarely exceeds 6 points.

Note: Why the agile kit says "task" for what Tidewater calls a story

The kit's own documentation calls a journal item a task and gives it the limit "under one sprint." That is the same thing Tidewater calls a story. Tidewater added a smaller level underneath, the one-week task, and keeps it only in GitLab. If you read the kit's help (:help agile) alongside this book, translate the kit's "task" as Tidewater's "story." The reason for the split is in Section 13.5, Where each level lives.

13.3.2 Why each limit is where it is

The limits are not arbitrary. Each one is the longest a piece of work can run before the team loses the ability to see whether it is going well.

A task under one week keeps every merge request small enough to review in under an hour. A merge request that changes forty lines can be read line by line; one that changes four thousand gets a glance and an approval, which is the review-by-screenshot habit of the Cameo years (Section 2.7, Reviewing a drop by screenshot) in a new form. It also means the pipeline gives feedback within days of the work starting, not at the end of a month.

A story under one sprint means every story either finishes and is demonstrated at the sprint review, or visibly does not. There is no "eighty percent done" in a sprint review; there is done, and there is carried over. A story that is carried over is a signal, and the team looks at why (see Section 13.3.3, Splitting work that is too big).

An epic under one semester keeps the medium-range plan honest. A semester is about the horizon over which a team can predict its own work with any confidence. An epic that would run longer is really two outcomes, and splitting it gives the program manager two points at which to say "that one is done."

A tome under one year matches the program's planning and funding cycle. The program plans and budgets by fiscal year; a tome that crosses two fiscal years becomes hard to fund and harder to report.

A project of years is whatever the mission needs. The limits below it are what make a long project tractable: a project of thirty-nine sprints is thirty-nine short, visible, re-planned cycles, not one long one.

Objection: "Real systems engineering work doesn't come in one-week pieces. An ICD takes months."

Answer

An ICD took months because it was one deliverable reviewed at the end. The work inside it was always made of smaller pieces: agree the message list, define each message, reconcile the units, review with the other segment. Each of those is a task or a story. What changes is that each piece is finished, reviewed and merged on its own, so the ICD is always in a known state instead of being "in work" for months. In Tidewater the equivalent of the ICD is the Interfaces package; it was ported, cleaned up and reviewed in five stories over three sprints, and was never in an unknown state. See Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named.

13.3.3 Splitting work that is too big

The skill the team practiced most in the first twelve weeks was not git or SysML. It was splitting. Every planning session found at least one story that was too big, and the team learned a handful of ways to cut it.

Table 13.2. Splitting stories that would not fit in a sprint
Too bigWhy it is too bigSplit it byResulting stories
Port the Stations package25 members, 18 TODO lines, two reviewerssub-areaStations level tags; Stations procured parts; Power system and parametric
Set up the pipelineunknown amount of learningfirst useful slicePipeline runs grammar and lint on every MR; then outline and TODO jobs; then trace
Import the requirementsthree DOORS modules, drift to investigateoutput vs investigationImport the DOORS modules; Report drift and gaps to the prime
Write the security planthe ISSM's review cycle is outside the teamwhat the team controlsDraft the toolchain description; ISSM review meeting; Answer the ISSM's comments
Behavior TODOsfour different constructsconstructState machine; fork, pin and object flow; constraint; interaction

Three rules of thumb came out of those sessions:

  1. Split by result, not by activity. "Analyze the Stations package" and "Fix the Stations package" are not a good split, because the first produces nothing anyone can see. "Stations level tags" and "Stations procured parts" each end in a merged change.
  2. Pull out the waiting. Anything that depends on someone outside the team (the ISSM, the enterprise GitLab administrators, the prime) becomes its own story or task, so the rest of the work does not wait with it.
  3. When in doubt, do the smallest useful thing first. The first pipeline story was two jobs. It was the most valuable story in sprint 1, because it proved the whole chain (branch, merge request, pipeline, approval, merge) worked end to end. Everything after it was adding jobs to a chain that already worked.

Here is the whole project as Jim laid it out in week zero. The sprint spans are the plan; Part III and Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle show how reality compared.
