Check the limits against the table: no tome runs more than 26 sprints (T3 runs 23), and no epic more than 13 (E14 runs exactly 13). The tomes overlap. That is deliberate: maintenance begins before the port is finished, because the prime's third drop arrives in sprint 14 whether the port is done or not.

Below the epics are stories. Here is sprint 1, the first plan the team ever made in this form, exactly as the kickoff recorded it (story ids are journal ids; the # numbers under each story are its GitLab task issues):

Seven stories and 17 tasks, 16.5 points. Two of the seven are not engineering at all: a learning story (practice lessons and the first chapters of this book, for all three) and a laptop story (Git for Windows, Vim and the kit on each machine, checked with kickoff.pl doctor). They are on the board because they take real time; a plan that hides them is a plan that slips. Every task is between half a point and a point and a half, well under the five-point limit. That is typical of a first sprint, when everything is new and the team does not yet trust its estimates; by sprint 4, three- and four-point tasks appear as people learn what a day of work in the new tools looks like.

13.5 Where each level lives

Each level lives in the place where the people who use it already look.

Stories, epics and tomes live in the team's journal, the plain-text ledger the agile kit keeps for each project (Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board). Each story is one journal item, with an id like TW-12 (the number is the story's GitLab issue number, so the two always match), a size in points, an epic (e:) and a tome (t:). The journal is where the sprint's commitment, capacity, done and carried-over work are recorded, and where velocity, burn-down and the weekly report come from. It is the part of the operating model Jim owns and reports from.

Tasks live only in GitLab. Each task is a GitLab issue, labeled type::task, linked to its story's issue ("Part of #12"), and, if it changes the model, closed automatically by the merge request that does the work. That is where Bob and Tom spend their day.

Why not put tasks in the journal too? Because the kit follows a rule that turned out to suit the team well: the architect's record holds what the architect is accountable for, and the team's day-to-day breakdown stays in the team's own tool. Jim is accountable for stories finishing in the sprint they were committed to; Jim does not need, and should not manage, which of Bob's three tasks is done by Wednesday. GitLab already records that, in detail, for anyone who wants to look.

The mapping to GitLab objects depends on which tier of GitLab the organization licenses. Tidewater's enterprise GitLab is the Free tier (GitLab's name for its unpaid edition, which in an enterprise installation is still supported by the administrators), so the team used labels and milestones for the upper levels:

Table 13.4. The levels in GitLab, by tier
LevelGitLab Free (what Tidewater used)GitLab Premium or Ultimate (if you have it)
Projecta group (tidewater) holding the model projectthe same
Tomea scoped label tome::porta parent epic (Ultimate supports multi-level epics)
Epica scoped label epic::structurea group epic, with child issues and a roadmap
Sprinta milestone "Sprint 3" with start and due datesan iteration in an iteration cadence
Storyan issue labeled type::storythe same, attached to its epic
Taskan issue labeled type::task, related to its storya child task (a GitLab "task" work item) or the same issue

A scoped label is a GitLab label whose name contains ::. An issue can carry only one label from each scope, so adding workflow::review to an issue automatically removes workflow::in-progress. That one feature is what makes labels usable as fields: an issue's type, epic, tome and workflow state are each exactly one value. Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab creates them from a file.

13.6 The cadence

Every sprint on Tidewater is ten working days, Monday of week one to Friday of week two, and every sprint has the same shape. The team's calendar invitations were created once, in week zero, and never changed.

Table 13.5. The two-week cadence
DayWhenEventLengthWhoProduces
Day 1 (Monday)09:00Sprint kickoff and planning90 minutesteam; program manager invited for the first 15the sprint goal, capacity, committed stories, task breakdown, poker estimates
Every day09:00Stand-up15 minutesteamthree terse lines per person (yesterday, today, blockers); blockers become actions
Every Friday15:00Weekly note20 minutes (Jim alone)Jimthe weekly quad page to the program manager
Wednesday of week 210:00Backlog refinement60 minutesteamnext sprint's stories meet the Definition of Ready; poker estimates
Day 10 (Friday)10:00Sprint review (demo)60 minutesteam, program manager, deputy program manager; prime's modeler when a drop is involvedlive demonstration from GitLab; scorecard; feedback
Day 10 (Friday)11:00Retrospective60 minutesteam onlystart, stop, continue; the pulse survey; one improvement for next sprint

Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro describes each event in detail, with the real chat pastes, poker rounds and retrospective notes from the twelve weeks. Here the point is the shape: about 7 hours of meetings per person per sprint (averaged over the first six sprints, from the meeting records), out of eighty hours. In the document era, Bob counted the team's recurring meetings in a typical fortnight (status meetings, working groups, review dry-runs, the CCB) and got eleven hours, not counting the review packages themselves.

Why two weeks? The team considered one week and three. One week was too short to finish anything that involved the ISSM or the prime, and planning every week would have eaten a day a month. Three weeks was too long to wait for feedback in the first quarter, when everything was new. Two weeks gave six sprints in the twelve weeks the directive allowed, which meant six reviews at which the program manager could see progress, and six retrospectives at which the team could fix what was not working.

Holidays do not move the cadence. When a holiday falls in a sprint (12 October in sprint 1, 11 November in sprint 3, 26 November in sprint 4, 25 December in sprint 6), the sprint keeps its dates and loses capacity. The events on the holiday move to the nearest working day. A cadence that shifts with every holiday stops being a cadence.

13.7 Capacity

Capacity is how many points the team can expect to finish in a sprint, worked out before planning from the calendar, not from hope.

Each person has a standing capacity per full sprint, agreed in week zero:

  • Jim: 5 points. Jim is the MBSE lead and spends roughly half of every sprint on things that are not stories: the program manager, the prime, the CCB, reviews of Bob's and Tom's merge requests, the weekly note. Five points is Jim's honest remainder.
  • Bob: 8 points. Ten working days, minus about two days for meetings, reviews of others' work, email and the unexpected.
  • Tom: 8 points. The same.

Then, before each planning session, the calendar is applied. A holiday removes a day for everyone; leave removes it for one person. Capacity is prorated by working days available out of ten. Sprint 1 had one holiday (Monday 12 October), so everyone had nine days:

Table 13.6. Sprint 1 capacity
PersonStanding capacityDays availableSprint 1 capacity
Jim59 of 104.5
Bob89 of 107.2
Tom89 of 107.2
Team21the sum

The kickoff record shows the result, and the commitment the team made against it:

The team then commits to between 85 and 95 percent of capacity. The margin is not padding; it is room for the unplanned work that every sprint contains (a pipeline that breaks, a question from the prime, a review that takes longer than it should). Sprint 1's commitment, in the record above, is inside that band.

Capacity is recorded in the journal with the stand-up verb cap on the first day of the sprint. The kit's metrics compare each sprint's load (committed divided by capacity) against two thresholds: above 110 percent is overload, below 70 percent is under-use. Both raise a signal in the weekly report (Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board).

Warning: The temptation in sprint 1

On the Friday before sprint 1, Jim's first draft plan held 26 points: everything the team wanted done by the first review. Tom did the capacity arithmetic on the whiteboard and the draft went to 16.5, with a learning story and a laptop story that the first draft had left out. Jim later said that cutting those points was the single most useful thing done in week zero, because it meant sprint 1 finished. A first sprint that finishes everything it committed to is worth far more to a skeptical team than one that attempts everything and finishes half.

13.8 Two ways to count "done"

The book uses two measures of finished work, and says which one every time:

  • Story points done is the journal's measure. A story counts only when all of its tasks are done; a story with one open task counts zero, and its remaining points carry over. This is the number behind velocity, predictability and the sprint report: sprint 4 finished 12 of 17 story points, because the Stations story carried over.
  • Task points done is GitLab's measure: every task closed in the sprint counts, including the finished tasks of a story that carried over. It is the number behind the work mix (engineering, platform, learning) in the Bottom line up front and the scorecard: sprint 4 closed 17 task points.

Neither is wrong. Story points done tells management what was delivered; task points done tells the team where the effort went. Mixing them in one sentence is the mistake.

13.9 Roles and decisions

Three people do the work. Their roles were assigned in Jim's email (Section 3.8, The email Jim sent that night) and written into the project's settings, so that GitLab enforces them.

Jim, MBSE lead. Owns the model's content and direction: what must be in it, which work comes first (the order of the backlog), what "done" means. Owns tomes and epics, plans each sprint with the team, approves merge requests as a code owner, creates baselines, reports to the program manager, and talks to the prime about the content of each drop. In GitLab, a maintainer.

Bob, MBSE engineer. Does most of the model work: converts, cleans up, writes what the converter cannot, reviews Tom's changes to the model. Owns the model's structure in day-to-day terms. In GitLab, a developer: Bob can push feature branches and open merge requests but cannot push to protected branches or create baseline tags.

Tom, configuration management and DevSecOps engineer. Owns the pipeline, the runner, the project settings, the vendor branch where prime drops land, and the mechanics of releases and baselines. Reviews Bob's changes to the pipeline and project files. In GitLab, a maintainer.

Around them:

Approve a model change (code owner)RRC
Change the pipeline or project settingsCCA/RCC
Create a baseline (tag and release)ACRICI
Accept a prime dropARRIIC
Raise a discrepancy report to the primeA/RRCII
Approve the toolchain for useCRIAC
Provide accounts, runner registrationRA
Report progressA/RCCII

A RACI table like this one is familiar from the document era; what is new is that most of its cells are enforced. Bob cannot create a baseline because the protected-tag setting allows only maintainers. A change cannot reach the integration branch without a code owner's approval because the protected-branch setting requires it. The ISSM's "A" on toolchain approval is not enforced by GitLab, which is why it is a story with its own tasks (Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated).

13.9.1 What happened to the CCB

The deputy program manager's first question, when Jim briefed the operating model, was: "Where does my CCB fit?"

The answer the team worked out, and the deputy accepted after the sprint 2 review, has three parts:

  1. Day-to-day model changes do not go to the CCB. They are made on feature branches, reviewed in merge requests, checked by the pipeline and approved by a code owner. The approval, the reviewer's comments, the pipeline results and the change itself are recorded together in GitLab, permanently. That record is more complete than any CCB minutes the program ever kept.
  2. Baselines go to the CCB. A baseline (a protected tag such as baseline-1, built from a release branch merged into main) is what analyses, contracts and other programs cite. Creating one requires Jim's approval in GitLab and the deputy's concurrence, recorded as a comment on the release merge request. The CCB reviews the release notes, which are generated from the merge requests since the last baseline, not written by hand.
  3. Disagreements go to the CCB. If a reviewer and an author cannot agree in a merge request, or a change would affect another program's interfaces, the merge request is labeled for the CCB and waits. In twelve weeks this happened once.

The deputy's question ("can a change be traced from request to approval to implementation?") is answered by a chain of links that GitLab maintains automatically: the issue that asked for the change, the merge request that made it (which says "Closes #N"), the pipeline that checked it, the approval, and the merge commit on develop. Section 5.5, One change, end to end follows one change along that chain.

13.10 Definitions of Ready and Done

Two short checklists govern the edges of every sprint. The Definition of Ready says when a story may be pulled into a sprint; the Definition of Done says when a story may be called finished. Both live in the project's wiki, under version control, and both changed several times in the twelve weeks as the team learned what mattered.

The Definition of Ready exists because the most common reason a story was carried over in the document era was that nobody knew what it meant when work started. The Definition of Done exists because "done" meant something different to each of the three people until it was written down. Jim's first draft of each was a page long. The versions that worked are below; the cut-down versions are what the team actually checked at refinement and review.

Tip: Keep them short enough to check aloud

If a definition cannot be read aloud at the review in under a minute, it will not be checked. The team's rule: every line must be something a person can answer yes or no by looking at GitLab, not by remembering.

13.11 The decisions the team wrote down

The last part of the operating model is a short list of decisions that shape everything else, each with its reason and the condition under which the team would revisit it. Jim kept them as a numbered list on the wiki's Home page and added to it whenever the team argued about something for more than ten minutes. These ten were made in week zero and sprint 1; each is explained fully in the chapter shown.

Table 13.8. The decisions behind the operating model
#DecisionWhyRevisit if
D-1The v2 model is SysML v2 textual notation in a git repositorytext can be compared, merged, checked and reviewed line by line; see Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelersthe program mandates a SysML v2 tool with its own repository
D-2Gitflow branching: develop is the default (integration) branch; main holds baselines onlybaselines are released to other programs; day-to-day work must never wait on a release; see Section 12.18, Branching strategiesreleases stop mattering (then switch to GitLab flow)
D-3Every merge is a merge commit; no squash, no fast-forwardthe history of who changed what feeds the metrics and the audit trailnever
D-4DOORS stays authoritative for requirement text; the model holds a converted copythe prime and the program manage requirements in DOORS; the trace job reports driftthe program moves requirements into the model
D-5Prime drops land on a vendor branch, converted and never hand-edited, and are merged into developgit can then merge the prime's changes with the team's own edits; see Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers and Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cyclethe prime delivers SysML v2 directly
D-6The team never edits the v1 model; problems in it go to the prime as discrepancy reportsthe prime owns the v1 model under the contractthe contract changes ownership
D-7Conversion debt (TODO lines left by the converter) is the primary port progress measureit is computed, countable and indisputable; see Section 3.6, Defining measurable progressthe TODO count reaches zero
D-8Tasks are at most 5 points; stories fit one sprint; tasks live in GitLab, stories in the journalsmall merge requests are reviewed properly; see Section 13.3.2, Why each limit is where it isthe team grows past about eight people
D-9The pipeline runs on a Windows shell runner with Git for Windows' Perlthe same tools as the laptops; nothing new to approve; see Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keepthe enterprise offers an approved Linux runner with Perl
D-10Everything that can be a file is a file under version control: settings, templates, pipeline, wiki, decisionsit can be reviewed, rebuilt and auditednever

A decision record need not be long. The team used this template in the wiki, one per decision, and the table above is their index:

Case study: Writing it down is the point

Bob, who argued hardest against several of these decisions, said at the sprint 3 retrospective that the decision list was the thing that made the arguments bearable. "When I lost an argument, it was written down with the reason and the condition for changing it. I didn't have to keep re-fighting it; I had to watch for the condition." Two of the ten were revisited in the eighteen months. Neither was reversed.

13.12 What the operating model is not

It is not Scrum, SAFe or any other branded method, although it borrows freely from them, and the team did not attend a certification course. Jim's view was that the program needed a way of working that three systems engineers could explain to a program manager in five minutes, not a method that needed a coach.

It is not a replacement for the program's systems engineering processes. Requirements are still managed in DOORS. The CCB still meets. The SEMP still exists, with a pointer to the wiki. What changes is the unit of work (small), the rhythm (two weeks, repeated), and the enforcement (by the platform).

It is not fixed. The operating model page changed eleven times in twelve weeks, every change through a merge request like any other file. The retrospective at the end of each sprint is where changes to it are proposed.

13.13 Applying this to your project

Copy these as they are:

  • The size limits. Task under a week, story under a sprint, epic under a semester, tome under a year. They work for any team of two to eight people doing model work.
  • Points as ideal person-days, with standing capacity per person and prorating for holidays and leave.
  • The cadence: one planning day, a daily fifteen-minute stand-up, a mid-sprint refinement, a review and a retrospective at the end. Book it all in the calendar once.
  • Writing decisions down with reason and revisit condition.

Adapt these to your situation:

  • The number of tomes and epics. Draw your own tree. Start from the outcomes your program manager will recognize, then check each against the size limits and split what does not fit.
  • The RACI around the team. Your CCB, security approver and contractor relationships will differ. The question to answer for each is: which of their decisions can be enforced by a GitLab setting, and which must be a story?
  • The GitLab mapping. If your organization licenses Premium or Ultimate, use epics and iterations; the operating model does not change.

Decide these locally, before sprint 1:

  • Each person's standing capacity. Be honest about how much of the lead's time goes to things that are not stories.
  • Who approves what, and who may create a baseline.
  • Your decision list. Ten decisions is a good start; do not try to decide everything in advance.

13.14 Exercises

Exercise 13.1: Size the tasks

Take a work package from your own program (a document section, an interface definition, a test procedure) and split it into stories that each fit in one sprint and tasks that each fit in one week. Give each task a size in ideal person-days. Which split did you find hardest, and which of the three rules of thumb in Section 13.3.3, Splitting work that is too big helped?

Exercise 13.2: Split a story

The story "Close the Behavior TODOs" covers a state machine, an interaction, a fork with pins and object flows, and a constraint expression. Bob estimated it at 11 points. Split it into stories of at most 6 points each, by the rule "split by result." Name each resulting story so that its end state is something that can be demonstrated.

Exercise 13.3: Compute a sprint's capacity

Sprint 4 runs 16 to 27 November 2026. Thanksgiving (26 November) is a holiday, and Jim takes leave on Friday 27 November. Using the standing capacities above, compute each person's capacity and the team's, and the range of points the team should commit to.

Exercise 13.4: Write a decision record

Write a decision record, in the template's format, for one decision your own team has argued about more than once (a naming convention, a review rule, a tool choice). Include the condition under which you would revisit it.

Exercise 13.5: Enforce a RACI cell

Pick three cells of your own team's RACI. For each, say whether a GitLab setting could enforce it (which one?), or whether it must be handled as a story with tasks. Use Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab once you have read it to check your answers.

14 Writing stories and tasks for model work

From what you know

You know

action items and work packages.

Here it is called

stories and tasks, each with acceptance criteria.

What is new

every story fits in two weeks and every task in one, and "done" is something a pipeline can check.

Survival kit

What you have

years of work breakdown structures, action item lists and IMS lines. You know how to break a program into deliverables, and you know how a schedule line that says "Model update -- 40% complete" can stay at 40% for three months.

What you need

to write the small pieces of work this process runs on -- a story that fits one sprint and ends in something you can show, tasks under a week that each end in a merged change -- and to write their "done" so that a machine can check most of it. You also need to budget the time it takes to learn all of this, before it gets taken from your evenings.

Note: Core path

This chapter is CORE: you write stories and tasks from the first sprint planning on. The splitting rules and the size limits themselves are in Section 13.3.3, Splitting work that is too big and Section 13.3.2, Why each limit is where it is; this chapter is about writing the issues.

14.1 The Monday the backlog was empty

Jim's first sprint planning, on 5 October, was supposed to take ninety minutes. It took three hours, and most of it went on a single question Bob asked about the first card on the board: "What does 'Port the Stations package' mean when it's done?"

Nobody could say. In the document years, a line like that meant "Bob is working on Stations," and it would be done when Bob said it was done, which would be at the review. In the Cameo years it meant the same thing, with a model instead of a document. The line had no edge. It could not be finished, only abandoned.

By the end of the three hours the team had rewritten that one line into four stories, and two of them still did not fit the sprint. The rest of this chapter is what they learned that afternoon and in the five plannings after it, written down so you can get there in less than three hours.

14.2 Stories, tasks and where each lives

Recall the levels from Section 13.3, The five levels: a project holds tomes, a tome holds epics, an epic holds stories, a story holds tasks. Two of those levels are written by the team every sprint, and they live in different places:

Table 14.1. The two levels the team writes every sprint
LevelSizeLives inWritten byEnds in
Storyless than one sprinta GitLab issue labelled type::story, and one line in the kit's journal (TW-&lt;issue number&gt;)the person who owns it, at refinement or kickoffsomething shown at the sprint review
Taskat most 5 points (a working week)a GitLab issue labelled type::task, linked to its storythe person doing it, at kickoffone merged change, or one recorded result

The journal tracks stories because the architect's view of the program is stories, epics and tomes; the hours and the one-day steps belong to the team (Section 13.5, Where each level lives). GitLab holds both, because the tasks are where the merge requests are.

14.3 A story in systems-engineering words

Software teams test a story against the acronym INVEST. Translated into the words of a systems engineer, the six letters are six questions you already ask of a work package:

Table 14.2. INVEST, translated
LetterSoftware wordThe question in SE wordsA Tidewater "no"
IIndependentCan this be done without waiting for another open item?"Close the Stations TODOs" while the layout decision is still open
NNegotiableIs the outcome fixed and the method left to the person doing it?"Use sed to replace the level TODO lines"
VValuableWould the program office care if it were done?"Reformat Interfaces.sysml"
EEstimableDo we know enough to size it, even roughly?"Fix whatever drop 2 breaks" before drop 2 arrives
SSmallDoes it fit in one sprint with room to spare?"Port the Stations package" (25 members, 18 TODO lines)
TTestableCould someone who did not do it check that it is done?"Improve the trace"

The last one is the one that matters most and the one engineers find hardest. "Improve the trace" is a direction, not a result. "No requirement in the Stations segment without a verify, checked by the trace job" is a result.

14.4 Writing the story issue

Every story is a GitLab issue made from the Story template (.gitlab/issue_templates/Story.md, Section I.3.1, Story). The template has four parts, and each one answers a question the program office will ask.

The title: a verb and an object. "Close the Stations level tags." "Grade our requirements with the recipe." "Data exchange table for the program review." Not "Stations," not "Recipe work," not "Support the review." A title with a verb can be done; a title that is a noun is a topic.

Why: one or two sentences, for the program. Who gains what. "The part tree shows every Stations element at its level, so the management site's tree view is readable and the outline check can count them." If you cannot write this line, the story is probably platform work disguised as engineering, or it is not worth doing this sprint.

What done looks like: a checklist someone else can tick. This is the acceptance criteria. Each line must be checkable by a person who did not do the work. The next section is about writing these lines so that a machine ticks most of them.

Tasks: one line per task issue, each under five points. The tasks are written at kickoff by the people who will do them, not by Jim the week before.

Here are three of Tidewater's real stories from the first twelve weeks, as they were filed, with their acceptance criteria (these come straight from sim/tidewater-plan.pl, the plan the simulation runs):

Table 14.3. Three stories and their acceptance criteria
Story (sprint)Done looks like
Laptops ready: Git for Windows, Vim, the kit (S1)kickoff.pl doctor passes on all three laptops
Close the Network TODO lines (S3)No TODO lines in Network.sysml; the pipeline is green
The trace job becomes a gate (S5)The trace job fails an MR that adds an orphan, an unverified requirement or drift

Every one of those lines can be checked by running something. None of them says "reviewed by Jim" or "looks good," because the review is part of every merge request already (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).

14.5 Acceptance criteria as pipeline checks

The habit that changed the team's plannings most was a simple one: write each acceptance criterion as something a job in the pipeline reports. Then "done" is not an opinion, and nobody has to remember to check.

Table 14.4. Acceptance criteria a machine can check
Instead ofWriteWho checks it
Stations is cleaned upNo // TODO lines in model/physical/stations/the todo job's count for that folder
Requirements are tracedThe trace job shows no new orphan, unverified or drifted requirementthe trace job (a ratchet from sprint 5)
The model is correctLint 0 errors 0 warnings; the grammar check passesthe lint and grammar jobs
The documents are updateddocs/ regenerated; the docs job is greenthe docs job
The spider web is smallerOne package dependency cycle fewer in the package viewmodel.pl draw pkg (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text)
Requirements are better writtenThe recipe report shows no finding for the Stations requirementsthe recipe job (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe)
Every Stations requirement is verifiedThe VCRM shows 100% verify coverage for Stationsthe vcrm job

Not every criterion can be a job. "The program office has seen the site" is a meeting. "DR-1 to DR-4 are sent to the prime through the contract channel" is a transmittal record. Those are fine: write them as a fact that anyone can confirm from a record ("the review notes list the program office attendees"; "the DR issues carry the transmittal date"). The rule is not "only machine checks"; the rule is "no opinions."

Tip: Write the criteria before the estimate

Planning poker (Section 24.3, Planning poker) goes faster when the criteria are already on the card. Half of Tidewater's estimate disagreements in sprint 1 were really disagreements about what done meant. In the poker for "Convert drop 1 and assess it" Bob voted 8 and Jim voted 3; once the criteria were written ("both converter reports attached, the TODO inventory by package on the wiki, the backlog estimated"), the second round was 3, 3, 3.

14.6 Writing the task issues

A task is the smallest piece anyone tracks: at most five points, done by one person, ending in one merged change or one recorded result. Tasks are GitLab issues of type task, made from the Task template, with three things the story does not have:

  • "Part of #N" on the first line of the description, naming the story, and a /relate #N quick action, so the story's page lists its tasks.
  • An estimate with /estimate 2d. The team uses days because a point is an ideal day (Section 13.3.1, What a point is).
  • The merge request closes the task, not the story. The MR description says Closes #42 for the task; the story closes when its last task does (Jim closes it at the review if nobody did).

Tasks for model work fall into a few recognizable kinds. Knowing them makes kickoff faster:

Table 14.5. The kinds of task in model work
KindExample from TidewaterTypical sizeEnds in
Close TODO linesLevel tags in Network1 to 3an MR that removes TODO lines
Hand-write a constructWrite the BuoyModes state def; exhibit it on MooredBuoy2 to 4an MR with new SysML v2 text
Pipeline jobAdd the trace job (report only) and the secrets job1 to 3an MR to .gitlab-ci.yml and ci/job.pl
Prime drop stepImport drop 1 onto vendor/prime1 to 2the vendor commit and the merge MR
DecisionDecide the layered layout; the layout map1an ADR in docs/adr/
Record or reportOpen DR-1 to DR-41 to 2issues sent to the prime
Meeting with an outcomeAgree the delivery interface with the prime0.5 to 1notes and a decision on the wiki
LearningPractice lessons 10-11; the survival kit, git and Vim chapters0.5 to 2a lesson checked as done

If a task does not end in one of those things, it is not a task yet. "Look at the Stations package" ends in nothing. "Write the TODO inventory by package" ends in a wiki page.

14.7 Try it: a story and its first task

Practice lesson 11's sandbox holds an offline GitLab with the Tidewater project and its templates. Make a story from the Story template and a task under it, then look at both. First, step into the clone and load the lesson's environment (it defines gl as a short name for gitlab.pl):

The story is issue #2 (the lesson already filed #1). Now the task, with its link and estimate given as quick actions in a note -- the same text you would type in the comment box on the web page (the block loads the environment again with . ../env.sh only because the book's test runs each block in a fresh shell; in your terminal once is enough):

The last command shows the task with the two system notes the quick actions left behind ("changed time estimate to 2d", "marked this issue as related to #2"). Open the story with gl issue show 2 and fill in its "Why" and "What done looks like" from the template's comments; in the real GitLab you would do that in the web editor or, as the team did, in Vim (Section 10.10, Commit messages, issues and merge requests in Vim).

Exercise 14.1: Rewrite three criteria

Rewrite these acceptance criteria so a pipeline job or a record can check them: (a) "The Behavior package is finished"; (b) "Traceability is improved for the segment requirements"; (c) "The prime has been told about the problems we found."

14.8 Splitting patterns for model work

Section 13.3.3, Splitting work that is too big gives the three rules (split by result, pull out the waiting, smallest useful thing first). Model work has its own natural seams, and these are the ones the team used most:

  1. By package. The converter writes one file per package, and packages are owned by people (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where). "Close the structure TODOs" became one story per segment folder: Network, Stations, DataCenter, Operations.
  2. By TODO kind. The converter's TODO lines name their kind (stereotype, state machine, interaction, include, fork, constraint). Level tags are quick and mechanical; a state machine is a design task. Never put both in one story: the quick ones finish and the hard one carries over, and the whole story shows as late.
  3. By requirement group. For trace and verification work, split by the DOORS module or the system requirement heading: "Stations verification cases," "Data center verification cases."
  4. By interface. An interface touches two owners. One story per interface keeps the reviews short and the right people on them.
  5. By drop change. When a prime drop arrives, its change requests (NWM-CR-... numbers in the drop's change list) are natural stories: one per significant change, each with its disposition (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).
  6. Investigation apart from result. "Find out why drop 3's Storm state does not appear in v2" is a one-day spike; "Add the Storm state by hand" is the task that follows.
Case study: The Stations story that would not fit

Bob's first try at the Stations work was one story of 9 points: level tags, procured parts, the power system's parametric and the state machine. Planning poker came back 5, 8, 13. Splitting it by TODO kind gave four stories: "Close the Stations level tags" (5, sprint 4, with its last two points carried into sprint 5), "Procured parts as metadata" (sprint 5, together with the DataCenter tags), the parametric (later, in the behavior and analysis epic), and "BuoyModes state machine by hand" (3, sprint 6). The level tags were the first visible dent in the TODO burn-down that management saw.

14.9 Sizing: points, poker and the first sprints

Sizes come from planning poker (Section 24.3, Planning poker): each person votes a number of points, the outliers explain themselves, and the team votes again. A few things the team learned about sizing model work:

  • The first time is always bigger. The first package with level tags took Bob three points; the third took one. Size the first of a kind generously and expect the next ones to shrink. Velocity in the first two sprints is not a forecast of anything.
  • Waiting is not effort. A task blocked for three days on the enterprise GitLab administrators is not a five-point task. Size the effort, mark the wait (/label ~workflow::blocked), and say it at stand-up as an ask.
  • Half points are fine, quarter points are not. A half-day task exists (send the DR, hold the meeting). Anything smaller is part of another task.
  • Engineering, platform and learning are labelled, not hidden. Every story carries work::engineering, work::platform or work::learning. The scorecard shows the mix sprint by sprint, so management can see the platform work shrinking and the engineering growing.

14.10 The learning budget

No line in the first plan Jim drafted said "learn git." The first plan held 26 points against a capacity of about 19, and every point was work. The team would have learned git anyway -- at night, at home, or by failing in front of each other in merge requests.

The plan that ran instead budgets the learning as stories, labelled work::learning, with real points:

Table 14.6. Tidewater's learning budget (share of each sprint's task points done, Section 13.8, Two ways to count "done")
SprintLearning shareWhat it covers
124%practice lessons 10 and 11; the survival kit, git, Vim and operating-model chapters
216%practice lessons 12 and 13; Vim for models; the diagrams chapter; the SysML v2 workbook, first half
3 and 417% and 9%the workbook, second half; talking about progress; reviewing a model change
5 and 66% and 4%the requirement recipe; memos and briefings

Sprint 1's learning story is a good model to copy. Its title is a verb and an object ("Learn the tools: survival kit, git, Vim, the operating model"); its done is checkable ("each of us finished practice lessons 10 and 11"; "each of us read the primer's Part II chapters for our role"); and its tasks are per person, sized for that person (Jim 1, Bob 1.5, Tom 1.5), because the three do not start from the same place.

Objection: "Management will see 20% of the sprint spent on training and cut it."

Answer

Management sees it either way. Unbudgeted learning shows up as missed commitments, carried-over stories and three tired engineers. Budgeted learning shows up as a line that shrinks every sprint while the engineering line grows -- which is exactly the picture Jim showed at the sprint 6 briefing (Chapter 35, The briefing). A visible, shrinking cost is a much easier conversation than an invisible one.

The same goes for the other setup work a new team forgets: laptops (one point each, plus the days waiting on the software request), the request for enablers memo, the conventions documents, the first demo rehearsal. If it takes time, it is a task. If it is a task, it is on the board.

14.11 The Definition of Ready, applied

A story is ready to bring into a sprint when the team can start it on Monday without a meeting. Tidewater's Definition of Ready is short (Section 13.10, Definitions of Ready and Done); in practice the refinement session checks five things for every candidate story:

Checklist: Ready for a sprint
  • ☐ The title is a verb and an object.
  • ☐ "Why" is written, in the program's words.
  • ☐ Every acceptance criterion is checkable by a job or a record.
  • ☐ Nothing it needs is waiting outside the team, or the waiting is its own task.
  • ☐ It has been through planning poker and fits the sprint with room to spare.

Stories that pass get the workflow::ready label. Stories that do not stay in the backlog, and the conversation about why is usually the most useful part of refinement.

14.12 A worked example: from an epic to its tasks

Here is one epic taken all the way down, as the team did it over sprints 2 to 6. The epic is E6, Structure: close the structure TODOs. Its outcome, from the epic issue: every structural TODO line in the converted model closed, the level tags in place, the clutter of the document port removed -- so the part tree and the outline check are true.

The stories. At the sprint 2 refinement Jim and Bob listed what "every structural TODO closed" meant, package by package and TODO kind by TODO kind, and wrote one story per result:

Table 14.7. Epic E6 as stories
SprintStoryOwnerWhy it is its own story
2Level conventions for the part treeBobeverything else needs the level tags to exist first
3Close the Network TODO linesBobone package, two kinds of TODO (levels, an include)
4Close the Stations level tagsBobthe biggest package; levels only
4Units and value typesBoba different kind of TODO (units), a different file
4Break the Network to Operations cycleToma spider-web result, judged by the package view
5Procured parts as metadata; DataCenter level tagsBobthe second TODO kind in Stations, plus a small package
5Untangle the Legacy Import packageTomclutter removal, with a DR to the prime
6Level tags in OperationsTomthe last package with level TODOs

No story mixes a quick kind of TODO with a slow one; no story spans two packages unless one of them is tiny; each has an owner; and the dependency (conventions first) is a story of its own at the start.

One story, written out. Here is "Close the Network TODO lines" as Bob filed it from the Story template:

The tasks. Each task issue says "Part of" the story, carries its estimate, and is closed by one merge request. The include task was two points, not one, because nobody had written a SysML v2 include use case before; Bob's merge request description says so, and links the workbook section Bob used (Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook). The next include, in a later sprint, took half a day.

14.13 The story in the journal

The kit's journal keeps one line per story, not per task (Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board). When a story is committed at kickoff, the stand-up file for that day gets two lines; when its last task closes, one more:

The id is TW- and the GitLab story issue number, so anyone can go from the journal to the issue and back. Points in the journal are the story's total (the sum of its tasks); the journal is what produces the sprint's committed, done and carried-over numbers, the velocity, and the quad (Section 24.8, Telling management every week).

14.14 Common mistakes, and their fixes

Every one of these happened on Tidewater in the first six sprints:

Table 14.8. Mistakes in the first six sprints
MistakeWhat it looked likeFix
A topic, not a result"Stations" as a story titlea verb and an object: "Close the Stations level tags"
An activity, not a result"Analyze the trace gaps"name what the analysis produces: "Write up the drift and the trace gaps"
Criteria as opinions"Reviewed and approved by Jim"the review happens on every MR anyway; write what the review is checking for
Hidden waiting"Runner online" sized at 4 points, 3 of them waiting on the administratorssize the effort; make the wait its own task and label it blocked
Two kinds in one storylevel tags and the state machine in one Stations storysplit by TODO kind (Section 14.8, Splitting patterns for model work)
A task over five points"Port the requirements" at 8it is a story; split it into tasks
Learning as overtimeno learning stories in the first planbudget it (Section 14.10, The learning budget)
A story nobody owns"Team: close the TODOs"one owner per story; tasks can go to others

14.15 When a story carries over

A story that is not done at the end of the sprint is carried over: its remaining points move to the next sprint in the journal (carry TW-67: the Stations story in sprint 4, Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed), and the story issue moves to the next milestone. Carryover is not failure; it is information. The question at the retrospective is always why:

  • It was too big. Split the rest before the next kickoff; do not carry the same oversized story twice.
  • It waited on someone outside the team. Was the waiting its own task? If not, next time it will be.
  • Something more urgent came in. Was it a real interrupt? The journal records unplanned work separately, so the pattern is visible over sprints.

In the first six sprints the plan carried over one story on purpose: "BuoyModes state machine by hand," started in sprint 6 and finished in sprint 7. Bob knew at kickoff that it would not finish, because the first hand-written state machine was a learning task as much as a modeling one. Writing that down at kickoff turned a surprise into a plan.

14.16 A backlog to start from

For a new port, the kit has a generic starting backlog, tools/gitlab/templates/backlog.csv, derived from Tidewater's plan with the Tidewater-specific words taken out: one row per task, with its tome, epic and story, its size, the role that usually does it, a sprint hint and an acceptance criterion. The first rows:

Load it into a spreadsheet, delete what does not apply, rename the epics for your system, and file the first two sprints as GitLab issues. It is a starting list, not a plan: the plan comes out of your own refinement sessions.

14.17 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the Story and Task templates, the habit of acceptance criteria as pipeline checks, the three work labels, and a learning budget that starts near a fifth of capacity and falls.
  • Adapt: the task kinds to your own model's TODO kinds and drop rhythm; the size limits to your sprint length.
  • Decide locally: who writes stories (Tidewater: the owner, at refinement), whether tasks live only in GitLab (Tidewater: yes), and how much learning time your management will accept on paper -- then ask for it in the request for enablers (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim).
Exercise 14.2: Split a story

"Port the Requirements package" is too big for one sprint. Using the patterns in Section 14.8, Splitting patterns for model work, split it into stories that each fit one sprint, and write one acceptance criterion for each that a pipeline job could check.

Exercise 14.3: Budget your own learning

Your team of four starts next month with no git experience. Draft the learning stories for the first two sprints: titles, done criteria, and the points per person.

You can now write a story issue with a title, a why and checkable criteria; write task issues linked to it with an estimate; recognize the kinds of task in model work; split stories along the model's seams; and budget learning as work.

15 Setting up GitLab

From what you know

You know

the CM plan, the CCB charter, and the list of who may approve what.

Here it is called

the GitLab project: members, protected branches, CODEOWNERS, labels and milestones.

What is new

the rules are settings GitLab enforces, written once in a project file.

Survival kit

What you have

a laptop with Git, Perl and Vim (Chapter 9, The survival kit), enough git to clone, branch and commit (Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers), and a directive that says "GitLab".

What you need

a GitLab project that works the way your configuration management plan says it should, before the first model file goes into it. By the end of this chapter you will have the project, its members, its protected branches and tags, its labels, its sprints, its templates and its code owners, all written down in one text file that you can review, re-apply and audit.

15.1 Tom's first request

On Thursday 8 October, once the laptops were ready, Tom opened a ticket with the enterprise GitLab administrators (task #14 in the sprint 1 plan). It was Tom's first real task in the new way of working, and it was not technical at all: it was a form. Tom had written hundreds of forms like it for the program's configuration management database. The request asked for three things:

  • a group named tidewater, with Jim as its owner;
  • the right for Jim and Tom to create projects inside the group;
  • a runner registered to the group, on a Windows machine the team could log into, with Git for Windows installed (what a runner is, and why the team needed its own, is the subject of Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero).

The administrators answered on Thursday: the group existed, the runner would take another week. Tom's stand-up status that Tuesday was the first one the team's lint flagged as blocked (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro shows it). That delay is typical, and it is why week zero in Chapter 3, The directive put access requests first. Everything else in this chapter can be done by the team itself, in an afternoon, once the group exists.

Warning: The administrators are on the critical path

In every organization the authors have seen, the slowest step of adopting GitLab is not learning it. It is getting the group, the runner and the network rules approved. Ask on day one, ask for everything at once, and put the request in your stand-up as a blocker until it is done, so management sees the wait.

15.2 What GitLab is, in systems engineering terms

GitLab is a web application that keeps git repositories and the work around them. If you have read Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers, you know that a git repository is a folder with its complete history: every version of every file, who changed it, when, and why. Git by itself lives on your laptop. GitLab is the shared place where the team's copy of the repository lives, plus everything a configuration management office would want around it: who may change what, who must approve, what was checked, what was released.

The vocabulary is new; the ideas are not. The table below maps the GitLab objects this chapter creates to the things a systems engineer already knows. The glossary in Appendix K, Glossary has the full list.

Table 15.1. GitLab objects and what they replace
GitLab objectWhat it isThe systems engineering thing it replaces
Groupa folder of projects with shared members and settingsthe program's CM library, one per program
Projectone repository plus its issues, merge requests, pipelines and wikione controlled item: the system model, with its own change history
Member and rolea person with an access level: guest, reporter, developer, maintainer, ownerthe access list on the CM library; who may draft, who may approve
Brancha named line of work inside the repositorya working copy, a draft revision
Protected brancha branch nobody may push to directlythe controlled baseline library: changes only through the board
Taga permanent name for one exact versiona baseline, a revision letter
Protected taga tag nobody may move or deletea released baseline under configuration control
Merge request (MR)a proposed change from one branch into another, with discussion and checksan engineering change proposal, small enough to review in an hour
Code ownerswho must approve changes to which filesthe signature authority matrix
Pipelineautomated checks run on every proposed changethe configuration audit and the peer review checklist, done by machine
Issuea unit of tracked workan action item, a work package, a discrepancy report
Labela tag on an issue, such as type::storya column in the action item spreadsheet
Milestonea dated container of issuesa schedule milestone; for this team, a sprint
Boardissues shown as cards in columns by labelthe status wall, the whiteboard of sticky notes
Wikipages of text kept with the projectthe SEMP appendices, the team's working agreements

Two of those rows deserve a moment, because they are where most of the value is and where most of the confusion starts.

A protected branch is GitLab's answer to the question Bob asks first about anything: "Who approves a change?" On a protected branch, nobody pushes directly; not Jim, not Tom, not the administrators. Every change arrives as a merge request, which runs the pipeline and collects the approvals the rules require. This is the configuration control board, scaled down to one change and made impossible to bypass by accident.

A merge request is the engineering change proposal you know, with three differences. It is small (an hour of review, not a binder). It shows the exact lines that change, side by side with the old ones, so nobody has to reconstruct the change from prose. And it carries its own audit: the pipeline's results are attached to it before anyone is asked to approve.

15.3 The decisions behind the settings

Before Tom clicked anything, the team spent an hour on Tuesday 6 October deciding how the project should behave. This section records those decisions and the reasoning, because the reasoning is what transfers to your project; the settings themselves are one file.

15.3.1 One project for the model, not one per segment

The team considered a project per package (stations, data center, operations) and rejected it. The packages import each other; a change to an interface touches two of them at once; splitting them would make every interface change two merge requests that must land together. One project per controlled item is the rule that held: the Tidewater model is one controlled item, so it is one project. The journal (the team's sprint ledger, Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board) is a different item with a different audience, so it lives in its own repository.

15.3.2 Gitflow, with develop as the default branch

Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers introduced branches. A branching strategy is the team's rule for which branches exist and how work moves between them. The three common ones are:

  • GitHub flow: one long-lived branch (main); every change is a short feature branch merged into it. Simplest.
  • GitLab flow: main plus environment or release branches downstream of it; fixes go into main first and are promoted ("upstream first").
  • Gitflow: two long-lived branches. develop is where work is integrated; main holds only released versions. Release branches stabilize a version before it goes to main; hotfix branches repair a released version and go back into both.

The team chose gitflow, for reasons that are about systems engineering, not software:

  • A baseline is a release. The program needs a small number of formal baselines, each reviewed and accepted. In gitflow, main contains only those; anyone who opens main sees the last accepted baseline and nothing else.
  • Integration happens continuously on develop. The day-to-day state of the model, checked on every change, is develop. That is what the team works against and what the model site shows.
  • The prime's drops need a branch of their own. Gitflow already thinks in terms of several long-lived branches, so adding vendor/prime (which holds exactly what the prime delivered, converted) is natural. Chapter 13, The operating model and Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle explain the vendor branch in full.

Because work lands on develop, the team made develop the project's default branch. That matters more than it sounds: GitLab closes an issue automatically when a merge request that says "Closes #12" is merged into the default branch. With main as default, no issue would ever close by itself.

Note: When to choose something simpler

If your program has no formal baselines and no contractor deliveries to absorb, GitLab flow (one main, short feature branches, tags for versions) is simpler and loses little. The rule of thumb: use gitflow when "released" and "current" must be different things that people can open separately.

15.3.3 Merge commits, never squash

GitLab can combine a merge request's commits into one ("squash") or keep them and add a merge commit. The tutorial material the team read treated squash as a matter of taste. For a model it is not: the team's metrics (lead time, review turnaround, who changed what) are computed from the merge history, and squash hides it. The project merges with a merge commit every time.

15.3.4 Pipelines must succeed; discussions must be resolved

These two switches turn the pipeline and the review from advice into rules. If the pipeline fails, the merge button is disabled. If a reviewer opens a thread ("this connection points the wrong way"), the merge waits until the thread is resolved. Bob, who spent years chasing comment matrices with no disposition column, liked the second one immediately.

15.3.5 Who may do what

Table 15.2. Members and roles in tidewater/model
PersonRoleWhy
Jimmaintainerowns the model's content, approves requirement changes, creates baselines
Bobdeveloperwrites most of the model changes; can merge into develop once approved
Tommaintaineradministers the pipeline, the runner, the vendor branch and the tags

Bob asked why Bob, who builds most of the model, was not a maintainer. The answer is the separation of duties the team already practiced with documents: the author does not approve the author's own work and does not cut the baseline. A developer can do everything the daily work needs; the two maintainers hold the keys to main and the tags. Least privilege is not an insult; it is what the ISSM will ask about first (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep, Chapter 42, Administration).

15.3.6 Which branches are protected, and how

Table 15.3. Protected branches
BranchPushMergeForce pushCode owner approval
mainnobodymaintainersnoyes
developnobodydevelopersnoyes
release/*maintainersmaintainersnono
hotfix/*maintainersmaintainersnono
vendor/primemaintainersnobodynono

vendor/prime is the unusual row. Nothing is ever merged into it, and only a maintainer (Tom) pushes to it, because its only content is the converter's output for each prime drop, committed by the drop intake procedure. Any human edit there would corrupt the comparison between drops.

Feature branches (feature/12-close-stations-todos) are not protected: they are the engineers' drafts.

15.3.7 Protected tags

Tags named baseline-* may be created only by maintainers, and once created they cannot be moved or deleted. A baseline is a promise to the program that a particular version existed and was accepted. A tag that could move would be a promise that could be quietly broken.

15.4 Settings as a file: project.conf

Every setting above can be clicked in GitLab's web pages under Settings. The team decided not to click them. Tom's argument, from a decade of CM audits: "If the settings live only in a web page, nobody can review a change to them, and nobody can prove what they were last March." So the settings live in a text file, project.conf, that is committed, reviewed in merge requests like any other change, and applied by a command.

Here is the beginning of the file the team used. Read it as you would read a SEMP appendix: every line is a decision from the previous section.

A few notes on the format, which is deliberately plain:

  • Sections are in square brackets. Lines are key = value. A semicolon after a space starts a comment, which is how each line carries its reason.
  • [members] uses GitLab's role names. [branches] uses push:, merge:, force: and codeowners: fields in the order of the protected-branches table.
  • The file never holds a password or a token. Those belong in the variables GitLab protects (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).

The rest of the file defines labels, sprints, the approval rule, two CI/CD variables and the two pipeline schedules:

15.4.1 Labels: scoped, and few

GitLab labels can be scoped: a label written type::story belongs to the scope type, and an issue can carry only one label per scope. Adding type::task to an issue removes type::story. Scoped labels turn a pile of tags into columns of a spreadsheet, each with exactly one value:

  • type:: what kind of item: epic, story, task, defect, discrepancy, drop, spike;
  • tome:: and epic:: which part of the plan it belongs to (Chapter 13, The operating model explains the hierarchy);
  • workflow:: where it is on the board: ready, in-progress, review, blocked, done;
  • priority::, severity::, owner::, phase::, area:: for sorting and for the metrics;
  • work:: engineering, platform or learning: the split the bottom line of this book is built on (Bottom line up front);
  • doc:: the review stage of a document the model generates, grey to green (Chapter 40, Documents still matter: review stages for generated documents);
  • disposition:: and prime-change, prime-tbd for the prime's drops (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).

The team kept the list short on purpose. Every label must answer a question someone actually asks. area:: mirrors the model's packages and the code owner sections, so "show me everything open on the stations" is one click. owner::prime marks a discrepancy the prime must fix, so Jim's pre-drop review of what the prime owes is one filtered list.

15.4.2 Milestones are sprints

The line sprints = 2026-10-05 39 2 creates thirty-nine milestones named "Sprint 1" to "Sprint 39", each two weeks long, starting on Monday 5 October 2026, each due on the Friday of its second week. Every story and task is put in the milestone of the sprint that commits to it. A milestone in GitLab is then exactly a sprint backlog: open it and you see what the team promised, what is done and what is not.

GitLab Premium has a separate feature, iterations, designed for sprints, with automatic cadences and burndown charts. The team's license was the Free tier for the first year, so milestones did the job. Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep lists which features need which tier.

15.4.3 The approval rule and the variable

Model review = 1 jim bob says that every merge request needs one approval from Jim or Bob. On GitLab Premium this becomes a real approval rule that blocks the merge; on Free, the code owner approval on the protected branches does most of the same work. The KIT variable tells every pipeline job where the agile kit is checked out on the runner; Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job uses it in every job. DOCKER_RUNNER says whether the runner can run Docker containers (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs explains why the team's cannot). The [schedules] section creates the nightly full check and the weekly status export as cron schedules, each run as the person who ran setup (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).

15.5 Applying the file

The command that applies project.conf is part of the kit. Run it from the model repository, where the scaffold (Chapter 50, Your project in twelve weeks: a playbook) put the file in .gitlab/:

It talks to GitLab through its web API (the same thing the web pages use underneath), authenticated by a personal access token that Tom created in Tom's own GitLab profile and kept in an environment variable, never in a file. The command creates the project if it does not exist, then makes every setting, member, label, milestone, protection and approval match the file.

You do not need a GitLab server to try it. The kit includes an emulator: a small, offline stand-in for GitLab that keeps its state in a folder, enforces protected branches with real git hooks, and runs pipelines on your machine. Everything in this book that talks to "GitLab" can be pointed at the emulator with --local DIR instead of --url. Type along in a practice folder ($KIT is your copy of the kit, set once in Chapter 9, The survival kit):

The first lines of the output:

and the last ones:

The whole run took about a quarter of a second. Clicking the same settings through the web pages took Tom most of an afternoon the first time, on a scratch project, and Tom missed two of them.

The two schedules were skipped, not lost: a schedule runs the pipeline on a branch, and develop does not exist until the next section creates it. Setup is safe to re-run: it creates what is missing, updates what differs and leaves the rest alone, so the second run, after develop exists, adds the schedules.

15.6 The first commit and the two long-lived branches

A brand-new project has no branches at all; protection rules wait for branches to appear. Tom cloned the empty project, added the pipeline file and its job script, the templates, the code owners file and the ignore list, made the first commit, and ran the kit's gitflow helper, which pushes main and creates develop from it. Then Tom ran setup a second time, for the schedules, and asked it what still differed from the file:

setup --diff reads and never changes anything. It compares the file with the live project and prints only what differs, one line per difference, and exits with status 1 when anything does. Tom put it on a monthly reminder: a setting someone changed by hand in the web pages shows up there, and the fix is a merge request to project.conf or a re-run of setup, never a second hand edit (Chapter 42, Administration).

The pipeline ran on that first push and failed: the lint job could not find a model/ folder, because there was no model yet. Tom's first red pipeline arrived before the first line of SysML. It was a useful lesson about what a pipeline is (a set of checks that assume the thing they check exists), and Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero returns to it. In the type-along, perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl --local ../gl --project tidewater/model pipeline list shows it.

Tip: The shorter way

tools/gitlab/kickoff.pl scaffold does the copying above in one command, and kickoff.pl start runs the whole week-zero sequence, setup included (Chapter 9, The survival kit). This section does it by hand once, so you know what those commands do.

15.7 Proving the protections work

Tom did not trust a setting until it had refused something. The team wrote down three tests, ran them, and kept the output as evidence for the ISSM.

A direct push to develop is refused. Tom committed a one-line change and tried to push it straight to develop. The || echo keeps your shell open and shows the refusal's status:

A merge with a failing pipeline is refused, even when approved. Bob's first merge request (the drop 1 import, Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated tells that story) had a failing check. Jim approved it anyway, to see what would happen, and tried to merge. In the type-along, a small README change on a feature branch plays that merge request; its pipeline fails for the same reason the first one did, because there is no model yet:

The "405 Method Not Allowed" is what GitLab's real API answers in the same situation; the emulator copies it so that scripts written against the emulator behave the same way against the server.

A baseline tag cannot be moved. That test waited until sprint 6, when the first baseline existed (Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0).

Case study: What the ISSM saw

The ISSM had approved document repositories for years by reading their access lists. The three refusals above, with the date and the command that produced them, were the first time a configuration control claim arrived with its own evidence. "I can test that myself," the ISSM said, and did. Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep has the rest of the security story.

15.8 Code owners: the signature authority matrix

The document era had a signature page: the requirements chapter needed the requirements lead's signature, the interface chapter needed both segment leads'. GitLab has the same idea in a file named CODEOWNERS, kept in the repository and therefore reviewed and versioned like everything else.

How to read it:

  • Each line pairs a path (a file or a folder, starting from the top of the repository) with the people who must approve changes to it, written @jim, @bob, @tom.
  • Lines are grouped in sections, the names in square brackets. A merge request that touches files in two sections needs an approval from each section.
  • A section that starts with ^ is advisory: its owners are asked, not required.
  • Within a section, the last matching line wins.

The team's split follows responsibility, not seniority. Jim is the first owner of requirements and verification, because those are the government's commitments to the program; Bob or Jim approve structure and behavior; Tom is the first owner of the pipeline file, the job script and the templates, because a careless change there disables the checks for everyone; the prime's drops (/imports/) need Tom (who imports them) or Jim (who accepts them).

Every section names at least two owners, and that is not generosity. GitLab never lets the author of a merge request approve it. A section whose only owner wrote the change could never be satisfied, and the merge request would wait forever. Jim's requirement changes are approved by Bob; Tom's pipeline changes by Jim.

With "code owner approval" switched on for develop and main (the codeowners:yes field in project.conf), GitLab enforces this file on every merge request. On the Free tier the file still works as a list of suggested reviewers; enforcement is a Premium feature. The emulator enforces it, so the team practiced the real rule from day one.

Tip: Change the file, not the setting

When someone joins, leaves or goes on long leave, do not loosen the protection: open a merge request that changes the owners, and another to change them back. The history of who could approve what, and when, is in the file's history.

15.9 Templates: the forms

Templates are Markdown files in the repository, under .gitlab/issue_templates/ and .gitlab/merge_request_templates/. When someone creates an issue or a merge request in the web page, a drop-down offers the templates; picking one fills the description. The team's templates are the forms of the new way of working:

Table 15.4. The issue and merge request templates
TemplateUsed forWhat it asks for
Storya slice of value that fits in one sprintwhy, acceptance criteria, the task table, the Definition of Ready
Taskone piece of work under a weekthe parent story, the steps, the one observable result
Defectsomething wrong in the government model or pipelinewhere, what, expected, evidence
Discrepancy Reportsomething wrong in the prime's v1 modelthe v1 element by xmi:id, the evidence, the drop that should fix it
Prime Dropintake of one prime deliverythe manifest, checksums, the intake checklist
Epica semester-scale group of storiesthe outcome, the stories, the exit criteria
Spikea time-boxed questionthe question, the time box, the decision it must produce
Default (MR)most merge requestswhat and why, the model changes, the checklist
Prime Drop (MR)the merge of a drop into developthe v1 delta, conflicts, rework tasks
Release (MR)a release branch into mainthe baseline contents and the checks
Hotfix (MR)a fix to a released baselinewhat was wrong, the fix, the back-merge

Each template is GitLab-flavored Markdown with HTML comments as instructions (<!-- like this -->, invisible once saved) and quick actions at the bottom: lines that start with a slash, such as /label ~"type::story" or /milestone %"Sprint 3", which GitLab executes when the description is saved and then removes from the text. The story template, for example, ends with:

The incomplete lines are blanks to fill in: the sprint number after Sprint , a user name after @, a number after /weight. Fill them before you save. On GitLab, an unfinished quick action is silently ignored, so a story saved with /milestone %"Sprint " simply has no sprint, which is a quiet way to lose work from a sprint backlog. The kit's emulator behaves the same way, so you can see it happen:

The labels from the template's first quick action are there; the milestone is -, nothing. Tom's rule after that: open every new story once after saving it and check the sprint.

Appendix I, Templates and GitLab Markdown, field by field reproduces every template, and Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep has filled-in examples of each Markdown field.

15.10 Wiki, README and CHANGELOG

Three more places hold text, each with a different job:

  • The README at the top of the repository is the front door: what the model is, how it is organized, how to run the checks. GitLab shows it on the project's home page.
  • The CHANGELOG is the human-readable list of what changed in each baseline. The pipeline copies a baseline's section into its release notes (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).
  • The wiki holds the team's working agreements: the Definition of Ready, the Definition of Done, the gitflow rules, the drop intake runbook, the baseline procedure, onboarding, administration and the glossary. The team seeded it from tools/gitlab/templates/wiki/ in sprint 1 (Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in).

A wiki in GitLab is itself a git repository, so its pages have history too. The team's rule: anything a newcomer must read is in the wiki; anything the pipeline needs is in the repository.

15.11 Signing in: SSH keys and tokens

Each person needs a way to prove who they are to the server, from the laptop's terminal. There are two, and the team used both.

An SSH key is a pair of files: a private key that never leaves the laptop and a public key you paste into your GitLab profile. Git then authenticates every clone, fetch and push with it. In Git Bash:

A personal access token is a long password-like string that a script presents to GitLab's API. The kit's gitlab.pl uses one, read from an environment variable. Create it under your avatar > Preferences > Access tokens, give it the narrowest scope that works (api for setup, read_api for reports), give it an expiry date, and put it in your shell's startup file rather than in any file inside a repository:

Warning: A token is a password

The pipeline's secrets job looks for GitLab tokens (they start with glpat-) in every file of every merge request, because sooner or later someone pastes one into a file. If it happens: revoke the token in GitLab first, then remove it from the branch. Deleting the line is not enough; the token is in the history. Chapter 42, Administration covers rotation.

15.12 What the enterprise administrators must do, and what the team does

15.13 Exercises

Exercise 15.1: Build the project

Using the emulator, create the three users and apply project.conf as shown in Section 15.5, Applying the file. Then run gitlab.pl --local gl --project tidewater/model issue list and gitlab.pl help setup. How many labels and how many milestones did setup create? Where in the file is each one defined?

Exercise 15.2: Make it refuse you

Clone the project, commit something, and try to push it straight to develop, then to main. Then create a tag named baseline-0 as Bob (--as bob) with gitlab.pl tag. Write down each refusal and explain which line of project.conf caused it.

Exercise 15.3: Redraw the signature page

Take the signature page of a document your team controls today. Write the CODEOWNERS file that would enforce the same signatures if the document were a folder of text files. Which signatures had no clear owner?

Exercise 15.4: Defend a branching strategy

Your program has no contractor drops and releases a new model version every month without a formal review. Which branching strategy would you choose, and which three lines of project.conf would you change?

15.14 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the idea of settings as a reviewed text file; protected integration and release branches; protected baseline tags; merge commits; "pipeline must succeed" and "discussions resolved"; code owners drawn from your signature authority; a short list of scoped labels; milestones as sprints.
  • Adapt: the branching strategy (gitflow if released and current must be separate, GitLab flow otherwise); the roles (match your separation of duties); the code owner sections (match your organization, not this team's); the label values (keep type:: and workflow::, change the rest).
  • Decide locally: which GitLab tier you have and therefore which rules are enforced or merely advisory; who in your enterprise creates groups and runners, and how long they take; where your tokens live.

16 The model repository: what goes where

From what you know

You know

a document tree and a numbering scheme for specifications and ICDs.

Here it is called

the model repository and its layered folders.

What is new

the layout itself says which layer may depend on which, and every prime drop lands in the same place.

Survival kit

What you have

a shared drive with folders named "SRS," "ICDs (current)," "ICDs (OLD - do not use)" and "Bob's working copy," and a Cameo project file that holds everything in one blob.

What you need

one repository whose folders mean something -- where the model lives and in what layers, where the prime's deliveries land and why nobody edits them, where decisions and conventions are written down, where the pipeline's own files live -- and a layout that every prime drop lands in the same way, so merges keep working for eighteen months.

Note: Core path

This chapter is CORE: the layout is decided in sprint 2, at the first import, and is very expensive to change later. The section on federation (Section 16.10, When one repository is not enough) is LATER.

16.1 Why the layout is decided at drop 1

Most decisions in this book can be revisited. The folder layout of the model is the exception, and the reason is the vendor branch (Section 12.19, The vendor branch). Every prime drop is converted and committed to vendor/prime, then merged into develop. Git can merge the new drop into the government's edited copy only when each package lands at the same path every time. Move Stations.sysml from one folder to another after drop 1, and drop 2's Stations arrives at the old path as a brand-new file while the edited one sits elsewhere. Every government edit to Stations then has to be redone by hand.

So in sprint 2 Bob had one decision to make before the first import, and a day budgeted for it: "Decide the layered layout; the layout map." This chapter is that day, written down.

16.2 Layers: dependencies point one way

A model's packages depend on each other. The spider web of the Cameo years (Section 2.3, Measuring the spider web) was dependencies pointing every way: Network used Stations, Stations used DataCenter, DataCenter used Network. Nothing could be understood, or changed, on its own.

The cure is old and simple: layers. Put the packages in an order, and allow a package to depend only on packages in its own layer or the layers below it. Tidewater's order, from the bottom:

Table 16.1. Tidewater's layers, bottom to top
LayerFolderWhat lives thereMay depend on
Librarymodel/library/types and units, interface and port definitions, the conventions (level tags, metadata)nothing in the model
Requirementsmodel/requirements/the DOORS modules (stakeholder, system, segment) and the requirement copy the Cameo model keptlibrary
Logicalmodel/logical/what the network does: the observation cycle and its stepslibrary, requirements
Physicalmodel/physical/what it is made of, one folder per segment, and the allocations of functions to partslibrary, requirements, logical
Analysismodel/analysis/constraint and calculation definitions (the energy balance)everything above it in this table
Verificationmodel/verification/the verification caseseverything above it

The order is written in sysml.conf (the layers key), and from sprint 5 the pipeline's complexity check fails any change that makes a package import from a layer above it (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web).

Case study: Why requirements sit below design

A new reader often expects requirements at the top, because they come first in the life cycle. In the dependency order they sit near the bottom: the design satisfies the requirements, so the design depends on them, not the other way round. A requirement that imports a part definition is a requirement that knows its own solution. When the layering check flagged one in sprint 5, it turned out to be exactly that: a segment requirement written around the prime's chosen modem.

16.3 The layout map
