The converters decide where each package lands. By default they write one folder per top-level package -- model/stations/Stations.sysml, model/types/Types.sysml -- which is fine for a first look and wrong for a project: every package at the same level, no layers. Given a layout map, they write each package where the map says, and they do it the same way for every drop.

Tidewater's map is examples/tidewater-v1/layout.map in the kit:

Three features of the map matter:

  • One line per package, by the name the package has in the prime's model. Stations = physical/stations/ puts Stations in model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml.
  • The same map for both converters. The XMI converter writes the model's packages; the ReqIF converter writes the DOORS modules (Stakeholder Needs = requirements/stakeholder/).
  • A catch-all line. * = unsorted/ sends any package the prime adds in a later drop to model/unsorted/, and the converter's report names it. A new package arriving in unsorted/ is a signal to decide where it belongs and add its line to the map -- before the first government edit to it.

Convert drop 1 with the map, in an empty folder, and look at what lands where:

Sixteen files: fifteen in the six layers, and one in legacy/, the clutter the team removes in sprint 5. Every later drop, converted with the same map, lands in the same files.

Warning: Change the map only with a plan

Changing a line of the map moves a package for every future drop. If you must (a package was put in the wrong layer), do it in one merge request that moves the file in develop and updates the map and re-imports the current drop on the vendor branch with the new map, so both sides of the next merge agree on the path. Treat it as an architecture decision and write an ADR (Section 16.8, Decisions and conventions on file).

16.4 The whole repository

The model is one folder of the repository. The rest holds what the pipeline, the reviewers and the next person on the team need. The kickoff script makes the skeleton (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab); here it is, made in a scratch folder, with drop 1 converted into it:

(The last line lists the folders git already tracks; the converted model is not committed yet.) Put together, the repository looks like this:

16.5 The files at the top, one by one

The top of the repository is a handful of files that each answer one question. Look at three of them in the scaffold.

sysml.conf -- what the model's roots are. The kit's model tools read it to know where the part tree starts, where the function tree starts, what the level tags are called, and (later) the layer order and the IDEF0 names:

The scaffold writes generic level tag names (L1System ...). Tidewater renamed them to its own (L1Network, L2Segment, L3Station, L4Subsystem, L5Assembly, L6Component) in the conventions story of sprint 2, so the tags read naturally in the model. Change them before the first level tag is written, not after.

CODEOWNERS -- who approves what. Each section names a folder and the people who must approve a change to it. Because the folders are the layers, ownership follows the architecture:

The interface definitions get two sections, so a change to them needs two approvals -- the systems lead's and one modeler's (Section 15.8, Code owners: the signature authority matrix).

.gitignore -- what never goes in. Every file a pipeline job writes into the project folder (logs, reports, the Pages site, exports) is listed, so a local run of the pipeline never leaves junk to commit by accident, along with the editor's swap files:

The rest of the top: .gitlab-ci.yml is the pipeline (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job); ci/job.pl does each job's work in Perl so the same pipeline runs under PowerShell on the Windows runner, Git Bash on a laptop, or a Docker image (Section 21.6, The lesson of the first week: PowerShell); .gitlab/ holds the issue and merge request templates and project.conf, the project's GitLab settings as a file; README.md says what the repository is and how to start; CHANGELOG.md gets one section per baseline.

16.6 What never goes in the repository

A repository is copied to every laptop, backed up, mirrored and read by everyone with access. Some things do not belong in it, however convenient:

Table 16.2. What never goes in
Never commitWhyWhere it goes instead
tokens, passwords, keysanyone with read access has them; deleting the commit does not delete themmasked CI/CD variables; the person's own credential store
the prime's .mdzip Cameo projectlarge, binary, proprietary, and nobody can review a change to itthe approved storage the CDRL names; the drop's XMI and ReqIF go in imports/
pipeline outputs (reports, logs, public/)they belong to the pipeline run that made themjob artifacts, kept by GitLab
personal working notesthey become everyone's, foreveryour own notes, or an issue comment
files with a higher marking than the repositoryspillagethe system accredited for them; rehearse what to do (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system)

16.7 The rules that make the layout work

A layout is only as good as the rules everyone follows inside it. Tidewater's rules, each with the check that keeps it true:

Table 16.3. Rules and the checks that keep them
RuleWhyKept true by
Layers import downward onlya change at the top cannot ripple into the bottomthe complexity job's layering check (sprint 5)
One folder per segment under physical/, owned by its CODEOWNERS sectionownership matches structure; reviews go to the right personCODEOWNERS approval on develop
Converter files are changed only to close a TODO line or by an accepted DRthe prime's content stays the prime's; drops keep mergingreview checklist; --impact lists hand edits per drop
imports/ is never editedthe record of what was received, and whenit arrives only through vendor/prime, which only Tom can push
Generated documents in docs/ are regenerated, never hand-editedthey always match the modelthe docs job fails when docs/ is stale
Decisions live in docs/adr/a new person learns why before working around itreview checklist
No secrets anywherethe repository is copied, backed up and read by manythe secrets job

16.8 Decisions and conventions on file

The scaffold gives every new model repository a small docs/ folder written for engineers new to all this:

  • docs/adr/ holds architecture decision records: one file per decision, numbered, each with its context, the decision and its consequences. Tidewater's first ten (D-1 to D-10, from week zero: gitflow, merge commits, the vendor branch, the layered layout ...) were written in sprint 2. When someone asks "why is it like this?", the answer is a file name.
  • docs/conventions/ holds the naming conventions, the markings guide the security officer fills in, and the review checklist every reviewer uses (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).
  • docs/onboarding.md is the first day for a new team member: run the doctor, do practice lessons 10 to 13, read these chapters.
  • docs/model-exchange-agreement.md is the agreement with the prime: what a drop contains, how often, stable ids, change notes, the return path for discrepancy reports (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).

Read one of the decision records the scaffold wrote:

16.9 Compared with a reference layout

Teams that have done this before publish reference layouts, and one the user of this book brought in is worth comparing line by line, because Tidewater departs from it in four places, each for a reason.

Table 16.4. A reference layout and Tidewater's, compared
Reference layoutTidewaterWhy Tidewater differs
model/ in layers: library, requirements, logical, physical, analysis, verificationthe same layers, via the layout map-- (the same idea)
model/external/prime/: only the interface surface of the prime's model, generated by scriptthe prime's whole model, mirrored on the vendor branch and edited to close TODO linesthe port is the goal: the government needs the whole system model in v2. A subsystem team consuming a prime's model should use the reference's way (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition); Tidewater does it for DOORS
tools/ with Python checks, generators and their tests, in the repositorythe agile kit, pinned by version (.kit-version); only ci/job.pl is in the repositorynothing to install on a locked-down laptop; the kit's tools have their own tests
reports/ never committed; documents rebuilt in CIdocs/ committed, with a gate that fails when stalereviewers see the rendered change in the merge request; the baseline tag's checksum covers docs/
prime-inputs/ as a restricted folder or separate repositoryimports/ on the vendor branchone repository is simpler for three people; the separate restricted repository is right when the prime's data has different access rules
docs/adr/, docs/conventions/, onboarding.md, model-exchange-agreement.mdthe same--
test/ harnesses and results/ with signed-off manual verdictsverification/results.csv, one schemaTidewater's tests are run by the prime's lab; the government records results (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop)

Neither column is "right." The reference is built for a team that owns its design and its tests; Tidewater is a government team porting and maintaining a model the prime owns. Choose the column whose reasons match your situation.

16.10 When one repository is not enough

This section is LATER: three people and one model fit one repository comfortably for the whole eighteen months.

A model outgrows one repository when more than one team changes it, or when other teams consume parts of it. The way to split is along the seams the layers already drew, into a GitLab group of repositories:

Each repository pins the versions of what it imports (a tag of the library, a tag of the system interfaces). The system repository's pipeline pulls the tagged releases of the subsystems and runs the integrated checks. It is the same layering, enforced across repositories instead of folders -- which is why getting the layers right in one repository first is the best preparation for ever needing more than one.

Warning: Do not federate early

Splitting a model across repositories before more than one team needs it buys version pinning, release coordination and cross-repository merges for no gain. Tidewater stayed in one repository for all thirty-nine sprints.

16.11 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the layers, the layout map used for every drop, the catch-all unsorted/ line, the docs/ folder with ADRs and conventions, and the rule that converter files change only to close TODO lines.
  • Adapt: the layer names to your domain (a spacecraft might add a separate operations/ layer); the folders under physical/ to your segments or subsystems; the map's lines to your prime's package names.
  • Decide locally, before the first import: whether the prime's model is mirrored whole (Tidewater) or only its interface surface (the reference), whether its drops live on a vendor branch or in a restricted repository, and whether generated documents are committed.
Exercise 16.1: Place a new package

Drop 4 adds a package named Drifters that the layout map does not list. Where does it land, how do you find out, and what three things do you change, in one merge request, before anyone edits it?

Exercise 16.2: Spot the upward import

model/requirements/segment/Segment_Requirements.sysml contains private import Stations::*;. Which rule does it break, why is it a smell, and what do you do about it given that the file came from the prime?

You can now explain why the layout is fixed at the first import, write a layout map, convert a drop into layers, name what goes in each folder of the repository and why, compare your layout with a reference, and say when a model needs more than one repository.

17 The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep

From what you know

You know

the tools the program bought, and the ones nobody used.

Here it is called

the DevSecOps tools in GitLab, each with its tier and its value.

What is new

each tool is adopted only when the team feels the problem it removes.

Survival kit

What you have

a GitLab project with its protections, labels, sprints and templates (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab).

What you need

to know which of GitLab's many features to turn on, in what order, and why each one is worth the trouble for three systems engineers with no software background. This chapter is the list, with the value of each tool stated in the terms management and the ISSM will ask about, the tier it needs, how to set it up, and when the Tidewater team adopted it. It also lists the features the team deliberately left off.

17.1 The problem with "DevSecOps platform"

GitLab's menus list more than a hundred features: security scanners for code and containers, dependency inventories, package registries, environments, feature flags, error tracking, incident management, compliance frameworks, value stream dashboards. Most of them exist for software teams shipping software. A team of three systems engineers porting a model needs a fraction of them, and turning on the rest has a cost: alerts nobody reads, jobs that fail for reasons nobody understands, and a growing sense that the tool is in charge.

The team's rule, which Tom wrote on the whiteboard in the first week and which survived the twelve weeks:

A tool goes on when a problem we already have costs more than the tool does. Not before.

— Tom, sprint 1 planning

That rule produced the adoption order in this chapter: one or two tools a sprint, each introduced as a story with a stated value, each measured afterwards. The order matters as much as the list. A tool turned on before the team feels the problem it solves is noise; the same tool turned on the week after the team felt the problem is a relief.

17.2 The list at a glance

Table 17.1. The GitLab tools the team uses, by tier and adoption sprint
ToolTierWhat it gives the teamAdopted
Issues, labels, milestones, boardsFreethe action item list, the sprint backlog and the status wall in one placesprint 1
Protected branches and tagsFreenobody changes the integration branch or a baseline except through reviewsprint 1
Merge requestsFreeevery change proposed, discussed, checked and approved in one pagesprint 1
Code ownersFree (enforced: Premium)the signature authority matrix, applied per filesprint 1
CI/CD pipelineFreethe configuration audit on every change, in minutessprint 1
Test report widget (JUnit)Freethe merge request says which check failed, on which filesprint 2
Code Quality widgetFreethe merge request lists the findings this change added or fixedsprint 2
Metrics report widgetPremiumthe merge request shows how the TODO count and lint numbers movedsprint 2
WikiFreeworking agreements, runbooks and the glossary, versionedsprint 2
Secret DetectionFreetokens and keys are caught before they reach the integration branchsprint 3
GitLab PagesFreethe model as a website for people who will never open a repositorysprint 4
Pipeline schedulesFreethe nightly check and the weekly status export run by themselvessprint 4
Generic package registryFreeeach prime drop kept, checksummed, exactly as deliveredsprint 5
ReleasesFreeeach baseline published with its notes and evidencesprint 5
Time trackingFreeestimates and time spent on issues, for the comparison with the old waysprint 5
EnvironmentsFreethe model site's deployments listed with the commit each one came fromsprint 6
Value stream analyticsFree (limited) / Premiumhow long work spends in each stage, from issue to mergesprint 6
Approval rulesPremium"one of Jim or Bob approves every change", enforcedwhen licensed
Push rulesPremiumthe server rejects commits without the right author e-mail or with large fileswhen licensed
Merge request and iteration burndownPremiumsprint burndown charts without a spreadsheetwhen licensed
DORA metricsUltimatedeployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restorenot used

The rest of this chapter takes them in adoption order, then lists what the team left off.

17.3 Sprint 1: the work and the gate

17.3.1 Issues, labels, milestones and boards

In the document era, the team's work lived in four places: an action item spreadsheet on a share drive, the integrated master schedule, e-mail, and Jim's notebook. The first tool replaced three of them. Every piece of work starts as an issue; the issue's labels say what kind of work it is and where it sits in the plan; its milestone says which sprint promised it; the board shows all of it as cards.

Value. One list, one status, linked to the change that does the work. When a merge request says Closes #12, issue 12 closes when the change merges, with a link from the issue to the exact lines that did it. Nobody has to update a status column.

Set-up. The labels and milestones come from project.conf (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab). The board is two clicks: Plan > Issue boards, create a board scoped to the current milestone, add one list per workflow:: label. Because the labels are scoped, dragging a card from "in progress" to "review" swaps the label.

Here is the board legend the team kept in the wiki:

Quick actions are what make issues fast to drive from a keyboard. Any comment can carry lines that start with a slash; GitLab runs them and records each as a system note. Bob's first task in sprint 1, driven entirely from comments in the emulator. Type it along in the sandbox of practice lesson 11 (perl $KIT/agile.pl practice 11 builds it; gl is the lesson's short name for perl $KIT/bin/gitlab.pl against its offline GitLab):

An excerpt of what issue show printed:

Every line with a * is a system note: GitLab's record of what changed, by whom, when. That record is what the document-era action item log never had. Nobody wrote it; it wrote itself.

17.3.2 Protected branches, merge requests and code owners

Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab set these up. Their value, in one sentence each, for the management briefing:

  • Protected branches: the model the program relies on cannot be changed by accident or in a hurry.
  • Merge requests: every change has a reason, a reviewer and an audit trail, in the same place as the change.
  • Code owners: the person accountable for a part of the model sees and approves every change to it.

17.3.3 The pipeline

The first pipeline had three jobs: the grammar check, the structure lint and the outline check. Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero explains what a pipeline is from zero; Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job walks through every job. Its value is the single biggest change in the twelve weeks: every proposed change is checked the same way, in minutes, before anyone is asked to review it.

17.4 Sprint 2: making the merge request say what is wrong

By the middle of sprint 2, Bob had a complaint that turned out to be the most useful complaint of the quarter:

When the pipeline is red I have to open the job, scroll through the log, find the line, and then find the file. The old comment matrix at least told me the page number.

— Bob, sprint 2, day 4

GitLab can show a check's findings directly on the merge request page, in widgets, if the job hands GitLab a report file in a format it understands. The kit's tools/gitlab/ci-reports.pl turns the model checkers' output into three such formats.

17.4.1 Test reports (JUnit)

JUnit is a file format invented for software tests, which GitLab reads to fill the merge request's test widget: how many checks ran, which failed, and why. For the model, each file the grammar checker reads is one "test", and the lint's zero-errors rule is another. When Bob broke a part type on purpose in a scratch branch (Hull typed as Hul), the lint job wrote this report. Do the same in the lesson's sandbox, on a scratch branch you then throw away:

Nobody reads that file. GitLab does, and the merge request shows "2 failed: model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml, lint 0/0" with the message beside each. That is the page number Bob asked for.

17.4.2 Code Quality

The Code Quality widget lists findings by file and line and, more usefully, compares them with the target branch: it shows the findings this merge request added and the ones it fixed. The same broken type produced:

The fingerprint is how GitLab recognizes the same finding in two pipelines: it is computed from the file and the message, so a finding that is still there after a change is "unchanged", not "new".

The team used Code Quality for something its designers did not intend: the port burn-down. The todo job reports every // TODO line the converter left as an informational finding. A merge request that closes TODO lines shows them in the widget as fixed; one that adds TODO lines (a careless re-import) shows them as new. Bob's satisfaction at seeing "29 fixed" on the Stations merge request in sprint 4 is recorded in Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed.

17.4.3 Metrics reports

A metrics report is a list of name value lines; GitLab Premium shows how each value changed against the target branch. The todo job's metrics for the raw drop 1 conversion, one line per layer of the model (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where):

The per-file count is one grep away when you want it: grep -c "// TODO" model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml prints 29.

On the Free tier the file is still kept as an artifact, and the team's scripts read it for the scorecard (Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard).

17.4.4 The wiki

Sprint 2 also put the wiki to work: the Definition of Ready and Done, the gitflow rules and the glossary moved from a Word document on the share drive into wiki pages, seeded from tools/gitlab/templates/wiki/. The value is modest but real: the agreements live next to the work, with history, and a newcomer finds them from the project's sidebar.

17.5 Sprint 3: the "Sec"

17.5.1 Secret Detection

A secret is anything that grants access: a GitLab token, a cloud key, a private key, a password. Secrets leak into repositories in mundane ways: a script tested with a real token, a configuration file copied from someone's laptop. Once committed, a secret is in the history forever, copied into every clone.

GitLab's Secret Detection is a Free-tier scanner, added to a pipeline with an include: of GitLab's template. The scanner runs inside a Docker container, so it needs a runner with the Docker executor. The team's runner is a Windows shell runner, where that job would wait "pending" forever and, with "pipelines must succeed", block every merge request. So the include is conditional on a project variable, DOCKER_RUNNER, which project.conf sets to false:

The always-on check is the pipeline's own secrets job, a few lines of git grep for the most common patterns, which runs on any runner and on a laptop (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). When the enterprise offers a Docker runner, setting DOCKER_RUNNER to true adds GitLab's scanner on top.

Value: the ISSM's first question about any repository is "how do you know nobody committed a credential?" The answer is now a job that runs on every change, with results the ISSM can read.

17.5.2 Why the ISSM blocked the team for three days

The team's security plan for the toolchain went to the ISSM in sprint 3. The ISSM's questions are worth listing, because yours will ask the same ones, and every answer is a GitLab setting or a fact about the pipeline:

Table 17.2. The ISSM's questions and where the answers live
The ISSM askedThe answer, and where it lives
Who can change the model?members and roles; protected branches (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab)
Who can approve a change?CODEOWNERS and the approval rule, in the repository
What runs on the runner, as which account?the pipeline file; the runner's service account has no rights outside its work folder (Chapter 42, Administration)
Can a pipeline reach the internet?no: the runner reaches the GitLab server only; the kit is a local checkout
Where are credentials kept?masked, protected CI/CD variables; never in the repository; Secret Detection on every change
How long are logs and artifacts kept?the project's artifact expiry; the audit events log (Chapter 42, Administration)
How is a baseline protected?protected tags; the baseline job's rebuild check (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job)
What happens if the server is lost?the group backup, and every laptop holds a full clone of the history

The block was not a disagreement. The ISSM was out for three days in week six, and the approval waited. Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named tells how the team kept working on everything that did not need the approval.

17.6 Sprint 4: the model as a website

17.6.1 GitLab Pages

Bob's objection in Chapter 3, The directive was that nobody outside the team would read SysML v2 text. Bob was right, and the answer is not to make them read it. GitLab Pages publishes a folder of files from a pipeline job as a website. The team's pages job builds that folder from the model on every merge into develop: the generated documents (the part tree, the function tree, the traceability report), the four diagrams drawn by the kit's view tools (part tree, trace, interconnection, packages) and the IDEF0 plates (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text), the requirement trace against DOORS, the verification matrix, the TODO burn-down and the complexity trend. Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job shows the job line by line.

Value: the program office, the deputy program manager, the prime's modeler and the review boards read the model's current state in a browser, without a license, without a repository, without asking the team for screenshots. The site was first shown at the sprint 4 review, and the deputy program manager's first question ("Is this today's?") was answered by the commit hash and date on the page.

Pages works on the Free tier. Access can be limited to project members, which is what the team did.

17.6.2 Pipeline schedules

A schedule runs a pipeline at set times, like a cron job or a Windows scheduled task. The team set two, under Build > Pipeline schedules:

  • nightly, 02:00 on weekdays (cron 0 2 * * 1-5), on develop: the full set of checks, so a problem caused by a change outside the repository (a new version of the kit on the runner, an expired certificate) shows up in the morning, not in the middle of someone's merge request;
  • weekly, Fridays 06:00 (cron 0 6 * * 5): the status job that exports issues, merge requests and pipeline results for the status metrics (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job, Chapter 36, Telling management).

A schedule is written as a cron expression: five fields for minute, hour, day of the month, month and day of the week. 0 2 * * 1-5 reads "minute 0, hour 2, any day of the month, any month, Monday to Friday". The team keeps its schedules in project.conf under [schedules], so gitlab.pl setup creates them and they are reviewed like any other setting; GitLab's web page (Build > Pipeline schedules) shows the same thing with a "next run" column.

One property of schedules surprises everyone once: a schedule runs as its owner, with the owner's permissions. If the person who created it leaves the project, the schedule stops running, silently. The team made Tom the owner of both schedules and put "take ownership of the schedules" on the off-boarding checklist (Chapter 42, Administration).

17.7 Gates, and what they cost

A gate is a check that must pass before work moves on. Systems engineers know gates as milestone entry and exit criteria; the difference here is that the gate is enforced by software, on every change, not by a board twice a year. Tidewater's gates are of two kinds:

  • pipeline gates: jobs that must pass (grammar, lint zero over zero, the outline ratchet, current docs, secrets);
  • merge gates: project settings that must be satisfied before the merge button works (pipeline succeeded, code owner approval, discussions resolved, protected branches and tags).

What they cost is a question management asks early, and the answer has three parts:

Table 17.3. What the gates cost (check GitLab's current pricing page; tiers and quotas change)
ItemCost
The agile kit and every check it runsnothing: it is a folder of Perl scripts
Pipelines on your own runner (self-managed GitLab or your own runner on GitLab.com)no per-minute charge; you pay for the machine
Pipelines on GitLab.com's hosted runnerscompute minutes: a free monthly quota, then paid
Pipeline gates, protected branches and tags, discussions resolvedFree tier
Approval rules, enforced code owner approval, push rules, merge trainsPremium
Security policies, compliance frameworks and pipelinesUltimate

Tidewater runs on its own runner, so the pipelines themselves cost nothing beyond the runner machine. The gates that need Premium were practiced on the emulator and requested for the second year. Prices and tier boundaries change often: check GitLab's pricing page and your organization's license before promising a feature to anyone.

17.8 Sprint 5: deliveries and releases

17.8.1 The generic package registry: keeping the prime's drops

Each prime drop is a contract deliverable. The government must be able to produce exactly what was delivered, on which date, years later. GitLab's package registry stores files under a name and a version; the "generic" kind takes any file. The drop-package job uploads each drop's XMI, ReqIF, CSV and manifest under prime-drop/v1.0, prime-drop/v1.1 and so on, authenticated by the job's own short-lived token. The emulator has the same commands; in the lesson sandbox, file the drop the lesson ships with:

Value: the deliverable and the model it became are kept together, with checksums, retrievable by version. The receiving inspection the contracting officer's representative used to do by e-mail now has a record.

17.8.2 Releases and baselines

A release in GitLab is a page attached to a tag: notes, links, the evidence of what was checked. For the team, a release is the published face of a baseline. When a baseline-* tag passes its rebuild check, the publish-package job files the baseline itself in the package registry as tidewater-model/<tag> (the model and its generated docs as one archive, the verification matrix, the toolchain inventory and a checksum list), and the publish-release job creates the release: that baseline's section of the CHANGELOG as the notes, links to those package files as the release's assets, and the sprint milestones it closes. A downstream team that wants "the model as of baseline 1" downloads one versioned archive; nobody e-mails a zip. The team rehearsed the whole procedure on a scratch project in sprint 5 and used it for real for the interim baseline in sprint 6 (Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0).

GitLab also collects release evidence: a snapshot, taken when the release is created, of the issues and milestones it names and the test reports of the tag's pipeline. For a baseline, that snapshot is the configuration status accounting record: what was in it, what was checked, when.

17.8.3 Time tracking

Issues and merge requests accept /estimate and /spend quick actions. The team used them for one reason: the twelve-week comparison with the document era needed effort numbers, and estimating after the fact is guessing. They did not use time tracking to judge individuals, and said so in the working agreements.

17.9 Sprint 6: showing the flow

17.9.1 Environments

An environment is GitLab's name for a place a pipeline deploys to. For a software team that is a test server or production. For the model team there is one: the model site. Naming the pages job's environment model-site gives a page (Operate > Environments) listing every deployment of the site with the commit and merge request it came from. When the deputy program manager asked "what changed on the site since Tuesday?", the answer was a list.

17.9.2 Value stream analytics

Value stream analytics measures how long work spends in each stage: issue created, first commit, merge request opened, merged. The Free tier shows a limited project-level view; Premium adds custom stages. The team used it once, for the management briefing, as a cross-check on the numbers its own scripts computed from the exported merge request history (Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard).

The same numbers are available on any tier from the kit, because they are computed from data every tier's API exposes: gitlab.pl analytics --by sprint prints the value stream stages, the four DORA measures translated for a model repository, pipeline success rates and durations, merge request throughput and issue flow, and --csv DIR writes them for a spreadsheet. Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics explains each number and which ones belong in a briefing. On the lesson's sandbox, with only a few days of history, most of them are still empty:

17.10 Tokens: which one, where

Tokens confused the whole team, so the team made a table. A token is a password for a program rather than a person. GitLab has several kinds, and choosing the right one is most of security in practice:

Table 17.4. GitLab tokens and what each is for
TokenWho or what holds itLifetimeThe team used it for
Personal access tokenone personuntil its expiry date (set one)gitlab.pl setup and ad hoc scripts on a laptop
Project access tokena bot user tied to one projectuntil its expiry datethe weekly status export (read_api only), stored as a masked variable
Deploy tokena machine outside the project, limited to named scopesuntil its expiry dateLATER: the prime's Jenkins uploads drops with write_package_registry only (gitlab.pl token deploy new, Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition)
CI job token (CI_JOB_TOKEN)one running jobonly while the job runsuploading drops to the package registry
Runner authentication tokenthe runneruntil the runner is re-registeredregistering the Windows runner (Tom and the admins)
Trigger tokena system outside GitLab that starts a pipelineuntil revokedLATER: the prime's Jenkins starts the intake pipeline after an upload (gitlab.pl trigger new)

The rules the team kept: prefer the job token (it expires by itself); give every other token an expiry date and the narrowest scope; store tokens in masked, protected CI/CD variables or in your shell's environment, never in a file in a repository; rotate them every 90 days (Chapter 42, Administration).

17.10.1 Protected and masked variables

CI/CD variables (Settings > CI/CD > Variables) are values the pipeline can read as environment variables. Two flags matter:

  • Masked: GitLab replaces the value with [MASKED] if a job prints it in a log.
  • Protected: the value is only given to pipelines running on protected branches and tags. A pipeline on someone's feature branch never sees it.

STATUS_TOKEN, the read-only token the weekly export uses, is both. KIT, the path of the kit on the runner, is neither: it is not a secret, and every job needs it.

17.11 What the team deliberately left off

Table 17.5. Features the team did not use, and why
FeatureWhy not, for now
SAST (static application security testing)scans source code for vulnerabilities; the repository holds a model, not code. Revisit if the team writes tools
Dependency scanninglists vulnerable software libraries; the model has none, and the kit is a separate, reviewed checkout
Container scanningscans Docker images; the runner uses no containers
GitLab Requirements Management (Ultimate)would create a second requirements database; DOORS stays authoritative, and the trace job compares against it
Merge trains (Premium)queue merges to keep a busy branch green; three people merging a few times a day do not need a queue
Auto DevOpsbuilds and deploys software by convention; it has nothing to build
Feature flags, error tracking, incident managementfor running software in production
Compliance frameworks and pipelines (Ultimate)enforce a pipeline across many projects; one project does not need it yet

None of these is a bad feature. Each was left off because the problem it solves was not one the team had. Two of them (SAST, if the team ever writes its own scripts into the repository, and compliance pipelines, if the organization puts several model repositories on the same rules) are on the list to revisit at the end of each semester (Chapter 42, Administration).

17.12 The cost side

Every tool above has a cost, and the briefing in Chapter 35, The briefing states it honestly:

  • Runner time: the pipeline takes well under a minute of checks per merge request on the team's runner (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job has the job timings); the nightly and weekly schedules add a few minutes a week.
  • Attention: each widget is one more thing on the merge request page. The team removed none, but the rule was that a widget nobody looked at for a sprint would be switched off.
  • Licenses: everything adopted in the twelve weeks runs on the Free tier, except the metrics widget and enforced code owner approvals, which the team practiced on the emulator and requested for the second year.

17.13 Exercises

Exercise 17.1: Apply the rule

List three problems your team has today with its documents or its model. For each, name the GitLab tool from this chapter that addresses it, and the problem it would create if you turned it on before anyone felt the original problem.

Exercise 17.2: Read a widget

Create a branch in your practice project, break one part type as Bob did, and run the pipeline locally (gitlab.pl ci --event merge_request_event --target develop). Open lint.xml and lint-cq.json. Which line of each would GitLab show on the merge request?

Exercise 17.3: Choose the token

For each job, choose a token from the token table and justify it: (a) a laptop script that lists open issues every morning; (b) the pipeline job that uploads a drop; (c) a scheduled export to a reporting server outside GitLab.

Exercise 17.4: Argue for one left-off tool

Pick one feature from the "left off" table and write the paragraph that would convince Tom to turn it on. What evidence would you need?

17.14 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the adoption rule (a tool goes on when a felt problem costs more than the tool); issues with scoped labels and milestones; protected branches and merge requests; a three-job pipeline on day one; report widgets as soon as people complain about reading logs; Secret Detection; Pages for everyone who will not open a repository; the package registry for contract deliverables; releases for baselines.
  • Adapt: the order (if your ISSM asks for secret scanning on day one, do it on day one); the tiers (check what your license has before promising a feature); the schedules (nightly may be weekly for a slow-moving model).
  • Decide locally: which tokens your organization allows; who may create project access tokens; how long artifacts and logs are kept; whether the model site may be visible beyond the project's members.

18 A local AI assistant on the laptop

From what you know

You know

asking a colleague to look over a draft.

Here it is called

a local AI model on the laptop.

What is new

a draft in seconds, never trusted, checked by the same gates as anything you write.

Survival kit

What you have

a model repository, a pipeline that checks every change (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job), Vim (Chapter 10, Vim for models), and a laptop with no discrete graphics card and somewhere between 16 and 32 GB of memory.

What you need

to know whether a language model running on that laptop (or on a shared server down the hall) can take some of the typing off the team -- and how to use one without letting it put a single unchecked line into the model. This chapter is the approval path, the two ways to host a model, a one-day bake-off to pick one, the SysML v2 caveat every reader must understand, the rules, and worked Tidewater uses in the order they pay off.

Every chapter so far has been about tools that are deterministic: the grammar check gives the same answer for the same file every time, and so does lint, and so does the pipeline. This chapter is about a tool that is not. A language model writes plausible text. Sometimes the text is right. Sometimes it is wrong in a way that looks exactly like right. The whole value of the chapter is in how the team keeps the first kind and catches the second, and the answer is the same one the rest of the book gives: the gates decide, not the author -- and the model is just another author.

Nothing in the Tidewater process needs an AI assistant. The kit runs without one, the pipeline runs without one, the twelve weeks in Part III were planned without one. Treat everything here as optional, and adopt it the way the team adopted every other tool (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep): when a problem you already have costs more than the tool does, and not before.

18.1 What a local model is, in plain words

A language model is a large file of numbers -- a few gigabytes -- that was built by feeding a program an enormous amount of text and adjusting the numbers until the program got good at one thing: given the beginning of a piece of text, guess the next word. Do that guess thousands of times in a row and you get a paragraph, an answer, a block of code. That is all it does. It has no model of Tidewater, no copy of the SysML v2 specification, no idea whether the text it produced will parse. It has a very good statistical sense of what text of that kind usually looks like.

A local model is one that runs on a machine you control: the laptop, or a server on the program's network. The program that runs it is called a runtime; the one this chapter uses is Ollama, a free runtime that downloads models, keeps them on disk, and answers questions about them on the laptop's own network port (11434). You type a question, the runtime feeds it to the model, the model's answer comes back as text. Nothing leaves the machine.

The systems-engineering analogy that works best: a local model is a junior analyst with a photographic memory of other people's documents and no access to yours. Fast, tireless, eager, frequently right about general things, confidently wrong about specific ones, and never the signature on anything. You would not let a new hire's first draft go to the CCB without review. The same rule applies here, and the pipeline enforces it.

Definitions
model
the file of numbers that writes text (a few GB); one model, many questions
runtime
the program that loads the model and answers questions (Ollama)
prompt
the text you give the model -- your question plus whatever context you paste in
context window
how much text the model can consider at once (prompt plus answer); tens of thousands of words for current models
parameters
the count of numbers in the model ("4B" = 4 billion); more usually means better and slower
mixture of experts
a model built so only part of it works on each word; big-model quality at a lower running cost
grounding
pasting the facts the model must use (spec excerpts, your names, good examples) into the prompt
hallucination
fluent, confident text that is false -- an invented library name, a keyword that does not exist

18.2 Why local, and not a cloud chatbot

Everyone on the team has seen a cloud chatbot. The question Jim got first, from Bob, was why not just use that.

Table 18.1. Cloud chatbot versus local model
QuestionCloud chatbotLocal model
Where does the prompt go?to a company's servers, over the internetnowhere: it stays on the machine
Can it see Tidewater files?only what you paste -- and pasting is the problemonly what you paste, and the paste stays local
Works offline / on a closed network?noyes, once the model file is on the machine
Approval patha cloud service authorization for the data's markinga software intake request, like any other install
Qualityusually higher (very large models)lower, especially on a laptop CPU
Speedfasta few words a second on a CPU; faster on a GPU server
Costper seat or per usethe hardware you already have, or one server

The deciding row is the first one. Model text, interface details and requirement wording are program information. On most programs, pasting them into a public chatbot is simply not allowed, whatever the chatbot's terms say, and the kit's own AI hook (lib/Ai.pm) repeats the same rule in its header: only use a service your organisation allows for the data's marking. A local model changes the question from "may this data leave the building?" (usually no) to "may this software run on this machine?" (a question the software intake process already knows how to answer).

That is the whole case for local. It is not that local models are better -- they are not. It is that they are the version of the tool the team can actually get approved.

18.3 Approval comes first

Before anyone types ollama pull, two things need approval, separately: the runtime (Ollama is an executable, installed like any other program) and each model (a multi-gigabyte data file with its own origin, license and training data). Approving one does not approve the other, and approving one model does not approve the next.

18.3.1 Model provenance is a policy question, not a technical one

The SysML-tuned model the kit documents in docs/OLLAMA.md, Babitdor/Qwen3-4B-SysMLv2, is a community fine-tune published by a single individual, with no stated license and no stated training data -- and it is built on Qwen3, a base model of Chinese origin. Many organizations' policies restrict the origin of AI models regardless of whether they run offline: the concern is the provenance of the numbers themselves, not where the prompts go. Read your organization's AI policy before pulling any model, and expect origin to be one of the first questions the approver asks.

If origin is restricted, the families to look at come from US and allied developers. Each publishes several sizes, and the Ollama library lists them; this book does not quote sizes, tags or benchmark scores, because they change faster than books do and none of them could be verified on the machine this chapter was written on:

Table 18.2. Model families from US and allied developers (check the Ollama library for current tags and memory needs)
FamilyDeveloperNotes for the request
gpt-ossOpenAIopen-weight models; check the license and sizes on the Ollama library page
GemmaGoogleseveral sizes; check the license terms on the model page
LlamaMetawidely used; check the license's use restrictions
GraniteIBMpositioned for enterprise use; check the license
PhiMicrosoftsmall models aimed at modest hardware
Mistral, DevstralMistral AI (France)Devstral is aimed at code and tooling work

None of these was trained to write SysML v2 text, and neither, in any depth, was the Qwen3 fine-tune (Section 18.7, The SysML v2 caveat). That matters less than it sounds, because the best uses for the team are not writing .sysml at all (Section 18.10, Worked uses, best fit first).

18.3.2 What to put in the request

Checklist
  • ☐ What: the runtime (Ollama, version, download source) and each model (name, tag, digest from ollama list, publisher, base model and its origin, license, size on disk)
  • ☐ Where: which machines (named laptops, or one shared server) and who has access
  • ☐ Data: what goes into prompts (model text, requirement text, pipeline logs) and its marking; a statement that prompts and answers stay on the machine
  • ☐ Network: whether the machine needs internet (only to download), and the offline route if it does not have it
  • ☐ Use: drafting and explaining only; every output passes the same review and pipeline gates as hand-written work; a human commits it
  • ☐ Measure: the bake-off results (Section 18.6, A one-day bake-off before you standardize) and what will be measured afterwards
  • ☐ Removal: how to uninstall and delete the model files (ollama rm, and the models folder)

Send it through the same channel as any software request, and copy the ISSM. The ISSM's questions will be about the runtime's network behavior (it listens on localhost:11434; confirm it is not exposed beyond the machine), the model file's integrity (the digest), and the data rule. Have the answers in the request and the review is short.

18.4 Two ways to host it: every laptop, or one shared server

The typical government laptop has no discrete GPU and 16 to 32 GB of memory. That rules out large models on the laptop and makes small ones slow: on a CPU, a small model produces a few words a second. Two hosting options follow from that, and the trade-off is worth deciding deliberately:

Table 18.3. Laptop installs versus a shared GPU server
Ollama on each laptopOne approved GPU server on the program network
Accreditationone approval, but installed on every laptop; each install is a change to a managed machineone system to accredit, once; laptops need nothing but a browser or curl
Model sizesmall models only, or mixture-of-experts models that run acceptably on a CPUlarger models; much faster answers
Works whenthe laptop is on, even disconnectedthe laptop is on the program network
Data pathprompt never leaves the laptopprompt crosses the program network to the server (still on the program network)
Administrationevery user updates their own runtime and modelsone administrator; one approved model list
Costnone beyond the laptopsa server with a GPU, and someone to run it

For a three-person team, the laptop route is quicker to start and the server route is easier to live with. A shared server is often easier to accredit than installs on every laptop, because it is one system with one boundary and one owner, and it allows bigger models that are noticeably better at the hard tasks. If the program already runs a GPU server for analysis or simulation, ask there first.

Pointing the tools at a server instead of the laptop is one setting. Ollama serves the same API in both places, so the kit's hook (ai_url in scrum.conf, Section 18.10.8, 8. The stand-up summary through the kit's AI hook) just names the server's address instead of localhost.

18.5 Installing on a laptop, without admin rights and offline

The steps are the ones in docs/OLLAMA.md; this section repeats them so the book stands alone. Requirements, from Ollama's Windows documentation: Windows 10 22H2 or newer, about 4 GB of disk for Ollama itself plus the model's size. A GPU is optional; without one Ollama runs on the CPU, more slowly.

  1. Download OllamaSetup.exe from https://ollama.com/download.
  2. Run it. It does not need Administrator: it installs into your home folder and adds a tray icon.
  3. Check it from Git Bash:

No installer allowed? Ollama also ships a standalone ollama-windows-amd64.zip (command line only): unzip it into a folder in your home directory, run ollama serve in one Git Bash window and use ollama from another.

Models go to C:\Users\<you>\.ollama\models. To keep them elsewhere (another drive, outside OneDrive), set the user environment variable OLLAMA_MODELS and restart Ollama.

Getting a model -- once the model is approved:

Check that the ID in ollama list matches the digest in the approval. If it does not, the model on the registry has changed since it was approved: stop, and re-approve before using it. The same rule applies to whichever model you are approved for.

When the work laptop has no internet, bring the model in by the approved offline route:

  1. On an approved machine with internet, install Ollama and pull the model.
  2. Copy the whole models folder (with its manifests and blobs subfolders) to approved removable media, and record a checksum of the archive:
  1. On the work laptop, check the checksum, unpack it into %USERPROFILE%\.ollama\ (or wherever OLLAMA_MODELS points), restart Ollama, and run ollama list to confirm the ID.

To remove it: ollama rm the model, then uninstall Ollama from Settings, "Add or remove programs", and delete the models folder yourself if you moved it.

18.6 A one-day bake-off before you standardize

Do not pick a model by reading about it. Pick it by giving two or three approved candidates the team's own tasks for one day and scoring the results the same way the team scores its own work: did it pass the gates, and how long did a person spend turning the draft into something mergeable?

Five Tidewater tasks make a good bake-off, because they cover the range from the model's best fit to its worst:

  1. Explain a TODO. Paste a converter TODO line and its v1 XMI fragment; ask what the v1 construct is and what the v2 equivalent would be. Score: correct explanation (Bob judges), minutes to read.
  2. Draft a state def. Ask for the v2 text of the BuoyModes state machine. Score: passes sysml.pl check (yes/no, how many tries), passes lint inside the model, minutes of hand fixing.
  3. Write a ci/job.pl helper. Ask for a small Perl function the pipeline needs (for example, count the TODO lines per package). Score: perl -c passes, it runs on the drop-1 conversion, the output is right, minutes.
  4. Draft a Discrepancy Report. Give the drift between DOORS and the model for TW-SYS-006; ask for a DR to the prime in the template's fields. Score: facts correct, tone usable, minutes of editing.
  5. Explain a pipeline log. Paste a failing lint job log; ask what failed and what to change. Score: correct cause, correct fix, minutes.

Each person runs each task once per candidate, with the same prompt (write the prompts down first; they are part of the result). Score into one sheet:

Table 18.4. Bake-off scoresheet (one row per task, per model, per person)
TaskModelPasses gateTriesMinutes to mergeableCorrect?Notes
1 Explain a TODOcandidate An/a1
2 Draft a state defcandidate Agrammar / lint
3 ci/job.pl helpercandidate Aperl -c / runs
4 Draft a DRcandidate An/a
5 Explain a logcandidate An/a
1 Explain a TODOcandidate Bn/a

Add a baseline row for each task: the same person doing it without the model. If the model's "minutes to mergeable" does not beat the baseline on at least two of the five tasks, the honest result is "not yet", and that is a perfectly good result to report. Keep the sheet; it goes in the approval request, and it is the first data point of the measurement the rules below require.

18.7 The SysML v2 caveat

Here is the most important paragraph in the chapter. Every general-purpose model is weak at SysML v2 textual syntax, because there was very little SysML v2 text on the internet when these models were trained. The language is new, the textual notation newer, and most published SysML is v1 diagrams. So the model has seen a great deal of UML, a great deal of SysML v1 described in prose, and a great deal of code in languages that look a little like SysML v2 -- and it blends them. The result is text that is plausible but invalid: v1 vocabulary in v2 clothing (state machine, region, block), keywords borrowed from programming languages, and library names that sound exactly right and do not exist. A SysML-tuned model reduces this; it does not remove it.

Two mitigations, and both are needed:

  • Grounding. Paste the facts into the prompt: the relevant excerpt of the specification (the textual notation for the construct you want), the model library names it may use (the kit ships the full list in tools/sysml/sysml-library-names.txt), and one or two good examples from your own repository. A crude but effective retrieval step is grep: find the existing text closest to what you want and paste it. The model is much better at "do it like this" than at "do it from memory".
  • The validate stage. Everything the model writes goes through sysml.pl check and model.pl lint, exactly like hand-written text, before a human even reviews it. The worked examples below show both gates catching real mistakes.

The consequence for how the team uses the assistant is the ordering of the next section: the best uses are the ones around the model -- small Perl helpers, pipeline YAML, report scripts, requirement and DR wording, explanations -- where the model's training is strong and the result is easy to test. Writing .sysml is the weaker fit, and comes last.

18.8 The rules

Warning: The rules for AI-assisted work

Never trusted. A model's output is a draft from an author with no accountability. It is read, checked and owned by a person before it goes anywhere.

Same gates. AI-drafted text goes through the same branch, merge request, pipeline and code-owner approval as everything else. No gate is relaxed for it, and no gate is added that hand-written work skips.

A human owns the commit. The person who commits it is the author of record. "The model wrote it" is never an answer in review.

Label it. A merge request that contains AI-drafted text carries the scoped label ai::assisted (add it under [labels] in project.conf; it is not in the template's set). The label is how the team measures.

Measure before claiming value. Use the bake-off sheet's columns -- gate passes, tries, minutes to mergeable -- on labeled merge requests. Report what the numbers say, including "it did not help with X".

Data rule. Prompts carry only what the machine is approved for. A local model does not change the marking of the text you paste into it.

Two practical limits belong next to the rules. A 4-billion-parameter model on a laptop CPU is slow (a few words a second; a state def takes a minute or two) and has a short attention span: long prompts with many instructions get partly ignored. And every answer can differ from the last one for the same prompt -- run it twice and you may get two drafts. Neither is a reason not to use it; both are reasons to keep prompts short and specific.

Prompt patterns that work, in the team's experience writing this chapter's examples:

  • One construct at a time. "The state def for BuoyModes", not "fix the Stations package".
  • Give it the three things it needs: the v1 XMI fragment, the converter's TODO line, and the surrounding v2 text the answer must fit (the package's imports and the owning part def).
  • Ask for text only. "SysML v2 text only, no explanation" -- then ask for the explanation separately if you want one.
  • Name the names. "Use the attribute defs Power and Energy from package Types" beats letting it guess.
  • Paste the error back. When the gate fails, paste the real error message and the draft and ask for a fix. Two rounds of that is the limit; after that, write it by hand.

18.9 Using it from Git Bash and from Vim

The commands in this section need Ollama and an approved model on your laptop, so the book's own test does not run them; the checks of the drafts they produce, later in the chapter, were run for real. From Git Bash, a one-shot question:

Or an interactive session (ollama run MODEL with no prompt; type /bye to leave). Qwen3-based models can print a <think>...</think> section before the answer; ignore it, or turn it off with /set nothink inside a session.

To keep a prompt you will reuse, write it in a file -- prompts are worth versioning like anything else -- and feed it in:

From Vim, three forms cover nearly everything. All three were checked in Vim with a stand-in ollama command; the model name is whichever one you were approved for:

Form 2 is the one to use for model text: the draft lands in a throwaway buffer, not in the model file. Save the buffer as a .sysml file in a scratch folder, press \mx (grammar-check this file, Chapter 10, Vim for models), fix, and only then copy the passing text into the real file -- where \ml (lint the model) checks it in context.

18.10 Worked uses, best fit first

Every assistant answer below is illustrative: the machine this book was written on could not run the model (its Ollama was too old for Qwen3-based models, and no model was pulled), so the answers are written to show the kind of text such a model produces, including its typical mistakes. Every check below is real: each draft was saved to a file and run through the kit's actual gates, and the output shown is the gates' actual output.

18.10.1 1. A helper script for the pipeline (best fit)

Small Perl helpers are where a model is strongest: Perl is all over its training data, the task is self-contained, and the result is easy to test. Bob wanted the TODO count per package, to decide which package to port next.

The prompt:

The draft (illustrative):

The real checks: perl -c and a run on the real drop-1 conversion.

Fifty-two TODO lines, the same total the converter's report and Part I give for drop 1, so the script agrees with an independent count -- that comparison is the test. It took one prompt and two minutes of reading. This is the kind of task the bake-off's third row measures, and it is the kind that usually wins.

18.10.2 2. Explaining a failing pipeline log

The second-best fit: a log is text, the model has seen a great many of them, and the explanation is checked by whether the fix works. Here is a real lint failure (the draft that caused it appears in Section 18.10.6, 6. SysML v2 text: the EnergyBalance constraint):

An explanation of the kind a model gives (illustrative):

That one is right, and it is checkable: grep the library list (tools/sysml/sysml-library-names.txt has PowerValue and EnergyValue, and no SolarPowerValue). The habit to build: when the explanation names a fix, confirm the fix exists before you make it.

18.10.3 3. Text for people: an MR description, a DR, a retro summary

Prose is a strong fit, and the review is the same as for any draft: facts first, then tone. Give the model the facts in the prompt -- it must not supply them.

A Discrepancy Report draft (illustrative), from the prompt "Draft a discrepancy report to the prime contractor in these fields: Title, Model element, DOORS object, What we found, Evidence, Requested action. Facts: TW-SYS-006 text differs: DOORS says the bulletin is published twice a day on a fixed schedule; the Cameo model's requirement text says only on a fixed schedule. Found by the trace job's drift check.":

Every fact in it came from the prompt; the model supplied the structure and the sentences. Jim's edit was one word. Notice what the reviewer checks: that it did not add a fact (a date, a paragraph number, a severity) that was not given. Models add plausible details; in a DR to a contractor, an invented detail is worse than a missing one.

The same pattern works for a merge request description ("here is the diff summary and the issue number; fill the Default template") and for a retrospective summary ("here are the sticky notes, verbatim; group them into start, stop, continue without changing any wording"). In both, paste the facts, ask for structure, check that nothing was added.

18.10.4 4. Explaining a converter TODO and its v1 construct

Useful for learning, especially in the first weeks when the team is still matching v1 vocabulary to v2. The prompt gives the TODO line and the XMI fragment it came from -- both real, from drop 1:

An explanation of the kind a model gives (illustrative): "This is a UML state machine owned by the MooredBuoy block. It has one region with an initial pseudostate and four states -- Observing, Degraded, Maintenance, Recovered -- and transitions triggered by named events such as lowBattery and charged. In SysML v2 the equivalent is a state def with states and transitions, exhibited by the part def; the triggers become accepted items or attributes, and the initial pseudostate becomes an entry action followed by the first state."

That is correct and is exactly the mental bridge a v1 modeler needs. Compare it with Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers, where the same mapping is shown by hand. The explanation is cheap to check -- every claim is visible in the fragment above.

18.10.5 5. SysML v2 text, the weaker fit: the BuoyModes state def

Now the hard part: three drafts of model text, each through the real gates. The first draft (illustrative) is what an under-grounded model typically writes -- the v1 vocabulary leaks straight through:

The real grammar check:

Exit status 1: in the pipeline this is a red grammar job. Read the error the way Chapter 10, Vim for models taught: line 2, column 19. The parser read state machine as "a state usage named machine" and then choked on the next word. There is no state machine in SysML v2, and no region, no initial ->, no source -> target : trigger -- all four are UML. Pasting the error back may get a better second draft; on a 4B model it often gets a different wrong one. Bob wrote it by hand, from Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers's pattern:

Then in context: the TODO line in model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml replaced by exhibit state modes : BuoyModes; inside MooredBuoy, and the state def and its five trigger attribute defs added to the package. The real checks on the whole drop-1 model afterwards:

The lesson is not "the model failed". The draft still saved time: the five state names and the six transitions were right, and copying them was faster than reading the XMI. The syntax was wrong, the gate said so in one line, and a person who knew the v2 pattern fixed it. That is the realistic shape of AI help on .sysml today.

18.10.6 6. SysML v2 text: the EnergyBalance constraint

The converter left two TODO lines in Analysis.sysml, one of them carrying the v1 expression in English: generation * sunHours >= load * 24. A grounded prompt ("here is the constraint def, here is the expression, write the v2 constraint body; parameters are inputs") gets close. This draft (illustrative) shows the other classic mistake -- invented library names that sound exactly right:

The grammar check passes it -- the syntax is perfectly good:

This is why the pipeline has two gates and not one. Spliced into the model, lint catches what grammar cannot: the names resolve to nothing.

There is a quieter lesson in the fix. ISQ::PowerValue and ISQ::EnergyValue exist, and swapping them in makes lint pass -- but the rest of Tidewater uses the model's own attribute defs Power and Energy (package Types), and the PowerSystem's bind lines connect this constraint to parts typed with them. The right fix is the model's own types, which is a judgment no gate makes for you:

Real result, in the model: lint: 14 file(s), 0 error(s), 0 warning(s) and the grammar check clean. Note too that the v1 expression mentions sunHours, which the v1 constraint block never declared as a parameter; the draft added it, correctly, and the reviewer has to notice that the model added a parameter -- a design decision worth a line in the merge request, and a question for the prime's modeler.

18.10.7 7. SysML v2 text: fork and flow in ObserveCoast

The behavior package has four TODO lines in ObserveCoast: a fork node after the quality check, an input pin, an object flow and a control flow. A draft for the fork and the flow (illustrative), grounded with the action def's real text:

Replacing the fork TODO, the first check then store; line, and the two edge TODOs with those lines, the real checks on the model:

That draft passed first time -- the construct is close to what the model has seen in other languages. The input pin TODO stays for a later task, and the helper from example 1 shows the effect of the three fixes together on a scratch copy of the model:

From 52 to 46. Passing the gates is necessary, not sufficient: the reviewer still asks whether the fork is where the v1 activity put it, whether 'log health' should run in parallel with archiving, and whether the flow goes to the right parameter. Those are engineering questions, and they are why a person owns the commit.

18.10.8 8. The stand-up summary through the kit's AI hook

The kit can hand the day's stand-up data to an AI and put the answer in the status mail. lib/Ai.pm has three backends: paste (the default: it writes the prompt to a file, you paste it wherever you are allowed to), mock (tests), and curl (an OpenAI-style chat endpoint -- which is what Ollama serves). In the journal project's scrum.conf:

Then perl bin/daily.pl ai (Vim: :SAi) sends the day's digest -- answers, flags, the sprint's numbers -- and parses the reply into five fixed sections: HIGHLIGHTS, RISKS, STUCK, QUESTIONS FOR LEADS, PROGRESS. On a shared server, ai_url names the server instead of localhost.

Two cautions. A SysML-tuned model was tuned for SysML, not for status writing; a general model from the approved list will usually write better summaries, and ai_model picks which. And the numbers never come from the AI: the kit computes every metric from the journal, and the AI only words the summary around them. If its wording contradicts a number, the number wins and the wording is edited.

18.11 What the team took from it

Case study: Bob's first try

Bob's first prompt was "convert the Stations package to SysML v2". The answer was four screens of confident text that did not parse, used block throughout, and invented a package import. Bob's verdict, after the grammar check listed the errors, was the one most engineers reach: "It's a fast typist that doesn't know the language." The second prompt -- one state def, with the XMI fragment and the surrounding text pasted in -- produced the draft in example 5: wrong syntax, right content, fixed in five minutes. The third prompt asked for the helper script in example 1 and was right the first time. The team's ranking of uses came out of that afternoon, and it matched what this chapter recommends.

The ranking, for the record: helper scripts and pipeline glue first, explanations second, prose drafts third, .sysml drafts last -- and every one of them through the same gates. A team that starts at the bottom of that list concludes AI is useless; a team that starts at the top concludes it is a useful junior analyst. Both are looking at the same tool.

Exercise 18.1: Write the approval request

Fill in the request checklist in Section 18.3, Approval comes first for your own organization: one runtime, one model you would choose from the families table, the laptops or server, the data rule. Find out which office approves model origin.

Exercise 18.2: Run a three-task bake-off

Pick three of the five bake-off tasks. Write the prompts down first. Run each with one approved model and without one. Fill the scoresheet: gate passes, tries, minutes to mergeable. Does the model beat the baseline on any task?

Exercise 18.3: Make the gates catch a hallucination

Take the invented-name EnergyBalance draft from Section 18.10.6, 6. SysML v2 text: the EnergyBalance constraint, splice it into a scratch copy of the drop-1 conversion, and run sysml.pl check and model.pl lint. Which gate catches it, and why can the other one not? Fix it with the model's own types and run both again.

Exercise 18.4: The scratch-buffer loop in Vim

Using form 2 from Section 18.9, Using it from Git Bash and from Vim, send a TODO line and its XMI fragment to a model (or, without one, to cat in place of ollama run ... to practice the keystrokes), save the scratch buffer as a .sysml file, and press \mx. Time the whole loop.

Exercise 18.5: Check a draft for added facts

Ask a model (or a colleague playing one) to draft the TW-SYS-006 DR from the facts in example 3. Underline every fact in the draft that was not in the prompt. How many were there, and which would have embarrassed you in front of the prime?

18.12 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the rules box, word for word; the ai::assisted label; the bake-off scoresheet; the scratch-buffer loop; the order of uses (tooling, explanations, prose, then model text).
  • Adapt: the model list to your organization's approved list and its origin policy; the hosting choice to what your program already runs (a shared GPU server, if one exists, is usually the better start); the bake-off tasks to five real tasks from your own backlog.
  • Decide locally: whether AI-assisted work is allowed at all on your network and for your data's marking; who approves models; whether the team needs it yet -- the honest answer after a bake-off may be "not yet", and that is a result.
  • Never adapt: the gates. AI-drafted text gets exactly the checks hand-written text gets. If a team ever proposes relaxing a gate "because the AI usually gets that right", the bake-off sheet is the answer.

19 CI/CD from zero

From what you know

You know

the configuration audit and the peer-review checklist, run before a milestone.

Here it is called

continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD).

What is new

the audit and the checklist run on every change, in minutes, and the products are rebuilt every time.

Survival kit

What you have

a GitLab project (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab), git on your laptop (Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers), and a sense from Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep that "the pipeline" is the most important tool in the box.

What you need

to understand what continuous integration and continuous delivery are, in words you already use; to know the parts of a pipeline by name; to read a job log, passing and failing; to run the pipeline on your own laptop before you push; and to explain a red pipeline to a manager. No programming. The next chapter, Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job, then walks through the team's real pipeline file line by line.

19.1 Tom's question

On the Wednesday of week one, Tom stood at the whiteboard with a marker and asked the question that the whole team had been too embarrassed to ask:

Everybody keeps saying CI/CD. I run configuration management for a living. Is this something I already do with a new name, or something new?

— Tom, sprint 1, day 3

The honest answer is: both. Continuous integration and continuous delivery are practices that systems engineering already has, done at a speed and a regularity that only a machine can manage. This chapter takes the two halves in turn, then the vocabulary, then the skill of reading what a pipeline tells you.

19.2 CI: continuous integration, in systems engineering words

Integration is a word systems engineers own. It is the moment the parts come together and you find out whether they fit. In the document era, integration of the descriptions of the system (the specification, the interface documents, the requirement matrix) happened at milestone reviews: every few months, someone gathered the latest version of each document, read them side by side, and wrote down where they disagreed. Between reviews, each document drifted on its own. The drift was found late, in a conference room, and fixed by hand.

Continuous integration means that every change is integrated into the shared description the same day it is made, and is checked automatically when it is. In the model's terms:

  • every change is made on a short branch and proposed as a merge request against develop, the shared model;
  • before anyone reviews it, a machine runs the same set of checks on the combined result (the change merged into the latest shared model), in minutes;
  • if a check fails, the change does not merge until it is fixed;
  • changes are small enough (one task, under a week of work, usually a day) that a failure points at a handful of lines, not a binder.

Compare that with two things Tom knew well:

  • A configuration audit checks that the configuration item matches its documentation. Done by people, it happens at a few milestones a year. CI runs a configuration audit on every change.
  • A peer review checklist asks the same questions of every document: are the requirements numbered, does every interface have two ends, is every term defined. Done by people, it depends on who has time. CI runs the checklist the same way every time.

So CI is the configuration audit and the peer review checklist, run by a machine on every change, before I sign.

— Tom, writing on the whiteboard

That sentence is the definition this book uses.

Note: What "integrate" does not mean here

Continuous integration of the model does not mean the hardware is integrated, or that the model is "complete". It means the shared description is always in a state that passed its checks. That is a smaller claim, and a much more useful one than the document era could make: on any given day, the model on develop is consistent with itself, by the rules the team wrote down.

19.3 CD: continuous delivery

Delivery is also a word systems engineers own: the contract data requirement says what must be delivered, in what form, when. In the document era, producing a deliverable was a project: export the diagrams, regenerate the tables, assemble the document, check the cross-references, convert to PDF, route for signature. It took days, and so it happened only when someone demanded it.

Continuous delivery means the products of the model are produced by the pipeline from the model, never by hand, and are always ready to hand over. For the Tidewater team the products are:

  • the generated documents: the part tree, the function tree, the traceability report;
  • the diagrams the kit's view tools draw from the text;
  • the requirement trace against DOORS;
  • the model website (GitLab Pages, Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep);
  • for each baseline, the release notes and the evidence that the baseline rebuilds identically.

None of these is ever edited by hand. If one is wrong, the model is wrong, and the fix is a change to the model.

The "D" is sometimes read as deployment: putting new software into service. For a model team there is almost nothing to deploy. The only deployment in this book is publishing the model website after each merge, and publishing a release when a baseline is tagged. When people at your organization say "CI/CD", they usually mean the whole idea; this book does too.

19.4 The anatomy of a pipeline

A pipeline is the set of automated checks and production steps that GitLab runs for one event (a push, a merge request, a tag, a schedule). It is described in one file at the top of the repository, .gitlab-ci.yml, written in a text format called YAML (indentation matters; Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job explains the few rules you need).

Here is the vocabulary, each word with its Tidewater example.

Definitions: The parts of a pipeline
pipeline
one run of the checks for one event. Example: the run GitLab starts when Bob opens a merge request that closes the Stations level-tag TODOs.
stage
a group of jobs that run together; stages run in order, and a stage starts only if the previous one passed. Example: check (grammar, lint, outline, todo, secrets), then trace (trace, vcrm), then docs.
job
one check or one production step; it runs a short script and passes or fails. Example: lint, which runs the kit's model linter and fails unless it finds zero errors and zero warnings.
script
the commands a job runs, the same commands you would type in a terminal. Example: perl ci/job.pl lint, which runs the linter and the report writer (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs explains why every job is one such line).
runner
the computer that runs the jobs. Example: a Windows machine with Git for Windows and the agile kit checked out, registered to the group by the enterprise administrators.
rules
when a job runs. Example: delta runs only on the branch that merges a prime drop; baseline only when a baseline-* tag is created.
artifact
a file a job keeps after it finishes, downloadable from the job page and passed to later jobs. Example: lint.txt, the linter's full output.
report
an artifact in a format GitLab understands and shows on the merge request page. Example: lint.xml, which fills the test widget.
variable
a named value the jobs can read. Example: KIT, the path of the kit on the runner.
cache
files kept between pipelines to save time. Example: none in this pipeline; the jobs are fast enough.
allow_failure
