a job whose failure shows yellow and does not block the merge. Example: the first version of trace, because most trace gaps are the prime's to fix (it later became a ratchet instead, Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).
manual job
a job that waits for someone to press its play button. Example: none yet.
environment
a named place a job deploys to, with a history of deployments. Example: model-site, the model website.

A picture helps. The merge request pipeline for an ordinary model change looks like this in GitLab's pipeline graph, one column per stage:

All six check jobs run at the same time (if the runner can run several at once; the team's runner ran them one after another, which made no practical difference at these durations). The trace stage starts when all of them pass, and docs when the three trace-stage jobs pass. After a merge into develop, a fourth stage, publish, rebuilds the model site (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

19.5 What starts a pipeline

Table 19.1. What starts a pipeline
EventGitLab's name for itWhat it is for, here
Someone pushes commits to a branch with no open merge requestpusha quick check of a draft; also every merge into develop or main
A merge request is opened or its branch is pushed againmerge_request_eventthe gate: the checks that must pass before the change may merge
A tag is createda tag pipeline (CI_COMMIT_TAG is set)the baseline audit and the release
A schedule firesschedulethe nightly check and the weekly status export
Someone presses "Run pipeline"weba manual re-run, for example after the runner was repaired

Two refinements matter.

One pipeline per change, not two. When a branch has an open merge request, a push to it would normally start both a branch pipeline and a merge request pipeline. The team's file has a workflow: section that suppresses the branch pipeline in that case (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). Fewer pipelines, less confusion about which result counts.

Schedules are cron. A schedule fires at times written as a cron expression (0 2 * * 1-5 is 02:00 on weekdays), on a branch you choose, and runs the pipeline as the schedule's owner. The team has two: nightly checks and the weekly status export (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep, Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

Merged results. The merge request pipeline runs on the result of merging the change into the current develop, not on the branch alone. If Bob's branch was started on Monday and Tom merged a change to an interface on Tuesday, Bob's Wednesday pipeline checks Bob's change together with Tom's. That is the integration in continuous integration. GitLab calls this a merged results pipeline; the kit's emulator does the same.

19.6 Every job starts from nothing

This is the idea that surprises everyone the first time, and it is the source of most "it works on my machine" puzzles. Each job runs in a fresh environment: the runner gets a clean copy of the repository at the commit being checked, runs the job's script, keeps the artifacts the job declared, and throws everything else away. The next job, even in the same pipeline, starts again from a clean copy.

Consequences:

  • A file one job writes is not there for the next job, unless the first job declares it as an artifact. Later stages download earlier stages' artifacts by default; a job can name the jobs it needs (needs: or dependencies:) to download only theirs.
  • Anything that must be the same for every job (the path of the kit, for example) is a variable, not something a job sets up and the next one inherits.
  • Something slow that does not change often (downloading tools, for software teams) can be kept in a cache between pipelines. A cache is a speed-up, never a correctness requirement: a job must still work if the cache is empty. The team's jobs take seconds and use no cache.
  • Your laptop is not fresh: it has files you created, settings you forgot, tools nobody else has. That is why the local run below runs each job's script in a controlled way, and why a pipeline is a better witness than "it worked for me".
Table 19.2. Artifacts, cache and variables
MechanismKeeps whatBetweenUse it for
Artifactfiles a job declaresjobs of the same pipeline, and for download afterwardsoutputs: reports, logs, the website
Cachefiles a job declares as cachepipelinesspeed-ups that are safe to lose
Variablea named valueevery jobsettings and secrets

19.7 Reading a pipeline

A pipeline answers three questions, in this order: did it pass, which job failed, and why. GitLab shows the first on the merge request (a green check mark or a red cross next to the pipeline), the second on the pipeline page (the graph above, with each job's status), and the third in the failed job's log: everything the job printed, line by line, with each command shown before its output.

19.7.1 A passing job, line by line

Here is the real log of the lint job on the team's import of drop 1, run on a laptop. Run it yourself in the sandbox of practice lesson 11 (perl $KIT/agile.pl practice 11 builds it), which holds the same import; GitLab's web page shows the same lines with timestamps and a few lines of runner preamble:

(The path of the kit, /opt/agile here, is wherever the runner's KIT variable points.) Read it as a transcript:

  • Lines starting with $ are commands; every other line is what the previous command printed.
  • The first line is the job's whole script, perl ci/job.pl lint. Everything after it was printed by that script, which shows each command it runs before running it (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs explains why every job is one such line).
  • Before running anything, the script checks that the KIT variable is set and points at the kit. If not, the job stops with a sentence that says what to fix: KIT is not set: add it under Settings > CI/CD > Variables (the kit's path on the runner).
  • The linter checked 17 files and 148 model elements and found nothing wrong.
  • The report writer turned that output into the files GitLab shows on the merge request (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).
  • Then the script applies the gate: the linter's last line must end in errors=0 warnings=0. It printed nothing more, because nothing was wrong. Silence after the last command is success.

19.7.2 A failing job, line by line

On a scratch branch, Bob typed the part type Hull as Hul and ran the same job:

The line that matters is the third: model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml:38:21: error: unresolved type 'Hul'. Every checker in the kit writes problems in the same shape: file, line, column, severity, message. Line 38, column 21, of the Stations file names a type that does not exist. The last line, lint is not 0/0, is the gate saying why the job failed. Everything between is supporting detail.

Tip: The habit

When a pipeline is red: open the failed job, search the log for error:, read the first one, go to that file and line. Fix the first error first; later errors are often caused by it.

19.7.3 When the line number points one line too late

The grammar checker reads the text the way a parser does: token by token, until something cannot follow what came before. A missing semicolon is therefore reported where the parser noticed, which is the next line:

Line 39 is the part mooring line, which is perfectly fine; the mistake is the end of line 38. When a grammar error seems to point at an innocent line, look at the end of the line above. The list after "expected" is what the parser would have accepted instead; a semicolon is not in the visible part of the list, which is the parser's way of being unhelpful. Bob kept a sticky note on the monitor: grammar error: look one line up.

19.7.4 From the log to the line, in Vim

Reading line numbers off a web page and typing them into the editor is the document era's page-number hunt. Vim does it for you. The kit sets up Vim's quickfix list for SysML: inside the model repository, open any .sysml file and type

Here is the same thing run on the scratch branch with the Hul mistake, ending with :clist, which prints the list:

Vim runs the same linter the pipeline runs, reads its file:line:col: error: message lines, and jumps to the first problem. :cnext goes to the next one, :copen shows the list. :make check does the same for the outline check. Outside a model repository, :make checks the current file's grammar. Chapter 10, Vim for models covers the rest of Vim for models; the point here is that the pipeline and your editor speak the same format, so fixing a red pipeline is the same motion as fixing a typo.

19.8 Running it on your own machine first

A pipeline that fails on the server costs a few minutes and a red mark on the merge request. A pipeline that fails on your laptop before you push costs seconds and nobody sees it. The kit's gitlab.pl ci reads the same .gitlab-ci.yml, decides which jobs GitLab would run for a given event using the same rules, and runs them in the current repository.

First ask what would run. Throw the scratch branch away, then list:

On Bob's branch with the drop 1 import, the answer was:

Ten jobs would run; the others are for other events (a drop branch, a delivery from the prime, a tag, the default branch, the schedule, and two simulation jobs that wait for a test harness the program does not have yet), and the list says which rule excluded each. The third column names the file each job came from, which matters once a pipeline is split into several files with include: local (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). GitLab's own template for secret scanning is listed but not run: it only exists on the server, and only with a Docker runner (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs).

Then run them, dropping --list. Each job's log goes to a folder you name with --logs, and a failing job's last lines are printed under it:

Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job shows the full run, including how the outline job lives with the violations the raw drop 1 conversion inherited.

Note: The CI/CD editor on the server

GitLab has the same idea built in: Build > Pipeline editor. It checks the YAML as you type, shows the pipeline as a graph ("Visualize"), validates it against a chosen branch ("Validate"), and shows the "full configuration" with every include: and extends: expanded. Use it when you change the pipeline file. Use gitlab.pl ci when you change the model, because it actually runs the checks.

19.9 Gates

A gate is a check that must pass before work moves on: a milestone entry criterion, enforced by software on every change. A pipeline job that blocks the merge when it fails is a gate (lint's zero over zero); a job that is allowed to fail is a warning light, not a gate (the first version of trace); a ratchet is a gate on change, not on state (outline, and trace later; Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). Project settings add gates of their own: the pipeline must succeed, a code owner must approve, discussions must be resolved. Deciding which checks are gates and which are warnings is one of the most consequential decisions in a pipeline, and it is a systems engineering decision, not a software one: block on what must never reach the shared model, warn on what someone else must fix. Most gates cost nothing; some settings need a paid GitLab tier, and hosted runners charge compute minutes (Section 17.7, Gates, and what they cost).

19.10 Shift left: catch it at the merge, not at integration

"Shift left" is DevSecOps jargon for a systems engineering truism: a defect found earlier is cheaper to fix. Draw the life cycle as a line from left (idea) to right (operations); every check you move to the left finds problems when they cost less.

For a model, the leftmost possible check is the merge request. An interface whose two ends disagree (a port typed one way on the stations side and another on the data center side) costs a few minutes to fix when the pipeline flags it on the merge request that introduced it. Found at an integration review three months later, it costs a meeting, a discrepancy report, two document revisions and the review's credibility. The status metrics in docs/STATUS-METRICS.html count exactly this, as metric H: interface mismatches caught at merge versus those that reached integration. For Tidewater the second number stayed at zero; Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard has the counts.

The pipeline is the team's safety net, not its judge. Three habits make that true:

  • Never merge red. The project setting enforces it, but the habit matters more: a red pipeline on develop means everybody's next merge request inherits the failure.
  • Fix forward, quickly. If something red reaches develop (it happened once, in sprint 6, when the runner's disk filled up, Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0), the first priority of whoever is free is to make it green again. The scorecard measures the time from the first red to the next green.
  • Fail fast. Cheap checks (grammar, lint) run first, so a typo fails in seconds instead of after the slow jobs.

19.11 The Sec in DevSecOps

Security in a pipeline is mostly unglamorous, and it is cheap precisely because it is automated:

  • Secrets never in the repository. The secrets job looks for tokens and keys in every change (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).
  • Secrets in protected, masked variables. The weekly export's token is given only to pipelines on protected branches, and never printed in a log.
  • A least-privilege runner. The runner's account can read the kit and write its own work folder; it cannot reach anything but the GitLab server, and it holds no credentials of its own beyond its registration (Chapter 42, Administration).
  • Protected branches and tags. Nobody, including the team, changes the shared model or a baseline outside a reviewed, checked merge request.
  • Verifiable baselines. Each baseline tag records a checksum of the generated documents; the baseline job proves the tagged model rebuilds them identically. Tampering with a baseline would require changing a protected tag, which nobody can do.

None of these needed a security specialist. Each is one setting or one job, and each answers a question the ISSM asks of every system (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep lists the questions).

19.12 Growing a pipeline one job at a time

The team's pipeline did not start with fifteen jobs. It grew the way Tom's rule from Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep says tools should: one job each time a problem repeated.

Table 19.3. How the pipeline grew
SprintJob addedThe problem it answered
1grammar, lint, outline"we can't tell whether a change broke the model"
2todo, docs, report widgets"how much is left?", "the generated docs are stale", "I can't find the error in the log"
3secrets, trace"the ISSM asked about credentials", "which requirements are unlinked today?"
4pages, schedules"management wants to see the model", "something broke overnight and nobody noticed"
5recipe, the trace ratchet, drop-package, baseline, publish-release"the DOORS text is vague", "a trace gap slipped in", "where is the exact delivery?", "prove the baseline"
6vcrm, delta (rehearsed for drop 2)"which requirements are verified, and how?", "what did the prime change that the converter can't show?"
latercomplexity, intake, publish-package, the SIL/HIL templates"is the spider web growing back?", "a drop arrived from the prime's Jenkins", "give other teams the baseline"

Each job has a cost: runner time, a log someone must read when it fails, false alarms. The team reviewed the pipeline at each retrospective with two questions: which job caught something real this sprint, and which job failed for a reason that was not a real problem? A job that never catches anything and sometimes cries wolf is a candidate for removal.

19.13 The minimum pipeline for any SysML v2 text repository

If you take one thing from this chapter to your own project, take this. It needs a runner with Perl, the agile kit checked out at the path in the KIT variable, and the kit's job script copied into the repository as ci/job.pl (from tools/gitlab/templates/ci/job.pl). Each script line is a single perl command, so the same file works on a Windows runner whose shell is PowerShell, in Git Bash and in a Docker image (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs tells how the team learned that the hard way):

Try it on the lesson's model, as if it were your project's only pipeline file:

Two jobs: every file is valid SysML v2, and every name in the model resolves. With "pipelines must succeed" switched on, that alone makes the model's integration branch trustworthy in a way no document set ever was. Everything else in Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job is added on top, one problem at a time.

One subtlety. Jobs with no rules: run in branch pipelines (every push), not in merge request pipelines: ask gitlab.pl ci --event merge_request_event --list and it answers "not added to merge request pipelines" for both. That is GitLab's default, and for the minimum pipeline it is fine: the branch pipeline on the merge request's source branch is the one GitLab checks before allowing the merge. The team's full pipeline uses rules: and a workflow: section so that the gate is a merged results pipeline instead (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

19.14 Explaining a red pipeline to a manager

Sooner or later the program manager will see a red mark and ask what it means. The answer the team gave, which worked:

A red pipeline means the checks caught a problem in a proposed change before it reached the shared model. That is the system working. The change will not merge until it is fixed, usually the same day. A red pipeline on the shared model itself would be a problem, and we measure how long it lasts: so far, once, for less than a day.

— Jim, to the deputy program manager, sprint 4 review

19.15 Exercises

Exercise 19.1: Break it and watch it fail

In your practice repository, create a branch, change one part's type to a name that does not exist, and run gitlab.pl ci --event merge_request_event --target develop --var KIT=$KIT --job lint. Find the error line in the log. Then fix it with :make lint in Vim and run the job again.

Exercise 19.2: One line up

Delete a semicolon at the end of a part line and run the grammar checker on that file. Which line does the error name? Explain the difference to a colleague in one sentence.

Exercise 19.3: Add a job

Add a job to the minimum pipeline that counts // TODO lines and prints the count, and never fails. Run it locally. What would you need to add so the count appears on the merge request page? (Hint: Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep.)

Exercise 19.4: Allowed to fail

Make the lint job of the minimum pipeline allow_failure: true and break the model again. What does the pipeline status become? Write two sentences on why this would be a bad idea for lint, and two on why the team first made trace allowed to fail and later replaced that with a ratchet.

Exercise 19.5: The manager's question

Write the three sentences you would say to your program manager about a red pipeline on a merge request, and the three you would say about a red pipeline on the integration branch.

19.16 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the definitions (CI = the configuration audit and peer review checklist on every change; CD = every product generated from the model, always ready); never merge red; run the pipeline locally before pushing; the two-job minimum pipeline on day one.
  • Adapt: the jobs to your checks (your organization may have its own modeling rules; each one that a program can check is a job); the triggers (a slower project may need only merge request and tag pipelines).
  • Decide locally: where the runner lives and who maintains it; which checks block a merge and which only warn; how you will explain red and green to your management, before the first red appears.

20 The pipeline, job by job

From what you know

You know

the checklist a reviewer works through before signing off.

Here it is called

the pipeline: jobs such as grammar, lint, trace and docs.

What is new

each checklist item is a script, and a red job stops the change.

Survival kit

What you have

the idea of a pipeline (Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero): stages, jobs, rules, artifacts, reports, a runner.

What you need

to be able to read, change and defend every line of the team's real pipeline file. This chapter takes .gitlab-ci.yml from the top, explains the few YAML rules you need, then goes job by job: what each job checks, the systems engineering question it answers, when it runs, what it keeps, what its output looks like on Tidewater's drop 1, and how it fails. The complete file is reproduced at the end.

20.1 Reading YAML in ten minutes

The pipeline file is written in YAML, a text format for nested lists and named values. You need six rules.

  1. Indentation is structure. Two spaces deeper means "inside". Never use a tab in a YAML file; in Vim, :setlocal expandtab makes the Tab key insert spaces.
  2. name: value is a named value. stage: check gives the job's stage the value check.
  3. A line starting with - is a list item. Under script:, each - line is one command.
  4. A # starts a comment (to the end of the line). The team's file is about half comments, on purpose.
  5. Quote a value that contains : (colon, space). Otherwise YAML reads it as another name: value. The kit's local runner refuses such lines with a message that says to quote them; GitLab refuses them too.
  6. &name marks a block to reuse; *name reuses it; <<: *name copies its contents in. The file uses this once, for the rules every model job shares.

That is all. There are no loops and no variables in YAML itself; anything that needs logic lives in a script the job runs.

20.2 The shape of the file

The file has two kinds of top-level entries: a few reserved names that configure the whole pipeline (stages, variables, workflow, include, default), and everything else, which is a job. A name that starts with a dot (.check) is a hidden job: a template other jobs copy, never run on its own.

The team settled on one principle after a lesson described in Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs: the YAML says when and where; the script says what. Every job's script: is a single line,

and the commands that job runs live in ci/job.pl, a short Perl script kept in the repository next to the pipeline file. The reason is portability: the Windows runner's default shell is PowerShell, where the shell commands in a typical pipeline (if [ ... ], $(find ...), $KIT) do not work, while perl ci/job.pl lint means the same thing in PowerShell, in Git Bash, on Linux and in a Docker container. A second benefit is that a person can run any job by hand with the same line, and see exactly what the pipeline sees.

So when this chapter says "the job runs the linter", it means: the YAML entry for lint says when the job runs and what files it keeps; ci/job.pl lint runs the linter, writes the report files and decides pass or fail. The log of each job starts with the perl ci/job.pl NAME line and then shows the commands job.pl runs and their output, in the same transcript form as Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero.

20.3 The header: stages, variables, workflow

The seven stages run in that order. check is the gate; trace reports requirement gaps; docs checks that the generated documents are current; delta runs only when a prime drop arrives; release only on baseline tags; publish only on the default branch; report only on the weekly schedule.

GIT_DEPTH: "0" asks the runner for the full history of the repository. By default GitLab fetches only the most recent commits to save time. The team's jobs read history: trace and delta compare imported drops, the burn-down counts TODO lines across merges, the baseline check reads the tag message. A shallow copy would make them wrong in confusing ways.

workflow: rules: decides whether a pipeline starts at all. GitLab reads the rules top to bottom and stops at the first that matches:

  1. a merge request event: yes, run (the gate);
  2. a push to a branch that already has an open merge request: no (the merge request pipeline covers it; without this rule every push would produce two pipelines);
  3. any other push to a branch (develop, main, vendor/prime, a draft branch with no MR yet): yes;
  4. a tag: yes;
  5. a schedule: yes.

The $CI_... names are predefined variables GitLab sets for every pipeline: CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE says what started it, CI_COMMIT_BRANCH is the branch (empty for tags and merge requests), CI_COMMIT_TAG the tag, CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS lists open merge requests for the branch. A bare $NAME in a rule is true when the variable is set and not empty.

20.4 The conditional include and the defaults

include: pulls in YAML from elsewhere, here one of GitLab's built-in templates: its secret scanner. The scanner runs in a Docker container, so it can only work on a runner that has Docker. The team's runner does not (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs explains why), and a job waiting for a runner that never comes stays "pending" forever, which with "pipelines must succeed" would block every merge request. So the include is conditional on a project variable, DOCKER_RUNNER, set to false in project.conf. The pipeline's own secrets job (below) is the always-on check. The kit's local runner lists the include as "runs on GitLab only".

default: sets things every job inherits. The team's default is the runner tags: every job asks for a runner tagged windows and mbse, which is the team's Windows shell runner (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs). On a Docker runner these tags change, and nothing else does. The check that KIT is set and points at the kit lives in ci/job.pl, so a misconfigured runner fails with a sentence that says what to fix rather than with a "file not found" deep in a job.

.model_rules is the rule shared by every job that checks the model, read top to bottom:

  1. never on a schedule unless that schedule sets the variable FULL to 1 (the nightly schedule does, and runs every check; the weekly status schedule does not, so it only exports reports);
  2. never in a pipeline the prime's delivery system starts (a trigger, Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition): that pipeline only takes in the files;
  3. never on vendor/prime, the branch that holds each drop exactly as delivered and converted. The checks run where the drop is merged, on its merge request into develop; on the raw branch they would stay red for structure only the prime can change;
  4. otherwise, always.

&model_rules names the block; <<: *model_rules copies it into .check, the hidden job the six check-stage jobs extend. Writing the rule once means changing it once.

All the job commands in this chapter can be typed in the sandbox of practice lesson 11, which holds the drop 1 import in the team's layout (perl $KIT/agile.pl practice 11 builds it):

20.5 Stage check: the gate

The six check jobs are the configuration audit. Each must pass (except where noted) for a merge request to merge.

20.5.1 grammar: is every file valid SysML v2?

The question it answers: is every .sysml file in model/ a valid sentence in the SysML v2 language? The document-era equivalent is the editor's first read: is the thing even well-formed?

What it runs: the kit's grammar checker over every model file, which is built from the official SysML v2 grammar (Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers), then ci-reports.pl grammar to write one JUnit test case per file and a Code Quality finding per error.

On drop 1: sysml: 17 file(s), 0 error(s), in about two seconds. The converter's output is always grammatical; this job earns its keep on hand edits, where a missing semicolon is the classic mistake (Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero shows the "one line up" error).

artifacts: when: always keeps the reports even when the job fails, which is exactly when you need them.

20.5.2 lint: does every name resolve?

The question it answers: is the model internally consistent? Does every part's type exist, does every import point at a real package, is anything declared twice? The document-era equivalent is the cross-reference check: does every "see section 3.2.1" point at a section that exists?

What it runs: model.pl lint, which ends with one summary line, then the report writer, then the gate: the last line must end errors=0 warnings=0. The team called it "zero over zero to merge", and it is the single most important rule in the file.

On drop 1:

elements=148 counts the model elements the linter understood. Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero shows the failing case (unresolved type 'Hul'), and Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep shows the JUnit and Code Quality files it produced.

20.5.3 outline: is the model's structure readable?

The question it answers: does every level of the part tree have between 2 and 9 children, and does every part definition carry the level tag (@L1Network down to @L6Component) that says where it sits? This is the kit's version of a rule every systems engineer knows from specification trees: fewer than two children is not a breakdown, more than nine is not readable, and every item knows its level.

What it runs: model.pl check, which reports level-tag mismatches and outline violations. On the drop 1 import, in the team's layered layout (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where):

(an excerpt; there are 20 lines). Each line is a count and the place it was counted: the Stations package has 25 members, the requirements copy 32, Battery one part, and many layer folders hold a single file.

Two kinds of violation are mixed here. The folder lines are an artifact of the layout: a layer with one file in it today (model/logical/ holds only Behavior) will fill as the model grows, or the team can decide one file is right for it. The package lines are about the model itself: the 25-member Stations package, the one-part Battery, the duplicate in the legacy package. The first kind is cheap to accept; the second is the prime's structure, which the government should not silently rearrange.

The level tags show zero mismatches only because there are no level tags yet: the converter turned every v1 stereotype into a TODO line. They appear as the team closes those TODOs (Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named, Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed).

20.5.4 The ratchet: why outline does not fail on day one

Twenty violations on the first day posed a real dilemma, and the team's resolution is one of the most transferable ideas in this book.

Option one: make the job fail on any violation. Then every merge request fails until all 20 are fixed, including the ones only the prime can fix (a 25-member package is the prime's structure; the government's copy should not silently diverge from it). Nobody could merge anything. The gate would be switched off within a week.

Option two: make the job allowed to fail. Then it is yellow forever, everybody learns to ignore it, and new violations creep in unnoticed.

Option three, which the team chose: a ratchet. A file in the repository, .ci/outline-max, holds the number of violations currently allowed: 20 on the day drop 1 was imported into the lesson's copy (the team's own count, with its own conventions file, is in Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated). The job fails if a change raises the count above that number, and tells the author to lower the number if the change fixed some. The number can only go down, one reviewed merge request at a time, until it reaches zero and the rule is absolute.

A ratchet turns an inherited problem into a measured, shrinking one without blocking the work, and it works for any rule you cannot satisfy on day one: unverified requirements, missing documentation, lint warnings in legacy content. The violations that only the prime can fix become discrepancy reports (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed); the ones the government can fix become tasks.

Tip: Lowering the ratchet is part of the change

When your merge request fixes outline violations, the job says fewer violations than allowed: lower .ci/outline-max to N in this MR. Do it in the same merge request. The reviewer checks that the number went down; Tom's rule was that nobody ever raises it without a written reason in the merge request and Jim's approval.

20.5.5 todo: the port burn-down

The question it answers: how much conversion debt is left? Every // TODO line the converter wrote is a v1 construct it could not carry into SysML v2 (Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers), and closing them is the port.

What it runs: a search for // TODO in model/, a count, and the report writer, which emits each TODO line as an informational Code Quality finding (so merge requests show the TODOs they closed as "fixed") and a metrics file. It never fails: the burn-down is information, not a gate.

On drop 1:

Fifty-two lines, forty-two of them in the physical layer and twenty-nine of those in Stations (grep -c "// TODO" model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml). That number is the first row of the scorecard (Chapter 3, The directive) and the spine of the sprint plans in Part III.

20.5.6 secrets: no credentials in the repository

The question it answers: did this change commit a token, a cloud key or a private key?

What it runs: a search of every tracked file for three patterns: GitLab personal tokens (glpat- followed by twenty characters), cloud access keys, and the header line of a private key file. If it finds one, it fails with the instruction "remove it, rotate it, then rewrite the branch before it merges". The order matters: a committed secret must be revoked first, because it is already in the history of the branch and in every clone of it.

The pattern list is short on purpose. It catches the common accidents with almost no false alarms. GitLab's own scanner, when a Docker runner is available, catches many more.

20.5.7 complexity: is the spider web growing back?

The question it answers: are the packages getting more tangled? The v1 model became a spider web one unreviewed link at a time (Chapter 2, The Cameo years); this job measures the web on every change so it cannot grow back unnoticed (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web).

What it runs: for every package, its fan-in (how many other packages depend on it) and fan-out (how many it depends on), the package dependency cycles, any dependency that goes up the layer order set in sysml.conf, and the number of relationship ends on each part definition. On a merge request it is a ratchet like outline: any new cycle or upward dependency fails, and fan-out or relationship ends fail when they get worse than on the target branch and are above the limits in sysml.conf (7 and 10 by default), so a new project's first parts and links pass; elsewhere it reports.

The cycles are the spider web's, inherited from the prime's model; ObservingStation, with its trace spaghetti, tops the relationship list. (This sandbox shows two tangled pairs; on the real project the job counted 2 tangled groups after the sprint 3 DOORS import.) Breaking the cycles is engineering work, not pipeline work: the team broke the Network and Operations loop in sprint 4 (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed), and the Stations and DataCenter loop was still open at the end of sprint 6 (1 group left).

20.6 Stage trace: DOORS against the model

The question it answers: for the requirements in the newest imported DOORS export, which are linked to the model (metric C), which have nothing satisfying them (orphans, F), which have nothing verifying them (G), what share is complete (I), and which have different text in DOORS and in the model (drift)? In the document era this was two days of spreadsheet work before each review (Chapter 1, Thirty years of documents). Here it takes a fraction of a second, on every change.

What it runs: reqif2sysml.pl --report --model against the latest imports/*/tidewater.reqif, then the report writer (one JUnit case per gap, so the merge request's test widget lists them). The model side of the comparison leaves out the requirement packages the job's own DOORS import generated (they carry a header saying so); otherwise DOORS would be compared with a copy of itself.

On drop 1, against the converted model (before the DOORS modules themselves were imported, see the warning below):

The command took 0.17 seconds. Bob's reaction to the drift line is in Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in.

20.6.1 Gate or warning? The trace ratchet

Gaps like these posed the same dilemma as the outline violations, with a twist: most of them are the prime's to fix. TW-SYS-012 has nothing satisfying it because the prime's v1 model has no satisfy relationship for it; the government's copy should not invent one. Blocking the government's merge requests on the prime's gaps would punish the wrong people.

The first version of the job was therefore allow_failure: true: it failed when there were gaps, showed yellow, and blocked nothing. The team soon noticed the cost of a permanent yellow light: nobody looks at it, so a merge request that removed a satisfy relationship by mistake would also show yellow, exactly as before, and pass.

The job became a ratchet, like outline. On a merge request it traces the model twice: once as the change leaves it, once as it was where the branch left the target branch (the merge base). It fails only if the change adds a gap: an orphan, an unverified requirement or a drifted text that was not there before. On develop and on schedules it reports and passes. The end of its log on the practice repository:

and, on a merge request that changes nothing in the trace, by no new trace gaps, and on one that makes things worse by this change adds trace gaps: ... naming the measure and its before and after. The prime's gaps stay visible in the widget, with a discrepancy report each (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed); the government's own mistakes cannot get in.

Tip: Two kinds of ratchet

The outline ratchet keeps the allowed number in a file someone lowers by hand. The trace ratchet compares with the target branch automatically, so it needs no file. Use the first when the number should only ever go down by a deliberate decision; use the second when "no worse than before" is the whole rule.

20.6.2 vcrm: the verification cross-reference matrix

The second job in the stage builds the VCRM, the verification cross-reference matrix every systems engineer has maintained in a spreadsheet: for each requirement, its verification method, the verification cases that verify it, and their latest results. The model supplies the first three (the verify relationships, Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers); results come from files under verification/ in a fixed format (requirement, case, verdict, commit, environment, timestamp, signed by), filled by the prime's test results in later drops and by people for analysis and inspection verdicts.

On drop 1 there are no results yet, and the job says so:

It writes the matrix as a web page and a CSV for Excel, never fails (missing cases are the trace ratchet's job), and its page joins the model site. In the document era the VCRM was a spreadsheet edited by hand before each review; here it is regenerated on every change, from the model, and nobody edits it.

20.6.3 recipe: are the requirement statements well written?

The third job in the stage grades every requirement statement against the requirement recipe (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe): a classification, a subject, one operative verb, a verifiable target verb, a threshold, an ID. It never fails: the DOORS text is the prime's, so its findings become a discrepancy report, not a blocked merge request. They show in the merge request's Code Quality widget, and the summary line feeds the scorecard.

Warning: Watch what you compare

The trace compares DOORS with the model. When the team imported the DOORS modules themselves into the repository as SysML (Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named), the first trace run over all of model/ found every DOORS id in the DOORS-generated packages and reported C 30 of 30 and text differs from DOORS 0: DOORS agreeing with itself. The job now leaves those packages out, by the header the import writes into them. The lesson stands for any measure: if your trace suddenly looks perfect, check what it is comparing before you brief it.

20.7 Stage docs: generated documents are current

The question it answers: are the documents generated from the model (the part tree, the function tree, the IDEF0 plates, the traceability report, all under docs/) the ones this version of the model produces?

What it runs: model.pl docs, then a check that git sees no difference in docs/. If the author changed the model and forgot to regenerate the documents, they differ, and the job fails with docs/ is stale: run model.pl docs and commit. The fix is two commands and a commit.

Why commit generated files at all? Because the baseline check below hashes them, and because a reviewer reading a merge request sees the effect of the model change on the documents (a part moved in the tree, a requirement newly traced) in the same diff. Committed, generated, checked: never edited by hand.

20.8 Stage delta: what the prime changed

The question it answers: between the two newest prime drops, which v1 elements were added, removed or changed, and which of those changes can the converter carry into v2 automatically, and which must be reworked by hand?

When it runs: on the vendor/prime branch (where each drop's converted output is committed) and on the merge request that brings a drop into develop (branches named feature/drop-...). The =~ /^feature\/drop-/ is a pattern match: "the branch name starts with feature/drop-".

What it runs: xmi2sysml.pl --delta OLD NEW on the two newest imports/*/tidewater.xmi, with the project's layout map so the paths are the repository's. On drop 1 alone it says "first drop: nothing to compare". With drop 2 (delivered 8 January 2027, Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle) it printed what you get by generating drop 2 yourself and comparing:

(an excerpt). Everything in drop 2 is carried; the "changed" line is the prime fixing the drift the team reported. Later drops have manual items (a new state in a state machine, which the converter does not carry), and those become tasks. This job is the reason the team rehearsed drop intake in sprint 6, before drop 2 arrived.

20.8.1 drop-package: keeping the delivery

On vendor/prime only, this job uploads each file of the newest drop to the project's generic package registry under prime-drop/<version>/, authenticated by the job's own token (CI_JOB_TOKEN, valid only while the job runs). On a laptop there is no registry, and the job says so and passes:

20.8.2 intake: a delivery from the prime's build system

The one job a trigger pipeline runs. When the prime's own build system (a Jenkins server, Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition) uploads a drop to the package registry and starts a pipeline with the variable DROP_VERSION, this job fetches the files, checks every checksum against the drop's manifest, keeps the drop as received (it never expires) and opens the Prime Drop issue that starts the vendor import. Tidewater used it from drop 4; until then drops arrived by file transfer and Tom ran the import by hand.

20.9 Stage release: the baseline audit

20.9.1 baseline: does the tagged model rebuild its documents?

The question it answers: is this baseline what it claims to be? This is the physical configuration audit, automated.

When it runs: only when a tag starting baseline- is created.

What it runs: regenerate docs/ from the tagged model and check nothing changed; compute a SHA-256 checksum over the list of every file under docs/ with its content hash; and compare it with the sha256= line written into the tag's message when the tag was created. If the documents do not rebuild, or the checksum differs, the job fails and the release is never published.

The job also writes toolchain.txt, an inventory of what produced the baseline, and keeps it, with the baseline's VCRM, as an artifact that never expires (expire_in: never): formal evidence for the life of the program.

A rehearsal tag, in the lesson's sandbox (the tag stays local; delete it after):

The baseline job's last line, and the start of the inventory:

(kit: names the kit version that ran the checks; on the runner it is a released kit version, which is exactly what the inventory is there to prove. The checksum and commit differ on your machine.)

20.9.2 publish-package: the baseline as a package

Also on baseline-* tags, this job files the baseline itself in the package registry for downstream users (other programs, the test range, the prime): tidewater-model/<tag>/ holding the model and its generated docs as one archive, the VCRM, the toolchain inventory and a SHA256SUMS list. On a laptop it leaves the files in a folder instead:

You never type the tag command by hand on the real project: gitlab.pl flow released creates the tag with the checksum after the release merge request merges (Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0, Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).

20.9.3 publish-release: the release page

Once baseline passes, this job copies the baseline's section from CHANGELOG.md into release notes, adds the verification summary, and GitLab's release: keyword creates the release page for the tag with those notes, links to the package files as the release's assets, and the sprint milestones it closes. The rehearsal had no CHANGELOG section for baseline-0, and the notes said so honestly:

needs: [baseline] makes the release wait for the audit; if the audit fails, there is no release.

20.10 Stage publish: the model site

The question it answers: what does the model look like today, for someone who will never open the repository?

When it runs: on every push to the default branch (develop), which in practice means after every merge, and on the nightly schedule; never on the weekly export or a delivery trigger.

What it runs: copies the generated documents into public/docs/, draws the four views (part tree, trace, interconnection and packages) into public/views/, copies the IDEF0 plates into public/idef0/, writes the trace report, the VCRM, the complexity trend and a TODO burn-down table (one row per merge, computed from the history), and writes an index page. GitLab publishes the public/ folder because the job is named pages; that name is the whole configuration. The environment: lines record each publication as a deployment of model-site.

The package view deserves a note. The kit's package drawer normally checks a security marking on every package (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system); the converted Tidewater model has none yet, so the drawer draws packages, dependencies and cycles only, and says it did not check markings. Its count of cycles (four on drop 1 in the layered layout, six in the converter's flat layout) is higher than the complexity job's, because the drawer counts each arrow that closes a loop, in the order it visits the folders, while the job counts groups of packages tangled together. Both are the spider web, seen at two levels of detail (Section 11.4, The five views, read).

20.11 Stage report: the weekly export

The question it answers: what does GitLab know this week, in a form the status metrics can read?

When it runs: only from the weekly pipeline schedule (the one without FULL=1): every Friday at 06:00 Eastern, cron expression 0 6 * * 5, on develop, set in project.conf under [schedules] (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab). A schedule runs the pipeline as the person who owns the schedule, with that person's permissions; if the owner leaves the project, the schedule stops (Chapter 42, Administration has the hand-over step).

What it runs: gitlab.pl export, authenticated with STATUS_TOKEN, a read-only project access token stored as a masked, protected CI/CD variable, which writes ci_jobs.csv, mrs.csv, issues.csv, defects.csv and one tracker file per sprint into exports/. If the repository holds a metrics.json, it also runs the status metrics collector. On the lesson's emulator the same export, by hand:

(the counts and times depend on how far you went in the lesson). Chapter 36, Telling management shows how the weekly export turns into the Friday status.

The second schedule, nightly (0 2 * * 1-5, weekdays at 02:00, on develop), runs the ordinary push pipeline, so a problem caused by something outside the repository (a kit update on the runner, an expired certificate) shows up in the morning.

20.12 The whole run, and what it costs

The merge request pipeline on the drop 1 import, run with the kit's local runner on a laptop:

About eight seconds of checks. On the GitLab server, each job also pays the runner's start-up cost (fetching the repository, preparing the shell), typically a few seconds to half a minute per job depending on the runner, so a merge request pipeline takes a minute or two from push to result. In the document era the same audit was a review meeting.

Table 20.1. Which jobs run for which event (checked with gitlab.pl ci --list for each event)
EventJobs that runPurpose
Merge requestgrammar, lint, outline, todo, secrets, complexity, trace, vcrm, recipe, docsthe gate
Push to develop (after a merge)the same ten, plus pagesintegration check and the model site
Push to vendor/primedelta and drop-package onlydrop intake: the raw drop is filed, not judged
Merge request from feature/drop-...the ten, plus deltareviewing a drop's merge
Tag baseline-*the ten, plus baseline, publish-package and publish-releasethe baseline audit and release
Trigger from the prime's build (DROP_VERSION set)intaketaking in a delivery
Weekly schedulestatusthe export for the status metrics
Nightly schedule (FULL=1, on develop)the ten, plus pagesearly warning
Warning: Local runs leave files behind

When you run the pipeline on your laptop, the jobs write their reports (lint.txt, lint.xml, lint-cq.json, lint.metrics and the rest) into your working copy, because that is where they run. On the server they are thrown away with the job's environment. Without care, the next git add -A commits them. The model repository's .gitignore lists them; the template the team started from (tools/gitlab/templates/.gitignore) already does: *.xml, *-cq.json, *.metrics, the jobs' .txt outputs, public/ and the package and log folders, with an exception for the manifests under imports/. Check with git status after a local run: it should show nothing new.

20.13 Changing the pipeline

The pipeline file is protected like everything else: CODEOWNERS makes Tom its owner, so every change to it is a merge request Tom approves, and the pipeline runs on the merge request with the changed file. That last point is a trap and a help. A change that breaks the pipeline file fails on its own merge request and never reaches develop. But a change that weakens a check (a deleted line, an added allow_failure) passes its own pipeline easily. The reviewer of a pipeline change must read the diff of the YAML as carefully as a reviewer of a requirement change reads the "shall".

Before pushing a change to the pipeline, check it locally (gitlab.pl ci --list for every event in the table above) and in GitLab's pipeline editor (Build > Pipeline editor > Validate).

20.14 The complete file

And the script every job calls, ci/job.pl (copied into the model repository from tools/gitlab/templates/ci/job.pl):

20.15 Exercises

Exercise 20.1: Which jobs, which event

For each event in the "which jobs run" table, run gitlab.pl ci --list with the matching --event, --branch, --tag options in your practice repository and compare the result with the table. Which job's rule surprised you?

Exercise 20.2: Turn the ratchet

Fix one outline violation in your practice model (give a one-child part a second child, or split a package). Run the outline job. What does it tell you? Make the change it asks for and run it again.

Exercise 20.3: Find your ratchet

Name a rule in your own organization that everyone agrees with and nobody meets today. Write the ratchet for it: what is counted, where the allowed number lives, who may lower it, who may raise it.

Exercise 20.4: Stale documents

Change a part's documentation comment in your practice model, commit without running model.pl docs, and run the docs job. Then fix it. Why does the team commit generated files at all?

Exercise 20.5: Review a pipeline change

A merge request adds allow_failure: true to the lint job with the description "lint is noisy this week". Write the review comment Tom should leave, and the alternative you would propose.

20.16 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: one-line job scripts that call a script in the repository (perl ci/job.pl NAME); GIT_DEPTH: "0" if any job reads history; a workflow: that gives one pipeline per change; a shared rule block; artifacts: when: always for reports; the zero-over-zero lint gate; the ratchet for inherited problems; a trace job that is allowed to fail; committed, checked generated documents; a baseline job that rebuilds and checks a checksum.
  • Adapt: the checks to your modeling rules; which jobs block and which warn; the schedules to your reporting rhythm; the site to your audience.
  • Decide locally: where the kit lives on the runner (the KIT variable); whether you have a Docker runner for GitLab's scanners; who owns the pipeline file; who owns the schedules.

21 Runners: where the pipeline runs

From what you know

You know

the lab machine that runs the analysis tools.

Here it is called

a runner: the machine GitLab sends pipeline jobs to.

What is new

it works unattended, and if it is offline, nothing merges.

Survival kit

What you have

a pipeline file (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job) and a GitLab project (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab).

What you need

a computer that actually runs the jobs. This chapter explains what a runner is, the kinds GitLab offers, why the Tidewater team chose a project runner with the Windows shell executor on a dedicated virtual machine, how it was registered and secured, what goes wrong ("pending", "stuck", offline), and how the team kept the same pipeline file working on Windows, on Linux, in Docker and on a laptop.

21.1 GitLab runs nothing

The most common misunderstanding about GitLab, and the one that cost Tom the most time in the first weeks, is that the GitLab server runs the pipeline. It does not. The server keeps the repository, decides which jobs a pipeline needs, and waits. A separate program, the GitLab Runner, installed on some other computer, asks the server every few seconds "is there a job for me?", takes one, runs it, sends the log and the artifacts back, and asks again.

In systems engineering terms, the server is the configuration management office that schedules the audit, and the runner is the auditor who shows up and does it. No auditor, no audit: a pipeline with no runner to take its jobs sits in the state GitLab calls pending, indefinitely. With "pipelines must succeed" switched on, that means no merge request can merge. An offline runner stops the whole team.

That is why the request to the enterprise administrators in Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab asked for a runner on day one, and why Tom's stand-up said "blocked" until it existed.

21.2 Who a runner serves: scopes

Table 21.1. Runner scopes
KindWho registers itWho it servesTypical use
Instance (shared) runnerthe GitLab administratorsevery project on the servergeneral-purpose jobs, usually Linux with Docker
Group runnera group ownerevery project in the groupa team's projects with shared needs
Project runnera project maintainerone project (or a few it is enabled for)special tools, special security rules
GitLab.com hosted runnerGitLabGitLab.com projectsno machine to maintain; billed in compute minutes

The Tidewater team used a project runner, registered to tidewater/model. Three reasons:

  • The tools. The jobs need Perl and the agile kit. The organization's shared runners were Linux machines running Docker containers built for software teams, with no kit and no way for the team to add one in the first quarter.
  • The security conversation. The ISSM wanted one machine, one service account, one purpose, a list of exactly what runs on it, and no other project's jobs on it. A project runner is that list.
  • The cost. On the organization's self-managed GitLab, a runner on the team's own virtual machine costs nothing per minute; on GitLab.com, the hosted runners bill compute minutes after a free quota (Section 17.7, Gates, and what they cost).

21.3 Hosted or your own: the decision

Many readers will not have a choice: the organization will have decided where pipelines may run. If you do have one, these are the questions that decided it for Tidewater.

Table 21.2. Hosted runners against your own
QuestionHosted runners (GitLab.com)Your own runner
May the model's data leave the organization's network?only if the data is cleared for the vendor's cloudstays where the runner is
Who patches the machine?GitLabyour administrators
What does a minute cost?compute minutes after a free quotanothing per minute; the machine's cost
Can you install the kit and its tools?in a container image you build and maintainon the machine, once
What does the ISSM have to approve?the vendor's service and the data flow to itone machine, one account, one network rule
What happens if it is down?GitLab's problem, GitLab's status pageyour problem; plan a second runner

For a model that is controlled, contractually sensitive or simply not cleared for a public cloud, the answer is almost always your own runner on the organization's network. For an open, unclassified training project like this book's exercises, hosted runners with the kit's Docker image are the quickest start.

21.4 What to put in the request

The enterprise administrators will need the same facts every time. Tom's request, which got the runner in about two weeks, listed:

  • Purpose: run the automated checks of the Tidewater model project's pipeline; no other project.
  • Scope: project runner for tidewater/model, tags windows, shell, mbse; runs untagged jobs; not protected in the first year.
  • Machine: a Windows Server virtual machine, 2 processors, 8 GB of memory, a 100 GB data disk for builds; patched on the organization's monthly schedule.
  • Software: GitLab Runner (the version matching the server), Git for Windows for all users; nothing else. The agile kit is a folder copied from the team's approved release.
  • Account: a dedicated service account with no interactive logon, rights only to the kit folder (read) and the builds folder (write).
  • Network: outbound HTTPS to the GitLab server only.
  • Owner: Tom, with Jim as backup; the administrators keep the machine.
  • Security documentation: the runner section of the toolchain security plan (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).

A request that answers every question the administrators will ask is a request that is not sent back. Ask for it on day one.

21.5 How a runner runs a job: executors

The executor is how the runner runs each job's script.

Table 21.3. Runner executors
ExecutorWhat it doesGood forWatch out for
shellruns the script directly on the runner's machine, as the runner's accountsimple jobs with tools installed on the machinejobs share the machine; nothing is isolated
dockerstarts a fresh container from an image for each jobclean, repeatable environmentsneeds Docker on the runner; images must be built and maintained
docker-windowsthe same with Windows containersWindows tools in containerslarge images, slow starts
kubernetesruns each job as a pod in a clusterlarge organizationsneeds a cluster and its administrators
customyour own scripts start and stop the environmentspecial casesyou maintain it

The team chose the shell executor on Windows: the runner machine is a Windows virtual machine with Git for Windows installed (which brings Perl, Git and a POSIX shell), and the agile kit checked out at a fixed path. Every job runs as the runner's service account, in a work folder the runner creates per project.

Why not Docker, which is cleaner? Because in the first quarter the organization had no Docker runners for the team's network, and the ISSM's approval for one would have taken longer than the twelve weeks. The kit does include an optional Docker image for later (Section 21.12, The Docker alternative), and the pipeline was written so that switching costs one line.

21.6 The lesson of the first week: PowerShell

When the runner came online at the start of sprint 2, Tom's first pipeline on the real server failed in a way it never had on the laptop:

followed by a PowerShell error about an unexpected token. The Windows shell executor runs PowerShell by default, not the Bash-style shell Git for Windows provides. In PowerShell, a variable is $env:KIT, not $KIT; test, [ ... ], $(find ...), | xargs and || either do not exist or mean something else. A pipeline written for one shell is a program in that shell's language.

There were three ways out:

  1. Configure the runner to use Bash (possible, but fragile on Windows, and different from every other runner the team might use later).
  2. Write the pipeline in PowerShell (and then it would not run on Linux, in Docker, or with the kit's local runner).
  3. Make every script line shell-neutral: one command that means the same thing in every shell.

The team chose the third. Every job's script became one line, perl ci/job.pl NAME, and the commands moved into ci/job.pl, a Perl script in the repository. Perl is the same program under PowerShell, cmd, Git Bash, a Linux runner, the Docker image and a laptop. The header of the script says why:

You can see both halves of the idea in the sandbox of practice lesson 11. The same line runs the job on a laptop that the runner runs on the server, and a missing KIT stops the job with a sentence instead of a cryptic error:

Exit status 2, not 1, means "the job could not run", as opposed to "the check failed": a runner problem, not a model problem.

Tip: The rule that came out of it

Keep the YAML for what GitLab needs to know (when a job runs, which runner, what it keeps); put what the job does in a script in the repository. You can then run any job by hand, on any machine, with the same line the runner uses.

21.7 Registering the runner

Registration connects a runner program to a GitLab project. Since GitLab 16 it goes in two steps: you create the runner in GitLab's web page, which gives you a runner authentication token, and you give that token to the runner program on the machine.

Step 1, in GitLab (Tom, as maintainer): Settings > CI/CD > Runners > New project runner. Fill in:

  • Tags: windows, shell, mbse. Tags are how jobs choose runners: a job with tags: [mbse] runs only on a runner that has the mbse tag.
  • Run untagged jobs: off. Every job in the team's pipeline asks for the tags windows and mbse (the pipeline's default: section sets them, Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job), so an untagged job from a careless edit waits visibly instead of running somewhere unexpected.
  • Protected: off for this runner (it must take merge request pipelines from feature branches). See Section 21.10, Protected runners for when to turn it on.
  • Description: tidewater-win-01.

GitLab shows the token once, starting glrt-. Treat it as a password.

Step 2, on the runner machine (the enterprise administrator with Tom, in an elevated PowerShell window). These are the commands they typed on the Windows virtual machine; the book's material has no server, so they are shown, not run:

The runner then appears in the project's runner list with a green dot. The registration writes config.toml next to the program; the parts that matter:

  • concurrent is how many jobs the runner runs at once. Two let a merge request pipeline and a develop pipeline run side by side; more did not help on a small virtual machine.
  • builds_dir is where each job's fresh copy of the repository goes. Put it on a data disk with room to spare.
  • shell = "pwsh" is the PowerShell default that taught the team the lesson above.

Step 3, the machine itself:

  • Install Git for Windows for all users, so perl and git are on the service account's path (C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin and C:\Program Files\Git\cmd).
  • Check out the agile kit at a fixed path (D:\agile-kit) and set the project's KIT CI/CD variable to it.
  • git config --system core.longpaths true, because Windows' 260-character path limit bites deep model folders under a deep builds folder.
  • Ask for antivirus exclusions for builds_dir: scanning every file of every fresh checkout made jobs several times slower in the first week.

21.8 The service account: least privilege

The runner runs as a dedicated Windows account, svc-tw-runner, with:

  • no interactive logon and no administrator rights;
  • read access to the kit's folder, write access to builds_dir and cache_dir, nothing else;
  • network access to the GitLab server and nothing else (the kit needs no network);
  • no credentials of its own: jobs receive the short-lived job token from GitLab, and the weekly export's token comes from a masked, protected variable.

These five lines were most of the ISSM's review of the runner (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep has the full list of questions). The shell executor's weakness is that jobs are not isolated from each other on the machine; the answers are that only one project's jobs run there and that every job starts from a fresh checkout.

21.9 Tags, pending and stuck

When a job will not start, GitLab shows one of two states:

  • pending: the job is waiting for a runner. Either every suitable runner is busy (it will start soon), or no online runner matches the job's tags and protection (it will wait forever). The job page says "This job is stuck because you don't have any active runners online or available with any of these tags assigned to them", with the tags.
  • stuck is GitLab's word for the second case.

The checklist Tom kept on the wiki:

  1. Is the runner online? Settings > CI/CD > Runners: a green dot and "last contact" a few seconds ago. If not, the service is stopped or the machine cannot reach the server.
  2. Do the job's tags: match the runner's tags? A job tagged docker will never run on tidewater-win-01.
  3. Is the job on a protected branch while the runner is protected, or the reverse?
  4. Is the runner paused?

The team's one "stuck" episode was self-inflicted, on a scratch project: Tom added GitLab's Secret Detection template unconditionally. Its job needs a Docker runner, so it waited forever, and with "pipelines must succeed" it blocked every merge request on that project until the include was removed. That is why the include is now conditional on DOCKER_RUNNER (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

21.10 Protected runners

A runner marked protected takes jobs only from pipelines on protected branches and tags. Organizations use this to keep jobs that hold secrets or publish things (releases, the model site, package uploads) on a machine that untrusted branches can never reach. A merge request from a feature branch cannot run there, so it cannot be tricked into printing a protected variable.

The team ran one unprotected runner in the twelve weeks and wrote down the plan for a second, protected one for the release, publish and drop-package jobs, to be added when the second year's license and machine arrived (Chapter 42, Administration). With only one runner, the protection comes from the variables instead: STATUS_TOKEN is protected, so only pipelines on protected branches receive it.

21.11 Keeping the runner healthy

Table 21.4. Runner care
WhatHow oftenWho
Runner online, last contact recentglance daily (the stand-up board shows it)Tom
Disk space on builds_dirweekly; alarm at 80%Tom and the admins
Runner version matches GitLab's major.minorafter each GitLab upgradeadmins
Windows patches and rebootmonthly window, announced in the stand-upadmins
Kit version on the runnerat each kit release, by merge request to the KIT pathTom
Runner token rotationyearly, or when someone with access leavesTom

The sprint 6 incident in Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0 is the disk row: builds_dir filled up, every job failed with a disk error, and develop was red for most of a day. Two changes came out of it: old builds are cleaned nightly, and a second runner went onto the plan, because one runner is a single point of failure for the whole team's ability to merge.

The runner's own log (the Windows event log, source gitlab-runner) is where to look when a job never reaches the runner at all; the job log in GitLab is where to look once it has.

21.12 The Docker alternative

If your organization offers Docker runners, the kit includes an image with Perl, Git and the kit, and a three-key file to switch the pipeline to it:

Because every script line is perl ci/job.pl NAME, nothing else in the pipeline changes. The image is built from a committed kit version and tagged with it, so the toolchain is baselined along with the model; tools/gitlab/docker/README.md has the build, test and care instructions. With a Docker runner, GitLab's managed scanners (Secret Detection and others) can run too.

21.13 The laptop is a runner too

gitlab.pl ci (Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero) is a runner that takes no orders from a server: it reads .gitlab-ci.yml, picks the jobs GitLab would pick for the event you name, and runs them in your working copy with Perl. It is not a substitute for the real runner (your laptop is not a fresh environment), but it answers "will my change pass?" in seconds before you push, and it is how every pipeline output in this book was produced.

21.14 Exercises

Exercise 21.1: Make a job pend

In a test project on your organization's GitLab (or with the emulator's gitlab.pl ci, by reading the --list output), add tags: [does-not-exist] to one job and push. What does GitLab say about the job? Fix it two ways: remove the tag, and register a runner with that tag.

Exercise 21.2: Translate a line

Take the line test -n "$KIT" || { echo "KIT is not set"; exit 1; } and write what it would have to be in PowerShell. Then explain in two sentences why the team chose perl ci/job.pl NAME instead of maintaining both.

Exercise 21.3: Write the runner's security description

In one page, describe a runner for your project the way the ISSM needs it: machine, account, rights, network, credentials, what runs on it, who maintains it. Use Section 21.8, The service account: least privilege as a model.

21.15 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: ask for the runner on day one; one purpose per runner; a least-privilege service account; shell-neutral job scripts (perl ci/job.pl NAME or the equivalent in your tool's language); a written "pending" checklist; disk monitoring; a plan for a second runner.
  • Adapt: the executor (Docker if your organization has it, shell if not); the scope (group runner if several model projects share tools); protected runners for publishing jobs.
  • Decide locally: who owns the runner machine and its patches; which network it may reach; whether hosted runners and their compute minutes are allowed for your data at all.

22 Reviewing a model change

From what you know

You know

red-lining a document and filling in the comment matrix.

Here it is called

reviewing a merge request: line comments, threads, approve or request changes.

What is new

you review only what changed, with the generated views and the pipeline results beside it.

Survival kit

What you have

decades of document reviews -- comment matrices, redlines, the review board where forty people looked at slide 37 -- and three years of Cameo reviews by screenshot, where nobody could tell exactly what had changed.

What you need

to review a merge request in under half an hour, knowing exactly what changed; to read a .sysml diff and the generated views beside it; to write findings that teach rather than blame; and to know when to approve, when to ask for a change, and when to say "this is too big to review."

Note: Core path

This chapter is CORE. Every model change on Tidewater is reviewed by a second person from the first week; the team budgeted half a point each in sprint 4 to learn to do it well.

22.1 Slide 37

Jim's last review before the directive was a Cameo model review for the prime's preliminary design. The model was presented as sixty slides of diagram screenshots. On slide 37, an internal block diagram of the power system, Jim noticed that the charge regulator now connected straight to the battery. Had that changed since the last review? Nobody in the room could say. The prime's modeler thought so; the screenshot from three months earlier was in another deck; the action item to find out took two weeks.

A merge request answers that question before anyone asks it. It shows exactly which lines changed, who changed them, why, what the automated checks found, and what the change does to every view of the model. The reviewer's job is no longer to discover what changed. It is to judge whether the change is right.

Objection: "We don't have time to review every change. We reviewed at milestones."

Answer

A milestone review of three months of changes takes the program days and finds problems weeks after they were made. A review of one small change takes fifteen to thirty minutes and finds the problem the day it was made. The total time is smaller, and the problems are cheaper. Tidewater's median review turnaround was measured every sprint (Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics); it fell below a day by sprint 4.

22.2 What the pipeline already checked

Before a reviewer opens a merge request, the pipeline has run on it (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). By the time it is green, these are already true, and the reviewer does not spend a minute on them:

  • Every .sysml file parses against the official SysML v2 grammar.
  • Lint reports 0 errors and 0 warnings; the outline and level rules hold.
  • The trace has no new orphan, unverified or drifted requirement (from sprint 5).
  • The generated documents in docs/ match the model.
  • No token, password or key is in the change.

That list is the reason a review can be short. If the pipeline is red, do not review. Say so in one line and wait; reviewing a change that does not yet pass is reviewing the wrong thing.

22.3 The reviewer's question

What is left is the part no machine can judge: is the change right? Tidewater's review checklist (docs/conventions/review-checklist.md in every scaffolded repository) breaks that question into a handful of things to look at. Here it is in full:

Two items on that list do most of the work in practice.

"It does what the issue asked, and no more." The most common problem in Tidewater's first sprints was not a wrong change; it was a change that did two things. Bob's first Stations merge request tagged levels and reformatted the indentation of the whole file, so the diff showed 180 changed lines for twelve real changes. Jim asked for it to be split, and the second version was reviewed in ten minutes.

"Converter files: lines that came from the prime are changed only to close a TODO line or by an accepted DR." This is the rule that keeps prime drops merging (Section 16.7, The rules that make the layout work). A reviewer who sees a change to a prime-delivered line that is not a TODO closure asks: is this the prime's to fix? If yes, it becomes a discrepancy report, not a merge request.

22.4 A review, start to finish

Practice lesson 11's sandbox has the Tidewater project in an offline GitLab, with a clone for Bob and the pipeline the team uses. Play both sides: Bob makes a small change and opens a merge request; Jim reviews it.

22.4.1 Bob: the change

Bob tags the station segment with its level -- one TODO line closed, one import added. (The perl -0pi line is a scripted stand-in for the edit you would make in Vim.)

flow finish pushes the branch, opens the merge request against develop, and runs its pipeline. The last line says which merge request it is and that its pipeline succeeded. Each block after this one starts with . ../env.sh: the book's own test runs every block in a fresh shell, so it loads the lesson's environment again. In your terminal you load it once, and it stays loaded until you close the window.

22.4.2 Jim: what changed, in text

The reviewer starts with the merge request itself -- its description, its pipeline, its test widget -- and then the diff. On the web these are the Overview and Changes tabs. From the clone:

The three dots in develop...feature/... mean "what the branch changed since it left develop," which is exactly what the merge request will bring in. The diff shows one line removed (the TODO), one added (@L2Segment;) and the import. That is a change you can review completely in two minutes.

How to read a .sysml diff:

  • Lines starting with - are gone, + are new. A changed line shows as one of each.
  • The @@ ... @@ lines say where. The text after the second @@ is often the enclosing package or definition, which tells you the context without opening the file.
  • Look at what each + line means, not only what it says. @L2Segment; means "this part is a segment." Is StationSegment a segment? (Yes: it is one of the network's three segments.)
  • Look for what is missing. A new satisfy without a verify; a new port with no connection; a requirement with no DOORS id. The pipeline catches some of these; the reviewer catches the rest.

22.4.3 Jim: what changed, in pictures

Text diffs show lines. Model changes are often easier to judge as pictures: what the change did to the part tree, the trace, the package dependencies. The kit draws the views of both versions with the differences colored (Section 11.8, Comparing two versions). Write them outside the clone, so they do not end up in a commit:

The summary line is the most useful single line a reviewer reads: how many changes, how many new trace gaps, how many new error findings. "0 new gaps" tells Jim the change cannot have broken traceability. The colored SVGs in ../review/ show where the change sits in the part tree.

In the real GitLab the reviewer often does not need this command at all: from sprint 4 the pipeline publishes the model site, and the merge request's pipeline has the drawn views as artifacts. Open the artifact, not the text.

22.4.4 Jim: the finding

The change is right. But Jim wants one more thing: a line of documentation saying why StationSegment is the L2 level, so a reader of the part tree does not have to guess. That is a finding, and it must be resolved before the merge:

The merge is refused: "discussions not resolved." The project setting all threads must be resolved turns every resolvable comment into a small gate. Bob answers the finding -- with a change, or with a reply that explains -- and resolves the thread; then the merge goes through:
