Notice what Jim did not do: Jim did not withhold the approval while waiting for a one-line doc comment. Jim approved the engineering and left a resolvable thread for the polish. The order matters to the author's day.

22.5 Suggestions: the redline you can apply

On the web, a reviewer who knows the exact replacement text can write it as a suggestion: a comment on a line with a fenced block marked suggestion. The author applies it with one click, and the merge request gets a commit with the reviewer's text. It is the redline, applied.

The first comment in that thread shows the form: three backticks, the word suggestion, an optional range (:-0+1 means "this line and the one after"), and the replacement lines. Use suggestions for exact wording, a missing unit, a name that breaks the convention -- anything where you already know the answer. Do not use them for design questions; ask those as questions.

22.6 Different changes, different questions

Not every merge request is reviewed the same way. The kinds of task in Section 14.6, Writing the task issues produce different kinds of change, and each has its own first question:

Table 22.1. What to ask first, by kind of change
ChangeTypical sizeThe reviewer's first questionLook at
TODO closure (level tags, procured parts)5 to 40 linesis each tag the right level for that part?the diff; the part tree view
Hand-written construct (state machine, flows, constraint)20 to 80 linesdoes it say what the v1 model meant?the v1 element in the drop (its xmi:id is in the TODO line); the IDEF0 or state view
Requirement changea few linesis it one testable statement, by the recipe?the recipe report; the trace view
Interface changea few lines, wide effectwho uses this port or item, and do they agree?the interconnection view; the second approver
Prime drop mergehundreds of lineswhat did the prime change, and what does it break of ours?the delta and impact report, not the diff
Pipeline change.gitlab-ci.yml, ci/job.pldoes every job still run, and does a red still block?the pipeline of the MR itself, all jobs listed
Decision record or conventionone fileis the decision clear, and are its consequences named?the text

22.7 Reviewing a prime drop merge

A prime drop merge request is the one review where reading the diff line by line is the wrong approach. A drop changes hundreds of lines, most of them exactly as the prime delivered them; the government does not review the prime's work line by line, it reviews what the drop does to the government's model.

So the drop's merge request carries the two reports from the converter, and the reviewer reads those first (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition):

  • The delta, xmi2sysml.pl --delta OLD.xmi NEW.xmi: every element the prime added, removed or changed, by its v1 id, each marked carried (the converter brings it over) or manual (the converter cannot, and someone must rework it by hand). The manual list is the reviewer's checklist: each item is a task, or already done in this MR.
  • The impact, --impact model: for each change, which of the government's requirements, verification cases, interfaces and allocations it touches, and which of the government's hand edits must be redone. A hand edit listed here and not redone in the merge request is a finding.

Then the conflicts: every file git could not merge on its own is listed in the merge request description, with how it was resolved. The reviewer checks that each resolution took the prime's side for the prime's content and re-applied the government's edits on top -- never the other way round (Section 51.3.4, Silent conflict resolution).

22.8 Writing findings that teach

The team's first reviews were stiff. Bob wrote "This is wrong." Tom wrote nothing and approved. Jim wrote three paragraphs. By sprint 4 they had settled on a few habits, which the review checklist's last table records:

  • Say what and why in one or two sentences, on the exact line. "The battery capacity has no unit; Energy would let the energy balance check it" teaches; "units?" does not.
  • Ask, when you are not sure. "Why does QualityControl depend on SensorSuite? It closes a cycle with Stations." The author may know something you do not.
  • Separate must from could. Prefix optional ideas with "Optional:" or "Nit:", and do not hold the merge for them.
  • Praise specifically, once. "Good split -- this is reviewable in ten minutes" tells the author what to repeat.
  • Never review the person. The comment is about the line, not about who wrote it. On a three-person team, every reviewer is reviewed by the people they review.
Case study: Tom approved everything

In sprints 2 and 3, Tom approved every merge request Tom was asked to review, usually within minutes, without a comment. At the sprint 3 retrospective Tom said why: "Who am I to tell Bob the model is wrong? Bob knows it better than I do." Jim's answer became a team rule: the reviewer's job is not to know more than the author; it is to be the second pair of eyes the change has never had. Tom's first real finding, in sprint 4, was a requirement satisfy pointing at the whole Network instead of the Telemetry Unit -- exactly the "trace at the right level" item on the checklist, and something Bob had not seen because Bob had written it.

22.9 Approve, ask for changes, or ask to split

A reviewer ends with one of three outcomes:

Table 22.2. The three outcomes of a review
OutcomeWhenHow
ApproveYou would sign for the change as it is, or with only optional commentsthe Approve button, or the /approve quick action
Ask for changesSomething must change before merginga resolvable thread on each finding (some GitLab versions also offer "Request changes" when you submit a review); do not approve yet
Ask to splitThe change is too big to review in about half an hour, or does two unrelated thingsone comment saying so and suggesting the split; do not review the rest

Approval is enforced, not ceremonial: CODEOWNERS names who must approve a change to each folder, and an interface change needs two approvals, Jim's as systems lead and the other modeler's (Section 15.8, Code owners: the signature authority matrix). GitLab will not let an author approve their own change.

22.10 Turnaround

A review that waits three days costs more than a review that finds a problem. The team agreed on three habits:

  • Review before you start new work in the morning. The GitLab To-Do list shows every merge request waiting for you.
  • A first response within one working day, even if it is "I'll look at this after the stand-up tomorrow."
  • Small changes get reviewed first. They are quick, and they unblock someone.

Review turnaround is one of the analytics the team reported to management from sprint 4 (Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics): the time from a merge request being opened to its first review comment or approval.

22.11 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the review checklist, the rule that a red pipeline is not reviewed, resolvable threads as gates, and the habit of reviewing the generated views, not only the text.
  • Adapt: the checklist's engineering items to your model's conventions and your program's review criteria; the CODEOWNERS sections to your team's ownership.
  • Decide locally: who reviews whom (on three people, everyone reviews everyone), whether a second approval is needed for interfaces, and the turnaround you will measure.
Exercise 22.1: Review a change

In the practice-11 sandbox, start a branch, change the doc comment of StationSegment and, in the same commit, remove the private import Interfaces::*; line from Stations.sysml. Open the merge request. Which of the two changes does the pipeline catch, and which would only a reviewer catch?

Exercise 22.2: Rewrite a finding

Rewrite these three review comments so they teach: (a) "wrong"; (b) "trace?"; (c) "This whole package is a mess, please clean it up."

You can now review a model merge request: check that the pipeline is green, read the description and the diff, compare the generated views of both versions, write a finding on the exact line, use suggestions, and choose between approving, asking for changes and asking for a split.

23 Stand-ups, the journal and the board

From what you know

You know

the status spreadsheet and the action-item list.

Here it is called

the journal of stories, and the GitLab board for tasks.

What is new

status is recorded once, as it happens, and every report is derived from it.

Survival kit

What you have

a GitLab project where tasks live as issues (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab, Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep), and an operating model that says work comes in tomes, epics, stories and tasks (Chapter 13, The operating model).

What you need

a record of the plan that management can trust: what each sprint committed, what it finished, what slipped, how fast the team goes, and where each epic and tome stands. This chapter sets up the agile kit's journal, a plain-text ledger of stories kept in Vim, explains how it divides the work with GitLab, and shows the reports it produces. Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro then shows the daily and fortnightly rhythm that feeds it.

23.1 Two records, one plan

By the end of sprint 1 the team had two places that knew about the work, and Bob asked the obvious question: why two?

If every task is an issue in GitLab, why do we also keep a journal? That's the double bookkeeping we were promised would go away.

— Bob, sprint 1 review

The answer is that the two records hold different things, for different readers, at different levels of the hierarchy.

Table 23.1. The hierarchy, and where each level is recorded
LevelSize ruleWhere it livesWho reads it
Projectyears; this one is 39 sprintsthe journal: one journal per projectthe program
Tomeunder a year (two semesters)the journal, t: on each story; a tome:: label in GitLabthe program manager
Epicunder a semester (13 sprints)the journal, e: on each story; an epic:: label in GitLabJim, management
Storyunder one sprintthe journal (id TW-N) and a GitLab issue labeled type::story (number N)Jim, the team
Taskunder a week (5 points or fewer)GitLab only: an issue labeled type::task, closed by a merge requestthe person doing it

The journal tracks stories and above: the commitments the team makes to management, sprint by sprint, and the roll-up into epics and tomes. GitLab tracks tasks and the stories they belong to: the day-to-day work, the merge requests that do it, the reviews and the pipelines.

The link between them is the number. A story is GitLab issue 12 and journal item TW-12. Anyone reading a stand-up note that mentions TW-12 opens issue 12 in GitLab to see its tasks, merge requests and discussion; anyone looking at issue 12 knows the journal tracks it as TW-12.

This is a deliberate application of a rule the agile kit has always had: the architect's journal holds commitments and their state, and task-level detail stays in the team's own tool. Tasks change daily; they are cut, merged, re-cut. A journal that tracked them would be noisy and always out of date. Stories change state a few times each, and every change is a fact management cares about: committed, done, carried, blocked.

Note: Why not GitLab for everything?

GitLab's Premium tier has epics and iterations with burndown charts, and with it a team could keep the whole hierarchy in GitLab. The team had the Free tier, and more importantly a need GitLab does not meet: a ledger in which points are never edited after the fact, only moved, so last month's numbers are exactly what they were last month. That property is what lets Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard compare sprint 1 with sprint 6 without anyone asking "has this been restated?"

23.2 Everything is a ledger

The journal is a text file, scrum.txt, in the format of ledger-cli, a decades-old plain-text accounting tool. That sounds odd for a scrum record until you see what it buys.

Every story has points (the team's estimate of its size: one point is one ideal person-day). The points sit in an account, and the account is the story's state:

When the team commits a story to sprint 1, its points move from Backlog:Model to Sprint:1:Model:Committed. When it is done, they move to Sprint:1:Model:Done. Nothing is ever edited; each event is a new entry that moves points. Re-estimating a story posts the difference, not a new number. Like money in double-entry bookkeeping, points are conserved: every entry balances, and the totals cannot drift.

Here is what the journal recorded on the first day of sprint 1, written by the kit from the planning notes (the compile step is below):

(an excerpt). The ~ Sprint 1 entry records the team's capacity for the sprint, 19 points. The Intake entry brings a new story into the backlog with its metadata after the semicolon: its epic, owner, priority and tome. The Standup entry moves its 4 points into the sprint's commitment.

You never write these entries by hand. You write terse notes, and the kit writes the ledger.

23.3 Setting up the journal

The journal is its own git repository, separate from the model, because it has a different audience and different rules (it is the team's management record; the model is a controlled item). The kit creates one:

scrum.conf holds the settings, one key = value per line. For a single team the ones that matter on day one are default_team = Model (the team's name in the journal; the new file leaves it empty) and unit = SP (story points, already set). In Vim it is one edit; from the shell, one command. The people go in roster.txt, with their names exactly as the meeting chat shows them, because the stand-up tools match chat names to the roster:

Jim keeps the journal repository on the team's share as well as in GitLab (a second project in the tidewater group, private to the three of them), and commits it at the end of each day with daily.pl commit.

23.4 The stand-up file

Each day's notes go in one small text file, standups/YYYY-MM-DD.txt, written in Vim (:SNew creates today's file with the open stories listed as comments). The notes use a handful of four-letter verbs, each one line:

Table 23.2. The stand-up verbs used most
VerbMeaningExample
sprint Nwhich sprint this file belongs tosprint 1
== Teamthe team the following lines are about== Model
cap Nthe team's capacity for the sprint, in pointscap 19
new ID PTS title ...a new story into the backlog, with p: priority, e: epic, t: tome, o: ownersee below
commit ID Ownercommit a story to the sprintcommit TW-1 Tom
done ID ...stories finished todaydone TW-3
block ID why / unblock IDa story is blocked, or no longerblock TW-1 waiting on the enterprise GitLab admins
carry ID ...at the sprint's end, stories that go to the next sprintcarry TW-11
est ID Na new estimate (posts the difference)est TW-7 5
note texta line for the record and the status mailnote Demo went well

Sprint 1's planning file, written by Jim on Monday 5 October after the kickoff. In Vim, Jim typed the lines into the file :SNew opened; to type along from the shell, write the same lines with a here-document (everything between the <<'PLAN' line and the PLAN line goes into the file):

(The story numbers in this chapter's examples come from a practice journal; Part III uses the numbers from the real run.) Quoted values (e:"E1 GitLab project and gitflow") may contain spaces; unquoted ones may not.

Then the compile step checks the file and, if every line is valid, appends the ledger entries to scrum.txt:

A stand-up file with a single mistake (an unknown story id, a done for a story that was never committed, a verb misspelled) is rejected whole, with every problem listed, and nothing is written. That is the journal's own gate: it never contains half a day.

In Vim the same steps are :SNew (today's file), :SCompile, and :SStatus. Chapter 10, Vim for models lists the rest.

23.5 What the journal tells you

Everything the journal reports is computed from the ledger when you ask; nothing is stored separately, so nothing can disagree.

The sprint view, the morning after planning (--today sets the date the journal reads as "today", so this works on any day you type it):

Load% is commitment divided by capacity: 17 of 19 points, 89%. The kit's metrics treat a load above 110% as a warning (the team is promising more than it can do) and below 70% as another (it is not using its capacity, or the capacity is wrong). Jim aimed for 85 to 95% every sprint.

The epics view, at the end of sprint 1:

(The column is headed "Tasks" because the kit calls every journal item a task; in this project every journal item is a story.)

Velocity, the points done per sprint, which becomes the basis for forecasts once there are three sprints of history:

And the ledger itself, through the kit's ledger tool, balances to zero, which is the proof that no points were created or lost. Right after planning, in your journal:

and in the practice journal at the end of sprint 1, after the stories were done and the next ones were filed:

Twenty-eight points came in (Equity:Intake is the counterweight of every intake); seventeen are done in sprint 1; eleven wait in the backlog for sprint 2.

23.6 Estimates that change

Estimates change, especially in the first weeks, when the team does not yet know how long anything takes. In the journal a new estimate is a posting of the difference. When the team re-estimated story TW-7 from 4 to 5 points in refinement (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro shows the poker round), the journal recorded:

The original 4 points and the added 1 are both visible forever. A forecast made on the 13th and one made on the 15th can each be reproduced from the journal as it stood that day; the kit can load the journal "as of" any date. In the document era, the action item spreadsheet had one estimate column, overwritten.

23.7 A story from end to end

It helps to follow one story through both records. Take the story Bob owned in sprint 1, "Convert drop 1 and assess it", four points.

Monday, planning. Jim creates the story as a GitLab issue with the Story template (its number becomes the id: in the practice project it was issue 1) and the journal line new TW-4 4 Convert drop 1 and assess it ... with commit TW-4 Bob. In GitLab the issue gets the labels type::story, tome::port, epic::drop-intake and the milestone "Sprint 1". Bob cuts it into tasks during the kickoff, each its own issue with the Task template and "Part of" the story:

Table 23.3. The tasks of one story
TaskPointsWhat it produces
Run both converters with --report1the two converter reports, attached to the story
TODO inventory by package2a table of the 52 TODO lines by package and kind, in the story
Estimate the port backlog with the team1candidate stories for the structure epic, poker-estimated

Tuesday to Thursday, the work. Each task moves across the board: workflow::in-progress when Bob starts it, a comment with the result and /spend when it is finished, /close. Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep shows the first task's history, driven entirely by quick actions. Bob's stand-up lines name the story, not the tasks (Y TW-4 read the converter report), because the journal knows stories.

Friday of week 2, done. When the last task closes, Bob says done in the stand-up; the answers step suggests the done TW-4 line; Jim confirms and compiles. In GitLab, Jim checks the story's acceptance criteria and closes it with a comment. The journal moved 4 points from Sprint:1:Model:Committed to Sprint:1:Model:Done, dated that day; GitLab recorded three closed tasks with their time and their outputs.

Neither record holds the other's detail, and neither needs to. Management sees the story in the quad; anyone who wants the details follows the number.

Tip: When a story will not fit

If, during the sprint, a story turns out bigger than the sprint, do not stretch it. Split it: the finished part is a story that is done; the rest is a new story in the backlog, estimated at the next refinement. The journal's carry exists for the story that is nearly done on the last day, not for the one that was never going to fit.

23.8 The board and the journal, day to day

The team kept the two in step with three habits:

  • The board is for tasks; the journal is for stories. The GitLab board, scoped to the current sprint's milestone, is what the team looks at during the day. The journal is updated once a day, after the stand-up.
  • A story is done when its last task closes. GitLab closes a task when its merge request merges; when a story's last task is closed, the owner says so in the stand-up (done TW-12), and Jim's journal records it.
  • Blocked is said out loud. A blocked task gets the workflow::blocked label in GitLab and a comment saying why; the story gets a block line in the journal the same day, so the weekly report to management shows it (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro, Chapter 36, Telling management).

23.9 The reports

The journal feeds every report the team sends upward. Each one is a command, and each was produced every sprint without anyone assembling a slide:

  • daily.pl review N: the sprint report at the review: committed, done, carried, velocity, predictability, and each epic's remaining points and forecast completion sprint. Sprint 1's began:
  • daily.pl quad: the weekly one-page status in four quadrants (technical priorities, watch items, schedule milestones, accomplishments), shown in Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro and Chapter 36, Telling management.
  • daily.pl health: every metric against its threshold, red, amber or fine.
  • daily.pl report: all of the above as HTML pages, plus the cockpit dashboard.
Warning: One hundred percent is not the goal

Sprint 1 in the practice journal finished 17 of 17, and so did the real sprint 1 (16.5 of 16.5). Sprint 4 did not: it finished 12 of 17 story points (Section 13.8, Two ways to count "done") and carried a walk-through into sprint 5, and that is fine (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed). A team that finishes everything every sprint is committing too little. The kit's metrics look for predictability (done over committed) of 80% or better, not 100%.

23.10 Exercises

Exercise 23.1: Make a journal

Create a journal with daily.pl init, add yourself and two colleagues to the roster, and write a planning file for a sprint of your own work with three stories. Compile it, then run daily.pl sprint and daily.pl epics.

Exercise 23.2: Break the compile

Add a line done XX-99 to a stand-up file and compile. What does the kit say, and what did it write to scrum.txt?

Exercise 23.3: Where does it go?

For each item, decide whether it belongs in the journal, in GitLab, or both, and why: (a) "write the state definition for BuoyModes, 3 points"; (b) "close the Stations TODO lines, 8 points"; (c) "the structure port"; (d) "Bob spent 4 hours on the review"; (e) "blocked: waiting for the ISSM".

Exercise 23.4: Re-estimate

Re-estimate one of your stories with an est line. Look at the ledger entries it produced. Why does the kit post the difference instead of replacing the number?

23.11 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: two records with a clear split (commitments and roll-ups in the journal, tasks in the team's tool); one number for a story in both; points that move and are never edited; a compile step that rejects a bad day whole; reports computed from the record, never assembled by hand.
  • Adapt: the hierarchy's names and size rules to your program; the capacity per person; the load band.
  • Decide locally: who keeps the journal (one person, usually the lead); where it lives; who may read it; which reports go to whom (Chapter 36, Telling management).

24 The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro

From what you know

You know

the weekly status meeting, the technical interchange meeting and the program review.

Here it is called

stand-up, planning poker, refinement, kickoff, demo and retrospective.

What is new

short meetings of fixed length at a fixed rhythm, each with one job.

Survival kit

What you have

a journal of stories (Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board), tasks in GitLab (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep), and two-week sprints.

What you need

the meetings that keep the plan honest, run in a way three systems engineers can sustain: a daily stand-up of terse written statuses, planning poker for estimates, a mid-sprint refinement, a kickoff on day one and a demo and retrospective on the last day. Each meeting produces a record the kit reads, so nobody writes minutes. This chapter shows each one with real chat pastes and the kit's real output.

24.1 Why meetings at all

The team's first reaction to the word "ceremonies" was predictable.

We already have too many meetings. Now we get a daily one and four more every two weeks?

— Tom, week zero

The answer the team arrived at, after a sprint of trying it, was that these meetings replace others rather than add to them. The weekly status meeting, the action item review, the monthly schedule review and most of the e-mail chains went away, because their questions were answered in fifteen minutes a day and two hours a fortnight, from records the meetings themselves produced.

Table 24.1. The two-week rhythm
WhenMeetingLengthProducesReplaces
Daily, 09:00stand-up15 minutesY/T/B statuses; blocks; done storiesthe weekly status meeting, the action item review
Day 1 (Monday, week 1)sprint kickoff and planning90 minutesthe sprint goal; capacity; committed stories; task issuesthe monthly schedule review
Wednesday, week 2refinement1 hourthe next sprint's candidate stories, estimated and readyad hoc tasking e-mails
Day 10 (Friday, week 2)demo (sprint review)60 minuteswhat was shown, feedback, accepted storiesreview-by-screenshot briefings
Day 10, after the demoretrospective60 minutesone or two changes; the pulse surveythe annual lessons-learned exercise
Every Fridayweekly status0 minutes of meetingthe quad, sent to managementthe weekly status slides

24.2 The daily stand-up: terse, written, linted

The team's stand-up is a Teams meeting at 09:00 whose main event is the chat. Each person posts one line with three parts, Y (what I did yesterday), T (what I will do today) and B (what blocks me), each naming the story it is about:

The kit reads two shapes. In sprints 1 and 2 the team posted the three parts on three lines, as most people do at first; this is Tidewater's first stand-up, from the meeting chat:

From sprint 3 they posted one line per person, drafted by talk.pl (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not) and edited before posting, with the outcome and a number first. The examples in this section use the one-line shape because it is shorter to type; the lint treats both the same way.

Then they talk only about the blockers and anything that needs two people. The statuses are the record; the talk is for help.

Why written, and why so terse? Because a written status can be checked by a program, compiled into the journal and compared with yesterday's, and a spoken one cannot. And because three engineers who had spent years writing status paragraphs for slides found that one line, with an id, said more.

The rules, from the team's wiki:

  • Every part is present. B none when nothing blocks you; an empty B is not "none", it is a missing answer.
  • Every Y and T names a story id (TW-4). Work with no id is invisible in the plan; if it matters, it should be a story.
  • A blocker goes in B, not in T. "Waiting on the admins" is not something you will do today.
  • Capital Y, T, B as delimiters; lower-case letters inside the text are just letters.

24.2.1 The lint

To type along, you need a journal with sprint 1 planned. If you made one in Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board, use it; otherwise these commands make the same one in a few seconds:

While people are still on the call, Jim pastes the chat into a file and runs the kit's lint on it: a check of every status against the rules. Here is the chat of Tuesday 6 October, sprint 1, day 2, the team's first real stand-up. Jim pasted it into standups/2026-10-06-chat.txt (in Vim, \sp does the paste; from the shell, a here-document does the same):

The lint reads Bob's longhand correctly but warns that there are no story ids. It refuses Tom's status: the B is empty, and the blocker is sitting in the T. The --reply option writes the lines to paste back into the chat, so people fix their own statuses during the call:

Tom and Bob reposted, and Jim pasted the new lines under the old ones:

and the second lint was clean (the parser keeps each person's last status):

--table shows what the parser understood, one row per person, which is how you check that it read what you meant:

In the first two weeks the lint flagged something almost every day. By sprint 3 the statuses were clean, and the kit's read-backs (a confirmation line for each clean status) stopped by themselves after a run of clean days, as scrum.conf's readback_clean_days sets.

In Vim, the whole loop is one layout: :STown opens the chat buffer, the lint table and the replies side by side; \sp pastes and lints, \sy copies the replies to the clipboard. Chapter 10, Vim for models has the details.

24.2.2 After the call: answers and flags

After the call, daily.pl answers reads the day's chat, writes the statuses into the record, raises flags, and appends suggested journal lines to today's stand-up file for Jim to confirm:

The suggested line in the stand-up file was block TW-1 waiting on the enterprise GitLab admins. Jim compiled it, and the block was on the record. The flags grow with the days: a blocker reported two days running is amber, three days red; the same "today" three days running is amber ("is this stuck?"); a story id that is not in the sprint, or not in the journal at all, is flagged; someone who says "done" in Y gets a suggested done line to confirm. None of these is applied automatically. The kit suggests, the lead confirms.

Case study: What the terse format did for the team

By the end of sprint 2 Bob, who had complained loudest about "status theater", said the one-line status was the first status format that had ever told Bob anything about the other two's work. It also made the blockers impossible to bury: the enterprise administrators' slow runner request was red on the weekly report by its third day, and management called the administrators before the team had to.

24.3 Planning poker

Planning poker is a way to estimate that avoids the loudest voice setting the number. Everyone votes at the same time, in points, without seeing the others' votes; if the votes differ, the highest and lowest explain their reasons, and the team votes again. The discussion is the point: a wide spread means people understand the story differently.

The team plays it in the meeting chat with the kit's #est rounds. Jim posts #est and the story; each person posts a number; the kit tallies the round from the pasted chat. Here is the refinement session of Wednesday 14 October, sprint 1, week 2, with three candidate stories for sprint 2:

Three things in that output are worth slowing down for.

The real disagreement was on TW-7. Bob voted 8 against two 3s, and explained: generating the model documents for the first time had produced warnings, so the docs job was not a routine job. After Bob's explanation the team voted 5, unanimously. The estimate moved because of information, not pressure. That is what poker is for.

Bob's explanation did not count as a vote. It contained a number ("that is not 3 days"), but the kit reads only answers as votes: a number with an optional unit, optionally after "actually" or "make it" and the like. Anything else in a round is discussion, so Bob's 8 stood, and the tally flagged it for re-discussion ("re-discuss with Bob"). People can still change their vote by posting a new answer ("actually 5"); the latest answer wins.

The kit suggests; Jim decides. The tally appends lines to the day's stand-up file, commented out, for Jim to accept by removing the semicolon:

Jim accepted the revote (est TW-7 5) and left the others commented. TW-6 stayed at the 3 it was proposed at.

Note: Which team section the lines go under

Est lines for tasks the journal already knows go under that task's team. The rest -- stories not filed yet, like TW-7 here, and the vote notes -- go under default_team from scrum.conf (the team set it to Model in week zero), or under the team in the chat file's name (standups/DATE-Model-chat.txt). Look at the end of the file the tally wrote:

With neither set, the tally says so (chat: no team for est lines of tasks not in the journal yet) and leaves those lines under a bare ==, where an uncommented est line would fail the compile. Set default_team once and the question never comes up.

24.3.1 How big is a point?

The team's scale was 1 point = one ideal person-day: a day with no meetings and no interruptions. A task may be at most 5 points (under a week); a story is a few tasks and must fit in one sprint; Jim's capacity was about 5 points a sprint (the rest of Jim's time went to management), Bob's and Tom's about 8. Using ideal days rather than abstract "story points" was a concession to the team's background: systems engineers estimate in days, and pretending otherwise would have cost more trust than it bought.

24.4 Refinement and the Definition of Ready

Refinement (also called backlog grooming) prepares the next sprint's stories so planning is quick. It happens on the Wednesday of the second week, so there is time to fix what it finds before Monday. Jim brings candidate stories; the team splits them, estimates them, and checks each against the Definition of Ready, kept in the wiki and in the Story template (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab):

Checklist: Definition of Ready (a story may enter a sprint when)
  • ☐ it fits in one sprint and names its epic and tome
  • ☐ its acceptance criteria are written so someone who did not do the work can check them
  • ☐ its tasks are cut, each at most 5 points (under a week)
  • ☐ its dependencies on the prime or on another story are linked
  • ☐ it has been estimated in poker, and the spread was explained

A ready story gets the workflow::ready label in GitLab. The refinement's journal file brings the new stories in with new lines (into the backlog, not yet committed), plus the accepted est lines:

(Jim rewrote the day's file with the refinement lines and the accepted estimate, replacing the tally's commented suggestions.) After compiling, the backlog showed the three stories with TW-7 at its new 5 points:

24.5 Kickoff and planning

The sprint starts on Monday morning with ninety minutes that do three things:

  1. The goal. One sentence that says what the sprint is for, in terms management would recognize. Sprint 1's: "A GitLab project the team can work in; drop 1 received and assessed." A goal lets the team make trade-offs during the sprint without asking: anything that serves the goal wins.
  2. Capacity. Each person's available days, minus holidays, leave and known meetings, summed into the cap line. Sprint 1 lost a day to the Columbus Day holiday; sprint 4 lost Thanksgiving and a day of Jim's leave.
  3. Commitment. The team pulls ready stories, highest priority first, until the total is about 85 to 95% of capacity. Each committed story gets the sprint's milestone in GitLab and its tasks are created (or confirmed) as task issues; the journal gets the cap and commit lines (Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board shows sprint 1's file).

The kickoff ends with the board reset: last sprint's closed cards gone, this sprint's stories in workflow::ready.

24.6 The demo

The sprint review, or demo, is where the team shows working results to the people who care about them: management, the deputy program manager who chairs the configuration control board, sometimes the prime's modeler. The rule that made the team's demos work was borrowed from the document era's worst habit and turned inside out:

Show the thing, not a slide about the thing.

— Jim's note on the demo agenda, sprint 1

So the demo shows real artifacts, in the tools: the merge request with its pipeline widgets, the board, the TODO count falling, the trace report, from sprint 4 the model website. Sprint 1's demo showed the project and its protections, a merge request blocked by a lint failure, and the drop 1 TODO inventory of 52 lines. It took twenty minutes.

At the end of the demo, Jim marks the stories the audience accepted as done in the journal, and runs the sprint report:

(from the practice journal; the real sprint 1 is in Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in). Unfinished stories are either carried into the next sprint (carry) or returned to the backlog, never quietly left open.

24.7 The retrospective

The retrospective is the team talking to itself about how it works, not what it built. The format the team used:

  1. The pulse survey, five questions answered anonymously on a 1 to 5 scale (Chapter 3, The directive defines them): I understand why we are working this way; I can do my work in the new tools without help; the checks catch problems I would have missed; I can see our progress; I would choose to keep working this way. Five minutes, on paper or a form. The averages go on the scorecard (Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard).
  2. Start, stop, continue. Each person writes what the team should start doing, stop doing and keep doing.
  3. One or two changes. Not ten. Each change becomes a story or a working-agreement edit, with an owner.
  4. Last sprint's changes. Did they help? Keep or drop.

The retrospective is the one meeting where nothing is recorded in the journal except the survey average and the changes. What people say stays in the room. That rule mattered: the team was discouraged at the start (Chapter 3, The directive), and the retrospective had to be a place to say so.

The changes that came out of the first six retrospectives (the report widgets, the ratchet, the "keep numbers out of chat comments" rule, the second runner) are told in Part III, and the pulse survey's arc in Chapter 38, How the team changed its mind.

24.8 Telling management every week

Every Friday, Jim sends management the quad: one page in four quadrants, generated from the journal. The practice journal's at the end of sprint 1:

(an excerpt; in your journal every story was done on the Friday, so the on-time line reads 5/5 this week, and the trend arrows differ). Watch items are where a blocker more than three days old appears with "PM help needed", which is how the runner request reached management in the real sprint 1. Chapter 36, Telling management covers the quad, the sprint mail and the twelve-week briefing in full.

24.9 Exercises

Exercise 24.1: Lint your own status

Write yesterday's work as a Y/T/B line in a chat file, in the Teams copy format above, with one deliberate mistake. Run daily.pl lint on it, then --reply. Fix it until the lint is clean.

Exercise 24.2: Play a round

With two colleagues, estimate three of your real tasks in an #est chat and tally it with daily.pl chat. Where did the spread come from? Did discussion change the number?

Exercise 24.3: Apply the Definition of Ready

Take a work item from your current plan and check it against the Definition of Ready. What would you have to do to make it ready? Which item failed first?

Exercise 24.4: Plan a demo without slides

Write the agenda for a twenty-minute demo of your team's last two weeks that shows only real artifacts. What would you show, in what order, and what question do you want the audience to answer?

24.10 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: terse written statuses with an id in every part, linted during the call; poker in the chat with a revote after the outliers explain; refinement mid-sprint against a written Definition of Ready; a one-sentence sprint goal; demos that show the thing; a short retrospective with a pulse survey and one or two changes; a weekly one-page status generated, not written.
  • Adapt: the times (a team across time zones may need asynchronous stand-ups in the chat alone); the scale (ideal days or abstract points, but pick one and keep it); who attends the demo.
  • Decide locally: what goes upward and what stays in the team; who confirms the kit's suggested lines; which meetings these replace, agreed with management in writing so the calendar actually gets lighter.

25 Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not

From what you know

You know

briefing a chief from a slide deck you rehearsed the night before.

Here it is called

talking about progress: the stand-up line, the demo and the weekly note.

What is new

one short sentence a day, outcome first, with one number, and tools that draft it for you.

Survival kit

What you have

a stand-up every morning (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro), a demo every second Friday, a weekly note to management, and a GitLab project that already knows almost everything you did.

What you need

words. Short ones, in an order management can follow, said out loud by people who have spent a career letting the documents speak for them. This chapter gives you a pattern, a ladder, a stakeholder map, a few scripts for bad news, and a tool that drafts the first version of every sentence from GitLab so you only have to correct it.

25.1 Why engineers go quiet

The first two weeks of Tidewater stand-ups produced statuses like these, copied from the meeting chat:

Each one is true. None of them tells the program manager, who started coming to the sprint reviews in sprint 2, whether the port is on schedule. And in the sprint 2 demo, Tom spent eleven minutes showing the pipeline file line by line, while the program manager checked e-mail and the deputy program manager said, at the end, "I did not follow the demo. What did we get for the two weeks?" Nobody answered for a long moment.

It is worth understanding why this happens, because the fix is different for each cause.

  • The precision instinct. Systems engineers are trained not to claim more than they can show. "On track" feels like a claim; "fixed lint warnings on the connector ends" feels like a fact. So the fact is said and the claim is left for the listener to infer, which the listener cannot do.
  • Fear of being wrong in front of managers. For thirty years the team's statements to management were reviewed, edited and signed before anyone said them. A live sentence with a number in it, said without a document behind it, feels exposed.
  • Not knowing what the audience needs. The program manager needs a different sentence from the ISSM, and both need a different one from Bob. Engineers default to the sentence they would want to hear: the mechanism.
  • Talking in mechanism. Mechanism is what the engineer spent the day on, so it is what is in their head. "Rebased my branch" is the most recent memory, not the most important news.
  • No practice. Nobody on the team had ever rehearsed a status. Documents were drafted, reviewed and redlined; spoken updates were improvised. Improvisation under mild stress produces mechanism or silence.

None of these is a character flaw, and none is fixed by telling people to "communicate better". Each is fixed by a structure: a pattern that puts the claim first, a number that backs it, a tool that drafts it, and a rehearsal.

I wasn't hiding anything. I just didn't know which of the forty things I did was the one they wanted.

— Bob, sprint 2 retrospective

25.2 The pattern: outcome, evidence, next or ask

Every status the team says to anyone outside the team follows one shape:

  1. Outcome: what is now true that was not true before, in the listener's words.
  2. Evidence: one number that proves it.
  3. Next step or ask: what happens next, by when; or what you need, from whom, by when.

The mechanism, the how, is kept in reserve. If someone asks, you have it; if nobody asks, nobody needed it.

Table 25.1. Stand-up statuses, before and after
Instead ofSay
"Y fixed lint warnings on the connector ends in PowerSystem""Y TW-12 Stations structure done: nine TODO lines closed, forty-three left. T TW-15 decide who owns the observation record, by Thursday. B none"
"B waiting on the runner""B TW-3 checks can't run on every change until IT approves the runner machine. Need: Jim to escalate today"
"T rebasing my branch after the vendor merge""T TW-31 the prime's January update: a list of what it changes for us by Wednesday"
"Y trace job is red""Y TW-22 the check found two requirements nothing satisfies. They're the prime's to fix; the report goes to them Friday"
"Refactoring the library package""Cleaning up shared definitions so the next change takes one edit instead of ten"

Notice three things about the right-hand column. Every line still fits the kit's terse format (Y, T and B, each naming a story), so the lint in Section 24.2, The daily stand-up: terse, written, linted still passes. Every line has exactly one number; two numbers make the listener choose, and they choose wrong. And every blocker is an ask with a name and a day, because management can act on "Jim to escalate today" and cannot act on "waiting".

Three sentence shapes cover most days. Copy them onto a card (Appendix H, Quick reference: saying it so they hear it) and keep it beside the keyboard:

  • "[X] of [Y] [things] are [done / covered / passing], up from [Z]." Forty-three of fifty-two TODO lines left, down from fifty-two.
  • "We caught [problem] at [early stage] instead of [late stage]." The check caught a broken interface at merge, the same day, instead of at integration.
  • "Blocked by [thing]. Need [specific help] from [person] by [day]."
Tip: The "so what?" test

Read your sentence and ask "so what?" as the program manager would. If the honest answer is "so nothing, I just did it", the sentence is mechanism: replace it with the outcome it served, or leave it out. If the answer is "so we're one step closer", say how close, with the number.

25.3 The ladder: one sentence, thirty seconds, five minutes

Management will give you one of three slots, and you rarely know in advance which. Prepare all three for anything you will talk about this week.

Table 25.2. The ladder
RungLengthWhat it holdsWhen you use it
One sentenceabout 10 secondsthe outcome and the numberthe hallway, the elevator, the start of every longer version
Thirty secondsthree or four sentencesoutcome, number, what it means for the next milestone, the askthe stand-up, a question in a meeting, the opening of the demo
Five minutesthe thirty seconds plus one piece of evidence shown and one before-and-afterthe demo, a briefing slotthe sprint review

Write the one-sentence version first. If you cannot, you do not yet know what the outcome is, and no amount of detail in the five-minute version will hide that. Then say each rung out loud, once, to a colleague or to the wall. Saying it is different from reading it: you will hear the word you trip over, and that word is usually jargon.

Here is Tidewater's sprint 4 review, on all three rungs, as Tom (the narrator that sprint) rehearsed it on Day 9:

One sentence: The model site management asked for is live, and the check now shows only 22 of the 52 conversion items left.

Thirty seconds: The model site is live and rebuilt every night, so anyone on the program can see the current model without asking us. The conversion is more than half done, and the checks found four gaps in the prime's requirements that we have reported to them. For the January drop, that means we can tell you what it changes for us within a day. We need the second runner approved by the 15th.

— Tom, sprint 4 review, rehearsed version

The five-minute version was the thirty seconds, then the live site on the screen, then one before-and-after, then the ask again. Nothing else.

25.4 Tools that draft the words

Writing the outcome-first sentence is the hard part, and it is hardest at 8:55 in the morning. Most of what it needs is already in GitLab: which tasks you closed, which merge requests merged, which issue is blocked and why. The kit's talk.pl reads that and drafts the sentence. It never posts anything; it prints a draft for you to correct.

talk.pl has four commands:

Table 25.3. talk.pl
CommandDraftsFrom
standup --as USERone Y/T/B line, outcome first, one number, a blocker as an askyour closed tasks and merged merge requests since the last working day; the task in progress; issues labelled workflow::blocked
review --sprint Na demo script: the question, the four headline numbers, what to show, a before-and-after, a safe live change, the ask, and the ladderthe sprint's milestone, issues, merge requests, pipelines and their metrics
weeklya plain-language note for management: a headline that is a conclusion, three numbers, risks, asksthe same, for the week
translate FILEa list of jargon in your text with plain alternatives, and the sentences that fail the "so what?" testyour draft

The kit also has daily.pl propose, which drafts each person's status from yesterday's answers in the journal (a "+1" in the chat accepts it). propose is good for days when nothing changed; talk.pl is good for days when something did, because it reads GitLab, where the change is recorded.

25.4.1 Try it on a practice project

The examples in this section run against the offline GitLab of practice lesson 11 (see Section 12.4, A practice repository). First, give it a small sprint to talk about: a story with three tasks for Bob, a blocked task for Tom with the reason in a comment, and two of Bob's tasks closed on Wednesday. Each gl command is an ordinary GitLab action; --now stamps it with a date, so the example reads the same whatever day you run it. Run everything in this section from the sandbox's work folder (cd work first).

You are now in the sandbox's work folder; the examples below stay there. (Each one sources ../env.sh again so it also works in a new window.) Now draft Thursday's stand-up for Bob. --prefix TW- makes the story ids look like the journal's; --why adds the line that says where each part of the draft came from.

The draft already has the shape: the outcome (the story's tasks), one number (two of three), the next step with a day (the end of the sprint, which is a default worth correcting to "by Thursday" if you know better), and a lint check, so the line will not bounce in the meeting. What Bob actually posted that morning was:

Bob kept the number, added what it means ("the part tree now shows every station's level"), dropped the review of !1 (true, but not what the team needed to hear that morning), and tightened the date. That is the intended use: the tool does the remembering, the engineer does the meaning.

Tom's draft turns the blocked task into an ask, using the reason Tom wrote in the issue's comment:

"Y none T none" is honest, and it is also the moment to say something out loud: what did Tom do on Wednesday? GitLab only knows what was recorded. If you spent the day on a meeting with the ISSM, the tool cannot know it, and you should write it in.

Warning: Read every number before you say it

A draft is a draft. In this practice project every change was made by a script in the same second, so talk.pl's timing figures come out as zero minutes; on a real project they are real. On every project, check each number against what you know before you say it in a meeting. The tool counts what GitLab recorded; you know what actually happened.

25.4.2 The weekly note

On Friday, the weekly note drafts the headline and the asks. Add an open discrepancy report so there is something to count, and a small file of document-era numbers (the "baseline") so the review can make its before-and-after:

Two edits make this sendable. "On track: 0 stories finished" will alarm a reader in week one of a sprint, so Jim adds the context the tool does not have ("two of three tasks in the first story are done; stories finish at the end of the sprint"). And the risk deserves a date: "if the runner is not approved by the 15th, changes wait for one machine". The note pairs with the kit's weekly quad (Section 24.8, Telling management every week), which carries the detail.

25.4.3 The review script

Before each sprint review, the person who will narrate drafts the demo script:

The script has seven parts, which are the seven moves of a demo in Section 25.6, Demos that land. On the practice project the numbers are thin: "n/a" for TODO lines and verify coverage, because practice lesson 11's pipeline has no TODO or trace job. On the Tidewater project those come from the pipeline's metrics, and Part III shows the real drafts for every sprint review next to what the team actually said.

25.4.4 Translating your own draft

The fourth command is for text you wrote yourself: a status, a demo opening, a paragraph for the weekly note. It does not rewrite your sentences. It lists the jargon it found with a plain alternative and a hint, and it flags the sentences that fail the "so what?" test, with a fill-in suggestion in the outcome, evidence, ask shape.

The rework of those two sentences, by Tom, became: "Done: my change to the power system is checked and accepted, with no errors found. Next: the verification matrix shows which requirements are verified, by Friday. Need: none." Longer than the original, and something a manager can repeat to their manager, which is the real test.

You can give translate your own glossary with --glossary FILE (lines term = plain alternative | hint), so the team's words, the prime's acronyms and your program's jargon get the same treatment.

25.5 Know your audience: the Tidewater stakeholder map

The same week sounds different to different people. Before a meeting, ask who is in the room and what one number each of them wants. The Tidewater team kept this table on the wiki and updated it after every review:

Table 25.4. Who wants which number
WhoCares aboutThe one number they wantSay it as
Program managerIs the money producing measurable results? Will the December review go well?TODO lines left, and the trend"22 of 52 left after sprint 4; about two sprints to go at this pace."
Deputy program manager (chairs the CCB)Can a change be traced from request to approval to implementation?changes accepted with a green pipeline and a code-owner approval"Every change this quarter is traceable from its issue to its merge."
ISSMIs the toolchain approved, and is anything leaking?open security findings, last secret-detection result"Secret detection ran on every change; zero findings since the runner was hardened."
The prime's modelerWhich of our discrepancy reports are open, and what do we need from the next drop?open DRs, oldest first"7 open, none closed yet; the oldest is the TW-SYS-006 wording, open since sprint 4."
The test organizationWhich requirements have a verification case and a result?verify coverage"9 requirements still have no verification case, and all of them are the prime's to close."
The team itselfAre we getting better at this?the pulse survey, the share of stand-up lines with an outcome and a number"Morale up from 1.9 in sprint 1; most statuses now have a number."

The numbers in this table are Tidewater's at the end of sprint 4 or 6, from the evidence; in Part III every sprint chapter shows them sprint by sprint.

25.6 Demos that land

The demo is where the quiet engineer is most exposed: a live screen, managers in the room, and no document to hide behind. Tidewater's sprint 2 demo went badly (Tom's eleven minutes on the pipeline file). The sprint 4 demo, after one retro change and a rehearsal, went well. The change was not "Tom should present better". It was a structure.

25.6.1 Three roles

Table 25.5. Demo roles
RoleDoesSays
Driverruns the keyboard: opens the merge request, the site, the boardnothing, or "here"
Narratortells the story in the listener's wordsthe question, the outcome, the before-and-after, the meaning
Note-takerwrites down every question, comment and requestnothing during; reads them back at the end

Splitting driving from narrating is the single most useful change. An engineer who is typing cannot also be choosing words for a manager; an engineer who is only talking can look at the audience. The note-taker turns the room's reactions into issues afterwards, so nothing said in the demo is lost.

The team rotates the roles every sprint. In sprint 4 Bob drove and Tom narrated and closed with the ask, because Jim was on leave that Friday (the meeting record, docs/tidewater/sprints/04/meetings.csv, lists Bob, Tom, the deputy program manager and the program manager); in sprint 5 Tom drove and Bob narrated. Rotation means everyone speaks to management at least once a month, and nobody becomes "the presenter" by default while the others stay quiet.

25.6.2 The Day 9 dry run

On Day 9 (Thursday of week 2), after refinement, the team spends thirty minutes running the demo once, out loud, with the roles they will have on Friday. Nothing is polished; the point is to hear it. The dry run catches:

  • The demo step that needs a password nobody has typed this sprint.
  • The jargon the narrator trips over ("so the MR's pipeline, I mean the merged-results pipeline...").
  • The number nobody can explain ("why did the TODO count go up on Tuesday?" Because the drop-2 preview added three).
  • The ask nobody has written down.

25.6.3 The six moves

A demo script, whoever drafts it, has six moves. talk.pl review drafts them; you edit them.

  1. Open with the question this sprint answered. "Can we show every station requirement has a verification? Yes, twenty-three of twenty-six. Here are the other three."
  2. Show the output, not the tool. The model site, the verification matrix, a merge request going from red to green, the data exchange table. Keep the .sysml text and the pipeline file ready in case someone asks.
  3. One before-and-after, with a number. "Finding where DOORS and the model disagree used to be done never, or once before a review. Now it takes two minutes, on every change."
  4. One safe live change. On a scratch branch, never on develop: remove one satisfy link and open a draft merge request; in about four minutes the trace check names the requirement that lost its design. Cause and effect, live, lands better than any slide. Close the merge request afterwards.
  5. What it means for the next milestone. "For the January drop, we'll know what it changes for us within a day."
  6. The ask, with a date. "We need the deputy program manager's decision on the delivery agreement by Friday."

And close the loop: the note-taker reads back the questions, and each becomes an issue before the end of the day.

25.6.4 The same four numbers, every time

Management learns to read a trend only if it sees the same numbers, in the same order, every review. Tidewater's four:

  1. TODO lines left: how much of the conversion is still to do.
  2. Verify coverage: how many requirements have a verification case.
  3. Open discrepancy reports and prime changes: what is waiting on the prime, or on us.
  4. Blocked items: what needs management's help.

They open every review, every weekly note and every memo. A headline states the conclusion of the numbers ("Trace: 29 of 30 linked, green"), not the topic ("Trace analysis").

25.7 Bad news, said so it builds trust

Engineers dread bad news more than managers do. Managers expect it; what they cannot forgive is hearing it late. These are the phrases the Tidewater team used, each tied to a real moment.

Table 25.6. Bad-news scripts
SituationSay
A check found a problem"Found early. That's the system working. Here is the impact and the fix."
A number got worse because you can now see it"It's not new, it's newly visible. The checks show twelve requirements without a test; here is the date each closes."
You are behind"This is behind by a week because the ISSM review moved. To recover we need the review slot on the 6th, or we can drop the second runner from this sprint."
You do not know"I don't know yet. I'll know by Thursday, after the impact report."
Something broke on your watch"The develop pipeline was red for a day after my merge. It's green now; the cause was X; the check that would have caught it is in this sprint."

Every row has the same skeleton: the fact, the cause in one clause, and what happens next with a date. None of them apologizes at length, and none of them blames.

25.7.1 Jim models "I don't know yet"

The hardest of these for the team was "I don't know yet", because for thirty years not knowing was something you fixed before the meeting. In sprint 3 the deputy program manager asked, in the review, whether the prime's January drop would be "a big one". Jim did not know, and said so:

I don't know yet. The prime's modeler said "a few sensor changes". I'll know by the Tuesday after it lands, because the delta report lists every change and what it touches in our model. I'll send you the count that day.

— Jim, sprint 3 review

Two things happened. The program manager wrote "Tue after drop: count" on a pad and moved on, which surprised the team. And in the next stand-up, Bob said "I don't know yet, I'll know by tomorrow" about the ObservationRecord ownership question, for the first time. The lead going first is what makes it safe for everyone else.

25.8 Measuring whether it is working

Like everything else in this book, the team measured its own talking. Each sprint, Jim counted the share of stand-up lines that had both an outcome and a number. In sprint 1 it was low: most lines were mechanism. By sprint 6 most lines had both. Part III gives the real counts per sprint (Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0), and the scorecard in Part IV includes it.

The pulse survey's question "I can explain our progress to management in one sentence" moved too. That question was the one Jim watched most closely, because it is the one that tells you whether the engineers will speak up when the lead is on leave.

25.9 Exercises

Exercise 25.1: Rewrite five statuses

Take your last five spoken or written statuses (or the three at the start of this chapter). Rewrite each in the outcome, evidence, next-or-ask shape, keeping the Y/T/B format and a story id. Run them through talk.pl translate and fix what it flags. Which one was hardest, and why?

Exercise 25.2: Climb the ladder

Pick one thing your team finished this week. Write the one-sentence, thirty-second and five-minute versions. Say each out loud to a colleague and ask them to repeat the one-sentence version back to you. If they can't, rewrite it.

Exercise 25.3: Your stakeholder map

Make the table in Section 25.5, Know your audience: the Tidewater stakeholder map for your own program: every person who hears your status, what they care about, the one number they want, and the sentence. Which of those numbers can your pipeline produce today?

Exercise 25.4: Draft from GitLab

In the practice-lesson-11 sandbox, close one more of Bob's tasks with a --now date, then draft Friday's stand-up with talk.pl standup. Edit the draft so it says what the change means, not only what was closed.

Exercise 25.5: Run a dry run

Plan next sprint's demo with three roles and the six moves. Hold a thirty-minute dry run on Day 9. Write down every place the narrator stumbled, and change the script, not the narrator.

25.10 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the outcome, evidence, ask pattern; the ladder; the demo roles and their rotation; the Day 9 dry run; the four headline numbers; the bad-news skeleton (fact, cause, next with a date).
  • Adapt: the stakeholder map (your program's people and their numbers); the four headline numbers (pick the ones that say whether your project is on track: for a new model rather than a port, "requirements with a design" might replace "TODO lines left"); the glossary for talk.pl translate.
  • Decide locally: whether drafts from talk.pl or daily.pl propose are the default; who keeps the stakeholder map current; how often the lead reviews the share of statuses with a number (Tidewater: once a sprint, in the retro).
Note: You can now...
  • say a status as outcome, one number, and next step or ask, in the stand-up format the kit lints;
  • prepare one-sentence, thirty-second and five-minute versions of anything you report;
  • draft stand-ups, weekly notes and review scripts from GitLab with talk.pl, and correct them;
  • find the jargon and the "so what?" sentences in your own text;
  • run a demo with three roles, six moves and a dry run;
  • say "I don't know yet" with a date, and deliver bad news in a way that builds trust.

Part III: Twelve weeks

Part II set up the shop: the operating model, the laptops, git, Vim, GitLab, the pipeline, the journal and the meetings. Part III is the work itself. Each of the next six chapters is one two-week sprint of Jim, Bob and Tom's first twelve weeks, from Monday 5 October to Friday 18 December 2026, told from the record the sprint left behind.

That record is real in the only sense that matters for a study book: every stand-up status, poker round, issue, merge request, pipeline log, quad and survey answer quoted in these chapters was produced by running the kit's own tools on the Tidewater scenario, and the numbers are cited from those files rather than typed. The files are in docs/tidewater/ beside the book; its README.md lists every one with a line on what it shows. When a chapter says a pipeline failed, you can open the log. When it says the team committed so many points, the number on the page was read from the sprint's scorecard when the book was built.

Each sprint chapter has the same shape, so you can read them in order or jump to the one that matches where your own team is:

  • The question and the mood. Every sprint answered one systems engineering question, and the pulse survey at the retrospective measured how the team felt about the answer.
  • The kickoff. The goal, the capacity, the plan, the planning-poker rounds, and the learning budget.
  • Week one and week two, day by day. The stand-ups as they were posted, the GitLab work as it happened, and the thought process behind each decision: what the team chose, what else it could have done, and what it would do differently now.
  • Refinement, review and retrospective. What was estimated for the next sprint, what was shown to management and how it landed, and what the team changed.
  • The numbers. The scorecard at the end of the sprint, and what Jim told management.
  • You can now..., exercises, and applying this to your project.

Two warnings before you start. First, the team is not good at this yet. In sprint 1 their stand-up statuses fail the lint, their first merge request has no pipeline, and their first local pipeline is red. In sprint 2 their first real pipeline dies on its first line and their demo loses the room. That is the point: the book shows what a first attempt actually looks like, so yours does not have to be perfect to be on track. Second, the early sprints are mostly about the shop rather than the model. The bottom line up front (Bottom line up front) shows how quickly that changes; by sprint 4 most of the board is systems engineering.

26 Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in

From what you know

You know

the first weeks of a new program: kickoffs, accounts, and a plan nobody believes yet.

Here it is called

sprint 1: planning, stand-ups, the first drop and the first pipeline.

What is new

by day ten, something real is finished and measured.

Survival kit

What you have

three laptops that have never run git, a prime drop that arrived the Friday before, a directive, and a team that would rather be writing documents.

What you need from this sprint: a GitLab project with its rules switched on, laptops that pass the kit's doctor, the drop converted and measured, and an honest estimate of what the port will cost. Nothing in the model changes yet.

26.1 The question, and the mood

Every sprint in this book answered one systems engineering question. Sprint 1's was the one a systems engineer asks first about any inherited work product: what do we actually have, and what will it cost to make it ours?

The prime's model had arrived the Friday before, by CDRL file transfer, as an XMI export, a DOORS ReqIF export, a CSV and a manifest. Nobody on the team had opened the XMI, and nobody wanted to. The team's mood at the kickoff is best captured by the first thing Bob said that morning, which the stand-up chat preserved:

The pulse survey at the end of the sprint put a number on it: a mean of 1.9 on a scale of one to five, the lowest of the twelve weeks. The five questions, and how each person answered them on Friday 16 October, were:

Table 26.1. The pulse survey at the sprint 1 retrospective (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree)
QuestionJimBobTom
I understand why we are working this way.212
I can do my work in the new tools without help.222
The checks catch problems I would have missed.222
I can see our progress.222
I would choose to keep working this way.212

Read that table as a baseline, not a verdict. Nobody understood yet why they were working this way, and nobody could work without help. The rest of Part III is, among other things, the story of those cells changing.

26.2 Week zero, briefly

Sprint 1 did not start from nothing. The week before it, the team spent about two person-days on things that had to happen before a sprint could: the directive meeting, the scorecard agreed with the program manager, the software request for Git for Windows and Vim, the first meeting with the ISSM, the decisions drafted, and the delivery call with the prime's modeler. The record is short enough to read whole:

Two things in it matter for what follows. First, those hours are outside sprint 1's capacity, on purpose: they were the cost of deciding to start, and the team did not want them hidden inside a sprint where they would make the first velocity look worse than it was. Second, the delivery call on 2 October is where Jim asked the prime for stable element ids and a manifest with every drop. Everything the team later automated about prime drops depends on that one conversation. If you take one thing from week zero into your own project, take that call (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).

The record is in the simulation's state too; this is the first command of the chapter, and like every runnable block in this book it is tested:

26.3 The kickoff: Monday 5 October, 09:00

The kickoff ran ninety minutes and replaced the day's stand-up. Jim opened with the goal Jim had written on the whiteboard the night before:

A GitLab project the team can work in; drop 1 received and assessed.

Then capacity. The standing numbers (Chapter 13, The operating model) are five points a sprint for Jim, whose other duties do not stop for a port, and eight each for Bob and Tom. Monday 12 October was a federal holiday, so each person's capacity was prorated by working days. Then the commitment, kept deliberately below capacity. The kit printed the result as the kickoff record, and this is the plan the team worked to for the next two weeks, exactly as it was recorded:

Read the plan from the top down and three decisions stand out.

The learning story comes first. TW-1, "Learn the tools," is a story with points, an owner per task and a done date, like any other. It is 24% of the sprint's task points done (Section 13.8, Two ways to count "done"). Jim's argument, made to the program manager in week zero and repeated to the team at the kickoff, was that the learning would happen either way: on the board, where it is visible and can be protected, or on nights and weekends, where it becomes resentment. Putting it on the board also made it measurable, which mattered later when management asked what the overhead had cost (Bottom line up front).

Most of the sprint is platform work. Laptops, the GitLab project, the first pipeline, the working agreements: none of it changes the model. That is the honest shape of a first sprint, and the team said so in the plan rather than dressing it up. Only TW-5 and TW-6, receiving and assessing the drop, are engineering.

The commitment is below capacity. The kickoff line says how far below. Jim's first draft had been much larger (Chapter 13, The operating model); cutting it was, by Jim's own account later, the most useful thing Jim did in week zero, because it meant sprint 1 finished.

The journal holds the same numbers. This is the sprint report the kit prints from the ledger, run against the simulation's journal:

26.3.1 Planning poker, the first time

Each story was estimated in the meeting chat with a #est round: Jim posted the story, each person posted a number, and the kit's tally (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro) read the chat afterwards. When the votes spread, Jim did what the method asks: the highest and lowest voters said what they knew, and the team voted again. The round that taught the team the most was the one for converting and assessing the drop:

The spread was wide. The high vote came from Bob, who had spent two years of evenings fighting Cameo's exports and expected the conversion to be a week of hand work. The low vote came from Jim, who had run the converter once in week zero and knew it does the bulk mechanically. The conversation in between was the useful part: the story was not "convert the model" but "convert it and measure what is left," and the measuring is a report, not hand work. The second round converged. Bob's worry did not disappear; it moved, correctly, into the later stories that close the TODO lines the converter leaves behind.

Tip: What poker is for

A spread is information, not a failure. If everyone votes the same number at once, either the story is well understood or nobody has thought about it. The second round matters less than the sentence each outlier says between the rounds. In the chat record the sentences are not there, only the numbers; write them into the story's notes when they change the plan.

26.4 Week one

26.4.1 Monday 5: the first stand-up, and the first lint

The stand-up is written (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro). Each person posts Yesterday, Today and Blockers in the meeting chat, and after the meeting Jim pastes the chat into the kit, which checks it. The very first stand-up looked like this:

and the kit's lint said:

The warnings are fair. "Meetings, reviews" is what everyone wrote on a Monday in the document era, and it tells the reader nothing about the plan. The fix is not to invent work for yesterday; it is to name the story the work served, or to write that the day was the kickoff. Nobody minded the warnings on day one. The point of the lint is that it is the same every day, so the habit forms without anyone having to nag.

26.4.2 Tuesday 6: the lint finds an error, and Bob finds a phrase

On Tuesday Bob wrote the status the way one would write an e-mail:

An error, not a warning: the kit could not find the three parts at all, so Bob's day did not reach the journal. Jim sent Bob the reply line the lint suggests, Bob reposted, and that was the end of it. It is worth noticing what did not happen: nobody had to read Bob's paragraph and decide whether it was a status. The format did that.

The same afternoon Bob finished the practice lessons and said the sentence the team quoted to each other for the rest of the twelve weeks:

Bob meant it as a complaint. It is also the best one-line description of git for a systems engineer that this book knows of.

26.4.3 Wednesday 7 and Thursday 8: three laptops pass the doctor

Each laptop was sized at one point in the laptop story, TW-2, after week zero had shown that a software request on a government laptop takes days, not minutes. Each person ran kickoff.pl doctor (Chapter 9, The survival kit) until it passed. Tom's final run:

The one warning is a missing SSH key. The team decided to use HTTPS with a personal access token instead, because the token was simpler to get approved, and wrote that down rather than leaving the warning unexplained. A doctor run with warnings is fine. A doctor run with warnings nobody can explain is how laptops drift apart.

26.4.4 Thursday 8: drift in two minutes

The best moment of sprint 1 happened on its fourth day, and it happened to the team's biggest skeptic. Bob ran both converters on drop 1 for TW-6, the first time anyone on the team had used them on the real drop. The XMI converter reported what it carried and what it could not:

Then the requirements converter compared the prime's DOORS text with the requirement text inside the prime's own model, and printed this at the bottom:

The last three lines are the drift: the same requirement, TW-SYS-006, says "twice a day" in DOORS and does not in the model. In the document era nobody would have found it until a review, if then, because finding it meant reading two documents side by side. Bob posted in the chat:

You can do what Bob did. These two commands convert the drop into a scratch folder with the team's layout map and run the trace against it:

and this counts the TODO lines the converter left, which is the port's starting debt:

Case study: Why the drift mattered more than the number

The converter's numbers were reassuring: everything in scope ported, and a manageable set of TODO lines. But numbers like that do not change minds; they confirm what the person who ran the tool already believed. The drift changed a mind, because it was a real defect in a real deliverable, found in two minutes by the person who least wanted to be there. If you are leading a team like this one, look for that moment early and let the skeptic have it.

The drift became the team's first discrepancy report to the prime later, in sprint 4 (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed). In sprint 1 it stayed a note on TW-6, because the team had not yet agreed how to report discrepancies, and Jim did not want the first thing the prime received from the new process to be improvised.

26.4.5 Friday 9: the project exists

Tom applied the project file to the GitLab group the enterprise administrators had created. The command is one line; its output is long, because it is the whole configuration of the project, read back:

Look at one setting in particular: only_allow_merge_if_pipeline_succeeds=false. In sprint 1 there was no runner, so there could be no pipeline, so the rule that a merge needs a green pipeline had to wait. The team turned it on in sprint 2, the day the runner came online (Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated). Switching on a gate before the thing it checks exists is a reliable way to make a team hate the gate.

The first weekly quad went to management that afternoon. Its first two lines told the story of the first week:

Less than half the sprint was done after half the sprint, which is normal when the first week is learning and laptops. The quad says so without anyone having to explain it.

26.5 Week two

Monday 12 October was a holiday. The second week was four days.

26.5.1 Tuesday 13: proving a refusal

Tom's task #15 sounds odd for a systems engineer: prove that a push is refused. But a rule you have never seen fire is a rule you do not know works. Tom pushed a commit straight to the protected integration branch, and GitLab answered:
