That rejection is the configuration management board's rule, enforced by software: nothing reaches the integration branch except through a reviewed merge request. Tom saved the output to the issue as evidence and closed it.

The same day Jim checked the drop against its manifest. Every file the prime delivered is listed in the manifest with a SHA-256 checksum, and checking them takes one line. The tr at the front removes Windows line endings from the manifest, which the prime's build writes:

The first time Jim ran it without the tr, every file "failed," which is the kind of thing that ruins a morning if you do not know about line endings. It is in the rescue appendix now (Appendix E, Rescue: when something goes wrong).

26.5.2 Wednesday 14: the first merge request, without a pipeline

Tom's first merge request committed the CODEOWNERS file, the issue and merge request templates, and the .gitignore. It is the first merge request the project ever had, and its description says something unusual:

It has no pipeline on purpose: the pipeline file arrives in sprint 2. Jim approved it, Tom merged it, and the project had its first reviewed change. Look at the checklist: only one box is ticked. The other three could not apply yet, because there was no pipeline to run, no docs job and no trace job, and Tom left them empty with the reason beside each. It is a small thing, and it is exactly the kind of small thing that decides whether a checklist means anything: tick only what you actually did.

The kit lets you read any merge request the team made, from the simulation's GitLab:

Bob closed the assessment the same day. The story issue shows what "done" meant for an engineering story in sprint 1:

and the task for running the converters, closed on Friday 9, shows the habit the team adopted for every task: the result goes in a comment on the issue, where the next person will look for it, not in an e-mail:

26.5.3 Thursday 15: the Definition of Done, and refinement

Jim wrote the working agreements into the wiki. The Definition of Done is the part the team argued about longest, because it is where "finished" stops being a matter of opinion:

At 10:00 the team held the sprint's refinement (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro): the stories for sprint 2, checked against the Definition of Ready and estimated with poker. The record:

Notice what the list says about the team's thinking at the end of its first week and a half. The drop is not merged yet; the plan is to bring it in through the vendor branch, in layers, which means Bob had already decided the model's folder layout would follow the layered structure rather than the converter's default (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where). That decision is cheap in sprint 2 and very expensive later, because every future drop must land in the same folders.

26.5.4 Friday 16: a red pipeline on a laptop

Tom's last task was to run the draft pipeline on Tom's laptop against drop 1, with the kit's local runner (Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero). There was still no GitLab runner, so this was the only way to see the pipeline work. It did not pass:

Grammar and lint passed: the converted model is valid SysML v2 and structurally sound. The outline check failed, because the converted packages and folders do not meet the rule that every parent has between two and nine children. That is not a defect Tom introduced; it is what the prime's model looks like.

This is the first real decision of the port, and it is worth slowing down for, because every team porting an inherited model will face it.

Objection: "Just turn the outline check off until the port is done"

That was Tom's first suggestion, and it is the most common one. The trouble is that a check you have turned off does not come back on by itself; the team would have shipped baseline-0 with the check still off.

Answer

The team kept the check and gave it an allowance: the number of violations the drop arrived with is recorded in a file in the repository, the pipeline fails only if a change makes the number bigger, and every change that makes it smaller lowers the allowance in the same merge request. The inherited debt is visible, counted and paid down; new debt is refused. This is a ratchet, and the team used the same idea later for the trace and complexity checks (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

The review on Friday morning was short. The deputy program manager attended, as the meeting record shows:

and the review record is plain:

The four headline numbers at the bottom show how little there was to show: no TODO lines because the drop was not in the model yet, no verification coverage because the trace did not run in a pipeline yet. The demonstration was a walk through the board and the GitLab project. The deputy's one question, recorded above, is the one every manager asks of a port: when does the model itself move? Jim's answer put a date on it, sprint 2, and named the mechanism that would check every change after that. The team took the question as the measure of sprint 2.

26.5.5 The retrospective

The start items are both about evidence. Writing the story id in every status is the lint lesson from Monday. Running the converter report before estimating is the poker lesson: the TW-6 round would have taken one vote instead of two if Bob had seen the report first. The stop item says the same thing from the other side. The continue items are about how the team learned: at the terminal, in pairs, with one issue per action so nothing lived only in someone's memory.

The scorecard (Chapter 3, The directive) was computed by the kit from GitLab and the journal at the end of the sprint:

Everything committed was done. The one gated-changes figure that reads badly, no change gated, is the merge request with no pipeline, and it is honest: there was nothing to gate it with yet. 26.7 What Jim told management

The weekly quad went to the program manager on Friday afternoon (Chapter 36, Telling management). Its top lines:

Jim added two sentences of Jim's own in the covering e-mail, and they are a fair model for a first-sprint report:

We have a project, protected branches, three working laptops and drop 1 measured: everything in scope converts, and the conversion debt is counted. We also found a requirement whose text differs between DOORS and the prime's model, which we will report to the prime formally once the reporting route is agreed.

No adjectives, no promises about December, one finding, and the next thing management will see: the model itself, on the integration branch, at the end of sprint 2.

26.8 Tools adopted this sprint, and the pain each removed

Table 26.3. What sprint 1 brought in

26.9 What went wrong, and why it was fine

  • The first stand-ups failed the lint. Expected, cheap to fix, and fixed by the habit rather than by a rule.
  • The first merge request had no pipeline. Unavoidable without a runner; the description said so, which is what made it acceptable.
  • Checklist boxes ticked by habit. Not caught in review. A template checklist is only worth what the person ticking it actually did.
  • The first pipeline was red. On a laptop, before anything depended on it, which is the cheapest place for a pipeline to be red. The red outline check produced the ratchet, one of the most useful ideas of the twelve weeks.
  • The drift was found and then parked. Deliberately: the team wanted an agreed discrepancy-report route before sending the prime anything.

26.10 You can now...

  • run kickoff.pl doctor and act on its output;
  • read a stand-up lint and fix a status that fails it;
  • run planning poker and use the spread, not just the result;
  • convert a prime drop, read the converter's report, and count the conversion debt;
  • run the trace and find text drift between DOORS and the model;
  • verify a delivery against its manifest;
  • explain why a gate is switched on only when the thing it checks exists;
  • explain a ratchet, and why it beats turning a check off.

26.11 Exercises

Exercise 26.1: The first status

Rewrite Bob's Tuesday status from the chat above so that the lint parses it and it names the story it served. Then write Monday's "meetings, reviews" line the way the lint would accept on a kickoff day.

Exercise 26.2: Read the drop yourself

In the tidewater sandbox, convert drop 1 as Bob did, then open s1/model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml in Vim and find the TODO line for the BuoyModes state machine. What v1 element does its id point at? (Practice lesson 10 walks through the same edit on a smaller scale; Chapter 10, Vim for models.)

Exercise 26.3: A spread worth having

Look at the TW-3 rounds in docs/tidewater/sprints/01/poker-2026-10-05.txt. Bob voted highest. Write the one sentence Bob might have said between the rounds, and the sentence you would add to the story's notes.

Exercise 26.4: Your week zero

List the hours your own team would spend before its first sprint, in the format of the week-zero record. Which of them would you be tempted to hide inside sprint 1, and why should you not?

26.12 Applying this to your project

  • Make the first sprint about the shop and say so. Laptops, the project, the rules, the first pipeline on a laptop. Do not promise model progress in sprint 1; promise a measured starting point.
  • Put learning on the board with points and owners. It is the first thing management will ask about later.
  • Measure the inherited work before you estimate it. Run the converters, count the debt, run the trace. The first real finding is your best argument; let the person who doubts the most find it.
  • Switch gates on in the order the things they check come into being, and prove each one refuses what it should.
  • Ratchet inherited debt instead of switching checks off.
  • Ask the prime for stable ids and a manifest before the first drop, not after.

27 Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated

From what you know

You know

the first delivery from a contractor, and the argument about where it lives.

Here it is called

the vendor branch and the first merge request into develop.

What is new

the prime's model arrives through a gate, and every change after it is checked.

Survival kit

What you have

a GitLab project with its rules, three working laptops, drop 1 converted on a laptop and measured, a pipeline that runs only on Tom's machine, and a team still unconvinced.

What you need from this sprint: a runner, so the pipeline runs on the server for every change; the drop on the integration branch through the vendor branch, in a folder layout that every future drop will land in; and the team's decisions written down where the next person will find them.

27.1 The question, and the mood

Sprint 2's systems engineering question was about configuration control: can the prime's model live on our integration branch, with every change to it checked and reviewed, without anyone editing the prime's model? If the answer was yes, the team had a baseline it controlled. If it was no, the whole port was a copy that would go stale with the next drop.

The answer was yes, and the pulse survey moved for the first time, to a mean of 2.4:

Table 27.1. The pulse survey at the sprint 2 retrospective
QuestionJimBobTom
I understand why we are working this way.322
I can do my work in the new tools without help.222
The checks catch problems I would have missed.232
I can see our progress.323
I would choose to keep working this way.323

Bob's answer to the third question moved first. The checks had caught something, and Bob had seen it. The sprint also had the twelve weeks' worst moment in front of management, which is why the last row is still low. Both stories are below.

27.2 The kickoff: Monday 19 October

The stories had been estimated at the sprint 1 refinement (Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in), so the kickoff was about capacity, the commitment and who did what. A full ten-day sprint gave more capacity than sprint 1, and the team committed a larger share of it, because the first sprint had finished and they trusted their numbers a little more:

The learning story shrank from sprint 1's, as planned. The platform share was still more than half, because the runner and the real pipeline were the sprint's main platform work and could not wait.

Two estimates had needed a second round at the refinement. The import of drop 1 through the vendor branch:

The high vote was Tom's. Tom had read the gitflow chapter (Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers) and knew the vendor branch meant two merges, one onto the vendor branch and one from it into the integration branch, plus a layout decision before either. The team settled between the two first votes. The other split was over Jim's own story, getting the team's enablers, decisions and conventions on record:

Jim gave the lowest vote on work Jim would do, which is the usual mistake: the person who will do the writing remembers the writing and forgets the reviews. The second round added the reviews back.

27.3 Week one

27.3.1 Monday 19: statuses with no outcome

The first stand-up of sprint 2 shows a habit that sprint 1 had not fixed:

The lint caught the missing story ids again. What the lint cannot catch is that not one of these lines says what is now true that was not true yesterday. That is what the scorecard's stand-up outcome share measures, and for sprint 2 it was 0: every line was a list of activities. Nobody flagged it at the time. It surfaced at the review, in the worst possible way.

27.3.2 Tuesday 20: the runner is online

The enterprise administrators registered the runner Tom had requested in sprint 1: a Windows virtual machine with Git for Windows, a shell executor, and the tags the pipeline asks for (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs). Tom's half-point task was to check the registration and the tags. It was the shortest task of the sprint and the one everything else waited on.

27.3.3 Wednesday 21: asking for what the team needs, in writing

Jim wrote the request for enablers that the operating model calls for (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim), using the memo template. The heart of it is a table of dated asks, each with what it buys and what happens if the answer is no:

The memo did two things a spoken request in a meeting would not. It made each ask specific enough to say yes or no to, and it put a date on the cost of no. The training hours in the first row are the learning budget, which until then had been protected only by Jim's say-so.

27.3.4 Thursday 22: the layout decision

Bob's task #39 was the most consequential half-day of the sprint: deciding where the converted model would live in the repository. The converter's default is one folder per v1 package, named after the package. The alternative is a layered layout, with libraries, requirements, logical behavior, physical structure, analysis and verification in their own folders and the packages placed in them by a layout map (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where).

The thought process went like this.

  • Every future drop must land in the same folders. The vendor branch works because git can compare the prime's new drop with the old one file by file. If a package moves between drops, git sees a deletion and an addition, and the merge with the government's edits becomes manual. So the layout chosen now is the layout for the life of the program.
  • The layers are how the team wanted to review. A reviewer looking at a change to a requirement package wants to know immediately that it is a requirement change, and the code owners for requirements are not the code owners for physical structure (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).
  • The layout map costs one file. A text file that says which package goes in which folder, applied by the converter on every drop. Moving a package later means editing that file and re-importing on the vendor branch, which is possible but not something to do casually.

Bob chose the layered layout, and the team recorded the choice in the merge request that imported the drop.

27.3.5 Friday 23: the pipeline dies on its first line

Tom committed the pipeline that had run on Tom's laptop the Friday before, opened a first merge request with a real pipeline, and watched it fail on every job:

Read the errors. The term 'FILES=$(find' is not recognized as the name of a cmdlet is PowerShell talking. The Windows runner's shell executor runs PowerShell by default, and the pipeline had been written in the Bash dialect that Git Bash uses on Tom's laptop. $(...), || and $KIT mean nothing to PowerShell. Tom's reaction is in the record:

The first pipeline on the real runner died on line one. PowerShell. Nobody told me the runner speaks PowerShell.

— Tom, sprint 2

This is the lesson of the runners chapter (Section 21.6, The lesson of the first week: PowerShell), and the team took the fix described there: every job's script became one line, perl ci/job.pl NAME, with the logic in a Perl script in the repository. Perl reads the same under PowerShell, Git Bash, Linux and Docker. The second pipeline on the same merge request:

Look at line five: no .sysml files under model/ yet. The pipeline is green because there is nothing in the repository for it to check. That is worth saying out loud, because a green pipeline on an empty model proves the plumbing, not the model. Jim approved the merge request on that understanding:

The simulation's GitLab still holds both pipelines. This is the failed one as GitLab lists it:

and the first lines of its grammar job's log:

The same afternoon Tom switched on "pipelines must succeed" and the merge request report widgets (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep). From that moment no change could reach the integration branch without a green pipeline. Bob's conventions package, the government's own library of level tags (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where), was the first model change to go through the full gate, and it passed on its first pipeline.

27.4 Week two

27.4.1 Monday 26: level tags and decision records

Bob named the level tags in sysml.conf, and Jim merged the team's decision records: the ten decisions drafted in week zero, plus the scaffold's own, as numbered files under docs/adr/ in the repository rather than slides in a briefing (Chapter 13, The operating model). The list is worth reading as a summary of how the team decided to work:

Each file is a page: the context, the decision, and its consequences. The point of keeping them in the repository is that a decision is changed the same way a model element is, by a reviewed merge request, and the history shows when and why.

27.4.2 Tuesday 27: the drop on the vendor branch

Tom imported drop 1 onto the vendor branch with gitlab.pl flow vendor (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition). The vendor branch holds nothing but the prime's deliveries, converted with the layout map, one commit per drop. Nobody edits it. The government's work happens on the integration branch, and each drop reaches it through a merge request from a short feature branch that merges the vendor branch in. That merge request was opened the same morning, and Jim said the sentence the team remembers from the sprint:

The model is on develop and nobody touched it with a mouse.

— Jim, sprint 2

It was not quite on develop yet. It was on its way through review, which is the point.

27.4.3 Wednesday 28: refinement for sprint 3

The list turned toward engineering for the first time: closing the conversion debt in the Network package, bringing the DOORS modules into the model, and the first drift and gap analysis. The platform stories that remained were about making the checks report something useful: the trace report and secret detection.

27.4.4 Thursday 29: the drop is merged

Bob reviewed the drop merge request. The review note is short, and it records the outline decision from sprint 1:

The pipeline on the drop merge request is the first one with the whole model in it. Its outline job shows the allowance at work:

The last two lines are the ratchet from sprint 1 in action: the drop arrives with its outline violations, they are reported, the allowance is set to that count, and from now on any change that adds a violation fails. The same merge request shows the code-quality widget in GitLab listing every one of those findings against the change that brought them in:

Bob and Jim both approved, because the drop touched folders owned by each of them, and the merge request was merged. The history of the integration branch now reads like a change log, one reviewed merge per line:

The same day Tom added two more jobs to the pipeline: todo, which counts the conversion debt on every change, and docs, which regenerates the model's generated documents and fails if the committed copies are out of date. The todo job's first count on the integration branch was 52, the number the port would burn down for the next four sprints.

27.4.5 Friday 30: the demo that lost the room

The review was the low point of the twelve weeks, and it is in the record:

Tom drove the demo, opened a terminal, scrolled through the pipeline file, explained the PowerShell problem, and finished on a green pipeline, which on that day was the most impressive thing Tom had seen in a month. The deputy program manager saw a terminal, a file full of words like rules and artifacts, and a green dot. The question at the end was fair, and nobody had an answer ready:

I did not follow the demo. What did we get for the two weeks?

— Deputy PM, sprint 2 review

What they had got was considerable: the prime's model under the government's configuration control, every change checked and reviewed, the conversion debt counted, the decisions on record. The team knew that. They had not said it in words the deputy could repeat to anyone else. The four headline numbers were at the bottom of the review record and nobody read them out.

Case study: Why the demo failed, in one sentence

The team demonstrated the machinery to someone who had come to see the result. The fix (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not) is a structure, not a talent: open with the question the sprint answered, show the output rather than the tool, give one before-and-after number, make one safe change live, and close with what it means and what you need. The team used exactly that structure in sprint 4, and it worked (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed).

27.4.6 The retrospective

The start items are the two lessons from the demo: rehearse it on Day 9, and rotate the driver so that nobody's first demo is in front of the deputy. The stop items are the two lessons from the week: no shell in the pipeline file, and no terminals in demos. The continue items are what was already working: running the pipeline locally before pushing, and small merge requests.

One more thing turned up at the review, in the GitLab To-Do lists the team looked at before the meeting:

The first issue in Tom's list is the intake issue for drop 1, opened when the drop arrived and never closed, although the drop had been received, checked and merged. It is a small housekeeping slip, and a useful one: the To-Do list is where it shows, and nobody had looked at the To-Do list until the review.

27.8 What went wrong, and what the team did about it

  • The pipeline was written for the wrong shell. Found on the first server run, fixed within the day, and the fix made the pipeline more portable than it would otherwise have been.
  • A green pipeline on an empty model. Not wrong, but easy to misread. The team learned to ask what a green pipeline actually checked.
  • The demo. The fix was a structure and a rehearsal, adopted at the retrospective and used from sprint 3.
  • Stand-up lines with no outcome. Not caught by the lint, caught by the deputy's question. The team started writing outcome-first statuses in sprint 3, with drafts from talk.pl (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not).
  • The intake issue for the first drop left open. Caught in the To-Do list at the review. Closing the intake issue belongs on the drop intake checklist (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).

27.9 You can now...

  • read a pipeline log and tell a shell error from a model error;
  • explain why every job runs perl ci/job.pl NAME, and what goes wrong without it;
  • explain what a green pipeline proves and what it does not;
  • import a prime drop onto the vendor branch and merge it through a feature branch;
  • choose a repository layout with the next drop in mind, and record it in a layout map;
  • write a request for enablers as dated asks with the cost of no;
  • recognise a demo that shows machinery instead of results, and restructure it.

27.10 Exercises

Exercise 27.1: Translate the failure

Take the first job in the failed pipeline log above. Write, in one sentence each, what a systems engineer who has never seen PowerShell needs to understand to fix it, and what Tom changed. (The runners chapter has the answer; Section 21.6, The lesson of the first week: PowerShell.)

Exercise 27.2: Re-run the demo

Write the sprint 2 demo script that should have been given, using the structure in Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not: the question, the output to show, one before-and-after with a number from the scorecard table above, one safe live change, and the ask. Keep it to five minutes.

Exercise 27.3: Read the integration branch

In the tidewater sandbox, list the integration branch's merges up to the end of sprint 2 with the git log command above. For each line, name the story it closed. Which merge brought the model in, and which merges changed only the machinery?

Exercise 27.4: A layout for your model

Sketch the layout map for a model you know: which packages go in the library, requirements, logical, physical, analysis and verification folders? Which package would you be least sure about, and what would it cost to move it after the third drop?

27.11 Applying this to your project

  • Run the pipeline on the real runner as early as you can, and expect the first run to fail for a reason that has nothing to do with the model.
  • Keep the pipeline's scripts shell-neutral from the start: one command per job, logic in a script in the repository.
  • Decide the repository layout before the first drop is merged, and write it down as a map the converter applies.
  • Bring the inherited model in through a vendor branch and never edit it there. Record the inherited debt as the starting point of a ratchet.
  • Write your asks down with dates and the cost of no. A memo gets decided; a remark in a meeting gets remembered differently by everyone who heard it.
  • Rehearse the demo and say the result before the mechanism. The first time you get it wrong in front of management is the last time you will need to be told.

28 Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named

From what you know

You know

the day a reviewer finds the mistake you missed.

Here it is called

a red pipeline.

What is new

the mistake is found minutes after you make it, by a machine, before anyone else sees it.

Survival kit

What you have

a pipeline that gates every change (Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated), drop 1 on develop through the vendor branch, the level conventions, and a team that has merged its first model changes but is still unsure it likes any of this.

What you need

the DOORS requirements inside the model next to the prime's copy, a report on every change that says which requirements have no design and no test, and a way of working with the pipeline when it says no. You also need to learn that a wait you do not say out loud is a blocker nobody can help with.

Sprint 3 ran from Monday 2 November to Friday 13 November 2026. It is the sprint the team remembers as the low point, and the survey agrees: the pulse fell from 2.4 at the end of sprint 2 to 2.2. Nothing went badly wrong. The pipeline stopped one of Bob's changes, the security office took three days to sign a form, and the burn-down chart barely moved. Those three things, each small, landed on people who had not yet seen the new way of working pay them back.

This chapter is worth reading slowly for that reason. Every team that makes this change has a sprint 3. The work gets done; the feeling lags behind it. What the team did about the feeling matters as much as what it did about the model.

28.1 The question this sprint answered

Sprint 2 put the prime's model into GitLab. Sprint 3 asked the first question a systems engineer actually cares about:

Do the requirements in our model match the requirements in DOORS, and which of them have nothing designed to meet them or nothing planned to verify them?

For thirty years the team answered that question with a spreadsheet, two days before a milestone review. Jim's scorecard records the document-era answer time as 2 working days of spreadsheet work (a notional figure, from the program's last document-era review cycle). At the end of this sprint the pipeline answers it on every change, in about 26 seconds of job time. That is the sprint's real result. The rest of this chapter is how they got there and what it felt like.

28.2 Kickoff: Monday 2 November

The kickoff ran from 09:00 to 10:30, as every kickoff does, and stood in for that day's stand-up. Jim brought the plan the team had refined and estimated on the Wednesday of the previous sprint. The kit wrote the record:

Three things in that record are worth pausing on.

The commitment is lower than last sprint's. The team committed 15 points against the capacity line above, where in sprint 2 it had committed 19. Sprint 2 went well: every committed point was done. The natural instinct after a good sprint is to commit more. Jim did the opposite, for two reasons Jim gave out loud at the kickoff. Wednesday 11 November is Veterans Day, a federal holiday, so the sprint has nine working days, not ten; the capacity line already accounts for that. And this sprint brings two things the team has never done: putting the DOORS export into the model, and a trace report that will show, for the first time, numbers about requirements that nobody has looked at systematically in years. Unknowns deserve slack.

Note: The thought process: commit to what you can finish, not to what you hope

A team that commits to everything it can imagine and finishes three quarters of it has told management nothing. A team that commits to less and finishes all of it has told management exactly what it can do. The second team gets trusted with more. Jim's rule, borrowed from the operating model (Chapter 13, The operating model), is to commit no more than about nine tenths of capacity and less when the sprint has a new kind of work in it.

Learning is still on the board. The story TW-50, "Learn: the workbook second half; talking about progress", carries 2.5 points: the second half of the SysML v2 workbook (Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook) for Bob, and for everyone the stand-up drafting tool talk.pl (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not). In sprint 1 learning was a quarter of the board; here it is 17% of the task points done (Section 13.8, Two ways to count "done"), and it keeps falling. That is the curve the BLUF promised management (Bottom line up front), and it only happens if the learning is on the board where everyone can see it being spent.

Platform work has shrunk. In sprint 2, building the shop took more than half the board. This sprint the platform share is 30% and engineering is 53% for the first time. Tom has two platform stories, the trace and secrets jobs and the runner hardening, and both exist because a real need showed up, not because a list of DevSecOps features said so.

Each story on that list was estimated with planning poker at the sprint 2 refinement and checked against the Definition of Ready. The kickoff did not re-estimate. It cut each story into tasks of at most a few days, assigned them, and committed. Ninety minutes, including the stand-up.

28.3 Week 1

28.3.1 Monday 2 November: drafting the stand-up

The sprint 2 retrospective had produced one change to how the team talks: statuses should lead with an outcome and carry one number. In sprint 2, not one stand-up line did; the scorecard's measure for it is 0. People reported motion ("worked on the pipeline") because that is what thirty years of status meetings had taught them to report.

So from this sprint the team drafts its statuses with talk.pl, which reads yesterday's GitLab activity and writes a line in the kit's terse format, outcome first. Each person then edits the draft before posting it. The kit keeps both:

Look at what changed between draft and posted line. Jim and Bob posted the draft as written, apart from the ellipsis where a long task title was cut. Tom changed the plan: "(first thing: read the review comments)", because a review waiting on Tom's merge request mattered more that morning than the task the draft picked. That is the honest finding from the evidence: most mornings the draft is right, and the edit, when there is one, is the engineer's judgement. Once the board is kept up to date, the draft is usually right, and editing it takes seconds. The value is not in the editing. It is that the draft starts from what actually happened, so nobody has to remember yesterday at 09:00 or invent a number.

For the sprint the share was 1, as a fraction: every stand-up line that reported work carried an outcome and a number. Chapter Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not explains why the draft helps engineers who would otherwise say nothing, and its limits.

28.3.2 Tuesday 3 November: the DOORS modules go onto the vendor branch

Jim's first task of the sprint was to put the DOORS export into the model. The prime's drop 1 included a ReqIF file alongside the Cameo XMI. In sprint 2 the team converted only the XMI. Now Jim re-ran the import with both converters, so the DOORS modules become SysML v2 packages under model/requirements/ next to the Cameo copy of the requirements.

Jim did it on the vendor branch, not on develop, and that choice deserves a sentence because it was argued. Bob's first instinct was to convert the ReqIF on a feature branch, since "it's just more files." Jim's answer was the rule the team wrote down in sprint 2 (ADR 0002, the prime boundary): anything that comes from the prime enters through vendor/prime and nowhere else. The DOORS export is the prime's. If it enters through a feature branch, the next drop cannot merge cleanly against it, because git has no record of the prime's version to merge from. Chapter Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition works through why the vendor branch is the only way the drops stay mergeable.

28.3.3 Wednesday 4 November: a green first pipeline

Bob opened merge request !8, "Level tags in Network", at 10:00: the TODO lines in the Network package that stood for the old Cameo level stereotypes, replaced by the @L metadata the team defined in sprint 2. The pipeline went green on the first try, Jim approved it, and Bob merged it the same afternoon. You can look at it in the team's GitLab:

The first line names the merge request and its branch, the second its author, labels, approver and pipeline. It is a small change and it is exactly what the team wanted every change to look like: one task, one branch, one merge request, green, reviewed, merged, closed.

28.3.4 Thursday 5 November: what a good stand-up line looks like

Here is Bob's line from Thursday's stand-up, as posted:

It names the story (TW-51), says what is now true ("Close the Network TODO lines: 1 TODOs closed, 51 left"), says what Bob will do today, and says nothing blocks the work. A manager reading it learns that one TODO line was closed and how many remain, without a meeting. The kit's lint checked it:

28.3.5 Friday 6 November: the red X

Bob opened merge request !9 at ten in the morning. The story was the last Network TODO line, a Cameo "include" between two use cases. The converter had left it as a comment, because it does not map UML includes:

Bob replaced the TODO with what Bob believed was the SysML v2 form. You can see the edit in Bob's clone. The commit is named by its subject, :/^Replace the Include TODO (the newest commit whose message starts with those words), because commit ids differ from one copy of the repository to the next:

The pipeline for !9 failed. Two jobs went red, grammar and lint, and the merge request showed a red X. This is the first time the team saw the gate stop a change, and here is the part of the log that matters:

The grammar job ran the kit's checker against the official SysML v2 grammar and found the problem on line 39, column 41: after include use case : it expected a name, a :> or another of the listed tokens, and it found QueryArchive queryArchive instead. Bob had written the type before the name, the way Cameo shows a property in a diagram compartment and the way many programming languages declare a variable. SysML v2 text puts the name first and the type after a colon: queryArchive : QueryArchive.

You can reproduce the error yourself from the commit, which is still in the repository:

And the fixed file, from the commit Bob pushed to the same branch:

28.3.6 Reading the log, line by line

Nobody on the team had read a job log before October. It is worth taking one apart once, slowly, because every red X from now on is read the same way.

Table 28.1. Reading a failing job log
Line in the logWhat it tells you
pipeline #23 (merge_request_event, refs/merge-requests/9/merge) failed, 5 jobswhich pipeline, why it ran (a merge request), what it tested (the merge of !9 into develop, not just Bob's branch), and the result
==== grammar check failedone job: its name, its stage, its result, how long it took
$ perl ci/job.pl grammarthe command the job ran, exactly as you can run it yourself
$ /usr/bin/perl $KIT/tools/sysml/sysml.pl check model/...what that command ran in turn: the grammar check on every model file
model/physical/network/Network.sysml:39:41: error: unexpected 'queryArchive'; expected ...the finding: file, line, column, what was found and what the grammar allowed there
sysml: 14 file(s), 1 error(s)the checker's summary
ci-reports grammar: 14 check(s), 1 failed, 1 finding(s)the same result turned into the test and code-quality reports GitLab shows on the merge request

Three habits follow from that table. Read the first line, so you know whether you are looking at your branch alone or at the merge result. Scroll to the first line with error: in it, not the last line of the log, because later jobs often fail because of the first error (here the lint job failed on the same syntax error). And copy the $ command: it runs the same way on your laptop, which is the fastest way to try a fix. In Vim, :make on the file puts the same error in the quickfix list and jumps to line 39, column 41 (Chapter 10, Vim for models).

Case study: What "include use case" means

In the Cameo model, the use case ReviewObservations had a UML include relationship to QueryArchive: reviewing observations always involves querying the archive. The converter has no mapping for UML includes, so it left a TODO line naming the include and its xmi:id.

In SysML v2 text an include is a usage inside the including use case: include use case queryArchive : QueryArchive; says that every performance of ReviewObservations includes a performance of QueryArchive, and gives that included performance a name, queryArchive, that other parts of the model can refer to. The grammar check confirms the line is well formed; the lint step confirms that QueryArchive resolves to the use case defined a few lines below. Both are needed. The grammar check alone would accept a misspelled type name; Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook shows the difference with a worked example.

The second pipeline, #24, was green, Jim approved, and Bob merged !9 at 15:00 the same day. The whole episode, from red X to merged, took one working morning.

Bob's reaction, recorded in the sprint's quotes, is the honest one:

A red X on my own MR. One missing word, and the machine found it before Jim did.

— Bob, sprint 3

There are two ways to hear that sentence, and the team heard both. One is embarrassment: a machine graded my work and I failed in front of my colleagues. The other is relief: the mistake never reached the model, never reached Jim's review, and never reached the prime or the program office. In the Cameo years, an error like this sat in the model until somebody tried to use the element, sometimes months later.

Objection: The machine is grading me

The objection, as Bob put it to Jim: "I have been doing this for twenty-six years. I do not need a script telling me my syntax is wrong in front of everybody."

Answer

the pipeline is not a judge, and nobody sees it but the team. A red X on a merge request is the cheapest possible place for a mistake to be found: before review, before merge, before anyone downstream relies on it. The retrospective turned the complaint into a practice the team kept: fix a red pipeline on the branch, not around it, and do not take it personally. The numbers back the habit: in this sprint 3 of 4 merge requests passed on their first pipeline, and the one that did not was green by lunch.

28.3.7 Friday 6 November, continued: DOORS and the trace report

Two more merge requests opened on the same Friday.

Jim's !10, "Prime drop v1.0 with the DOORS modules", merged the vendor branch, now carrying the DOORS packages, into develop. Its pipeline was green. Bob reviewed it the following Tuesday, and the review note is a good example of what reviewing a drop looks like: not reading every converted line, but reading the delta report and the conflict table.

Tom's !11 added the trace report to the pipeline, and a secrets check. The trace job runs the DOORS-to-model trace on every pipeline. Here is what it printed on the first run, from the log of pipeline #29:

Read it slowly; this is the most important output of the sprint.

  • C, linked: 29 of 30 DOORS requirements have a counterpart in the model with the same DOORS id. One does not: TW-SYS-016 is in DOORS and not in the prime's model at all.
  • F, orphans: 2 requirements have nothing in the model that satisfies them.
  • G, unverified: 9 requirements have no verification case.
  • I, completeness: 66.7% of requirements are both satisfied and verified.
  • Drift: TW-SYS-006 says something different in DOORS than in the model's copy.

The drift line is the easiest to see with your own eyes. Both copies of TW-SYS-006 are in the model now, one from the prime's Cameo export and one from the DOORS export:

The Cameo copy says the data center shall publish a marine bulletin on a fixed schedule. DOORS says twice a day, on a fixed schedule. Which wording is right is not the government team's call to make by editing a file: DOORS is the requirements baseline the prime is contracted to, and the model is supposed to match it. The gap goes back to the prime as a discrepancy report, DR-1, in Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed.

How does the trace job know which copy is which? Every file the DOORS converter writes starts with a line that says so:

The trace job compares DOORS, as exported, against the model without those generated packages; otherwise it would compare DOORS with its own copy and find nothing. Chapter Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job shows the rule in the job.

None of these gaps were made by the government team. They are in the prime's model and the prime's DOORS module, and they had been there, unseen, since drop 1 arrived. The trace job made them visible. That is why Tom added it as report only: the job prints the gaps and never fails a pipeline because of them. If it failed, every merge request on the team would go red for problems none of them could fix, and the team would learn to ignore red. Chapter Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job shows the job; Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself shows the day it becomes a gate, and why only then.

Note: The thought process: a check you cannot pass teaches people to ignore checks

Tom's rule for adding a job: if the team cannot make it green by its own work, the job reports; it does not fail. The gaps here belong to the prime. The right response is a discrepancy report to the prime (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed), not a red pipeline for Bob. A gate is for problems the person merging can fix.

The secrets job is the "Sec" in DevSecOps, at its smallest useful size. It scans every tracked file for things that look like keys, tokens or passwords and fails if it finds one. On the first run it found none in the repository's tracked files. It took Tom less than an hour, it runs in seconds, and it closes the most likely security incident for a modeling team: someone pastes a credential into a file and pushes it. Chapter Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system puts it in context.

28.4 Week 2

28.4.1 Monday 9 to Thursday 12 November: a wait said a day late, with no one to ask

Tom's second story, TW-54, was runner hardening: the GitLab runner that executes every pipeline job is a Windows machine running jobs under an account, and the security office wanted that account to be a service account with the least privilege it needs, approved by the ISSM, with a hardening checklist in the wiki. Tom started the task on Monday 9 November; it closed on Thursday 12 November.

Most of those days were waiting: the checklist was quick, the ISSM's signature on the service account was not. Here are Tom's stand-up lines from the three working days of that wait (Wednesday 11 November was a holiday), as posted:

Read the last field, day by day. On Monday it says B none, although the request was already sitting with another office. On Tuesday the block appears, a day late, and the kit records it in the journal. But look at the ask: "a date from the ISSM". It names no one who can get that date. On Thursday it is still there, and the ask has become "help to unblock it", still with no name and no date. The kit's lint could not catch either problem, because a status that says "none", or a blocker with a vague ask, is a valid status.

At the retrospective, Tom said what had happened:

Three days waiting on a signature. The pipeline was the fast part.

— Tom, 10 November

and the team wrote it down as the sprint's one thing to stop:

This is the most useful failure in the twelve weeks, because it is the one every engineer recognizes. Engineers do not like to say they are blocked. It sounds like an excuse, or like asking for help, or like criticizing another office. So they say "none" and wait. The stand-up exists to catch exactly this, and it only works if waiting is said out loud, with a date and an ask:

Said on Monday, that line would have started the block a day earlier, named the person who could act, and put the ask in Jim's hands that morning. Chapter Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not has the templates; the change the team made was simply to agree that a wait on anyone outside the team for more than one day is a blocker and gets said.

28.4.2 Tuesday 10 November: the DOORS modules merge

Bob merged !10 on Tuesday, after reading the delta. The review note mentions the outline allowance. That is the file .ci/outline-max, which records how many outline violations (packages with too few or too many members, folders with a single file) the model is allowed to have. The prime's drop brings its own: the converted Requirements package has more members than the 2-to-9 rule allows, because Cameo put every requirement in one package. The outline job does not fail the drop for that. It records the new count as the allowance, and from then on any change that adds a violation fails, while any change that removes one must lower the number. You can see the allowance move in the history, one line per commit that changed the file, with the number it recorded:

Read it from the bottom up: 1 at the start, 17 after the first import of drop 1, 19 once the DOORS modules came in, and back to 17 in December when Tom removed the Legacy Import clutter and lowered the number, as the ratchet requires.

That pattern, a measure that may only get better, is called a ratchet. The team uses it for every measure it cannot make perfect on day one: outline violations here, trace gaps from Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself, package complexity later (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

From this point the DOORS requirements live in the model, under model/requirements/stakeholder/, system/ and segment/, and the Cameo copy of the requirements lives beside them under model/requirements/model/. Two copies of the same requirements may look wasteful. It is the opposite: DOORS is the authoritative wording, the Cameo copy is what the prime's model actually links to, and keeping both is what lets the trace job see where they disagree.

28.4.3 Wednesday 11 November: Veterans Day

No stand-up, no work. The capacity line accounted for it. It is worth saying because new teams often forget holidays when they plan, then discover at the review that they were short a day.

28.4.4 Thursday 12 November: refinement and planning poker

At 10:00 the team ran refinement for sprint 4: the stories Jim had drafted, checked against the Definition of Ready, and estimated with planning poker in the meeting chat. The kit tallied the votes. Most rounds went straight to consensus. One did not:

Jim voted 3 for "Close the Stations level tags"; Bob and Tom voted 5. The tally shows no consensus, so Jim asked the question the operating model says to ask: what does the high vote know? Bob knew something Jim did not. The Stations package is the largest in the model: it holds the buoys, the shore stations and everything inside them, and a good part of those parts are procured items from suppliers, which in the prime's model carry an extra stereotype with supplier and part-number tags. Bob expected those to take longer than the plain level tags. On the second round all three voted 5.

That conversation is the reason planning poker exists. The numbers matter less than the moment the outlier explains themselves. In Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed you will see that even 5 was not enough, and why.

Bob's stand-up on Thursday and Friday said "T none": all of Bob's committed work was finished and the next sprint's stories were not yet started. The operating model's answer to an empty "today" is to pull the top story of the next sprint forward rather than to look busy. An empty "today" is a planning signal, not a problem.

Tom's lines on those two days show a different and smaller lesson:

Tom's drafted status names the drop-intake issue for prime drop 1 (TW-25), due "by Oct 16". That issue was still open: the sprint 1 work it tracked was done, but the issue itself was never closed. talk.pl drafts from the board, so a forgotten open issue shows up as somebody's "today". The analytics for the sprint list it as the oldest open issue, and it was still showing up in Tom's drafts at the end of sprint 4. The fix takes ten seconds: close it. The lesson is the one every tool on the team teaches sooner or later: the tools are only as good as the board you keep.

28.4.5 Friday 13 November: review and retrospective

Jim closed the last story of the sprint at 10:00, the write-up of the drift and the trace gaps. Then the review:

Every committed story was done: 15 of 15 story points. The four headline numbers are the ones the team reports at every review (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not): TODO lines left, verify coverage, open discrepancy reports, and blocked items.

The demo script, as talk.pl review drafted it, is in the evidence. Its fourth and sixth sections are worth reading as a lesson in reading your own numbers:

The first half is useful: the median time from opening a merge request to its first review, and the time from first edit to accepted change, measured in hours, against a document-era change cycle that took weeks. The second half is a trap. The draft divides the TODO lines left by this sprint's rate of closing them and announces that the port will take about twenty-five more sprints. That is arithmetically correct and practically wrong: this sprint's engineering was DOORS and the trace report, not TODO lines, so this sprint's TODO pace says nothing about the next one's. Delete that line before anyone reads it aloud. Every forecast a tool drafts for you is a hypothesis; you are the one who knows whether the assumption behind it holds.

The review showed the sprint's merge requests and their pipelines, including the trace report on a real merge request. Anyone watching asks the obvious question: who fixes the gaps? The plan for sprint 4 answers it: a discrepancy report to the prime for each gap, through the contract.

Jim's Friday note to management is built from two things the kit already wrote: the review script's thirty-second version and the weekly quad. In words, it says this:

Note: Sprint 3, the Friday note

The note leaves out the morale dip. Whether, how and to whom a lead reports the team's mood is a judgment call, and Chapter 41, For the lead: leading a reluctant team is about exactly that kind of judgment.

28.8 You can now

  • Read a failing pipeline log, find the file, line and column, and reproduce the error locally with the grammar check.
  • Explain the SysML v2 naming order (name : Type) and spot the v1 habit that writes it backwards.
  • Read the trace report's C, F, G, I and drift lines and say which gaps are yours and which are the prime's.
  • Explain why a new check starts as report only and becomes a gate only when the team can pass it.
  • Say a wait out loud as a blocker, with a date and an ask.
  • Use planning poker's outlier question to surface what one person knows.
Exercise 28.1: Make the grammar check say no

Do practice lesson 11 (Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated shows the setup). It plants exactly the kind of mistake Bob made: a model change with a syntax error. Watch the pipeline fail, read the job log, find the line, fix it on the branch, and push again. Then write the stand-up line you would post the next morning, outcome first, with one number.

Exercise 28.2: Read the trace report

In the Tidewater sandbox, show pipeline #29's trace job log with perl "$KIT/bin/gitlab.pl" --local gitlab --project tidewater/model pipeline show 29, open the trace log it names, and list the two orphans and the drifted requirement. For each, decide: is this ours to fix, or the prime's? Write one sentence per gap saying why.

Exercise 28.3: Rewrite Tom's stand-up

Rewrite Tom's posted lines from 9 and 10 November so the three-day wait would have reached Jim on the first morning. Run your line through the kit's lint (daily.pl lint, Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro) to check it parses.

28.9 Applying this to your project

  • Expect a sprint 3. Somewhere around week five or six, the novelty is gone and the payoff has not arrived. Measure it (a five-question pulse costs a minute) so you can see it, and do not argue with it.
  • Put your requirements source into the model next to the model's copy, and run a trace on every change. The first report will show gaps that were always there. Decide in advance whose they are and how they will be reported.
  • Add every new check as report-only first. Make it a gate only when the people merging can make it green.
  • Agree that waiting on anyone outside the team for more than a day is a blocker, and that it is said at the stand-up with a date and an ask.
  • Close the issues you finish. Every tool that reads the board, from the stand-up draft to the analytics, repeats your board's mistakes back to you.

29 Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed

From what you know

You know

the program review where the slides are the only evidence.

Here it is called

the model site, and a demo.

What is new

management looks at the live model, not at screenshots of it.

Survival kit

What you have

the DOORS requirements in the model, a trace report on every change that lists the prime's gaps (Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named), a team that has seen the pipeline say no and survived it, and a pulse survey that says morale is low.

What you need

the structure of the model's biggest package tagged and checked, one of the inherited dependency cycles gone, every gap the trace found sent back to the prime through the contract, and something management can open without a briefing. You also need a demo that tells management what they got for two weeks, because the last one did not.

Sprint 4 ran from Monday 16 November to Friday 27 November 2026. Thanksgiving fell on Thursday 26 November, so the sprint had fewer working days than a full one; the capacity line in the kickoff record accounts for the holiday and the leave around it.

It is the sprint in which the work started to pay the team back. The pulse went from 2.2 to 3. The TODO count fell from 50 to 22. And at the review, the program manager opened the model on a phone.

29.1 The question this sprint answered

Sprint 3 asked whether the requirements match. Sprint 4 asked three questions about structure and one about communication:

Is every part in the Stations package at the right level of the part tree? Which of the dependency cycles the prime handed us can we break? What exactly do we ask the prime to fix? And can management see the model without us?

The first three are systems engineering questions the team had always asked, in reviews, with screenshots. The fourth is new: in the Cameo years nobody outside the team ever looked at the model directly. They looked at slides made from it.

29.2 Kickoff: Monday 16 November

The commitment is higher than sprint 3's: 17 points, against 15. Jim committed more because sprint 3 had finished everything and because the kinds of work in sprint 4 were familiar: level tags (Bob had done Network), a dependency edit (small), a pipeline job (Tom's third), and discrepancy reports (writing, which the team had done all its career). The one story with real uncertainty is TW-67, "Close the Stations level tags", which the team had argued up to a higher estimate at the previous refinement (Section 28.4.4, Thursday 12 November: refinement and planning poker).

Look at the work mix. Engineering is 74% of the task points done (Section 13.8, Two ways to count "done"); platform has fallen to 18% and learning to 9%. Three sprints earlier, platform and learning together were most of the board. This is the moment the team stops building the shop and starts working in it.

The learning story is small and practical: how to review a model change (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change), and a rehearsal of the sprint review. The rehearsal is there because of what happened at the sprint 2 review, and it deserves its own section.

29.2.1 Why the demo gets rehearsed

At the end of sprint 2 Tom demonstrated the new pipeline: the terminal, then the YAML, then a green pipeline, in that order, with the vocabulary Tom had spent two weeks learning. The deputy program manager's feedback, recorded in the review notes:

Nothing Tom said was wrong. It was the wrong order and the wrong words for the audience. The team's sprint 2 retrospective decided two things: the demo is rehearsed on the Wednesday of week 2, after refinement, and the person who drives the screen rotates. Chapter Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not explains the six moves of a demo that lands; this sprint is the first time the team used them.

29.3 Week 1

29.3.1 Monday 16 November: learning to review

All three closed their learning tasks on the first morning: Jim worked through the review checklist the team keeps in docs/conventions/review-checklist.md, Bob practiced line comments and suggestions on a scratch merge request, and Tom wrote the first draft of the demo plan for 27 November. Reviewing is a skill the team had in the document era, where it meant red pen on a printed specification. It transfers better than they expected. What is new is that the change under review is small, the reviewer sees exactly the lines that changed, and the pipeline has already checked the mechanical things, so the reviewer's attention goes to whether the change is right.

29.3.2 Thursday 19 November: breaking a cycle in two lines

The prime's model came with two package dependency cycles, measured in Chapter 2, The Cameo years: Stations depends on DataCenter and DataCenter on Stations, and Network depends on Operations and Operations on Network. A cycle means neither package can be understood, reviewed or changed without the other. In a diagram-based tool they are hard to see; in text they are a line each.

Tom took the Network and Operations cycle. The Operations package depended on Network for one reason only: a dependency from ServiceVessel to Technician, a left-over trace from the document port that said nothing a systems engineer would miss. The fix removed it, and the import of Network that existed only to serve it:

Two removed lines. Jim approved !12 the same day, and Tom merged it. The cycle count the scorecard tracks went from 2 to 1.

The cycle was two lines. In Cameo it was a week of looking at a diagram.

— Tom, sprint 4

Note: The thought process: is it ours to break?

Operations.sysml is a file the converter writes from the prime's drop. Editing it means the next drop will try to put the dependency back, unless the prime removes it too. Tom asked that question before writing the change, and the answer has two parts. First, the government's v2 model is the government's: if a dependency is meaningless, the v2 model should not carry it, and the vendor-branch merge will show the conflict when the prime's next drop arrives (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition works through how such edits survive). Second, the prime should know, so the team keeps a list of the clutter it removes for the discrepancy reports. The other cycle, Stations and DataCenter, is harder: it involves the observation record that both packages use, and deciding who owns it is a design decision, not a cleanup. It went to Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself.

29.3.3 Friday 20 November: the Stations tags, a red X, and a question for the prime

Bob opened merge request !13, "Level tags in Stations", at ten in the morning. It replaced the package's level-stereotype TODO lines with @L metadata, the same mechanical change Bob had made in Network, on a much larger package. The grammar and lint jobs passed.

The pipeline failed anyway. Not grammar, not lint: the outline job. Here is the part of its log that matters:

and at the end of the same job:

Two findings. The outline violation count went up by one, which the ratchet does not allow. And the level-tag check found a part that is tagged at the wrong level: WaveSensor is tagged L5, an assembly, but the first place it appears in the part tree is directly inside MooredBuoy, an L3 station, which makes it an L4 subsystem. The extra outline violation comes from the same root.

You can reproduce the finding from Bob's commit:

Bob's tag was not a typo. Bob had copied the level from the prime's Cameo stereotype, exactly as the TODO line said. The prime's model is inconsistent with itself: the stereotype says L5, the structure says L4. In the document era this kind of inconsistency was found, if it was found at all, by someone reading two documents side by side.

This is the decision point the sprint is remembered for. Bob and Jim had three options:

  1. Tag WaveSensor L5 as the prime says, and raise the outline allowance so the pipeline passes. The pipeline's own message forbids this: "fix them, do not raise .ci/outline-max".
  2. Wait for the prime to fix its stereotype, leaving the Stations tags unmerged until a later drop.
  3. Tag it L4 in the government's copy, where the structure says it belongs, and send the inconsistency to the prime as a discrepancy report so their model and the government's converge.

They chose the third, and the commit says so in the model itself:

Jim opened DR-7 the same day. The second pipeline was green, Jim approved, and Bob merged !13 that afternoon.

29.3.4 Reviewing !13: what Jim actually checked

Jim's approval came after the second pipeline, not the first. That is the first line of the team's review checklist, learned on the Monday of this sprint:

A red pipeline means the change is not finished; reviewing it wastes the reviewer's time and invites the author to argue with the machine through the reviewer. Once the pipeline was green, Jim's review was about the engineering. The size was fine: the change touched one file, mostly one kind of line, about fifty lines in all. The levels matched the part tree, which the outline job had now confirmed mechanically, so Jim did not need to count levels by eye. And one rule of the checklist applied directly to this change:

The WaveSensor line changed something the prime wrote, beyond closing a TODO. The rule allows such a change only with a discrepancy report behind it, and the line names one in its comment. Jim's review took minutes, and most of those minutes went to the one line that mattered. That is what a review checklist is for: it moves the reviewer's attention from the mechanical to the consequential.

Objection: We should not change the prime's model

The objection, in Bob's words: "If we change their levels, we own a model that disagrees with the contract deliverable."

Answer

the government's v2 model already disagrees with the prime's v1 model in every place the team has closed a TODO; that is the point of the port. What must not happen is a silent disagreement. The change carries the DR number in a comment on the line itself, the DR goes to the prime through the contract, and when the prime's drop fixes the stereotype the vendor-branch merge brings the two back together. A disagreement that is written down, reported and tracked is configuration management. One that is not is the spider web again.

29.3.5 Friday 20 November, continued: discrepancy reports to the prime

While Bob dealt with WaveSensor, Jim did the sprint's most important piece of systems engineering, and it involved no model edits at all. Jim turned each gap the trace report had found the sprint before into a discrepancy report: an issue in GitLab, from the team's Discrepancy Report template, labeled for the prime, and transmitted through the contracting channel.

(The list is the team's GitLab today, at the end of sprint 6; the reports about the Legacy Import clutter and the DOORS wording were opened in Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself.) Here is the first of them, as Jim wrote it:

Table 29.1. Anatomy of a discrepancy report
Part of the reportWhat goes in itWhy
DR numberthe team's own sequence, assigned when the issue is openedso every later reference, in a model comment or a drop's MANIFEST, can cite it
Prime trackingleft blank until the prime assigns its own numberthe two organizations will each track it; both numbers end up on the issue
Found in dropthe drop version and its delivery datethe prime fixes what it delivered, not what it has now
DOORS idthe requirement, if there is onethe trace job reports by DOORS id, so closure can be checked mechanically
Severitythe team's scale, from the templateso the prime and the program office can order their work
What we foundone or two sentences, in engineering words, and how it was foundthe prime must be able to reproduce it without the government's tools
What we askexactly what the government wants changed, not howthe model is the prime's to change
Closurecheckboxes: sent, by whom, when; fixed in which dropstays open until a drop actually fixes it

The report says what was found, where, how it was found, and exactly what the government asks the prime to do. It does not say how to fix it inside Cameo; that is the prime's business. And it has a closure section that stays open until a drop actually fixes the problem, which is how the team will know, months later, whether the prime did what it was asked.

Note: The thought process: why not just fix their model?

Every gap on that list would take Bob a minute to "fix" in the government's v2 model: add a satisfy for TW-SYS-012, copy TW-SYS-016 in from DOORS, write the missing verification case for TW-SYS-011. Jim said no to all of them, and the retrospective agreed (see below). The requirements and their satisfaction are the prime's contractual responsibility. If the government quietly patches its copy, the prime's model stays wrong, the next drop reintroduces every gap, and the government has taken on design responsibility nobody funded. The discrepancy report puts the fix where it belongs. The trace job will show, drop by drop, which reports the prime has closed.

The scorecard shows 5 discrepancy reports opened in the sprint and none closed yet; the first closure comes with drop 2 in January.

29.3.6 The weekly status, 20 November

The week-1 sprint progress in that quad looks alarming next to sprint 3's finish, and it is not. Points count when a story is done, and the large Stations story was still open on Friday even though its main merge request had merged. Read the quad's "improving" and "degrading" arrows across weeks, not one week's percentage.

29.4 Week 2

29.4.1 Monday 23 November: the Stations package in numbers

Bob's stand-up on Monday:

One merge request closed a large share of the remaining TODO lines. That is the shape of a port: long stretches of small, careful changes, and a few large mechanical ones once the pattern is proven on a small package. Network in sprint 3 was the proof; Stations in sprint 4 was the payoff.

The story was not finished, though. Its second task was to walk the Stations part tree with the prime's modeler and record what they confirmed: which parts are procured, which supplier and part-number tags the prime's stereotypes carry, and whether the tree matches what the prime is actually building. That needed a meeting with someone outside the team, and Bob's stand-up already names it as today's work.

29.4.2 Tuesday 24 November: the model site

Tom's !14 added the pages job to the pipeline. On every merge to develop, and every night on a schedule, the job builds a small web site from the model and publishes it with GitLab Pages: the generated documentation (the part tree, the function tree, the IDEF0 plates, the trace report), the diagrams the kit draws, and the TODO burn-down. Nothing on the site is written by hand. If the model changes, the site changes with it, the same day.

The site is small on purpose. Each page answers a question someone outside the team used to ask the team, usually the week before a review:

Table 29.2. The model site in sprint 4, page by page
PageThe question it answersWho asks it
The part tree (docs/, the generated Nouns page and the tree view)What is the system made of, and at what level?the program manager, new engineers, the prime
The function tree and the IDEF0 platesWhat does the system do, and what does each function take and produce?the test organization, the operations community
The trace reportWhich requirements have a design and a verification, and which do not?the program office, the independent reviewers
The diagram viewsWhat connects to what?everyone, in a review
The TODO burn-downHow much of the port is left?the program manager, every Friday

None of the pages is a new kind of information. Every one of them used to be a slide, a table in a document, or an answer to an e-mail, prepared by hand from the model. What is new is that they are never out of date and nobody has to prepare them.

The nightly rebuild is a pipeline schedule, the first the team created:

It runs at 02:00 Eastern on weekdays, against develop, with every check switched on. If anything broke during the day, it is red before the stand-up. Chapter Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep explains why the site was the single most valuable tool the team adopted, for an audience the team had never served directly: everyone else.

The same Tuesday, Jim prepared the sprint review with the program office (task #82), and on Wednesday Jim met the prime's modeler about how future drops should be delivered (task #83). That conversation, about stable element ids, change notes, and eventually letting the prime's Jenkins deliver straight into GitLab, is the subject of Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition.

29.4.3 Wednesday 25 November: refinement, and an outlier again

Refinement for sprint 5, with planning poker. One round split:

Tom voted 5 for "Procured parts as metadata; DataCenter level tags"; Jim and Bob voted 3. This time the high vote knew what the team had just learned the hard way: procured parts carry supplier and part-number tags that must become metadata with values, not just a level tag, and the Stations walk-through had not even happened yet. The second round settled at 3.5, which is the sprint 4 lesson written as an estimate.

The demo script for the review was drafted with talk.pl review (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not) and rehearsed out loud before the meeting; the rehearsal was Tom's task on Wednesday 25 November, Day 9, and the script itself is in the evidence (docs/tidewater/sprints/04/review-script.md).

29.4.4 Thursday 26 November: Thanksgiving

29.4.5 Friday 27 November: units, a carryover, and the review

Bob merged !15 in the morning: the value types Power and Energy now specialize the ISQ quantity kinds from the SysML v2 standard library, so a power is a power and not just a number:

The three TODO lines for the Cameo unit instances went with it.

Then the carryover. The Stations walk-through needed the prime's modeler, and it could not start until the last day of the sprint, so it did not fit. Bob closed the task and continued it in sprint 5, with its estimate, and the journal moved the story's remaining points into the next sprint:

Delivery for the sprint: 12 of 17 story points, or 71%. That is the first sprint the team did not finish everything it committed, and it is handled the way the operating model says: the story carries, visibly, with its remaining points, and the quad shows it as a watch item (Chapter 13, The operating model).

At 10:00, the review:

The review notes record how the rehearsed demo ran: it led with the question, showed the model site, gave one before-and-after, made one live change, and closed with the ask. Those are the six moves of Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not, and here is what each one looks like for a sprint like this one:

  1. The question first. What did this sprint settle about the model, in the audience's words: is the structure right, and can they see it without the team? Not "here is what we built".
  2. The output, not the tool. The model site, not the terminal. The part tree, the trace report and the burn-down, as pages anyone can read.
  3. One before-and-after. The notes name the one used: the cycle, two lines removed, against a week of reading a diagram in the Cameo years.
  4. One safe live change. The script's suggestion: on a scratch branch, delete one satisfy line and open a draft merge request; a couple of minutes later the trace report names the requirement that lost its design. Then close the merge request.
  5. What it means for the next milestone. How far the structure TODOs have to go, and when the interim baseline for the program review is due.
  6. The ask. One decision or one kind of help, with a date.

The program manager's reaction is in the review notes, and it is the moment the team remembers:

I can open this on my phone? I have never seen the model without a briefing.

— Program manager, sprint 4 review

The same four headline numbers as every review: 22 TODO lines left; verify coverage unchanged at the level the trace found in sprint 3; 5 discrepancy reports open with the prime; nothing blocked.

Warning: Verify coverage did not move, and that is correct

If management asks why the share of requirements with a verification stayed flat while everything else improved, the answer is the discrepancy reports. Every remaining verification gap is in the prime's model: TW-SYS-011, the stakeholder needs, and the requirement that is not in the model at all. The government team will not paper over them with its own verification cases. Coverage moves when the prime's drops close the DRs, and the trace job will show exactly when. A flat line here is a measure working honestly, not a team failing.
