29.8 You can now

  • Break a package dependency cycle by finding the one dependency that creates it, and decide whether it is yours to break.
  • Read an outline and level-tag finding, reproduce it on your own checkout, and decide between fixing your copy, waiting for the prime, and doing both.
  • Write a discrepancy report that says what was found, how, and what you ask the prime to do, and keep it open until a drop closes it.
  • Explain why verify coverage can stay flat while the model improves.
  • Set up a model site and a nightly schedule, and say what each one is for.
  • Run a demo with the six moves, and carry a story honestly when it does not fit.
Exercise 29.1: Find a cycle

In the Tidewater sandbox, draw the package view with perl "$KIT/tools/sysml/model.pl" draw pkg -o pkg.svg in Bob's clone and find the cycle that remains. Name the dependency you would remove to break it, and say why that is a design decision, not a cleanup (Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself shows what the team decided).

Exercise 29.2: Write a discrepancy report

Pick a gap from the trace report in Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named that does not already have a discrepancy report (hint: look at the unverified stakeholder needs). Write the discrepancy report from the team's template, in Vim, and open it as an issue on a practice sandbox with gitlab.pl issue new --template "Discrepancy Report".

Exercise 29.3: Rehearse a demo

Take the sprint 4 review script in docs/tidewater/sprints/04/review-script.md. Rewrite it so it opens with the question, shows the model site first, has one before-and-after with a number, one safe live change, and one ask with a date. Read it aloud against a five-minute timer.

29.9 Applying this to your project

  • Publish the model where management can open it, generated from the model on every merge, as early as you can. It changes the conversation more than any metric.
  • Run a nightly full check so problems are red before the stand-up, not found next week.
  • Send the prime's gaps back as discrepancy reports, one per gap, with a closure section. Do not patch the prime's model quietly in your copy; when you must diverge, write the DR number on the line.
  • Rehearse the demo, with the question first and the ask last. Rotate the driver.
  • Expect your first carryover when a task depends on someone outside the team. Carry it visibly with its remaining points; the quad and the journal are built for it.

30 Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself

From what you know

You know

requirement review comments, and the trace matrix you rebuild before each review.

Here it is called

the recipe check and the trace gate.

What is new

the trace defends itself: a change that breaks it cannot merge.

Survival kit

What you have

a model whose structure is nearly closed, a pipeline that checks every change, a model site the program office has seen once, and a team that has started to trust the checks (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed).

What you need from this chapter: how the team turned two questions into machinery -- are the requirements we inherited good enough to verify? and can we stop a change that quietly breaks the trace? -- and how a mistake that used to survive until the next milestone review was caught in four minutes on a Friday morning.

30.1 The question this sprint answered

Every sprint chapter in this part starts with the systems-engineering question the team answered, because that is how the team learned to start every sprint. Sprint 5's question was one Jim kept coming back to after the sprint 4 review, where the program manager had opened the model site on a phone and said they had never seen the model without a briefing: if the model is checked, what is it checked against? If the requirements are weak, a checked model is a well-organized mistake.

The question was fair, and it split into two questions the team could work on:

  1. Are the requirements good enough to be verified? Not "are they right" -- that is the stakeholders' call -- but are they written so that someone could design to them and test them? That is what the requirement recipe (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe) measures.
  2. Can the model defend its own trace? By now the pipeline reported trace gaps on every merge request: requirements nothing satisfies, requirements nothing verifies, text that differs from DOORS. Reporting is not the same as preventing. Nothing stopped an engineer from deleting a satisfy line by accident.

The mood had turned. The pulse survey at the sprint 4 retrospective came in at 3 out of 5, up from the sprint 3 dip; Bob, who had asked in week one why they could not just send the Word document, now opened merge requests without being asked. The team was not yet enthusiastic. It was, in Jim's words at the kickoff, "past the point of wanting to go back."

30.2 Kickoff: a carried story, a small learning budget, mostly engineering

The kickoff ran on Monday 30 November, 09:00 to 10:30, and stood in for that day's stand-up. The record the kit wrote:

Three things in that record are worth reading slowly.

The first story is a carryover. TW-67, Close the Stations level tags, was committed in sprint 4. Its first task (#76, the level tags themselves) finished in sprint 4; its second task -- walking the Stations part tree with the prime's modeler and recording what they confirmed -- did not happen in sprint 4. The story carried into sprint 5 with its remaining points. Nobody hid it: the sprint 4 review said so, the journal recorded a carry, and the weekly quad marked the story late. A carried story is not a failure. A carried story nobody mentions is.

The learning budget is small now. Learning was 24% of sprint 1's task points done (Section 13.8, Two ways to count "done"). In sprint 5 it is 6%: one story, TW-89, in which Jim and Bob read the recipe chapter of this book and Jim drafted a memo from pipeline numbers. The budget fell because the team needed it less, not because the plan squeezed it out. That distinction matters when you explain the curve to management (Bottom line up front).

Engineering dominates. 64% of the task points done are engineering work -- requirements, structure, trace -- and 30% is platform work (the trace gate and the release rehearsal). In sprint 2 those shares were almost reversed.

The goal Jim wrote on the board was three clauses long: Procured parts and DataCenter closed; Legacy Import untangled; trace becomes a gate. Two of the three are engineering. The third is the one this chapter is mostly about.

30.3 Week 1: clutter out, a ratchet in

30.3.1 Monday 30 November: the recipe, read before it is run

Jim spent the morning on task #97, half a point from the learning story: read Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe and draft a memo from the pipeline's numbers. The order was deliberate. The team had learned in sprint 2 that running a new checker before anyone understands what it checks produces a list of findings nobody trusts. Jim wanted to be able to explain every finding to the prime before the prime saw a single one.

30.3.2 Tuesday and Wednesday: the Legacy Import package

The drop-1 model carries a package called Legacy Import: the residue of the document port years ago. It holds a duplicated block (Battery_old), a copy of a subsystem (Copy of SensorSuite), an unused placeholder (TBD Component) and a "requirement" that is really a slide title. Chapter 2, The Cameo years measured it as part of the spider web.

Tom's task (#102) was to remove it from the government's v2 model. Jim's task (#103) was to ask the prime to remove it from the v1 model, as discrepancy report DR-5.

The thought process behind doing both is worth spelling out, because it is the pattern for every piece of clutter the team inherits:

  • Deleting it in v2 alone is not enough. The Legacy Import file is converter output. It lives on the vendor branch (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job), and every future prime drop will bring it back. Git will see the government's deletion on develop and the prime's unchanged copy on vendor/prime, and every drop merge will raise a delete/modify question until the prime deletes it upstream.
  • Waiting for the prime alone is not enough either. The clutter inflates the spider-web measures, confuses every new reader, and the prime's next drop is weeks away.
  • So: delete it now, and file the DR. The deletion makes the government's model clean today. The DR makes the problem the prime's to fix, with an id both sides can cite. When the prime's drop finally removes the package, the conflict disappears on its own.

Tom's merge request, !16, removed the package. Its pipeline went green on the first run. Jim sent DR-5 the same morning:

Notice what the DR does not say. It does not say you made a mess. It names the elements, says why they are a problem, and asks for one concrete action. A discrepancy report is an engineering request between two teams that will work together for years; write it the way you would want to receive it.

You can see the deletion in the team's history. In the Tidewater sandbox, from Tom's clone:

The second line of the output is the drop-1 import that created the file; the first is Tom's removal. That is the whole history of the package in the government's model: arrived with the prime's drop, left by a reviewed merge request. Compare that with the Cameo years, when a package like this could be deleted from a shared model by anyone with a license and nobody would know who or why.

30.3.3 Wednesday: Bob and the prime's modeler

Bob closed the carried task the same day: a walk through the Stations part tree with the prime's modeler, on a shared screen, with the generated part tree from the model site (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text) instead of a Cameo diagram. It also gave both sides a second look at DR-7, opened in sprint 4: WaveSensor is tagged as a level-5 assembly in the v1 model while being a direct part of the level-4 MooredBuoy. DR-7 is still open at the end of the sprint -- correctly, because only the prime can say which of the two is wrong.

The walk-through is the first time the team used the model site with the prime. It will not be the last. A generated, read-only view that both sides can look at removes the oldest argument in a model review: "that's not what my diagram shows."

30.3.4 Thursday: stand-ups that say something

By sprint 5 the stand-up statuses had changed character. Here is Thursday's, pasted from the meeting chat as the kit stores it:

and the kit's lint of it:

Compare that with sprint 1 (Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in), when the lint flagged missing story ids and statuses that described keystrokes ("rebased my branch"). Every line now names a story, says what is true (a story done, with its tasks counted), and names a date for what is next. The share of stand-up lines with an outcome and a number -- one of the twelve-week measures from Chapter 3, The directive -- was 1 for the sprint, as a fraction of lines.

Each line was drafted by talk.pl standup (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not) from the previous day's GitLab activity, and each person edited or posted the draft. The evidence keeps both:

The drafts and the posted lines are identical, every day of the sprint. That can mean two things. The good reading: the drafts were already in the form the team wanted, so there was nothing to fix. The worrying reading: people had stopped reading their own statuses. You cannot tell which from the record, and that is the point. The rule worth adopting is simple -- read the draft before you post it; if it would not make sense to the deputy PM, change it. A drafting tool is a starting point, not a substitute for knowing what you did yesterday.

30.3.5 Friday 4 December: the trace becomes a ratchet

One job in the pipeline changed this week, in Tom's story TW-93. Until then, the trace job reported gaps and was allowed to fail: red in the job list, green for the merge. The reason was sound. The model inherited gaps that only the prime can close -- requirements the v1 model never satisfied, never verified, or worded differently from DOORS -- and a gate that failed on every one of them would have blocked every merge request the team ever opened.

The ratchet keeps that reason and adds a rule: a merge request may not make the trace worse. The job runs the trace twice -- once on the merge result, once on the target branch -- and compares the sets of orphan, unverified and drifted requirement ids. A gap that is already on develop is old news and is reported. A gap that this change adds fails the job, names the requirement, and blocks the merge.

!17 put the ratchet in. Its own pipeline was green. The interesting part came a week later.

Case study: The decision: gate, ratchet, or report

The team considered three designs before Tom wrote a line, and the reasoning is the part to copy.

Make the trace a hard gate. Every orphan, every unverified requirement, every drifted text fails the merge request. Clean, simple, and unusable: the inherited gaps would fail every merge request until the prime fixed its model, which could take months. Within a week someone would set the job to allow_failure, and the gate would be a decoration.

Keep reporting. Leave the job allowed to fail and trust people to read it. That is what the team had been doing since sprint 3 (Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named). It works until the day someone is in a hurry, and a reporting job that is always red trains everyone to ignore red.

Ratchet. Fail only on what this change makes worse. The inherited gaps stay visible in every report and on the model site; a new gap blocks the merge and names the requirement. The cost is complexity in the job -- it has to check out the target branch and run the trace twice -- and one subtle requirement: the comparison must be between sets of requirement ids, not counts. A change that fixes one orphan and creates another leaves the count the same and the model worse; a ratchet that compared counts would let it through. Test your ratchet with exactly that case.

The same pattern -- report everything, block only what gets worse -- is how the team handles every inherited problem: outline violations, complexity, recipe findings. It is the single most useful idea in this sprint.

Jim closed #105 the same Friday, having read the recipe findings for the DOORS modules and decided which ones to send to the prime. That is the next section.

The week ended with the first of two weekly quads for management (Chapter 36, Telling management):

30.4 The recipe: grading the requirements

The story Grade our requirements with the recipe (TW-94) is the engineering heart of the sprint. The recipe (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe) describes a requirement as a single sentence with up to eighteen parts, six of them required, and lists the target verbs that are rarely verifiable ("provide", "have", "be", "be able to"). req-recipe.pl reads each requirement, decomposes it into those parts, and reports what is missing or weak.

Jim ran it on the three DOORS modules -- the stakeholder needs, the system requirements and the segment requirements -- in the government's model, where the DOORS text lands unchanged. You can run the same command in the Tidewater sandbox:

The summary line says the DOORS text holds 30 graded requirements and that none of them is missing a required part. The findings are about quality, not completeness. Here is the first one in the full report the pipeline kept:

The network "shall provide marine weather observations." Provide how? To whom, how often, within what? A test engineer cannot write a pass criterion for provide. That is not pedantry: it is the difference between a requirement that can be verified at acceptance and one that will be argued about.

30.4.1 Why a discrepancy report, and not an edit

The obvious next step would have been to fix the wording in the model. Jim did not, and the reason is ADR 0008 (DOORS stays authoritative for requirement text), recorded in sprint 2 (Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated). The DOORS text is the prime's, under the contract. If the government rewrites it in the v2 model, the model and DOORS disagree -- which is exactly the drift the trace job exists to catch -- and the next drop will undo the edit anyway.

So the findings went to the prime as DR-6, sent on Tuesday 8 December:

The DR quotes the tool's summary and four representative findings, and asks for one action. It does not list every finding: the prime can run the same tool on the same text (it is in the kit) and get the same answer. Making the check reproducible on the other side is worth more than a long attachment.

You can open the DR in the sandbox's GitLab, as Jim did:

Its labels say a lot in a small space: type::discrepancy, owner::prime, severity::2, area::requirements, phase::port. Anyone in the program can filter the board for everything the prime owes us without a spreadsheet.

30.4.2 Why the recipe is not a gate yet

The obvious question once Jim's findings came in was: should the recipe fail the pipeline? Not yet, and the reason is ownership. Every finding in the DOORS text is the prime's to fix; a gate on it would block the government's merge requests for the prime's wording. What the team did instead was add the recipe to the pipeline as a report -- its findings show up in the merge request's code quality widget and as metrics on the model site -- so that a merge request which adds a requirement in the government's own packages can be held to the recipe in review, and so that the count is visible when the prime's next drop arrives. When the government writes its own requirements, later in the program, a recipe ratchet on its own packages is the natural next step.

30.4.3 The stand-ups that week

Monday 7 December shows the lint doing a small, useful thing:

The lint warns that DR-6 is not in the journal. It is right: DR-6 is a GitLab issue, not a story in the journal, and the lint matches anything that looks like an id. The warning costs Jim nothing -- warnings do not stop the compile -- and it is a reminder of the boundary the kit keeps on purpose (Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board): the journal holds the team's stories; discrepancy reports, tasks and everything else live in GitLab. Jim could have written the status around the story id (TW-94) alone; naming the DR is still worth the warning, because DR-6 is what anyone outside the team would ask about.

Two other things in the week's statuses are worth a second look. Bob's line on Tuesday 1 December says Y none: the drafting tool found nothing of Bob's in GitLab from Monday, because Monday was the kickoff and a learning task Bob had not started. None is honest. It is also the line most likely to make a manager wonder what Bob did all day. When the truthful answer is "meetings and reading", say so -- Y kickoff; read the recipe chapter -- rather than letting the tool's none stand. And several lines end in an ellipsis, where the tool shortened a long story title. Nobody minded. A stand-up line is for the people in the meeting, who know the stories; it does not need to be a complete sentence.

Objection: "This is just more paperwork for the prime."

It is less. Before, requirement quality came up at a milestone review, as red ink on a PDF, months after the text was written, with no way for the prime to check the reviewer's opinion. Now it arrives as a reproducible check with named findings, early enough to fix before anyone designs to the weak text.

30.5 Week 2: metadata, a dry run, a tabletop and a catch

30.5.1 Monday 7 December: procured parts as metadata

Bob's !18 replaced the converter's TODO lines for the v1 Procured stereotype with SysML v2 metadata: each procured part now carries @Procured { supplier = "..."; partNumber = "..."; } from the government's Conventions package. It is a small change with a long tail. Supply-chain questions -- which parts come from which supplier? -- become a search over the model instead of a call to the prime (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system returns to this).

The design choice behind it is worth a paragraph, because every v1 profile a team inherits raises the same question. The v1 model expressed "procured" as a stereotype from a project profile, with the supplier and part number as tagged values. SysML v2 offers three ways to carry the same information: plain attributes on each part definition, a specialization of a ProcuredPart part definition, or metadata. Bob chose metadata, for two reasons. Procurement is a fact about the part, not a property of the system -- the buoy does not behave differently because its modem came from a particular vendor -- and metadata is the v2 construct for facts about elements. And metadata is what the kit's checks and views read: the same pattern the level tags use (Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook). One rule for all the metadata keeps the model's conventions few enough to remember.

Sprint 4's retrospective had already said stop estimating procured parts as if they were simple. Procured parts carry more than they show: every one needs a look before its metadata can be written, because a v1 profile enforces that the stereotype is applied, not that its tagged values are consistent or complete.

30.5.2 Wednesday 9 December: refinement and planning poker

Refinement for sprint 6 took the second half hour of Wednesday morning. The stories had been written during the week; refinement applied the Definition of Ready to each and estimated it with planning poker in the meeting chat (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro). The record:

Three of the eight stories took two rounds. The tally the kit printed for one of them shows how the conversation went:

In the first round for the VCRM story, Jim voted low and Bob and Tom voted high. Jim asked the question the facilitation prompt in the chat suggests -- what does the high vote know? The answer was the inspection verdicts: someone has to enter and sign a verdict for every requirement verified by inspection, and both high votes had counted that work. The plan already gave it to Jim, as Jim's own task (#126), because a signed verdict needs the lead's authority. With that settled, the second round agreed. That is what planning poker is for: not the number, but the minute in which the team finds out it was imagining two different stories.

30.5.3 Wednesday 9 December: DataCenter closed; the release rehearsal

Bob's !19 closed the level-tag TODO lines in DataCenter. Tom spent two days on #107: rehearsing the release and hotfix flows in a sandbox project, tidewater/sandbox, before doing either for real. The release path is the gitflow path (Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers, Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job): a release/ branch from develop, a merge request into main with the CCB's concurrence, a tag, and a back-merge into develop. The hotfix path starts from main and ends in both branches.

Rehearsing in a sandbox is cheap insurance. The first real baseline -- baseline-0, three weeks later -- went to the program office with the CCB watching. Tom wanted to have made the mistakes already, in a project nobody else could see.

30.5.4 Thursday 10 December: the spillage tabletop

Tom, as the team's part-time security owner, ran a tabletop with the ISSM (#108): a marked file has been pushed to the model repository by mistake. What do you do? The steps the team walked through are the ones in Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system: stop pushing, tell the ISSM before doing anything else, do not "fix" history yourself (a rewritten branch on a server does not remove the data from clones, caches and backups), and let the security office decide the containment.

The issue's record of the tabletop is one line: Done: Spillage tabletop: a marked file pushed by mistake. That is not good enough, and it is worth saying plainly because it is the most common way a tabletop is wasted. Its value is in what you learned -- who to call, how long the first hour took, what you did not know -- and a closed issue with no notes preserves none of it. A tabletop's record should hold three bullets: what we did, what surprised us, what we change.

30.5.5 Friday 11 December: the ratchet catches a real mistake

Bob's last story of the sprint was TW-91, Prune ObservingStation's trace spaghetti: the v1 model gives ObservingStation more relationship ends than any other block, many of them duplicate trace links made during the document port. Bob's task was to remove the duplicates and keep the real ones.

Bob opened !20 at 10:00. Its first pipeline failed. Here is the end of the trace job's log, from the evidence:

The second-to-last line is the target branch -- develop -- with the gaps it already had. The last line is the verdict: this change adds trace gaps: orphans 2 -> 3 (new: TW-SYS-002). Among the links Bob had judged duplicates was a satisfy that was not a duplicate at all: it was the only link from the design to TW-SYS-002, Scheduled transmission. Without it, nothing in the model satisfied the requirement.

The ratchet stopped me. I deleted a satisfy I thought was a duplicate. It was not.

— Bob

In the document era this mistake would have survived until someone built a traceability matrix by hand for a milestone review -- weeks or months later, by which time nobody would remember which edit removed the link. Here it was caught on the merge request that made it, before review, with the requirement named. Bob restored the line, pushed, and the second pipeline passed:

You can find both verdicts in the sandbox's pipeline records:

Open !20 in the sandbox's GitLab and look at its test report:

Warning: A green merge request with "failed" tests

The pipeline is green, yet the test widget lists the inherited trace gaps as failed tests. They are the old gaps -- TW-SYS-012, TW-SYS-016 and the rest -- that belong to the prime and that the ratchet deliberately lets through. Teach your reviewers to read the job's last line (no new trace gaps), not the widget's count. (The outline job already reports its inherited findings as skipped; the trace job's JUnit report should do the same, and this is on the team's list for the tooling.)

30.6 Reading the sprint's own numbers

At every sprint end the pipeline's records go through gitlab.pl analytics (Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics). Sprint 5's report starts like this:

Three readings matter, and one of them is a trap.

The trap: "issue created -> first commit". The median is the longest stage in the value stream by far. Read naively, it says the team let issues sit for a week before touching them. Read correctly, it says the team filed sprint 5's stories and tasks at the sprint 4 refinement and the sprint 5 kickoff, and started each task on its planned day. That is a queue by design, not a delay. A value stream measures waiting; whether the waiting is a problem depends on whether anybody needed the work sooner.

The real signal: "MR opened -> first review" and "first review -> merged". A merge request waited a few hours for its first review and was merged within minutes of approval. In the document era, a model change waited for a review board measured in weeks (Chapter 3, The directive has the notional baseline). The scorecard's review turnaround, 3.3 hours, is the same fact.

Change failure rate: zero. No merge to develop needed a revert or a fix-forward. The one failed pipeline of the sprint was !20's first run -- a merge request pipeline, which is where failures should happen. A failure on a merge request is the system working; a failure on develop is the system missing something. Keep the two apart when you talk about pipeline health, or a good sprint will sound like a bad one.

30.7 What went wrong, and what the team did about it

A case study that only reports successes teaches nothing. Sprint 5's problems were small, and each one taught something.

  • A real satisfy was deleted as a duplicate. Caught by the ratchet on the merge request, fixed in the same merge request (Section 30.5.5, Friday 11 December: the ratchet catches a real mistake). The retrospective turned it into practice: prune trace links from the generated trace report, never by eye.
  • The spillage tabletop left no lesson behind. One closed issue and a one-line comment (Section 30.5.4, Thursday 10 December: the spillage tabletop). The fix is a three-bullet record, and it costs five minutes.
  • The intake issue for the first drop is still open. Tom's stand-up on Friday 11 December still lists TW-25 intake prime drop v1.0 (2026-10-02), by Oct 16 as today's work -- a task due two months earlier. The drop was imported and merged in sprint 2; nobody closed the intake issue, so the drafting tool keeps offering it. The analytics for sprint 6 will list it as the oldest open issue. An issue that is really done but not closed pollutes every report built on issues; close what you finish, or the tools will keep reminding you of things that are not true.
  • On-time delivery was seven of eight, not eight of eight. The quad counts TW-67 as late because it carried over from sprint 4 (Section 30.10, What Jim told management). That is correct. A story that crosses a sprint boundary is late, even when nobody did anything wrong. Do not argue with the measure; explain it once.

30.8 The review: numbers someone asked for

Two days before the review, on Wednesday 9 December, the deputy program manager asked Jim for the trace numbers. Jim did not build a slide.

The deputy PM asked for the trace numbers. I sent a link.

— Jim

The link was the model site's trace page (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep), regenerated by the pipeline on every merge to develop. In the document era the same question meant two days of spreadsheet work, notionally (Chapter 3, The directive). That small exchange is the whole argument of this book in two sentences.

The review itself ran on Friday 11 December, 10:00 to 11:00, in the rehearsed format the team adopted in sprint 4 (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed, Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not): lead with the question, show the output, one before-and-after, one safe live change, the ask. The demo script started as a talk.pl review draft:

The draft's title says edit before the meeting, and the team did: the live change -- delete a satisfy on a scratch branch, watch the trace job name the requirement -- had just happened for real to Bob that morning, so the demo could point at !20 instead of staging it.

The review record shows what was accepted and the four numbers:

Every committed story was demonstrated: delivery was 18.5 of 18.5 story points (100%), the first full sprint since sprint 3. The TODO burn-down went from 22 to 14 lines of conversion debt. Verify coverage did not move -- and should not have: the unverified requirements are gaps in the prime's model, and the way to close them is through the discrepancy reports, not by the government inventing verification cases.

At the review, GitLab's own To-Do lists (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep) showed who owned what next:

Jim's list is long, and it is mostly discrepancy reports waiting on the prime. That is the shape of the job for a government lead on a program like this one: the government's model work is done in the team; the prime's is tracked in the team.

30.9 The retrospective

Two of the three actions came straight from the week. Stop cleaning up trace links by eye is Bob's lesson from !20; the ratchet will catch a bad deletion, but a pruning task should start from the generated trace report, not from memory. Start lowering .ci/outline-max in the same merge request that fixes a violation closes a gap the outline ratchet left open: an engineer who fixes an outline violation and does not lower the allowance leaves room for someone else to add one back.

The pulse rose to 3.8. The survey is anonymous in the meeting, but the evidence keeps each person's answers (Chapter 3, The directive lists the five questions), and the lowest are Bob's: on I understand why we are working this way, on I can see our progress, and on I would choose to keep working this way. On the checks catch problems I would have missed Bob answered higher -- in the week the ratchet caught Bob's mistake. A lead reading those answers should not try to argue the low ones up. They are a prompt for a conversation, one to one, about what would make the why and the progress visible to the person doing the work.

30.10 What Jim told management

The weekly status on Friday 11 December was the quad, as the kit printed it:

The covering note on top of a quad like this one needs only two sentences, for example: Sprint 5 delivered everything it committed. The pipeline now refuses a change that breaks the requirement trace; it caught one this morning, before review. It does not need to explain how the ratchet works. If management wants to know, they will ask, and the answer is a link (Chapter 36, Telling management).

  • Run the requirements recipe on DOORS text and decide which findings to send to the prime, and how.
  • Explain why the government does not edit the prime's requirement text, and what it does instead.
  • Read a trace ratchet verdict: tell the target branch's old gaps from the gaps a change adds.
  • Remove inherited clutter from the v2 model and file the discrepancy report that removes it upstream.
  • Run a planning-poker round where the second vote matters more than the first.

30.13 Exercises

Exercise 30.1: Grade a module

In the Tidewater sandbox, run req-recipe.pl on model/requirements/segment alone. Pick the two lowest-scoring requirements and rewrite them to the recipe, as a reply to DR-6 would (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe has the pattern). Check your rewrites with req-recipe.pl --strict on a text file.

Exercise 30.2: Break the trace on purpose

Do practice lesson 11 (perl agile.pl practice 11) if you have not. Then, on a branch in the Tidewater sandbox's work/bob clone, delete one satisfy line, commit, and run perl ci/job.pl trace with both CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE=merge_request_event and CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME=develop in the environment (with only the target branch set, the job treats the run as a branch pipeline and says "not a merge request: reported only"). Find the line that names the requirement you orphaned.

Exercise 30.3: Write a discrepancy report

Choose one finding from recipe-doors.txt that DR-6 does not quote. Write a DR for it from the Discrepancy Report template (Appendix I, Templates and GitLab Markdown, field by field): what we found, why it matters to verification, what we ask the prime to do. Keep it under a hundred words.

Exercise 30.4: Read the record of a tabletop

Read issue #108 in the sandbox (gitlab.pl issue show 108). Write the three bullets the team's new template asks for, as if you had run the tabletop: what you did, what surprised you, what you would change.

30.14 Applying this to your project

  • Grade the requirements before you design to them. Run a recipe-style check on the inherited text in your first month, not before your first review. Send the findings to whoever owns the text.
  • Make the trace a ratchet, not a gate. If you inherit gaps you cannot close, a gate that fails on every gap will be turned off within a week. A gate that fails only on new gaps will stay on for the life of the program.
  • Delete inherited clutter in your model and upstream at the same time. One without the other leaves you fighting the same file at every delivery.
  • Rehearse your first release where nobody can see it. A sandbox project costs nothing and turns the first real baseline into the second attempt.
  • Record what a tabletop taught you. A closed issue with no notes is a meeting nobody can learn from.

31 Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0

From what you know

You know

the interim design review, and the baseline you freeze for it.

Here it is called

baseline-0: a release branch, a protected tag and a briefing.

What is new

the baseline rebuilds identically, on demand, with its evidence attached.

Survival kit

What you have

a model whose structure is almost closed, a trace that defends itself (Chapter 30, Sprint 5: Grading the requirements, and a trace that defends itself), a recipe-graded set of requirements, and a team that has rehearsed a release in a sandbox.

What you need from this chapter: how a three-person team finished its first twelve weeks with something management could hold -- a tagged, reproducible baseline, a generated table of what crosses each interface, a verification matrix -- and how it handled the sprint's real events: a failed nightly pipeline, a token committed by mistake, a review comment that blocked a merge, a story that could not finish, and a number that almost told management the wrong thing.

31.1 The question this sprint answered

Sprint 6 ended with the twelve-week briefing to program management. The question behind every story in it was the one a program manager asks at any milestone: can you hand me something I can rely on? In the document era the answer was a set of documents with signatures. For this team it had to be three things:

  1. A baseline: a tagged, reproducible version of the model, approved by the CCB, that can be rebuilt byte for byte and named in a contract letter.
  2. An answer to "what crosses each interface?" -- the question every interface control working group asks -- generated from the model, not typed into a spreadsheet.
  3. An honest answer to "which requirements are verified, and how?", in the form a test organization uses: a verification cross-reference matrix (VCRM).

The pulse at the sprint 5 retrospective was 3.8. Nobody on the team would have predicted that number in week one. The risk now was the opposite of discouragement: a team pleased with itself, with a short sprint, holidays, and an audience waiting.

31.2 Kickoff: a short sprint with a big ending

Capacity is the lowest of the twelve weeks: the sprint ends on Christmas Eve, and Bob is on leave for its whole second week. Read the plan with that in mind and one line stands out. TW-112, BuoyModes state machine by hand, is a three-point task scheduled to start on Friday 18 December -- the day before Bob's leave -- and to finish on 29 December, in the next sprint. Nobody planned to fail it. But a task that starts the day before a week of leave and is due after the sprint ends is not a commitment; it is a hope. The team committed it because BuoyModes had to start before the January drop, and it carried, exactly as the dates said it would (Section 31.6, The carryover).

The work mix shows how far the team had come. Platform work is 14% of the task points done (Section 13.8, Two ways to count "done") and learning 4%; engineering is 82%. In sprint 1 the engineering share was 27% (Bottom line up front).

31.3 Week 1: the quiet days and the busy one

31.3.1 Monday to Wednesday: Operations closed, verdicts signed

Jim spent Monday morning on the last learning task of the twelve weeks: the memo and briefing chapters of this book (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim, Chapter 35, The briefing), because the briefing was Jim's to give in ten days.

Tom's !21 closed the level-tag TODO lines in the Operations package. Its first pipeline was green. By sprint 6 a green first pipeline on a structure change is unremarkable, which is the point: the team had stopped noticing the checks on routine work, the way an engineer stops noticing a calculator.

On Wednesday Jim opened !22, Inspection verdicts, signed. Some Tidewater requirements are verified by inspection -- someone looks at the thing and signs that it complies -- and the results schema the team adopted in week zero (ADR 0003) puts those verdicts in a file in the repository, with the name of the person who signed. A signed verdict is a configuration item like any other: it goes through a merge request, it has an author and an approver, and it is in the baseline. Jim's merge request entered the verdicts Jim could sign from the drop-1 evidence; the VCRM job, later in the sprint, reads them. Here is the file, in Tom's clone of develop:

Each row is one verdict: the requirement, the verification case, the verdict, the commit of the model it was judged against, how it was judged, when, and who signed. Read the commit column twice. It is what turns a signature into evidence: years from now, anyone can check out exactly the model Jim inspected. In the document era an inspection record named a document revision, and the revision named nothing that could be rebuilt.

The file is named results-gov.csv because it holds the government's own verdicts. When the prime's test results arrive with later drops (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop), they land in a sibling file in the same schema, and the VCRM reads both. One schema for every source of verdicts is ADR 0003's whole point.

31.3.2 Thursday 17 December: Bob's day

Thursday was the busiest day of the twelve weeks, and it is told in full, hour by hour, in Chapter 39, A day in the life, week twelve. The short version, from GitLab's own record:

Four things happened before lunch, and each one is a pattern worth knowing.

A failed nightly pipeline, triaged at the stand-up. The scheduled 02:00 full check failed in every job before running any check. Bob saw it first, opened an issue at 09:15 and linked the failing pipeline; Tom took it at the stand-up and closed it by 10:30:

The cause had nothing to do with the model: the runner's disk was full. The fix had two parts, and the second is the one that matters -- clearing the disk fixes today; making the runner clean up after each job fixes the next month (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs). The scorecard records how long develop was red: the worst time to restore in the sprint was 8.5 hours, from the failed 02:00 run to the green rerun.

A draft merge request that failed on purpose. Bob opened !23, the fork, pin and object flow in ObserveCoast, as a draft at 10:00 -- a draft says "not ready for review, but run the checks". Its first pipeline failed the trace job:

While editing the behavior, Bob had also touched the text of TW-SYS-007 in the model's copy of the requirements. The model's text no longer matched DOORS: a new drift. The ratchet named it, Bob restored the DOORS wording, and the second pipeline passed. Bob marked the merge request ready at noon. Notice the order: the check ran before anyone was asked to review. Reviewers never saw the mistake.

A review comment that blocked a merge. Tom's !24 documented the flow properties in Interfaces -- what each interface carries -- so the data exchange table could be generated from them. Bob reviewed it at 14:05 and asked for a change, with a suggestion block:

"Late" assumes a schedule nobody had written down. At 14:20 Tom tried to merge anyway and GitLab refused: discussions not resolved (1 open). That refusal is the project setting the team chose in week zero (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab): a merge request cannot merge while a reviewer's thread is open. Tom applied the suggestion, Bob resolved the thread, Jim and Bob approved, and it merged at 15:10. You can see the approvals in the sandbox:

Two approvals, because Interfaces.sysml sits in a CODEOWNERS section that needs both the package owner and Jim as systems lead (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).

An assumption made visible. Tom's reply on !24 says the assumption "goes in the next prime-tbd list". This is the team's practice for work that cannot wait for the prime (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition): proceed on a written assumption, label it prime-tbd, and close it when a drop confirms or corrects it. The suggestion put the assumption into the model's own doc text, so it shows up in everything generated from the model -- including, the next day, the data exchange table.

Six things happened before lunch and I knew about every one of them from GitLab, not from email.

— Bob, 17 December

Bob's GitLab To-Do list at 14:05 held exactly one item -- Tom's review request:

31.3.3 Friday 18 December: the table, and a token

Tom's !25 generated the data exchange table: for each interface, the flows, their direction, their type, their fields, and the notes from the model's doc text. Its first pipeline failed -- not on the model, on the secrets job:

Tom had pasted a personal access token into a helper script to test it, and committed the script. The pipeline stopped it before it reached develop. What Tom did next is the whole procedure for a leaked credential, and its order matters:

Revoke first, because the token may already have been copied from the branch. Replace it with a narrower one stored as a masked, protected CI/CD variable (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep). Then rewrite the branch so the token is in no commit. Deleting the line in a new commit is not enough: the old commit still holds it (Appendix E, Rescue: when something goes wrong).

The table itself is a generated document in docs/, committed with the model and rebuilt by the pipeline. Here it is in the sandbox, as of the end of the sprint:

Look at the HealthIF row: the assumption from Thursday's review is in the table, labeled as an assumption to confirm with the prime. In the document era, that assumption would have lived in someone's head or in a comment on a PDF. Here it is part of the deliverable, and it will stay visible until the prime answers.

The week's quad went to management on Friday:

31.4 Week 2: two of three, and the ending

Bob was on leave. The attendance record shows it -- stand-ups with two people from Monday 21 December on -- and the plan had accounted for it in the capacity. Jim and Tom finished the sprint.

31.4.1 Monday 21 December: the VCRM job

Tom's !26 added the vcrm job and the baseline jobs to the pipeline. The VCRM reads every requirement, its verification method, the verification cases that claim to verify it, and the verdicts in the results files, and writes vcrm.html and vcrm.csv. In the sandbox:

Read that line carefully, because the team almost did not. Hardly any requirement is verified, most are not run, and some have no case at all. That sounds like a disaster. It is not: it says something different from the trace.

31.4.2 The number that almost misled management

The trace measure the team had reported for twelve weeks -- verify coverage -- asks: does every requirement have a verification case that claims to verify it? For Tidewater that was 29 of 30 linked requirements with 9 unverified, the same as at the drop-1 import, because the gaps are the prime's.

The VCRM asks a different question: has the verification actually been done, with a recorded verdict? In a program that has not reached test, almost nothing has been. The verified ones are the inspection verdicts Jim signed in !22.

When Jim drafted the review script with talk.pl review, the tool did what tools do: it found a newer verification measure and used it.

Verify coverage: 6.7% verified (VCRM) (down 63.3 from 70). Read naively, that line tells the program manager that verification collapsed in the last sprint. It did not collapse; a second, stricter measure appeared. The draft was corrected before the meeting -- the review record uses the measure the program had been seeing all along:

This is the most important lesson about drafting tools in this book (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not): read every number before you say it, and never compare two measures as if they were one. The fix is not a better tool; it is a person who knows what each number means.

The kit's talk.pl was changed after this sprint, because of exactly this near miss: it now keeps the two measures apart and labels the second one as a different measure. Run it on the same sprint in the sandbox and compare its lines with the draft above:

That is how a tool should improve: a person caught a misleading number, and the tool was changed so the next person does not have to.

31.4.3 Tuesday and Wednesday: the briefing, and refinement for January

Jim wrote the twelve-week briefing and its memo on Tuesday (#128). The briefing's content is in Chapter 35, The briefing; here is its outline as the evidence keeps it:

Every number in it came from the pipeline's records: the TODO lines, the lead time, the gated changes, the pulse. None was typed into a slide from memory. The written twin of the briefing is the progress memo (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim).

Wednesday's refinement prepared sprint 7: breaking the last package cycle, the DailyUpload interaction by hand, the EnergyBalance constraint expression, retiring the profile TODO, and pinning the kit version.

Case study: The decision: an interim baseline, now

The plan called for the first real baseline -- baseline-1, the port's acceptance -- in sprint 20. Jim proposed an interim baseline-0 for the twelve-week review, and the reasoning is worth copying.

Against: the model was not finished. BuoyModes was still a TODO line, the trace still had the prime's gaps, the package view still showed a cycle. A baseline of an unfinished model, the argument went, would look like a claim that it was finished.

For: a baseline is not a claim of completeness; it is a claim of identity. Baseline-0 says: this is the model on 24 December, these are its known gaps (the release notes and the VCRM list them), and anyone can rebuild it exactly. That is precisely what a program needs before a review -- a fixed point to discuss -- and it is what the document era could never provide: the "baseline" was a set of PDFs whose source nobody could reproduce. The other reason was practice. The release path has steps that only run on a tag: the baseline audit, the toolchain inventory, the release. Running them first in December, with nothing riding on them, was cheaper than running them first for baseline-1.

The CCB agreed on the second argument. The deputy program manager's concurrence comment on !27 says what the board reviewed: the change list and the pipeline.

31.5 Thursday 24 December: baseline-0

The interim baseline is the first time the team's work went out under the CCB's name. Tom had rehearsed the path in sprint 5 in a sandbox project. The real path, on the real project:

  1. A release/baseline-0 branch from develop, with the CHANGELOG section and regenerated docs.
  2. A merge request into main, !27, with the release template's checklist and one line the CCB writes itself.
  3. The deputy program manager's concurrence, recorded as a comment on the merge request -- the CCB's approval, in the same place as the engineering approvals:
  1. The merge into main, the annotated tag baseline-0 whose message carries the sha256 of the generated docs, and the back-merge into develop.
  2. The tag pipeline: it regenerates the docs from the tagged model, checks the hash against the tag message, writes the toolchain inventory, rebuilds the VCRM and publishes the release.

The tag in the sandbox:

And the end of the tag pipeline's baseline job:

baseline-0 rebuilds identically. That one line is a physical configuration audit, done by a machine in a minute, on every baseline, forever. The toolchain lines below it say which kit, Perl and git produced the baseline, so the audit can be repeated years from now with the same tools.

The scorecard counts it: 1 baseline tagged, 1 reproducible.

31.6 The carryover

At 16:30 on Christmas Eve the journal recorded the sprint's one carryover: Bob's BuoyModes task, #120, continued as #138 in sprint 7 with its remaining points.

Delivery for the sprint was 11 of 14 story points (79%). The carryover was predictable from the kickoff -- the task's dates ran past the sprint -- and that is the lesson: when the plan already says a task cannot finish, either split it so the first part can, or leave it out and say why. Committing it anyway made the sprint look worse than the team's work was. The converter's TODO line for the state machine is still in the model, and the TODO burn-down counts it.

31.7 Reading the sprint's own numbers

The sprint-end analytics (Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics) tell the story of the busy Thursday in four lines:

Time to restore is no longer empty, as it was in sprint 5: develop was red once, from the 02:00 nightly failure to the green rerun. That is the disk-full incident, and the number is honest about it -- the nightly failed at 02:00 and nobody looked until the stand-up. A team that wants that number smaller has two choices: a runner that cannot fill its disk (the fix Tom made), or a notification that wakes someone up. For a model repository, the first is the right answer; nobody's model needs to be green at 03:00.

Pipeline success rate dropped from sprint 5. Look at the job failures line before worrying: the secrets failures are Tom's token (the merge request pipeline, a rerun, and the push to the branch), and the other single failures are the nightly run, where every job failed for the same disk-full reason. Not one failure was a model error that reached develop. A falling success rate with that explanation is a sign the checks are working; the same number without the explanation would worry a manager for nothing. Always bring the explanation.

Change failure rate is still zero. Seven merges to develop, none reverted or fixed forward.

31.8 What went wrong, and what the team did about it

  • The runner's disk filled up. Fixed the same morning; the runner now cleans up after each job. The lesson for administration is in Chapter 42, Administration: a runner is a server, and servers need the same care as anything else.
  • A personal access token was committed. Caught by the pipeline before it reached develop; revoked, replaced with a masked project token, history rewritten. The retrospective made it a rule: no tokens in scripts, even test ones (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system).
  • A story was committed that could not finish. BuoyModes, planned across Bob's leave (Section 31.6, The carryover).
  • A drafting tool nearly misreported a measure to management. Corrected before the review (Section 31.4.2, The number that almost misled management).
  • A requirement's text was changed by accident. Bob's edit to TW-SYS-007 in !23, caught by the trace ratchet in a draft merge request, before any reviewer saw it.

None of these reached the model on develop. In the document era, the same five mistakes -- a lost day of work, a leaked credential, an over-committed plan, a misleading slide, an altered requirement -- would have surfaced, if at all, at the next milestone review.

31.9 The review and the retrospective

The review on 24 December had the largest audience of the twelve weeks: the deputy program manager and the program manager joined Jim and Tom. The demo used the model site as its home page and ended on the baseline. The program manager's feedback was short:

Keep doing this. Show me the same numbers in March.

— Program manager, 24 December

The retrospective:

Stop pasting tokens into scripts, even test ones is Tom's lesson from Friday. Start writing acceptance criteria as pipeline checks is the sprint's most important process change: a story is done when a named check says so, not when someone feels finished (Chapter 14, Writing stories and tasks for model work). Continue reviews with line comments instead of red-pen PDFs is the team recognizing what Thursday's review of !24 was: the same scrutiny as a document review, two hours after the change instead of three weeks.

The pulse: 4.1, the highest of the twelve weeks, from 1.9 at the end of sprint 1. Jim's answers were the highest on the first and last questions -- I understand why we are working this way and I would choose to keep working this way. For the person who carried the directive into the room in week zero, those are the two that count.

Objection: "The morale numbers are the team grading its own homework."

They are, and the book does not pretend otherwise. Three people answering five questions is not a survey; it is a conversation starter. What makes the numbers worth reporting is that they were defined in week zero, asked the same way every sprint, and published even when they went down -- sprint 3's dip is in every briefing. A measure you only report when it is good is advertising. The other eleven measures on the scorecard do not depend on anyone's mood.

31.10 Twelve weeks, in the measures agreed on day one

The scorecard was defined in Chapter 3, The directive before the first sprint. These are its values at the end of each sprint, from the pipeline's own records:

31.11 What Jim told management

The briefing on 24 December (Chapter 35, The briefing) and the progress memo (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim) carried the twelve-week story. A covering note for the last quad of the year needs one sentence: Baseline-0 is tagged, reproducible and CCB-approved; the model, the trace, the verification matrix and the data exchange table are on the model site, and they will stay current without anyone rebuilding them.

31.12 Tools adopted this sprint, and the pain each removed

31.13 You can now...

Note: You can now...
  • Cut a baseline through a release branch, record the CCB's concurrence on the merge request, tag it, and read the pipeline's proof that it rebuilds identically.
  • Tell verify coverage (a case exists) from verification status (a verdict exists), and keep them apart in a briefing.
  • Respond to a committed credential in the right order: revoke, replace, rewrite.
  • Generate a document -- the data exchange table -- from the model, with its assumptions visible.
  • Read a sprint plan and spot the task that cannot finish before the sprint starts.

31.14 Exercises

Exercise 31.1: Audit baseline-0

In the Tidewater sandbox, check out the baseline-0 tag in Tom's clone, run perl ci/job.pl baseline with CI_COMMIT_TAG=baseline-0 in the environment, and confirm the rebuild line. Then rename one part definition in a model file (for example Thermometer in model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml), run it again, and read what the job says. Why would changing a file under docs/ instead not trip the audit? (Restore the tree afterwards with git checkout -- ..)

Exercise 31.2: Two measures, one slide

Write the two-line statement Jim could have put on a slide about verification at the end of sprint 6: one line for verify coverage, one for the VCRM, each saying what it measures, with its number. Have someone outside the team read it and tell you what they think it means.

Exercise 31.3: Fix the plan, not the sprint

Rewrite TW-112 from the sprint 6 kickoff so that its first task can finish inside the sprint despite the leave. What would "done" mean for that first task, as a pipeline check?

Exercise 31.4: An assumption to the prime

Using the Discrepancy Report or Prime Drop template (Appendix I, Templates and GitLab Markdown, field by field), write the request that asks the prime to confirm or correct the "late = two missed transmissions" assumption in the data exchange table. Say what changes in the model if the prime disagrees.

31.15 Applying this to your project

  • End your first twelve weeks with a baseline. A tagged, reproducible, CCB-approved version is the thing management can hold; everything else is a promise.
  • Put the CCB's approval where the engineering approvals are. A comment on the release merge request is a record nobody can lose and everybody can find.
  • Introduce a new measure next to the old one, never in its place. Name both; explain the difference once.
  • Make assumptions part of the generated documents. An assumption in the model's doc text shows up in every table the pipeline builds, until somebody confirms it.
  • Plan around leave and holidays before the sprint, not at the review. A carryover you could see on day one is a planning error, not bad luck.

Part IV: Making the case

Part III followed the team through twelve weeks, one sprint at a time. Part IV steps back and asks the question management asked on 24 December: was it worth it? The answer has to be built from measurements the team agreed before the work started, computed by the system rather than typed into slides, and honest about what did not move.

The chapters run in the order Jim prepared them. Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics shows the views GitLab offers for free and what each one says about a model team. Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard puts the twelve measures from Chapter 3, The directive side by side, before and after. Chapter 34, Proving the port is complete and correct answers the question every port must answer: is the v2 model complete and correct? Chapter 35, The briefing is the briefing itself, slide by slide, with the demo script. Chapter 36, Telling management is the weekly rhythm of reports that made the briefing a summary rather than a surprise. The last chapters of the part turn to the people: how the team changed its mind, a day in the life at week twelve, and how documents still matter.

Everything quoted here comes from docs/tidewater/, the evidence of the simulated run. Where this part says a number, it cites the file it came from.

32 Measuring with GitLab analytics

From what you know

You know

the metrics slide assembled the night before a review.

Here it is called

GitLab analytics, and gitlab.pl analytics.

What is new

the numbers come from the work itself, every day, and nobody counts by hand.

Survival kit: Before you start

What you have

twelve weeks of issues, merge requests and pipelines in one GitLab project, and the kit's journal of stories.

What you need

to know which of GitLab's analytics views answer a question a systems engineer or a program manager actually asks, which of them your license includes, and how to get the same numbers when it does not.

Jim's first instinct, when the program manager asked for "the metrics," was to open GitLab's Analytics menu and screenshot whatever was there. Tom talked Jim out of it. Half the menu was greyed out on their license tier, and the other half answered questions nobody on the program had asked. "Deployment frequency" sounds impressive until someone asks what Tidewater deploys. This chapter is the sorting Jim and Tom did in sprint 6: what each view measures, what it means for a team whose product is a model, and how to get the numbers without buying a tier you do not need.

32.1 Two kinds of numbers

The team keeps two records, and each one is good at different questions.

  • The journal (the kit's scrum.txt, Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board) holds stories: what was committed, done, carried, blocked, and how many points each was worth. It answers planning questions: are we delivering what we commit to, and how fast does the backlog shrink?
  • GitLab holds tasks, merge requests, approvals, pipelines and tags. It answers flow and quality questions: how long does a change take from proposal to acceptance, how often does a check catch something, how long are we red?

Neither replaces the other. The scorecard in Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard takes its delivery and morale measures from the journal and the retrospectives, and its flow and quality measures from GitLab. This chapter is about the second kind.

32.2 The views GitLab offers

GitLab's analytics are spread over several pages, and which ones you see depends on the license tier. Tiers and the features in them change from release to release, so treat the tier column below as a guide and check GitLab's current pricing page before you plan around a view.

Table 32.1. GitLab's analytics views, as a systems engineer reads them.
ViewTier (check current pricing)What it measuresThe question it answers for a model team
Value stream analyticsFree (basic), Premium (custom stages)time an issue spends in each stage, from created to closedwhere do our changes wait: before work starts, in review, or after merge?
CI/CD analyticsFreepipeline success rate and duration over timedo our checks run reliably, and how long does a change wait for them?
Repository analyticsFreecommits, languages, contributorswho is touching the model, and how often?
Merge request analyticsPremiumthroughput, time to mergehow many changes did we accept, and how long did each take?
Code review analyticsPremiumopen merge requests and their review activitywhich proposed changes are stuck waiting for a reviewer?
Issue analyticsPremiumissues opened and closed per monthis the backlog of discrepancies and tasks growing or shrinking?
Contribution analyticsPremium (group level)events per memberis the work spread across the team or resting on one person?
Milestone burndown and burnupPremiumissues and weight closed against a milestoneare we on track for this sprint?
DORA metricsUltimatedeployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restorehow fast and how safely do changes flow?
Insights and analytics dashboardsUltimatecharts you configure in YAMLanything above, on one page

The Tidewater project ran on the Free tier for the first twelve weeks; the tier decision was one of Jim's asks in the request for enablers (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim). That meant value stream, CI/CD and repository analytics in the web pages, and everything else from the API.

32.3 The Free-tier route: gitlab.pl analytics

Every number in the paid views is computed from data that every tier exposes through GitLab's REST API: merge requests with their commits, notes and approvals; issues with their labels and dates; pipelines and their jobs; deployments and releases. The kit's gitlab.pl analytics reads that data and prints the same five sections a manager would want from the paid pages. It works the same way against a real GitLab server and against the offline stand-in the book uses.

Here it is on the Tidewater project at the end of sprint 6. The sandbox is a copy of the simulated project, with its GitLab state in gitlab/:

The same report, as the team filed it with the sprint 6 evidence:

Against a real server, the only change is the first two options: --url https://gitlab.example.gov --token-env GITLAB_TOKEN instead of --local gitlab. The token needs only the read_api scope.

32.4 Reading the five sections

Value stream. Each row is one stage of a change's life, with the median and the 85th percentile in hours. The stage that matters most for a model team is MR opened -> first review: that is the wait for a colleague's eyes, and it is where document-era reviews used to take weeks. In sprint 6 the median was 3.3 hours. The long stage at the top, issue created -> first commit, is not a problem: stories are filed at refinement, a week before work starts, so that stage measures planning lead, not delay.

DORA, for a model repository. The four DORA measures were defined for software teams that deploy services. A model team deploys too, just not to production servers. The table below is the translation the kit uses.

Table 32.2. The four DORA measures, translated for a model repository.
DORA measureSoftware meaningModel meaning in gitlab.pl analytics
Deployment frequencyreleases to productionpublishes of the model site (the pages environment) and baseline releases
Lead time for changescommit to running in productionfirst commit on a branch to merged on develop
Change failure ratedeployments that caused an incidentmerges that needed a fix-forward or a revert merge request
Time to restoreincident to recoverydevelop pipeline red to the next green

Two of these belong in front of management and two do not. Lead time (3.5 hours median in sprint 6) is the direct answer to "how long does a change take now?", and time to restore (the worst case in sprint 6 was 8.5 hours, the night the runner's disk filled up) shows the safety net works. Deployment frequency is mostly the nightly schedule rebuilding the site, so it measures a cron line, not the team. Change failure rate was zero in the first twelve weeks, which says more about the small number of merges than about the team's skill; quote it only with its denominator.

CI/CD. Pipeline runs, failures and duration. The job failure line is the one to read: it says which checks caught something. In sprint 6 most failures were the secrets job, which is the planted test token in Bob's day in the life (Chapter 39, A day in the life, week twelve) doing exactly what it should.

Merge requests. Throughput, time to merge and review turnaround per sprint, and merged-over-opened per author. The per-author line is useful to the team and dangerous in a briefing: it reads as a productivity ranking, and in sprint 6 it mostly shows that Tom prepared the baseline and the release.

Issues. Opened and closed by type, and the oldest open items. The discrepancy reports to the prime sit at the top of the oldest list. That is correct: they are the prime's to close, with the next drop.

32.5 The trend across the twelve weeks

One sprint is a snapshot. The case for management is the trend, so run the report over the whole period, by sprint, and write the tables as CSV files for a spreadsheet:

The two flow measures the team agreed to report, taken from each sprint's scorecard:

Table 32.3. Flow measures by sprint, from the scorecard files.
SprintLead time, median hoursReview turnaround, median hoursChanges gated
12.220 of 1
23.63.36 of 6
34.24.14 of 4
43.53.34 of 4
53.53.35 of 5
63.53.37 of 7

Read it the way the program manager will. Lead time and review turnaround are measured in hours from the first sprint, against a document-era baseline measured in working days and weeks. They do not improve much after sprint 2, and that is the honest finding: the gain came from the way of working, not from the team getting faster at it. The one ungated change is merge request !1 in sprint 1, made before the pipeline file existed; its description says so.

32.6 Small numbers and other traps

A three-person team produces a few merge requests a week. Statistics on numbers that small are fragile, and the team learned to say so before anyone else did.

  • Quote the count with the median. "Median 3.5 hours over 7 merges" is honest; the median alone invites a comparison with a team of fifty.
  • Do not chase a measure. If review turnaround becomes a target, reviewers approve faster and catch less. The team watched it as a symptom, never as a goal.
  • Watch the definitions. The talk.pl review draft for sprint 6 reported "verify coverage" from the verification matrix, which counts requirements with a passing recorded result. The scorecard reports requirements with a verification case. The draft therefore showed coverage collapsing from seventy percent to almost nothing, the week the matrix job arrived. Tom caught it in the Day-9 rehearsal; Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard explains the two measures.
  • Separate the prime's numbers from the team's. Open discrepancy reports and unverified requirements belong to the prime until a drop closes them. A government team that reports them as its own backlog looks stuck.

32.7 What goes in the briefing

Jim put three numbers from GitLab into the December briefing, and left the rest in the appendix:

  1. Lead time for a change, with the document-era baseline beside it.
  2. Changes gated: every change since sprint 2 passed the checks and a code owner's review.
  3. Pipeline health: share of develop pipelines passing, and the worst time to restore.

Value stream stages, DORA deployment frequency, per-author counts and issue ages stayed in the team's own review. The reasoning is in Chapter 35, The briefing: management can act on three numbers with a trend; it cannot act on twenty.

32.8 How this relates to the kit's other measures

The kit already had measures before GitLab arrived. daily.pl health checks the journal against the thresholds of the operating model (blocked items, load, velocity, carryover). The weekly quad (Chapter 36, Telling management) reports sprint progress and on-time delivery. bin/status-metrics.pl computes the A to Z status metrics of a port from a model repository's git history. GitLab analytics adds the flow view on top: the same project seen through its merge requests and pipelines. When two sources disagree, believe the one that is closest to the work, and find out why.

Exercise 32.1: Run the report yourself

In the Tidewater sandbox, run gitlab.pl analytics for sprint 3 alone (2 to 13 November). Which stage of the value stream is longest, and why is that not a problem? Then run it for sprint 6 with --by week.

Exercise 32.2: Translate a DORA measure

Write one sentence a program manager would understand for each of the four DORA measures, using the model meanings in the table above. Which two would you leave out of a briefing, and why?

Exercise 32.3: Find the trap

Open docs/tidewater/sprints/06/review-script.md and docs/tidewater/sprints/06/review.txt. The draft and the final version disagree about verify coverage. Which one is right, and what would have happened if the draft had been read out?

32.9 You can now

  • name the GitLab analytics views, what each measures and roughly which tier it needs;
  • get the same numbers on the Free tier with gitlab.pl analytics, by sprint, with CSV output;
  • translate the DORA measures into model terms, and say which belong in front of management;
  • spot the traps of small numbers and mismatched definitions before management does.

32.10 Applying this to your project

Decide the three flow numbers you will report before the first sprint, write them into your scorecard, and run gitlab.pl analytics --by sprint at every sprint end into the sprint's evidence folder, as Tidewater did. Do not buy a tier for its dashboards until you have used the Free-tier report for a few sprints and know which questions you keep asking. If your license includes the paid views, use them for the team's own retrospectives and keep the briefing to the few numbers you defined in advance.

33 The twelve-week scorecard

From what you know

You know

the stoplight chart.

Here it is called

the twelve-week scorecard.

What is new

every measure was agreed in week zero and is computed from the evidence, including the one that did not move.

Survival kit: Before you start

What you have

the twelve measures the program manager signed on 1 October (Section 3.6, Defining measurable progress), and a scorecard file the pipeline and the journal filled in at the end of every sprint.

What you need

to read the scorecard the way a skeptical manager will: measure by measure, before against after, including the measures that did not move.

The scorecard was the team's insurance. Bob had said it in the first week: "If we don't write down now what counts as progress, in December they'll judge us on whatever they happen to look at." So the measures were agreed before sprint 1, each with a definition, a source and a target, and each sprint's numbers were written by the system into docs/tidewater/sprints/NN/scorecard.json. Nobody typed them. This chapter reads the last of those files against the first, measure by measure.

To see the source for yourself, open the last scorecard file in the Tidewater sandbox:

33.2 Conversion debt: the TODO burn-down

The converter leaves a // TODO line for every v1 construct it cannot carry. Counting those lines on every change was the team's port burn-down (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). Nothing was imported in sprint 1, so the first count arrived with drop 1 in sprint 2:

Table 33.2. TODO lines left on develop, from the pipeline's todo job.
