The steep fall in sprint 4 is the Stations package: most of its level tags closed in one story. The lines left at the end are behavior and analysis, the constructs the converter never carries: the BuoyModes state machine (carried into sprint 7), the energy-balance expression, and the profile note. You can count them yourself on the integration branch:

33.3 Flow: lead time, review and gating

These three are the measures that changed the program manager's mind, because the document-era numbers beside them are measured in working days and weeks. A requirement change used to take 23 working days through the CCB; a model change now goes from the first commit to merged in a median of 3.5 hours, and every one of them was checked by the pipeline and approved by a code owner who did not write it. Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics shows the sprint-by-sprint trend.

Two cautions keep this honest. First, the comparison is not like for like: a CCB change carried a requirement through several organizations, while a merge request carries one model change through one team. The fair claim is that the team's own part of the work is now measured in hours. Second, the baseline numbers are notional, taken from the program's last document-era cycle as the team remembered it; they were never measured the way the new numbers are. The scorecard says so in its own file, under document_era_baseline_notional.

33.4 Trace: computed every time, and flat

The trace job compares the prime's DOORS export with the model on every change. Its measures did not move in twelve weeks, and they were not supposed to.

Table 33.3. Trace measures at the end of sprint 6, identical to sprint 2.
MeasureValue at sprint 6
C: requirements linked29 of 30
F: orphans (nothing satisfies them)2
G: unverified (no verification case)9
I: completeness66.7%
Text drift between DOORS and the model1

The gaps were planted in the prime's model before the government touched it: two requirements nothing satisfies, a set without verification cases, one requirement whose DOORS wording differs from the model. They are the prime's to fix, through discrepancy reports, and the drops that close them arrive from January. A government team that edited the v2 model to close them would have made its model disagree with the contractual baseline. So the right twelve-week result is not "coverage went up"; it is "every gap is found by a program on every change, and every gap has a discrepancy report with an owner and a due drop." That is what measure 5 asked for.

Warning: Two different "verify coverage" numbers

The scorecard counts requirements that have a verification case (G above: the rest are covered, which is the seventy percent the reviews quote). The verification matrix, new in the last sprint, also counts requirements with a passing recorded result, and on that definition almost none qualify yet (the "Verification" line of the baseline-0 release notes gives the count): the prime's test results only start arriving with drop 4. The talk.pl review draft for sprint 6 quoted the matrix number as if it were the scorecard's and announced a collapse. Name the definition every time you say "coverage."

33.5 Discrepancy reports

By the end of sprint 6 the team had opened 7 discrepancy reports to the prime and closed 0. Closed zero sounds bad and is correct: a discrepancy report closes when a prime drop fixes the problem, and the first drop after the port started arrives in January (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition). What management should see is that every gap the trace found became a written, numbered, dated request to the prime within a sprint, where in the document era such gaps went into an email, if anywhere.

33.6 The spider web: better, not gone

Measure 7 is the one the team did not meet, and the briefing said so.

Table 33.4. Spider-web measures of the v2 model, from the pipeline's complexity job.
After sprintPackage cyclesDuplicatesMax fan-outMax relationships per part
210419

Three things happened. The worst block, ObservingStation, lost its trace spaghetti in sprint 5: the maximum relationships per part fell to less than half. Sprint 4 attacked both package cycles from Chapter 2, The Cameo years. The Network and Operations cycle is gone. The DataCenter and Stations cycle is not: the story removed the dependency it was written against (QualityControl on SensorSuite), and the complexity job still reports cycles: DataCenter <-> Stations, so another reference between the two packages remains. The team reported that at the review rather than declaring the story's goal met, and finding the remaining edge went into the sprint 7 backlog. And the "duplicates" column jumped in sprint 3, when the DOORS modules were imported: the model now holds each requirement twice, once as the Cameo copy and once as the DOORS module's conversion. That doubling is deliberate (DOORS is authoritative, and the trace compares the two), but the measure cannot tell a deliberate copy from clutter. The team reported the number as it was and explained it, rather than redefining the measure to make the column look better. Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web covers what it would take to finish.

33.7 Pipeline health and baselines

In sprint 6, 16 of 17 pipelines on develop passed. The one failure was the night the runner's disk filled up; the worst time from red to green was 8.5 hours, inside the one working day the scorecard allowed. The interim baseline-0 was tagged on 24 December, and the pipeline's baseline job rebuilt it and matched the checksum recorded in the tag. In the document era a baseline was a revision letter on a cover page, and nobody could rebuild one.

33.8 Delivery and morale

Delivery against plan was the measure that kept the team honest about its own estimates:

Table 33.5. Delivery and morale by sprint, from the journal and the retrospectives.

Two sprints fell below the eighty percent target, and both for the same reason: a story carried over. In sprint 4 the Stations walk-through moved to sprint 5; in sprint 6 the hand-written BuoyModes state machine moved to sprint 7. Both were the hardest engineering of their sprint, and in both cases the team chose to finish the work properly rather than to call it done. The journal records the carry; the quad marks the story as late.

The pulse survey asked the same five questions at every retrospective. It started at 1.9, dipped to 2.2 in sprint 3 (a grammar error on a hand edit and a three-day wait for the ISSM, the same week), and ended at 4.1. Chapter 38, How the team changed its mind tells that story; the scorecard only says it was measured every sprint, by the same questions, and reported even when it was low.

33.9 Measures beyond the twelve

The sprint files carry three more numbers that the team found useful, though they were not on the signed scorecard:

  • Work mix. The share of done points that was engineering, platform or learning, by sprint. It opens this book (Bottom line up front): engineering grew from a quarter of sprint 1 to most of sprint 6.
  • Stand-up outcome share. The share of stand-up lines that stated an outcome and a number. It went from 0.48 in sprint 1 to 1 from sprint 3 on (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not). Sprint 2 scored lower than sprint 1 because sprint 1's statuses happened to quote counts while sprint 2's described mechanism.
  • First-pipeline pass rate. How many merge requests passed their checks on the first try: 4 of 6 in sprint 6. A failure on the first pipeline is the system working; the measure shows how much the checks are doing.

33.10 What the scorecard does not say

A scorecard is a set of chosen numbers. This one does not measure the quality of the engineering decisions (whether the cycle break put ObservationRecord in the right package), it does not compare cost with the document era, and its "before" column is memory, not measurement. The team said so in the briefing. A scorecard that admits its limits is easier to believe than one that does not.

Pick the three measures you would challenge first if you were the program manager. For each, write the question you would ask and find the evidence file that answers it.

For your program, write down the document-era equivalent of measures 2, 4 and 10, with where the number comes from. Mark each one "measured" or "remembered."

33.11 You can now

  • read a sprint's scorecard file and trace each value to the job or record that produced it;
  • explain why trace coverage stays flat during a port, and why that is the right result;
  • separate a measure that missed for a good reason from one that missed for a bad one, and say which is which;
  • present a scorecard that includes its misses and its limits.

33.12 Applying this to your project

Write your scorecard before sprint 1, with a definition, a source and a target for each measure, and have the program manager sign it. Make the pipeline and the journal write it at every sprint end, so no number is typed. Include at least one measure you might miss, and one that measures the team rather than the model. Keep the "before" column honest: label remembered numbers as notional, and replace them with measured ones the first time you can.

34 Proving the port is complete and correct

From what you know

You know

the configuration audit, and the sign-off on a data conversion.

Here it is called

proving the port: counts, the TODO burn-down, the trace against DOORS and a sampled review.

What is new

most of the evidence is produced by scripts anyone can rerun.

Survival kit: Before you start

What you have

the prime's drop 1 (the v1 model and the DOORS export), the converted v2 model on develop, and the pipeline's reports.

What you need

an answer to the first question management asks about any port, in a form an independent reviewer can check: is the new model complete, and does it say the same thing as the old one?

The deputy program manager put the question plainly at the sprint 4 review: "How do I know nothing fell on the floor between the Cameo model and the new one?" In the document era the answer would have been a person's signature on a comparison spreadsheet. The team's answer was a set of evidence a reviewer can regenerate: counts the converter produces, a burn-down the pipeline keeps, a trace a program computes, a sample a person checks, and a baseline anyone can rebuild. This chapter lays out that evidence, shows where Tidewater stood at the end of the twelve weeks, and says what is still missing before the port can be accepted at baseline-1.

34.1 Complete, and correct

The question has two halves, and they need different evidence.

  • Complete: every element of the v1 model that matters is either in the v2 text or accounted for. Nothing was silently dropped. This is mostly counting.
  • Correct: what the v2 model says matches what the v1 model and DOORS say. Names, structure, relationships and requirement text agree. This is counting plus comparison plus a human look.

A port is acceptable when both halves are evidenced and someone with the authority to accept it has signed. For Tidewater that someone is the deputy program manager, through a concurrence comment on the baseline-1 release merge request (Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).

34.2 Evidence 1: the converter accounts for every element

The converter's report lists every v1 element type it read, how many it mapped to v2 text, how many it folded into a parent, and how many it left as a TODO line. Nothing is dropped without a line in that table. Run it on drop 1 in the Tidewater sandbox:

Read the totals row and the line below it: every in-scope element (classes, ports, properties, connectors and activities, the filter the status metrics use) was ported. The --map option also wrote map.csv, one row per v1 element with the v2 name, kind, file and line it became. That map is the backbone of the rest of the evidence:

Each v2 kind is a count a reviewer can compare with the v1 side of the report: requirements in, requirements out; part definitions in, part definitions out. A difference must be explained by a fold (a v1 element that became part of another v2 element) or a TODO line.

34.3 Evidence 2: the TODO burn-down reaches zero

Every TODO line is a v1 construct the converter could not carry, waiting for a person. A complete port has none. Tidewater's count, from the pipeline's todo job at the end of each sprint, stood at 5 at the end of sprint 6. Count it on the integration branch:

The remaining lines are behavior and analysis: the BuoyModes state machine (carried into sprint 7) and the energy-balance expression, both written by hand. Acceptance waits for zero.

34.4 Evidence 3: the trace agrees with DOORS

DOORS is authoritative for requirement text. The trace job compares the prime's DOORS export with the requirements in the model on every change, leaving out the DOORS-generated packages so the model is not compared with itself:

Four numbers and two lists come out. Linked says how many DOORS requirements the model carries (29 of 30 at the end of sprint 6: the missing one exists only in DOORS and is a discrepancy report). Orphans and unverified are gaps in the prime's model, also reported. The drift list names requirements whose text differs between DOORS and the model, with both versions printed. For the port, the rule is simple: every number must be either identical to the v1 model's own trace, or explained by a discrepancy report. A port that changed the trace has changed the meaning.

34.5 Evidence 4: a sampled side-by-side review

Counts prove nothing was lost; they do not prove nothing was garbled. For that, a person compares a sample of elements in both forms. The team picked every twenty-fifth row of the map, which is reproducible (anyone running the same command gets the same sample) and spreads across packages:

For each sampled row the reviewer opens the v1 element in the XMI and the v2 text at the file and line the map gives, and records "same", "same, reworded", or "different" in the review issue. One of the sample, side by side:

At the end of sprint 6 the sample had been drawn but not reviewed: it is a story for the semester that ends with baseline-1, done by Jim and the prime's modeler together, so the prime agrees with the result.

34.6 Evidence 5: the views say the same thing

The v1 model was mostly diagrams. The v2 model regenerates its views on every change (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text): the part tree, the requirements trace, the interconnection view and the package view. A reviewer who knows the old diagrams compares them with the generated ones for the same packages. This is a quick check that catches a wrong parent or a missing connection that the counts would not. It is also the check that convinces people who learned the system from diagrams.

34.7 Evidence 6: the baseline rebuilds

The accepted port is a baseline, and a baseline is only evidence if it can be rebuilt. The interim baseline-0 of sprint 6 records the checksum of its generated documents in the tag:

The pipeline's baseline job regenerates the documents from the tagged model and compares the checksum, and writes the toolchain inventory beside it (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). The baseline-0 audit passed: the scorecard shows 1 reproducible of 1 tagged.

34.8 Where Tidewater stood at twelve weeks

Table 34.1. Port acceptance evidence, interim status after twelve weeks.
EvidenceStatus at the end of sprint 6Needed for acceptance
Converter accounts for every elementin-scope elements all ported; every fold and TODO listeddone
TODO burn-down5 lines left (behavior, analysis)zero
Trace against DOORScomputed on every change; gaps are discrepancy reports to the primeunchanged, or explained
Drift listone requirement, reportedreported and dispositioned
Sampled reviewsample drawn, review not yet donerecorded in an issue, with the prime's modeler
Views comparedviews generated on every changereviewer's note in the same issue
Baseline rebuildsbaseline-0 reproduciblebaseline-1 reproducible
Sign-offnot yetdeputy PM's concurrence on the baseline-1 release merge request

The completeness report that ties these together, with every count and the sign-off in one document, is produced at baseline-1 in sprint 20, when the TODO count reaches zero and the sampled review is done. That is beyond the twelve weeks this part covers; Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle describes it.

Checklist: Port acceptance
  • ☐ The converter report shows every in-scope element ported, and every fold and TODO accounted for
  • ☐ The TODO count on the integration branch is zero
  • ☐ The trace numbers equal the v1 model's own trace, or each difference has a discrepancy report
  • ☐ The drift list is empty, or each drifted requirement has a disposition
  • ☐ A reproducible sample of elements has been compared side by side, and the result recorded
  • ☐ The generated views have been compared with the v1 diagrams of the same packages
  • ☐ The baseline tag rebuilds to its recorded checksum, with the toolchain inventory kept
  • ☐ The accepting authority has concurred, in writing, on the release merge request
Exercise 34.1: Draw your own sample

In the Tidewater sandbox, change the sampling rule to every fifteenth row and include satisfy rows. Pick two sampled elements and compare them side by side as the chapter does. Which are "same", and which "same, reworded"?

Exercise 34.2: Explain a difference

The converter report shows elements that were folded. Find two in map.csv (kind folded) and write one sentence each on why folding them is not a loss.

34.9 You can now

  • produce the counts that show a port lost nothing, from the converter's report and its map;
  • show that the port did not change the meaning of the requirements, with the trace and the drift list;
  • draw a reproducible sample for a side-by-side review and record the result;
  • list what is still missing before a port can be accepted, and who signs.

34.10 Applying this to your project

Agree the acceptance evidence with whoever will accept the port before you start converting, and write it into the scorecard or the definition of done for the port epic. Keep the converter's report and map for every drop in the repository, so the counts can be regenerated. Make the sample reproducible, and do the review with someone from the organization that owns the old model. Do not call the port done until the TODO count is zero and someone with authority has said so in writing.

35 The briefing

From what you know

You know

the program review briefing.

Here it is called

the twelve-week briefing.

What is new

every number on it traces to a file in the repository, and the demo is live.

Survival kit: Before you start

What you have

six sprints of evidence, the scorecard (Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard), and twenty minutes on the program management review agenda on 24 December.

What you need

a briefing that a program manager who has never opened GitLab can follow, that leads with conclusions, shows the real thing working, admits what did not work, and ends with an ask.

The directive of September promised management a briefing "at the December PMR." For twelve weeks that line hung over the team. Bob's fear, said out loud in week one, was that the briefing would be judged on how polished the slides were, the way briefings always had been. Jim's answer was to build the briefing the same way the team now built everything else: from the evidence, rehearsed, reviewed, with as few slides as possible and one live demonstration. This chapter is that briefing, slide by slide, with the reasoning behind each choice.

35.1 Preparing it

The preparation took one story in sprint 6 ("Retrospective, the management briefing and the plan for next semester," two points, Jim) and used the same rhythm as every sprint review since sprint 4 (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not):

  1. Draft from the system. talk.pl review drafts a demo script from GitLab and the journal: the question the sprint answered, the four headline numbers with their change, what to show, a before-and-after, a safe live change and a place for the ask.
  2. Edit for the audience. The draft is a starting point. Jim cut it to what the program manager asks about and added the document-era comparison.
  3. Rehearse on Day 9. Bob and Tom played the program manager and the deputy and interrupted with the questions they expected. The rehearsal caught the one mistake that would have hurt most (below).
  4. Write the twin. The briefing has a written twin, the twelve-week progress memo (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim), so the numbers survive after the meeting.

Here is the draft the system produced for sprint 6, run in the Tidewater sandbox:

Warning: The number that nearly went to management

The draft's second section says verify coverage fell by more than sixty points. It did not. The draft took "coverage" from the new verification matrix, which counts requirements with a passing recorded result, while every earlier review had used the trace's count of requirements with a verification case. On the trace's definition coverage was unchanged at seventy percent. Tom spotted it in the rehearsal because the number looked too dramatic to be true. The final script (Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard explains both measures) used the trace's number and said which definition it was. Read every drafted number before you say it.

35.2 The briefing, as given

Jim's outline, as filed with the sprint 6 evidence:

Six points, one demonstration, one ask. The sections below take them in order.

35.3 Slide 1: where we started

Headline: "We started with documents, then a Cameo model nobody could merge or review."

One slide, two numbers from the drop-1 assessment of Chapter 2, The Cameo years: the diagram count and the package cycles. Jim did not criticize the Cameo work; the people in the room had paid for it, and Bob and Tom had built it. Jim said what it could not do: two people could not change it at the same time and merge the result, a review meant screenshots in a briefing, and nobody could say which version of a diagram was current. The point of the slide is to name the problem the next five slides solve.

35.4 Slide 2: what we built

Headline: "Every change to the model is now checked and reviewed before it is accepted."

A picture, not a list: the flow from a proposed change through the pipeline's checks and a code owner's review to the model site. Jim named four things and no tool names: a project where the model lives, a set of automatic checks, the model itself in SysML v2 text, and a web site that management can open on a phone. The vocabulary on the slide was systems engineering vocabulary (Chapter 5, DevSecOps in systems-engineering words): "configuration control," "peer review," "audit," "baseline."

35.5 Slide 3: the scorecard, sprint by sprint

Headline: "The measures you signed in October, computed by the system."

The table on the slide is the one in the outline above: TODO lines, lead time, gated changes and morale for each of the six sprints. Jim chose four columns because each one answers a question the program manager had asked during the twelve weeks:

  • TODO lines: "How much of the port is left?" From 52 after drop 1 to 5.
  • Lead time: "How long does a change take now?" A median of 3.5 hours in sprint 6.
  • Gated: "Is anything getting in unchecked?" Every change since sprint 2: 7 of 7 in sprint 6.
  • Morale: "Is the team going to quit?" The program manager had not asked this out loud. Jim put it on the slide anyway, dip and all, because the dip in sprint 3 was the most believable number in the table.

The full twelve-measure scorecard went in the handout, with the one measure that missed (Section 33.6, The spider web: better, not gone) explained in a sentence: "We broke one of the two package cycles; the other is still there, and finding its last edge is in the January backlog."

35.6 Slide 4: before and after

Headline: "A requirement change took weeks. A model change takes hours, reviewed and checked."

The comparison management had asked for, with its honesty built in. The document-era number, 23 working days through the CCB, is labelled notional on the slide, and Jim said why: it is the program's memory of its last document-era cycle, not a measurement. Jim also said what the comparison does not prove: a CCB change crossed several organizations, a merge request crosses one team. The claim Jim made was narrower and true: the government team's part of a change is now measured in hours, and every one is reviewed and checked.

35.7 Slide 5: the demonstration

Headline: "Watch the model catch a mistake."

The demonstration followed the review moves the team had practised since sprint 4: start from the question, show the output and not the tool, make one safe live change, and say what it means. The live change was the same one in every rehearsal: on a scratch branch, never on develop, delete one line that says a part satisfies a requirement, and let the trace check name the requirement that lost its design.

Rehearse it yourself in the sandbox. First, a scratch copy of the integration branch and the deletion:

Then remove the line, commit, and run the trace check the way a merge request pipeline runs it:

The last line of the output is the whole demonstration: "this change adds trace gaps," naming the requirement. In the meeting Jim opened the draft merge request on the projector, the pipeline turned red in about two minutes, and clicked through to the line, then closed the merge request. The program manager's question was the one Jim had hoped for: "And that runs on every change?" It does.

The model site came second: the part tree, the trace report and the data exchange table Tom had generated in sprint 6, all from the same model, all current as of that morning's nightly pipeline.

35.8 Slide 6: next semester, and the ask

Headline: "January: the prime's first new drop. We will show what it changes within a day."

The next milestones in one line each: the prime's drops of January and April, the behavior modeling the converter cannot carry, and the first full baseline in sprint 20. Then the ask, with dates, carried over from the request for enablers of October: approval of a second runner machine, and the GitLab tier decision, both by 15 January. An ask without a date is a hope; an ask with a date is a decision management can make in the room.

35.9 What management asked, and how the numbers answered

The questions came in the order the team had predicted in the rehearsal, with one surprise.

Table 35.1. Questions at the December briefing.
QuestionWho askedThe answer, and its source
"How do I know nothing fell on the floor in the port?"deputy PMthe converter's counts and the trace, every change; the sampled review is next semester (Chapter 34, Proving the port is complete and correct)
"What happens when the prime sends the next version?"program managera vendor branch, a change report, an impact report, and one issue per change for the CCB (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition)
"Is this approved to hold program data?"ISSMthe runner and repository were reviewed in sprints 2 to 5; markings are decided before real content (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system)
"Can I see this without asking you?"program managerthe model site, rebuilt nightly, and the weekly note (Chapter 36, Telling management)

The surprise was the last comment, recorded in the sprint 6 quotes: the program manager's "Keep doing this. Show me the same numbers in March." Jim's reading of it, at the retrospective an hour later, was that the scorecard had become the program's, not the team's.

35.10 What the briefing left out

It left out the tools. Nobody on the slides said "GitLab," "pipeline," "YAML" or "merge request" without a plain translation beside it. It left out the per-person numbers, which read as a ranking. It left out DORA measures and value stream stages, which are for the team's own review (Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics). And it left out the parts of the story that belonged to the team: the night the runner's disk filled up was one line on the scorecard, not a slide.

Exercise 35.1: Rewrite a slide headline

Slide 2's first draft headline was "Our DevSecOps toolchain." Write three alternatives that state a conclusion, and pick the one a program manager would remember.

Exercise 35.2: Rehearse the demo

Run the two demo blocks above in the sandbox, then change the deletion to a verify line instead of a satisfy line. What does the trace check say now, and how would you say it in one sentence to the program manager?

Exercise 35.3: Find your ask

Write the ask for your own first management briefing: one decision, one date, and what happens if it is not made.

35.11 You can now

  • build a management briefing from evidence, with a conclusion as every headline;
  • draft a review script with talk.pl review, then check every number it drafted before you say it;
  • run a safe live demonstration on a scratch branch that shows the checks catching a real mistake;
  • answer the predictable questions with a source for each answer, and close with a dated ask.

35.12 Applying this to your project

Agree the date of the first management briefing before sprint 1, and work backwards: the scorecard it will show, the evidence each number comes from, the demonstration you will rehearse. Keep it to a handful of slides with conclusions as headlines, put the full scorecard in a handout, and rehearse with someone playing the skeptic. Show one thing working live. Say what did not work. End with an ask that has a date.

36 Telling management

From what you know

You know

the weekly status report and the quad chart.

Here it is called

the weekly quad, the sprint mail and the weekly note.

What is new

they are drafted from the journal and GitLab, so writing them takes minutes.

Survival kit: Before you start

What you have

a journal of stories, a GitLab project, and a program manager who will not open either.

What you need

a rhythm of short reports, each built by the system from the same records, so that management sees progress every week and the December briefing is a summary rather than a surprise.

The briefing in Chapter 35, The briefing worked because nothing in it was new to the program manager. Every number on its slides had appeared, a few at a time, in reports that arrived every Friday and every second Friday for twelve weeks. This chapter is about that rhythm: what each report is, what is in it, how it is produced, and how the team learned to write the parts a program cannot produce.

36.1 Three rhythms

Jim agreed three kinds of report with the program manager in week zero (Section 3.10, What management needed to hear, and when):

Table 36.1. The reporting rhythm agreed in week zero.
ReportWhenWhat is in itBuilt from
Weekly note and quadevery Fridayone paragraph of headline, three numbers, risks, asks; the one-page quad behind itthe journal (daily.pl quad), GitLab (talk.pl weekly)
Sprint reviewevery second Fridaywhat was finished, shown live; the four headline numbers; the askGitLab, the journal, the pipeline; the demo script
Program reviewend of sprint 6, then quarterlythe scorecard, before and after, a demonstration, the askeverything above (Chapter 35, The briefing)

The rule behind all three: the system produces the numbers, a person writes the sentences. Nobody types a count into a report.

36.2 The weekly quad

The quad is a one-page weekly status the program already used before Tidewater, in a slide template the team's lab had used for years. The template, Quad Explanation, describes four quadrants under a "Weekly Status" title with the lab's name and an "As of" date. The kit's daily.pl quad produces the same page from the journal. Here is the template's meaning, element by element, and where each element comes from in the kit.

36.2.1 The four quadrants

Table 36.2. The quad's quadrants, the template and the kit.
QuadrantWhat the template says it holdsWhat the kit puts there
Technical Prioritiesthe current sprint backlog: every task, tagged with its statethis sprint's stories from the journal, each with a four-letter word, points and owner
Watch Items / PM Help Neededtasks with a blocker or that could not be completed on time, marked for the program managerblockers older than three days as (PM), fresh blockers, holds, carryovers and unassigned work as (WI)
Schedule Milestonesthe 30-60-90 day backlog: what is due 30, 60 and 90 days out, priority 1 to 3epics whose forecast finish falls in each window, with progress and the forecast date
Accomplishmentsitems from the DONE list, marked on time or latestories done this week, marked on time unless they were ever carried over or reworked

36.2.2 The four-letter words

The Technical Priorities quadrant tags every item with one word, so the program manager can read the state of the sprint at a glance:

Table 36.3. The quad's four-letter words.
WordMeaning in the template
TODOa task that needs to be completed: on the backlog, not started
OPENa task that has begun
DONEa completed task
WAITa task that cannot proceed because of a blocker outside the team
HOLDan open task interrupted by a higher priority
PASS [team]handed to another team, to overcome a blocker or because they can do it better
DROPa task that should not be done after all
REDOdone, but the demonstration showed it was wrong, so it is back in the sprint
PUNTtoo hard as written: back to the backlog to be re-cut
SYNCcoordinated across teams, with a shared DONE

The stand-up verbs map onto them: hold and resume, punt, redo, pass, sync in the stand-up file set the word the quad prints (Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board).

36.2.3 The two SWAT marks

Watch items carry one of two marks, and the difference matters to a program manager:

  • (PM) SWAT: the program manager needs to help remove a blocker. This is an ask.
  • (WI) SWAT: the program manager needs to be aware of an item. This is information.

The kit raises an item to (PM) when a blocker is older than three days or a team is loaded over a hundred and ten percent of its capacity; everything else on the watch list is (WI).

36.2.4 The legend

The template's legend has three groups. Schedule movement: pushed right (a milestone slipped later), pulled left (it moved earlier). Issue level: minor or no issues, significant issues requiring PM awareness, show stopper issues. Trend: improving, degrading, no change. The kit prints the first and third group as marks (->, <-, =, and the sprint progress trend in the header). It does not draw the three issue levels; the (PM) and (WI) marks carry most of that meaning, and a show stopper on a three-person team is a phone call, not a quad entry.

36.2.5 The two metrics

The template's second slide makes the quad do double duty as a metrics report: "Weekly Status satisfies both Metrics."

  • Sprint Progress: the share of the current sprint backlog (the Technical Priorities quadrant) that is done. The kit prints it in the header, with its trend against the previous week.
  • On-Time Delivery of Milestone Products: the share of accomplishments delivered on time, marked with a tick or a cross in the Accomplishments quadrant. The kit prints this week's and this sprint's counts beside it.

36.2.6 Tidewater's quads

The first quad of the project, Friday of sprint 1's first week:

And the last of the twelve weeks:

Read them the way the program manager did. The header gives the two metrics. Technical Priorities shows the sprint; in the first quad, two of its first stories are learning and laptops, which is the learning budget of Bottom line up front showing up where management can see it. The milestones quadrant shows the epics converging. The accomplishments are all ticked. The watch list is empty in both; across the twelve weeks only one item ever reached it, the Stations story carried out of sprint 4, as a (WI).

That empty watch list is worth a second look. In sprint 3 the toolchain review waited three days for the ISSM, and the quad of that Friday does not show it, because the wait began and ended between two Fridays. A weekly snapshot can miss a short block; the daily stand-up record (Chapter 23, Stand-ups, the journal and the board) has it.

You can produce a quad yourself from the Tidewater journal, as of any date:

The numbers will differ from the evidence copy above: the journal now holds the whole sprint, so "as of 18 December" is computed with the later stand-ups in it. The evidence copy is the page Jim actually sent that Friday afternoon. That is a lesson in itself: file the report you sent, not one you can regenerate.

36.3 The weekly note

The quad is the detail. The note is the headline: one paragraph a program manager reads on a phone between meetings. talk.pl weekly drafts it from GitLab, with a conclusion as its first line ("On track," "At risk" or "Needs help"), three numbers, the risks and the asks:

Jim edited every draft before sending it. The risks section of this one lists the discrepancy reports to the prime by age, each on its own line; in the note Jim sent, Jim folded them into one sentence ("our discrepancy reports to the prime, the oldest four weeks old, all due with the January drop") because the program manager reads a list of identical lines as that many separate problems. The draft is a starting point; the sentence is the lead's job (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not).

36.4 The sprint review report

Every second Friday the review notes go to the program manager and the deputy: the sprint goal, what was demonstrated, what carried over, the artifacts shown, any feedback, and the four headline numbers. Sprint 6's review, as filed:

The four headline numbers were the same at every review from sprint 2 on: TODO lines left, verify coverage, open discrepancy reports, blocked items. Keeping them identical was deliberate. By sprint 4 the deputy program manager stopped asking what they meant and started asking why one had changed.

The reviews also recorded the feedback, including the feedback that hurt. Sprint 2's says the deputy did not follow the demo; sprint 4's records the program manager asking whether the model site works on a phone. Both are quoted in Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not, and the change between them is the reason the team rehearses.

36.5 How the reports changed management's questions

In September the program manager's question about the model was "Is it done?" By November it was "Which of these watch items needs me?" By December it was "Show me the same numbers in March." The reports did not just inform management; they changed what management asked for, from a yes or no to a trend. That is the point of a rhythm of small, regular, system-built reports: the conversation moves from whether the team is working to what the work shows.

Exercise 36.1: Read a quad

Open docs/tidewater/sprints/04/quad-2026-11-27.txt. What is the one watch item, what does its mark mean, and what would you expect the program manager to do about it?

Exercise 36.2: Write the note

Run talk.pl weekly for 13 November in the sandbox. Rewrite the draft as the note you would send: one conclusion, three numbers, at most one risk, and an ask if there is one.

Exercise 36.3: Map your own template

If your program already has a weekly status template, map each of its elements to a source the system can fill, as the quadrant table in this chapter does. Which elements have no source, and who writes them?

36.6 You can now

  • read and explain every element of the weekly quad: quadrants, four-letter words, SWAT marks, legend and metrics;
  • produce a quad from the journal and a weekly note from GitLab, and edit the draft into what you send;
  • keep a sprint review report with the same headline numbers every time;
  • explain why a weekly snapshot can miss a short block, and where to look instead.

36.7 Applying this to your project

Use the status template your management already reads, and have the system fill it, rather than inventing a new format they must learn. Agree the rhythm in week zero, and keep the headline numbers identical from report to report. Let the tools draft and let a person write the sentences. File every report you send with the sprint's evidence, so the briefing at the end of the quarter is assembled, not written.

37 Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim

From what you know

You know

the DoD memo: office symbol, MEMORANDUM FOR, numbered paragraphs, signature block.

Here it is called

Markdown memos rendered with md2memo.

What is new

you write the memo in Vim, render it with one command and review it like a model change.

Survival kit

What you have

Vim, a model repository, and a management chain that still runs on signed memoranda.

What you need

a way to write a proper memorandum (office symbol, date, MEMORANDUM FOR, FROM, SUBJECT, numbered paragraphs, signature block, portion markings when required) without leaving Vim, without a word processor template that fights you, and with the memo under review in the repository like any other change. The kit has it: md2memo.pl turns Markdown into a memorandum PDF in pure Perl, and memo-build.pl wraps it for templates.

37.1 Why memos still matter

Everything in the earlier chapters is live: the board, the pipeline, the model site, the stand-up. Management can look at any of it at any time. So why write a memorandum?

Because some things have to be on the record, in the form the organization files and forwards:

  • Requests that need a signature. Training time, hardware, licenses and tool approvals are decided by someone who will forward the request up a chain. A chat message does not travel; a memo does.
  • Decisions that must outlive the people who made them. A memorandum for record (MFR) of why the team chose gitflow, or how the change board dispositioned a prime drop, is what an auditor or a successor reads in three years.
  • Results reported upward. The twelve-week progress memo is what the program manager attached to their own report. The live site is the evidence; the memo is the claim, signed.
  • Correspondence with the prime. Discrepancy reports go to the contractor through the contracting officer, as formal correspondence, not as a GitLab issue the contractor cannot see.

The team's objection, in week two, was that this was the old way coming back in by the side door. Jim's answer was that the memo was now the thin layer: one page that points at evidence the system produces, instead of a forty-page document that was the evidence. Writing it took twenty minutes instead of two days, because every number in it came from the pipeline or talk.pl (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not).

37.2 The format, and how Markdown maps to it

A DoD-style memorandum has a fixed shape. md2memo.pl maps plain Markdown onto it:

Table 37.1. Markdown to memorandum
Memo partMarkdownRendered
Organization (letterhead)# Tidewater Coastal Observation Programcentered, upper case
Office symbol## TW-SEflush left, upper case
Date## 24 December 2026flush left
MEMORANDUM FOR## Memorandum for Tidewater Program Managerupper case
FROM, SUBJECT, REFERENCES## From: ..., ## Subject: ..., ## References: (a) ...; (b) ...upper case
Numbered paragraphseach top-level paragraph1., 2., 3. ...
Subparagraphsa list right after a paragrapha., b., c. (then (1), (a) ...)
Emphasis*word* or **word**underlined
Tablespipe tablesa ruled grid in the PDF, box characters in text
Signature block## JIM then ## Tidewater MBSE Leadupper case, after the last paragraph
Portion marking{CUI}text{/} (and U, C, S, TS with controls)a portion mark in the margin; banners top and bottom

The output is US Letter with one-inch margins, Times 12 by default (--font courier for the typewriter look), as a PDF, PostScript or plain text. Nothing needs installing: it is the same core Perl as the rest of the kit.

37.3 The five templates

Writing a memo from a blank page is how memos get long. The kit ships five templates in tools/gitlab/templates/memos/, and kickoff.pl scaffold copies them into every new model repository as docs/memos/templates/. Each one carries its guidance in comments that never print, and marks every blank as <<placeholder>>.

Table 37.2. The memo templates
TemplateUse it whenThe rule it teaches
memorandum-for-record.mda decision must be on the record: gitflow, a baseline, a waiverstate the decision, the options rejected, and who can change it
request-for-enablers.mdthe team needs time, hardware, licenses or approvalsevery ask has what, why (in management's terms), by when, and what happens if not
progress-memo.mdmanagement needs measured progress: the twelve-week memo, a quarterly memothe outcome in the subject line; the agreed measures in a table; before and after; the ask
drop-disposition.mdthe change board has dispositioned the changes in a prime dropone row per prime change: accept, accept with impact, reject or clarify, no impact
discrepancy-report-transmittal.mddiscrepancy reports go to the prime through the contracting channelcite the prime's own element ids so the contractor can find each one

Here is the start of the request-for-enablers template; the comment block is its instructions, and it does not print:

The rule in that comment is the one that matters: "We're not ready" sounds like foot-dragging; "we need X by date Y, or the trace report slips two weeks" is an engineering position management can act on. It is the same outcome, evidence, ask pattern as the stand-up in Section 25.2, The pattern: outcome, evidence, next or ask, in a more formal register.

37.4 Writing one

37.4.1 From the shell

Start from the template, in the repository's docs/memos/ folder, and ask the build script what is still blank:

--check exits with status 1 while anything is still blank, so it can also run in the pipeline: a memo with a placeholder never reaches develop. Fill in the blanks in Vim (next section), then build it. Here is Jim's finished memo from sprint 2, built from the same template:

The .txt beside the PDF is the same memo as plain text, which is what you paste into an e-mail when the PDF is an attachment, and what git diff can show in review:

Look at what Jim did. The subject line names the outcome ("brief measured results at the December program management review"), not "resources". Paragraph 1 says where the team stands with one number. The asks are a table, because management reads the table first, and each row says what happens if the answer is no. The full memo is in docs/tidewater/memos/, with the four others the team wrote in the twelve weeks and the first prime drop after them.

37.4.2 From Vim

The whole loop stays in Vim. Open the memo, write, and build with one Ex command; % is the current file:

To read the result beside the source, open the text version in a split:

and to find the blanks left in a template, search for the placeholder marker:

n jumps to the next one. When memo-build.pl --check % stops complaining, the memo is ready for review.

If you want md2memo.pl itself (for options such as --font courier or a default marking), call it directly; but it prints the template's instruction comments, so use memo-build.pl for anything that started from a template. Options for md2memo.pl go after --:

37.4.3 Portion marking

Tidewater is notional and unmarked, so the team's memos carry no markings. Your program's memos may need them, and md2memo.pl handles them: tag a portion with {CUI}...{/} (or U, C, S, TS with dissemination controls), and every paragraph gets its portion mark and every page its banner, rolled up from the portions on it. Here is a discrepancy report transmittal with one paragraph tagged, as a demonstration (the CUI label is notional, like everything in Tidewater):

Warning: The tool marks what you tag; it does not decide what is controlled

md2memo.pl applies the markings you put in the text and rolls them up correctly. Deciding what is CUI, export controlled or classified is the security office's job, under your program's classification guide. Agree the rules before the first marked memo, and record them in docs/conventions/markings.md.

37.5 Memos under review, like model changes

The team keeps its memos in the model repository, under docs/memos/, with the date first in the file name so the folder lists them in order. A memo is a change like any other:

  1. Open an issue ("Twelve-week progress memo for the December review"), with the doc::grey label from the document review stages (Chapter 40, Documents still matter: review stages for generated documents).
  2. Write the memo on a feature branch, from the template.
  3. Open a merge request. The reviewers are the people whose numbers are in it: Bob checks the model figures, Tom the pipeline figures.
  4. The pipeline runs memo-build.pl --check on every changed memo, so a placeholder or a missing subject line fails the merge request.
  5. The issue's doc:: label moves through the stages as reviews finish; at doc::white Jim signs and sends the PDF.
  6. Merge. The memo, its PDF and its text are now in the history, next to the model they describe, at the same commit.

That last point is the quiet benefit. A year later, "what did we tell management in December, and what did the model look like when we said it?" is one git log away: the memo and the model share a commit.

37.6 Tidewater's memos

The team wrote five memos in its first four months. All five are in docs/tidewater/memos/ as Markdown, PDF and text.

Table 37.3. The Tidewater memos
DateMemoFromTemplate
24 Sep 2026the directive: adopt DevSecOps practices for systems engineering artifacts (Section 3.1, The memo)the program managernone: it came first
21 Oct 2026request for enablers: training hours, the ISSM slot, a Cameo seat, a second runner, the GitLab tier decisionJim, sprint 2request-for-enablers.md
23 Oct 2026memorandum for record of decisions D-1 to D-10 (Section 13.11, The decisions the team wrote down)Jim, sprint 2memorandum-for-record.md
24 Dec 2026twelve-week results for the December reviewJim, sprint 6progress-memo.md
13 Jan 2027disposition of prime drop v1.1Jim, as chair of the model change boarddrop-disposition.md

37.6.1 The twelve-week progress memo

The most important of the five is the one that told management the twelve weeks worked. Its subject line is a conclusion: Twelve-week results: the Tidewater model is under configuration control and checked on every change. Its second paragraph is the scorecard agreed in week zero (Section 3.6, Defining measurable progress), with the value at the start, the value now and the target, and the source of each number:

The "Now" column is filled from the simulation's sprint 6 evidence (the scorecard and the analytics report), the same numbers the briefing in Chapter 35, The briefing shows. The rest of the memo follows the progress template: one before-and-after paragraph, one honest paragraph about what did not go well and what the team did about it, what the results mean for the next milestone (the January drop), and the ask with a date. It is the written twin of the sprint 6 briefing, and it went to the program manager the day after.

37.6.2 The disposition memo

The drop-2 disposition memo shows the change board's work in the form a contracting officer files: one row per change the prime delivered, the board's disposition, and the issue that tracks each. It also closes DR-1, because drop 2 fixed the TW-SYS-006 wording. Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition explains the disposition process; the memo is its record.

37.7 The progress memo, step by step

Jim wrote the twelve-week memo on the Monday of sprint 6's second week, in about forty minutes, and it went through one review round. The order Jim worked in is the order to copy, because each step uses something the system already produced.

  1. Start from the measures, not the prose. Copy progress-memo.md and fill the measures table first: the "At start" column comes from week zero's scorecard (Section 3.6, Defining measurable progress), the "Now" column from the latest pipeline metrics and talk.pl review (Section 25.4, Tools that draft the words), the "Source" column says where each number lives so a reader can check it. If a number cannot be sourced, it does not go in the table.
  2. Write the subject line as the conclusion the table supports. Not "Twelve-week status", but what the numbers say: "the model is under configuration control and checked on every change". If the table does not support a conclusion you would sign, the memo is not ready, and the conversation with management should happen before the memo, not in it.
  3. Paragraph 1: the most important result, in one sentence with one number. The same rule as the one-sentence rung of the ladder (Section 25.3, The ladder: one sentence, thirty seconds, five minutes).
  4. One before-and-after paragraph. Pick the comparison management will repeat. For Tidewater it was finding the difference between the prime's DOORS text and the model: never done systematically before, now done on every change in under a minute.
  5. One honest paragraph about what did not go well, and what the team did about it. Sprint 3's dip went in, with its two causes and the two fixes. A progress memo with no bad news reads as a sales document, and management discounts it.
  6. What it means for the next milestone. The next thing management cares about (the January drop) and what the team can now do for it.
  7. The ask, with a date, and a reference to where it was first asked. The twelve-week memo repeated two asks from the October request-for-enablers memo that were still open, and cited it.
  8. Attachments that are evidence, not decoration. The briefing and a link to the model site. Not a printout of the pipeline.

Then memo-build.pl --check, a merge request with Bob and Tom as reviewers (Bob checks every model number against the site, Tom every pipeline number against the job logs), and a review in the document stages before Jim signs.

37.8 Which record for what: memo, ADR, issue, wiki

The team found itself with four places to write things down and, for a sprint, wrote some things in all four. The rule they settled on:

Table 37.4. Where to write it down
RecordForAudienceLives inChanges by
Issuework to be done, and the conversation about itthe team, the reviewersGitLabcomments, labels, closing
ADR (architecture decision record)a decision about the model or the toolchain, with context and consequencesengineers now and laterdocs/adr/ in the repositorya new ADR that supersedes it
Memorandum for recorda decision the organization must be able to cite, in its own formatauditors, successors, the program officedocs/memos/ (and the official file)a new memo
Wiki pagehow the team works: the definitions of ready and done, the runbooks, the glossarythe team, newcomersthe GitLab wikiediting, with history
Memo to someonea request, a report, correspondencea named person outside the teamdocs/memos/, then sentnot changed once sent

Some decisions belong in two places. The ten decisions of week zero were written as ADRs, because engineers need the reasoning next to the model, and summarized in one memorandum for record, because the program office needed a document it could cite. The memo points at the ADRs; it does not repeat them.

Tip: One fact, one home

If the same fact appears in an ADR, a memo and the wiki, it will drift. Give each fact one home and point at it from the others. The memo is the thinnest layer: it cites, it does not restate.

37.9 What md2memo cannot express

The tool covers what a working memorandum needs, and the team found its edges quickly. They are worth knowing so you do not fight them:

  • Header lines are upper case. The ## lines become upper case, so a long reference list prints in capitals.
  • The date cannot sit flush right on the office-symbol line. Runs of spaces collapse; the office symbol and the date go on separate lines.
  • The signature block is flush left, not started at the center of the page.
  • Attachments are a small table. A list after the signature would continue the paragraph numbering, so the templates use a two-column table instead.
  • References are one line, not (a) and (b) subparagraphs under the header.
  • Wide tables wrap mid-word in the text output. The PDF measures widths and is fine; the 65-column text version breaks long cell words.
  • Instruction comments print if you call md2memo.pl directly on a template; memo-build.pl strips them first.

If your organization's correspondence manual requires any of the first four exactly, render the PDF and fix the last mile in the office's word processor; keep the Markdown as the reviewed source. Most program offices accepted the output as is.

37.10 Exercises

Exercise 37.1: Ask for what you need

Copy request-for-enablers.md and write the request your team would need to adopt this book's practices: training time, a runner machine, a tool approval, one more. For each ask write what, why in management's terms, by when, and what happens if not. Run memo-build.pl --check until it is silent, then build it.

Exercise 37.2: Record a decision

Pick one decision from Section 13.11, The decisions the team wrote down (or one your team made this month) and write a memorandum for record with the memorandum-for-record.md template: the decision, the options rejected and why, and who can change it. Compare it with the same decision as an ADR in docs/adr/: what does each one do that the other does not?

Exercise 37.3: Build from Vim

Open a memo in Vim, change one paragraph, and rebuild it with :w | !perl $KIT/tools/memo/memo-build.pl %. Open the text version in a vertical split. Then commit the memo on a branch and look at git diff of the .txt: is the change easy to review?

Exercise 37.4: Draft the progress memo from evidence

Using talk.pl weekly and review output for a sprint (Section 25.4, Tools that draft the words), fill in the measures table of progress-memo.md for that sprint. Which numbers came from the pipeline, which from GitLab, and which did you have to supply yourself?

37.11 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the five templates; memos in the repository under docs/memos/, dated file names, reviewed by merge request; memo-build.pl --check in the pipeline; the rule that every number in a memo comes from the system.
  • Adapt: the letterhead, office symbols and signature blocks to your organization's correspondence manual; the marking rules to your security classification guide (write them in docs/conventions/markings.md first).
  • Decide locally: which decisions need an MFR as well as an ADR; who signs which memo; whether the PDF from md2memo.pl goes out as is or through the office's word processor for the last mile.
Note: You can now...
  • write a DoD-style memorandum in Markdown, in Vim, from a template, and render it to PDF and text;
  • find what is still blank with memo-build.pl --check, and keep placeholders out of the repository;
  • tag portions for marking and get the banners rolled up correctly;
  • keep memos under review in the model repository, at the same commit as the model they describe;
  • know where the tool's format stops and the correspondence manual takes over.

38 How the team changed its mind

From what you know

You know

the objections people raise to any new process: some fair, some fear.

Here it is called

the objections, revisited.

What is new

each one is answered with evidence from the twelve weeks, not with a promise.

Survival kit: Where this chapter fits

What you have

twelve weeks of evidence -- stand-up chat, retrospectives, a pulse survey every second Thursday, quotes people did not expect to have written down.

What you need

an honest account of how three skeptical engineers moved from "why can't we just send the Word doc?" to "keep doing this", without pretending the middle was smooth. You also need a way to measure that change on your own team, because management will ask, and because the team deserves to see it.

In Chapter 3, The directive the team raised nine objections in one meeting. They were not excuses. Each one was a real fear held by a person who had been burned before: by a document port that took two years, by a tool nobody else could read, by an approval that never came, by management goals that moved. This chapter takes the objections one at a time, in the order they were raised, and sets beside each one the evidence the twelve weeks produced. Where the evidence does not answer the objection, the chapter says so.

38.1 The pulse, sprint by sprint

At every retrospective each person answered the same five questions, anonymously, on a scale of one (strongly disagree) to five (strongly agree). The questions were chosen in Chapter 3, The directive before any work started, so nobody could tune them to the result.

Table 38.1. The pulse survey's mean, from each sprint's morale.json.
SprintMeanWhat happened that sprint
11.9Learning the tools, the GitLab project, drop 1 received
22.4The first pipeline died on the PowerShell runner; drop 1 reached develop
32.2Bob's first red merge request; three days waiting on the ISSM
43The model site on a phone; the first cycle broken
53.8The trace gate stopped a mistake before it merged
64.1Interim baseline; the management briefing

The shape matters more than the end point. The line rose in sprint 2, fell in sprint 3, and only then climbed. The dip is the most useful number in this chapter. It came in the sprint where the team stopped learning in a sandbox and started being judged by the pipeline on real work -- and in the same sprint, a security approval sat unsigned for three days. If you run this survey on your own team and see a dip in the third or fourth sprint, it does not mean the change is failing. It means the change has become real.

The five questions moved differently. Here are sprint 1 and sprint 6, person by person:

Table 38.2. The five pulse questions, sprint 1 and sprint 6.
QuestionJim, S1Bob, S1Tom, S1Jim, S6Bob, S6Tom, S6
I understand why we are working this way.212544
I can do my work in the new tools without help.222444
The checks catch problems I would have missed.222444
I can see our progress.222444
I would choose to keep working this way.212544

Bob started lowest on the first and last questions -- Bob did not see why, and would not have chosen this. Those are the two that changed most. Nobody's answer reached the top of the scale on "I can do my work in the new tools without help" by sprint 6. That is honest: twelve weeks makes a team competent, not expert, and the book does not claim more.

You can read every answer yourself. The survey files are plain JSON in the evidence:

38.2 The objections, revisited

38.2.1 "We already did this once. Modeling took two years and gave us a spider web."

Bob's objection was the deepest, because it was about the last time. The Cameo port had been sold as the end of document drift; it delivered a model that only three people could open and that nobody trusted.

The evidence is partial, and that is worth saying. The v1 drop arrived with 1 package dependency cycle remaining in the v2 model by sprint 6, against two in drop 1 -- the Network and Operations cycle was broken in sprint 4; the DataCenter and Stations cycle is still there at the end of sprint 6. The worst part definition dropped from fourteen relationship ends in v1 to 8 in v2. Tom's reaction to the first cycle break, in sprint 4:

The cycle was two lines. In Cameo it was a week of looking at a diagram.

— Tom, 24 November 2026

The measurement is in Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web. What changed Bob's mind was not the numbers, though. It was that the complexity was visible on every change instead of discovered at a review. A spider web grows one innocent link at a time; a check that runs on every merge request stops the innocent link.

38.2.2 "Why can't we just do systems engineering the old way?"

Tom asked it; Bob said it out loud on the first morning:

Why can't we just send the Word doc? It worked for twenty years.

— Bob, 5 October 2026

The answer in Chapter 3, The directive was that nothing changes what a requirement or a baseline is; what changes is how the team keeps them. The evidence for that answer came three days later, from Bob:

I found the drift in two minutes. It used to take a week, and we only looked before a review.

— Bob, 8 October 2026

That sentence was the first time anyone on the team compared the new way to the old way in a unit they cared about. It was also the first number in the scorecard (Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard): the trace answers in 24 seconds what the document era answered in 2 days (notional, from the program's last document-era review cycle).

38.2.3 "We're systems engineers, not programmers."

Nobody wrote a program in twelve weeks. They edited text files in Vim, which all three already used, and typed git commands they learned in an afternoon (Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers). Bob's verdict after that afternoon:

Spent the afternoon in the practice repo. Branch, commit, merge. It is configuration management with fewer forms.

— Bob, 6 October 2026

The harder moment came in the third sprint, when the pipeline said no to Bob for the first time:

A red X on my own MR. One missing word, and the machine found it before Jim did.

— Bob, 4 November 2026

That quote is from the dip sprint, and it is not a happy one. It became one of the reasons the pulse rose afterwards: the red X was private, immediate and fixable, which a red-pen review two weeks later never was.

38.2.4 "The contractor owns the model. Anything we do is a copy that will go stale."

This objection is only partly answered by the first twelve weeks, because only one prime drop arrived in them. What the twelve weeks proved is the mechanism: drop 1 came in on the vendor branch (Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated), the government's own edits sat beside it without being overwritten, and every gap the government found went back to the prime as a discrepancy report -- 7 of them by the end of sprint 6, none closed yet, because the prime closes them in later drops. Whether the copy stays current is answered by the drops in Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition, not by this chapter.

38.2.5 "Nobody outside our team will be able to read SysML v2 text."

Jim raised it as devil's advocate. The answer turned out to be that nobody outside the team needed to read the text: they read the model site the pipeline publishes. The program manager's reaction in the sprint 4 review:

I can open this on my phone? I have never seen the model without a briefing.

— Program manager, 20 November 2026

Fewer people could read the Cameo model, which needed a licence. More people read the v2 model than ever read the v1 one, because it was a web page.

38.2.6 "The ISSM will never approve this in time."

Tom was half right, and the evidence shows it. The toolchain review did slow the team down:

Three days waiting on a signature. The pipeline was the fast part.

— Tom, 10 November 2026

That wait is part of the sprint 3 dip. The lesson the team drew, recorded in the sprint 3 retrospective, was to stop "waiting for the ISSM without a date" -- to ask for a date, and to keep working on what did not need the approval. The approval came. The objection was right about the delay and wrong about the outcome.

38.2.7 "We'll spend twelve weeks learning tools and have nothing to show."

The BLUF (Bottom line up front) answers this with the time split: learning and platform work fell from most of sprint 1 to a small share of sprint 6. The scorecard answers it with results: TODO lines from the conversion fell to 5, every change in sprint 6 was gated (7 of 7), and an interim baseline was tagged and reproduced (1). There was something to show from sprint 2 onward; the problem in sprint 2 was that the team showed it badly (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not).

38.2.8 "Management will just move the goalposts."

Tom said this quietly, at the end of the meeting. The defense was the scorecard, agreed in writing in week one. At the sprint 6 review the program manager did not move the goalposts; they asked for the same ones again:

Keep doing this. Show me the same numbers in March.

— Program manager, 24 December 2026

38.2.9 "In three years there'll be another directive."

Probably true, and the twelve weeks cannot disprove it. What the team kept from them is not a tool but a habit: the system's description as reviewed text under configuration control, with checks that run on every change. The text is in an open standard, the checks are scripts the team owns, and the history is in git. Whatever the next directive brings, it starts from a model that can be read, diffed and converted -- which the v1 model could not.

38.3 What actually changed minds

Reading the quotes in order, three things recur:

  • A number in a unit the engineer cared about. "Two minutes, it used to take a week." Not a dashboard, not a velocity chart -- a comparison to their own experience.
  • A mistake caught privately and early. The red X on Bob's merge request, the trace gate that stopped Bob deleting a satisfy Bob thought was a duplicate (sprint 5). Being stopped by a machine before a colleague saw the mistake built trust in the checks faster than any explanation.
  • Being seen by management without a briefing. The program manager on the phone; Jim answering the deputy PM's trace question with a link instead of a week of slides:

The deputy PM asked for the trace numbers. I sent a link.

— Jim, 9 December 2026

What did not change minds: being told the new way was better, the GitLab feature list, and the sprint 2 demo, which showed the terminal instead of the answer. Management's feedback on that demo was blunt -- "I did not follow the demo. What did we get for the two weeks?" -- and it is in the evidence too.

Exercise 38.1: Run the pulse on your own team

Take the five questions above. Ask them at your next three retrospectives, anonymously, on a one-to-five scale. Plot the mean. Before you look at the result, write down which sprint you expect the dip in, and why.

Exercise 38.2: Write your team's objections down

In your kickoff meeting, write every objection on the whiteboard in the speaker's words, with the speaker's name if they agree. Put the list in the wiki. At the end of each sprint, add the evidence for or against each one. Which objections are still unanswered after six sprints?

38.4 You can now

  • Measure a team's change of mind with a short, fixed pulse survey and read its shape, not just its end point.
  • Answer an old-way objection with evidence from your own project instead of argument.
  • Recognize the third-sprint dip as a sign the change has become real.

38.5 Applying this to your project

Copy the five questions and the habit of writing objections down in the speaker's words. Adapt the scale and the timing to your retrospectives. Decide locally whether the survey is anonymous (Tidewater's was) and who sees the raw answers. Do not promise management a rising line; promise them the measurement, and explain the dip in advance.

39 A day in the life, week twelve

From what you know

You know

an ordinary day in the Cameo years: e-mail, meetings, screenshots, a briefing to update.

Here it is called

Bob's day in week twelve.

What is new

the day goes to engineering, and the machinery does the bookkeeping.

Survival kit: Where this chapter fits

What you have

Bob's Thursday, 17 December 2026 -- the second-to-last week of the twelve -- exactly as GitLab and the stand-up chat recorded it.

What you need

a concrete picture of what the work feels like once the tools are learned, beside the same kind of day three years earlier in the Cameo era. Managers ask "what does a normal day look like now?" This is the answer.

Nothing on this day was staged for the book. It is an ordinary working day in sprint 6, chosen because it has most of what a small model team meets in practice: a failed overnight check, a change that the pipeline sends back, a review that requests changes, a merge that is refused until a discussion is resolved, and the next morning a secret that nearly got into the repository. Every time below is Eastern time, as GitLab recorded it.

39.1 09:00 -- the stand-up, and the night's failure

The first thing Bob saw was not an email. It was the GitLab To-Do list and the board: the scheduled "Nightly full check" pipeline from 02:00 had failed, in every job, before any check ran. Bob opened an issue for it at 09:15, labelled it, and linked the failing job:

The failure was not in the model. The runner -- the Windows machine that runs the team's pipeline -- had filled its disk with old build directories. At the stand-up it took one sentence to hand over ("Tom, the nightly died on disk space, #132"), and Tom had it cleared and re-run by 10:30. In the Cameo era the equivalent -- a tool failing overnight -- would have been discovered when someone opened the model and it would not load.

The stand-up itself was three lines in the meeting chat, drafted with talk.pl and edited before posting (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not):

You can open the issue Bob filed in the simulation's GitLab:

39.2 10:00 -- a draft that the pipeline sends back

Bob's own work that week was the hand-written flows in the ObserveCoast activity: the fork, the pin, the object and control flows that the converter could not carry from v1 (Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook). Bob opened merge request !23 as a draft at 10:00 -- a draft is a merge request that says "look, but do not merge yet" -- and the pipeline ran on it straight away. It failed. The grammar, lint and outline checks were green; the trace check was red:

Bob had tidied a doc comment on requirement TW-SYS-007 while in the file, and the new wording no longer matched DOORS. The trace job compares the model's requirement text with the DOORS export on every change; a new difference fails the merge request (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). The old difference, TW-SYS-006, is the prime's and is tracked as a discrepancy report, so it does not fail anything. Bob put the wording back, pushed, and the next pipeline (#87) was green. Bob marked the draft ready at noon. In the Cameo era a reworded requirement in the model would have been found -- if at all -- at the next DOORS synchronisation, weeks later, by someone else.

39.3 14:05 -- reviewing Tom's change

At 14:05 Bob's To-Do list showed one item: Tom had asked Bob to review !24, "Document what crosses each interface". Bob did not read the raw text diff alone. Bob read the generated documentation the pipeline attached, then went to the line that looked wrong and left a line comment with a suggestion -- a proposed replacement the author can apply with one click -- and requested changes:

The comment is the review culture the team built in Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change: it names the problem ("late" assumes a schedule nobody wrote down), cites the requirement, and offers a concrete fix that keeps the uncertainty visible as an assumption to confirm with the prime.

At 14:20 Tom tried to merge. GitLab refused: the project requires every discussion on a merge request to be resolved first (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab), and Bob's thread was open. Tom applied the suggestion; Bob resolved the thread at 14:50 and approved; Jim, as the code owner for interfaces, had already approved; Tom merged at 15:10. The same click closed task #123, because the merge request description said "Closes #123".

The merge request's page shows its checks as GitLab's widgets would:

One rough edge is visible there, and the book does not hide it: the test widget lists the requirement gaps the government has already reported to the prime as failed tests, even though the pipeline is green, because the trace report marks every gap, old or new, as a failure. The pipeline itself only fails on new gaps. Until the report is changed to mark inherited gaps as skipped, read the widget's "failed" count together with the trace job's verdict line.

39.4 15:30 -- the day closes

Bob merged !23 at 15:30, which closed Bob's task #121. By the end of the day both changes were on develop, both had passed their checks on the merge request, both had been reviewed and approved by someone other than the author, and the board, the burn-down and the model site all showed it without anyone writing a status report. The nightly schedule would run the full check again at 02:00.

Six things happened before lunch and I knew about every one of them from GitLab, not from email.

— Bob, 17 December 2026

The next morning, Friday, Tom's merge request !25 failed a different check: the secrets scan found a test access token pasted into a helper script. By 11:30 it was fixed: revoke the token, issue a new one as a masked CI/CD variable, and rewrite the branch so the token never reached develop (Appendix E, Rescue: when something goes wrong). The sprint 6 retrospective's "stop" list has one line that came from that morning: "Pasting tokens into scripts, even test ones."

39.5 The same Thursday, 2023, the Cameo way (notional)

Note: This half is notional

Nothing below comes from the simulation. It is a composite of how the team described their Cameo-era days in Chapter 2, The Cameo years, written as one day so it can be compared. Treat the times as typical, not measured.

Table 39.1. One Thursday, three years apart. The left column is notional; the right column is the evidence above.
TimeDecember 2023, Cameo and documentsDecember 2026, GitLab and SysML v2
08:30Email from the prime: the model export for the review will be late.GitLab To-Do: the nightly check failed; an issue is open by 09:15.
09:00Status meeting, forty minutes, everyone reads their slide.Stand-up, fifteen minutes, three lines in chat, drafted from GitLab.
10:00Bob checks out a Cameo project lock; Tom has it, Bob waits.Bob opens a draft merge request; the pipeline runs on it in minutes.
11:00Bob edits the activity diagram; layout takes most of the hour.The pipeline finds a reworded requirement before anyone else sees it.
13:00Screenshots pasted into a review briefing, slide by slide.Bob reads Tom's change in the generated docs and leaves a line comment.
14:30The review comments come back as a marked-up PDF.The comment is a suggestion Tom applies with one click.
15:30Someone asks which requirements are unverified; "I'll get back to you".The trace answer is on the model site, current as of the last merge.
16:30A requirement changed in DOORS last month; nobody noticed.Every DOORS difference is checked on every change.

The point of the comparison is not that the old day was lazy. The engineers worked as hard in 2023. The difference is where the effort went: in 2023 most of it went into moving information between tools and people by hand, and the checks happened at reviews, weeks later. In 2026 the moving and checking are done by the pipeline on every change, and the people spend their day on the model and on each other's work.

Exercise 39.1: Write your own two-column day
