Pick one ordinary day from last month. Write what you did, hour by hour, in the left column. In the right column write what the same work would look like with a merge request, a pipeline and a model site. Which rows would change most? Which would not change at all?

39.6 You can now

  • Describe a normal working day in a GitLab model team, hour by hour, with the evidence a manager can check.
  • Explain why a draft merge request that fails its pipeline is good news, not bad.
  • Read a merge request's widgets and know which numbers are new problems and which are inherited ones.

39.7 Applying this to your project

Copy the shape: a To-Do list instead of email, a nightly full check, draft merge requests, required discussion resolution, suggestions in reviews. Adapt the times to your team's hours and your stand-up. Decide locally whether a nightly failure is picked up at the stand-up (Tidewater) or by whoever is on call that week.

40 Documents still matter: review stages for generated documents

From what you know

You know

color-team reviews and document maturity grades.

Here it is called

review stages for generated documents, as doc:: labels.

What is new

some of the criteria are checked by the pipeline, so a grade means something before the reviewers open the document.

Survival kit: Where this chapter fits

What you have

a model that generates most of what used to be hand-written -- the data exchange table, the trace report, the verification matrix -- and a handful of documents that are still written by people: the briefing memo, the request for enablers, the drop disposition.

What you need

a shared, simple way to say how finished a document is, that management already understands, and a clear line between what the pipeline can check and what still needs a human reader.

A model does not abolish documents. Management still reads memos; the customer still receives deliverables; the prime still gets formal letters. What changes is that most of a document's content now comes from the model and is regenerated on every change, so the question "is this document ready?" splits in two. Part of the answer is mechanical and the pipeline can give it. Part of it is judgment, and only a reviewer can.

The team kept the document maturity scale the program already used: the Document Review Stages chart, a colour and a grade for each stage of a document's life. Everyone on the program knew it, and the point of this chapter is that the team did not invent a new vocabulary for documents just because the model moved to GitLab.

40.1 The scale

Table 40.1. The Document Review Stages, from the program's grading chart.
ColourStageGradesPercent completeWhat it means
(none)TODO--0The document is in the queue.
GreyCollectionG-, G, G+1 to 24A loose collection of content has been started.
BlueCompliantF-, F, F+25 to 45The outline is complete.
PinkCompleteD-, D, D+46 to 63The content is stable and consistent.
RedCompellingC-, C, C+64 to 78Graphics, tables, data, spelling, acronyms and grammar are finalized.
GoldComprehensiveB-, B, B+79 to 90The document is sound, coherent and actionable.
WhiteCopy ReadyA-, A, A+91 to 99It is ready for hard-copy review.
GreenDone--100It is releasable.
Note: Two versions of the chart

The deck the program circulates has two slides. The first (above) gives the full grading scale. The second gives shorter descriptions with different percentage bands -- for example, it calls Pink 45 to 75 percent and uses Green for "analysis underway" and White for "done". This book follows the first slide, which is the more detailed one. If your program uses the chart, agree which slide governs before the first document is graded.

40.2 The stages as GitLab labels

A document that people write is tracked by an issue, the same as any other piece of work. Its stage is a scoped label -- doc::grey, doc::blue and so on -- and because the labels are scoped, an issue can carry only one of them at a time: moving a document to Pink removes Blue automatically. The labels are defined in the project file (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab); the document's source lives in the repository, and each change to it goes through a merge request like a model change.

Warning: The label descriptions in the template do not match the chart

The project file template (tools/gitlab/templates/project.conf) describes the doc:: labels in proposal colour-team terms -- for example, Red as "the reader's view, scored as the customer would score it". The program's chart above describes Red as "graphics, tables, data, spelling, acronyms and grammar are finalized". When you adopt the labels, copy the descriptions from the chart your program uses, so the label tooltip in GitLab and the chart on the wall say the same thing.

40.3 Sprint 6: two documents through the stages

In sprint 6 the team produced two documents for the program review: the twelve-week progress memo (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim) and the data exchange table, which is generated from the model's interface definitions. Each had an issue, and Jim moved each issue through the stages as reviews finished. You can read the history in the simulation's GitLab:

Both documents went from Grey on 16 December to Green on 24 December, the day of the review. The simulation moves them one stage per working day; real documents usually spend longer in Pink and Gold, where the arguments happen. What matters is not the speed but that the stage is visible on the board, dated, and attributed: anyone could see on Monday that the memo was still Red and the table was already Gold.

40.4 What the pipeline can check, and what it cannot

The stages were written for hand-made documents, where every one of them was a human judgment. For a document built from a model, several of them become checks that run on every change. The line between the two is the useful thing to agree on.

Table 40.2. Mechanical checks and human judgment, stage by stage.
StageWhat the pipeline can checkWhat still needs a person
GreyThe file exists in the repository; it renders.Whether this is the right document to write.
BlueEvery required heading is present; required header fields (for a memo: Memorandum for, From, Subject).Whether the outline answers the reader's question.
PinkNo placeholders left; every number cited from evidence, not typed; no TODO markers.Whether the content is consistent in meaning, not just in form.
RedGenerated tables are current (the docs job); figures render; banner and portion markings present.Spelling and grammar in the prose; whether the graphics say what the text says.
GoldNothing new.Whether it is sound, coherent and actionable -- the management review.
WhiteThe PDF builds cleanly; the marking rolls up correctly.A last read on paper.
GreenThe release or merge is recorded; the issue is closed.The decision to release.

The memo tool shows the Pink line directly. Run its check on a fresh copy of the progress memo template, before anyone fills it in:

A memo that still has placeholders cannot be Pink, whatever its author feels. That is the kind of rule the pipeline is good at. Whether the memo's ask is the right ask is not.

For generated documents the mechanical part is even larger. The data exchange table is rebuilt from the model on every merge request, and the docs job fails if the committed copy is stale (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). So the table can never be "Red" in the sense of out-of-date data: if the data were stale, the merge request would not merge. What review adds for a generated table is the reader's question -- does this table say what the interface owners need to know? -- and that question belongs in Gold.

Exercise 40.1: Grade a document both ways

Take a document your team is writing now. Grade it on the chart by hand. Then list which of the "pipeline can check" items in the table above it would pass today. Where the two disagree, which one is right?

40.5 You can now

  • Track a document's maturity on the board with scoped labels, using the stages the program already knows.
  • Separate the mechanical part of a document review from the judgment part, and automate the mechanical part.
  • Explain to management why a generated table cannot be "out of date" once it is checked on every merge request.

40.6 Applying this to your project

Copy the idea of one scoped label per stage and of moving a document's issue as reviews finish. Use your own program's stage names, colours and descriptions -- if your program has no chart, the proposal colour-team names in the kit's template are a reasonable start. Decide locally which slide or version of a chart governs, and who is allowed to move a document to Gold and to Green.

41 For the lead: leading a reluctant team

From what you know

You know

leading engineers through a schedule crunch.

Here it is called

leading a reluctant team through a change of method.

What is new

learning time is protected explicitly, and small wins are made visible.

Survival kit

What you have

a directive you did not ask for, a deadline, two or more good engineers who did not ask for it either, and the same lack of experience they have.

What you need

a way to lead the change without pretending to know more than you do: a team that feels safe to be slow and wrong for a few weeks, protected time to learn, early wins that are real, a workload that does not quietly become nights and weekends, and a management chain that hears dated plans instead of excuses. This chapter is Jim's view of the twelve weeks, written for whoever is in Jim's chair on the next project.

41.1 What Jim was handed

The directive arrived on a Thursday (Section 3.1, The memo). By the following Tuesday Jim had read it four times, sat through the program manager's explanation, and come out with three facts. The program would adopt DevSecOps practices for its systems engineering artifacts. The team would show measurable progress in twelve weeks. And nobody on the team, including Jim, had ever done any of it.

The team's reaction was not subtle.

We did documents for twenty years and the system flew. Then they made us do Cameo, and we did it, and now the model is a hairball nobody can review. Now this. What happens in three years when the next thing comes along?

— Bob, the first team meeting about the directive

Jim's private reaction was close to Bob's. What made the difference over the next twelve weeks was not that Jim became an expert first. It was a handful of decisions about how to lead three beginners, one of them Jim, through a change none of them had chosen. Each is a section of this chapter.

41.2 Make it safe to be slow and wrong

For the first month, everyone on the team would be worse at their job than they had been for years. Bob, who could find any block in the Cameo model blindfolded, would spend twenty minutes on a merge conflict. Tom, who had run the program's CM database for a decade, would push to the wrong branch. Jim would forget the command to create a branch in front of the program manager. That is not a risk to manage; it is a certainty to plan for.

Psychological safety, for a team of three systems engineers, comes down to a few concrete habits:

  • A red pipeline is information, not an accusation. The pipeline will fail on everyone's changes, often, and most of all in the first weeks. The team agreed, in the first retro, that nobody says "who broke it" in the stand-up; they say "what did it catch". The pipeline's job is to be wrong-detector; a failure means it worked.
  • The lead goes first. At the sprint 1 kickoff Jim did practice lesson 11 live, on the shared screen, with the whole team watching, including the lesson's planted mistake: the merge request goes red on a missing semicolon. Jim read the log out loud, found the line with the quickfix list in Vim (Section 10.6, Checking from Vim), fixed it and pushed again. It took six minutes. Nobody remembers the semicolon; everybody remembers that the lead's change went red first and that it was fine.
  • "I don't know yet" is an acceptable answer with a date attached (Section 25.7, Bad news, said so it builds trust). The lead says it out loud in front of management, early, so the team learns that it is safe.
  • No question is a nuisance during pairing. The rule the team wrote on the wiki: "If you have been stuck for fifteen minutes, ask. If someone asks you, stop and help." Fifteen minutes is short enough that nobody suffers in silence and long enough that people try first.
  • Complaints are heard, then turned into changes. The retrospective is where "this is pointless" gets said, and Jim's rule was to answer a complaint with one of three things: a change for next sprint, an explanation of why not, or "I'll ask management", with a date.
  • Measure how people feel, not only what they ship. The pulse survey at every retro (Section 24.7, The retrospective) is five questions, one to five, anonymous. It costs two minutes and it is the only early warning the lead gets.
Case study: The semicolon

Jim nearly did not share the screen for that lesson. The plan had been to rehearse it the night before, so the demonstration would go smoothly. Jim decided against it: the team needed to see a failure handled, not a performance. In the sprint 1 retrospective, Tom wrote on the "continue" list: "Jim breaking things first."

41.3 Protect the time to learn

The most important decision Jim made was to put learning into the plan as work, with points, where everyone could see it.

The temptation is the opposite. Management wants measurable progress in twelve weeks; every hour spent on a practice lesson is an hour not spent closing TODO lines. So the learning happens "on the side": at lunch, after hours, at weekends. It always does happen, because the work cannot be done without it. But then the plan is a lie (the team's capacity looks bigger than it is), the people doing the learning resent it, and the first time the schedule slips, the learning is what gets cut.

Tidewater's plan carries learning as stories, labelled work::learning, with a reserve that falls as the team gets better: 24% of the task points done in sprint 1 (practice lessons 10 and 11, the survival kit, git from zero, Vim for models), less in sprint 2 (lessons 12 and 13, the diagrams chapter, the first half of the SysML v2 workbook), and a small remainder by sprint 6. Part III gives the real numbers for each sprint.

Making learning visible takes one label. In GitLab, a learning story looks like any other (here in the work folder of practice lesson 11's sandbox):

Three things follow from making it visible:

  1. The plan is honest. Velocity in sprint 1 is low, and everybody knows why. When the program manager asked in the first review why only part of the conversion was done, Jim pointed at the learning stories: "That is the training you approved, in the plan where you can see it."
  2. The learning is protected. A story on the board is harder to cut than an evening nobody sees. Jim asked for it formally in the request-for-enablers memo (Section 37.6, Tidewater's memos): four protected hours a week per person, with what happens if not ("the conversion burn-down slows by about a third").
  3. The shrinking reserve is itself a result. The scorecard shows learning time falling as competence rises. Management reads that as the investment paying off, which it is.
Tip: The lead learns first

Jim did practice lessons 10 and 11 in week zero, before the team, alone, and got stuck twice. That made the first pairing sessions easier: Jim could say "I got stuck there too; here is what helped." A lead who has not done the lessons can only say "it's in the book".

41.4 Pair at the terminal

Pairing is two people at one keyboard: a driver who types and a navigator who reads, thinks ahead and catches mistakes. They swap every twenty minutes or so. For a team learning a new toolset together it is the fastest way to spread skill, because the person who knows a thing teaches it while doing real work.

Tidewater's pairing in the twelve weeks:

Table 41.1. Who paired with whom
WhenPairOn
Sprint 1Tom drives, Bob navigatesthe first git commands in the practice repository: branch, commit, push
Sprint 1Bob drives, Jim navigatesthe first conversion report and the TODO inventory
Sprint 2Tom drives, Jim navigatesthe first pipeline, and the PowerShell failure on the real runner
Sprint 2Tom drives, Bob navigatesthe first vendor-branch import; Bob then reviews and merges its merge request
Sprint 3Jim drives, Bob navigatesthe DOORS import and the first trace report
Sprint 4 onwardas neededconflicts, new job types, the first release

Two lessons from that table. First, the person who knows less drives. When Tom drove the first git commands with Bob navigating, Tom learned git and Bob learned how to explain it, which is the step where Bob's own understanding became solid. Second, the lead pairs too, as navigator and as driver. Jim at the keyboard with Bob navigating was the moment Bob stopped treating the new tools as Jim's project and started treating them as the team's.

Pairing feels slow. Two people on one task looks like half the throughput. In the first weeks it is the opposite: two beginners together get unstuck in minutes, where one alone loses an afternoon. The team stopped pairing by default in sprint 4, when it was no longer needed for routine work, and kept it for anything new.

41.5 Pick the first wins on purpose

A discouraged team needs evidence, early, that the new way does something the old way could not. The lead's job is to make sure the first wins are real, are noticed and are the team's.

Jim chose the first win before sprint 1 started: run the trace report on drop 1 and look for places where the prime's DOORS text and the model disagreed. In the document era that comparison was done once before a major review, by hand, over a week, if at all. Bob ran it on the fourth day of sprint 1, from the command line, and found the TW-SYS-006 drift in about two minutes.

I found the drift in two minutes. It used to take a week, and we only looked before a review.

— Bob, sprint 1, day 4 (from the team chat)

That sentence did more for the transition than anything Jim said in twelve weeks, because Bob said it, about Bob's own work.

The pattern for choosing first wins:

  • It answers a question the old way could not answer cheaply. Drift between DOORS and the model; requirements with no verification; which packages depend on each other in a cycle.
  • The skeptic does it. A win the lead announces is a claim. A win the skeptic discovers is evidence.
  • It takes days, not weeks. The first win had to land in sprint 1. The model site for management (sprint 4) was a bigger win, but it would have been too late to be the first one.
  • It is shown, not told. Jim asked Bob to show the drift in the sprint 1 demo, live, on the command line.

And then the lead makes sure the win is noticed: in the stand-up ("Bob found the drift in two minutes"), in the demo (Bob shows it), in the weekly note to management, and in the retro ("what worked this sprint?").

41.6 Watch the workload

A team learning a new way of working while delivering under a deadline is a team at risk of quiet overwork. Nobody announces it. The signs are small: statuses posted at 6 a.m., merge requests opened at 9 p.m., a stand-up line that says "Y caught up on the vendor merge" on a Monday after a weekend.

Jim's routine for watching it took ten minutes a day:

  1. Read the stand-up statuses for time stamps, not just content. Work after hours shows in the chat times and in the merge request times.
  2. Check blocked items daily, because a blocked person often works around the block alone, late. A blocked item that is three days old is the lead's problem, not the engineer's (Section 24.2, The daily stand-up: terse, written, linted).
  3. Commit below capacity. The team committed about nine-tenths of capacity in each sprint, never all of it; the remainder absorbs the surprises (a prime question, an ISSM review that moves) that always come.
  4. Look at the pulse survey's workload question at every retro. A drop of one point is a conversation, not a statistic.

The blocked-items check is one command. Here a blocked task is added to the practice project, then listed:

When Jim saw the signs, in sprint 3, the response was not "work smarter". It was to drop scope: one story moved to the next sprint, explicitly, with a note in the weekly report to management saying why.

41.7 Manage up with dated plans

The lead stands between the team and the management chain that issued the directive. Done badly, the lead passes pressure down and excuses up. Done well, the lead passes plans up and protection down.

What worked for Jim:

  • Agree the measures before the work starts. In week zero, Jim and the program manager agreed the twelve-week scorecard (Section 3.6, Defining measurable progress): which numbers would show progress, where they started, what the targets were. Every report after that was against an agreed yardstick, so nobody could move the goalposts and nobody could claim success by picking flattering numbers.
  • Report the same numbers every week, in the same order (Section 25.6, Demos that land), in a one-page note that pairs with the kit's weekly quad. Management learns to read the trend and stops asking for special reports.
  • Ask for enablers formally, with dates and consequences. The request-for-enablers memo of sprint 2 (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim) turned "we need more time" into five specific asks, each with what it buys, by when, and what happens if not. What management approved, and when, is told in Chapter 27, Sprint 2: Drop 1 on develop, every change gated and Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named; an ask that is not approved becomes a known risk, on the record, rather than a surprise.
  • Bring management to the demo, not the demo to management. The program manager attended sprint reviews from sprint 2 onward. Seeing the merge request go green, live, did more than any slide.
  • Never surprise them. Bad news went into the next weekly note or the next stand-up summary, the week it was known, with a date for the fix (Section 25.7, Bad news, said so it builds trust).
Objection: "Management just wants the slide with green on it."

Some managers do. But a directive that says "show measurable progress" is a manager asking to be given something they can defend upward. The weekly note with four numbers, a trend and a dated plan is that thing.

Answer

Give them the numbers in the form they forward. The Tidewater program manager attached Jim's weekly notes to the program's own monthly report unchanged by sprint 4. That is when the slide requests stopped.

41.8 Say no with a date

The lead's most frequent hard conversation is not with the team. It is with a manager or stakeholder who wants something now that is not in the sprint: a special report, a slide, "just a quick change to the model" before a meeting.

Saying yes to every request breaks the sprint and teaches everyone that the plan does not matter. Saying a flat no sounds like obstruction. The middle is no, with a date:

Table 41.2. No, with a date
RequestSay
"Can you add the thermal interfaces to the model before Thursday's review?""Not this sprint: it's not in the plan and it would push the Stations work. It goes to refinement on Wednesday; the earliest it lands is sprint 5. For Thursday I can show you where it will go."
"I need a one-off report of every requirement the prime changed.""The delta report does that on every drop. The next one is in January; I'll send you its summary the day after it lands."
"Just update the briefing slide with the new numbers.""The model site is updated every night with the numbers; here's the link. If you need a slide, the weekly note has them in the order you used last time."
"Can Bob help the other program for a week?""Not without moving the conversion: Bob owns the Stations package this sprint. If it's urgent, I'll put it to you as a trade: Bob for a week, Stations moves to sprint 5. Your call."

Each answer has the same parts: what you will not do now, why (in the requester's terms), when it could happen, and often what you can offer today. The last row is the most useful form of all: turn the request into a trade and give the decision back to the person who has the authority to make it.

The deputy program manager, who chairs the change board, made exactly this kind of request in sprint 4 (a change to a requirement before the board had seen it). Jim's answer was to open a merge request for it, so the board could approve it in the normal flow the same week. That became the team's standard answer to "just a quick change": a merge request is quick, and it is on the record.

41.9 Know when to slow down

There will be a sprint where it goes wrong. For Tidewater it was sprint 3: Bob's hand edit broke the grammar check on a merge request, the ISSM was unreachable for three days and the toolchain review stalled, and the pulse survey dropped for the first time. Bob wrote "this is the Cameo year again" in the retro.

The signs that the team needs to slow down, not push harder:

  • The pulse survey drops, especially on "I could explain our progress" or "my workload is sustainable".
  • Stand-up statuses get shorter and vaguer ("Y stuff T stuff B none"), or stop naming outcomes.
  • A red pipeline stays red for a day and nobody mentions it in the stand-up.
  • Merge requests get bigger, because people stopped believing in small ones.
  • Someone asks, for the first time, whether they could "just do it the old way this once".

What Jim did in sprint 3, and what the book recommends:

  1. Name it, out loud, in the retro. "This sprint was hard. The numbers show it, and so do you." Pretending it was fine would have cost the trust earned in sprints 1 and 2.
  2. Cut scope, not learning. One engineering story moved to sprint 4. The learning reserve stayed.
  3. Remove the cause, not the symptom. The ISSM block was the real problem; Jim booked the ISSM's next two review slots two weeks ahead, so it could not happen again. The grammar failure was fine: the pipeline caught it before it reached anyone else, which is its job, and Jim said so.
  4. Pause new tools. No new pipeline job or GitLab feature was introduced in sprint 4 beyond what was already planned. A team that is struggling does not need one more thing to learn.
  5. Tell management the same week, as a dated plan: "Sprint 3 delivered less than planned for two reasons; here is what changes in sprint 4; the twelve-week targets still hold."

Sprint 4's pulse recovered. Slowing down is not losing; it is how the twelve weeks stay twelve weeks and do not become a year of burnout.

41.10 Hand over ownership, on purpose

In week zero, the transition was Jim's project: Jim got the directive, Jim set up the meetings, Jim talked to management. By the end of the twelve weeks it had to be the team's way of working, or it would stop the day Jim went on leave. That does not happen by itself; the lead has to give things away, one at a time, and let them be done differently.

What Jim handed over, and when:

Table 41.3. What the lead gave away
WhenWhatToHow Jim let go
Sprint 1the pipelineTomTom chose the jobs and their order; Jim reviewed but did not redesign
Sprint 2the vendor-branch import of each prime dropTom, with Bob reviewingthe drop runbook became Tom's wiki page
Sprint 3security owner, with the ISSMTomTom ran the ISSM meetings; Jim attended the first only
Sprint 4the Stations package and its code-owner sectionBobBob approves Stations changes, including Jim's
Sprint 4narrating the demorotatingJim closes with the ask, and only that
Sprint 5preparing the change board's agenda from the open prime changesBobBob briefs the deputy program manager; Jim chairs
Sprint 6the weekly note to managementrotating, drafted with talk.pl weeklyJim reads it before it goes, and changes only facts

Two things made the hand-overs stick. First, each one was recorded where the system enforces it: CODEOWNERS names Bob as an owner of the Stations folder, so Jim's own Stations changes wait for Bob's approval. A hand-over that is only spoken is reclaimed the first time the lead is in a hurry. Second, Jim accepted that the new owner would do it differently. Tom's pipeline ran jobs in an order Jim would not have chosen; it worked, and changing it would have taken the pipeline back.

The first time my approval was the one holding up Jim's merge request, I thought I'd done something wrong. Then I realized that was the point.

— Bob, sprint 4 retrospective

41.11 The lead is a beginner too

Jim had twenty-six years of systems engineering and zero weeks of git. The temptation for an experienced lead is to hide the second fact behind the first: to stay in the management role, delegate the tools and never be seen not knowing.

Jim did the opposite, deliberately:

  • Did the practice lessons first, and told the team where they got stuck.
  • Took real tasks, with points, every sprint: the DOORS import in sprint 3 was Jim's, from the command line, with Bob navigating.
  • Asked questions in the stand-up, in front of everyone: "How do I see which pipeline job failed?" Tom answered in one sentence, and two other people learned it.
  • Used the tools the team used. Jim's weekly note was drafted with talk.pl, edited in Vim and built with the same memo tool everyone else used. A lead who keeps a private Word template is telling the team the new tools are for them, not for leads.

The effect was that the team never had to pretend in front of Jim, because Jim was visibly learning alongside them. It also meant Jim's judgment about what was hard was accurate: a lead who has not done the work under-estimates it, and that is how teams end up with plans they cannot meet.

41.12 The lead's fortnight

Most of the lead's work in the new way is a rhythm, not heroics. Jim's two weeks, once it settled down in sprint 4:

Table 41.4. Jim's two weeks
WhenThe leadTime
Every dayreads the stand-up chat (times as well as content); checks blocked items; answers one question in the chat or pairsabout 20 minutes
Day 1runs the kickoff: the goal, capacity including the learning reserve, the commitment90 minutes
Days 2 to 8takes one or two real tasks; reviews merge requests in their code-owner areasabout half the time
Day 9refinement and planning poker; the demo dry run; the ask for Friday written down2 hours
Day 10closes the demo with the ask; runs the retrospective and its pulse survey90 minutes
Every Fridayreads the weekly note before it goes; sends it with the quad15 minutes
Every second weekthirty minutes with the program manager: the four numbers, the trend, the open asks30 minutes

What is not on the list is as important: status meetings, slide preparation and chasing people for updates. The records the meetings produce replaced them (Section 24.1, Why meetings at all). That is the time the lead gets back, and Jim spent it on two things: real modeling work, and the conversations with management that protect the team.

41.13 Exercises

Exercise 41.1: Budget the learning

Plan the first three sprints of your team's transition with an explicit learning reserve: what each person learns, which practice lessons and chapters, how many points per sprint. Write it as stories with a learning label. What engineering scope did you have to move to make it fit?

Exercise 41.2: Choose the first win

List three questions about your current model that the old way could only answer slowly. For each, name the tool that answers it in minutes, and the skeptic on your team who should be the one to run it. Which one can land in sprint 1?

Exercise 41.3: Say no with a date

Write your answer to three requests you expect from management in the first month (a special report, an urgent model change, borrowing a person). Each answer: what not now, why, when, and what you can offer today, or the trade.

Exercise 41.4: Read the signs

Look back at your team's last two weeks of statuses, merge requests and chat. Which of the slow-down signs do you see? What would you change in the next sprint, and what would you tell management?

41.14 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the lead goes first (shares their own failing change); a visible learning reserve as labelled stories; pairing with the less experienced person driving; first wins chosen on purpose and shown by the skeptic; the daily ten-minute workload check; the measures agreed with management before the work starts; no with a date.
  • Adapt: the size of the learning reserve to your team's starting point (a team that already uses git needs less); the pulse survey questions to what your team worries about; the format of your weekly note to what your management already reads.
  • Decide locally: who in management gets the weekly note and attends the demo; how much scope the lead may move without asking; what the team does when the lead is away (someone has to say "I don't know yet" first).
Note: You can now...
  • make it safe for a team to be slow and wrong while it learns, starting with yourself;
  • put learning in the plan as visible, protected, shrinking work;
  • pair to spread skill quickly, and stop pairing when it is no longer needed;
  • choose first wins that convince skeptics because the skeptics find them;
  • watch for quiet overwork and respond by cutting scope;
  • manage up with agreed measures, dated plans and formal requests for enablers;
  • say no with a date, and turn requests into trades;
  • recognize a sprint that has gone wrong and slow down on purpose.

Part V: Living with it

The first twelve weeks are a sprint in both senses: a burst of effort, watched closely, with a briefing at the end. What follows is longer and quieter. Tidewater's model has to stay correct for years after the briefing, through staff changes, server upgrades, expiring tokens, a contractor who keeps delivering Cameo drops, and the slow temptation to stop doing the dull parts because nothing has gone wrong lately.

This part is about that long tail. Chapter 42, Administration covers the recurring administration that keeps the environment trustworthy: who has access, which tokens exist, whether the runner is patched, whether a backup can actually be restored. Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle covers the engineering rhythm after the port: taking in each prime drop, cutting baselines, fixing a released baseline in a hurry, and retiring the tools that only the port needed. Chapter 51, Pitfalls and anti-patterns collects the ways teams like Jim's go wrong when they move from documents and Cameo to a model in GitLab, each with the symptom you will notice first, why it happens, and what to do.

None of it is glamorous. All of it is what separates a demonstration from a capability. The program manager put it to Jim after the sprint 6 briefing, in a sentence Jim wrote on the whiteboard and left there: "Now show me it still works in a year."

42 Administration

From what you know

You know

the CM manager's routine: accounts, access lists, audits and backups.

Here it is called

administering GitLab, runners and tokens.

What is new

most of the routine becomes a scheduled check that reports drift.

Survival kit: The upkeep

What you have

a GitLab project that works, a runner that runs, three people who know their way around both, and a model that passed its first baseline.

What you need

a short list of recurring chores, each with a cadence, an owner and a checklist, so the environment is still trustworthy a year from now when nobody remembers how it was set up.

42.1 The Friday the nightly pipeline went red

Eleven weeks after the briefing, on a Friday morning, Tom opened the project page and saw the nightly status pipeline in red. Nothing in the model had changed since Wednesday. The job log ended with a single line from the export step: the server had answered 401 Unauthorized.

It took Tom twenty minutes to find the cause, and most of that time was spent remembering where things were. The scheduled pipeline exported GitLab's records for the status metrics, and to do that it used a project access token stored in a masked CI/CD variable. The token had been created during week zero with GitLab's default expiry. It had expired at midnight.

The fix took two minutes: create a new token, paste it into the variable, re-run the job. The lesson took longer to absorb. In the document era, the team's tools had not expired. A Word template did not stop working on a date, and a shared drive did not need its permissions reviewed for the system to keep running. The new environment is made of parts that need upkeep: credentials that age, a runner whose operating system needs patches, protections that can drift when someone with the right role clicks the wrong box, backups that are worthless until someone restores one.

That afternoon Jim and Tom wrote down every recurring chore they could think of, with how often it had to happen and who would do it. The list became a page in the wiki and a standing story on the board. This chapter is that list, explained.

Note: Administration is configuration management

None of this is new in kind. A CM office has always kept access lists, verified backups, audited baselines and tracked tool versions. What is new is that GitLab records most of it automatically, so the chore is usually a review of a record, not the creation of one.

42.2 The administration calendar

Every item in this chapter appears in one table. Tom printed it and taped it beside the monitor; it also lives in the wiki as the Administration page (the version the team started from, wiki/Administration.md, is shown in Appendix I, Templates and GitLab Markdown, field by field).

Table 42.1. The administration calendar
ChoreCadenceOwnerTypical timeEvidence it was done
Access review: members, roles, the prime's accountsquarterly, and the same day someone leavesJim30 mina comment on the Admin story with the member list
Token inventory and rotationmonthly check; rotate before expirytoken owner, checked by Tom15 min per tokenthe inventory table in the wiki, updated
Runner patching: operating system, gitlab-runner, Git for Windows, the kitmonthlyTom1 houra green pipeline after the update; versions in the runner page
Runner health: last contact, disk, job queue timesweeklyTom10 mina note in the Friday quad if anything is wrong
Pipeline schedules: owner current, last run passedmonthly, and on every departureTom5 minthe schedules page; owner noted in the wiki
Container image rebuild and scan (only if the Docker image is used)monthlyTom30 mina new image tag in the registry
Protection audit: settings versus project.confmonthly, and after any admin changeTom20 minthe settings pages match project.conf (setup re-applied if not)
Project export (backup of issues, MRs, wiki)each baseline, and monthlyTom20 minthe export file in the package registry, with its checksum
Restore testquarterlyTom, watched by Jim2 hoursa scratch project restored and its pipeline green
Audit event reviewmonthly (Premium)Jim20 mina comment on the Admin story
Milestones two sprints aheadeach sprint planningJim5 minthe next two milestones exist
Label and board tidy-upeach refinementJim10 minno unlabelled open issues
Upgrade watch: GitLab release notes for CI and API changesmonthlyTom30 mina note in the wiki's Administration page
CODEOWNERS matches the teamon every membership changeJim5 minan MR changing CODEOWNERS

The total is about four hours a month in a normal month and a day in a quarter-end month. Tom tracked it with /spend on the standing Admin story so the cost was visible in the sprint report rather than hidden in overtime.

Tip: Make the chores into issues

A chore that lives only in someone's head stops happening when that person is on leave. The team created one story per sprint titled "Administration, sprint N" from a template with the sprint's chores as a checklist. It was deliberately small (two or three points) and it never carried over: an unchecked chore was moved to the next sprint's story with a comment saying why.

42.3 Members and access reviews

42.3.1 The five roles

GitLab gives every member of a project one of five roles. The names sound like a hierarchy, and they are, but what matters for a model project is what each role can do to the controlled configuration.

Table 42.2. GitLab roles as Tidewater uses them
RoleWho on TidewaterCan doCannot do
Guestnobody (sometimes a reviewer from another program)see issues, commentsee the repository on a private project
Reporterthe prime's modeler, the ISSM, the program officeread the model, issues, MRs, pipelines; comment; download packagespush, merge, change settings
DeveloperBobpush feature branches, open and approve MRs, run pipelines, merge into develop where the branch rule allowspush to protected branches, change settings or protections, create protected tags
MaintainerJim, Tomeverything a developer can, plus merge into main, create baseline-* tags, manage CI/CD variables, protections and membersdelete the project, transfer it (owner only)
Ownerthe group owner (the enterprise admins)everythingn/a

Two choices in that table were argued over.

Bob is a developer, not a maintainer. Bob objected at first: Bob does most of the model work and felt a lower role was a statement of trust. Jim's answer was about separation of duties, the same principle that kept engineers from signing their own CCB approvals in the document era. A developer can do everything the daily work needs. The maintainer-only powers are the ones that change the rules (protections, tokens, baselines), and the team agreed those should sit with two people, neither of whom does most of the model edits.

The prime's modeler is a reporter. The prime's modeler can read the government model and comment on issues, which makes discrepancy reports a conversation instead of an email chain. The prime's modeler cannot push, because the government v2 model is the government's record; the prime's changes arrive as drops on the vendor branch (see Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).

42.3.2 Adding a person

Checklist: Onboarding one person
  • ☐ Account exists on the enterprise GitLab (the enterprise admins create it; the person signs in once)
  • ☐ Added to the project with the lowest role that lets them do their job ([members] in project.conf, then gitlab.pl setup)
  • ☐ SSH key or personal access token set up on their laptop (Chapter 9, The survival kit)
  • ☐ Added to CODEOWNERS if they will own a package, by MR
  • ☐ Added to roster.txt in the journal (daily.pl roster add ...) and to the stand-up invitation
  • ☐ Walked through the Onboarding wiki page; first task is a small one with a pairing partner
  • ☐ Their first MR merged within their first week

Membership is in project.conf so that the list is reviewed like any other change. When Jim added the deputy program manager as a reporter in sprint 8, it was a two-line MR: one line in [members], one line in the wiki's contact page, approved by Tom.

42.3.3 Removing a person

Offboarding is the one chore with a same-day deadline. Access that outlives its need is the most common finding in any security review, and it is the easiest to prevent.

Checklist: Offboarding one person (the same day)
  • ☐ Removed from the project and from the group (a group membership grants the project too)
  • ☐ Their personal access tokens revoked by an admin, or confirmed expired
  • ☐ Any CI/CD variable they could read (maintainers can read all of them) rotated
  • ☐ Their pipeline schedules taken over by a current member (a schedule runs as its owner)
  • ☐ Their open issues and MRs reassigned, with a comment saying to whom and why
  • ☐ CODEOWNERS updated if they owned a package (the approval rule would otherwise wait for someone who is gone)
  • ☐ Removed from roster.txt and the stand-up invitation
  • ☐ The runner machine's local accounts checked if they had one

42.3.4 The quarterly access review

Every quarter Jim opens the project's member list and compares it with reality: who is on the team, who still needs read access, which accounts have not signed in for ninety days. The review takes half an hour and produces one comment on the Admin story, listing the members and any change made. Over eighteen months the review removed four accounts: a program-office analyst who had moved on, two of the prime's staff who no longer worked on the model, and a test account Tom had created during week zero and forgotten.

Warning: Inherited membership is invisible from the project page

A person who is a member of the tidewater group is a member of every project in it, with the group role. When you review a project's members, include the inherited ones (the member list shows them with the group's name beside them). Most forgotten access is inherited.

42.4 Tokens and rotation

42.4.1 What a token is, in plain terms

A token is a password issued to a program rather than to a person. When the pipeline needs to call GitLab's API, or a script on Tom's laptop needs to create issues, it cannot type a password into a login page. It sends a long random string instead, and GitLab checks the string against its list of tokens, each with an owner, a set of permissions (called scopes) and an expiry date.

GitLab has several kinds of token. A team new to all this needs to know which kind to use where, because using the wrong kind is the commonest security mistake.

Table 42.3. Kinds of token and where Tidewater uses each
TokenBelongs toUse it forTidewater example
Personal access tokenone personscripts that person runs from a laptopJim's gitlab.pl calls from Vim
Project access tokena bot user in one projectautomation that must outlive any one personthe nightly status export
Group access tokena bot user in a groupautomation across several projects (Premium on gitlab.com)not used
Deploy tokenthe projectread-only access to the repository or packages from outsidethe program office's read-only mirror
CI_JOB_TOKENone running jobcalls from inside a pipeline job; expires when the job endsuploading a prime drop to the package registry
Runner authentication tokenone runnerthe runner talking to GitLabglrt-... in the runner's config.toml
Pipeline trigger tokenthe projectstarting a pipeline from outsidenot used

The rule the team adopted fits on one line: use CI_JOB_TOKEN inside the pipeline whenever it can do the job; use a project access token for automation; use personal tokens only for a person's own interactive work. CI_JOB_TOKEN is the best kind because nobody has to store, rotate or protect it; it exists only while a job runs.

42.4.2 Scopes: the least that works

Each token carries scopes that limit what it can do. The scope names are GitLab's: read_api, api, read_repository, write_repository, read_registry, and a few others. A token for the nightly export only reads, so it gets read_api and nothing else. A token that creates issues needs api, which is broad: it can do anything the token's user can do through the API. Give api only to tokens whose bot user has a role no higher than the work needs (a project access token can be created with the reporter or developer role, not just maintainer).

42.4.3 Where tokens live

A token used by the pipeline is stored as a CI/CD variable in the project's settings (Settings, CI/CD, Variables), with two flags set:

  • Masked: GitLab replaces the value with [MASKED] if a job prints it to the log. This protects against the most common leak, a debugging echo left in a script.
  • Protected: the variable is only given to pipelines on protected branches and tags (develop, main, baseline-*). A feature branch pipeline does not see it, so a change on an unreviewed branch cannot read it.

The nightly status job runs on develop, so a protected variable is fine for it. A job that must run on feature branches cannot use a protected variable; if such a job needs a secret, that is a design smell worth a conversation with the ISSM.

Tokens never go in files in the repository, not even in a branch that will be deleted: git keeps history, and the secret detection job (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job) exists to catch exactly that mistake. On laptops, personal tokens go in an environment variable set by the user's shell profile (GITLAB_TOKEN for gitlab.pl, as gitlab.pl help says), never in a script.

42.4.4 The token inventory and rotation

Tom keeps a table on the wiki's Administration page, one row per token: what it is for, its kind, its scopes, the variable or place where it is stored, who owns it, and when it expires. GitLab shows the expiry dates too, and sends email a week before a personal or project token expires, but the email goes to the token's owner, and a bot user has no inbox anybody reads. The inventory is how the Friday incident is prevented.

Checklist: Rotating a project access token
  • ☐ Create the new token (Settings, Access tokens) with the same scopes and role, expiry at most ninety days out
  • ☐ Paste the value into the CI/CD variable (Settings, CI/CD, Variables), keeping Masked and Protected set
  • ☐ Run the job that uses it (gitlab.pl pipeline run develop --source web, or the Run pipeline button) and check it passes
  • ☐ Revoke the old token
  • ☐ Update the expiry date in the inventory table

Ninety days was a compromise. The ISSM's first position was thirty days, which would have meant a rotation every other week for the team's three tokens. Tom showed the inventory and the checklist, and the ISSM agreed to ninety days with a monthly check, on the condition that the rotation itself was recorded. It is: each rotation is a comment on the Admin story.

42.4.5 When a token leaks

If a token is ever seen where it should not be (pasted into an issue, committed to a branch, printed in a log before masking was set), the order of actions matters:

  1. Revoke it first. Settings, Access tokens, Revoke. Everything else can wait five minutes; this cannot.
  2. Create a replacement and update the variable.
  3. Find where it appeared and remove it (edit the comment; for a commit, the secret is in history even if the file is fixed, which is why revocation comes first).
  4. Check the audit events for use of the old token since it leaked (Premium), or ask the instance admins.
  5. Tell the ISSM, with the times. A leak reported in an hour is an incident handled; a leak found later is a finding.

The team never had a real leak. They rehearsed the procedure once, in sprint 9, with a deliberately created and deliberately "leaked" token on a scratch project, and timed it: seven minutes from "found" to "reported".

42.5 The runner

42.5.1 What the runner is, and what this section covers

The runner is the machine that executes pipeline jobs. GitLab the server runs nothing itself: when a pipeline starts, the server queues its jobs, and a runner program on some machine asks for work, runs the job's script and sends back the log and the result. With no runner available, jobs sit in pending forever, which is exactly what happened to Tidewater's first pipeline for the two days before Tom's runner was registered (Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in).

Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs explains runners from the beginning: scopes, executors, registration, tags and why Tidewater chose a project runner with the Windows shell executor on a dedicated virtual machine, running the same Git for Windows Perl as the laptops. This section is about keeping that runner healthy for years: the chores, their cadence, and what breaks when they are skipped.

42.5.2 The runner's set-up, as a record

Tom kept the runner's installation as a short runbook in the wiki, because the second runner (below) had to be built the same way and so will its replacement after the virtual machine is retired. The essentials:

  1. A dedicated Windows virtual machine from the enterprise, never a person's laptop: a laptop sleeps, travels and is reimaged, and every MR would wait for it.
  2. Git for Windows at the laptops' version; perl -v matches; the kit cloned to C:\agile at the agreed tag and its tests passing there (perl tests/run.pl).
  3. A local service account, svc-runner, with no administrator rights and no interactive logon; gitlab-runner installed as a Windows service running as that account.
  4. The runner created in GitLab (Settings, CI/CD, Runners, New project runner) with tags windows, shell and mbse, then registered on the machine with gitlab-runner register --url https://gitlab.example.com --token glrt-... and the shell executor.
  5. config.toml adjusted (below), the service restarted, a trivial branch pushed and its first job watched from pending to passed.

The shell executor on Windows runs each job's script in PowerShell (pwsh) unless told otherwise, and PowerShell reads $KIT differently from Git Bash and has no $(find ...). Rather than depend on a particular shell, every line of Tidewater's pipeline is one shell-neutral command, perl ci/job.pl NAME, and the Perl script does the work. The same .gitlab-ci.yml therefore runs under pwsh on this runner, under Git Bash on a laptop with gitlab.pl ci, and inside the optional Docker image. The KIT variable reaches the script through the environment in every case.

42.5.3 Least privilege on the runner

A runner executes whatever is in .gitlab-ci.yml on the branch being tested, so anyone who can push a branch can run commands on the runner machine as the runner's account. That is the main security fact about runners, and the ISSM asked about it in the first meeting. The team's answers, each a setting:

  • The service account has no admin rights and cannot log on interactively, so a job cannot install software or read other accounts' files.
  • The runner is a project runner, registered to tidewater/model only, not shared with projects whose members the team does not know.
  • The runner machine holds no secrets beyond its own glrt- token. Tokens jobs need come from protected, masked CI/CD variables, which feature-branch pipelines never see.
  • Only members can push. The prime's modeler is a reporter and cannot push, so the prime cannot run code on the government runner.
  • The machine follows the program's workstation baseline: patching, antivirus, logging.

GitLab's protected runner flag makes a runner take jobs only from protected branches and tags. The checking runner cannot be protected, because merge request pipelines run on feature branches and checking those is the point. From sprint 8 the team ran a pattern the ISSM liked: the general runner, unprotected, for checks; and a second, protected runner with an extra tag, release, for the jobs that publish or hold credentials (pages, the package upload, the release job), which carry tags: [release]. A change on an unreviewed branch can never reach the protected runner.

42.5.4 Antivirus, long paths and disk

Three Windows details caused most of the runner's trouble in the first months.

  • Antivirus. Real-time scanning of the builds folder made each job several times slower, because a checkout writes thousands of small files. The enterprise security team agreed to exclude D:\runner\builds and the kit folder from on-access scanning, with a scheduled full scan nightly instead. Ask for this in writing; do not just turn scanning off.
  • Long paths. Windows limits paths to 260 characters unless told otherwise, and a builds folder plus a deep model path plus a generated file name can exceed it. The fix is git config --system core.longpaths true on the runner (and the laptops) and a short builds_dir, as above.
  • Disk. Each job leaves a checkout and its artifacts behind. The sprint 6 incident, when the builds drive filled and every pipeline failed for most of a day (Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0), led to a scheduled task that deletes build folders older than a week, and a free-space check as the first line of the weekly health look.

42.5.5 Updates, health and a second runner

Once a month Tom updates the runner, in this order, running a pipeline after each step so a failure points at its cause:

  1. Windows updates, by the enterprise's normal process.
  2. gitlab-runner. Its version tracks GitLab's: the runner's major and minor version should match the server's, so a server upgrade is followed by a runner upgrade within the month.
  3. Git for Windows, only to the version the laptops move to, after the kit's tests pass under it on one laptop.
  4. The kit, to the agreed tag (Section 42.9, Upgrades).

Every Friday Tom spends ten minutes on health: the runner page in GitLab (Settings, CI/CD, Runners) shows each runner's last contact; a runner that has not contacted GitLab for more than a few minutes is offline, and an offline runner means every MR is blocked. Tom also checks free disk space and the queued duration of the week's jobs; a job that waited more than a minute or two for a runner means the runner is busy or sick. When the runner stops, the gitlab-runner service's own log (Windows Event Viewer, Application log) usually says why.

From sprint 7 a second Windows virtual machine runs an identical runner with the same tags. Either can take any checking job, so one runner being patched or broken no longer stops the team. Two runners cost the enterprise one more small virtual machine; the day the first runner's disk filled cost the team three person-days.

42.5.6 The Docker image, if you use one

The kit offers an optional container image, mbse-ci (tools/gitlab/docker/), for organizations whose GitLab offers only Docker runners. Tidewater did not use it, but a reader's project may. If you do, the image is part of the toolchain baseline and needs the same upkeep as the runner:

  • Pin the base image by digest, not by a moving tag, so a rebuild is deliberate.
  • Rebuild monthly, or when the base distribution publishes a security update, and give each rebuild a new tag.
  • Tag the image with the kit's version. A pipeline that names mbse-ci:1.0 always runs the same checks; never use :latest in a pipeline.
  • Scan it with whatever your security office uses before pushing it to the registry, and keep no credentials in it.

42.5.7 Pipeline schedules and who owns them

The project has two scheduled pipelines: a nightly full check of develop on working days (cron 0 2 * * 1-5) and the weekly status export on Friday mornings (0 6 * * 5). Both are listed in project.conf's [schedules] section, so they are recreated by gitlab.pl setup, and gitlab.pl schedule lists and runs them.

A schedule runs as the user who owns it. When that user leaves, or loses the role the jobs need, the schedule stops or fails, and nobody notices until a Friday report is missing. Two rules followed: schedules are owned by a team member who is not about to leave (Tom, with Jim as the named backup), and the offboarding checklist has a line to take over the leaver's schedules (Build, Pipeline schedules, Take ownership).

42.5.8 What the pipeline costs

The kit and its checks cost nothing. On a self-managed GitLab with the team's own runners, there are no per-minute charges: the cost is the virtual machines and the time to look after them, about an hour a month each. On GitLab.com with GitLab's hosted runners, jobs consume compute minutes: each plan includes a quota, and more must be bought. Tidewater's pipeline is small (a few minutes per MR), but a reader on hosted runners should estimate MRs per month times minutes per pipeline before choosing.

Some gate settings need a paid tier: required approval rules, enforced code-owner approval, push rules and merge trains are Premium; security policies and compliance frameworks are Ultimate (Section 42.10, License tiers). Prices and the features in each tier change; check GitLab's current pricing page before planning a budget.

42.6 Protection audits

42.6.1 What drifts and why

Protections are settings, and settings drift. Someone with the maintainer role unprotects a branch "for five minutes" to fix something and forgets to protect it again. A new GitLab version changes a default. A group setting overrides a project setting. In the document era the equivalent was a controlled document quietly edited outside the CCB; the defence then was a configuration audit, and it is now.

The difference is that GitLab's protections are in a file. project.conf says what the project's settings should be, and gitlab.pl setup applies it; running it again re-applies the file, so a setting someone changed by hand in the web pages goes back to what the file says. Running setup with --dry-run prints every API request the file asks for, without contacting the server at all:

That is a preview of what the file says, not a comparison with the server: because a dry run reads nothing, it prints the full list every time. To audit drift, Tom runs the read-only comparison once a month and after any administrative change by anyone. gitlab.pl setup --diff FILE reads the live project, prints one line per difference, and exits 1 when anything has drifted. Here someone has turned force push on for develop in the web pages:

The file says no force push; the live project says yes. A difference is investigated before it is fixed: the question is not only "what changed" but "who changed it and why", which the audit events answer on Premium (and the instance admins can answer on Free). Then setup puts the project back. On a new project the two schedules also show as missing until develop exists; that is expected.

42.6.2 The monthly audit

Checklist: Monthly protection audit
  • ☐ the project's settings pages match project.conf; gitlab.pl setup project.conf re-applied if they did not
  • ☐ main and develop: push allowed to no one, merge by the intended role, force push off, code owner approval on (Premium)
  • ☐ vendor/prime: push by maintainers only, merge by no one
  • ☐ baseline-* tags protected, create by maintainers only
  • ☐ Merge settings: merge commit, no squash, pipelines must succeed, discussions must be resolved
  • ☐ CODEOWNERS on develop names only current team members
  • ☐ Every merge into develop since the last audit had a passing pipeline and an approval by someone other than the author (scorecard measure 3; gitlab.pl export gives the MR list)
  • ☐ No CI/CD variable is unprotected or unmasked unless the inventory says why

The seventh line is the important one. It checks the outcome, not the setting: even with every setting right, the question a reviewer will ask is "can you show me that every change was reviewed?", and the export answers it with the evidence.

42.7 Backups and restore tests

42.7.1 What is already safe and what is not

Git is distributed: every clone holds the full history of every branch it has fetched. With three engineers and a runner, the model's history exists in at least five places, and losing the server would not lose a single commit. New users often stop there. They should not, because the repository is only part of what the team now depends on.

Table 42.4. What a git clone does and does not protect
WhatWhere it livesSafe if the server is lost?
The model, its history, tagsevery cloneyes
Issues, comments, the board, labels, milestonesthe server onlyno
Merge requests, reviews, approvalsthe server onlyno
The wikithe server (it is a git repository you can clone)only if someone clones it
Pipeline history, job logs, artifactsthe server onlyno
CI/CD variables, protections, membersthe server; mostly in project.confpartly
Packages (the prime drops, baseline bundles)the server's package registryno
The journal (data/tidewater/journal)Jim's laptop and its own GitLab projectyes, if pushed

Merge requests and their approvals are the audit trail the whole process rests on. Losing them would be like losing every signed CCB form.

42.7.2 Three layers of backup

  1. The instance backup belongs to the enterprise GitLab administrators, who back up the whole server daily. Tom asked them, in writing, what is backed up, how often, how long it is kept and when a restore was last tested. The answers went in the wiki. The team does not run this layer, but it should know what it covers.
  2. The project export. GitLab can export a project (Settings, General, Advanced, Export project) into one archive holding the repository, issues, MRs with their discussions, labels, milestones, the wiki and more. Tom exports at every baseline and once a month, and uploads the archive to the package registry under a project-export package, versioned by date, so its checksum is recorded.
  3. The clones. Everyone pushes their work daily, and the wiki is cloned onto Tom's laptop and pulled weekly.

42.7.3 The restore test

A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. Once a quarter Tom restores the latest project export into a scratch project (a project in Tom's personal namespace, deleted afterwards) and checks it:

Checklist: Quarterly restore test
  • ☐ Import the latest export archive as a new project
  • ☐ The default branch, main, develop and every baseline-* tag are present
  • ☐ A merge request from the last sprint shows its discussion and approvals
  • ☐ The wiki's Home page and Administration page are present
  • ☐ Register nothing new: point the existing runner at the scratch project temporarily, run the pipeline on develop, and check it passes
  • ☐ Rebuild the latest baseline's docs and compare the checksum with the tag message
  • ☐ Record the date, the archive's checksum and the result on the Admin story; delete the scratch project

The first restore test, in sprint 10, failed on the fifth item: the scratch project had no CI/CD variables (an export does not carry them, by design, because they hold secrets). That was the useful result. The team added the variable list, without values, to project.conf's [variables] section, so recreating them is part of the setup file.

The offline emulator (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep) let Tom rehearse the whole procedure on a laptop before touching the server: the emulator's state is one file, and restoring it is copying that file and the bare repository back.

42.8 Audit events

GitLab Premium records audit events: who added a member, changed a protection, created or revoked a token, changed a CI/CD variable, and similar administrative actions, with the time and the source address. (Who pushed what and who merged what is in the repository and the MRs on every tier.) Jim reviews the project's audit events once a month, looking for three things:

  • Any change to protections or merge settings. Each should match an MR to project.conf or a comment on the Admin story. One that matches nothing is asked about the same day.
  • Membership changes. They should match the onboarding and offboarding records.
  • Token creation and revocation. They should match the token inventory.

On the Free tier there is no audit event page for projects. The team's fallback was the monthly protection audit above, plus the instance administrators' logs on request. That is weaker, and Jim said so in writing when the Premium question came up (see Section 42.10, License tiers).

42.9 Upgrades

Four things in the environment change version, and each needs a different kind of care.

GitLab itself. The enterprise administrators upgrade the server, usually monthly. GitLab announces deprecations in its release notes months ahead, and occasionally removes a CI keyword or an API field. Tom reads the release notes each month for two sections only: CI/CD (anything about keywords the pipeline uses) and the REST API (anything gitlab.pl calls). After each server upgrade, Tom opens the pipeline editor (Build, Pipeline editor), which validates .gitlab-ci.yml against the server's current rules, and runs a pipeline on develop.

gitlab-runner. Upgraded monthly with the runner patching, within the version range the server supports.

Git for Windows and its Perl. Upgraded on the laptops and runner together, a few times a year. The kit's tests run first on one laptop under the new version (Appendix A, Command reference has the command); only when they pass does everyone upgrade.

The kit. The kit is a dependency like any other. The runner and the laptops use the same tag of the kit, never whatever is newest. Upgrading the kit is a story: read the kit's changes, run its tests, run the model's pipeline locally with the new kit (KIT=/c/agile-new perl bin/gitlab.pl ci --event merge_request_event --target develop), then move the runner and laptops together. A new kit that changes a converter's output changes what the next vendor import produces; that is planned, not discovered.

Warning: Never upgrade on a drop week

The week a prime drop arrives is the week the team most needs the environment to behave exactly as it did last time, so the delta shows only the prime's changes. Upgrades wait for the sprint after.

42.10 License tiers

GitLab comes in three tiers: Free, Premium and Ultimate. Several features this book uses are Premium or above, and the team spent part of sprint 2 working out which they actually needed. The honest answer was that the process works on Free with a few manual substitutes, and that Premium buys enforcement of things Free can only ask people to do.

Table 42.5. Features by tier, and what Tidewater did on each
FeatureTierHow Tidewater uses itOn Free instead
Protected branches and tagsFreedevelop, main, vendor/prime, baseline-*n/a
Merge request approvals (optional)Freeone approval per MRn/a
Required approval rules, code owner approval enforcedPremiuma code owner must approve; merge is blocked otherwiseCODEOWNERS suggests reviewers; the team's rule and the monthly audit check it was followed
Pipelines, artifacts, schedules, Pages, releases, package registryFreeall of themn/a
JUnit and Code Quality reports on the MRFreethe MR widgetsn/a
Metrics report on the MRPremiumscorecard numbers shown with their changethe numbers are in the job log and artifact
Scoped labels (key::value, one per key)Premiumworkflow::, type::, priority::plain labels; the board still works; two workflow labels can coexist by mistake
Milestone burndown chartsPremiumthe sprint burndownthe journal's sprint report
Epics, roadmapsPremium (multi-level: Ultimate)not neededepic:: and tome:: labels, the journal's roadmap
IterationsPremiumnot usedmilestones named Sprint N
Push rulesPremiumreject commits with secrets or large files at push timethe secrets job in the pipeline
Audit events (project)Premiumthe monthly reviewthe protection audit and the instance logs
DORA metrics, value stream analytics dashboardsUltimate (VSA basics on Free)not essentialgitlab.pl export and the status metrics

The program bought Premium for the team in the second quarter, on the strength of one argument Jim made in the sprint 6 briefing: on Free, the rule "every change approved by a code owner other than its author" is a team habit checked monthly; on Premium, it is a setting the server enforces on every merge. For a program that has to show an auditor its change control, the difference was worth the licence cost of three seats.

42.11 Applying this to your project

  • Copy the administration calendar and turn it into a recurring story. Adjust the cadences to your organization's policies, but keep every row; each one exists because a team like Tidewater's got hurt without it.
  • Copy the token rule (job token inside pipelines, project tokens for automation, personal tokens only for a person's own work) and the token inventory. Agree the rotation period with your security officer before you create the first token, not after the first expiry.
  • Adapt the runner to your environment. If containers are allowed and your tools run in them, a Linux container runner is simpler to keep clean. Keep the principle that the runner runs the same tool versions as the engineers.
  • Adapt the role assignments to your separation-of-duties rules. Write down why each person has the role they have; you will be asked.
  • Decide locally which tier you need. List the rules your program must be able to prove, and check which of them your tier can enforce rather than merely record.
  • Do not skip the restore test. The first one will find something, as Tidewater's did.

42.12 Exercises

Exercise 42.1: Assign the roles

Your project has five people: a model lead, two modelers, a CM engineer who runs the pipeline, and a contractor liaison who must read the model and comment on discrepancy reports. Assign each a GitLab role and write one sentence per person justifying it in terms of separation of duties.

Exercise 42.2: Choose the token

For each automation, name the kind of token and its scopes: (a) a pipeline job that uploads the prime's drop to the package registry; (b) a nightly job that exports MR and pipeline records for the status metrics; (c) Jim's script that creates the sprint's milestones from a laptop; (d) a read-only mirror of the repository for the program office.

Exercise 42.3: Find the drift

Using the offline emulator, apply tools/gitlab/templates/project.conf to a fresh emulator directory with gitlab.pl --local DIR setup. Then edit the file to allow force push on develop and apply it again: what does setup print for the protected branch? Now preview the same file with --url https://gitlab.example.com --dry-run (a dry run contacts nothing). Why does the preview list every request, not only the changed one? How would you have noticed the change if someone had made it in the web pages instead of the file? (Try gitlab.pl setup --diff on the original file. --dry-run also works on the offline emulator: it prints the requests and applies nothing.)

Exercise 42.4: Plan a restore test

Write the checklist you would use to restore your own project from an export. Which items on Tidewater's checklist would fail on your server, and why? (Hint: think about what an export deliberately leaves out.)

Exercise 42.5: Make the tier case

Your program is on GitLab Free. Write the three-sentence argument for or against Premium for your team, naming the one rule you most need the server to enforce rather than record.

43 Maintenance through the life cycle

From what you know

You know

the long sustainment phase: ECPs, contractor deliveries and re-baselines.

Here it is called

maintaining the model against prime drops, with baselines and hotfixes.

What is new

each delivery is compared automatically, and its impact on your model is listed before anyone decides.

Survival kit: Staying current for eighteen months

What you have

a SysML v2 model under configuration control, a pipeline that checks every change, an interim baseline, and a prime contractor who will keep delivering changes to the old SysML v1 model for as long as the contract runs.

What you need

a routine that takes each new drop in without drama, cuts baselines on a schedule, fixes an urgent error in a released baseline without waiting for the next one, and keeps the change board, the discrepancy reports and the archive in order -- until the day the model is retired.

The first twelve weeks were a port. Everything after them is maintenance: the steady work of keeping the government's SysML v2 model equal to the system the prime is building, while the engineering on top of it grows. On Tidewater that is thirty-three more sprints, six more prime drops, three baselines and one hotfix. This chapter is the routine for that period, shown end to end on real drops in a sandbox you build yourself.

Note: What is evidence and what is plan in this chapter

Sprints 1 to 6 of Tidewater have been simulated and their evidence is in docs/tidewater/. Sprints 7 to 39 have not run yet. In this chapter the prime's drops are real (each one is generated by sim/tidewater-v1.pl, with its manifest and change requests), and every command runs on them. What the team does in sprints 7 to 39, and when, is taken from the team's plan, sim/tidewater-plan.pl, and is marked From the plan. A later edition replaces those passages with the simulated sprints' evidence.

43.1 The eighteen months at a glance

The prime delivers a drop roughly every quarter under CDRL A003. Each drop comes with a manifest that lists its change requests, which is what the government's change board dispositions. These are the seven drops as the prime delivered them:

Table 43.1. The prime's drops, from their manifests

Make the first three drops now. The rest of this chapter works on them:

Three of the drop 3 change requests are engineering decisions the prime made for its own reasons (a storm mode, a fuse, a deleted requirement). Two are answers to the government's own discrepancy reports: the requirement that nothing satisfied, and the duplicate block left by the 2023 document import. That mix is normal. A healthy maintenance relationship sends questions upstream and gets answers back in the next drop.
