Over the whole plan, engineering is 72% of the work (see Bottom line up front); the maintenance routine itself is small, which is the point of making it routine.

43.2 The drop intake runbook

Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition explains each step of the drop loop and why it exists. Here is the routine as a team runs it every quarter, start to finish, on a project you build in the sandbox. It takes the first drop through the project's week zero, then takes the second drop through the full loop.

First, the project. kickoff.pl start is the week-zero sequence from Chapter 50, Your project in twelve weeks: a playbook; with the layout map it puts every prime package into the layered folders from the first drop:

env.sh gives you the gl shortcut for the project's GitLab (here the kit's offline stand-in). In a real terminal you source it once; the blocks below each start with . ../env.sh because each one is tested on its own.

Week zero left drop 1 on its own branch, feature/drop-v1.0, ready for review. The prime's structure arrives all at once, and with it the prime's outline violations (packages with one member, folders with one file). The government did not make them and does not fix them in the drop's merge request. It records them, so that from now on the outline gate fails only on violations the government adds. flow vendor, which kickoff.pl start ran for drop 1, records the new allowance in a commit of its own and regenerates the documents in another. Look at the branch, then open the merge request:

Tom opened the merge request; Jim and Bob approved it. The project's approval rule wants one reviewer, the interface files want a code owner other than the author (Bob), and no one approves their own change. That is the drop loop's first pass. The second drop shows every step.

1. Receive and verify. The drop arrives (by file transfer in the first months, later from the prime's Jenkins, see Section 45.9, The prime's Jenkins: a delivery interface). Before anything else, check that every file is the file the prime sent:

The manifest is written with Windows line endings, so tr strips them before sha256sum reads the list. A failed check stops the intake: the drop goes back to the prime with a request to resend, and nothing is imported.

2. Assess the impact against the government's model, before importing. Run the impact report on develop, the model as the government has it today. Run it before the import: on the drop's own branch, the drop's changes are already in the files and the report mistakes them for government edits.

The report groups the changes by the prime's change requests and lists, for each, the requirements, verification cases, interfaces and allocations it touches. "Hand edits to redo" is the line that matters most in maintenance: every TODO the government closed by hand, and every definition it edited, that the drop changes underneath. Here it is zero, because this sandbox's model has no hand edits yet; on Tidewater's real develop the drop 3 report flags the hand-written state machine, because the prime added a storm mode the converter cannot carry (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition shows that run).

3. Disposition. Each significant change request becomes an issue with a disposition:: label, decided at the change board (Section 43.5, The change board in GitLab). Nothing is merged before its disposition.

4. Import on the vendor branch and merge the drop into a feature branch. flow vendor converts the drop, commits the raw conversion on vendor/prime (never edited by hand), and merges it into feature/drop-v1.1, listing any conflicts:

Two lines in that block are the lessons of past drops. The docs are regenerated on the drop's branch, because the documents are generated from the model and kept in the repository: a drop changes the model, so it changes the documents, and the pipeline's docs job refuses a merge request whose documents are stale. And the outline allowance is checked again whenever a drop adds structure; this drop added none.

5. Rework. Conflicts and hand edits to redo become tasks on the drop's story, and the government's edits are re-applied on top of the prime's new text (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition and practice lesson 12 show a conflict resolved in Vim).

6. Close the loop. Close the Prime Drop issue, close the discrepancy reports the drop answers, open new ones for what it got wrong, and record the drop latency (delivered to merged on develop) for the monthly status.

Checklist: The drop intake runbook
  • ☐ Checksums verified against the manifest; markings checked; the drop archived as received
  • ☐ Prime Drop issue opened with the transmittal record and the change requests listed
  • ☐ Impact report run on develop, before the import; attached to the issue
  • ☐ Every significant change request dispositioned at the CCB (disposition:: label, deputy PM concurrence)
  • ☐ flow vendor: raw conversion on vendor/prime; merged into feature/drop-VERSION
  • ☐ Conflicts resolved by taking the prime's text and re-applying the government's edits
  • ☐ Hand edits to redo done as tasks; docs regenerated; outline allowance recorded if the drop added structure
  • ☐ Merge request green, approved by two people other than the author, merged to develop
  • ☐ DRs answered by the drop closed; new DRs opened; Prime Drop issue closed; latency recorded

From the plan: the drops' latency is a measured result of sprints 7 to 39 and is reported in a later edition. The plan's target is that a drop is merged on develop within its sprint, and from drop 4 on (sprint 17's intake automation) within days of delivery.

43.3 Baselines and releases

A baseline is the configuration the program agrees to stand behind: the model, its generated documents, its verification matrix and the tools that produced them, all at one commit, tagged and published. Tidewater plans four: baseline-0 (the interim baseline at the end of the first twelve weeks, sprint 6), baseline-1 (port acceptance, sprint 20), baseline-2 (sprint 30) and baseline-3 (the end of the eighteen months, sprint 39).

Every baseline follows the same path through gitflow: a release branch from develop, a changelog section, a merge request to main with the change board's concurrence, a tag, a release, and a back-merge so develop has everything main has. Cut baseline-1 from the two drops now on develop:

Tom prepared the baseline; Jim and Bob approved it. On Tidewater the release merge request also carries the deputy program manager's concurrence as a comment: in GitLab terms that comment is the change board's signature (Section 43.5, The change board in GitLab). flow released then tags main as baseline-1 (the tag's message records the checksum of the generated documents), publishes the release, and opens the back-merge request to develop:

The tag's pipeline did the rest. The baseline job rebuilt the documents and checked their checksum against the tag, which is the physical configuration audit done by machine. The release jobs published the baseline as a package, so other teams can take a versioned copy without access to the repository:

The package holds the model and documents as a tarball, the verification matrix, the toolchain inventory (which versions of the kit, Perl and git produced the baseline) and a checksum file. The release links to each of them and names the sprint milestones it closes; GitLab keeps the release's evidence (the milestones' issues and the test report at release time) with it.

Tip: The release branch is the last place to fix, not to change

A release branch takes only fixes that make the baseline correct: a changelog line, a missing document, an outline allowance a drop should have recorded. New work goes to develop and waits for the next baseline. If a fix is needed on the release branch, it goes back to develop in the back-merge, so nothing is lost.

From the plan: baseline-1 at sprint 20 also carries the port completeness report (Chapter 34, Proving the port is complete and correct) and the deputy program manager's sign-off of the port; baseline-2 at sprint 30 is the first with signed tags (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system) and retires the prime's legacy test matrix for Stations (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop); baseline-3 closes the eighteen months.

43.4 Hotfixes

Sometimes a released baseline is wrong in a way that cannot wait for the next one. From the plan: in sprint 24 the program office finds a satisfy relationship in baseline-1 that points at the wrong element. The fix goes on a hotfix branch from main, is merged to main as a patch baseline, and is merged back to develop:

Two things are easy to miss. The satisfy line lives in a file the converter writes from the prime's model, so the hotfix is also a discrepancy report to the prime: unless the prime corrects its v1 model, the next drop puts the wrong satisfy back, and the impact report will flag it as a hand edit to redo. And the patch baseline gets its own tag, baseline-1.1, so anyone holding baseline-1 knows a corrected version exists.

43.5 The change board in GitLab

Tidewater's change control board did not go away; it moved. The board's decisions are now records in GitLab:

Table 43.3. The change board's records, before and after
Board activityWhere it lives in GitLab
An engineering change proposalA merge request, with the impact report attached
A prime change request to dispositionA prime-change issue with a disposition:: label: accept, accept with impact, reject or clarify, no impact
The board's approval of a baselineThe deputy program manager's concurrence comment on the release merge request
The board's agendaThe open prime-change issues and release merge requests, listed by gl issue list --label prime-change
The minutesThe issues' and merge requests' comment threads, kept forever

The board meets once a month (the plan's "Monthly status and CCB items" story, every other sprint). Most decisions are quick, because the impact report has already done the analysis a board used to spend its meeting on. The ones that take time are the ones that should: a change with cost or schedule impact, or a change the prime made without a reason. From the plan: drop 5's rename comes with no rationale; the board dispositions it "reject, clarify", sends a discrepancy report asking why, and closes it when drop 6 answers. Drop 4's drifting buoys are "accept with impact": they add verification work, and the board records the cost.

43.6 Discrepancy reports, upstream and back

A discrepancy report is the government's formal question to the prime about its model: a requirement nothing satisfies, a wording difference between DOORS and the model, a duplicate block, a change with no reason. On Tidewater they are GitLab issues labelled type::discrepancy and owner::prime, sent through the contracting channel with a transmittal memo (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim), and kept open until a drop answers them.

The drops show the loop working. Drop 2's NWM-CR-0014 aligns TW-SYS-006 with DOORS, closing the first drift the team found in sprint 1. Drop 3's NWM-CR-0018 and 0019 answer the reports about TW-SYS-012 and the duplicate SensorSuite. Drop 4's NWM-CR-0022 brings TW-SYS-016 into the model. Drop 6's NWM-CR-0028 deletes the Legacy Import package the team untangled in sprint 5. Each change request names the report it answers in its rationale, which is why the team asked for change notes in week zero.

43.7 The life cycle beyond the port

Tidewater's eighteen months sit inside a longer life. The same repository, pipeline and routine serve every phase; what changes is where the pipeline's emphasis sits:

Table 43.4. The life cycle and the pipeline's emphasis
PhaseRepository activityPipeline emphasis
ConceptStakeholder needs, use cases, early tradesValidation, trade analysis
Requirements (to SRR)Requirement models, satisfy linksTrace coverage, completeness, the recipe
Architecture (to PDR)Structure, interfaces, behaviorInterface consistency, budgets, the data exchange table
Detailed design (to CDR)Refined parts, parametersFull analysis, simulation hooks
Integration and testVerification cases, results linked backThe verification matrix, results ingestion (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop)
Production and sustainmentOne configuration per fielded blockChange impact on old baselines, fixes upstream first

Tidewater uses gitflow, with baselines as releases on main. When a program fields several configurations at once (block 1 in service while block 2 is designed), the alternative is a long-lived release branch per fielded configuration, cut from its baseline tag: fixes land on develop first and are cherry-picked onto each fielded branch that needs them. That is GitLab flow's release-branch variant, and the choice is worth a decision record the day the second configuration is fielded.

43.8 Retirement and archival

Every model ends. The prime's contract closes, the system leaves service, or a successor model takes over. Plan the end while the team still remembers how everything works:

  • Freeze. Cut a final baseline, protect every branch so nothing more can merge, and archive the GitLab project (archived projects are read-only and stay searchable).
  • Keep what an auditor will ask for. The baseline packages, the release evidence, the toolchain inventory and the drops as received are formal records; their retention is set by the program's records schedule, not by GitLab's default artifact expiry. Copy them to the program's records system with their checksums.
  • Keep the tools that read them. A tagged copy of the kit (the slim release.pl --profile mbse zip) beside the archive means the model can be checked and its documents rebuilt years later, on whatever Perl is current then.
  • Hand over or shut down. Transfer the project to its successor, or revoke every token, remove the runners and close the schedules (a schedule runs as its owner: an owner who leaves stops it, which is the one clean-up that happens by itself).
  • Write it down. The runbook and lessons learned are the plan's last story (sprint 39). The next team that ports a model will read them before they read this book.
Exercise 43.1: Run a drop through the loop yourself

Which of drop 3's change requests appear in the impact report as "manual", and why can't the converter carry them?

Exercise 43.2: Cut the next baseline

After drop 3 is merged, cut baseline-2 the way baseline-1 was cut. What must the changelog section say, which change requests does it list, and what does the release link to?

Exercise 43.3: A hotfix that the prime must also fix

43.9 Applying this to your project

  • Make the drop loop a checklist on day one and run it the same way every time; the second drop is where teams either have a routine or have a crisis.
  • Run the impact report on your integration branch before the import, never on the drop's branch.
  • Record inherited counts (outline, complexity, trace gaps) in the drop's merge request so the gates measure only what your team adds.
  • Baseline on a calendar the program understands (milestones, quarters), and publish each baseline as a package with its toolchain inventory.
  • Put the change board's decisions in the issues and merge requests; the board's minutes then write themselves.
  • Plan retirement before the people who built the model move on.

43.10 You can now...

  • take a prime drop from delivery to merged: checksums, impact report on develop, disposition, vendor import, regenerated documents, two approvals;
  • record what a drop brings in so the gates measure only your team's changes;
  • cut a baseline, publish it as a package with its toolchain inventory, and merge it back to develop;
  • ship a hotfix to a released baseline and tell the prime why it must change its model too;
  • run the change board in GitLab, and plan the model's archival.

44 Verification as a closed loop

From what you know

You know

the VCRM spreadsheet and the test reports that feed it.

Here it is called

the verification matrix generated by the pipeline, and one results schema.

What is new

results flow in from every source, and the matrix is current every day.

Survival kit: Where this chapter fits

What you have

requirements in the model with verify relationships to verification cases; a pipeline; a prime contractor and a test organization who actually run the tests.

What you need

a way to turn "which requirements are verified, and by what evidence?" into a report the pipeline regenerates on every change -- and a plan for moving testing onto that footing under management pressure, without putting formal verification evidence at risk.

Testing is where a program proves the system works and where the customer accepts it. It is the worst place for a big-bang tool change. This chapter shows what the Tidewater team built for verification in the first twelve weeks, which is deliberately small, and then the staged plan for the rest of the program. Everything after sprint 6 in this chapter is the plan, not the evidence; it says so where it applies.

44.1 The loop

Verification in a model repository is a loop with three parts.

  1. Plan the tests in the model. Each requirement has a verify relationship to a verification case, and the case states its method (test, analysis, inspection or demonstration), its subject and its objective (Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook).
  2. Execute the tests wherever they run -- the prime's lab, a simulation, an engineer's inspection.
  3. Feed the results back in one results format, and let the pipeline regenerate the verification cross-reference matrix (VCRM) on every change.

The government team owns the first and third parts for Tidewater. The prime and its test organization own the second. That split is the most important design decision in this chapter: the government does not need to run the prime's tests to know, at any moment, which requirements have evidence behind them.

44.2 One results format

Every verdict -- automated or not, the prime's or the government's -- goes into a CSV file in the model repository's verification/ folder, with the same columns:

The verdict is passed, failed or not run. commit names the version of the model the test was run against, so a result can never be mistaken for evidence about a later design. signed_by is empty for an automated result and carries a person's name for an inspection, analysis or demonstration -- the results that will never come out of a test harness, and that matter just as much. Keeping them in the same file is what keeps the matrix complete: an inspection verdict signed by Jim counts exactly like a passed automated test.

44.3 Sprint 6: the VCRM in the pipeline

In sprint 6 Jim's story "VCRM: which requirements are verified, and how" added the vcrm job to the pipeline and entered the government's first signed inspection verdicts. From then on every merge request's pipeline printed the matrix's summary line. Here it is from the last merge request of the twelve weeks:

Read it the way a test lead would. Of the requirements in the model, a few have passing evidence, many have a verification case but no result yet -- the prime has not run those tests -- and some have no verification case at all. The last group is the one that matters: those are the requirements the trace reports as unverified (9 of them at the end of sprint 6), and they are the prime's to fix, raised as discrepancy reports. That is why verify coverage stayed flat through the first twelve weeks: the team made the gap visible and reported it; it did not, and should not, write verification cases for the prime.

You can regenerate the matrix yourself from the simulation's model at the end of sprint 6. Bob's clone is in the sandbox; switch it to develop and run the job exactly as the pipeline does:

The government's signed verdicts are the results file the job read:

And the matrix itself is a CSV the model site publishes, one row per requirement:

44.4 The testing transition, under pressure

Management's pressure to "move testing to DevSecOps" arrived in the same directive as everything else. The team's answer was to move testing last, in stages, and never to put formal evidence at risk. These are the ground rules it adopted, and the five stages, each with what Tidewater did or plans to do.

Ground rules.

  • Don't break what is contractually committed. Test plans, procedures and reports are often contract deliverables with an agreed format and approval chain. The new approach has to produce them, or the customer has to agree to a change, before it replaces the old one. Check with the program office and contracts first.
  • Protect the test schedule from the tool change. If a test event is near, freeze the method for it, and change between campaigns, never during one. For Tidewater the prime's Station acceptance test campaign (notional, spring 2027) is a frozen window: no verification-process change merges during it.
  • Separate the three changes. SysML v2, a DevSecOps pipeline and agile ways of working are three transitions that management tends to bundle. Tidewater sequenced them: ways of working and git first, the port next, testing last.
Table 44.1. The five stages and Tidewater's mapping. Only stage 1 is evidence; stages 2 to 5 are the plan.
StageWhat it isTidewater
1. Traceability firstVerification cases in the model and a generated VCRM; tests executed exactly as today.Done: the trace report from sprint 3, the VCRM from sprint 6.
2. Automate result captureExisting test harnesses emit a standard format (JUnit XML or the results CSV); the pipeline ingests it.Planned: the prime's results arrive with each drop from drop 4.
3. Pilot one subsystem in parallelThe full approach for one contained package, run beside the legacy process for one cycle; differences reconciled.Planned: the Stations VCRM beside the prime's legacy test matrix for drops 4 and 5.
4. Shift testing leftModel-level checks on every merge request; long regressions nightly; hardware time for what only hardware can prove.Planned: the energy-balance and latency checks of the engineering epic.
5. Scale and retirePackage by package; retire legacy artifacts only once the customer accepts the new ones.Planned: the legacy matrix retired at baseline-2, with the program office's agreement.

Managing the pressure. Report what management cares about: verification coverage, time from a design change to test feedback, problems found before the lab versus in it, hours spent assembling review packages. Push back with specifics and a date ("we switch at the campaign boundary, after the pilot, with the customer's agreement"), not with "we're not ready". Ask for the enablers in writing: training time, a test-automation engineer, runner hardware for the lab, the tool approvals (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim). Bring the test team in from the start to co-own the verification case format and the results schema; a process designed without them fails at the bench. Accept that some verification stays manual, and make sure its results flow into the same matrix. Get the customer and any independent test organization to accept model-generated evidence early, by showing them the pilot's output.

Risks to watch.

  • Tool maturity. Keep the model and the results in plain, tool-neutral text so a tool that falls short does not strand the evidence.
  • Model-test drift. If test procedures change outside the model, the matrix lies. Procedure changes go through merge requests like model changes.
  • Over-automation theater. A green pipeline that checks trivial things breeds false confidence. Every automated check should map to a real verification objective.
  • Hardware contention. Automated hardware tests can starve manual testing of bench time; schedule the bench.

44.5 Higher fidelity: model, software and hardware in the loop

Tidewater's government team owns no lab, so it runs no software-in-the-loop (SIL) or hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) tests. The kit's pipeline template still carries both, switched off, so a program that does have a simulation or a bench starts from a tested template. The levels are:

Table 44.2. Increasing fidelity, and where each level runs.
LevelWhat runsWhereTrigger
Model in the loopConstraint and calculation checks, executable behaviorThe normal runnerEvery merge request
Software in the loopReal software against a simulated environmentA normal or high-performance runnerNightly schedule
Hardware in the loopReal hardware on a lab benchA runner attached to the benchBy hand, gated
QualificationThe full system, formal proceduresThe test facilityAt the test readiness review baseline

The HIL job in the template shows the GitLab features a lab needs: a runner tag that only the bench's runner has, a resource group so two pipelines never fight over one bench, when: manual so a person confirms the bench is ready, and an environment so the bench's history of what ran on it is recorded:

Both jobs are off unless a project variable switches them on. You can confirm which jobs a pipeline would run, on your laptop, without a lab:

The local runner accepts the resource group and the manual rule, but only a real GitLab enforces them -- one job at a time on the bench, and a protected environment that only authorized test engineers can start. Test those on the server before the first bench run.

Formal evidence has to outlive GitLab's default artifact expiry. The template marks the verification jobs' artifacts expire_in: never; for qualification evidence, also archive the results to the package registry with the baseline (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

44.6 Closing the loop on failures

When a test fails, the result goes into the results file like any other, the matrix shows it red on the next pipeline, and an issue is opened as the discrepancy report -- linked to the requirement, the verification case, the failing job and its artifacts. The fix goes through the normal merge request flow, and the test runs again as regression. In Tidewater's plan the first failed result arrives with drop 5 and opens a discrepancy report automatically (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).

Tag the configuration under test -- a test readiness baseline, a qualification baseline -- so every result names exactly which design it tested. A result without a commit is an anecdote.

Exercise 44.1: Read the matrix

In the tidewater sandbox, regenerate the VCRM as above and open vcrm.csv. Pick one requirement with status "no case". Find it in the trace report. Who should write its verification case, and how would you ask them?

Exercise 44.2: Map your program to the stages

Write the five stages down for your own program. For each, name the owner (government, prime, test organization), the date it could start, and the test campaign it must not interrupt.

44.7 You can now

  • Keep every verdict -- automated, inspection, analysis -- in one results format with the commit it applies to.
  • Regenerate a VCRM on every change and read what its numbers mean for who has to act.
  • Plan a testing transition in stages that management can track and that never gambles a qualification.

44.8 Applying this to your project

Copy the results schema and the rule that every verdict names a commit. Adapt the VCRM's columns to your contract's deliverable format. Decide locally who owns each stage, which test campaigns are frozen windows, and when the customer sees the pilot's output. Start with stage 1 even if nothing else is possible: a generated matrix that shows the unverified requirements is the quickest visible win in testing.

45 The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition

From what you know

You know

contractor deliverables under a CDRL, and the review cycle that follows each one.

Here it is called

prime drops: receive, assess, disposition.

What is new

each delivery is compared element by element, its impact on your model is computed, and every decision is an issue.

Survival kit: The prime keeps changing the model you just ported

What you have

a SysML v2 model the team built from the prime's Cameo export, a contract that says the prime maintains the authoritative v1 model, and a calendar with a new drop on it every quarter.

What you need

a way to take each drop in without losing a week, without losing your own work, and without accidentally accepting a change nobody authorized. This chapter is that way, end to end, with every command run against real drops.

The port was never a one-time conversion. Northwind Marine Systems, the prime, kept its Cameo model and kept changing it: a new sensor, a new operating mode, a deleted requirement, a renamed activity, test results from its lab. Seven drops arrive over the eighteen months of the Tidewater project, and every one of them lands on a model that Jim, Bob and Tom have been editing in the meantime.

In the document era this was the problem everybody dreaded and nobody owned. A new revision of the SRS arrived as a PDF with change bars, somebody compared it by eye with the old one, and the differences that mattered to the government's own documents were found weeks later, often at a review, often by the customer. Bob remembered it well:

Rev D of the ICD came in on a Friday. By the next Friday I had found eleven changes. The twelfth one we found at the PDR, in front of the program manager.

— Bob, at the sprint 6 retrospective

This chapter shows the loop the team built instead. It has six steps, each with a tool, and each step produces a record someone can audit later:

  1. Receive the drop and check it is exactly what the prime sent.
  2. Archive it unchanged, where nobody can edit it.
  3. Compare it with the previous drop, element by element, by the prime's own element IDs.
  4. Assess what each change touches in the government's model.
  5. Disposition each significant change at the change board, as an issue with a decision.
  6. Implement the accepted changes through ordinary merge requests, and report problems back to the prime.

Before any of that, there is one question that is not about tools at all.

45.1 Contract first

A change in the prime's model is not direction. This is the single most important sentence in this chapter. The prime maintains its Cameo model under a contract data requirement (CDRL A003 on Tidewater). When the prime adds a hygrometer to the sensor suite in its model, that tells you what the prime has done. It does not tell the government team to do anything. If Bob updates the government model because "the prime's model changed," and the change was never approved through the contract, Bob has just spent government effort on work nobody authorized, and possibly accepted a change the program office would have rejected.

So before the first drop, three questions go to the program office and the contracting officer's representative, in writing:

  • What is the prime's model, contractually? Is it the authoritative source for requirements and interfaces, or supporting data? On many programs the specifications and interface control documents still govern, and the model is a deliverable that illustrates them. On Tidewater the System Requirements Specification in DOORS governs; the Cameo model is "supporting data, maintained by the contractor."
  • Which version is on contract? The drop that was delivered last is not necessarily the one the program accepted. Tidewater's rule: a drop becomes the reference only after the change board has dispositioned it.
  • Through which channel do changes become direction? A contract modification, technical direction letter, an approved engineering change proposal, or an interface change approved by the interface control working group. The drop itself is never the channel.

Jim's answer to the third question became the rule the team works by: every drop goes through the change board, with the program office and contracts represented, before anything in it changes the government model. The board is small on Tidewater (Jim and the deputy program manager), and it meets in GitLab, but it exists, and its decisions are recorded.

Objection: "We are the government. We can just change our model."

Bob said it in sprint 2: the government team owns the v2 model, so why ask anybody's permission to keep it in step with the prime?

Answer

you can change your model whenever you like. What you cannot do is let the prime's model decide what your model says without a decision on record. If the prime renames an activity, follows it with three more changes, and one of them conflicts with a requirement the program office cares about, the record has to show who looked at it and what they decided. The change board costs Jim and the deputy program manager twenty minutes per drop. The alternative is an audit finding, or an unfunded change.

45.1.1 The model exchange agreement

The second thing to settle before the first drop is how drops arrive. Tidewater wrote it down as a short model exchange agreement, a page in the repository's docs/ folder that both sides signed in week zero. It is the interface control document for the interface between two organizations' engineering processes, and like any ICD it says what crosses, in what format, how often, and what happens when something is wrong:

Two clauses in that agreement made every later step possible, and they are worth asking for on any program:

  • Stable element IDs. Cameo gives every element an ID (xmi:id). If the prime's export keeps those IDs from one drop to the next, a program can compare drops element by element and know that a renamed activity is the same activity. If the export generates new IDs each time, every comparison degrades to guessing by name. The prime's modeler agreed in week zero; it cost them a checkbox in the export settings.
  • Change notes with every drop. A list of the prime's own change requests, each with an ID, a one-line rationale and the elements it touches. The prime already had this list for its own change control; the agreement just asks for it to be delivered.

45.2 Receive: what arrived, and is it what was sent?

To follow along you need drops. The kit's generator writes the same seven drops the Tidewater team received, each with the prime's manifest and change list. Make the first five:

A drop is four or five files: the Cameo model as XMI (tidewater.xmi), the DOORS modules as ReqIF and as CSV, the prime's change list (CHANGES.csv), and a manifest. From drop 4 on there are also the prime's test results. The manifest is the transmittal record. Read it first, every time:

It names the delivery (version, date, CDRL), who built it and with what (the prime's Jenkins job and build number, its repository commit, the tool versions), the change requests in this drop, and a SHA-256 checksum for every file. The checksums are what make "is this what was sent?" a question with a yes-or-no answer instead of an opinion. Check them before anyone opens a file:

(The tr -d '\r' is there because the prime's Windows build writes the manifest with Windows line endings; without it sha256sum looks for a file whose name ends in an invisible carriage return.) Every line must say OK. A single FAILED means the file is not what the prime's build produced: it was damaged in transit, edited on the way, or the manifest itself is wrong. Either way the drop is not imported. The team does not fix it; the prime sends it again.

Tip: Why a checksum and not a careful look

A checksum is a fingerprint of the file's exact bytes. Change one character anywhere in a 120 KB XMI file and the fingerprint changes completely. It is the same idea as the configuration audit's check that the delivered configuration matches the documented one, done by a program in a second instead of by a person in an afternoon.

45.3 Archive: keep it exactly as delivered

The received drop is evidence. Months later someone will ask "what exactly did the prime deliver on 2 April?", and the answer has to be the files themselves, not a converted copy that has since been edited. Tidewater keeps every drop in two places, neither of which anybody edits:

  • The vendor branch (vendor/prime) of the model repository. Each drop is converted there, as delivered, and committed with the raw files under imports/<version>/. Nobody commits anything else to that branch; its protection rule allows only the configuration manager to push, and nobody to merge into it. The vendor branch is the reason a new drop can be merged into a model the team has been editing: git compares the new drop with the old drop as converted, and carries only the prime's changes across. Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers explains the idea, and practice lesson 12 lets you do it.
  • The Generic Package Registry of the GitLab project, as prime-drop/<version>. The pipeline's drop-package job files every drop there automatically, with its checksum, so the CDRL deliverable sits next to the model it became and can be downloaded by version.

If your program's access rules for the prime's data differ from those for the model, the archive moves to its own restricted project and the model project references it by version. The loop stays the same.

45.4 Compare: what changed, element by element

Converting a drop is the easy part. The hard question is what changed since the last drop, because that is what the team has to assess. The converter answers it directly from the two XMI files, matching elements by the prime's IDs:

Read the first four lines before anything else. They say how big the change is, and they split it in two:

  • Carried by the converter. Re-converting the drop reproduces the change in SysML v2 text. The vendor-branch merge brings it across without anyone retyping it.
  • Manual. The converter does not carry this kind of element (state machines, interactions, constraint expressions, which it leaves as TODO lines). A person has to rework the government's v2 text by hand. These are the expensive changes, and the report lists them at the end as a checklist.

Drop 2 is all carried. Drop 3 is not. Its change to the buoy's operating modes (a new Storm state) sits inside a state machine, which the converter leaves as a TODO; the government team wrote the state machine by hand in sprint 6. Look at the manual list:

Five manual items, all inside BuoyModes: the Storm state, two transitions, and their two triggers. Without the element-level comparison this change would have been invisible: the converted v2 text of drop 3 is the same as drop 2's around the state machine, because both just say TODO there. A diff of the converted files would have shown nothing. This is the strongest argument for stable IDs and an element-level delta.

Note: Why compare v1 with v1, not v2 with v2

It is tempting to convert both drops and diff the SysML v2 text. That catches everything the converter carries and misses everything it does not, which is exactly the part that needs a person. The comparison has to happen on the prime's model, in the prime's terms, with the converter's coverage reported per change.

45.5 Assess: what does it touch in our model?

The delta says what changed in the prime's model. The change board needs to know what that touches in the government's model: which requirements, which verification cases, which interfaces, and which hand edits the team made that now need redoing. That is impact analysis, and it needs one more piece of information: where each of the prime's elements ended up in the government's v2 text.

The converter writes that as a map when it converts a drop. Start the government's model from drop 1, laid out in layers with the same layout map the team uses (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where), and keep the map:

Each row ties one of the prime's elements (its xmi_id) to the v2 name, kind, file and line it became. Now ask the question the board needs answered, for drop 2:

The summary is the change board's agenda in eight lines: three requirements touched (the new humidity requirement TW-SYS-017, the stakeholder need it derives from, and TW-SYS-006, whose wording the prime aligned with DOORS), two verification cases, one interface and one allocation, grouped under three of the prime's change requests. Above the summary, the full report walks through each change request with its rationale and every v2 element it touches, with file and line, so a reviewer can open exactly those lines.

45.5.1 Change requests: the prime's own reasons

Because the drop carries the prime's change list, the impact report is grouped by the prime's change requests rather than by element. That turns a list of forty element changes into three or four decisions:

Drop 5 has two change requests. NWM-CR-0024 adds a reserve term to the energy balance constraint, with a reason. NWM-CR-0025 renames the activity PublishBulletin to IssueBulletin, and the rationale column is empty. The impact report says so plainly:

A rename with no reason is not something to accept by reflex. Names in the model are referenced from requirement text, from test procedures, from the government's own hand-written behavior and from documents outside the model. The board needs to know why before it agrees. That case, a change request with no rationale, is the textbook reason for the "reject or clarify" disposition below.

45.5.2 Hand edits that need redoing

The most valuable line in the impact summary is the last one: hand edits to redo. The government team closes the converter's TODO lines by hand, writing the state machines, interactions and constraint expressions the converter could not carry. When the prime then changes one of those constructs, the vendor-branch merge brings nothing across (the converter carried nothing), and the team's hand-written version silently goes stale. The impact analysis looks for exactly that: a TODO line the converter would write, which is no longer in the government's model because someone replaced it.

Play the part of Bob in sprint 6, closing the BuoyModes TODO by hand:

Then drop 3 arrives, with the prime's new Storm state:

The report names the hand edit, the file and the line: Bob's state machine needs a Storm state, and nothing else in the loop would have said so. On Tidewater this became a task in the drop-3 intake story, assigned to the person who wrote the original edit.

45.6 Disposition: one issue per significant change

The impact report is the input to the change board. The board's output is a decision per change request, recorded where the work happens: in GitLab issues. Tidewater opens one issue per drop (the intake, from the Prime Drop template) and one issue per significant change request, labeled prime-change, with exactly one of four disposition labels:

Table 45.1. The four dispositions a change request can get
DispositionMeaningWhat happens next
disposition::acceptAccepted as deliveredThe vendor-branch merge brings it in; nothing more
disposition::accept-with-impactAccepted, and it adds government workLinked tasks for the extra work; the cost and schedule effect noted on the issue
disposition::reject-clarifyNot accepted yetA discrepancy report asks the prime for the rationale or a correction; the issue stays open until the prime answers
disposition::no-impactCosmeticNothing for the government model to do

On Tidewater, drop 4's drifting buoys were accepted with impact (new verification cases, a new part of the station segment to review); drop 5's unexplained rename was sent back for clarification; most change requests were simply accepted; and the documentation edits in drop 7 had no impact. Which drops and change requests got which disposition is part of the simulation's later sprints, and the counts belong to its evidence rather than to this page.

The issues themselves take a minute to open. Create a scratch GitLab and the project from the team's project file:

Then open the intake issue and one issue per change request, straight from the impact CSV the converter wrote:

Each disposition is a quick action in a comment, so the decision, who made it and when are all in the issue's history:

The deputy program manager concurs in a comment on the intake issue. That comment is the change board's minutes.

Objection: "This is a lot of ceremony for a sensor."

Tom raised it at the drop-2 intake: three issues and a board decision for one hygrometer and a requirement.

Answer

the ceremony is proportional. A drop with three change requests takes three issues and one twenty-minute conversation. The issues are generated from the impact report, so nobody types the list. And the record is what lets the team answer, six months later, "when did we accept the humidity requirement, and who agreed?" in one search instead of an archaeology project. When a drop is truly trivial, the board dispositions everything as accept in one comment, and the intake closes the same day.

45.6.1 prime-tbd: when you cannot wait for the drop

Sometimes the government team needs a change before the prime delivers it. In sprint 6 the team knew from the prime's modeler that a humidity sensor was coming, and Bob needed something in the model for the data exchange table. Waiting for drop 2 would have stalled the table for a month. So Bob modeled an interim HumiditySensor on develop, and the team opened an issue labeled prime-tbd: work that rests on an assumption about the prime's next drop, closed when the drop lands.

When drop 2 arrived, the vendor-branch merge conflicted exactly where Bob's interim sensor sat, which is the point: the conflict forces the decision. The team kept the prime's hygrometer, deleted the interim, and closed the prime-tbd issue in the same merge request. Practice lesson 12 replays that merge, and you can run its first steps here:

The conflict is the system working: two teams changed the same thing, and git stopped to ask a person which one wins. Finish the lesson to resolve it in Vim (agile.pl practice 12).

45.7 Implement, and report back

Accepted changes reach the government model through the normal merge request flow, nothing special:

  • The vendor-branch import and its merge into a feature/drop-<version> branch are done by the configuration manager (gitlab.pl flow vendor), and the merge request carries the delta and impact reports in its pipeline (the delta job runs on drop branches automatically).
  • Each hand edit to redo becomes a task, linked to its change request issue, and goes in on its own branch with its own review. The merge request description cites the prime's change request ID, so the history reads "Storm state added to BuoyModes (NWM-CR-0015)."
  • Conflicts are resolved upstream-first: the prime's version wins, then the government's edit is reapplied on top of it. Never the other way around, or the next drop will conflict again.

Problems the team finds go back to the prime as discrepancy reports: GitLab issues labeled type::discrepancy and owner::prime, transmitted through the contracting channel with the memo template in docs/memos/templates/ (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim), and kept open until a later drop fixes them. The prime's change requests cite them when they do, which closes the loop visibly. Drop 3's NWM-CR-0018 and NWM-CR-0019 say "Answers government DR" in their rationale; drop 4's NWM-CR-0022 brings TW-SYS-016 into the model in answer to another. The discrepancy report numbers in this paragraph are the ones the prime's change notes cite; the simulation's issue numbers for them are in its evidence.

45.7.1 Returning the government's model

The exchange runs both ways. When the prime needs the government's design data (at a baseline, or for an interface the government owns), the team returns it as a controlled deliverable: built from a baseline tag, never from a working branch, with a transmittal record just like an incoming drop. Here is the mechanics, on a scaffolded model repository:

On Tidewater the pipeline does this on every baseline tag (the publish-package job puts the archive, the verification matrix and the toolchain inventory in the package registry), and the transmittal memo goes out with it. Be honest with the prime about one limit: the kit has no SysML v2 to SysML v1 converter. The government returns SysML v2 text, the generated tables and the verification matrix. Whether the prime's Cameo can import SysML v2 text depends on the prime's tool version; settle it in the model exchange agreement, not on delivery day.

45.8 Two strategies at the v1-to-v2 boundary

Tidewater mirrors the prime's whole model: every drop is converted in full onto the vendor branch, and the government's model is that conversion plus the government's edits. There is a second strategy, and on many programs it is the better one.

Table 45.2. Mirroring the whole model versus translating only the interface surface
Full mirror (Tidewater)Interface surface
What is convertedthe whole v1 model, every droponly what you consume: your allocated requirements, your external interfaces, the parameters you depend on
Where it livesthe government model itself, layered foldersone generated package (for example model/external/prime/), never hand-edited
How your design uses ityou edit the converted text in place, closing TODO linesyour design satisfies and connects to elements of the generated package
What a new drop doesa 3-way merge on the vendor branch; conflicts where both sides editedthe package is regenerated; validate and trace checks show what broke
Best whenthe government needs the whole system model in v2 (the port is the goal)you are a subsystem or segment team consuming a prime's model

Tidewater chose the full mirror because the government's goal was the system model itself. It already uses the interface-surface pattern in one place: the DOORS modules. They are converted by script into model/requirements/ on every drop and never hand-edited; the government's design satisfies them. If your team owns a subsystem and the prime owns the system, start with the interface surface: it is smaller, the generated package never conflicts, and the boundary is explicit.

45.9 The prime's Jenkins: a delivery interface

Northwind builds its drops in Jenkins, a continuous integration server older than GitLab's and still common in industry. The government team uses GitLab. Nobody on Jim's team needs to run Jenkins, and the government never asks the prime to migrate. What the team does need is to understand what Jenkins hands them, and to agree how.

45.9.1 Jenkins in GitLab terms

Most Jenkins words have a GitLab counterpart. You need them to read the prime's build records and to talk to the prime's build engineer:

Table 45.3. Jenkins and GitLab, side by side
JenkinsGitLabIn systems-engineering words
Jenkinsfile.gitlab-ci.ymlthe procedure, written down and versioned
agent (a build machine, by label)runner (by tag)the bench the procedure runs on
stage / stepsstage / scriptthe procedure's sections and lines
environment { }variables:the procedure's settings
withCredentialsa masked CI/CD variablea credential handed over for one step, never written down
JUnit plugin (junit 'results.xml')artifacts: reports: junit:test results read into a trend
archiveArtifacts ... fingerprint: truejob artifacts, package registrythe delivered items, kept with their checksums
build number, job URLpipeline ID, pipeline URLthe record's serial number
shared workspace between stagesa fresh workspace per jobGitLab starts each job clean; pass files on as artifacts

The last row is the one that surprises people moving between the two: a Jenkins job usually keeps one working folder for all its stages, while GitLab gives each job a fresh checkout. Chapter 19, CI/CD from zero explains why.

45.9.2 Three ways a drop can arrive

From least to most automated, these are the delivery patterns a model exchange agreement can choose between:

  1. File delivery. The prime's Jenkins builds the drop and archives it; someone transfers the files under the CDRL to approved government storage; Tom runs the intake by hand. This is how Tidewater's first three drops arrived, and it is the right place to start: nobody has to grant anybody network access.
  2. Push into GitLab. The prime's Jenkins uploads the drop to the government project's Generic Package Registry, using a deploy token that can do nothing but write packages, and then fires a pipeline trigger with the drop's version. The government's intake job runs on its own. Tidewater switched to this from drop 4.
  3. GitLab pulls from Jenkins. A scheduled government job fetches the prime's last successful build over the prime's API. Possible, and usually blocked: it needs a network path from the government enclave into the contractor's, and credentials for the prime's server held by the government. Few security officers approve it.

The illustrative Jenkinsfile in the kit shows what pattern 2 looks like on the prime's side. The kit does not run it (there is no Jenkins here); read it for the shape:

45.9.3 Two tokens, each able to do one thing

Pattern 2 needs two credentials, created by a maintainer of the government project and handed to the prime through the contracting channel. Each can do exactly one thing, and each expires:

The deploy token can upload packages. It cannot read the model, push code, open issues or see anything else. If it leaks, the worst an attacker can do is upload a fake drop, which the intake job will reject because its checksums will not match the manifest the prime's build wrote.

The trigger token can start a pipeline and pass it variables. It cannot change anything. The triggered pipeline runs the government's own intake job, as the token's owner, with the government's rules. Both tokens live in Jenkins' credential store on the prime's side, and in the government's token inventory (Section 42.4, Tokens and rotation) with an owner and an expiry date.

With the deploy token, the prime's build uploads the drop; in the scratch GitLab you can play that part:

45.9.4 The intake job: the government's gate

The triggered pipeline runs one job: intake. It is in the team's pipeline file, and short:

It fetches every file of the drop, checks each one against the checksum in the manifest the prime's build wrote, keeps the drop as received (an artifact that never expires: it is formal evidence), and opens the Prime Drop issue. A green build on the prime's side is evidence that the prime's checks passed. It is not acceptance. Acceptance is the government's own gates on the import merge request, and the board's disposition.

You can run the intake exactly as the trigger would, locally, against a folder instead of the registry. It needs a model repository with the team's pipeline, which the scaffold you made above has:

Now the case the intake exists for: a file changed somewhere between the prime's build and the government. One line added to the XMI, the kind of edit nobody would notice by eye:

The pipeline fails, the log names the file and both checksums, and the drop is not imported. The team tells the prime, and the prime's build sends it again. Nobody spends an afternoon working out what changed.

45.9.5 The ICD between the two pipelines

Everything above is an interface between two organizations' processes, and it deserves the same treatment as any other interface: written down, agreed, and changed under control. Tidewater's version is a section of the model exchange agreement. Its checklist, which you can lift for your own program:

Checklist: The pipeline interface, agreed with the prime
  • ☐ What crosses: the file list per drop (XMI, ReqIF, CSV, CHANGES.csv, results, MANIFEST.txt)
  • ☐ Formats and versions: Cameo version and export settings (stable IDs on), DOORS export options
  • ☐ The manifest fields: version, date, CDRL, Jenkins job URL and build number, prime repository commit, tool versions, a checksum per file, the change requests
  • ☐ How it crosses: file delivery, or registry upload plus trigger (and who may change the pattern)
  • ☐ Who holds which credential: the deploy token and the trigger token, their scopes, expiry and rotation
  • ☐ What the government does on receipt: the intake checks, the board, the disposition time
  • ☐ What happens when something is wrong: rejected drop, resend, discrepancy reports and their return path
  • ☐ Markings: the prime's proprietary and export markings, preserved through every conversion

45.10 Cautions

A few things went wrong, or nearly did, on Tidewater and on programs like it:

  • You will probably still need a Cameo seat. If the prime delivers .mdzip project files instead of XMI, or if an export goes wrong and someone has to look at the original, the government needs at least one Cameo licence to open it. Budget for one during the transition rather than discovering the need on drop day. The model exchange agreement should ask for XMI and ReqIF so the seat is rarely used.
  • The prime's markings travel with the data. Proprietary and export-control markings in the prime's model apply to every conversion of it: the v2 text, the generated documents, the packages. Preserve them, mark the vendor branch and the archive accordingly, and restrict access to the people the markings allow. If those people are fewer than the model team, the archive goes in its own project (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system).
  • Don't freeze waiting for the prime. If a drop is late, keep working against the last accepted one, and record every assumption about the next drop as a prime-tbd issue. The conflict at the next merge will make the team revisit each one.
  • Never edit the vendor branch by hand. It is tempting to "just fix" a converter quirk there. The next drop's import overwrites it, or worse, merges around it. Fix converter problems in the converter, and government changes on develop.
  • Keep the drop loop's records in GitLab, not in email. The intake issue, the change-request issues, the dispositions and the discrepancy reports are the configuration management record of the boundary. An email thread with the prime's modeler is fine for the conversation; the decision goes in the issue.

45.11 Applying this to your project

  • Before the first drop: get the three contract answers in writing, write the model exchange agreement, and ask for stable IDs and change notes. Those two requests cost the supplier almost nothing and make everything else in this chapter possible.
  • Choose your boundary strategy: full mirror if the model itself is your deliverable, interface surface if you consume someone else's model.
  • Start with file delivery, move to registry-and-trigger once the intake job has proven itself on a few drops.
  • Copy the six steps (receive, archive, compare, assess, disposition, implement) and the four disposition labels. The tools are in the kit; the discipline is the change board meeting on every drop.
  • Measure the loop: the time from delivery to merged on the integration branch, the share of change requests with a disposition within a week, and the open discrepancy reports. These are the numbers that tell management the boundary is under control.
Exercise 45.1: Read a drop like a change board

Generate drops 3 and 4 (perl "$KIT/sim/tidewater-v1.pl" --drop N DIR) and run the delta between them with --impact against a model converted from drop 3. For each change request, propose a disposition and write one sentence of justification. Which change adds government work, and what work?

Exercise 45.2: Write the clarification

Draft the discrepancy report for NWM-CR-0025 (the rename with no rationale) from the Discrepancy Report issue template: what you need from the prime, why the rename matters to the government model, and by which drop you need the answer.

Exercise 45.3: Break the intake on purpose

Copy a drop, change one character in tidewater.reqif, and run the intake job locally against the copy. Then fix the copy by regenerating the file instead. What does the intake report each time, and why is "regenerate" the only acceptable fix?

Exercise 45.4: Choose a strategy

Your team owns the data center segment; the prime owns the system model. Sketch which elements of the Tidewater model would go in an external/prime package under the interface-surface strategy, and which the data center team would own.

46 Systems engineering work, not pipeline work

From what you know

You know

the engineering itself: requirements, architecture, interfaces, analyses and verification.

Here it is called

work::engineering, as distinct from work::platform and work::learning.

What is new

the board shows how much of the team's time goes to engineering, sprint by sprint.

Survival kit: The work is the engineering

What you have

a backlog full of stories, and a nagging feeling that too many of them are about GitLab, runners and YAML, and too few are about the system.

What you need

a clear line between systems engineering work (deciding and proving what the system is) and platform work (building and keeping the machinery that checks and renders it), a way to see the balance sprint by sprint, and a catalog of real engineering stories to fill the backlog with once the machinery runs.

46.1 The line

Bob asked the question in the second sprint, and the question was a fair one:

Two sprints in, and I have written a pipeline description, a runner request and a branching guide. When do I do systems engineering again?

— Bob, sprint 2

It is the right question, and the answer has to be a number, not a reassurance. Every story on the Tidewater board carries one of three labels:

Definitions: The three kinds of work

work::engineering: deciding or proving what the system is. Requirements, architecture, interfaces, behavior, analysis, verification, change decisions. The output is model content or an engineering judgment someone signs. work::platform: building or keeping the machinery that checks, renders and protects the model. Pipelines, runners, GitLab settings, templates, access, the kit version. The output is a working tool. work::learning: becoming able to do either. Practice lessons, chapters of this book, pairing at the terminal. The output is a person who can do something they could not do last sprint.

A quick test for a story you are not sure about: would a systems engineer from the document era recognize the output as engineering? A closed TODO line that adds @L2Segment; to a part: yes, it is a configuration decision about the system's structure. A new pipeline job that counts TODO lines: no, it is a tool, however useful. A data exchange table generated from the interface items: yes, it is the interface control document, produced differently. Deciding who owns ObservationRecord so a dependency cycle can be broken: very much yes, it is an architecture decision.

The label is not a value judgment. Platform work is how the engineering becomes cheap to check, and learning is how a team that had never seen a merge request learned to run one. The point of the label is to make the balance visible, so that platform and learning shrink as they should, and so that nobody has to argue from feelings.

46.2 The balance, sprint by sprint

The split comes straight out of the plan file the simulation runs (sim/tidewater-plan.pl), so it cannot be rounded in anyone's favour:

The shape is the one to aim for. In the first two sprints platform and learning take most of the points: there is a project to create, a runner to get approved, three laptops to set up, git and Vim to learn. From sprint 3 engineering takes the larger share, and by sprint 6 most of the work is engineering again, which is the answer to Bob's question, and the one to give with these numbers on the screen. GitLab can show the same split live: filter the board or the issue list by work::engineering, and the milestone page sums the points.

Two warnings about the number. It is a planning measure, not a productivity score: a sprint that is half platform because the runner died is a sprint that kept the team working. And it does not go to zero: maintenance sprints still carry a story or two of platform work (a runner upgrade, a token rotation, a kit version bump), which is how the machinery stays trustworthy.

The work is the disposition: which of the prime's changes the government accepts, which it questions, which cost money, and what each one does to requirements and verification. 46.5 A generic catalog for your project

The catalog below is the pattern to build your own backlog from. It follows a list of thirty-eight planned-work items collected while this book was written, from a small team modeling a different system; the list mixed engineering and platform work in roughly the proportion a team reaches after its first semester, which is itself a useful benchmark. Each line is a story title, the model change, and the check that makes it done.

46.5.1 Concept and requirements

  • Capture stakeholder needs from the concept of operations. A requirements package per stakeholder group, each need tagged with its source document. Check: the package resolves (lint).
  • Define the top-level use cases. A use case per mission thread, with actors and objectives. Check: a generated use-case table for the customer walkthrough.
  • Derive system requirements from the needs. Requirements with measurable constraints and derivation links. Check: the trace fails any system requirement without a parent.
  • Add a requirement metadata schema. Verification method, priority, owner, status as metadata. Check: a job fails a requirement missing a required field.
  • Import the legacy requirements spreadsheet. A script that turns the CSV into requirement text, run once, kept for the next import. Check: the merge request's diff, reviewed.
  • Establish the units and quantities library. Shared value types on ISQ quantities; requirements refactored to use them. Check: lint (no unresolved types).

46.5.2 Architecture

  • Define the logical decomposition. Part definitions for the function blocks, composed into the system context. Check: the part tree view.
  • Model a subsystem's interfaces. Port and interface definitions, connections, a satisfy to the interface requirement, a verification case stub. Check: trace coverage for the subsystem.
  • Allocate functions to physical components. Allocations at the agreed level. Check: the trace flags unallocated functions.
  • Model the power subsystem and its budget. Power draw per part and a roll-up per mode. Check: a job fails when a mode exceeds supply.
  • Model the mass properties. Mass with margin per part, rolled up. Check: the mass report.
  • Model the data bus and its messages. Item definitions with fields and rates. Check: the generated ICD table.
  • Model the thermal interfaces. Heat flows and dissipation. Check: the values handed to the thermal team as a file.
  • Define an external interface. The external system as a part, with the agreed protocol and timing. Check: the interface lead is a code owner of the package.

46.5.3 Behavior

  • Model the operating modes. A state definition with transitions and guards, linked to the budgets per mode. Check: grammar and lint; the budgets run per mode.
  • Model the startup sequence. An action with ordered steps and timing. Check: total startup time against its requirement.
  • Model fault detection and recovery. Fault states and recovery actions, each linked to the hazard it mitigates. Check: a fault-to-response table for the safety review.
  • Model the end-to-end data timeline. Latency on each step. Check: the sum against the end-to-end requirement.

46.5.4 Analysis and trades

  • Run a trade study. Candidate variants with their attributes and a weighted scoring. Check: the trade table.
  • Hook up an external simulation. A wrapper that reads parameters from the model, runs the simulation, writes results back. Check: the job's artifact.
  • Allocate reliability. Failure rates and a series-parallel roll-up. Check: a job fails below the requirement.
  • Run a sensitivity analysis. Sweep the key parameters through a budget. Check: the chart for the review package.

46.5.5 Verification

  • Write the verification cases for a subsystem. A case per requirement with method, objective and criteria. Check: verify coverage for the subsystem reaches 100%.
  • Ingest test results. A script that maps results to verification cases. Check: the VCRM regenerates.
  • Record analysis and inspection verdicts. A signed results format for what is not automated. Check: the VCRM merges them.

46.5.6 Baselines and sustainment

  • Prepare a review baseline. Close the trace gaps, defer what remains, all checks green. Check: the baseline tag and its document set.
  • Process an engineering change after a review. The change, its impact report and the change-board approval on the merge request. Check: a minor baseline tag.
  • Branch for a delivered configuration. A protected release branch from the qualification tag; fixes land upstream first. Check: the branch rules.
  • Model a field discrepancy and its fix. The discrepancy linked to parts and verification cases, a regression case added. Check: the regression passes on both branches.
  • Retire obsolete requirements. Mark them retired rather than deleting them. Check: coverage metrics exclude them.

46.5.7 And the platform items in the same list

Model style checks; generating the review document package; pinning the tool image; enabling secret and dependency scans; code owners per subsystem; an impact report posted on each merge request. Six of thirty-eight: about one in six. That is roughly the steady state to expect once the machinery exists, and a useful target when you plan the second semester.

46.6 Splitting an engineering story into tasks

A story fits in a sprint; a task fits in a week, at most five points (Chapter 13, The operating model). Engineering stories split along the engineering, not along the tools. "Close the Stations level tags", split by what an engineer decides, could look like this:

  1. Tag the segment and the station parts (L2, L3): 1 point. The levels everyone agrees on.
  2. Tag the subsystems and assemblies (L4, L5): 1 point. Where the v1 profile is most often inconsistent, and a question to the prime's modeler may be needed.
  3. Tag the components (L6) and run the level check: 1 point. The leaves, and the proof.

A split along the tools ("edit the file", "run lint", "open the MR") produces tasks nobody can demo and nobody can estimate. A split along the decisions produces tasks a reviewer can check one at a time.

46.7 Applying this to your project

  • Label every story work::engineering, work::platform or work::learning from the first sprint, and show the split at every review. The trend answers "when do we do engineering again?" better than any promise.
  • Expect the first two sprints to be mostly platform and learning, and say so to management before they start.
  • Fill the backlog from the catalog, starting with the requirements and architecture stories your converted model already demands: every TODO line is an engineering decision waiting for a story.
  • Look for the engineering inside tooling-shaped stories (prime drops, baselines, hotfixes) and label them by their decisions, not their commands.
Exercise 46.1: Label your backlog

Take the next ten stories in your backlog (or Tidewater's sprint 7 plan in sim/tidewater-plan.pl) and give each one of the three labels. For every story you labelled platform, write one sentence naming the engineering story it makes cheaper. If you cannot, ask whether the story is needed now.

Exercise 46.2: Split along the decisions

Split "Break the Stations to DataCenter cycle" into tasks of at most five points each, along the decisions an engineer makes rather than the commands they type. Compare your split with the plan's.

47 Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web

From what you know

You know

the Cameo model that grew into a spider web.

Here it is called

layering, ownership, complexity metrics and gates.

What is new

the pipeline measures the tangle on every change and refuses changes that make it worse.

Survival kit: Where this chapter fits

What you have

a v2 model that started life as a converted v1 spider web (Chapter 2, The Cameo years), a pipeline, and a team that now changes the model every day.

What you need

the practices that stop a text model from growing the same web, which of them Tidewater already follows, and a way to measure the web so you notice it growing.

Bob's objection in Chapter 3, The directive -- "we already did this once, and it gave us a spider web" -- deserves a better answer than "SysML v2 is different". SysML v2 text does not prevent a spider web. A text model can be just as tangled as a diagram model; it is only easier to see the tangle and to stop it growing. This chapter is about the seeing and the stopping.

47.1 How tangled was v1, and how tangled is v2?

The v1 model the prime delivered measures itself when the drop is generated. Run it on drop 1:

The v2 model at the end of sprint 6 is measured by the pipeline's complexity job. Run it on develop in Bob's clone of the simulation:

Table 47.1. The spider web measured, v1 against v2. v1 numbers from the drop's own measures; v2 from the complexity job. The cycle row compares two different counts of the same tangle (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text explains the three ways to count it).
Measurev1, drop 1 (Cameo)v2, end of sprint 6
Package cycles2 pairs of packages that depend on each other (DataCenter and Stations; Network and Operations)1 tangled group (the complexity job's count: DataCenter and Stations)
Most relationship ends on one part definition14 (ObservingStation)8
Largest package fan-outnot measured in v13
Hand-drawn diagrams to keep current47, some stalenone: every view is generated
Unused and duplicated blocks (the Legacy Import clutter)4 unused, 2 duplicatedremoved from the v2 model in sprint 5

Two things in that table need a word. First, one cycle is still there: Network and Operations was broken in sprint 4 (story TW-69); DataCenter and Stations was not planned for the first twelve weeks and is still on the backlog. Second, the complexity job reports a large number of duplicates -- 29 -- which is not clutter. It counts requirement names defined twice: once in the Cameo copy of the requirements the XMI carries and once in the DOORS conversion. That is a known, deliberate duplication while DOORS stays the authoritative source; the job reports it so nobody mistakes one copy for the other.

The package view draws the same web for people (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text):

The view counts dashed arrows: six in this flat-layout figure, four in the layered layout. The job counts tangled groups: one on drop 1. Use the job's number for the trend and the picture for the conversation.

47.2 Twenty practices

These are the practices that keep a model untangled, grouped as the user's reference grouped them. Each is marked applied (Tidewater does it), adapted (Tidewater does a version of it, for a stated reason) or later (not in the first twelve weeks, with when it would make sense).

47.2.1 Structure

Table 47.2. Structure practices.
PracticeTidewaterHow
1. Layer the model; dependencies point one way onlyAppliedFolders by layer (library, requirements, logical, physical, analysis, verification) from the layout map at drop 1 (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where); the complexity job reports any upward dependency.
2. Modularize by ownershipAppliedOne folder per subsystem under physical/; CODEOWNERS maps each folder to its owner.
3. Explicit, narrow importsAdaptedGovernment-written files may not use wildcard imports (the job counts them). Files converted from the prime's drops keep the converter's wildcard imports: editing them would make every new drop conflict.
4. Federate into several projects when the model outgrows one teamLaterOne three-person team, one project. Split along the layers when a second team or an outside consumer appears (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where).

47.2.2 Reuse and abstraction

Table 47.3. Reuse practices.
PracticeTidewaterHow
5. Separate definitions from usagesAppliedThe converter writes part, port and interface definitions and uses them as typed usages.
6. A versioned project libraryAdaptedmodel/library/ holds the conventions, value types and interfaces, versioned with the model's baselines; publishing it as its own package comes with federation.
7. Interfaces as contracts at subsystem boundariesAppliedPort and interface definitions in the library; subsystems connect through them.
8. Model variability explicitlyLaterNo variants in the first twelve weeks; the drifting buoy in drop 4 arrives as a specialization of the station, and variant modeling is the planned way to handle more.

PracticeTidewaterHow
9. Trace at the right granularityAdaptedObservingStation's trace spaghetti was pruned in sprint 5; the remaining links are the prime's to rationalize, raised as a discrepancy report.

Table 47.5. View practices.
