12. Diagrams and documents are generated viewsAppliedmodel.pl draw and the model site; no diagram is drawn by hand (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text).
13. Standard viewpoints per stakeholderAdaptedThe model site for management, the VCRM for test, the data exchange table for interface owners; formal view def elements in the model come later.

47.2.5 Semantics and metadata

Table 47.6. Semantics practices.
PracticeTidewaterHow
14. Metadata instead of stereotype sprawlAppliedThe v1 profile's stereotypes became a handful of metadata definitions in the Conventions package.
15. Executable constraints over proseLaterThe energy-balance constraint is still a converter TODO at the end of sprint 6; writing it and evaluating it in the pipeline belong to the engineering epic after the port.

47.2.6 Process guardrails

Table 47.7. Process practices.
PracticeTidewaterHow
16. Automate complexity metrics with thresholdsAdaptedThe measures are on the scorecard every sprint; the complexity job as a merge-request gate (a ratchet: fail only when a measure gets worse) is planned after sprint 6, so the first twelve weeks stayed lean (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).
17. Small, reviewable changesAppliedOne issue, one branch, one merge request; the sprint 3 retrospective added "split MRs before they reach 300 lines".
18. Refactor continuouslyAppliedCycle breaking, the Legacy Import clean-up and the trace pruning were planned stories with points, not spare-time work.
19. Tool-neutral text as the source of truthAppliedThe .sysml text in git is the model; everything else is generated from it.
20. Architecture decision recordsAppliedDecisions D-1 to D-10 as ADRs in docs/adr/ from sprint 2.

47.3 Why the web grows, and how the guardrails stop it

A spider web is never designed. It grows one link at a time, each link reasonable when it is made: a trace "just to be safe", an import of a whole package to reach one definition, a copy of a block "for now". In the Cameo years the links were made in diagrams, nobody saw the whole, and nothing measured it until the model was too tangled to change.

The guardrails above work because they act at the moment a link is made. A wildcard import in a government file is counted on the merge request that adds it. An upward dependency is reported before it merges. A new cycle shows up in the complexity report the same day. None of these checks is clever; what matters is that they run on every change, so the web cannot grow unnoticed. The other half is the work: the cycle break and the clean-up stories were in the backlog with points (Chapter 46, Systems engineering work, not pipeline work), not left to good intentions.

Exercise 47.1: Measure a model you own

Run the complexity job (or the package view) on a model you work on. Which package has the largest fan-out? Is there a cycle? For each one, write down whether it is a real engineering dependency or an accident of how the model was built.

Exercise 47.2: Mark the twenty practices for your project

Copy the tables above and mark each practice applied, adapted or later for your own project, with one line on why. Which three would make the biggest difference in the next sprint?

47.4 You can now

  • Measure a model's tangle -- cycles, fan-out, relationships per part, duplicates -- and read what each number means.
  • Explain why a text model can still become a spider web, and which guardrails stop it.
  • Decide which of the twenty practices to apply now and which to defer, with a reason for each.

47.5 Applying this to your project

Copy the layering, the ownership folders, the generated views and the decision records from the first sprint; they cost almost nothing and are hard to add later. Adapt the import rule to how your model arrives: if most of it is converted from someone else's tool, keep their files as delivered and hold your own files to the stricter rule. Decide locally when to turn the complexity measures into a merge-request gate -- after the inherited web is measured and the team has seen the numbers for a few sprints.

48 Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system

From what you know

You know

the ISSM, the security classification guide, marked documents and the authorization package.

Here it is called

protecting the engineering environment, and engineering security into the system.

What is new

markings, secret scanning and security requirements are checked in the pipeline, not only at accreditation.

Survival kit: Two kinds of security

What you have

a GitLab project, a runner, a model, and an ISSM who has started asking questions. You also have a system to design, which will one day face people who want to misuse it.

What you need

to see that "security" means two different jobs. One is protecting the place where the engineering happens: the repository, the pipeline, the laptops, the data. The other is engineering security into the system itself: requirements, trust boundaries, threats, verification. Small teams usually do the first, because the ISSM insists, and forget the second, because nobody asks until the review where everyone asks.

48.1 Why the second half gets forgotten

On Tidewater, "security" arrived in sprint 2 as a meeting with the ISSM about the runner. For the next six weeks it meant hardening checklists, service accounts, secret scanning and a tabletop exercise. All of that was necessary. None of it said anything about whether a spoofed buoy could feed false observations into the marine bulletin, which is the security question a mariner would ask.

That is the normal pattern. The environment half has an owner from day one (the ISSM, who must authorize the toolchain) and a deadline (no authorization, no GitLab). The system half has neither: it lives in the requirements, the architecture and the verification plan, which the program assumes "the engineers" will get to. In the document era it got done, if at all, in a security annex written near the end. In a model it can be done the way everything else is: as model content, checked by the pipeline on every change.

This chapter walks through twenty-six points, from a note Jim kept from a program security briefing, and marks each one for Tidewater as applied (done in the first year), adapted (done in a reduced or different form, with the reason), or LATER (planned, with the sprint or epic). Tidewater is a civilian, notional program and nothing in it is sensitive, so some points are taught here as general practice for programs that are. The table at the end (Section 48.8, The twenty-six points at a glance) lists all twenty-six.

48.2 Half one: protecting the engineering environment

48.2.1 Data classification and handling

1. Know what the model contains, before the first commit. Requirements, interface details and performance parameters can be controlled information, export-controlled, or classified. Decide the handling level with the security office before anything is committed, because a repository cannot be made "less sensitive" afterwards: its history keeps every version. Tidewater: applied. The decision is a decision record, "Data handling and markings", written by Jim with the ISSM in week zero and committed before the first drop was imported. It says the content is notional and unmarked, and it names the conditions that would change that (any real performance parameter, any real site).

2. Watch for aggregation. A model's purpose is to pull scattered facts into one connected, queryable whole. Individually harmless facts can become sensitive together: the list of every station, its location, its power budget and its link schedule says more than any one document did. Tidewater: adapted. There is no real content to aggregate, but the habit is practised: the ISSM reviews the model as a whole before each baseline is tagged, not one merge request at a time. Add that review to your release checklist; it is not in the kit's templates by default.

3. Mark at the package level, and let the pipeline enforce it. Use a metadata definition for markings, put one on every package, and let the pipeline fail a model with an unmarked package; generated documents then carry the right banner because the generator reads the marking. The kit ships this: the SecMeta vocabulary and model.pl gate, shown working in Section 48.5, A worked example: the security gate. Tidewater: LATER, in the maintenance tome: the story "Markings on every package; model.pl gate in the pipeline". Until then every package is notional and unmarked by decision (the data-handling record), which is itself a marking decision on record.

4. Separate by sensitivity. When parts of a system sit at different handling levels, split them into separate repositories on networks accredited for each level. Access controls inside one repository are not a separation mechanism. Tidewater: adapted. One repository is enough because everything is at one level. The option is recorded in the data-handling decision: if the prime's drops ever carry markings the team's repository is not approved for, the drops move to a separate, restricted project and are referenced by tag. Write the same clause into your model exchange agreement with the prime.

48.2.2 Platform and access

5. Self-host on an accredited network. GitLab and its runners run inside the program's enclave; shared cloud runners and software-as-a-service tools are out for controlled data unless specifically authorized. Tidewater: applied. The project lives on the enterprise GitLab, and the runner is a project runner on a government Windows VM (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs).

6. Least privilege. Roles scoped to need: Jim and Tom are maintainers, Bob is a developer. main and develop are protected, merges need a code owner's approval, and nobody pushes to them directly. Membership is reviewed when someone joins or leaves. Tidewater: applied (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab, Chapter 42, Administration).

7. Strong authentication. Enterprise single sign-on with multi-factor or PKI for the web interface; SSH keys or short-lived tokens for git; no long-lived personal access tokens in scripts. Tidewater: applied. Project access tokens carry an expiry date and a single scope, and their rotation is a recurring task in Chapter 42, Administration.

8. Sign commits and tags. A signed baseline tag proves who approved which configuration. That is configuration management evidence first and security second. Git can sign with an SSH key, which every laptop already has from Chapter 9, The survival kit, so there is nothing extra to install. Tidewater: LATER, the story "Signed baseline tags" in the maintenance tome. The mechanics take one minute and are shown in Section 48.6, Signing a baseline tag.

48.2.3 Pipeline and supply chain

9. Treat runners as privileged. A runner sees every file of every job it runs and every variable those jobs use. Harden it, run it as a service account with no other rights, and keep jobs that hold secrets (release, package upload, Pages) on a protected runner that only protected branches and tags can use. Tidewater: applied (runner hardening with the ISSM in sprint 3; the protected runner in Chapter 42, Administration).

10. Pin and vet the tools. Use specific versions, from internal mirrors where the network requires it, never "latest" pulled from the internet, and keep an inventory of the tools that produced each baseline. Tidewater: adapted. The kit is pinned by version in the model repository (.kit-version, checked by every job), each baseline's evidence includes toolchain.txt (kit version, Perl, git, operating system, runner), and the optional Docker image is pinned by digest (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs). There is no internal package mirror because the kit needs no packages.

11. Manage secrets properly. Masked, protected CI/CD variables; a secret-detection job on every change; and when something leaks, rotate it at once, because deleting the commit is not enough. Tidewater: applied. The secrets job runs from sprint 3, GitLab's managed Secret Detection runs where a Docker runner exists, and the recipe is in Section E.13, "I pushed a secret".

12. Scan your own code. The team's tooling gets the same treatment as any software. Tidewater: adapted. The team writes almost no code of its own: ci/job.pl and the kit's tools are tested in the kit's own pipeline, on both Perls, before a kit version is pinned. Static analysis and dependency scanning are not used, because there are no dependencies to scan (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep lists the features deliberately left off).

13. Retain artifacts deliberately. Keep formal evidence for the life of the program; let everything else expire, because a throwaway artifact can still contain something sensitive. Tidewater: applied. Baseline audits, the verification matrix at each baseline, and each prime drop as received are kept with expire_in: never; every other artifact uses the project's default expiry (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

48.2.4 AI tools

14. Keep model content out of external AI services. Only models approved for the data's handling level, which in practice means a local model on the laptop or an approved server inside the enclave, and only after the model's origin has been checked against policy. Tidewater: applied (no cloud AI; the local assistant goes through approval first, Chapter 18, A local AI assistant on the laptop).

15. Treat AI output as untrusted input. Generated text goes through the same gates and the same review as anything a person writes, and the merge request says so with the ai::assisted label. Tidewater: applied.

48.3 Half two: engineering security into the system

The second half is systems engineering, not administration. Every point below is model content: something you write in .sysml text, review in a merge request, and check in the pipeline. That makes it the same kind of work as a power budget or an interface, which is the argument for doing it in the model instead of an annex.

16. Security requirements are requirements. Confidentiality, integrity, availability and authentication requirements, derived from the threat analysis and the program's control baseline, with the same trace and verification coverage as any other requirement. Tidewater: LATER. The requirements belong to the prime's DOORS modules, so the government raises them as discrepancy reports, and they arrive as TW-SEC-* requirements in a later drop (the story "Security requirements TW-SEC through DRs to the prime").

17. Model threats and trust boundaries. Mark each part with the trust zone it sits in. Every interface that crosses from one zone to another is a boundary crossing, and each crossing must trace to a security requirement that covers it. Each threat in the register names the asset it attacks and the requirement that mitigates it. The kit's model.pl gate checks both rules (Section 48.5, A worked example: the security gate). Tidewater: LATER (stories "Trust zones on the part tree" and "A notional threat register"), and demonstrated now on a small model.

18. Model data flows with their sensitivity. Tag item definitions (the things that flow) with their handling level, and check that sensitive data never flows through an interface not rated for it. Tidewater: LATER, not planned. All Tidewater data is public weather data; the pattern is the package-marking pattern applied to item definitions.

19. Behavior under attack. Model what the system does when it detects an attack: detect, contain, degrade gracefully, beside the fault-recovery behavior. Tidewater: LATER, for the observation ingest path: what the data center does with records from a station that fails authentication.

20. Plan security verification. Verification cases for authentication, signing and access-control tests, with their results in the same verification matrix as everything else. Tidewater: LATER (the story "Security verification cases in the VCRM").

21. Generate certification evidence. An authorization package needs traceability from controls to design to test evidence. If the model already traces them, the pipeline produces most of that package: the gate's report, the trace report and the verification matrix at a baseline tag are evidence nobody assembles by hand. Tidewater: adapted. The baseline evidence includes the trace and the verification matrix; there is no authorization package for Tidewater's system because it is notional.

22. Model the supply chain. Record where components come from, so a counterfeit or provenance concern can be traced to the parts it affects. Tidewater: applied. The prime's model already carried a Procured stereotype with supplier and part number; the port turned it into @Procured metadata in sprint 5, so a question about a supplier is one search.

48.4 Process

23. Name a security owner. On a small team one person owns the security requirements, the threat model and the pipeline's security posture, part-time, so that "someone" means someone. Tidewater: applied. Tom, named in week zero, with the ISSM as the authority.

24. Bring the ISSM in before standing up the toolchain. Retrofitting an authorization onto a running pipeline is painful. Tidewater: applied. The ISSM was contacted in week zero, the toolchain review started in sprint 2, and the runner hardening in sprint 3 was done with the ISSM, which is also why sprint 3 had a three-day block waiting for the ISSM's calendar. That block was the cheap version of the lesson.

25. Use frameworks as checklists. The NIST SP 800-53 control baseline under the Risk Management Framework, NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC for controlled unclassified information, NIST SP 800-218 (the Secure Software Development Framework), and the DoD Enterprise DevSecOps reference design. Nobody implements all of them on day one; read them as checklists that stop you missing a whole category. Tidewater: adapted. They are used as checklists in the quarterly access and toolchain reviews (Chapter 42, Administration); this book does not restate their contents, and your ISSM will tell you which ones apply.

26. Rehearse incidents. The most likely serious incident for a modeling team is marked information pushed to the wrong place (spillage), and the response is time-critical. Tidewater: applied. A one-point tabletop exercise in sprint 5, Jim and Tom with the ISSM; the script is below (Section 48.7, The spillage tabletop).

48.5 A worked example: the security gate

This example builds a small Tidewater model in a scratch folder: a buoy in the untrusted zone, the data center in the trusted zone, a public site in between, one security requirement, two threats. It is notional and tiny, so that every line can be read. The security vocabulary comes from the kit (a copy ships with the Halberd example model); its comments are stripped on the way in.

Three things in that text are security engineering, not decoration:

  • @TrustZone { zone = Zone::untrusted; } on MooredBuoy says where the part sits. A buoy at sea is untrusted: anyone with a radio in range can talk to it.
  • The two interface lines are the boundary crossings. Each names the zone at both ends and the security requirement that covers it (secReq). The publication link to the public site has none yet.
  • The threat register has two entries, each with its STRIDE category and CAPEC identifier; one is mitigated by secR01, the other by nothing yet.

Now the gate. It runs five checks: the text, the trace, the markings, the zones and the threats, and it fails if any of them finds an error.

Two findings, both real security work, neither a typing mistake:

  • the publication link crosses from the trusted data center into the semi-trusted public zone with no requirement covering it;
  • the bulletin-tampering threat has no mitigation.

The fix is engineering: a requirement that the data center signs every bulletin it publishes, which covers the crossing and mitigates the threat at once, satisfied by the data center and verified by an inspection.

(In real work you would make these edits in Vim, not with sed; the commands are here so the book can be tested.)

Finally, the marking rule. Remove the marking from one package and the gate stops it, which is point 3 working:

model.pl gate also draws what it checked, if you ask: --svg DIR writes the package view with each package's marking and the interconnection view with the zones shaded, which is the picture the ISSM wants at a review (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text). The kit's Halberd example model (examples/halberd) carries the same vocabulary at full size, with planted gaps, if you want a larger model to read.

48.6 Signing a baseline tag

A signed tag records, cryptographically, who created it. Git can sign with an SSH key, so the key you already use for GitLab can sign baselines. This example uses a fresh key in a scratch repository; on the project, the signing key and the list of allowed signers are set up once by the security owner.

GitLab shows a Verified badge on a signed tag or commit when the signing key is registered on the signer's profile. The allowed-signers file is what lets anyone check a signature offline, years later, without GitLab.

48.7 The spillage tabletop

A tabletop exercise is a meeting in which you walk through an incident that has not happened, out loud, with the people who would handle it. Tidewater's took one point of Jim's and Tom's time in sprint 5, with the ISSM. The scenario:

Thursday, 14:10. Bob notices that a file pushed to Bob's feature branch an hour ago contains a paragraph pasted from a marked document. The merge request is open; the pipeline ran; GitLab sent notification e-mails to Jim and Tom.

The questions the ISSM asked, and the answers the team wrote down:

  1. What does Bob do first? Stops. Does not delete the branch, does not force-push, does not edit the file "to make it go away": all of those spread or destroy evidence. Calls Tom (security owner) and the ISSM, in that order, by phone.
  2. Who else has a copy? Everyone who fetched since 13:10, the runner's build directory, the pipeline's artifacts and logs, the notification e-mails if they quoted the text. Tom lists them from GitLab's audit events and the job list.
  3. How is it contained? The ISSM directs it. A maintainer can make the project private to the team and pause the runner; nobody rewrites history until the ISSM says how, because the program's procedure may require the systems to be handled as spilled equipment.
  4. What does the team learn? The source of the paste, and whether a check could have caught it. On Tidewater the answer was the markings rule (point 3), moved earlier in the plan as a result.

The written answers became a page in the wiki, linked from the onboarding page, and the first step of the rescue recipe for a leaked secret became "call the security owner" (Section E.13, "I pushed a secret").

Most of the "applied" marks are in the first half and most of the "LATER" marks in the second: that is the pattern this chapter opened with, and Tidewater did not escape it either. The difference is that the second half is in the backlog with stories and sprints, not in a sentence that says "security will be addressed".

48.9 Applying this to your project

  • Copy: the data-handling decision record before the first commit; the security owner by name; the ISSM in week zero; the secrets job and the rotate-first rule; the spillage tabletop; the twenty-six-point table, filled in for your program and reviewed each quarter.
  • Adapt: the marking levels in SecMeta (Tidewater's are notional labels), the trust zones (three is a starting point, not a rule), and which framework your ISSM uses as the checklist.
  • Decide locally, early: whether your data needs separate repositories (point 4) and whether the program's GitLab tier gives you approval rules and push rules, or whether those controls are procedural (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).
  • Put the second half in the backlog with real stories, owned by a systems engineer, measured by the gate. If the system half has no stories, it is not planned; it is hoped for.
Exercise 48.1: Close a boundary crossing

In the worked example's folder, add a fourth part, MaintenanceLaptop, in the untrusted zone, with an interface to the data center that has an empty secReq. Run model.pl gate and read the finding. Then write the security requirement that covers it, satisfy it, verify it, and run the gate until it says PASS. What did you have to decide that was engineering, not typing?

Exercise 48.2: Your twenty-six

Copy the table above into your project's wiki and mark each point for your program. For every LATER, name the story or epic; for every adapted, write the reason in one sentence. Which three points would your ISSM ask about first?

49 Scaling up: segments, blocks and a ladder of fidelity

From what you know

You know

big programs. Several major systems built by different organizations, each with its own schedule; interface control documents signed by both sides; hardware that takes a year to qualify; a test range booked months ahead; a program schedule that lines all of it up at the reviews.

Here it is called

a system of systems, run as segments with their own cadences, synchronized at integrated baselines. Hardware moves in blocks, each a full Vee; software moves in sprints underneath; verification climbs a ladder of fidelity from model checks to sea trials; the model in GitLab holds every interface.

What is new

one model and one pipeline tie the segments together, so an interface change on one side shows its effect on the other the same day, and the baselines that line the segments up are tags a machine can audit.

This chapter is LATER. Jim, Bob and Tom are a three-person government team porting one system model; in their first twelve weeks nothing here is their job. Read it when the program around your model is larger than your team: several segments, hardware with long lead times, a test campaign, a simulation that has to earn credit. It explains how the practices of this book stretch to that size, and where they need help from other disciplines.

Note: Where this chapter comes from

Adapted from a reference sketch the author uses for a weapon-system program, rewritten for this book's civilian example. The process lessons carry over unchanged; the weapon-specific content does not, and none of it appears here.

49.1 A system of systems

Tidewater is small enough to describe in a paragraph, and it is already a system of systems. Moored buoys and shore stations observe; telemetry units carry the observations ashore; the data center ingests, checks, archives and publishes the marine bulletin; the field crew keeps the stations running. Each of those is a major system in its own right, built and maintained by different people, and the places where they meet -- the observation interface, the health interface, the public interface -- are where integration problems show up.

The three kinds of segment move at different speeds, and pretending otherwise forces one of them to work at the wrong pace.

Table 49.1. Tidewater's segments and their cadences.
SegmentWhat it is mostlyNatural cadenceWhat sets the pace
Stations and buoyshardware: hulls, moorings, sensors, powermonths to a year per changelong-lead parts, environmental testing, a field season to install
Telemetrymixed: radios plus firmwarea few months per radio change, weeks per firmware changeradio approvals, field updates of firmware
Data centersoftware: ingest, quality control, archive, publicationevery sprintthe pipeline; nothing physical has to move

49.1.1 Interfaces are owned at the system level

Interface management is the systems-engineering job at this size. Each segment owns its own part of the model, under its own code owners (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where); the interfaces between segments are owned at the system level, by the people who answer for the whole. In the model, an interface is a port definition and the items that flow through it. In Tidewater they live in the library layer, where every segment can use them and none can change them alone:

Each line is a row of what the document era called an interface control document. The observation record, the health report and the bulletin are the messages; the port definitions are the connectors; the data exchange table the team generated in sprint 6 (Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0) is the ICD's table, produced from these lines rather than typed. When a segment changes its side of an interface, the change is a merge request against the library, the system-level code owners must approve it, and every segment that uses the interface sees the effect in its next pipeline.

The rule that matters most: one copy of each interface. The most common failure at this size is two segments each keeping their own copy of an ICD and editing it separately. With the interface in the model, there is nothing to copy.

49.1.2 An integration lab with stand-ins

Segments should integrate long before real hardware meets in the field. A system integration lab does that with stand-ins: a buoy emulator that sends observation records over the real interface to the real ingest service, a telemetry emulator that drops and delays messages the way a bad link does, a test copy of the data center. The stand-ins are built from the interface definitions in the model, so they speak exactly what the real segments speak. Integration problems then appear on a bench in the first months, not on a pier in the second year.

49.2 Integrated baselines

The segments synchronize at integrated baselines: defined points where every segment's configuration is frozen, put together and tested end to end. Tidewater's baselines are exactly that, at the scale of one model; a larger program does the same across segments.

  1. Freeze. In the last sprint of the period, each segment tags its configuration: the hardware build state, the software build, the firmware, and the model version. In GitLab each segment's repository gets its tag, and the system model gets a release branch (Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).
  2. Integrate. The frozen configurations are loaded together in the integration lab, with stand-ins for anything not yet built.
  3. Test end to end. Scripted scenarios run through the whole system: a buoy observes, the observation crosses the link, the data center ingests it, checks it, archives it and publishes the bulletin.
  4. Record. Results go into the verification matrix (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop) and calibrate the simulation; every discrepancy becomes a story in the next period.
  5. Tag. The combined configuration becomes one system baseline: a protected tag, audited by the pipeline, the reference for the period's review (Chapter 4, The Vee, kept: the systems-engineering V in MBSE DevSecOps).

49.3 The work plan, shared across segments

Every segment plans with the same four levels and the same timeboxes, so a station story and a data-center story mean the same size of commitment, and every segment's planning periods end on the same baseline.

The reference this chapter is adapted from names the levels slightly differently from this book. It calls the thirteen-sprint planning period an epoch and the multi-year capability block a tome. This book uses epic for work that fits in a semester (thirteen sprints) and tome for work that fits in a year (Chapter 13, The operating model). The mapping is simple:

Table 49.2. The levels of the work plan in this book and in the reference.
This bookThe referenceTimeboxWhat "done" means at this size
TaskTaskunder a weekmerged, reviewed, the pipeline green
StoryStoryone sprintacceptance criteria met and demonstrated
EpicEpochup to thirteen sprintsevery segment frozen, integrated and tested end to end: an integrated baseline
Tome(part of a block)up to a yeara capability verified
ProjectTome (a block)yearsa capability block fielded

Four habits make the shared plan work across hardware and software.

  • Reviews land on epic boundaries. A hardware Vee spans several epics, and each of its reviews is scheduled as the closing event of an epic. Integration and the review become the same milestone.
  • Waiting is a dependency, not a big task. Long-lead parts and environmental tests still break into tasks under a week: preparation, execution, data reduction, model calibration. The months of waiting for a hull or a test slot are tracked as a dependency between stories, not hidden inside an oversized task.
  • Field events close an epic. Harbor tests and sea trials are scheduled as the closing stories of an epic, so their results calibrate the simulation at the start of the next one.
  • The last sprint hardens. The thirteenth sprint of an epic is for integration fixes, the baseline freeze and the documents generated from the model, not for new features.

49.4 The spine: requirements, functions, logical, physical

At this size the model is organized as a chain often called RFLP: requirements, functions, logical architecture, physical implementation. Each layer traces to the one before it, so a requirement change shows its downstream impact without anyone searching for it. Tidewater's layered folders follow the same chain: requirements, logical (behavior), physical (structure), with the library and the verification layer around them (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where).

The physical layer becomes the product tree, one branch per segment. Decompose each branch until every leaf is a configuration item: something procured, built or written as a unit, with its own specification, its own verification and its own place in configuration management. Deeper than that belongs in the segment's own design; higher than that leaves requirements with nobody clearly answerable for them. The tree for Tidewater's stations:

Each leaf -- an anemometer, a modem, a charge regulator -- is a candidate configuration item. Whether it is one is a program decision (is it bought as a unit, specified and verified as a unit?), recorded in the model with the procured metadata the team added in sprint 4 (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed).

49.4.1 Views worth generating

Programs that work under an architecture framework (DoDAF, or its successor the Unified Architecture Framework) review a standard set of views. Generate them from the model rather than drawing them; a drawn view is out of date at the next change (Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text). For a civilian observation network the useful ones read like this:

Table 49.3. Architecture views generated from the model, with Tidewater's content.
ViewWhat it shows for Tidewater
OV-1the operational concept: buoys and shore stations along the coast, the link ashore, the data center, the forecasters and mariners who use the bulletin
OV-2, SV-1who exchanges what with whom: station to data center (observations, health), data center to the public (bulletin, latest observations)
OV-5bthe observation cycle as activities: sample, transmit, ingest, check, archive, publish
SV-4which part performs which function: the allocations in the model
SV-6each message's content, rate and latency budget: the data exchange table
SV-7performance measures: observation latency, data availability, station uptime

49.5 Hardware: blocks, not one big Vee

Each hardware-dominant segment follows a formal Vee with real review gates (Chapter 4, The Vee, kept: the systems-engineering V in MBSE DevSecOps), and the system runs an overarching Vee above them. A single Vee that takes years delivers nothing until its end. Instead the program fields a first capability as Block 1, then runs overlapping Vees for the next blocks. Each block is a complete, verified, fieldable baseline; in the work plan, each block is a tome. Sprints run continuously underneath.

Tidewater's blocks are not invented for this chapter: they are in the prime's drops. Drop 4 brings the drifting buoy as a change request, and the change report shows the new block arriving in the model:

49.5.1 What each review must show

Each step of a hardware Vee is gated by a review, and at this size the evidence for every review comes from the model and the pipeline, not from a document set assembled for the occasion.

Table 49.4. Reviews and the evidence each takes from the model.
ReviewThe question it answersEvidence from the model
SRRDo we understand the need?requirements baselined, traced to needs, a verification method on each
SFRDoes the functional design meet the requirements?functions allocated to segments; latency and availability budgets closed
PDRCan the preliminary design meet its allocations?the allocated baseline, interface definitions at version 1, simulation predictions against the measures
CDRIs the design ready to build?the product baseline, message-level interfaces, verification procedures
TRRAre we ready to test?test cases, the lab configuration, simulations accredited for the event
SVR, FCADoes the system meet its requirements?the verification matrix closed, deviations dispositioned

49.6 Software: sprints with a pipeline

The data center is software: ingest, quality control, archive, publication. So is the firmware in the loggers and telemetry units. All of it is developed in two-week sprints, rolled up into the same epics as the hardware.

The pipeline is what makes sprinting safe on software that runs in the field. The practices that carry over from safety-critical programs, scaled to an observation network:

  • A coding standard enforced by the pipeline, with each deviation recorded and approved rather than silently allowed.
  • Structural test coverage scaled to criticality. Firmware that can strand a buoy needs more than the archive's reporting scripts.
  • Reproducible builds. The exact build that passed the tests, identified by its hash, is the one loaded in the field -- the same idea as the baseline's checksum (Chapter 4, The Vee, kept: the systems-engineering V in MBSE DevSecOps).
  • Tests tagged with requirement ids, so pipeline results update the verification matrix automatically.
  • Interface code generated from the model where the toolchain allows, so message definitions cannot drift from the interface definitions.
  • Software loads under configuration control, the same as hardware configuration items.

Security belongs in the pipeline from the first sprint (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system). The data center is networked and public-facing, so it carries the largest attack surface, and it is the strongest candidate for a continuous authorization: the pipeline's evidence keeps the authorization current instead of re-certifying each release.

49.7 Verification: a ladder of fidelity

Sea trials are expensive, rare and at the mercy of the weather; a storm cannot be scheduled. Most verification evidence therefore comes from lower rungs, with each rung anchoring the one below it.

  • Model checks run on every merge request: grammar, lint, trace, the verification matrix (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).
  • Simulation models the network and its weather: station failures, link drop-outs, storms, the data center's load. This is where availability and latency statistics come from, thousands of runs a night.
  • The bench in the loop runs real equipment against a simulated sea: a real data logger and modem fed by a scripted sensor stream, the real ingest service fed by a buoy emulator.
  • Harbor and shore tests connect real stations, the real link and the real data center end to end, in sheltered water.
  • Sea trials run a real buoy in real weather. They are the anchor points, and each is designed as much to validate the simulation as to demonstrate the system.

The pipeline template already carries the two middle rungs, switched off until a program has a simulation and a bench (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop). Switch them on in the question and the nightly schedule shows them:

sil-regression runs every night on its own; hil-test waits, manual, for a person who has checked the bench.

49.8 The digital twin is a calibrated simulation

For a system like Tidewater the digital twin (Section 4.13, Digital thread and digital twin) is, in practice, the network simulation kept honest by field data. The station models are calibrated against recorded observations, the link model against measured drop-outs and delays, the data center model against measured processing times. Every test result flows back to calibrate the models, and the calibrated models flow back into the system model's budgets: the latency and availability numbers the requirements promise.

Warning: Accredit the simulation from the start

A simulation that has not been accredited for a specific use cannot earn verification credit, and accreditation late in a program is slow and painful. Plan the verification, validation and accreditation of the simulation itself from the first epic, as stories with owners. MIL-STD-3022 gives documentation templates for it.

49.9 Standards to plan around

These are the general standards a program of this size usually has to plan around. Which ones apply, and which revision, is set by your contract: check the current revisions and the contract before you plan.

Table 49.5. Standards to plan around. Check current revisions and your contract.
StandardCovers
ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288system life-cycle processes; the backbone of the Vee
DoDI 5000.97digital engineering expectations on defense programs
DoDAF, UAFarchitecture views generated from the model
MIL-STD-882Esystem safety: hazard analysis and risk acceptance
MIL-STD-810environmental testing: vibration, shock, thermal, salt fog
MIL-STD-461, MIL-STD-464electromagnetic interference and compatibility, equipment and system level
MIL-STD-1472human engineering for consoles and crew stations
MIL-STD-3022documentation for model and simulation verification, validation and accreditation
RMF (DoDI 8510.01)cybersecurity authorization

A civilian program would swap some of these for its own sector's standards; the planning habit is the same: list them in the first epic, give each an owner, and trace the requirements they impose into the model like any other requirement.

49.10 Where it breaks: the handoffs

Large programs rarely fail inside a segment. They fail at the handoffs between segments, and each failure point is a schedule risk worth tracking explicitly.

  • Interface copies drift. Each segment edits its own copy of an ICD. Keep one copy, in the model, owned at the system level.
  • Software baselines out of step with hardware reviews. The software that was reviewed is not the software that was integrated. Freeze both at the same integrated baseline, by tag.
  • Documents edited by hand. Once someone edits a generated document, the model stops being authoritative. The baseline audit catches it (Chapter 4, The Vee, kept: the systems-engineering V in MBSE DevSecOps); the habit prevents it.
  • A simulation that never gets accredited. All the verification credit it was supposed to earn evaporates at the end. Start accreditation in the first epic.

49.11 Exercises

Exercise 49.1: Name the cadences

List the segments of your own program (or of a program you know). For each, write its dominant kind (hardware, software, mixed), its natural change cadence, and what sets that pace. Then mark where the integrated baselines would have to fall for all of them to be frozen together at least twice a year.

Exercise 49.2: One copy of the interface

In the practice project from lesson 11, find the observation record and every place that uses it (grep -rn ObservationRecord model/). Which code owners would have to approve a change to it, and why should a segment not be able to change it alone?

Exercise 49.3: Find the next block in the drops

Using the drops (perl "$KIT/sim/tidewater-v1.pl" --drop N DIR), find which drop introduces partner data sharing, its change-request id, and the requirement it adds. Where in the block picture does it fall?

Exercise 49.4: Put a check on its rung

For each of these, name the rung of the ladder where it belongs: a missing verify relationship; a link model that drops one message in twenty; a buoy that loses power in a storm; a bulletin published late because the archive was slow; a modem that resets when its firmware is updated over the air.

49.12 You can now

  • Explain why a system of systems needs several cadences and how integrated baselines line them up.
  • Keep interfaces as one copy in the model, owned at the system level.
  • Map the reference's epochs and blocks onto this book's epics and tomes.
  • Decompose a product tree to configuration items and name the views worth generating.
  • Plan hardware as overlapping blocks and verification as a ladder whose rungs calibrate each other.
  • Name the handoffs where large programs break.

49.13 Applying this to your project

Start with the inventory, not the tools: list your segments, their cadences and their interfaces, and put every interface in the model as one copy with system-level owners before anything else. Then pick the integrated baselines from the slowest segment's natural rhythm, map your planning periods onto epics that end on them, and switch on the pipeline's simulation and bench jobs only when there is a simulation and a bench to run. Plan the simulation's accreditation in the same first epic as the standards list.

50 Your project in twelve weeks: a playbook

From what you know

You know

the program plan you write at the start of a new effort.

Here it is called

a twelve-week playbook for your own project.

What is new

a plan you can copy, already tested on Tidewater, with the decisions you must make locally marked.

Survival kit: Your turn

What you have

this book's account of what three engineers did with Tidewater, the kit, and a program of your own with a model in Cameo (or in documents), a supplier who keeps changing it, and a manager who wants to see progress.

What you need

a plan for your own first twelve weeks that keeps what worked on Tidewater, drops what was specific to it, and starts on Monday. This chapter is that plan, with the decisions you have to make locally and the commands that set it up.

Tidewater is a worked example, not a template to copy word for word. Your program has a different system, a different supplier, a different network, different people. What carries over is the shape: a week of setup, two sprints of building the shop while learning to use it, four sprints in which the engineering takes over, and a briefing at the end built from measurements. This chapter gives that shape in generic terms, marks every decision that is yours to make, and shows the kit's path through week zero on a project that is not Tidewater.

50.1 The shape of the twelve weeks

Table 50.1. A generic twelve-week plan, from week zero to the first baseline
WhenGoalTypical storiesDone when
Week zeroAgreements and accessScorecard agreed with management; supplier exchange agreement; ISSM contact; software requests in; laptops checkedEvery person has run kickoff.pl doctor; the scorecard page is signed
Sprint 1 (weeks 1-2)A project the team can work in; the first drop received and assessedGitLab project from the project file; first pipeline drafted and run locally; receive and check the first drop; TODO inventory; working agreements; practice lessons 10-11Direct pushes to the integration branch are refused; the drop's checksums verified; the backlog estimated
Sprint 2 (weeks 3-4)The drop on the integration branch through the vendor branch; every change gatedRunner online; pipeline gates every merge request; vendor import of drop 1; conventions; decision records; laptops and Vim; request for enablersEvery merge is green and approved by someone else; the TODO count is the baseline
Sprint 3 (weeks 5-6)First packages closed; requirements in the model; the trace on every changeClose the first package's TODOs; units and value types; DOORS into the model; trace and secrets jobsThe trace report runs on every merge request
Sprint 4 (weeks 7-8)The largest package closed; gaps reported to the supplier; something to show managementThe biggest structure package; dependency cycles broken; discrepancy reports; model site on Pages; nightly pipelineManagement has seen the model site
Sprint 5 (weeks 9-10)The remaining structure closed; clutter removed; trace becomes a gateRemaining packages; duplicate and legacy clutter; the trace ratchet; requirements graded with the recipe; release rehearsalNo merge can add a trace gap
Sprint 6 (weeks 11-12)Behavior started; an interim baseline; the briefingHand-written state machines and activity flows; a data exchange table; the verification matrix; baseline-0; the briefing and memoThe baseline tag rebuilds; the briefing is given from measured numbers

Two features of this plan are not negotiable, in the sense that every team that skipped them regretted it:

  • Something visible for management by sprint 4. The team that shows nothing until week twelve spends weeks nine to twelve answering "is this working?" instead of working. On Tidewater the model site on GitLab Pages, shown at the sprint 4 review, did more for the program's confidence than any status slide.
  • Engineering takes over the board from sprint 3. If platform work is still most of the points in sprint 4, something is wrong with the plan, not with the team: the pipeline is gold-plated, or the setup is blocked, or the learning budget was not taken. Look at the split (Section 50.8, What to measure) every sprint.

50.2 Week zero, with the kit

Week zero is the week before sprint 1. It is mostly conversations: the scorecard with management (see Section 3.6, Defining measurable progress), the exchange agreement with the supplier (Section 45.1.1, The model exchange agreement), the first meeting with the information system security manager (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system), the software requests for every laptop. The kit's part is short. On each laptop, the doctor checks that everything the team needs is in place and says exactly what to fix:

Expect warnings the first time (a missing Vim setup line, an SSH key not yet made). kickoff.pl doctor --fix sets the recommended git settings and prints each one; everything else is a line in the output with its fix.

Then one person, usually the configuration manager, runs the week-zero sequence. Read the plan before running it:

Twelve steps: check the laptop, make the model repository from the kit's templates, create the GitLab project from the project file, push, start gitflow, add the schedules, create the sprints, import the first drop onto the vendor branch, start the journal, write the wiki pages, and open the first stories. Without --yes it only prints the plan. With --yes it does it, against the offline GitLab here or against your real server with --url:

Against a real GitLab, the same command runs with --url https://your.gitlab --token-env GITLAB_TOKEN. If a step fails (a permission your account does not have yet, a runner not registered), the output says which step and how to continue from it with --from N. On Tidewater the runner request took until the start of sprint 2; plan for that.

Warning: Two things the kickoff cannot do for you

It cannot get your runner approved, and it cannot get your supplier to keep element IDs stable. Both take weeks of other people's time. Ask for them in week zero, in writing, with a date.

50.3 Sprint by sprint: what to watch

The table above says what each sprint is for. This section says what usually goes wrong in it, how you will see it coming, and what Tidewater did about it. None of it is specific to SysML or to GitLab; it is what happens when a team that knows its system well meets tools it does not know.

50.3.1 Sprint 1: the urge to plan everything

The first sprint's risk is a plan that is too big. A lead who has finally been given permission to change things tends to put the whole port on the board. Jim's first draft of sprint 1 held more points than the team had capacity for, before any learning time; the team cut it at the kickoff, after the planning poker made the gap obvious (Section 24.3, Planning poker).

Watch for: stories with no acceptance criterion a program can check; a sprint committed above about nine tenths of capacity; nobody on the board with a learning story. Fix it at the kickoff, not at the review.

The other risk in sprint 1 is silence. People who are unsure of the new tools say "working on it" at stand-up for three days in a row. The kit's stand-up lint flags a status with no story ID or no change since yesterday, and the "same plan three days" flag in Section 24.2, The daily stand-up: terse, written, linted exists for exactly this. Treat it as a request for help that nobody dared make.

50.3.2 Sprint 2: the runner, and the first red pipeline

The runner is almost always late, and the first pipeline on a real runner almost always fails on something the laptop run did not show (on Tidewater, the Windows runner's default shell was PowerShell, and every script line written for Git Bash failed: Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs tells the story). Neither is a reason to slip the sprint. Plan the runner as a blocked item with an owner and a date from the first day of the sprint, and keep the team working with the local pipeline (gitlab.pl ci) until it arrives.

Sprint 2 is also when the first real merge conflict happens, usually in the drop import. Treat the first one as a team event: resolve it together, at one screen, with the conflict markers explained (Chapter 10, Vim for models, and practice lesson 12). The second conflict is then just work.

50.3.3 Sprints 3 and 4: the dip

Most teams have a dip around sprint 3. The novelty is gone, the setup work is still not quite finished, and the engineering has not yet sped up. On Tidewater the pulse survey fell in sprint 3, when an approval blocked the security work for three days and Bob's first hand-written edit failed the grammar check in front of everyone.

Watch for: the pulse survey's second question ("I can do my work in the new tools without help") falling; merge requests sitting unreviewed for days; the same person doing all the reviews. Fix: pair the struggling person with the most fluent one for a day; rotate reviews; make the sprint 4 review the moment something visible goes in front of management, so the team sees the work land.

50.3.4 Sprints 5 and 6: gold-plating, and the briefing

By sprint 5 the team is fluent, and the risk turns around: the pipeline grows jobs nobody asked for, and platform work creeps back up. Every new job should answer a problem the team actually had, named in the story ("we merged a trace gap twice; the ratchet stops it"). If you cannot name the problem, the job waits.

Sprint 6 ends with the briefing. Start it in sprint 5: decide the four or five numbers it will show, check they are computed by programs, and rehearse it at the sprint 5 review. Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not and the memo templates in Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim are the tools; the numbers come from the measures agreed in week zero, and nothing new should appear in the briefing that management has not seen in a weekly note first.

50.4 Selling the plan in week zero

The plan has two audiences before it has a single story done: the team, who may not want it, and management, who asked for it but may expect too much. Each needs a different conversation.

For management, the plan has three points, in this order. First, the measures: what "measurable progress" will mean in twelve weeks, computed by programs, agreed now so nobody argues about them in December. Second, the cost: the split of the first two sprints is mostly platform and learning, on purpose, and it falls by sprint 4; the enablers (learning time, a runner, approvals, a tier decision) are asks with dates. Third, the checkpoint: something visible at the sprint 4 review, so management does not wait twelve weeks to know whether it is working.

For the team, the conversation is about what does not change. They still own the engineering. Their judgment still decides what the system is. What changes is where the work is recorded, how it is checked, and how often it is integrated. A line that says it plainly: "We are not becoming software developers. We are keeping our model the way software teams keep their code, because it is checked on every change." The objections are real; let each one be said, as Jim did in Chapter 3, The directive, and point at the chapter that answers it.

50.5 The decisions that are yours

Every decision below was made one way on Tidewater. The column on the right says what should drive yours.

Table 50.2. Decisions to make locally, and what should drive them
DecisionTidewater's choiceWhat should drive yours
Branching modelgitflow: develop for integration, main for baselines, a vendor branch for the supplier's dropsBaselines delivered under contract favor gitflow; a model nobody "releases" can use GitLab flow (Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers)
Merge methodmerge commits, never squashKeep merge commits if you will measure from history; squash only if nobody will
Boundary with the supplierfull mirror of the supplier's modelFull mirror if the model is your deliverable; interface surface if you consume theirs (Section 45.8, Two strategies at the v1-to-v2 boundary)
Repository layoutlayered folders through a layout mapThe layers suit any system; the folder names should match your subsystems (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where)
Requirements sourceDOORS authoritative, converted on every drop, never hand-editedWhatever your contract says governs; never two editable copies
Runnera Windows shell runner on a dedicated VM with Git for Windows' PerlWhat your enterprise can approve; a Docker runner works with the optional image (Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs)
GitLab tierstarted on Free, Premium decided in sprint 2Approval rules and code-owner enforcement are the Premium features worth paying for first (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep)

Primary progress measureTODO lines left by the converterAny count the strongest skeptic would accept, computed by a program
Story sizetasks at most five ideal days, stories within a sprintKeep the limits; the numbers are what make a sprint plannable
Ceremony timesstand-up 09:00, refinement Wednesday week 2, review and retro Friday week 2Whatever the team will actually attend; protect them from other meetings

Record each one as a decision record in docs/adr/ in the model repository, with the context and the reason. The scaffold starts the folder with ADR 0001; Chapter 13, The operating model shows Tidewater's list. A new team member reading those files learns in an hour why the repository is the way it is.

50.6 The learning budget

No one on Jim's team had used git, written a pipeline or read SysML v2 text before sprint 1. The plan budgeted for that, in points, on the board, as stories labeled work::learning: practice lessons, chapters of this book, pairing at the terminal. On Tidewater the learning share started at about a quarter of sprint 1 and fell to a few percent by sprint 6 (the exact figures are in Bottom line up front, cited from docs/tidewater/work-split.json).

Copy the budget, not the numbers. Two rules:

  • Budget the learning, or it happens on nights and weekends. A team that is expected to learn git on top of a full sprint learns it badly, resents it, and tells management the new way does not work. Learning time on the board is visible, defensible, and shrinks by itself as competence grows.
  • Learning is on the plan, not in the margins. Each person's learning stories have tasks and acceptance criteria like any others: "practice lesson 11 checks as done," "can open a merge request without help."

A reasonable starting reserve for a team new to all of it is a fifth of sprint 1, a sixth of sprint 2, a tenth of sprints 3 and 4, and a few percent after. Adjust at each retrospective from the pulse survey's second question ("I can do my work in the new tools without help").

50.7 Your backlog

The kit ships a generic backlog for a v1-to-v2 port: tomes, epics, stories and tasks with points, an owner role, a sprint hint and an acceptance criterion written as something a person or the pipeline can check. It is written in neutral terms (the supplier, the integration branch), so it fits a program that is not Tidewater:

Sum it by sprint before you change anything, to see the shape:

Then change it: replace the system's names, cut the stories your program does not need (no supplier drops, no DOORS), add the engineering stories your program does need (Chapter 46, Systems engineering work, not pipeline work has a catalog), and re-estimate with your own team in planning poker (Section 24.3, Planning poker). Do not keep a story because Tidewater had it.

The kit has no command that loads the CSV into GitLab in one go; a short loop does it. Here the sprint 1 rows become task issues in the project the kickoff made:

In practice, load one sprint at a time, at each kickoff, after the team has refined it. A backlog loaded eighteen months ahead is a backlog nobody reads.

50.8 What to measure

Measure from day one, with programs, and agree the measures with management before sprint 1. Three layers of measures served Tidewater, and each answers a different audience.

50.8.1 The split: where the time goes

Every story carries work::engineering, work::platform or work::learning, and the split of points by label, sprint by sprint, goes on the first page of every status (Bottom line up front). Tidewater's is computed from its plan by one script; it shows how:

The shape to look for: platform and learning high in sprints 1 and 2, engineering the larger share from sprint 3, mostly engineering by sprint 6. A flat line means the setup never finished.

50.8.2 The four headline numbers

At every review, the same four numbers, so management learns to read the trend (Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not):

  1. Conversion debt (TODO lines left by the converter), from the pipeline's todo job.
  2. Verify coverage (requirements with a verification case), from the verification matrix or the trace.
  3. Open discrepancy reports and supplier changes awaiting disposition, from GitLab labels.
  4. Blocked items, from the board.

The first one is there from the moment the first drop is converted. In the repository the kickoff made, on the drop's branch:

50.8.3 The scorecard

The twelve measures Jim agreed with management before sprint 1 (Section 3.6, Defining measurable progress) are the case at week twelve. Copy the rule more than the list: every measure is computed by a program from the repository or GitLab, and every measure is one a skeptic in the room would accept. Then pick the measures your management cares about. The ones that carried the most weight on Tidewater:

  • change lead time and review turnaround, against the document era's numbers (labeled notional if they are reconstructions);
  • the share of changes gated (it must be 100%, and GitLab's protected branches make it a setting);
  • the time to answer "which requirements are unverified?" (two days of spreadsheet work before, a pipeline job's seconds after);
  • reproducible baselines;
  • the team's own pulse survey, which the program manager insisted on and was right to.

GitLab's analytics give the flow measures on any tier through the kit (Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics):

On a project a day old the tables are empty. By the sprint 2 review they have a story to tell.

50.9 What to copy from Tidewater, and what not

Table 50.3. Copy the shape, adapt the details
CopyAdaptLeave behind

Something visible for management by sprint 4What it is (a model site, a data exchange table, a VCRM)The Pages site, if your network forbids it
