Three things from Tidewater are easy to copy and wrong to copy:

  • The spider-web cleanup stories. Tidewater's v1 model had specific clutter (a Legacy Import package, two dependency cycles). Yours has its own. Measure it first (Section 11.4.4, Packages shows the package view), then plan.
  • The planted problems. The simulation planted gaps, drift and failures so the book would have something to show. Your real model will have different ones, and probably more.
  • The cast. Your team is not three people with these roles. A one-person team can run the same loop with approvals from a colleague in another group; a ten-person team needs more code-owner sections and a second runner. Keep the separation of author and approver, whatever the size.

50.10 When things go differently

50.10.1 No supplier drops

If your v1 model is your own and nobody else will change it, drop the vendor branch, the change board for drops and the impact analysis. Convert once, onto a branch, review it, merge it, and from then on the v2 text is the model. Tidewater's tome 3 (maintenance against drops) disappears, and the months it took go to engineering.

50.10.2 Documents, not Cameo

If the starting point is documents and spreadsheets rather than a v1 model, the port is writing, not converting. The plan's shape still holds, but sprint 1's "convert and assess" becomes "inventory and decide the package structure," and the TODO count is replaced by a count of requirements and interfaces captured. The requirements recipe (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe) and the workbook (Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook) become the core of sprints 2 to 4.

50.10.3 A bigger team

Above about six people, split into teams along the model's layers or segments, give each team a CODEOWNERS section, and consider one repository per segment with the system repository consuming tagged releases of each (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where describes the federation). The twelve-week shape holds per team.

50.10.4 A slower organization

If the runner, the GitLab tier and the tool approvals take a quarter instead of a sprint, start anyway: the kit's offline GitLab and local pipeline (gitlab.pl ci) let the team learn and work on laptops while the approvals move. Tidewater's practice lessons are exactly that. Keep the request-for-enablers memo (Chapter 37, Writing it down: DoD-style memos from Vim) current and show it at every review: the blocked items are the fourth headline number for a reason.

50.11 The first Monday

Checklist: Before the first sprint 1 stand-up
  • ☐ The scorecard page agreed with management, with the document-era baselines labeled
  • ☐ The supplier's exchange agreement drafted, with stable IDs and change notes asked for
  • ☐ The ISSM met; the marking decision recorded as a decision record
  • ☐ Every laptop: kickoff.pl doctor shows no FAIL, or the software request is in with a date
  • ☐ The runner request submitted, with a date asked for
  • ☐ kickoff.pl start run against the real GitLab (or the offline one while access is pending)
  • ☐ Sprint 1 refined and estimated in planning poker, learning stories included
  • ☐ The ceremony times in everyone's calendar, the stand-up format agreed (Section 24.2, The daily stand-up: terse, written, linted)
  • ☐ The first drop received, its checksums verified
  • ☐ The request-for-enablers memo drafted, to go out in sprint 2

50.12 Applying this to your project

This whole chapter is the application. If you keep three things from it:

  • Agree the measures before you start, and compute them with programs. Everything else in the case follows from numbers nobody can argue with.
  • Put the learning on the board. A team that is given time to learn will tell management the new way works, because for them it does.
  • Show something by sprint 4. Confidence is built in the middle of the twelve weeks, not at the end.
Exercise 50.1: Your twelve-week table

Copy the twelve-week table into your program's terms: your system's packages, your supplier (or none), your reviews. For each sprint, write the goal as an outcome management would recognize, and the "done when" as something a program can check.

Exercise 50.2: Your decision records

Write ADRs 0002 to 0005 for your program from the decisions table: branching model, supplier boundary, merge method and primary progress measure. One page each: context, decision, consequences.

Exercise 50.3: Your sprint 1

Take the first two sprints of backlog.csv, rewrite them for your program, sum the points, and check them against your team's capacity with a learning reserve. What do you cut first?

Exercise 50.4: Run week zero offline

Run kickoff.pl start --yes --local DIR for an invented project of your own with drop 1 of Tidewater, then open DIR with gitlab.pl --local DIR issue list and read the stories it made. Which ones would you rewrite for your program?

51 Pitfalls and anti-patterns

From what you know

You know

lessons-learned reports that nobody reads.

Here it is called

pitfalls and anti-patterns.

What is new

each pitfall has a symptom you can spot early in your own project.

Survival kit: Knowing the ditches

What you have

a working process and, by now, some habits, good and bad.

What you need

a way to recognize the bad habits early, from the first symptom you would actually notice, before they cost a sprint. Every team moving from documents and Cameo to a text model in GitLab falls into some of these. Tidewater fell into more than half of them.

51.1 How to read this chapter

Each pitfall has the same four parts:

  • Symptom: what you will see first. Usually it is small: a number that stops moving, a conversation that keeps recurring, a pipeline colour nobody comments on any more.
  • Why it happens: the reason a sensible team ends up there. None of these pitfalls is stupidity. Most of them are an old habit, correct in the document era, applied in a place where it no longer fits.
  • Fix: what to do, as concretely as possible.
  • At Tidewater: where the team met it, and what happened.

The pitfalls are grouped by where they bite: the model, the change process, the pipeline, the measures, and the people. A checklist version, for a monthly look in the mirror, closes the chapter.

51.2 Pitfalls in the model

51.2.1 Porting the spider web

Symptom. The v2 model has the same duplicated blocks, stale packages and dependency cycles as the v1 model. Someone finds Battery_old in the part tree and asks whether it is real.

Why it happens. The converter is faithful: it carries what is in the XMI, clutter included, because it cannot know which blocks are clutter. A team under schedule pressure measures progress by TODO lines closed and treats everything the converter did not flag as done.

Fix. Treat untangling as its own work, with its own stories, measured by scorecard measure 7 (cycles, duplicates, the most-connected block). Do not delete clutter silently: raise a discrepancy report so the prime removes it upstream, and remove it in the government model in an MR that cites the report. Until the prime's drop removes it, the next vendor import will bring it back as a conflict, which is the reminder you want.

At Tidewater. The drop-1 conversion carried the Legacy Import package with its copied blocks, and the two package cycles from Chapter 2, The Cameo years. Bob's first instinct was to delete the package in one commit. Jim stopped it: the deletion would conflict with every future drop until the prime removed it too. The team raised discrepancy reports, removed the clutter in the government model with the report numbers in the MR, and watched the prime's later drops remove it upstream (the Copy of SensorSuite block went in drop 3, the whole Legacy Import package in drop 6).

51.2.2 Reformatting the converter's output

Symptom. Every prime drop produces dozens of merge conflicts, in files where nobody changed anything that matters.

Why it happens. Converter output is not how a person would lay the text out, and a tidy engineer reformats it: reorders members alphabetically, re-indents, splits long lines, moves the doc comment above the tag. Each change is harmless alone. Together they mean that the next vendor import, which writes the converter's layout again, differs from the government file on nearly every line, and git's three-way merge can no longer tell the prime's changes from the government's.

Fix. Edit converter output in place and minimally: replace a // TODO line with the line that closes it, add a line where one is needed, and leave every other line exactly as the converter wrote it. Put government-only content (new packages, the conventions library, views) in separate files the converter never writes (on Tidewater, model/library/conventions/ and its neighbours), which the vendor branch never touches. Write the rule into the Definition of Done.

At Tidewater. Tom reformatted Interfaces.sysml in sprint 2 to make it "readable" and the change sailed through review because the diff looked like pure layout. Drop 2's import then conflicted on forty lines of that file. Resolving them took Tom most of a day, after which the team wrote the in-place rule into the Definition of Done and reverted the reformatting.

51.2.3 Hand-editing the vendor branch

Symptom. A delta report shows changes the prime says it never made, or a vendor import does not reproduce when run again from the same drop.

Why it happens. The vendor branch looks like any other branch, and a quick fix there (a converter glitch, a typo in the prime's requirement text) seems faster than a discrepancy report.

Fix. The vendor branch holds exactly what the converters produce from the drop, nothing else. Protect it so only maintainers can push and nobody can merge into it. Fixes go on develop (government edits) or to the prime (a discrepancy report). If a converter is wrong, fix the converter, re-import, and record the converter version in the import commit.

At Tidewater. Never happened, because vendor/prime was protected from week zero with merge set to no one. Tom tested the protection in sprint 2 by trying to push a one-line change to it and kept the rejection message as evidence.

51.2.4 Changing requirement text in the model

Symptom. The trace job's drift count goes up after a government MR, not after a drop.

Why it happens. An engineer sees a badly worded requirement in the model, knows what it should say, and fixes the doc text. It feels like the obvious improvement.

Fix. DOORS is the authority for requirement text, and the prime owns DOORS. The model's requirement text is a copy. A wording problem is a discrepancy report to the prime; the fix arrives in a later drop, through both the ReqIF and the XMI. The government model may add notes or analysis around a requirement, never different words in it.

At Tidewater. TW-SYS-006 drifted from the start (Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers). Bob wanted to align the model text by hand in sprint

  1. Jim raised a discrepancy report instead, and drop 2 fixed both sides. The drift count fell to zero through the

process rather than around it, which is what the scorecard needed to show.

51.2.5 Trusting the TODO count alone

Symptom. The TODO count is zero, the pipeline is green, and a reviewer finds that the government's hand-written state machine is missing a state the prime added months ago.

Why it happens. The converter writes a TODO line for each construct it does not carry. When the prime changes something inside such a construct (a new state inside a state machine, a new message in an interaction), the TODO line in the converted output is unchanged, so the vendor import shows no difference at all. The TODO count cannot see it.

Fix. Run the v1 delta on every drop: xmi2sysml.pl --delta OLD.xmi NEW.xmi. It compares the two drops element by element by xmi:id and marks every change the converter does not carry as manual. Each manual line becomes a task.

At Tidewater. Drop 3 added a Storm state to BuoyModes. The converted v2 output did not change at all. The delta listed five manual changes inside the state machine, and Bob's drop-3 story carried a task to add the state by hand (Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle).

51.3 Pitfalls in the change process

51.3.1 The big-bang merge request

Symptom. An MR has thirty files and two thousand changed lines, it stays open for a week, and the review is a single comment saying "looks fine".

Why it happens. The document era trained people to batch: a document revision collected months of changes because each revision cost a CCB meeting. The instinct carries over: finish everything, then ask for review.

Fix. One task, one MR; one task, less than a week. If an MR touches more than one package or takes more than fifteen minutes to review, split it. Small MRs are reviewed properly, merge without conflicts, and keep lead time (scorecard measure 2) low.

At Tidewater. Bob's first structure MR in sprint 3 closed every TODO in two packages at once. Jim's review took two sessions and missed a wrong level tag, which a later MR had to fix. From sprint 4 on the team cut stories into package-sized tasks, and median review turnaround fell below a working day.

51.3.2 Long-lived branches

Symptom. A feature branch is two weeks old, and merging develop into it produces conflicts in files the branch's author never touched.

Why it happens. The engineer is "nearly done" for days, and keeping the branch private feels safer than showing an unfinished change.

Fix. Branches live days, not weeks. Merge develop into your branch daily if it must live longer, and push it so the MR pipeline checks the integration. If a task will take longer than a week, it is two tasks.

At Tidewater. The only branch older than a week was the behavior work in sprint 6, which straddled Bob's leave. Its merge needed a manual conflict resolution in Behavior.sysml. The retrospective added a rule: before leave, merge or hand over.

51.3.3 Rewriting shared history

Symptom. A colleague's git pull fails with "diverged" messages, or a merge request suddenly shows commits that were already merged.

Why it happens. Tutorials teach git rebase and git push --force as tidy ways to clean up a branch, and they are, on a branch only you use. On a shared branch they rewrite history other people have.

Fix. Protected branches forbid force push; keep it that way. On your own feature branch, tidy before you push for the first time, not after. The project uses merge commits and no squash, because the merge history is part of the record (who merged what, when, after which review) and feeds the status metrics.

At Tidewater. Tom followed a tutorial's advice to squash commits in sprint 2, on a test project. When the team saw that squashing would make the merge history unable to show which engineer made which change, they set squash to never in project.conf and wrote the reason beside it.

51.3.4 Silent conflict resolution

Symptom. After a vendor merge, a change the prime announced in its manifest is not in the government model.

Why it happens. Conflicts are uncomfortable, and git offers one-word ways out: take our side, or take theirs, for a whole file. Taking ours drops the prime's change; taking theirs drops the government's edits.

Fix. Resolve conflicts hunk by hunk in Vim (Chapter 10, Vim for models), or take the vendor side and re-apply the government's edits deliberately, which is the method the Drop Intake Runbook prescribes. Either way, the MR description lists each conflicted file and how it was resolved, and the reviewer checks the manifest's changes against the merged result.

At Tidewater. Drop 5 changed the EnergyBalance constraint expression in a TODO line the government had already replaced by hand. The conflict was real: both sides changed the same line. Tom took the vendor side and re-applied the hand-written constraint with the new expression, and listed the file in the MR. gitlab.pl flow take exists for the wholesale case, but the runbook uses it only on files the government never edits.

51.3.5 Old reviews in new clothes

Symptom. Every merge request is approved, and then a monthly meeting reviews the same changes again from slides.

Why it happens. The organization does not yet trust the MR approval as the review of record, so it keeps the old board as a safety net. Nobody says out loud that the MR review is now redundant or that the board is.

Fix. Decide which review is the review of record, write it into the configuration management plan, and make the other one a summary. For Tidewater, the MR approval by a code owner is the change approval; the CCB meets monthly to look at the outcomes (baselines, discrepancy reports, metrics), not at individual changes.

At Tidewater. The deputy program manager, who chairs the CCB, asked in sprint 4 for "the list of model changes for the board". Jim answered with the merged MR list from gitlab.pl export and offered to replace the change-by-change review with a fifteen-minute review of the export. The board agreed after seeing two months of it.

51.4 Pitfalls in the pipeline

51.4.1 Red is normal

Symptom. The pipeline on develop has been red for three days, and the stand-up no longer mentions it.

Why it happens. A failing check that blocks nothing becomes background. Usually it started with a job that failed for a reason outside the team's control (a runner problem, a server outage), and when the reason went away nobody re-ran it.

Fix. A red pipeline on develop or main is the team's first priority, above any story, until it is green. The stand-up asks one question first: "is develop green?" Scorecard measure 8 measures the time from a failure to the next pass so that the habit is visible.

At Tidewater. The runner's disk filled in sprint 6 and every job failed. The fix took Tom an hour once noticed, but it was noticed only the next morning. The team added "is develop green?" as the first line of the stand-up and a disk-space check to the weekly runner look (Chapter 42, Administration).

51.4.2 Allowed to fail, forever

Symptom. Half the jobs are yellow (allowed to fail) and nobody can remember why.

Why it happens. allow_failure: true is the easy way to add a check that does not pass yet. It is meant to be temporary and almost never is.

Fix. Every allow_failure has a comment in .gitlab-ci.yml saying why and until when, and an issue to remove it. Tidewater's trace job is allowed to fail by design (the planted requirement gaps are the prime's to fix, and the discrepancy reports track them); that reason is written beside the job.

At Tidewater. The outline check started as allowed to fail during the port because the converter's layout broke the outline rule. It had an issue, a waiver in the wiki, and a removal date tied to the end of the structure epic. When the date came the waiver was removed in an MR, and the job went back to blocking.

51.4.3 Bypassing the gate

Symptom. A protected branch was unprotected "for five minutes" to push a fix directly, and the audit shows it.

Why it happens. Urgency, and a maintainer's role that permits it. In the document era, the equivalent was walking a change past the CCB because the review was next month.

Fix. The gate has no bypass that leaves no trace. Urgent fixes go through a hotfix branch and a merge request like everything else; a small MR with a green pipeline merges in minutes. The monthly protection audit (Chapter 42, Administration) checks that nothing was unprotected, and the audit events (Premium) show who did it.

At Tidewater. Nobody unprotected a branch, which Jim attributes to the sprint 1 exercise: the team deliberately opened an MR with a lint error and watched the merge button refuse (Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in). Seeing the gate work made it feel like protection rather than obstruction.

51.4.4 Unpinned tools

Symptom. The pipeline fails on develop with no model change, and the failure is in a check's behavior.

Why it happens. The runner uses whatever version of the kit or the converters is newest, and someone updated it.

Fix. The runner and the laptops use the same pinned version of every tool. Upgrading a tool is a story with its own MR and its own pipeline run (Section 42.9, Upgrades).

At Tidewater. The runner and laptops ran the same tagged kit from week zero, after Tom saw what a moving dependency did in the vendor import rehearsal: re-running the drop-1 import with a newer converter produced a different Stations.sysml, which would have shown up as a phantom prime change.

51.4.5 Tools before habits

Symptom. In week two the project has a board with nine columns, forty labels, epics, iterations, value stream analytics and a security dashboard, and the team still cannot say what the next task is.

Why it happens. GitLab has a feature for everything, and the enthusiastic member of the team turns them all on.

Fix. Adopt one tool when it pays for itself, and say what it pays for. Tidewater's adoption timeline (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep) added one or two features per sprint, each when a problem made it worth the cost of learning it.

At Tidewater. Tom proposed a full security scanning suite in week zero. Jim asked what it would scan: the model had no code, so SAST and dependency scanning had nothing to look at. Secret detection, which did have something to look at, went in at sprint 3.

51.5 Pitfalls in the measures

51.5.1 Measuring by hand

Symptom. The status chart is assembled on Thursday night from three spreadsheets, and the numbers on it cannot be reproduced the following week.

Why it happens. It is how status was always done, and the automated numbers are not yet trusted.

Fix. Every number in a status report comes from the repository, GitLab's records or the journal, produced by a script or the pipeline. If a number cannot be produced that way, it is not on the scorecard. The rule was set in Chapter 3, The directive and it is the one that made the sprint 6 briefing believable.

At Tidewater. In sprint 2 Jim was tempted to report "percent of model ported" from a judgment. The TODO count was not yet automated, so Jim reported nothing for that measure and said why. The todo job came in that sprint.

51.5.2 Gaming the TODO count

Symptom. The TODO count falls faster than the work could possibly have been done, and some MRs delete TODO lines without replacing them.

Why it happens. Any measure that becomes a target invites shortcuts. Deleting a TODO line is a one-keystroke "closure".

Fix. The Definition of Done says a TODO line is closed only by the construct that replaces it, and the reviewer checks the replacement. The v1 delta and the trace job catch missing content later, but review catches it first. Report the TODO count together with measures that would move if it were gamed (trace completeness, lint warnings).

At Tidewater. It did not happen, partly because Bob, the strongest skeptic, was also the one closing most TODO lines and saw the count as proof of work rather than a target set by others.

51.5.3 Reporting only the good numbers

Symptom. The sprint report shows four measures; last sprint it showed six.

Why it happens. Two measures looked bad, and leaving them out felt kinder than explaining them.

Fix. Report every agreed measure, every sprint. A bad number with a reason and a plan is credible; a missing number is noticed and remembered.

At Tidewater. Sprint 3 was bad: the pipeline caught Bob's grammar error, the ISSM blocked the security story for three days, and morale dipped (Chapter 28, Sprint 3: the first red X, DOORS in the model, and a wait nobody named). Jim reported all of it. At the sprint 6 briefing the program manager said that the sprint 3 report was the reason the sprint 6 numbers were believed.

51.6 Pitfalls with people

51.6.1 The hero

Symptom. Only one person can fix the pipeline, run a vendor import or cut a baseline, and that person's leave is planned around.

Why it happens. The person who set it up knows it best, and it is faster for them to do it than to teach it.

Fix. Rotate the chores. Every procedure has a wiki runbook, and every runbook has been followed at least once by someone other than its author. Pair on the first instance of anything.

At Tidewater. Tom built the pipeline and could have stayed its only mechanic. From sprint 4 on, Bob did one pipeline change per sprint with Tom reviewing, and Jim ran the drop-2 vendor import with Tom watching. When Tom was on leave in sprint 9 nothing stopped.

51.6.2 Forcing it on the skeptic

Symptom. The skeptic complies, silently, does the minimum, and the old way continues in a spreadsheet on the side.

Why it happens. Management directed the change, so arguing feels pointless; the skeptic's objections are treated as resistance instead of requirements.

Fix. Write the objections down and answer each one with evidence, as Chapter 3, The directive did and Chapter 38, How the team changed its mind revisits. Give the skeptic the measure they would believe and let them run it. Never ask anyone to pretend to be enthusiastic.

At Tidewater. Bob's objections were the most specific, and so the most useful. Bob's question "how will I know the model is right?" became the lint and trace jobs. Bob's quote from sprint 1 ("I found the drift in two minutes, it used to take a week") came from running one of them.

51.6.3 Stand-up as a status meeting

Symptom. The stand-up takes forty minutes, each person reports to Jim, and problems are solved in the meeting.

Why it happens. The team's last daily meeting format was a status meeting with a manager, and that is what a daily meeting feels like.

Fix. Terse statuses: yesterday, today, blockers, with story ids, posted in the meeting chat and checked by the kit's lint (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro). Problems get named in the stand-up and solved after it, by the people involved.

At Tidewater. The first stand-up ran twenty-five minutes. By sprint 3, statuses were one line each, the lint found nothing to complain about, and the meeting took ten minutes.

51.6.4 Tasks too big to finish

Symptom. Stories carry over sprint after sprint, and tasks sit in the "in progress" column for more than a week.

Why it happens. Estimates in the document era were in weeks or months, and a five-point ceiling feels artificial.

Fix. Enforce the sizes: a task is at most five points (five ideal days) and is cut further if it might not finish in a week; a story fits in a sprint. A carried-over story is discussed at the retrospective, not just moved.

At Tidewater. The Stations story in sprint 4 carried two points into sprint 5 (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed). The retrospective found that its level-tag task was really two tasks. Carryovers were rare after that.

51.7 A monthly look in the mirror

Checklist: Pitfall check, once a month at the retrospective
  • ☐ The v2 model has no duplicate blocks, no package cycles, and no clutter without a discrepancy report
  • ☐ Converter output is edited in place only; government-only content is in files the converter never writes (model/library/conventions/ and the like)
  • ☐ Nobody pushed to vendor/prime except imports
  • ☐ Requirement text changes came only from drops
  • ☐ Every drop had a v1 delta, and its manual items became tasks
  • ☐ No MR this month was larger than a task; no branch lived longer than a week
  • ☐ No force push, no squash, no unprotected branch
  • ☐ Every conflicted file in a vendor merge is listed in its MR with how it was resolved
  • ☐ develop was never red for more than a working day
  • ☐ Every allow_failure has a reason and an issue
  • ☐ Tools are pinned; upgrades were stories
  • ☐ Every reported number came from a script; every agreed measure was reported
  • ☐ Each runbook was followed by someone other than its author at least once
  • ☐ Stand-ups took fifteen minutes or less
  • ☐ No story carried over twice

51.8 Applying this to your project

  • Copy the monthly checklist into your retrospective template. It costs five minutes.
  • Adapt the pitfalls to your sources. If your v1 model has no prime contractor and no vendor branch, the vendor pitfalls become pitfalls about your own Cameo exports, but reformatting and in-place editing matter just as much.
  • Decide locally which pitfalls your organization is most prone to. A team with a strong CCB culture will fall into old reviews in new clothes; a team with an enthusiastic tool-builder will fall into tools before habits. Watch for your own two.

51.9 Exercises

Exercise 51.1: Diagnose the symptom

For each symptom, name the pitfall and the first thing you would do: (a) a vendor merge conflicts on 60 lines of a file the government only added level tags to; (b) the drift count rose after a government MR; (c) the TODO count is zero but the prime's manifest mentions a new state; (d) develop has been red since Tuesday.

Exercise 51.2: Your two pitfalls

Pick the two pitfalls your own organization is most likely to fall into. For each, write the symptom you would expect to see first in your environment, and one rule that would prevent it.

Exercise 51.3: Prove the TODO count blind spot

Generate drops 2 and 3 with perl sim/tidewater-v1.pl --drop 2 /tmp/d2 and --drop 3 /tmp/d3. Convert both with xmi2sysml.pl --out and compare the two stations/Stations.sysml files. Then run xmi2sysml.pl --delta /tmp/d2/tidewater.xmi /tmp/d3/tidewater.xmi. Which change appears in the delta and not in the converted files, and why?

The appendices are for use at the keyboard. Appendix A, Command reference lists every command the book uses, with its options, checked against the tools' own help. The three quick reference guides, Appendix B, Quick reference: Vim for MBSE DevSecOps, Appendix C, Quick reference: git, gitflow and the GitLab tools and Appendix D, Quick reference: SysML v1 to v2, are meant to be printed and kept beside the monitor. Appendix J, Checklists gathers every checklist in the book in one place, Appendix K, Glossary translates between systems engineering, DevSecOps and SysML v2, and Appendix N, Answers to the exercises answers the exercises.

This appendix lists every command the book uses, grouped by tool, with the options that matter for the process. The syntax lines are taken from each tool's own help, which is always the final word: run the help command shown at the top of each section when in doubt. Commands are run from Git Bash on Windows (or any shell on Linux) at the root of the kit unless the section says otherwise; perl bin/... paths are relative to the kit. In the model repository the pipeline reaches the same tools through the KIT variable, as perl "$KIT/tools/sysml/model.pl" and so on.

--template NAME reads .gitlab/issue_templates/NAME.md from the current directory, so run it inside a clone of the model repository. The target defaults to the project's default branch (develop). merge refuses, with GitLab's own reason, until the pipeline has succeeded, the approvals (including code owners) are in and every resolvable discussion is resolved. mr show prints the pipeline's report summaries (tests, code quality, metrics), as the MR page's widgets do.

sysml.pl check checks each file against the official SysML v2 grammar and prints FILE:LINE:COL: error: ... for each problem, a form Vim's quickfix list reads directly (\mx checks the current file).

A.6 The pipeline's helpers

Every job in the model repository's .gitlab-ci.yml runs one shell-neutral line, perl ci/job.pl NAME, where NAME is the job (grammar, lint, outline, todo, trace, vcrm, recipe, complexity, docs, delta, baseline, ...; perl ci/job.pl alone lists them all). The script calls the tools below and the kit's model tools through KIT, so the pipeline runs unchanged under PowerShell, Git Bash or a container. To run one job's work by hand in a clone: perl ci/job.pl lint.

ci-reports.pl turns a check's output into the report files GitLab shows on a merge request: JUnit XML for the test widget, Code Quality JSON for the code quality widget (one finding per error, warning or TODO line) and metrics text. It only reports; the job still passes or fails on the check's own exit status. pages-index.pl writes the front page of the model site that the pages job publishes.

Appendix D Quick reference: SysML v1 to v2

The converters are bin/xmi2sysml.pl (Cameo XMI to SysML v2 text) and bin/reqif2sysml.pl (DOORS ReqIF or CSV to requirements, and the trace). Nothing in the v1 model is dropped silently: what the converter cannot carry becomes a // TODO line naming the v1 type and its xmi:id, and the --report lists it. The kit's one-sheet port card is docs/SYSML-PORT-QRG.pdf; this appendix adds the hand fixes and the drop cycle.

Block, Class, Component, Actorpart def; Generalization becomes :>
InterfaceBlock (or a Class used only as a port type)port def; FlowProperty becomes an in/out/inout feature
ConstraintBlockconstraint def with its parameters; the expression becomes a TODO
Signalitem def
DataType, ValueType, PrimitiveTypeattribute def (UML primitives map to ScalarValues::*)

Reference property (non-composite, Block-typed)ref part
Value property (value-typed or untyped)attribute (default value kept)
Signal-typed propertyitem
Port, ProxyPort, FullPort, FlowPortport n : PortDef; (conjugated: ~PortDef); atomic flow ports become port { in attribute ... }
Connectorconnection NAME connect a.p to b.q;
BindingConnectorbind a = b;
Activityaction def with parameters, call actions, control flows as first/then
UseCaseuse case def (skeleton)
Requirement and Cameo's requirement kindsrequirement with doc, doorsId, title, verificationMethod
TestCaseverification def
Satisfysatisfy R by X;
Verifyverify R; inside the test case's verification def objective

ownedCommentdoc /* ... */

Requirements are named from their DOORS id by both converters (TW-SYS-001 becomes TW_SYS_001), so satisfy and verify written by one resolve against the other.

Appendix E Rescue: when something goes wrong

From what you know

You know

the restore-from-backup request to IT.

Here it is called

rescue recipes for git and Vim.

What is new

almost every mistake can be undone by you, in a minute, because nothing committed is ever really lost.

Survival kit: Before you panic

What you have

a mistake. A commit on the wrong branch, a merge full of conflict markers, a red pipeline, a Vim window that says a swap file exists. Perhaps a sinking feeling.

What you need

the one recipe for this mistake, and the reassurance that nearly everything here can be undone. Every recipe in this appendix was run, start to finish, in a sandbox when this book was built: first the mess is made, then it is cleaned up.

E.1 Three facts that make mistakes cheap

Your clone is yours. Until you push, nothing you do on your laptop reaches anyone else. A wrong commit, a bad merge, a deleted branch: all of it is local, and all of it can be put back.

Git almost never forgets. Every commit you have made in the last few months is still in your clone, even after a reset or a deleted branch, and git reflog lists where your branch has been. Losing work in git takes real effort.

The protected branches protect you too. Nobody can push straight to develop or main; changes reach them only through a merge request that passed the pipeline and a review. So the worst a slip on your laptop can do is make a red merge request, which is what merge requests are for.

The one thing that is hard to undo is a secret (a token, a password) that reached GitLab. That has its own recipe, and the first step is a phone call, not a git command (Section E.13, "I pushed a secret").

E.2 The practice set-up

The recipes below share one sandbox: a bare repository standing in for GitLab, and a clone of it called work with main and develop. To follow along, make an empty folder, open Git Bash in it, and type this first.

Every recipe below starts with cd work, because each one is typed in a fresh Git Bash window.

E.3 "I committed to develop by mistake"

You meant to start a feature branch, forgot, and committed on develop. You have not pushed (you could not: the branch is protected). The fix is two moves: make a branch where you are, which keeps the commit, then put develop back where GitLab has it.

git reset --hard origin/develop moves your local develop to match GitLab's and throws away uncommitted changes, so make the branch first. If you had uncommitted edits too, commit them on the new branch before you switch back.

Tip: The habit that prevents it

Start every piece of work with gitlab.pl flow start feature NN-words or git switch -c feature/NN-words. Your shell prompt in Git Bash shows the branch in brackets; glance at it before git commit.

E.4 "I want my last commit back as edits"

The commit was premature: the message is wrong, or you want to add one more file. git reset --soft takes the commit away and leaves its changes staged, ready to commit again.

Only do this to commits you have not pushed. Once a commit is on GitLab, add a new commit instead of rewriting the old one.

E.5 "I am editing on the wrong branch"

You started editing, then noticed the prompt says develop. If the right branch does not exist yet, git switch -c takes your uncommitted edits with it. If it does exist, park the edits with git stash, switch, and bring them back.

E.6 "I lost a commit"

You ran a reset you did not mean, or deleted a branch, and a commit seems to be gone. It is not. git reflog lists every place your HEAD has been; HEAD@{1} is "where I was one move ago".

If the lost commit is further back, read down the git reflog list until you see its message, and use its hash: git branch rescue 1a2b3c4 makes a branch that points at it, without moving anything else.

E.7 "The merge is full of conflicts and I want out"

A merge stopped with CONFLICT and the file is full of <<<<<<< markers. If you are not ready to resolve them now, you do not have to: git merge --abort puts everything back exactly as it was before the merge.

When you are ready, resolving the conflict is described in Chapter 10, Vim for models: pick the right text between the markers, delete the markers, git add the file, git commit.

E.8 "I merged, and it was the wrong thing"

The merge finished, but it should not have happened: the wrong branch, or a resolution you regret. Before you push, ORIG_HEAD remembers where you were before the merge.

E.9 "A change on develop is wrong"

This is the one case where the mistake has already been reviewed and merged. Nobody rewrites develop: you make a new change that undoes the old one, and it goes through a merge request like any other. git revert -m 1 undoes a merge commit (the -m 1 says "keep the side that was develop").

(The local develop was used here as a stand-in for what GitLab did when it merged the merge request. On the real project, start from origin/develop after git pull.) In the merge request, say what was wrong and link the original one. GitLab also has a Revert button on a merged merge request that does the same thing.

E.10 "The pipeline is red"

A red pipeline is not a mistake; it is the safety net working. Read the first failed job's log from the top down to the first line that says error: it names the file and line. Reproduce it on your laptop, fix it, and push a new commit to the same branch. The merge request picks it up and the pipeline runs again.

The message points at line 3 because that is where the parser noticed; the missing ; is at the end of line 2. That is common: when the error line looks fine, look at the line above.

Never force-push a branch other people have, and never delete and re-open a merge request to "get a clean pipeline": the history of the red run is part of the record. Appendix F, Model error catalog lists the messages you will meet and their fixes.

E.11 "I changed a file I should not have"

You opened a converter-written file "just to look" and reformatted it, or a search-and-replace went too far. git restore puts the file back as it was in your last commit; git restore --staged unstages it without touching your edits.

E.12 "My clone is a mess"

Untracked files everywhere, branches you no longer understand. First look without deleting: git clean -n lists the untracked files it would remove. When you are sure, git clean -fd removes them. If the whole clone has become confusing, keep it aside and clone again; your pushed work is all on GitLab.

E.13 "I pushed a secret"

A token, a password or a private key reached GitLab in a commit. The pipeline's secrets job may have told you, or a reviewer did. The order matters:

  1. Tell the security owner now (on Tidewater, Tom, with the ISSM). Do not wait until you have fixed it.
  2. Rotate the secret: revoke the token in GitLab, change the password. This is the fix. Anything you do to the repository afterwards only tidies up, because a secret that was pushed must be treated as seen.
  3. Remove it from the branch before the merge request merges: amend or rewrite your own feature branch, with the security owner watching, and put the new value in a masked CI/CD variable (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).
  4. If it already merged to a protected branch, a maintainer and the security owner decide together whether the history is rewritten; that is never a solo decision.

Marked information pushed to the wrong place (spillage) follows the same first step, and then the program's spillage procedure: stop, notify, contain, and do not delete history yourself (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system).

E.14 "Vim says a swap file exists"

Vim keeps a swap file (.Stations.sysml.swp) while a file is open, so that a crash or a closed laptop lid does not lose your edits. When you open the file again, Vim warns that the swap file exists and offers choices:

  • [R]ecover if Vim crashed or the window was closed: your unsaved edits come back. Check them, :w to save, then quit and open the file again, answer [D]elete to remove the old swap file.
  • [E]dit anyway or [Q]uit if the file is open in another window right now: go back to that window instead.

From the shell, vim -r lists the swap files Vim can recover. Inside Vim, u undoes, Ctrl-R redoes, and :earlier 10m takes the buffer back to how it was ten minutes ago, which rescues most "I deleted the wrong block" moments without git at all.

E.15 "I broke a practice lesson"

The practice lessons (Appendix A, Command reference) are sandboxes; breaking them is allowed. Reset the lesson and set it up again.

Without --dir, the lessons live in the kit's data/practice/ folder and perl agile.pl practice reset N removes them there.

E.16 When to ask for help

Ask at once, without trying another command, when:

  • the mistake involves a secret or marked information;
  • you are about to use --force with git push, or to delete a branch other people use;
  • a recipe here did not do what it says (that is a bug in this book or the kit, and the team wants to know).

On Tidewater, asking was a stand-up sentence: "B TW-21 my clone of the model is tangled after the drop merge; need: ten minutes with Tom after stand-up." It took nine minutes, and Tom wrote the fix down as a new recipe.

Appendix F Model error catalog

From what you know

You know

Cameo's validation messages.

Here it is called

the model error catalog: grammar, lint, outline and recipe messages.

What is new

each message names a file and a line, and every one here was produced for real.

Survival kit: When a check says no

What you have

a message from the grammar check, lint, the outline check, a pipeline job or the recipe checker. It is terse, and it was written by a program, not a person.

What you need

what it means in plain words, the usual cause, and the fix. Every message in this appendix was produced by a runnable example when this book was built: the example breaks a real Tidewater file, shows the real message, and puts the file back.

F.1 How to read a message

Most messages share one shape:

From left to right: the file, the line, the column (characters from the left edge), the severity (error must be fixed before a merge; warning should be; note is information), and the message. In Vim, :make or the kit's \ml (lint) and \mx (grammar) put these lines in the quickfix list, and :cnext jumps from one to the next (Chapter 10, Vim for models).

Two habits save most of the time spent on errors:

  • Fix the first message first. One missing ; can produce a cascade; the first message is the cause, the rest are often echoes.
  • When the line looks fine, look one line up. Parsers notice a problem where the text stops making sense, which is usually just after the mistake.

The messages come from five places, in the order the pipeline runs them:

Table F.1. Where model errors come from
ToolWhat it checksPipeline job
tools/sysml/sysml.pl checkthe text against the official SysML v2 grammargrammar
tools/sysml/model.pl lintnames resolve, no duplicates, brackets balance, imports existlint
tools/sysml/model.pl checklevel tags and the 2-to-9 outline ruleoutline
ci/job.plthe pipeline's own rules: lint at 0/0, ratchets, secrets, docs currentevery job
tools/sysml/req-recipe.plrequirement wording against the recipe (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe)recipe

F.2 The practice model

The examples share one sandbox: a model repository made with kickoff.pl scaffold, with Tidewater's drop 1 converted into it in layers, exactly as the team's first import, with the two roots of the part and function trees named in sysml.conf (the scaffold leaves them for you to set). To follow along, run this in an empty folder.

In the examples below, a check that finds a problem is followed by || echo "exit status $?". A check that passes exits with status 0; one that finds errors exits with 1 (2 means it could not run at all). The pipeline reads exactly that number to colour a job red or green, and the echo shows it to you. Each example starts with git checkout -q -- model, which puts the model files back the way the last commit had them, so one broken example never spills into the next.

F.3 Grammar check messages

The grammar check reads each file against the official SysML v2 grammar. Its messages all say unexpected something, then list a few of the things it would have accepted there. The list is a hint about what kind of text belongs at that spot, not a menu: read the word it calls unexpected, and the line above it.

F.3.1 unexpected ...; expected ',', '.', ':' ... -- a missing semicolon

Means. Line 3 ends without ;, so the parser read on into line 4 and stumbled on port. Fix. Add the ; at the end of the line above the one named. Every member line ends with ; or a { ... } body.

F.3.2 unexpected end of file -- a brace never closed

Means. The file ended while a { was still open. Fix. Count braces from the top; in Vim, put the cursor on a { and press % to jump to its partner. The kit's lint names the line of the brace that is never closed (Section F.4.5, is never closed), which is often quicker.

F.3.3 unexpected 'Name' after a SysML v1 word

Means. state machine and region are SysML v1 vocabulary. The v2 grammar read state as the start of a state usage named machine, and did not expect a second name. Fix. Write the v2 form: state def BuoyModes { entry; then Observing; state Observing; ... }, and exhibit it on the part with exhibit state modes : BuoyModes;. Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook shows the full pattern; this is the mistake a v1 modeler makes most, and a local AI assistant makes it too (Chapter 18, A local AI assistant on the laptop).

F.3.4 unexpected 'doc' -- a doc comment in quotes

Means. Two mistakes, and the parser reports the first one it can see: line 3 has no ;, so doc on line 4 is unexpected. Fixing that reveals the second: a doc comment is written doc /* text */, not in quotes. Fix. attribute mass = 1.5; and doc /* A buoy. */.

F.4 Lint messages

Lint runs on the whole model at once, so it can see what the grammar check cannot: whether a name you use is declared somewhere. It ends with one line the pipeline reads, elements=N errors=E warnings=W; the lint job fails unless both counts are zero.

F.4.1 unresolved type

Means. Hul is not declared in any file of the model, nor in the standard library. Fix. Correct the spelling, or add the private import of the package that declares the type. If the name comes from the prime's model, it may have been renamed in a newer drop: xmi2sysml.pl --delta ... --impact lists renames (Appendix D, Quick reference: SysML v1 to v2).

F.4.2 duplicate member

Means. Two members of one package have the same name. Usually a copy-and-paste, or a hand-written element that the next prime drop also brought in. Fix. Keep one. If both are real, rename yours and raise a question with the prime.

F.4.3 a SysML keyword cannot be a name

Means. Words such as state, action, port, in and out are part of the language. Fix. Choose another name (hullState), or quote it ('state') when it must match a name in the prime's model.

F.4.4 import of unknown package

Means. The package named in the import does not exist (here Station for Stations). Fix. Correct the name. Package names are the file's top-level package, not the file name.

F.4.5 is never closed

Means. A { has no matching }. Lint names the line where the unclosed brace opens, which the grammar check cannot. Fix. Add the } where the element ends.

F.5 Outline and level-tag messages

model.pl check prints two sections. Level tags: each part definition carries a level tag (@L2Segment;), and the tag must match the level where the part tree first reaches it. Outline: every folder and package should hold between 2 and 9 entries, the span a person can take in at a glance.

F.5.1 tagged Ln, first reached at Lm

Means. StationSegment is two steps below the network (level 2), but someone tagged it as a level-4 subsystem. Fix. Use the tag the TODO line named (@L2Segment;). The converter's TODO line always says which stereotype the prime applied; copying it is the safe choice.

A misspelled tag (@L2Segmnt;) is not reported by lint or by the check: it is a different, undeclared name that nothing reads. The outline job's level count and practice lesson 10's checker catch it (Chapter 10, Vim for models); a review should too.

F.5.2 outline violations

Means. The model has folders or packages with fewer than 2 or more than 9 entries. On a fresh conversion this is normal: the prime's packages were never shaped to the rule. The pipeline therefore treats the outline as a ratchet: .ci/outline-max records the number the team accepted, and the job fails only when a change makes it worse. A new scaffold's allowance is its own few violations plus a little room for the first folders, so a whole converted drop goes far over it. Fix. On the first import, record the starting number in .ci/outline-max in the same merge request, with the reason in the description. After that, never raise it: split the folder or package that grew, and lower the number when it falls.

F.6 Pipeline job messages

These come from ci/job.pl, the small script every job runs (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). They are written for the person reading the job log, so most of them already say what to do.

Table F.2. Messages from ci/job.pl
MessageMeansFix
lint is not 0/0 (elements=N errors=E warnings=W)lint found somethingread lint.txt in the job's artifacts, or run model.pl lint locally
this change adds outline violations (N > M): fix them, do not raise .ci/outline-maxthe outline ratchetsplit what grew; see Section F.5.2, outline violations

this change adds trace gaps: orphans 1 -> 2 (see trace.txt)the merge request removed a satisfy or verify, or added a requirement nothing satisfiesrestore the link, or link the new requirement, before merging

the kit on this runner is X, but .kit-version pins Ythe runner has another kit version than the model asks forupdate the runner's kit, or bump .kit-version in a reviewed merge request

Four of them, produced:

The token in the third example is assembled when the example runs, so the kit's own secret scan never sees a real- looking token in this book's source.

F.7 Requirement recipe findings

req-recipe.pl reads requirement text the way a careful reviewer does (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe). Its findings are graded: major (the statement cannot be verified as written), minor (it can, but something is missing), info.

Table F.3. Common recipe findings
FindingMeansFix
weak target verb 'provide' (also have, be, be able to, support, ensure ...)no test can show "provide"name the action: send, store, measure, report
2 operative verbs (shall, shall)two requirements in one sentencesplit it; each gets its own ID
'measure' with no measurable thresholda verb that implies a quantity, without oneadd the number and unit, or "at least", "within", "every"
passive 'shall be kept'the subject that must act is missingmake the specification target the subject
vague 'in time' (also as appropriate, user-friendly, fast ...)a word two readers read differentlyreplace it with the measure behind it
missing part Requirement IDno project-unique IDevery requirement needs one

On Tidewater the requirements belong to the prime's DOORS modules, so the fix for a finding there is a discrepancy report to the prime, not an edit in the government model (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).

F.8 When the message is not here

  • Search the kit's help: perl $KIT/agile.pl help error "the message" finds the entry for most kit messages.
  • Run the check on the one file alone (sysml.pl check FILE); a smaller input gives a clearer message.
  • Undo your last edit (git diff shows it) and redo it in two halves; the half that brings the message back holds the mistake.
  • Ask, with the exact message copied, the command you ran, and git status (Section E.16, When to ask for help).

Appendix G Modeling style guide

From what you know

You know

the drafting standard and the document style guide.

Here it is called

the modeling style guide.

What is new

much of it is checked by the pipeline.

A style guide exists so that three people write one model, not three. Every rule here is short, has a reason, and is the same rule the model repository's docs/conventions/naming.md states, which kickoff.pl scaffold puts in every new project. When the two disagree, the repository's copy wins: it is the one the team reviews and changes by merge request.

There is one rule above all the others:

Warning: Government text and the prime's text follow different rules

Files the converter writes from the prime's drops keep the prime's names and layout, exactly as delivered, with only the // TODO lines replaced. Every rule below about names, order and formatting applies to what the government writes. Changing the prime's text for style makes every later drop conflict (Chapter 51, Pitfalls and anti-patterns); ask the prime through a discrepancy report instead.

G.1 Names

Table G.1. Names in the model
ThingRuleExampleNot
packageUpperCamelCase noun, the subject it holdsStations, PowerSystemstations_pkg, Pkg1
definition (part, port, item, interface, state)UpperCamelCase nounMooredBuoy, ObservationIFmoored_buoy, Block1
action definitionUpperCamelCase verb phraseCheckQuality, PublishBulletinQC
usage (part, port, attribute, action)lowerCamelCase, the role it playsbuoys, obsOut, stateOfChargeMooredBuoy1, p1
requirement usagethe DOORS id, - and . as _TW_SYS_006req6
requirement idas DOORS has it, never reusedTW-SYS-006a new number for an edited requirement
verification definitionverb + what it showsTestDataFlow, InspectVesselAccessTest1
metadata definitionwhat it marksProcured, L3StationStereo7
quoted namesonly to match a source that used spaces'Stakeholder Needs' (from DOORS)in new government text

A name says what the thing is, not where it sits in a diagram or a document. Copy of SensorSuite, Battery_old and TBD Component came from the v1 model's spider web; they do not come back. Acronyms are written as words in names (ObservationIf would be correct by the rule; ObservationIF is kept because the prime chose it), and abbreviations are avoided unless the program uses them in speech.

G.2 Files and folders

  • One top-level package per file, named after the package: Stations.sysml holds package Stations.
  • Folders are layers, in this order: library/, requirements/, logical/, physical/, analysis/, verification/. A package may depend on its own layer or a lower one, never a higher one; the complexity job checks it (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web). For the prime's packages the layer is set by the converter's layout map, so every drop lands in the same folder (Chapter 16, The model repository: what goes where).
  • Government-only additions go in the layer they belong to (library/conventions/Conventions.sysml, logical/GovBehavior.sysml), never inside a converter-written file, and begin with a comment that says why they exist.
  • Generated files are never edited by hand: docs/ comes from model.pl docs, the DOORS requirement packages from reqif2sysml.pl. Change the source and regenerate.

G.3 Inside a file

A government-written file, in the order its parts appear:

  • The opening comment answers three questions in two or three lines: why this file exists, which decision allowed it, who owns it.
  • The package's doc comment says what the package holds, in one sentence a reviewer can check against its contents.
  • Imports come first and name exactly what is used (private import ScalarValues::Real;). A wildcard (::*) is allowed only in files the converter writes, where it is the converter's choice.
  • Every definition has a doc comment that says what the thing is or does, in the program's words, not the model's: "Send battery state, mode and faults to the data center", not "ReportHealth action def".
  • Members in a stable order: parts, then ports, then attributes, then connections and satisfy relationships, then behavior. Not alphabetical: grouped by kind, so a diff shows what kind of thing changed.
  • One statement per line, four spaces of indentation, no tabs. Lines under about 120 characters; a long requirement text is the exception, because its doc is the requirement.

G.4 Metadata, not stereotypes

  • Use metadata definitions for what v1 did with stereotypes: level tags (@L3Station;), procurement (@Procured { supplier = "..."; partNumber = "..."; }), markings (@Marking { level = Level::U; }), trust zones.
  • Keep the set small and declared in one place, the conventions library. A new metadata definition is a decision: it needs a merge request that says what will read it.
  • A tag nobody reads is decoration. If no check, view or report uses a metadata definition, remove it.

G.5 Relationships

  • Declare each relationship once, on the element that owns the responsibility: the part satisfys the requirement, the verification case verifys it. Reverse views (which parts satisfy this requirement?) are generated, never maintained by hand.
  • Trace at the level that actually satisfies, and no lower. A requirement satisfied by the data center is satisfied by DataCenter, not by each of its five services.
  • Allocate at the agreed level (Tidewater: the segment and station level), not every step to every component.
  • No dependency used as a vague "related to": it is how the v1 model grew its cycles. If two elements are related, say how (satisfy, allocate, connect) or leave them alone.

G.6 Requirement text

Requirement statements follow the recipe (Chapter 7, Requirements a pipeline can check: the recipe): one requirement per statement, a measurable threshold where the verb implies one, no weak verbs (provide, support, be capable of), the specification target as the subject, and the project-unique ID. The prime's DOORS modules own the wording on Tidewater, so a recipe finding there becomes a discrepancy report, not an edit.

G.7 TODO lines

  • A converter // TODO line is replaced by the line or block that closes it, in place, without moving or reformatting the lines around it. The next drop then merges cleanly.
  • A TODO you cannot close yet stays as it is; do not delete it to make the count fall. The count is the port's burn-down, and it has to be true.
  • Government text has no TODO lines of its own. Open an issue instead, and put the issue number in a comment if the reader needs to know.

G.8 Commits and merge requests

  • Commit message: a first line under about 60 characters, in the imperative ("Add the Storm mode to BuoyModes"), then a blank line and why. The "what" is in the diff.
  • Merge request title: what the model gains, as a verb phrase someone could demo ("Close the Stations TODO lines").
  • One story's worth per merge request. A merge request that touches four packages for four reasons is four merge requests.
  • Decisions in ADRs: one decision per file in docs/adr/, with the context, the decision and the consequences. Anything a new team member might "fix" without knowing why it is that way deserves one.

G.9 Branches, tags and issues

Table G.2. Names outside the model
ThingRuleExample
feature branchfeature/<issue number>-<a few words>feature/41-sys006-wording
release branchrelease/baseline-Nrelease/baseline-1
hotfix branchhotfix/<what>hotfix/satisfy-sys-014
drop branchmade by gitlab.pl flow vendorfeature/drop-v1.1
tagbaseline-N, annotated, made by gitlab.pl flow releasedbaseline-0
story titlesomething you could show at the reviewBreak the Stations to DataCenter cycle
task titleone piece of work under a weekMove the ObservationRecord dependency to Interfaces
discrepancy report titlethe v1 element and the problemDR: TW-SYS-012 has no satisfy in drop 1

G.10 Changing this guide

The style guide is the team's, not this book's. Change docs/conventions/naming.md by merge request, with the reason in the description, and say in the review what existing text will be brought in line and when (never "all at once": a style sweep across converter-written files is exactly the reformatting Chapter 51, Pitfalls and anti-patterns warns about).
