Appendix I Templates and GitLab Markdown, field by field

From what you know

You know

document templates and CDRL formats.

Here it is called

GitLab templates for issues, merge requests and wiki pages, in Markdown.

What is new

a template opens pre-filled every time, with checklists a reviewer can tick.

This appendix prints every template the Tidewater project uses and every filled-in sample of a GitLab text field, with notes on the Markdown each one uses. The files are in the kit under tools/gitlab/templates/ (copied into the model repository) and tools/gitlab/samples/. Read it with GitLab open in another window and try each feature in a scratch issue.

I.1 How GitLab uses templates

GitLab looks for description templates in two folders of the repository's default branch:

  • .gitlab/issue_templates/NAME.md appears in the Choose a template list when someone creates an issue;
  • .gitlab/merge_request_templates/NAME.md appears in the same list on a new merge request. A merge request template named Default.md is filled in automatically on every new MR.

Because templates are files in the repository, they are changed like the model: by merge request, reviewed by their code owner (Tom), and recorded in history. The Definition of Done can therefore say "the MR description follows the Default template" and mean a specific, versioned text.

Three things in templates do work beyond filling in text:

  • HTML comments (<!-- ... -->) are prompts. They are visible while you edit and invisible once the description is saved, so a template can explain each section without the explanation cluttering the issue.
  • Quick actions on their own lines at the end (/label ..., /milestone ..., /assign ...) run when the issue or MR is created, so every story starts with the right labels without anyone remembering them. A quick action with nothing after it (/assign @ with no name) does nothing and is removed, which lets a template remind the author to fill it in.
  • Task lists (- [ ] item) become checkboxes that anyone with access can tick without editing the text, and GitLab counts them in the issue list ("2 of 5 checklist items").

I.2 GitLab Markdown in fifteen features

Table I.1. The GitLab Markdown this project uses
FeatureYou writeUsed in
Headings## What and whyevery template
Tablesrows of cells between | characters, a |---|---| line under the headerstories, MRs, DRs, releases
Task lists- [ ] item and - [x] itemStory, Task, MR checks, DoR, DoD
HTML comments<!-- prompt -->every template
Quick actions/label ~"type::story" on its own lineevery issue and MR template
Issue and MR references#19, !19, tidewater/model#19stories, MRs, comments
Milestone references%"Sprint 4"Story, Task, release notes
Label references~"workflow::review"comments, the board legend
Mentions@jimMR reviews, DRs
Closing keywordsCloses #19 in an MR descriptionDefault, Hotfix
Table of contents[[_TOC_]]the wiki, the README
Collapsible sections<details><summary>Log</summary> ... </details>Story (the DoR), MR pipeline logs
Alertsa quote starting > [!note] (or [!tip], [!important], [!warning], [!caution])wiki, README, release notes
Diagramsa fenced block tagged mermaidGitflow, Drop Intake Runbook, the README
Suggestionsa fenced block tagged suggestion:-0+1 in a review comment on a diff lineMR reviews

Footnotes ([^1] in the text and a line [^1]: the note at the end) are used in wiki decision records. Mathematics ($...$) and front matter are available but the project never needed them.

I.3 Issue templates

I.3.1 Story

Line by line:

  • The opening comment states the size rule (one sprint, tasks under a week) and the naming rule. It disappears when the story is saved, so it is a reminder, not clutter.
  • Why asks for the outcome in one or two sentences. Jim insisted on it after sprint 1, when two stories turned out to be the same work described differently; the why makes duplicates obvious.
  • What "done" looks like is the acceptance criteria as a task list. Two items are pre-filled because they apply to every story that changes the model: a green pipeline and no new trace gaps. The reviewer ticks them.
  • Tasks is a table of task issues with points and owners. GitLab turns #21 into a link showing the task's title and state, so the table is also a live status view.
  • The Definition of Ready sits inside <details>, collapsed, so it is there for the refinement session and out of the way afterwards.
  • The quick actions label the story (type::story, workflow::ready, a priority), and leave the milestone, assignee and weight for the author: %"Sprint " without a number reminds without guessing.

I.3.2 Task

A task is the smallest unit and the template is correspondingly short. Part of # links it to its story. Do is a checklist the reviewer can follow; its pre-filled line, "Run gitlab.pl ci locally before pushing", is the habit that keeps pipeline failures off the shared branches. Done when asks for one observable result, such as "grep finds no TODO in model/physical/stations/Stations.sysml". /estimate 1d sets a default estimate the author changes; GitLab shows estimate against /spend time on the issue.

I.3.3 Defect, Discrepancy Report, Prime Drop, Epic, Spike

A defect is something wrong in the government's own model or pipeline. Its labels say where it was found (phase::port or phase::maintenance) and what kind it is (area::interface for problems between packages, the status metrics' measure H).

A discrepancy report is a problem in the prime's v1 model or DOORS. The government does not fix it; it reports it. The two-column table without a header row (| | | then |---|---|) is a GitLab idiom for a form: labels on the left, values on the right. The Closure checklist has two steps, sent and fixed, and the second names the drop intake issue that confirmed the fix. That link is how a DR's life is traced from finding to closure.

The prime drop template is the intake checklist for one delivery. Its task list follows the drop cycle in Appendix D, Quick reference: SysML v1 to v2 step by step, so the issue itself records that every step was done, by whom and when.

On GitLab Free there are no group epics, so an epic is an ordinary issue labelled type::epic whose description lists its stories. On Premium the same text goes in a real epic, and the stories are attached to it.

A spike is time-boxed investigation that ends in a decision, not in a model change. Its output is usually a wiki decision record (sample 12 below).

I.4 Merge request templates

The Default template is filled in on every new MR. Its opening comment calls the MR what it is in systems engineering terms, a change request in miniature. Closes # and Part of # connect the MR to its task and story: when the MR merges into the default branch (develop), GitLab closes the task automatically. Checks is the author's own checklist, deliberately overlapping the pipeline: the author runs the same checks before asking anyone to review. /assign_reviewer @bob is a default the author changes; the code owner rules decide who must approve regardless.

The Prime Drop MR template carries the delta summary and a conflict table: one row per conflicted file with how it was resolved. The reviewer checks the table against the drop's manifest.

Release and hotfix MRs target main. The Release template records the baseline in a two-column form (which commit of develop, which prime drops, which sprints), the release checklist and the gaps accepted with it. The Hotfix template asks for what is wrong in the released baseline, the smallest change that corrects it, and an after-merge checklist: tag baseline-N.1, back-merge to develop, tell the baseline's users. After either merges, gitlab.pl flow released IID tags main, creates the release and opens the back-merge MR.

I.5 Repository files

I.5.1 CODEOWNERS

CODEOWNERS is not Markdown but it lives with the templates. Each [Section] lists default owners after its name; each path below it can name its own. GitLab reads the file from the MR's target branch. A ^ before a section makes it advisory: the generated docs/ are listed so reviewers are suggested, but no approval is required for them. With code owner approval enforced on develop (Premium), an MR touching model/doors/ cannot merge until Jim approves.

I.5.2 README, CHANGELOG, release notes

The README is the first page anyone sees in the repository. It uses an alert to say up front that everything is notional, a table for who does what, a layout table and a mermaid diagram of the branches.

The CHANGELOG follows the common Keep a Changelog layout: one section per baseline, newest first, with Added, Changed and Fixed. Its entries come from the Changelog: trailer the team puts in commit messages (sample 13). The link at the bottom compares the last baseline with develop; ../-/compare/ is GitLab's relative path for a comparison page.

Release notes are the description of a GitLab release. > [!important] makes the "cite this baseline by its tag" rule impossible to miss. The Known gaps task list records what the baseline ships with on purpose, so nobody mistakes an accepted gap for an oversight.

I.5.3 The project file

The full file continues with the area, owner, workflow, priority and severity labels, the sprint milestones, the approval rule and the variables. gitlab.pl setup applies it (Appendix A, Command reference); every comment beside a setting says why that setting was chosen, which is the record an auditor or a newcomer needs.

I.6 Wiki pages

The wiki is a git repository of Markdown pages beside the code. The team's pages started from these templates and were changed by the team over the project; gitlab.pl wiki put TITLE FILE publishes one.

The Definition of Done is a task list grouped by level (task, story, sprint, baseline). Pasting it into a story's comment gives a checklist to tick; keeping it in the wiki gives one place to change it.

The Glossary wiki page (wiki/Glossary.md) carries the same translations as Appendix K, Glossary, in the wiki's tables.

I.7 Filled-in samples

Each sample is what one GitLab field looks like after the team has filled it in, set in sprints 1 to 6. The index:

I.7.1 Planning: epic, story, task

The story's task table shows how references work as a status view: each #N renders with the task's title and an open or closed icon. The task is short because the story carries the context.

I.7.2 Problems: defect, discrepancy report, prime drop

I.7.3 Change: merge request, review, comments

The MR description's pipeline table sits inside <details>, so the review starts with what changed and why, and the log is one click away.

The review thread shows the three moves of a GitLab review: a comment on a line (resolvable, so the MR cannot merge until it is resolved), a suggestion the author applies with one click, and quick actions (/relate, /approve, /merge) that do the bookkeeping in the same comment.

Comments on a story double as its log: each stand-up-sized update carries a /spend and a workflow label change, so the board and the time report update themselves.

I.7.4 Time and record: milestone, release, wiki, commits

A decision record in the wiki: status, who decided, the context, the decision, the consequences, a diagram and a footnote. It is the document era's memo for record, with the difference that it is versioned and linked from the issues it affects.

Commit messages are not a GitLab field, but GitLab shows them everywhere and links their references. The format is the common git convention: a subject in the imperative under 72 characters, a blank line, the reason, and trailers (Changelog:, Issue:, Reviewed-by:) last.

I.7.5 The board and references

I.8 Applying this to your project

  • Copy the folder structure (.gitlab/issue_templates/, .gitlab/merge_request_templates/) and the Default MR template on day one; they cost nothing and shape every change from the start.
  • Adapt the labels and the quick actions in each template to your own label set. Keep scoped labels for anything that has exactly one value at a time (type, workflow state, priority).
  • Decide locally which fields your auditors will look for (the closure of a discrepancy report, the approval of a baseline) and make sure a template asks for each one.

I.9 Exercises

Exercise I.1: Write a story

In a scratch project, or on the emulator with gitlab.pl --local /tmp/gl issue new ... --template Story, write a story for "Close the DataCenter TODO lines" with three tasks under five points each. Make every quick action run.

Exercise I.2: Find the features

Pick three samples and list every GitLab Markdown feature each uses, from the table in Section I.2, GitLab Markdown in fifteen features. Which feature would you add to the Discrepancy Report template, and why?

Exercise I.3: Write a discrepancy report

Run the trace on drop 1 (reqif2sysml.pl --report --model) and write the discrepancy report for one orphan requirement, using the template. What exactly do you ask the prime to change, and how will you verify it in the next drop?

Appendix J Checklists

From what you know

You know

entry and exit criteria for reviews.

Here it is called

checklists for each step of the rhythm.

What is new

many items are confirmed by the pipeline instead of by a signature.

Every checklist in the book, in the order the work meets them. Print the ones you use; tick them in a GitLab issue comment (paste the lines as - [ ] items) when the record matters. Each names the chapter that explains it.

J.1 Week zero

From Chapter 3, The directive and Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab.

Checklist: Before sprint 1
  • ☐ Ask the enterprise GitLab administrators for the group, the project, the accounts and a runner (lead time: about a week)
  • ☐ Book the security officer (ISSM) for a toolchain briefing in sprint 2
  • ☐ Check every laptop: Git for Windows (Git Bash, Perl), Vim, the kit at the agreed tag; perl tests/run.pl passes
  • ☐ Agree the scorecard with management: measures, how each is computed, targets, old-way baselines; signed
  • ☐ Ask the prime for stable xmi:ids across drops and a MANIFEST.txt with checksums in each drop
  • ☐ Log the first drop's delivery against its CDRL; store it on approved storage; do nothing else with it yet
  • ☐ Put stand-ups, planning, refinement, review and retrospective in the calendar for the whole quarter
  • ☐ Enter holidays and planned leave, so the first capacity is honest
  • ☐ Make the journal project: daily.pl init, daily.pl roster add ... for each person

J.2 Project set-up

From Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab and Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep.

Checklist: The GitLab project, first day
  • ☐ project.conf written: settings, members, branches, tags, labels, sprints, approvals, variables (no secret values)
  • ☐ gitlab.pl --dry-run setup project.conf reviewed, then applied
  • ☐ Default branch is develop; merge method is merge commit; squash never; pipelines must succeed; discussions must be resolved
  • ☐ main and develop protected: push allowed to no one, force push off, code owner approval on (Premium)
  • ☐ vendor/prime protected: push by maintainers, merge by no one
  • ☐ baseline-* tags protected: created by maintainers only
  • ☐ CODEOWNERS, issue templates and MR templates committed through the first MR
  • ☐ Runner registered on a dedicated machine (project runner, tags, service account without admin rights, core.longpaths, antivirus exclusion for the builds folder) and a first job has run
  • ☐ .gitlab-ci.yml with grammar, lint and outline jobs; a deliberately broken MR has been seen to fail and be blocked
  • ☐ Board with workflow columns; sprint milestones two sprints ahead
  • ☐ Wiki: Home, Definition of Ready, Definition of Done, Glossary

J.3 The sprint

From Chapter 13, The operating model and Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro.

Checklist: Kickoff and planning (day 1)
  • ☐ Last sprint's carryover discussed, not just moved
  • ☐ Capacity per person from the calendar (holidays, leave, training); cap in the stand-up file
  • ☐ The sprint goal written in one sentence, in the milestone description
  • ☐ Stories pulled in priority order until about 85 to 95 percent of capacity
  • ☐ Every pulled story meets the Definition of Ready; every task is 5 points or fewer
  • ☐ Estimates settled by #est rounds in the chat; outliers explained before a re-vote
  • ☐ commit lines in the stand-up file; issues moved to the sprint milestone and workflow::ready
  • ☐ The board shows only this sprint's milestone
Checklist: Daily stand-up (15 minutes)
  • ☐ First question: is develop green? If not, fixing it comes first
  • ☐ Each person posts one terse line: Yesterday, Today, Blockers, with story ids
  • ☐ daily.pl lint while people are still on the call; replies pasted back for any status it flags
  • ☐ Blockers named, owners agreed; the discussion happens after the stand-up
  • ☐ After the call: daily.pl answers, confirm the suggested lines, daily.pl compile, daily.pl commit
Checklist: Refinement (day 9)
  • ☐ New work entered as stories (new lines and issues from the Story template)
  • ☐ Each candidate story checked against the Definition of Ready; tasks cut to 5 points or fewer
  • ☐ #est rounds for anything not yet sized
  • ☐ Stale stories pruned with a reason
  • ☐ Dependencies on the prime or another story linked
  • ☐ The next sprint's top stories labelled workflow::ready
Checklist: Review and demo (day 10)
  • ☐ Demonstrate from the real system: the merged MRs, a pipeline with its widgets, the model site, the trace
  • ☐ Show the scorecard, every agreed measure, including the bad ones
  • ☐ Record management's feedback as issues, not as notes
  • ☐ Close the stories that meet the Definition of Done; the rest carry over with a reason
Checklist: Retrospective (day 10)
  • ☐ The pulse survey (five questions, 1 to 5), anonymous
  • ☐ Start, stop, continue: one change the team will actually make next sprint, written as a story or a rule
  • ☐ The monthly pitfall check (Section 51.7, A monthly look in the mirror) once a month
  • ☐ Last retrospective's change: did it happen?
Checklist: Weekly communication (Friday)
  • ☐ daily.pl quad reviewed and sent: priorities, watch items, milestones, accomplishments
  • ☐ The scorecard numbers refreshed from the export, not typed
  • ☐ Anything management must decide is stated as a decision with a date

J.4 A change

From Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers, Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job and Appendix I, Templates and GitLab Markdown, field by field.

Checklist: Author, for every task
  • ☐ Branch from up-to-date develop: gitlab.pl flow start feature IID-slug
  • ☐ Converter output edited in place and minimally; government-only content in files the converter never writes (model/library/conventions/ and the like)
  • ☐ \mx on each edited file, \ml on the model, gitlab.pl ci --event merge_request_event --target develop before pushing
  • ☐ docs/ regenerated (\md) and committed
  • ☐ Commit messages: imperative subject under 72 characters, the why, a Changelog: trailer
  • ☐ MR from the Default template: what and why, Closes #task, model changes, checks ticked
  • ☐ Pipeline green on the merged result; every discussion answered
Checklist: Reviewer, for every MR
  • ☐ The change matches the task; nothing unrelated is in it
  • ☐ Every closed TODO line is replaced by the construct that closes it
  • ☐ No requirement text changed outside a drop
  • ☐ Pipeline green; JUnit and code quality widgets show no new failures; TODO count did not rise without a task
  • ☐ Trace: no new orphan, unverified or drifted requirement, or a DR is linked
  • ☐ Comments are resolvable and specific; suggestions used for small fixes
  • ☐ Approve only what you would sign

J.5 A prime drop

From Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle and Appendix D, Quick reference: SysML v1 to v2.

Checklist: Drop intake (one story, finished in the sprint it arrives)
  • ☐ Files in a dated folder outside the repository; every sha256 matches MANIFEST.txt
  • ☐ Prime Drop issue opened from the template in the current sprint
  • ☐ Files uploaded to the package registry (prime-drop, the version)
  • ☐ gitlab.pl flow vendor DROPDIR VERSION: vendor/prime committed and pushed, feature/drop-VERSION started
  • ☐ xmi2sysml.pl --delta OLD NEW read; each manual line is a task
  • ☐ Each conflict resolved by taking the vendor side and re-applying the government edit; listed in the MR
  • ☐ No conflict markers left; grammar, lint 0/0 and outline pass
  • ☐ Trace read: DRs fixed by this drop closed, new gaps raised as DRs
  • ☐ MR from the Prime Drop template, approved by a code owner, merged; CHANGELOG.md updated
  • ☐ Drop latency (delivery to merged) recorded
Checklist: Discrepancy report to the prime
  • ☐ Facts only: what the model says, what DOORS says, what the trace or delta printed
  • ☐ The v1 element's qualified name and xmi:id; the DOORS id
  • ☐ One requested change, specific enough to verify in the next drop
  • ☐ Severity set; sent through the contract channel; the prime's tracking number recorded
  • ☐ Closed only by the intake issue of the drop that fixes it

J.6 A baseline and a hotfix

From Chapter 43, Maintenance through the life cycle.

Checklist: Baseline
  • ☐ Content decided: which drops and stories are in; the rest moved to the next milestone
  • ☐ gitlab.pl flow start release baseline-N; only release fixes on the branch
  • ☐ CHANGELOG.md [Unreleased] moved under the baseline heading; docs regenerated
  • ☐ Release MR from the template: content, accepted gaps listed and accepted by the model lead
  • ☐ Merged into main; gitlab.pl flow released IID tags baseline-N with the docs hash and opens the back-merge
  • ☐ Tag pipeline: the baseline job reports that the baseline rebuilds identically
  • ☐ Release notes published; project exported and stored; milestones closed
  • ☐ Back-merge MR to develop merged
Checklist: Hotfix to a released baseline
  • ☐ The defect is in the released baseline and someone depends on it now (otherwise it waits for the next baseline)
  • ☐ gitlab.pl flow start hotfix slug from main; the smallest change that corrects it
  • ☐ Hotfix MR to main; pipeline green; approved
  • ☐ Tagged baseline-N.1; the users of baseline-N told
  • ☐ The same fix back-merged to develop

J.7 Administration

From Chapter 42, Administration; each is explained there.

Checklist: Onboarding one person
  • ☐ Account, project role (the lowest that works), SSH key or token, CODEOWNERS if an owner
  • ☐ roster.txt and the stand-up invitation
  • ☐ Onboarding wiki page with a pairing partner; first MR merged within a week
Checklist: Offboarding one person (the same day)
  • ☐ Removed from the project and the group; tokens revoked; readable CI/CD variables rotated
  • ☐ Open issues and MRs reassigned; pipeline schedules taken over; CODEOWNERS, roster and invitation updated
Checklist: Monthly
  • ☐ Token inventory checked; any token expiring within a month rotated
  • ☐ Runner patched (operating system, gitlab-runner matching the server's version, Git for Windows with the laptops, the kit at its tag)
  • ☐ Pipeline schedules owned by a current member and passing
  • ☐ Container image rebuilt from a pinned base and scanned (only if the Docker image is used)
  • ☐ Protection audit: the settings pages match project.conf (setup re-applied if not); every merge had a passing pipeline and a non-author approval
  • ☐ Audit events reviewed (Premium)
  • ☐ Project exported to the package registry
  • ☐ GitLab release notes read for CI and API changes
Checklist: Quarterly
  • ☐ Access review, inherited memberships included
  • ☐ Restore test from the latest export into a scratch project

J.8 Before you call the port done

Checklist: The port's exit criteria
  • ☐ TODO count zero, or every remaining TODO has an issue and an accepted reason
  • ☐ No duplicate blocks, no package cycles; the clutter has DRs and the prime is removing it upstream
  • ☐ Trace: every requirement linked; every orphan, unverified or drifted requirement has a DR
  • ☐ Every outline waiver removed; all jobs blocking except those allowed to fail by design, with reasons
  • ☐ A baseline tagged on main that rebuilds identically
  • ☐ At least one prime drop taken through the full intake cycle after the first import
  • ☐ Every runbook followed at least once by someone other than its author
  • ☐ The scorecard reported every sprint, including the bad sprints

Appendix K Glossary

From what you know

You know

the acronym list at the back of every SEMP.

Here it is called

the glossary: systems engineering, DevSecOps and SysML v2 side by side.

What is new

each new term is mapped to the one you already use.

Three vocabularies meet in this book: systems engineering and configuration management, which the reader already speaks; GitLab and DevSecOps, which Jim, Bob and Tom learned in twelve weeks; and SysML v2, which replaces the SysML v1 they knew from Cameo. The first table translates between the first two, the second defines the DevSecOps and GitLab words, the third maps SysML v1 terms to v2, and the last two cover the agile words and the terms this book and its kit coined. The project wiki's Glossary page (tools/gitlab/templates/wiki/Glossary.md) uses the same translations.

Warning: CI means two things

In configuration management a CI is a configuration item. In GitLab, CI means continuous integration, the automatic checks. This book writes "configuration item" in full and uses CI only for the checks.

K.3 SysML v1 and SysML v2

Appendix L A twelve-week study plan per role

From what you know

You know

a training plan with courses and dates.

Here it is called

a twelve-week study plan per role.

What is new

the learning time is budgeted on the team's board, not taken from evenings.

This book is long because it is a reference as well as a story. Nobody should read it front to back before doing anything. This appendix is the order the Tidewater team read it in, week by week, with the practice lessons and the exercises that go with each week, and the learning time the plan budgeted for it. Use it as a starting point for your own team: the roles matter more than the names.

The three roles:

  • The lead (Jim). Owns the model, the backlog's tomes and epics, the change board and the conversation with management. Reads for decisions and for the case to make; types fewer commands than the others.
  • The modeler (Bob). Does most of the model work: closing TODO lines, writing behavior by hand, reviewing. Reads for SysML v2 and Vim, and practises the most.
  • The pipeline owner (Tom). A systems engineer who took on the GitLab project, the runner and the pipeline. Reads for setup, CI/CD and administration.

L.1 Where the hours come from

Learning time is planned work, not evenings and weekends (Chapter 41, For the lead: leading a reluctant team, Chapter 14, Writing stories and tasks for model work). On Tidewater it is a work::learning story every sprint, with a task per person, sized like any other task (one point is one ideal day, about eight hours). The plan file is the source; print each person's learning tasks from it:

Table L.1. Learning hours per person per sprint, from the plan (printed by the block above)
SprintJimBobTom
18 h12 h12 h
24 h12 h8 h
34 h8 h8 h
44 h4 h4 h
54 h4 h0 h
64 h0 h0 h

The learning share falls as competence rises: see the sprint-by-sprint split in Bottom line up front. Reading this book's chapters and doing the practice lessons is what those hours buy. The practice lessons are offline, run on the laptop against the kit's GitLab stand-in, and take about forty-five minutes each (perl agile.pl practice N; perl agile.pl practice check N says what to do next).

L.2 Week zero: everyone

Before sprint 1, all three read the same short list, so the team starts with one vocabulary. The list climbs the ladder in the preface (From what you know to what you do not): what you know first, then what is new.

  • Bottom line up front and Preface: what the twelve weeks are, and what they cost.
  • Chapter 3, The directive: what management asked for, and the scorecard that will measure it.
  • Chapter 4, The Vee, kept: the systems-engineering V in MBSE DevSecOps: the systems-engineering Vee you already know, and where each piece of it lives in GitLab.
  • Chapter 5, DevSecOps in systems-engineering words: every DevSecOps term in systems-engineering words.
  • Chapter 9, The survival kit, up to the end of the laptop checks; then perl "$KIT/tools/gitlab/kickoff.pl" doctor on each laptop.

The lead also reads Chapter 13, The operating model and Chapter 50, Your project in twelve weeks: a playbook, because week zero is when the scorecard, the exchange agreement with the prime and the first meeting with the security officer happen.
