L.6 Check yourself

At the end of each sprint, each person should be able to say yes to that sprint's "You can now..." list in the sprint chapter (Chapter 26, Sprint 1: A GitLab project the team can work in to Chapter 31, Sprint 6: Behavior by hand, a table for the program, and baseline-0). If the answer is no for two sprints running, the learning budget is too small or the backlog too full; that is a conversation for the retrospective, not a private worry.

Exercise L.1: Build your own plan

Copy the three tables into your team's wiki, rename the roles to your people, and move rows to match your program (a team with no supplier drops can skip the drop-loop rows until it has one). Then print your own plan's learning tasks the way the block above does, and check that the hours in the tables match what the backlog actually reserves.

Appendix M Further reading

From what you know

You know

the applicable documents list.

Here it is called

further reading.

What is new

nothing; this is where to go deeper.

Titles only, deliberately: web addresses move, and an address printed in a book is wrong within a year. Every item below is easy to find by its title, and most are free. Check with your security office before downloading anything to a work laptop; several are available in the program's library.

M.1 SysML v2 and the language underneath

  • OMG Systems Modeling Language (SysML), Version 2.0, the specification. Read Part 1 (the language) for the textual notation; dip into the rest as needed. The kit's grammar check is built from the official grammar that comes with it.
  • OMG Kernel Modeling Language (KerML), Version 1.0, the foundation SysML v2 is defined on. Useful when a SysML construct behaves unexpectedly and you need the underlying rule.
  • OMG Systems Modeling Application Programming Interface (API) and Services, the standard API for model repositories, if your program plans to publish models to an API server.
  • The SysML v2 Pilot Implementation, the open-source reference implementation and its training material, including the textual notation examples. The kit's model.pl validate can call it for full semantic checking.
  • The SysML v2 release repository's training and examples folders, the most direct way to see idiomatic v2 text.

M.2 Systems engineering

  • INCOSE Systems Engineering Handbook, the shared vocabulary for the processes this book renames (configuration management, verification, technical reviews).
  • NASA Systems Engineering Handbook, free, and a good second view of the same processes from a program that writes everything down.
  • The DoD Digital Engineering Strategy, for the policy background behind the directive in Chapter 3, The directive.

M.3 Git, GitLab and DevSecOps

  • Pro Git, by Scott Chacon and Ben Straub, free online. Chapters 1 to 3 cover everything in Chapter 12, Git from zero, for systems engineers and more; chapter 7 is the rescue kit (Appendix E, Rescue: when something goes wrong) in depth.
  • The GitLab documentation, especially the user guides for merge requests, protected branches, CODEOWNERS, CI/CD YAML syntax, runners, and the Generic Package Registry. GitLab's documentation is versioned: read the version that matches your instance.
  • The GitLab Runner documentation on the shell and Docker executors, for Chapter 21, Runners: where the pipeline runs.
  • The DoD Enterprise DevSecOps Reference Design and its playbooks, the program-level picture of what this book does at team scale.
  • NIST SP 800-218, the Secure Software Development Framework, as a checklist for the pipeline's security posture (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system).

M.4 Security frameworks named in this book

  • NIST SP 800-53, security and privacy controls, used under the Risk Management Framework (NIST SP 800-37).
  • NIST SP 800-171, protecting controlled unclassified information, and the CMMC program built on it.
  • Your program's security classification guide and marking instructions, which outrank everything else on this list.

M.5 Agile, for systems engineers

  • The Scrum Guide, by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, short and free. Tidewater's rhythm is a light version of it (Chapter 13, The operating model).
  • The Agile Manifesto and its twelve principles, one page, worth reading for what it does not say.

M.6 Vim

  • Vim's own help, which is better than any book: :help user-manual for the guided tour, :help quickref for the one-page summary, and :help agile for the kit's commands (Chapter 10, Vim for models).
  • vimtutor, the thirty-minute interactive lesson that ships with Vim: run vimtutor in Git Bash.

M.7 The kit's own documents

These ship with the kit, in docs/, and need no download:

  • docs/GITLAB.html, the GitLab guide written for this team's process.
  • docs/SYSML-PORT.html and docs/SYSML-PORT-QRG.pdf, the port guide and its one-sheet card.
  • docs/VIM-CHEATSHEET.html, one page for every Vim mode.
  • docs/OLLAMA.md, installing a local model, approvals first (Chapter 18, A local AI assistant on the laptop).
  • docs/HELP.html, the kit's help, the same text as :help agile and perl agile.pl help.

Appendix N Answers to the exercises

Every exercise in the book has an answer here, in book order. Where an exercise asks you to run something, the answer runs it, and the output shown is what the kit really prints; the blocks are tested like every other command in the book, so if your output differs, the difference is worth a look. Where an exercise asks for judgement, the answer is a model answer: one good response, the reasoning behind it, and what any good answer must contain. Your answer can differ from a model answer and still be right; it cannot leave out what the "must contain" lines name.

Many exercises ask about your own program. Those answers show what a good response looks like for Tidewater, so you can see the shape, and then say what to look for in yours.

The commands below run in three places. A scratch folder holds drops, small models and offline GitLab projects made for the answer. The tidewater folder is the simulation's state after sprint 6, the same one the sprint chapters use. A few answers read the kit itself. Each block says which.

N.1 Part I: where they start

Exercise 1.1: Count the copies

A typical result for one interface requirement on a document-era program: the system specification (owned by the systems engineering lead, updated at the last revision), the interface control document (owned by the interface lead, two revisions behind), the requirements database export (owned by the requirements manager, refreshed monthly), the verification matrix spreadsheet (owned by the test lead), and two briefings. Six places; on most programs two or three agree word for word.

You cannot find out without reading them all, which is the point of the exercise. A good answer names the one tool that would answer it mechanically: a comparison of the text with the same identifier in each place. In this book that is the trace job's drift list, which compares DOORS text with the model's text for every requirement on every change (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job).

Must contain: every place, an owner for each, a date for each, and an honest "I could not check this one" where that is true.

Exercise 1.2: Reconstruct a change

Lay the change out as dated events: request raised, impact assessment started and finished, board scheduled, board held, document updated, document re-baselined, downstream documents updated. Then mark each interval deciding (a person working on it) or waiting (in a queue, an inbox, a calendar). On most programs the waiting is well over half the elapsed time; the chapter's example was mostly waiting for the next board and for the document owners.

Must contain: the elapsed time, the decided time, the fraction waiting, and the one queue that held it longest. That queue is the first thing a merge request with automatic checks removes.

Exercise 1.3: The five virtues

A model answer for Tidewater's document era:

  • Readable by anyone: a Word file opens everywhere. Cost: anyone can read it, nobody can check it mechanically.
  • Contractually meaningful: the specification is a deliverable with a signature. Cost: changing it takes a board.
  • Reviewed: every revision went through a review meeting. Cost: weeks of calendar time per review.
  • Baselined: revision letters and a document register. Cost: the register and the documents drift apart.
  • Traced: a verification matrix spreadsheet. Cost: two days to rebuild it before every review.

Keep the page. After Chapter 33, The twelve-week scorecard, each line should have a GitLab counterpart: a text file anyone can read, a merge request with approvals, review in hours, a protected tag, a trace job.

Exercise 2.1: Measure it yourself

Generate drop 1 and search it:

There are two: Battery and Battery_old. The real battery is the one something uses. A block is real if another element has it as a type:

Battery is the type of the power system's battery part; Battery_old sits in the "Legacy Import" package and nothing refers to it. Deciding by use, not by name, is the habit to keep.

Exercise 2.2: Read the manifest

The checksums match. If one did not, the file you hold is not the file the prime's build recorded: corrupted in transit, edited by someone, or from a different build. Do not import it. Call the prime's modeler (the contract's named technical contact) and ask for the drop to be sent again; record the event on the Prime Drop issue (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).

Exercise 2.3: Belief and fact

A model answer sorts each belief into one of three columns:

  • About the language: "SysML cannot express our constraints" (it can, with constraint blocks; the team never used them), "a requirement must be a diagram element" (it is an element; diagrams are views of it).
  • About the tool: "the model is the diagrams", "you cannot merge two people's work", "you need a seat to read the model". These are Cameo's file format and licensing, not SysML.
  • About how the team was asked to work: "the model must contain every document paragraph", "every slide needs a diagram", "nobody may delete anything". These came from how the port was ordered.

Must contain: at least one belief in each column. Most teams find the third column is the longest, which is good news: it is the one they can change.

Exercise 3.1: Read your own directive

Three columns: what it says (quote it), what it requires (the minimum that would satisfy an auditor), what it leaves open (everything else). For Tidewater's directive (Chapter 3, The directive), "adopt DevSecOps practices" says a lot and requires little: a version-controlled model, automated checks, a demonstration within twelve weeks. It leaves open the tools, the branching model, the measures and the team's pace.

The open items belong to the person who will be held to the result, which for an MBSE team is the model lead, with the program manager's concurrence. Write them down as decisions (Chapter 13, The operating model) so they stop being open.

Exercise 3.2: Write down the objections

The exercise is the method; a good result looks like Tidewater's list in Chapter 3, The directive: nine objections in the speakers' words, each with a column "answered where, with what evidence". Typical entries: "we will lose the diagrams" (answered by generated views, Chapter 11, Seeing the model: diagrams from text); "nobody will read text" (answered by the model site the program office reads, Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep); "this is a software process" (answered by the systems engineering share of the work, Bottom line up front).

Must contain: the speaker's own words, not a paraphrase, and a planned date for each answer. An objection without a date is a promise nobody is held to.

Exercise 3.3: Pick your measures

Five that work for most ports, each computable without judgement:

  1. TODO lines left after conversion, from the pipeline's todo job; target zero; old-way baseline: none (nobody counted).
  2. Requirements with a verification case, from the trace job; target: every requirement the government owns; old-way baseline: the last verification matrix, counted by hand.
  3. Merge requests that went through a green pipeline and an approval, from GitLab; target: all of them after the first sprint; old-way baseline: changes made without a recorded review.
  4. Change lead time, from GitLab analytics (Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics); target: days, not weeks; old-way baseline: the board cycle.
  5. The team's pulse survey; target: rising; old-way baseline: the first retrospective.

The skeptic usually rejects the pulse survey ("feelings are not data") and the lead time ("you are comparing a typo fix with a board decision"). Both objections are fair. Answer the first by keeping the survey anonymous and the questions fixed; answer the second by comparing like with like, and by saying so on the slide.

Exercise 4.1: Map your program's Vee

A good answer names every rung on the right arm, puts "nobody" or "a person, before each review" against at least one of them, and circles a rung below system verification: those are the repetitive ones. Tidewater's answer circles the verification matrix, which used to take two people a week before each review.

Exercise 4.2: Find the three Vees

A merge request's Vee: any change into develop, with the ten jobs gitlab.pl ci --list --event merge_request_event --target develop shows. A baseline's Vee: a baseline-N tag, with the thirteen jobs --event tag --tag baseline-N shows, three of them the release jobs. The program's Vee: the next technical review, which reads the latest baseline's release package.

Exercise 4.3: Break and mend a horizontal line

The job reports orphans 2 -> 3 (new: ...) and fails. Two sentences for the program manager: "The check stops a change that breaks a link between a requirement and the design that meets it. The nine gaps already in the model are the prime's, reported to the prime, and they are counted every day instead of blocking our work."

Exercise 4.4: The thread before the twin

Most programs moving from documents have none of the four on day one; a good answer says so and names the first step, usually stable ids from the prime and doorsId on every requirement. The decision a twin would change must come with a number, for example "how many buoys to recover before winter, worth one vessel day each".

Exercise 5.1: Make your own list

A starting list, with the systems engineering term beside each:

DevSecOps termClosest SE / CM term
repositorycontrolled document library
commita change to a controlled item, with author and date
brancha working copy for one change
merge requestengineering change request with its review
pipelineconfiguration audit plus review checklist, run by machine
tagbaseline
releasepublished baseline with its release notes
runnerthe machine the audit runs on (no equivalent)
artifactreview package, generated
code ownerapproval authority for an item

"Runner" and "pipeline schedule" usually have no equivalent; that is fine. Compare with the translation table in Chapter 5, DevSecOps in systems-engineering words and keep the words your team already uses for the rest.

Exercise 5.2: Which idea first?

For Tidewater the time-saver was automatic checks on every change (the grammar and lint jobs found in minutes what review meetings found in weeks) and the most resisted was small changes reviewed one at a time ("we will drown in reviews"). They are usually different ideas, and that matters: lead with the time-saver, because it pays for the patience the resisted idea needs. A good answer names both and says which one you will introduce first.

Exercise 5.3: Follow a change

Write your change against the ten steps (issue, branch, edit, local check, commit, push, merge request, pipeline, review and approval, merge). In a document-era process, steps 1, 7 and 9 usually exist (a change request, a review, a signature), steps 4 and 8 do not exist at all (no automatic check), and step 10 is a person re-typing the change into the master document. The time goes into the review queue and into re-typing. A good answer marks each step "existed / missing / done by hand" and puts a duration on each existing one.

Exercise 6.1: Convert and count

Fifty-two, which matches the table "Drop 1's conversion debt, by kind" in Chapter 6, SysML v2 for SysML v1 modelers.

Exercise 6.2: Read a package

The data segment has four parts (ingest, quality control, archive, publisher), three external ports (observations in, health in, the public interface out) and five connections in a chain: observations into ingest, ingest to quality control, quality control to the archive, the archive to the publisher, the publisher out to the public port. Most readers draw it in a few minutes, faster than finding the right diagram among the forty-seven in the v1 model, and the text cannot be out of date with itself.

Exercise 6.3: Find a hidden error

There is only one, the energy balance. A discrepancy report for it: "The constraint balance on EnergyBalance (xmi:id in the drop) uses sunHours, which is not a parameter of the constraint block. Please declare sunHours (with its unit) or state where its value comes from. Impact: the government's v2 model cannot evaluate the constraint until it is declared." Name the element by its id, say what is wrong, say what you need, say why it matters.

Exercise 6.4: Write a state machine

One new line, named so it reads as a sentence, reusing the existing CrewOnSite event.

Exercise 7.1: Decompose by hand, then check

By hand: classification (missing; Tidewater is unmarked, so optional here), state and trigger (missing), specification target "the power system", operative verb "shall", target verb "report", precise object "the battery state of charge", modifier and modification (missing), reference (missing), exceptions (missing), ID TW-SEG-003. All required parts are present. A test engineer needs the optional parts the sentence lacks: to whom it reports, how often, and how accurately. Without them the requirement cannot fail a test.

The checker agrees: every required part found, one minor finding, no threshold.

Exercise 7.2: Split TW-SYS-001

What you had to decide: how often each quantity is measured (the original had no rate), whether waves are measured only by buoys (the original said "each buoy shall also"), and in which mode the requirement applies. The rates above are notional; on a real program they come from the stakeholder need, and asking for them is a discrepancy report to whoever owns the wording.

Exercise 7.3: A need that can be traced

"Mariners shall be able to obtain the latest marine bulletin and the latest observation from every station through a public service, at any time, without an account." It stays a stakeholder need (it names the mariner and the outcome, not a system element) and becomes verifiable by demonstration: the program office watches a mariner, with no account, read the latest bulletin and observations. The evidence is the demonstration record. The weak verb "be able to read" is replaced by an outcome someone can watch happen.

Exercise 7.4: Add a constraint

The sentence carries the recipe for people; the constraint carries the same rule for the tools.

Exercise 7.5: Write the DR

One screen: a title ("DR-6: thirteen DOORS requirements do not meet the requirement recipe"), a table of the thirteen IDs with one-line findings (TW-STK-001 weak verb "provide"; TW-STK-003 and TW-STK-004 "be able to"; TW-SYS-001 two operative verbs; TW-SYS-012 "be serviceable"; the rest "no measurable threshold"), and the suggested wording for the five in recipe-rewrites.txt.

Ask the prime to fix TW-SYS-001 and TW-SYS-012 first: TW-SYS-001 is two requirements in one sentence, so one of them cannot be verified separately, and TW-SYS-012 has no satisfy in the model and no verifiable verb, so it blocks both traceability and verification. The "no threshold" findings matter too, but they can wait for the wording owner's next revision.

N.2 The SysML v2 workbook

Each answer below writes its snippet into the scratch folder and checks it. The snippets are complete files, so you can run any one of them on its own.

Exercise 8.1: Break it three ways

Only the misspelled prat is reported on the line that is actually wrong (line 3, at the word after prat, because the checker read prat as a name and then found another name). The missing ; is reported one line later, where the next statement starts. The missing } is reported at the end of the file, wherever that is. The two rules from Chapter 8, SysML v2 by example: a workbook in action: fix the first error first, and look one line up.

Exercise 8.2: Narrow the imports

Fourth sees Hull and Mooring (Stations' own public members) and ObservationPort, because Stations imports it publicly and so re-exports it. It does not see StationMode, which Stations imports privately. A public import is a promise to every package that imports you; make imports private unless you mean that promise.

Exercise 8.3: Document a decision

The forecaster's document wants the doc: what quality control is. The decision belongs in review and in the decision log; if it matters for years, it belongs in a decision record (Chapter 13, The operating model), and the comment points to it.

Exercise 8.4: A shore station

A cell in a buoy in the segment is four levels down from the segment: segment, buoy, battery, cell. The buoy inherits the battery from ObservingStation, so the depth is the same in a shore station.

Exercise 8.5: A shore-station suite

Now without the :>>, in a lint project:

Lint says nothing, and that is the lesson. Without :>> the suite declares a second attribute with the same name that hides the inherited one; it is legal text and the kit's lint does not flag the shadowing. A full SysML v2 tool with semantic checks (the OMG pilot implementation, model.pl validate with Java) reports it. Until then, reviewers look for the same name declared twice in a specialization (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).

Exercise 8.6: A health interface
Exercise 8.7: Two flows

One connection is enough: the connection says the two parts are joined, and each flow says what crosses. Two flows on one connection is usually clearer to a reviewer, because it mirrors the hardware (one cable, two kinds of traffic). A second connection is right only when there really are two physical paths.

Exercise 8.8: A power budget's inputs

A fraction from zero to one, constrained, is the simplest honest "percentage". Reading the library turns up dimensionless ratio types too; use whichever your team agrees on, once, in the library package, so every model says it the same way.

Exercise 8.9: A reserve

The English: "The usable energy of the station's batteries shall exceed one day of a 15 W load." The text form is exact about units and arithmetic; the English is what a reviewer checks against intent. Keep both: the sentence in the doc, the expression in the constraint.

Exercise 8.10: The battery requirement
Exercise 8.11: Trace a new requirement

The trace job would list TW-SYS-013 as unverified: something satisfies it, nothing verifies it. On a merge request the ratchet fails only if that is a new gap compared with the target branch (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job); adding a new requirement without its verification case is exactly that, so write the case in the same merge request.

Exercise 8.12: Inspect the vessel access

Record the method on the requirement (verificationMethod, as the converters write it from DOORS), because the VCRM job reads it from there (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop); the verification case's doc repeats it for the human reader.

Exercise 8.13: The Storm mode

The prime's drop 3 adds the same state with triggers named stormWarning and calm. Your names may differ; when the drop lands, use the prime's names so the next delta stays clean, and say so in the merge request.

Exercise 8.14: Join and finish
Exercise 8.15: Use the calc

A reviewer checks this form more easily: each calc has a name that says what it computes, and the constraint reads "generation covers load". The one-line expression is shorter but hides the units of sunHours and 24.

Exercise 8.16: Allocate the cycle

Allocate PublishBulletin to the publisher, not to the data center: allocate to the lowest element that actually performs the function, but no lower (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web). An allocation to the whole data center says nothing a reviewer can check, and the IDEF0 plates show the publisher as the mechanism, which is what the forecaster expects.

Exercise 8.17: A marking

On a real program the value is decided by the original classification authority, through the security classification guide; the team applies it, and the ISSM reviews it. The model records the decision; it does not make it (Chapter 48, Security: protect the environment, engineer it into the system).

Exercise 8.18: Read a bulletin

No include: reading the latest bulletin never requires a query of the archive; a mariner who wants history performs a different use case. Including it would make every bulletin read depend on the archive.

Exercise 8.19: A hybrid

The trade study needs the same attributes on every variant, with units: cost, power draw, data rate, coverage at sea, and availability. Put them on Modem so each variant must give a value; a variant without one cannot be scored.

Exercise 8.20: A test view

Expose the verification package and the requirements packages, and nothing structural: the test organization needs the cases, what they verify and the methods. That view is, in effect, the VCRM (Chapter 44, Verification as a closed loop).

Exercise 8.21: Find three types

The degree Celsius symbol is quoted ('°C') because it is not a plain name. A temperature range is two values, minimum and maximum; a single attribute called range would hide which is which.

Exercise 8.22: Review a file in five passes

DataCenter imports Interfaces and Stations; Stations imports it back, which is the Stations and DataCenter cycle (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web). Its five TODO lines are all level stereotypes. One doc is not a description of the element: the second doc on QualityControl is pasted from a briefing ("From the Ops Concept briefing, slide 22 ..."), and the dependency from QualityControl to SensorSuite is what closes the cycle.

To the prime, as a discrepancy report: the pasted briefing text and the dependency, because both are in the prime's model and come back with every drop. The government's to fix: the level tags (TODO lines the government closes in its own copy).

Exercise 8.23: Grow the mini model

The workbook's mini model, rebuilt from the workbook's own text so this answer stays in step with it:

Adding the state machine to Network.sysml as the exercise says gives Network ten members, and the outline check fails: two to nine children per parent. The state machine is behavior, so the better home is Behavior.sysml, with Network importing it:

Now break the trace by removing the new verification case:

On a merge request the pipeline's trace job would fail: the target branch had no unverified requirement and this change adds one (Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job). That is the ratchet: existing gaps are reported, new ones stop the merge.

Exercise 8.24: Your first TODO

The TODO line on ObservationNetwork reads // TODO stereotype Tidewater_Profile:L1Network on this element (xmi:id ...) not converted. It is replaced by the one line @L1Network;, and the package gains private import Conventions::*;, where the Conventions package (in model/library/conventions/) defines the level tags.

N.3 Part II: week zero

Exercise 13.1: Size the tasks

A model answer for "write the interface section of the ICD for the observation link": stories "Observation link defined in the model" (port def, interface def, the item and its fields; 5 points) and "Observation link reviewed by both owners" (review, comments, merge; 2 points). Tasks: "write the item def and its fields" (2), "write the port and interface defs" (2), "connect it in the network" (1), "review with the data center owner" (1), "answer the review" (1).

The hardest split is usually the review: it waits on someone else. Rule 2 of Section 13.3.3, Splitting work that is too big, pull out the waiting, is the one that helps: the review becomes its own task, so the modeling finishes on time even when the reviewer is busy.

Exercise 13.2: Split a story

Split by result, one construct per story, each ending in something that can be shown:

  1. "BuoyModes state machine passes lint and appears on the model site" (3 points).
  2. "DailyUpload interaction written and grammar-checked" (2 points).
  3. "ObserveCoast fork, pins and object flows written; the IDEF0 plate shows them" (3 points).
  4. "EnergyBalance constraint written with declared parameters" (3 points).

Eleven points become four stories of at most three, and each one's end state can be demonstrated: open the model site, show the plate, run the check.

Exercise 13.3: Compute a sprint's capacity

Sprint 4 has nine working days (Thanksgiving is a holiday). Prorate each standing capacity by the days each person is there:

PersonStanding (10 days)Days presentCapacity
Jim58 (holiday and Friday's leave)5 × 8/10 = 4.0
Bob898 × 9/10 = 7.2
Tom898 × 9/10 = 7.2
Team18.4

Commit 85 to 95 percent of it: about 15.6 to 17.5 points. The team's real sprint 4 kickoff recorded the same capacity and committed seventeen:

Exercise 13.4: Write a decision record

A model record, in the template's shape:

Must contain: the context in one paragraph, the decision in one sentence, the consequences including the cost, and a condition that would reopen it.

Exercise 13.5: Enforce a RACI cell

Three typical cells:

  • "The interface lead approves every interface change": enforceable. A CODEOWNERS entry for the interfaces folder plus "code owner approval required" on develop (Chapter 15, Setting up GitLab).
  • "Only the CM lead creates baselines": enforceable. A protected tag rule baseline-* with create:maintainer, and only the CM lead is a maintainer for that purpose.
  • "The model lead is consulted on scope changes": not enforceable by a setting. It is a ceremony: the change goes on the board as a story, and refinement is where the lead is consulted (Chapter 24, The rhythm: stand-ups, poker, refinement, kickoff, demo, retro).

The pattern: approvals and permissions are settings; consultation and judgement are stories and meetings.

Exercise 9.1: Find a requirement

Five requirements are verified by inspection (TW-SYS-010, TW-SYS-012, TW-SYS-015, TW-SEG-001 and TW-SEG-008), and TW-SYS-012 appears in the converted requirements package of the Cameo model.

Exercise 9.2: Count the debt by package

Stations holds 29 of the 52, because it is the biggest package: most of the model's part definitions live there, and each one carries a level stereotype the converter could not carry (L3Station down to L6Component). Most of the debt is that one mechanical kind, which is why it was closed first (Chapter 10, Vim for models).

Exercise 9.3: Break a checksum

sha256sum -c prints FAILED for the changed file and a warning that one checksum did not match. With a real delivery: stop, do not import, record it on the Prime Drop issue, and ask the prime to send the drop again (Chapter 45, The prime's model changes: receive, assess, disposition).

Exercise 9.4: Make each mistake on purpose

Read each one aloud: "command not found" (the name is wrong, or the program is not installed), "No such file or directory" (the path is wrong; check where you are with pwd), "not a git repository" (you are outside the clone; cd into it). None of them changed anything.

Exercise 12.1: The practice afternoon

The recoveries, each as one command:

MistakeRecovery
broke a file you had not committedgit restore FILE
staged a file by mistakegit restore --staged FILE
wrong commit message on the last commitgit commit --amend -m "..." (only before pushing)
a commit that should not have happened, already sharedgit revert COMMIT
a merge that went wrong, still in progressgit merge --abort

The one to remember: on anything already pushed, use revert, never amend or reset. Appendix E, Rescue: when something goes wrong has each one played out.

Exercise 12.2: A conflict with three sides

Two conflicts, one per merge: the first branch conflicts with the change on main, and after you resolve it the second branch conflicts with the result. git log --oneline --all --graph shows two merge commits on main, each with two parents. Resolve each so the line says what you mean, not by keeping both versions side by side; with merge.conflictstyle diff3 set, the middle section shows the original line, which tells you what each side changed.

Exercise 12.3: The auditor's questions
Exercise 12.4: A vendor branch of your own

A change on one side and a deletion on the other is a conflict: git cannot know whether the deletion or the new doc should win, so it shows the government's version against an empty prime side. The team accepts the prime's deletion, because the prime owns the structure, and checks first whether anything still uses Hull. If the doc mattered, it goes to the prime as a discrepancy report so it survives the next drop.

Exercise 12.5: Choose a strategy

For Tidewater the facts are: formal baselines (yes), others depending on specific versions (yes, the program office and the prime), released versions corrected (yes, a hotfix in sprint 24), publication (every change, through the model site). Those point to gitflow: main holds baselines, develop holds integration, hotfixes are possible.

A program with no formal baselines, one team and continuous publication points to GitLab flow. The decision record says which facts decided it, so the decision is revisited when the facts change.

Exercise 10.1: The debt as a jump list

Grouped by kind, drop 1's fifty-two TODO lines are:

Thirty-six level stereotypes, four activity constructs, three procured parts, three units and six others (the state machine, the interaction, the include, the constraint expression twice, the profile). Close the level stereotypes first: they are mechanical, one substitution per package, and they move the burn-down the most.

Exercise 10.2: Close the level tags in one package

In Stations, the level tags are 25 of the 29 TODO lines; after the substitution four remain:

Three procured parts (metadata to write) and the BuoyModes state machine (a design task for later).

Exercise 10.3: Break it three ways
  • Misspelled type: the grammar check passes; lint reports unresolved type on the line of the usage.
  • Missing semicolon: the grammar check reports it, on the next line, where the following statement starts.
  • Level tag on the wrong level: the grammar check and lint both pass; model.pl check reports a level-tag mismatch on the part def. A misspelled tag name such as @L1Netwrk; passes all three, which is why the practice lesson's own check exists (Chapter 10, Vim for models).
Exercise 10.4: Resolve with the ancestor

For a single conflict, the marker search (/^<<<<<<< then ]c-style editing) is faster: you see the three versions in place and edit one line. For ten conflicts, git mergetool with Vim's three-way diff is better, because it walks you from conflict to conflict and shows the base beside each side. Either way, the diff3 middle section (the ancestor) is what tells you who changed what.

Exercise 10.5: Write a merge request description in Vim

A good description says what changed (the Stations level tags, 25 TODO lines closed), why (the structure epic, story id), how it was checked (\mx and \ml clean, the outline count unchanged), and what the reviewer should look at (that each tag matches the part's level in the tree). With git diff --stat inserted, a reviewer can approve from the description and the diff: the change is mechanical and the checks prove the mechanics; the reviewer checks the levels.

Exercise 14.1: Rewrite three criteria
  • (a) "The todo job reports zero TODO lines in model/logical/, and the IDEF0 plates regenerate without warnings."
  • (b) "The trace job reports zero unverified segment requirements, or each one has an open discrepancy report linked from this story."
  • (c) "A Discrepancy Report issue exists for each finding, labelled owner::prime, and the transmittal memo is recorded on it."

Each names a job, a number or a record someone can check.

Exercise 14.2: Split a story

By requirement group and by investigation versus result (Section 14.8, Splitting patterns for model work):

  1. "Stakeholder needs in the model" (the DOORS stakeholder module converted and merged): the grammar and lint jobs pass and the trace links all stakeholder needs.
  2. "System requirements in the model": the trace job shows every system requirement linked.
  3. "Segment requirements in the model": the same for the segment module.
  4. "Drift and gaps reported" (investigation): one Discrepancy Report issue per drift or gap the trace lists.
Exercise 14.3: Budget your own learning

Sprint 1, about a fifth of capacity: "Learn the tools: survival kit, git, Vim" (2 points each; done when practice lessons 10 and 11 check as done), "Laptops ready" (1 point each, plus the software request's wait; done when kickoff.pl doctor passes). Sprint 2, about a sixth: "Learn the pipeline and a prime drop" (2 points each; done when lessons 12 and 13 check as done and each person has merged one real change). Label them work::learning so the reserve is visible (Chapter 14, Writing stories and tasks for model work, Bottom line up front).

Exercise 11.1: Find a cycle

The Stations and DataCenter cycle is closed by two lines in the prime's files: dependency from QualityControl to SensorSuite in DataCenter, and dependency from DataLogger to IngestService in Stations (plus the imports they need). The shared element is the observation record, which already belongs in the library's interfaces; with both segments depending only on the library, the cycle disappears. Both dependencies are in the prime's model, so the fix is a discrepancy report, not a government edit (Chapter 29, Sprint 4: the model site, a cycle broken, and the demo that landed).

Exercise 11.2: Read a plate

For the Check step, from the plates of the converted model:

Input: the ingested observation record. Output: the checked observation record. Mechanism: Quality Control, supplied by allocate CheckQuality to QualityControl; in the allocations package.

Exercise 15.1: Build the project

Setup created seventy-two labels (the [labels] section, one line each) and thirty-nine milestones (the one sprints = ... line in [milestones], which expands to a milestone per sprint).

Exercise 15.2: Make it refuse you

Each refusal comes from one line of project.conf: develop = push:none ... and main = push:none ... in [branches] (nobody pushes; changes arrive by merge request), and baseline-* = create:maintainer in [tags] (Bob is a developer, so cannot create a baseline).

Exercise 15.3: Redraw the signature page

A specification's signature page usually reads: prepared by (author), reviewed by (subsystem leads), approved by (chief engineer), CM release (CM lead). As a CODEOWNERS file over a folder of text files:

The CM release is not a code owner: it is the protected baseline-* tag. Signatures with no clear owner are usually "reviewed by" lines that list a role nobody holds; those become an open question for the lead.

Exercise 15.4: Defend a branching strategy

GitLab flow: main is the integration branch and the published model, releases are tags on main, and there is no develop. In project.conf: set default_branch = main, remove the develop line from [branches] (and make main merge:developer), and drop the vendor/prime line, since there are no drops. Monthly versions become tags without a release branch.

Exercise 16.1: Place a new package

With Tidewater's map, an unlisted package lands under unsorted/ (the map's * = unsorted/ line), and the converter says so in its report: "layout map: Drifters is not listed; written to unsorted/...". The delta job's report on the drop merge request shows the same. In one merge request, before anyone edits it: add the package to the layout map in the right layer, move the file there on the vendor branch by re-importing the drop with the new map, and add the folder to CODEOWNERS (and to layers in sysml.conf if it is a new layer).

Exercise 16.2: Spot the upward import

It breaks the layering rule: requirements are a lower layer than the physical architecture, and lower layers never import higher ones. It is a smell because a requirement should not depend on a design; that is how the spider web starts. The file is generated from the prime's export, so do not hand-edit it: the complexity job reports upward imports in generated files instead of failing on them, and the fix goes to the prime (or to the converter's layout, if the import is the converter's own) as a discrepancy report (Chapter 47, Keeping SysML v2 from becoming a spider web).

Exercise 17.1: Apply the rule

A model answer:

Problem todayGitLab toolThe problem it creates if turned on too early
nobody knows which version of the ICD is currentprotected tags and releasesceremony around every small change before anyone has felt the version problem
reviews happen in e-mail threads nobody can findmerge requests with approvalsapprovals queue up behind one reviewer if code owners are drawn too narrowly
status slides take a day each weekthe model site on Pages, analyticsa dashboard nobody asked for, numbers nobody trusts yet

The rule in Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep: a tool appears when the team has felt the pain it removes.

Exercise 17.2: Read a widget

The JUnit report (lint.xml) has one testcase per check with a failure element carrying the message; GitLab shows that message in the merge request's test widget as one failed test. The Code Quality report (lint-cq.json) has one finding with description, location.path and location.lines.begin; GitLab shows it in the code quality widget and on the diff line. The line to look for in both: the unresolved type message with its file and line.

Exercise 17.3: Choose the token
  • (a) A personal access token with read_api, owned by the person who runs the script, with an expiry date.
  • (b) No stored token at all: the pipeline's CI_JOB_TOKEN, which exists only while the job runs.
  • (c) A project access token with read_api only, stored as a masked, protected CI/CD variable, with an owner and an expiry in the token inventory (Chapter 42, Administration).
Exercise 17.4: Argue for one left-off tool

For merge trains: "Twice this month two merge requests were green alone and red together on develop, and develop was red for half a day each time. A merge train tests each merge request on top of the ones queued before it, so develop stays green." The evidence needed: the count of red develop pipelines caused by two green merge requests, from analytics (Chapter 32, Measuring with GitLab analytics). Without that evidence, Tom is right to leave it off.

Exercise 18.1: Write the approval request

A complete request names one runtime (Ollama, a specific version), one model family and size from an allowed developer, where it runs (three laptops, or one approved server), the data rule ("only information our marking rules allow on that machine"), and that the model's origin and license were checked. The office that approves model origin is usually the one that approves software intake, with the ISSM concurring; find out by asking both, in writing.

Exercise 18.2: Run a three-task bake-off

The answer is your scoresheet. A good one has, per task: the prompt written in advance, the number of tries, whether the result passed the gates (grammar, lint, the recipe for text), and the minutes to a mergeable result, with and without the model. A typical finding: the model helps on the helper script and the discrepancy report text, and loses on SysML v2 text, where its first draft fails the gates.

Exercise 18.3: Make the gates catch a hallucination

The grammar check passes: invented names such as ISQ::SolarPowerValue are perfectly good grammar. Lint catches them, as unresolved type errors on the lines that use them, because lint resolves names against the model and the library and the grammar check does not. With the model's own Power and Energy types both gates pass. Section 18.10.6, 6. SysML v2 text: the EnergyBalance constraint shows the real runs.

Exercise 18.4: The scratch-buffer loop in Vim

With cat standing in for the model, the loop is: select the TODO line and the XMI fragment, :'<,'>w !cat > /tmp/prompt, :new, :r !cat /tmp/prompt, :w answer.sysml, \mx. Most people time it at a minute or two once the keys are familiar; the time is in reading the answer, not in the keys.

Exercise 18.5: Check a draft for added facts

Typical added facts: a date the defect was found, a test that "failed", a section number in a document the prompt never named, and a severity. The one that would embarrass you in front of the prime is any invented reference, such as "per SRS paragraph 3.2.1": the prime will look it up. Delete every added fact or verify it before sending.

Exercise 20.1: Which jobs, which event

Running gitlab.pl ci --list for each event reproduces the table in Chapter 20, The pipeline, job by job. The rule that usually surprises people: a job with no rules: does not join merge request pipelines at all, on GitLab and locally. Every check job in the template has an explicit merge-request rule for that reason.

Exercise 20.2: Turn the ratchet

After fixing one violation the outline job passes and says "fewer violations than allowed: lower .ci/outline-max to N in this MR". Lower the number in .ci/outline-max in the same merge request and run it again: it passes with the new allowance, and nobody can add a violation back without the job failing.

Exercise 20.3: Find your ratchet

Example: "every requirement has a verification method". Counted: requirements with an empty method in the DOORS export. The allowed number lives in a one-line file in the repository, like .ci/outline-max. Anyone may lower it in a merge request that fixes some; only the lead may raise it, and only with a recorded reason, enforced by a CODEOWNERS line for that file.

Exercise 20.4: Stale documents

The docs job fails: it regenerates the documents and finds the committed ones differ ("docs are stale"). Fix it by running model.pl docs and committing the result. The team commits generated files so a reviewer sees, in the merge request diff, what the change does to the documents people read, and so a baseline's checksum covers the documents as well as the model.

Exercise 20.5: Review a pipeline change

"Request changes. allow_failure on lint means a model with unresolved names can merge, and nobody will notice until the next release. If lint is noisy, that is information: which messages are noise? Let's fix those (or ratchet the count, as we do for the outline) and keep lint blocking." The alternative: a ratchet on the lint warning count, with errors still blocking.

Exercise 19.1: Break it and watch it fail

The lint job fails and its log names the file and line with unresolved type 'NAME'. In Vim, :make lint fills the quickfix list from the same message, :cnext jumps to the line, the fix is the correct type name, and the job passes on the next run.

Exercise 19.2: One line up

The error names the line after the one missing the semicolon (the workbook answer above shows it: m1.sysml:3:5, when the semicolon was missing on line 2). In one sentence: "The checker only notices a statement did not end when the next one starts, so it points at the start of the next statement."

Exercise 19.3: Add a job

To show the count on the merge request page, write it to a metrics file and declare it as artifacts: reports: metrics:; GitLab then shows it in the metrics widget, with the change since the target branch (Chapter 17, The DevSecOps tools that earn their keep).

Exercise 19.4: Allowed to fail

The pipeline becomes "passed with warnings" and the merge request can merge. That is a bad idea for lint because lint errors are real defects (unresolved names), and a warning icon is easy to ignore; a broken model would reach develop. The team first made trace allowed to fail because its gaps were the prime's, inherited and outside the team's control, so failing on them would block every merge. The ratchet replaced it because it separates what the team inherited (reported) from what a change adds (blocked).

Exercise 19.5: The manager's question

On a merge request: "The automated checks found a problem in a proposed change before it was accepted. Nothing in the model is affected. The author is fixing it today."

On the integration branch: "The accepted model currently fails a check, so every new change is on hold. We know the cause and expect it green by this afternoon. The last good baseline is unaffected."

Exercise 21.1: Make a job pend

GitLab shows the job as pending with "This job is stuck because you don't have any active runners online or available with any of these tags assigned to them: does-not-exist". Locally, gitlab.pl ci --list still lists the job (the local runner ignores tags), which is itself the lesson: tags are a property of the server's runners. Fix it by removing the tag, or by registering (or editing) a runner with that tag.

Exercise 21.2: Translate a line

In PowerShell: if (-not $env:KIT) { Write-Output "KIT is not set"; exit 1 }. The team chose perl ci/job.pl NAME because a Perl command line is the same in PowerShell, cmd, Git Bash and Docker, so one pipeline file works on every runner, and the logic lives in one script that has its own tests instead of two shell dialects to keep in step.

Exercise 21.3: Write the runner's security description

One page, in this order: the machine (a dedicated Windows VM, its name and network segment), the account (a service account with no interactive login and no administrator rights), what it can reach (the GitLab server only, outbound), the credentials on it (the runner token, stored by the runner service; no personal tokens), what runs on it (the model project's pipeline jobs only, through a project runner with tags), who maintains it (Tom, patched monthly with the runner version kept in step with GitLab's), and how it is cleaned (build folders removed after each job). Section 21.8, The service account: least privilege is the model.

Exercise 22.1: Review a change

The pipeline catches the removed import: lint fails with unresolved names (ObservationIF, HealthIF) on the port lines. Only a reviewer catches the doc change, because it is valid text with a different meaning; the generated documents in the diff make it visible, and the review checklist asks whether each changed doc still says what the element is (Chapter 22, Reviewing a model change).

Exercise 22.2: Rewrite a finding
  • (a) "This satisfies TW-SYS-003 with the archive, but the requirement is about ingest. Should it be IngestService?"
  • (b) "TW-SYS-013 has no verification case after this change; the trace job will flag it. Can you add the case here, or link the story that will?"
  • (c) "The package has two cycles and a duplicated block (see the pkg view). Could we take the cycle in this merge request and open a story for the duplicate?"

Each says what, where, why it matters, and asks for a specific action.

Exercise 23.1: Make a journal
Exercise 23.2: Break the compile

The kit names the unknown task and writes nothing: a stand-up file with any error is rejected whole, never half applied.

Exercise 23.3: Where does it go?
  • (a) GitLab: a task, under one week, closed by a merge request.
  • (b) The journal and GitLab: a story in the journal (points, sprint), its tasks in GitLab.
  • (c) The journal: an epic, as the e: tag on its stories.
  • (d) Neither: hours stay in the team's own time records (GitLab's /spend if the team uses it); the journal never holds hours.
  • (e) The journal (a block line on the story, so the quad shows it) and GitLab (the workflow::blocked label on the task, with the reason in a comment).
Exercise 23.4: Re-estimate

The kit posts the difference (two more points) instead of replacing the three, because the journal is a ledger: history is never rewritten, so the original estimate and the change both stay visible, and velocity can be computed honestly afterwards.

Exercise 24.1: Lint your own status
Exercise 24.2: Play a round

The tally shows the spread and the outlier for each round. The spread usually comes from one person knowing something the others do not (Bob's high vote on TW-3 in sprint 1 came from experience of the export). Discussion should change the number when it surfaces that knowledge; if it does not, take the higher of the converged votes and note the risk on the story.

Exercise 24.3: Apply the Definition of Ready

The first item that usually fails is "has acceptance criteria a pipeline job or a record can check". Making it ready means writing those criteria (as in the stories exercises above), sizing it under a sprint, and naming the owner. If a dependency outside the team exists, it becomes its own task first.

Exercise 24.4: Plan a demo without slides

Twenty minutes: the question the two weeks answered (two minutes), the model site's front page with the four headline numbers (three), one merge request from red to green, opened live (five), one before-and-after with a number (three), one safe live change (five), and the ask with a date (two). The question for the audience: "Is this the evidence you need for the next milestone, and if not, what is missing?"

Exercise 25.1: Rewrite five statuses

For the three at the start of Chapter 25, Talking about progress: helps for engineers who would rather not, outcome first with one number:

  • "Y TW-12 Stations level tags done: 9 TODO lines closed, 43 left. T TW-15 decide who owns ObservationRecord, by Thursday. B none"
  • "Y TW-22 the trace found 2 requirements nothing satisfies; they are the prime's, report goes Friday. T TW-22 draft the report. B none"
  • "Y TW-3 runner request sent. T TW-4 pipeline draft. B TW-3 waiting on IT approval of the runner machine -- need: Jim to escalate today"

The hardest is usually the blocker: it must name what you need and from whom, which feels like complaining. It is not; it is the one sentence management can act on.

Exercise 25.2: Climb the ladder

For "the model site is live": one sentence, "The program office can now see the current model, its checks and its numbers on a web page that updates on every change." Thirty seconds: add what is on the page and the one number that moved. Five minutes: open the page, show the part tree, the trace page and the burn-down, and say what it replaces. If the colleague cannot repeat the one sentence, it had a mechanism in it ("Pages", "pipeline"); take it out.

Exercise 25.3: Your stakeholder map

For Tidewater: the program manager (schedule and risk; the one number is TODO lines left against the plan), the deputy program manager (change control; the open prime changes), the ISSM (security; open security findings), the prime's modeler (the drop loop; open discrepancy reports), the test organization (verification; requirements with a verification case). The pipeline produces all of these except the program manager's plan comparison, which comes from the journal.

Exercise 25.4: Draft from GitLab

talk.pl standup --as bob drafts the closed task as done and the next open task as today, with a number. The edit that matters turns "closed #N" into what it means: "Stations tags done: the structure epic is 60% through, and the model site shows the new tree."

Exercise 25.5: Run a dry run

The narrator usually stumbles at the transitions: from the question to the first screen, and from the live change to the ask. Fix the script by writing the transition sentence into it ("That is what changed; here is what it means for the review"), and by moving any screen that needs explanation before it makes sense to the end or out.

The id points at the uml:StateMachine named BuoyModes, owned as a behavior in the v1 model. In Vim, /TODO.*BuoyModes finds the line, and the id is what you search for in the XMI (or quote in a discrepancy report) to find the original.

Exercise 26.3: A spread worth having

The rounds went 2, 5, 3 and then 3, 3, 3:

Bob's sentence, a model answer: "Creating the project is an hour; proving the protections refuse a push, and getting the runner requested, is the rest." The note on the story: "Includes proving the branch protection refuses a direct push (task #15) and the runner request; the runner's approval is outside the team." Both moved into the plan: task #15 is "Prove a direct push to develop is refused".

Exercise 26.4: Your week zero

Tidewater's own record, for comparison:

A model answer lists the same kinds of hours: the directive meeting, the kickoff with management, software requests, the repository skeleton, the first security conversation, the decisions, the practice repository, and the delivery agreement with the prime. The ones people are tempted to hide in sprint 1 are the waits and the security meeting, because they produce nothing on a board. Do not: hidden hours make sprint 1's velocity look worse than it was and the next team's plan too optimistic, and the waits are exactly what management can shorten if it sees them.

Exercise 27.1: Translate the failure

What a systems engineer needs: "The runner reads each job's script as PowerShell, not as the Bash we tested on our laptops, so $(...) and || mean nothing to it and the job dies on line one." What Tom changed: "Each job's script became one line, perl ci/job.pl NAME, which reads the same in every shell, with the logic moved into a Perl script in the repository."

Exercise 27.2: Re-run the demo

A five-minute model script:

  1. The question (30 seconds): "Can the program trust that every change to the model is checked before it is accepted?"
  2. The output (1 minute): the merge request list, six of six changes merged with green checks, and the model now on develop.
  3. One before-and-after (1 minute): "Review turnaround is 3.3 hours, median. Before, a model change waited for the next review board."
  4. One safe live change (2 minutes): on a scratch branch, misspell one type; the pipeline goes red with the file and line; fix it; green.
  5. The ask (30 seconds): "We need the runner machine approved by 13 November, or the checks stay on our laptops."

The merges, oldest first (the log lists them newest first; your commit ids will differ, the branch names will not):

Exercise 27.4: A layout for your model

A model answer for a typical model: the library gets value types, units, port and interface definitions and the conventions; requirements get the DOORS modules; logical gets the functional architecture and the activities; physical gets one folder per segment; analysis gets constraints and trade studies; verification gets the cases. The least sure package is usually the one that mixes interfaces and structure (Tidewater's Interfaces). After the third drop, moving it costs one layout-map line, one re-import on the vendor branch, a CODEOWNERS change, and a merge that touches every file importing it; the converter's --delta shows how many.

Exercise 28.1: Make the grammar check say no

The lesson's checks say when it is done (perl agile.pl practice check 11). A model stand-up line for the next morning: "Y TW-61 Stations port merged after a red grammar check: 1 syntax error found by the pipeline, 0 by the reviewer. T TW-62 ... B none".

Exercise 28.2: Read the trace report
  • TW-SYS-012, orphan: the prime's. Nothing in the prime's model satisfies it; adding a satisfy would put a design decision in a file the next drop overwrites.
  • TW-SYS-016, orphan: the prime's, for the same reason; it is also unverified, so one report covers both gaps.
  • TW-SYS-006, drift: the prime's. The model's text no longer matches DOORS, and DOORS is the prime's master, so the prime decides which wording is right.

All three become discrepancy reports, not government edits.

Exercise 28.3: Rewrite Tom's stand-up

On 9 November the wait had already started; the rewrite names it in the B line with what Tom needs from whom:

(The scratch journal's dates differ from the story; the lint checks the form, which is what matters here.) A blocker in the B line goes into the quad's watch items the same day, so Jim would have seen it on the first morning, not the third.

Exercise 29.1: Find a cycle

The remaining Stations and DataCenter cycle is made by two dependencies: DataLogger to IngestService in Stations and QualityControl to SensorSuite in DataCenter. Remove one by moving the element both sides share (the observation record) into the library, so both segments depend downward. That is a design decision because it decides which segment owns the data's definition and changes the interface both owners review; it also touches the prime's files, so it goes through a discrepancy report.

The record says only that it was done. The three bullets, as a model answer:
