Exercise 31.1: Audit baseline-0

A changed character under docs/ does not trip the audit: the job regenerates the documents from the model and hashes what it built, so the hand edit is overwritten. A change to the model does trip it, because the documents it generates no longer match the tag. The exercise's docs edit therefore shows the opposite of what it implies; edit a model file to see the failure.

Exercise 31.2: Two measures, one slide
  • "Verify coverage: 21 of 30 requirements (70%) have a verification case that claims them. Unchanged since drop 1; the nine gaps are the prime's."
  • "Verification status (VCRM): 2 of 30 requirements have a recorded verdict, both by inspection. Expected: the program has not reached test."

An outside reader should say "most requirements have a plan to verify them, and two are verified so far". If they say "verification dropped", the slide still needs work.

Exercise 31.3: Fix the plan, not the sprint

Split TW-112 so its first task fits before Bob's leave: "BuoyModes states and transitions written from the v1 diagram" (1 point, Bob, 14 to 17 December) inside the sprint, and "BuoyModes triggers, guards and review" (2 points) in sprint 7. Done for the first task, as a pipeline check: the grammar and lint jobs pass on the merge request, the BuoyModes TODO line is gone (the todo job's count drops by one), and the outline job reports no new violation.

Exercise 31.4: An assumption to the prime

If the prime disagrees, the health flow's doc text changes, the data exchange table regenerates, and the alarm logic and verification case in DataCenter change with it; the prime-tbd label closes with the drop that settles it.

N.5 Part IV: making the case

Exercise 32.1: Run the report yourself

The longest stage is issue created to first commit, about four days at the median. That is not a problem: the team files the sprint's issues at the kickoff, so each one waits for its turn by design. The stages after the first commit (opening the merge request, review, merge) take hours, and they are the ones that measure the flow.

Exercise 32.2: Translate a DORA measure
  • Deployment frequency: "How often the published model is updated: the model site rebuilt, or a baseline released."
  • Lead time for changes: "How long a change takes from the first edit to being part of the accepted model."
  • Change failure rate: "How often an accepted change had to be corrected or undone."
  • Time to restore: "When the accepted model fails its checks, how long until it passes again."

Leave out deployment frequency, because it mostly counts the nightly schedule, and change failure rate, because at zero it says nothing yet. Keep lead time and time to restore: they answer "how fast" and "how safe".

Exercise 32.3: Find the trap

The final version is right. The draft's line, "6.7% verified (VCRM) (down 63.3 from 70)", compares two different measures: the VCRM's verdict recorded against the trace's case exists. Read out, it would have told the program manager that verification collapsed in sprint 6, when nothing got worse: a stricter measure appeared. The review record keeps verify coverage at 70% and reports the VCRM separately.

Exercise 33.1: Read it like a skeptic

A model answer:

MeasureThe questionThe evidence
2, change lead time"Is 3.5 hours a real change, or only typo fixes?"the merge request list in the analytics output, per author, and each MR's diff
4, trace answer time"Who timed 22 seconds, and on what?"the trace job's duration in the pipeline logs (gitlab/pipelines/.../trace.log)
12, morale"Is three people's anonymous answer meaningful?"sprints/NN/morale.json, with the question wording

The skeptic is right to ask: with three people, morale is a conversation starter, not a statistic, and the scorecard should say so.

Exercise 33.2: The measure that missed

"We set out to remove both package cycles inherited from the old model; we removed one, and the other is still there because a second reference between DataCenter and Stations remains. Finding and removing that last reference is planned for sprint 7, and the complexity job reports the count on every change, so you will see when it reaches zero." The briefing's own sentence is shorter and says the same thing (Section 35.5, Slide 3: the scorecard, sprint by sprint).

Exercise 33.3: Your own baseline

The answer is your program's numbers. A good one says, for each: lead time (a change board log: days from a change request to its approval, measured if the log has dates), trace answer time (how long the last "which requirements are unverified?" question took, usually remembered), and review turnaround (comment-matrix dates, measured if the matrices are filed). Mark remembered numbers as such on every slide that uses them.

Exercise 34.1: Draw your own sample
  • IngestService: same. The class became a part def of the same name, with its documentation and ports.
  • Observation history (TW-STK-005): same, reworded. The v1 class was named by its title; the v2 requirement is named by its DOORS id, keeps the title as an attribute, and carries the DOORS text in its doc.
Exercise 34.2: Explain a difference

Two folds from drop 1's map:

  • The multiplicity of a part (a LiteralInteger and a LiteralUnlimitedNatural, two v1 elements) folds into the [4] on the usage: v2 writes the bounds inline, so nothing is lost; there are just fewer elements.
  • A generalization folds into the :> of the definition, for example attribute def Power :> PowerValue. v1 stores the inheritance as its own element; v2 writes it as part of the declaration.

The test of a fold is the same each time: can you point at the v2 text that carries the information? If so, it is not a loss.

Exercise 35.1: Rewrite a slide headline
  • "Every model change is now checked automatically before anyone accepts it."
  • "The model answers in seconds questions that used to take days."
  • "Twelve weeks in, two thirds of the team's work is systems engineering again."

A program manager remembers the second: it names a pain they have felt, and a number.

Exercise 35.2: Rehearse the demo

In one sentence: "This change removed the only test for TW-SYS-003, and the check caught it before anyone accepted the change."

Exercise 35.3: Find your ask

A model ask: "Approve the runner machine request by 13 November. Without it, the automated checks run only on our laptops, nothing stops an unchecked change, and the December baseline cannot be rebuilt by anyone but us." One decision, one date, one consequence the decision-maker cares about.

Exercise 36.1: Read a quad

The one watch item is TW-67, the Stations level tags story, carried into the next sprint. (WI) marks a watch item (for awareness); (PM) would ask for the program manager's help. The program manager should note it and do nothing: the team owns it, and the story finishes early the next sprint.

Exercise 36.2: Write the note

A note to send:

On track. Three stories finished this week; 50 converter TODO lines remain; 21 of 30 requirements have a verification case (70%); the nine without are the prime's and are reported. One risk: the runner's security review has waited three days for the ISSM. Ask: a date from the ISSM by Tuesday.

The draft lists no risk, because the ISSM wait was in stand-up chat, not in GitLab. Jim adds what only people know.

Exercise 36.3: Map your own template

A typical program weekly template: accomplishments (merged MRs and closed stories), next week (the open milestone's issues), schedule (the quad's milestones, from the journal), risks (blocked issues and old discrepancy reports), metrics (the pipeline's scorecard), staffing (no source), budget (no source). Staffing and budget have no source in the system; the lead writes them, or they come from the finance system, and the note says which.

Exercise 37.1: Ask for what you need

The finished memo passes the check silently and builds:

Your own asks, as a table row each: "Training time, 4 points per person in sprint 1 and 2 in sprint 2; so the team learns on the board, not on weekends; by the sprint 1 kickoff; if not, the transition takes twice as long." Do the same for the runner (by sprint 2, or checks stay on laptops), the tool approval, and the GitLab tier decision.

Exercise 37.2: Record a decision

The memo for record is signed, dated and addressed to a reader outside the team: it is what an auditor or the contracting officer files. The ADR lives beside the model, is versioned with it, and is read by the next engineer. The memo carries authority; the ADR carries context and is easy to supersede. Keep both for decisions that bind the program (the branching model), and only the ADR for decisions that bind the team.

Exercise 37.3: Build from Vim

Yes: the .txt diff shows the changed paragraph as a few changed lines, with the rest unchanged, because the build wraps text the same way every time. The PDF diff is binary and unreadable. That is why the team commits the .txt beside the PDF.

Exercise 37.4: Draft the progress memo from evidence

From the pipeline: TODO lines, trace numbers, pipelines passing. From GitLab: stories done, merge requests, review turnaround. From you: the plan comparison, the risks only people know (the ISSM's wait), and the document-era baselines. A memo with more of the third kind than the first two needs more evidence before it goes out.

Exercise 38.1: Run the pulse on your own team

The answer is your team's data. Tidewater's dip came in sprint 3, when the new tools were in use and the old shortcuts were gone; most teams predict sprint 2. A prediction made in advance and checked afterwards is the point: it tests whether you know your team.

Exercise 38.2: Write your team's objections down

The answer is your team's list. The objections still open after six sprints are usually about the supplier ("the prime will never change its model") or the organization ("the CCB will not accept a merge request"); the tool objections ("git is too hard") are usually answered by sprint 3, with evidence.

Exercise 39.1: Write your own two-column day

Rows that change most: waiting for a review (hours instead of weeks), finding the current version (the branch, not an e-mail hunt), and building status slides (generated). Rows that do not change: thinking about the design, talking to the people who own the requirements, and meetings with the supplier.

Exercise 40.1: Grade a document both ways

The pipeline is right about what it can check (references resolve, nothing is missing, the text matches DOORS); the hand grade is right about what it cannot (whether the design is good, whether the reader understands it). Where they disagree on something the pipeline checks, trust the pipeline and find out why the hand grade missed it.

Exercise 41.1: Budget the learning

A model plan: a fifth of sprint 1, a sixth of sprint 2, a tenth of sprint 3, as work::learning stories with practice lessons as acceptance criteria. The engineering scope that moves is usually the second package of conversion work: with learning on the board, sprint 2 holds one package, not two (Section 50.6, The learning budget).

Exercise 41.2: Choose the first win

Three typical questions: "which requirements have no verification?" (the trace job), "what changed in the supplier's last drop?" (the converter's delta), "who changed this requirement and when?" (git blame on the requirements file). The trace is the one for sprint 1: it needs only the drop and the converter, and the skeptic who has answered it by hand for years is the right person to run it.

Exercise 41.3: Say no with a date
  • "Not this sprint: the special report needs the trace job, which is ready in sprint 3. Today I can send last review's numbers."
  • "Not today, unless it replaces something: the model change goes on the board for Wednesday's refinement. If it is urgent, tell me which story it displaces."
  • "Not until the sprint ends on the 23rd: Bob is committed to the drop import. From the 26th, for two weeks."
Exercise 41.4: Read the signs

The answer is your team's. The common signs: stand-up lines that list activities with no outcome, merge requests open for days, a red develop nobody mentions. Change one practice per sprint, and tell management the sign and the fix in the same sentence.

N.6 Part V: living with it

Exercise 42.1: Assign the roles
  • Model lead: Maintainer. Owns protections and baselines; the only one who can change who approves what.
  • Two modelers: Developer. They push branches and open merge requests, but cannot merge into protected branches alone or change the rules that check them.
  • CM engineer: Maintainer, for tags and releases, with the protections still requiring another person's approval on merges, so running the pipeline does not mean approving content.
  • Contractor liaison: Reporter. Reads the model and comments on issues, cannot push: the supplier's view never becomes the supplier's write access.
Exercise 42.2: Choose the token
  • (a) The job's own CI_JOB_TOKEN, which can publish to the project's package registry; no stored token.
  • (b) A project access token with read_api, stored as a masked, protected variable, with an owner and expiry.
  • (c) Jim's personal access token with api, short expiry, kept out of any file; or a project access token with the Maintainer role if the script becomes routine.
  • (d) A deploy token with read_repository only.
Exercise 42.3: Find the drift

Setup prints the protected branch with force:yes. The preview lists every request because a dry run reads nothing from the server: it cannot know what is already set, so it shows the whole file. A change made in the web pages shows up with setup --diff, which compares the file with the live project (the last line above, after the file was put back); re-running setup puts the setting back. Two corrections to the book: --dry-run now works with --local too (it prints and applies nothing), and the read-only comparison the admin chapter says the kit lacks is setup --diff.

Exercise 42.4: Plan a restore test

The checklist: import the export into a scratch group; check the repository, branches and tags; issues, merge requests and comments; labels and milestones; the wiki; then re-create what an export leaves out on purpose. An export carries no CI/CD variables or secrets, no runners, no protected-branch and tag rules in some versions, no group-level settings, and no container or package registry contents. Those items fail on any server, by design; they must be re-applied from project.conf and the token inventory.

Exercise 42.5: Make the tier case

"On Free, the rule that a model change needs another engineer's approval is a habit we record; on Premium, GitLab refuses the merge without it, and the code owner of the interface files must be one of the approvers. For a model the government will baseline under contract, an approval the server enforces is the evidence an auditor needs. The cost is a few seats a year against one finding at a configuration audit."

Exercise 43.1: Run a drop through the loop yourself

The delta from drop 2 to drop 3 marks five elements manual, all of the storm mode:

NWM-CR-0015's new state, two transitions and two triggers (stormWarning, calm) sit inside the BuoyModes state machine, which the converter leaves as a TODO line: there is no v2 text for them to land in, so an engineer adds them to the hand-written state machine. The fuse, the deleted requirement, the new satisfy and the deleted duplicate block are all carried.

Exercise 43.2: Cut the next baseline

The changelog section names the baseline and date, the drop merged (v1.2) and its change requests (NWM-CR-0015 to 0019, with the storm mode marked "reworked by hand"), and the discrepancy reports the drop closed. The release links to the package (model and documents tarball, VCRM, toolchain inventory, checksum file) and names the sprint milestones it closes; the tag message records the documents' checksum.

Exercise 43.3: A hotfix that the prime must also fix

"In baseline-1 the requirement TW-SYS-007 is satisfied by BulletinPublisher, which does not provide the public interface the requirement is about; we corrected it to DataSegment::publicOut in baseline-1.1. That relationship is generated from your v1 model on every drop, so the next drop will put the old satisfy back and our correction will appear as a hand edit to redo. Please change the satisfy in your model to the public interface, and tell us which drop carries it."

Exercise 44.1: Read the matrix

TW-SYS-011, for example, has an analysis method and no case; the trace lists it as unverified, and it has no satisfy gap. The case is the prime's to write, because the prime owns the system model's verification; ask through a discrepancy report naming the requirement, its method, and the drop you need the case in.

Exercise 44.2: Map your program to the stages

The answer is your program's table. The five stages are traceability first (government, now), automated result capture (the prime or test organization, once their harness can write the format), a parallel pilot on one subsystem (joint, between campaigns), shifting checks left (government and prime, after the pilot), and scaling and retiring legacy artifacts (with the customer's agreement). A good answer names the campaign each one must not interrupt, such as a qualification test series.

Exercise 45.1: Read a drop like a change board
Change requestDispositionWhy
NWM-CR-0020 salinityaccepta new field in the observation record, with a reason; the converter carries it
NWM-CR-0021 drifting buoysaccept with impacta new part in the station segment that touches both network interfaces
NWM-CR-0022 TW-SYS-016acceptit answers the government's own discrepancy report
NWM-CR-0023 TW-SYS-002 intervalaccept with impactthe requirement changed, so its verification case must change

The drifting buoys add government work: the observation and health links now carry a new kind of station, so the interface owners review the links, the data exchange table regenerates, and the verification of the links needs a drifting-buoy case.

Exercise 45.2: Write the clarification
Exercise 45.3: Break the intake on purpose

The first run rejects the drop and names the file with both checksums; the second accepts it. Regenerating is the only acceptable fix because the manifest's checksums describe what the prime built: editing the file back by hand might match by luck or not at all, and editing the manifest would make the check worthless. On a real program the "regenerate" step is the prime's build sending the drop again.

Exercise 45.4: Choose a strategy

In model/external/prime/, generated and never edited: the system and segment requirements allocated to the data center, the port and interface definitions the data center connects to (ObservationIF, HealthIF, the observation record), and the parameters the data center depends on (reporting intervals). The data center team owns its own design: IngestService, QualityControl, the archive and the publisher, their behavior, the satisfy links to the generated requirements and the verification cases.

Exercise 46.1: Label your backlog

Tidewater's sprint 7 plan: "Break the Stations and DataCenter cycle", "The DailyUpload interaction by hand", "The EnergyBalance constraint expression" and "Retire the Tidewater Profile TODO" are engineering. "Pin the kit version" is platform, and makes every later engineering story cheaper to verify: a baseline rebuilt next year uses the same checks as the one cut today. If a platform story cannot name the engineering it speeds up, it can probably wait.

Exercise 46.2: Split along the decisions
  1. Find every reference between Stations and DataCenter and decide which are real design dependencies (2 points).
  2. Decide where the shared element belongs (the library, or one segment) and move it (2 points).
  3. Remove or redirect the remaining accidental references, and confirm with the complexity job that the cycle count is zero (1 point).

The plan has one task, "Remove the QualityControl to SensorSuite dependency" (2 points). That is the split along a command, and it is why the cycle survived: it removed the dependency it was written against, and nobody had looked for the other reference first.

Exercise 47.1: Measure a model you own

On Tidewater, as a stand-in:

The DataCenter and Stations cycle is an accident: two trace-style dependencies drawn on v1 diagrams, not a design need, since the two segments exchange data through the network's interfaces. The largest fan-out (3) is the network package, which is a real dependency: the network is what connects the segments.

Exercise 47.2: Mark the twenty practices for your project

The answer is your table. For most teams the three with the biggest effect in the next sprint are layering with a one-way rule (1), small reviewable changes (17), and generated views (12), because each one prevents new tangle without needing the old tangle fixed first.

Exercise 48.1: Close a boundary crossing

Rebuild the worked example, add the laptop and its interface, and run the gate:

Then the requirement, the satisfy and the verification:

The engineering decisions: which zone a maintenance laptop belongs in (untrusted, because it travels), what the data center should trust about it (an issued device and a token, not a password), whether the requirement also mitigates a threat worth adding to the register (an unauthorized maintenance session), and how to verify it (a test with a laptop that should be refused). The sed lines are the typing.

Exercise 48.2: Your twenty-six

The answer is your table. Most ISSMs ask first about point 1 (what the model contains, and at what level), point 4 (separating repositories by sensitivity) and point 9 (runners as privileged machines), because those decide whether the system can be authorized at all. Every LATER needs a story or epic name; "later" without one is the pattern the chapter warns about.

Exercise 49.1: Name the cadences

A good answer separates the segments by what limits them, not by who builds them. Hardware is limited by lead times, qualification and field access; software by the pipeline. The baselines fall where the slowest segment can freeze: for Tidewater, the station segment's field seasons set them, and the data center's sprints line up underneath.

Exercise 49.2: One copy of the interface

It is defined once in model/library/Interfaces.sysml and used in the stations, the data center and the observation cycle's behavior (model/physical/stations, model/physical/datacenter, model/logical). CODEOWNERS gives that file two sections, both of which must approve: the systems lead (Jim) and one of the people who build on both sides (Bob or Tom, whoever did not write the change). If a segment could change it alone, the other segments would find out at integration; with one copy and system-level owners, they find out in the merge request.

Exercise 49.3: Find the next block in the drops

Drop 6 (v1.5): its CHANGES.csv carries NWM-CR-0026, "Add partner sharing TW-SYS-019", with the rationale of a data-sharing agreement with partner agencies; it adds TW-SYS-019, the data center sharing observations with partner agencies. It is Block 3 in the picture, starting while Block 2 is still in verification.

Exercise 49.4: Put a check on its rung

The missing verify is a model check, on every merge request. The link model belongs to simulation. The storm power loss is a sea-trial finding that then calibrates the simulation. The late bulletin is a simulation result (load) that a harbor test should confirm end to end. The modem reset belongs on the bench, with the real modem and logger.

Exercise 50.1: Your twelve-week table

The answer is your program's table. A good row reads like Tidewater's: "Sprint 2: the first drop on the integration branch, every change gated. Done when: the drop's merge request merged with a green pipeline, and a direct push to develop is refused." Each goal names an outcome a manager recognizes; each "done when" is a pipeline result, a record or a merged change.

Exercise 50.2: Your decision records

Each ADR has the template's four parts: context, decision, consequences and when to revisit (Exercise 13.4 has a model). The merge-method record is the one most teams get wrong: if you will measure lead time or review turnaround from history, choose merge commits, and say so as the reason.

Exercise 50.3: Your sprint 1

Ten and twelve points as written, before multiplying the "one per person" tasks by the team's size (for three people, sprint 1 grows by five points). Against a three-person capacity of about nineteen with a fifth reserved for learning, it fits. What to cut first: the stories your program does not need (no supplier, no drop intake), then anything that is not on the path to the first gated change.

Exercise 50.4: Run week zero offline

Five stories: the protected project, the first pipeline, receiving the drop, converting it, and the working agreements. Programs without a supplier rewrite the two drop stories; most programs rewrite the conversion story's acceptance criteria to name their own packages.

Exercise 51.1: Diagnose the symptom
  • (a) Reformatting the converter's output (Section 51.2.2, Reformatting the converter's output). Diff the government's file against the vendor branch with whitespace ignored, and revert everything but the level tags.
  • (b) Changing requirement text in the model (Section 51.2.4, Changing requirement text in the model). Find the merge request in the drift report and restore the DOORS wording; send the improvement to the prime as a discrepancy report.
  • (c) Trusting the TODO count alone (Section 51.2.5, Trusting the TODO count alone). Run the converter's --delta on the drop and rework the manual lines by hand.
  • (d) Red is normal (Section 51.4.1, Red is normal). Stop merging, name an owner for the red pipeline today, and fix it before anything else.
Exercise 51.2: Your two pitfalls

The answer is your organization's. A good one names a symptom you can observe in your own tools ("the drift count rose after our MR"), not a feeling, and a rule that a setting or a check enforces, not a reminder.

Exercise 51.3: Prove the TODO count blind spot

The converted files differ only by the fuse. The storm mode appears only in the delta: it is inside the BuoyModes state machine, which the converter writes as one TODO line in both drops, so the TODO count does not change while the content behind it does.
